4 The probability of extinction
Denote by \(q\) the probability of extinction, i.e., \(q= \mathbb {P}\left(\exists n \in \mathbb {N}: \;  X_n = 0\right)\). Then the following statement holds.







Lemma 3 The extinction probability \(q\) of a branching process with offspring distribution \(\xi\) is the smallest nonnegative root of the equation \[
  z=G_{\xi }(z),
\tag{2}\] i.e., it is a fixed point of the function \(G_{\xi }\).










ExampleExample 4





Prove lemma Lemma 3.






SolutionSolution





Note that each person in a generation produces (among their descendants) a copy of the original Galton-Watson process, which is independent of the other people in the generation and their descendants. That is, for the process to die out, either it must die out immediately at step 1 (i.e., \(\xi_1^{(1)} = 0\)), or all \(\xi_1^{(1)}\) independent copies of the G-W process must eventually die out. The probability of this (given \(\xi_1^{(1)} = k\)) equals \(q^k\) by independence. Altogether,
\[
\begin{align}  q = \mathbb {P}\left(\xi _1^{(1)} = 0\right) + \sum _{k=1}^\infty q^k \mathbb {P}\left(\xi _1^{(1)} = k\right) = G_\xi (q) \end{align}
\]
Another proof: the events \(\left\{ X_n = 0\right\}\) increase in \(n\) (an extinct process does not come back to life), and their union is the extinction event. By continuity of the probability measure, \(\mathbb {P}\left(X_n = 0\right) = G_{X_n}(0)\) is nondecreasing in \(n\) and converges to \(q\). Using continuity of \(G\), we have
\[
\begin{align}  G_\xi (q) & = G_\xi (\lim _{n \to \infty } G_{X_n}(0)) = \lim _{n \to \infty } G_\xi (G_{X_n}(0)) = \lim _{n \to \infty } G_{X_{n+1}}(0) = \\ & = q \end{align}
\]
From this we can also deduce that \(q\) is the smallest nonnegative root of the equation \(z = G_\xi (z)\). Let \(z \geq 0\) be an arbitrary root. Then \(z\) is a fixed point of all the compositions as well: \(G_{X_n}(z) = z\). Generating functions are monotone on \([0, +\infty )\), so
\[
\begin{align}  G_{X_n}(0) \leq G_{X_n} (z) = z \end{align}
\]
Taking the limit in \(n\) on the left-hand side, we get \(q \leq z\).






Equation (Equation 2) is the first remarkable formula in the theory of branching processes. Note that \(z=1\) is always a solution of (Equation 2). However, when other roots are present, we need to be able to pick out the extinction probability among them. A complete classification of the situations is given by the theorem on the extinction probability.







Theorem 2 Let the random variable \(\xi\) not be identically \(1\), i.e., \(\mathbb {P}\left(\xi = 1\right) < 1\). Denote \(\mu = \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right]\) (possibly \(\mu = +\infty )\). Then

If \(\mu \leqslant 1\), equation (Equation 2) has only one solution \(z=1\) on \([0,1]\). In this case \(q=1\).
If \(\mu >1\), equation (Equation 2) has a unique solution \(z_{0} \in [0,1)\). In this case \(q=z_{0}\).

Thus, the extinction probability is the smallest root of the equation \(z=G_{\xi }(z)\) in the interval \([0,1]\).




Note that the theorem has a rather vivid interpretation: if the mean number of offspring in the process is no greater than 1, the process is doomed to extinction; otherwise there is a nonzero probability of the population existing forever.
Iterations of the generating function: the staircase \(0 \to G_\xi(0) \to G_\xi(G_\xi(0)) \to \ldots\) (red) depicts the growth of the probabilities \(\mathsf P(X_n = 0) = G_{X_n}(0)\) toward the extinction probability \(q\) — the smallest fixed point of \(G_\xi\) on \([0,1]\) (the point where it meets the diagonal). The offspring law is \(\operatorname{Geom}(p)\), \(\mathsf P(\xi = k) = p(1-p)^k\), with mean \(\mu = \frac{1-p}{p}\). Move the slider \(p\): as \(\mu\) crosses the critical value \(1\) (i.e., as \(p\) crosses \(\frac12\)), the intersection point of the curve \(G_\xi\) with the diagonal “breaks away” from \(1\), and the extinction probability \(q\) becomes less than one. ExampleExample 5





Find the extinction probability of a branching process with a geometric \(\operatorname {Geom}(p)\), \(p \in (0,1)\) offspring distribution (i.e., \(\mathbb {P}\left(\xi = k\right) = p(1-p)^{k}, \;  k \in \mathbb {Z}_{+}\)).

\[

\(q = 1\), if \(p \geqslant \frac{1}{2}\); \(q= \frac{p}{1-p}\), if \(p < \frac{1}{2}\).

5 The total number of particles
Let us now discuss the question of the total number of particles in the branching process. Denote \(Y_{n}=1+X_{1}+\ldots +\) \(X_{n}\), the total number of particles in the process up to and including time \(n\). Then the following recurrence relation holds between the generating functions of \(Y_{n}\) and \(Y_{n-1}\), analogous to the relations in Lemma 1 for \(X_{n}\) itself:
\[
  G_{Y_{n+1}}(z)=z G_{\xi }\left(G_{Y_{n}}(z)\right)
\tag{3}\]






ExampleExample 6





Prove ().






HintHint





See Example @G-W_proc:prob_of_extict_lem_proof.









SolutionSolution





Note that each member of the first generation produces, among its descendants, a Galton-Watson process independent of the other members and their descendants. Moreover, the number of members of the first generation is distributed according to the law of \(\xi\) and is independent of the subsequent number of offspring. That is, we have \(Y_{n+1} \overset {d}{=} 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{\xi } Y_n^i =: \tilde{Y}_{n+1}\), where \(Y_n^i\) are independent copies of \(Y_n\) (independent of each other and of \(\xi\)). Moreover (for more detail, see the solution of G-W_proc:prob_of_extict_lem_proof) \[
\begin{align}  G_{\tilde{Y}_{n+1}}(z) & = \mathbb {E}\left[z^{\tilde{Y}_{n+1}}\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[z \cdot z^{\sum _{i=1}^{\xi } Y_n^i}\right] = \\ & = z \cdot \mathbb {E}\left[z^{\sum _{i=1}^{\xi } Y_n^i}\right] \enclose {circle}{=} \\ \mathbb {E}\left[z^{\sum _{i=1}^{\xi } Y_n^i}\right] & = \mathbb {E}\left[\mathbb {E}\left[z^{\sum _{i=1}^{\xi } Y_n^i} \mid \xi \right]\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[G^\xi _{Y_n}(z)\right] = G_{\xi }(G_{Y_n}(z)) \\ & \enclose {circle}{=} \;  z \cdot G_{\xi }(G_{Y_n}(z)) \end{align}
\] Since we are dealing with expectations, we may make substitutions up to equality in distribution of the quantity under the expectation. Altogether \[
\begin{align}  G_{Y_{n+1}}(z) = z G_\xi (G_{Y_n}(z)) \end{align}
\]






Let \(Y\) be the total number of particles in the branching process over all time: \(Y = \lim_{n \to \infty } Y_{n}\). \(Y_{n}\) converges to \(Y\) pointwise (i.e., for every \(\omega\)), and hence also a.s. and in distribution. One can show that this implies pointwise convergence of the generating functions:
\[
  G_{Y}(z) = \lim _{n \to \infty } G_{Y_n}(z), \qquad \text{for any } \left|z\right| < 1
\]
\(G_{Y}\) can be found as the limit of \(G_{Y_n}\), or from the second remarkable equation in the theory of branching processes.







Lemma 4 The function \(G_{Y}(z)\), \(\left|z\right| < 1\) satisfies \[
  G_Y(z) = z G_{\xi }(G_Y(z)).
\]

ProblemProblem 8





On the final level of the computer game “Heroes of Loofah and Soap III: The Breath of Moidodyr,” the player must battle the evil Soap Bubble. Each time the player attacks the Bubble, one of two equally likely events occurs: the Bubble may pop, or it may split into two new Bubbles. To win, the player must destroy all Soap Bubbles.

What is the chance of clearing this level?
Let \(\tilde{Y}\) be the total number of Bubbles that popped. Find the generating function and distribution of \(\tilde{Y}\).
Compute \(\mathbb {E}\left[\tilde{Y}\right]\).










ProblemProblem 9





Let \(\tilde{Y}\) be the total number of particles with no offspring in a Galton-Watson branching process with geometric offspring distribution \(\operatorname {Geom}(2/3)\) (that is, \(\mathbb {P}\left(\xi =k\right) = \frac{2}{3} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^k\) for \(k \in \left\{ 0,1,2, \ldots \right\} )\). Compute \(G_{\tilde{Y}}\) and \(\mathbb {E}\left[\tilde{Y}\right]\).

This lecture note is still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished passages. If you find something, please let the author know (contact information on the course page).
Informally, a random process (or stochastic process) is a collection of random variables scattered in time. Formally, let \(T \subset \mathbb {R}\) be some subset of the real numbers, which is usually interpreted as time. Then a collection \(X=\left(X_{t}, t \in T\right)\) of random variables \(X_{t}=X_{t}(\omega ) = X(t,\omega )\), defined on one and the same probability space \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mathbb {P})\) for all \(t \in T\), is called a random process (or stochastic process) on the set \(T\).
As a rule, \(X_t\) for different \(t\) are not independent. If \(\left(t_1, t_2, \ldots , t_n\right)^T\) is a vector of elements of the set \(T\), then the distribution of the random vector \(\left(X_{t_1}, X_{t_2}, \ldots , X_{t_n}\right)^T\) is denoted
\[
  \mathbf{P}_{t_1,\ldots ,t_n}
\]
and is called the finite-dimensional distribution of the process \(X_t\) at the points \(t_1, \ldots , t_n\).
crumbs: 1. Basic concepts of the theory of random processes. Some examples

title: Basic concepts of the theory of random processes. Some examples
text:
2.1 The Poisson process
An important special case of a renewal process is the Poisson process. Suppose the intervals between jumps \(\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) (let \(\xi\) be a random variable with the same distribution) have an absolutely continuous distribution on \(\mathbb {R}_+ = [0, +\infty )\) and possess the memoryless property: for \(0 < s, t\) we have
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\xi > t + s \mid \xi > s\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(\xi > t\right)
\]
Recall that the only continuous distribution on \([0,+\infty )\) with the memoryless property is the exponential distribution: \(\xi \sim \operatorname {Exp}(\lambda )\) for some \(\lambda > 0\). A renewal process \(N_{t}\) with such inter-jump intervals (exponentially distributed with parameter \(\lambda\)) is called a Poisson process of intensity (rate) \(\lambda > 0\).


                                                
Left — two trajectories of a Poisson process of rate λ (filled dots belong to the trajectory, open dots do not: N_t is right-continuous with left limits) and a dashed line for the mean 𝔼N_t = λt. Right — a histogram of N_T over 4000 trajectories against the exact Pois(λT). Move the λ slider.


Why is the process called Poisson? Why is \(\lambda\) called the intensity (rate)?






ExampleExample 4





Find the finite-dimensional distributions of the Poisson process.






SolutionSolution






Notice that the event \(\left\{ N_{t} = n\right\}\) means that the \(n\)-th person arrived before time \(t\), and the \((n+1)\)-th after. Hence,
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}\left(N_{t} = n\right) & = \mathbb {P}\left(S_{n} \leq t, \;  \underset {=S_{n} + \xi _{n+1}}{S_{n+1}} > t\right) = \\ & = \mathbb {P}\left(S_{n} \leq t, \;  \xi _{n+1}> t - S_{n}\right) = \\ & = \int _{0}^{t} \mathbb {P}\left(\xi _{n+1} > t-x\right) \cdot \frac{\lambda ^n}{\Gamma (n)}x^{n-1}e^{-\lambda x} \;  dx = \\ & =\int _{0}^{t} e^{-\lambda \cdot (t-x)} \cdot \frac{\lambda ^n}{\Gamma (n)}x^{n-1}e^{-\lambda x} \;  dx = \\ & = \frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!}e^{-\lambda t}. \end{align}
\]
That is, \(N_{t} \sim \operatorname {Pois}(\lambda t)\). In particular, \(\mathbb {E}\left[N_{t}\right] = \lambda t\).
Now consider two time instants \(0 < t_1 < t_2\) and find the joint distribution of \(N_{t_1}\) and \(N_{t_2}\). Let \(n_1 \le n_2\). The event \(\left\{ N_{t_1}=n_1, N_{t_2}=n_2\right\}\) means:

the \(n_1\)-th person arrived before \(t_1\), the \((n_1+1)\)-th after \(t_1\),
in total, \(n_2\) people had arrived by time \(t_2\).

Using the definition:
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}\left(N_{t_1}=n_1, N_{t_2}=n_2\right) & = \mathbb {P}\left(S_{n_1} \le t_1 < S_{n_1+1}, \;  S_{n_2} \le t_2 < S_{n_2+1}\right) = \\ & = \text{<4 integrals>}. \end{align}
\]
Working through these integrals carefully, we obtain the following answer:
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}\left(N_{t_1}=n_1, N_{t_2}=n_2\right) & = \frac{(\lambda t_1)^{n_1}}{n_1!} e^{-\lambda t_1} \\ & \quad \cdot \frac{[\lambda (t_2 - t_1)]^{\,  n_2 - n_1}}{(n_2 - n_1)!} e^{-\lambda (t_2 - t_1)} \end{align}
\]
The left-hand side equals \(\mathbb {P}\left(N_{t_1} = n_1, N_{t_{2}} - N_{t_1} = n_2 - n_1\right)\). The right-hand side equals (as we essentially derived above) \(\mathbb {P}\left(N_{t_1} = n_1\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(N_{t_{2}} - N_{t_1} = n_2 - n_1\right)\). Altogether, we obtain that \(N_{t_1}\) and \(N_{t_{2}} - N_{t_1}\) are independent.
The same can be done for an arbitrary number of points to obtain the finite-dimensional distribution. Altogether, the Poisson process is a process with independent increments, and moreover these increments follow a Poisson law with parameter proportional to the time increment (i.e., the increments are stationary). More formally: for arbitrary \(0 < t_{1} < t_{2} < \ldots < t_k\) (\(k \in \mathbb {N}\)), the increments
\[
\begin{align}  & N_{t_1} - \underbrace{N_{0}}_{=0 \text{ a.s.}}, \quad N_{t_2} - N_{t_1}, \quad N_{t_3} - N_{t_2}, \\ & \quad \ldots , \quad N_{t_{k}} - N_{t_{k-1}} \end{align}
\]
are jointly independent, and \(N_{t} - N_{s} \sim \operatorname {Pois}(\lambda (t-s))\), \(0 \leq s < t\).

Along the way we have answered the questions posed before the example: the process is called Poisson because \(N_t \sim \operatorname {Pois}(\lambda t)\) (and all the increments are Poisson-distributed), and \(\lambda\) is called the intensity (rate) because \(\mathbb {E}\left[N_t\right] = \lambda t\): on average \(\lambda\) events occur per unit of time.












ExampleExample 5





An insurance agent handles the settlement of insurance claims. Claims are filed on business days according to a Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda = 5\) per day.

If two claims were filed on Monday and three on Tuesday, what is the probability that by the end of Friday the total number of claims filed this week will be \(16\)?
In the new calendar year, the agent starts work on Monday, January 12. On which day does he expect to receive the \(30\)-th claim?







SolutionSolution





Let the process \(N_{t}\) model the filing of claims, with \(t\) measured in days.






Enum-item1.



We use the independence of increments:
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}\left(N_{5} = 16 \mid N_{1} = 2, N_{2} - N_{1} = 3\right) & = \mathbb {P}\left(N_{5} - N_{2} = 11 \mid N_{1} = 2, N_{2} - N_{1} = 3\right) = \\ & = \mathbb {P}\left(N_{5} - N_{2} = 11\right) = \frac{(3\lambda )^{11} }{11!}e^{-3\lambda } \approx 6.6\%  \end{align}
\]








Enum-item2.



The arrival time of the \(30\)-th claim is \(S_{30}\), the sum of \(30\) independent \(\operatorname {Exp}(5)\) intervals: \(\mathbb {E}\left[S_{30}\right] = 30 \cdot \frac{1}{5} = 6\) business days. The sixth business day after starting on Monday, January 12, is Monday of the following week, January 19.














ProblemProblem 3





Requests for equipment repair arrive at a technical service center. Requests arrive on business days according to a Poisson process \(N_t\) with intensity \(\lambda = 4\) requests per day.

In the new month, the center starts work on Monday, February 5. On which day does it expect to receive the 20th request?
What is the probability that at most 1 request arrives during a single business day?
If 3 requests were filed on Monday and 5 on Wednesday, what is the probability that by the end of Friday the total number of requests for the week will be 20?
Find the probability that \(3\) requests were filed from the start of the week through the end of Tuesday, and at most \(7\) requests by the middle of Thursday. In other words, find \(\mathbb {P}\left(N_{2} = 3, \;  N_{3.5} \leq 7\right)\).

title: Mathematical Statistics
text: A course in mathematical statistics: from the basic notions of point estimation to linear regression and statistical hypothesis testing. The first part of the course is devoted to estimation theory — statistics, consistency and unbiasedness, methods for constructing estimators (moments, maximum likelihood), comparison of estimators, sufficient statistics, and confidence intervals. The second part covers the Bayesian approach, linear regression, and hypothesis testing, including in linear models, goodness-of-fit tests, and correlation coefficients.

title: Goodness-of-Fit Tests
text:
WarningDraft



This text is still being edited: it may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished passages. If you find something, please let the author know (contact information on the course page).
The next class of hypotheses that we consider in this text concerns whether an unknown distribution coincides with a known one. In other words, let \(X\) be an observation with unknown distribution \(\mathbb {P}\), whose distribution function equals \(F\). We pose the hypotheses
\[
  H_0: \;  \mathbb {P} = \mathbb {P}_0, \qquad H_1: \;  \mathbb {P} \neq \mathbb {P}_0
\]
for some given distribution \(\mathbb {P}_0\). The alternative distributions are left entirely unspecified; a priori only the type of distribution (e.g. discrete or absolutely continuous) and the set of possible values of the observation \(X\) may be known. Tests for such hypotheses are called goodness-of-fit tests. The best known among them are the Kolmogorov test and the chi-squared test, which we discuss in this chapter. The first is based on comparing the theoretical and empirical distribution functions, and the second on comparing the theoretical and empirical densities.
For goodness-of-fit tests it is customary to use ones that have the property of consistency.

title: Goodness-of-Fit Tests
text:
1.1 The Kolmogorov goodness-of-fit test
The Kolmogorov statistic is the distance between the functions \(F_n^*\) and \(F_0\) in the supremum metric:
\[
  D_n := \sup _{x \in \mathbb {R}}\left|F_n^*(x) - F_{0}(x) \right|.
\tag{1}\]


                                                
The theoretical distribution function \(F_0(x)\) and the empirical distribution function \(F_n^*(x)\) for a sample of size \(n=12\). The Kolmogorov statistic \(D_n=\sup_x|F_n^*(x)-F_0(x)|\) is marked on the graph.








ExampleExample 1





Prove that if \(H_0\) holds, then the distribution of \(D_n\) depends only on \(n\). In particular, it does not depend on \(F_0\).






SolutionSolution





If \(H_0\) holds, then with probability \(1\) every sample element falls in the set \(Q_0((0,1))\), where \(Q_0\) is the quantile function of the distribution \(P_0\). The whole sample falls in \(Q^n_0([0,1])\) with probability \(1\). Hence,
\[
  D_n \stackrel{\text{a.s.}}{=} \sup _{x \in Q_0((0,1))}\left|F_n^*(x) - F_{0}(x) \right|
\tag{2}\]
Next, apply to the sample \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) the probability integral transform: \(Y_i := F_0(X_i), \;  i \in \left\{ 1,\ldots , n\right\}\). Since \(F_0\) is continuous, \(\mathbb {P}_0\) has no points of nonzero mass, \((0,1) \subset F_0(\mathbb {R})\), and \(F_0(\cdot )\) is a one-to-one map between \(Q_0((0,1)) \subset \mathbb {R}\) and \((0,1)\): \(F_0^{-1} = Q_0\). So \(Y_1, \ldots , Y_n\) is a sample from \(\operatorname {U}[0,1]\).
Note that one-to-one transformations of the argument cannot change the value of the supremum in Equation 1, Equation 2. Hence,
\[
  D_n \stackrel{\text{a.s.}}{=} \sup _{y \in (0,1)}\left|F_n^*(Q_0(y)) - y\right|.
\]
Moreover, \(F_n^*(Q_0(y))\) is, a.s., the empirical distribution function for the sample \(Y_1, \ldots , Y_n\):
\[
  F_n^*(Q_0(y)) = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n \; \mathbb {1}_{X_i \leq Q_0(y)} \stackrel{\text{a.s.}}{=} \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n \; \mathbb {1}_{F_0(X_i) \leq y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n \; \mathbb {1}_{Y_i \leq y}
\]
Thus,
\[
  D_n \stackrel{\text{a.s.}}{=} \sup _{y \in (0,1)}\left|\tilde{F}_n^*(y) - y \right|,
\]
where \(\tilde{F}_n^*\) is the empirical distribution function for the sample \(Y_1, \ldots , Y_n\) from \(\operatorname {U}[0,1]\).






The distribution of \(D_n\) depends only on \(n\), but for finite \(n\) it is given by overly cumbersome formulas. The limiting distribution of the statistic \(D_n\) looks somewhat simpler.







Theorem 2 (Kolmogorov) Suppose the hypothesis \(H_{0}\) holds, i.e. the distribution \(\mathbb {P}_0\) with distribution function \(F_0\) is the true distribution of the sample \(\overrightarrow {X}\). Then the asymptotic distribution of the statistic \(D_n\), scaled by \(\sqrt{n}\), is a certain known distribution not depending on \(\mathbb {P}_0, F_0\), called the Kolmogorov distribution (notation: \(\operatorname {K}\)):
\[
  \sqrt{n}D_n \xrightarrow [n\to \infty ]{d_0} \operatorname {K}
\]
The Kolmogorov distribution \(\operatorname {K}\) can be defined via the distribution function \(F_{\operatorname {K}}\):
\[
  F_{\operatorname {K}}(t) = \sum _{j=-\infty }^{+\infty }(-1)^{j} e^{-2 j^{2} t^{2}} \cdot \; \mathbb {1}_{t \geq 0}
\]











Corollary 1 Under the conditions of Kolmogorov’s theorem, \[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\sqrt{n}D_n \leq t\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} F_{\operatorname {K}}(t), \quad \forall t > 0
\]




The Kolmogorov test of significance level \(\alpha\) is written as follows: \(\left\{ \sqrt{n} D_{n}> Q_{\operatorname {K}}(1-\alpha )\right\}\), where \(Q_{\operatorname {K}}(\cdot )\) is the quantile function of the Kolmogorov distribution. The Kolmogorov test is asymptotic, since we use not the exact distribution of \(D_n\) for each \(n\), but only the limiting distribution. The Kolmogorov test is customarily applied when \(n \geq 20\).


                                                
The density of the Kolmogorov distribution (the limiting distribution of the statistic \(\sqrt n D_n\)).








ExampleExample 2





Prove that
\[
  D_{n}=\max _{1 \leq k \leq n} \max \left\{ \frac{k}{n}-F\left(X_{(k)}\right), F\left(X_{(k)}\right)-\frac{k-1}{n}\right\}  .
\]






SolutionSolution





Indeed, for any \(k \in \{ 1, \ldots , n-1\}\), on the interval \(\left[X_{(k)}, X_{(k+1)}\right)\) the function \(F_{n}^{*}\) is constant and equal to \(\frac{k}{n}\), while \(F(x)\) is nondecreasing, so on this interval any value of \(\left|F_{n}^{*}(x)-F(x)\right|\) does not exceed \(\max \left\{ \frac{k}{n}-F\left(X_{(k)}\right), F\left(X_{(k+1)}\right)-\frac{k}{n}\right\}\) (note that the second term has the form \(F(X_{(j)}) - \frac{j-1}{n}\) with \(j = k+1\)). Furthermore, on the interval \(\left(-\infty , X_{(1)}\right)\) the function \(F_{n}^{*}\) equals 0, so on this interval \(\left|F_{n}^{*}(x)-F(x)\right| \leq F\left(X_{(1)}\right)\). Finally, on the interval \(\left[X_{(n)}, \infty \right)\) the function \(F_{n}^{*}\) equals 1, so on this interval \(\left|F_{n}^{*}(x)-F(x)\right| \leq\) \(1-F\left(X_{(n)}\right)\). Since every value on the right-hand side of the claimed equality is attained by the function \(\left|F_{n}^{*}(x)-F(x)\right|\) (as one-sided limits at the points \(X_{(k)}\)), the equality is proved.












ProblemProblem 2





Prove the consistency of the Kolmogorov test.









ProblemProblem 3





We have a sample \(X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}\) of size 3. To test the hypothesis that the sample is drawn from the uniform distribution on \([0,1]\), the following version of the Kolmogorov test is used: the hypothesis of uniformity is rejected if \[
  \sup _{y \in [0,1]}\left|F_{3}^{*}(y)-y\right|>1 / 3 .
\] What is the significance level (size) of this test?

title: Goodness-of-Fit Tests
text:
1.2 The Cramér-von Mises-Smirnov test
The Cramér-von Mises-Smirnov statistic is the squared distance between the functions \(F_n^*\) and \(F_0\) in the space \(L^{2}\left(\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right), \mathbb {P}_0\right)\):
\[
  \omega ^2 := \int _{\mathbb {R}} \left|F_n^*(t) - F_0(t)\right|^2 \mathbb {P}_0(dt) = \int _{-\infty }^\infty \left|F_n^*(t) - F_0(t)\right|^2 dF_0(t).
\]
The last integral is a Lebesgue-Stieltjes integral.
As with the distribution of the Kolmogorov statistic, the distribution of the statistic \(\omega^2\) does not depend on \(F_0\) when \(H_0\) holds.






ProblemProblem 4





Prove that if \(H_0\) holds, then \[
  \omega ^2 \stackrel{d}{=} \int _{0}^1 \left|\tilde{F}_n^*(y) - y\right|^2 dy,
\] where \(\tilde{F}_n^*(y)\) is the empirical distribution function for a sample from \(\operatorname {U}[0,1]\). That is, the distribution of \(\omega^2\) depends only on \(n\). In particular, it does not depend on \(F_0\).



As with \(D_n\), the distribution of \(\omega^2\) for finite \(n\) is given by overly cumbersome formulas, but the limiting distribution looks more or less simple.







Theorem 3 (Smirnov) Suppose the hypothesis \(H_{0}\) holds, i.e. the distribution \(\mathbb {P}_0\) with distribution function \(F_0\) is the true distribution of the sample \(X\). Then the asymptotic distribution of the statistic \(\omega^2\), scaled by \(n\), is a certain known distribution not depending on \(\mathbb {P}_0, F_0\), called the omega-squared distribution (notation: \(\operatorname {OS}\)):
\[
  n\omega ^2 \xrightarrow [n\to \infty ]{d_0} \operatorname {OS}
\]
The distribution \(\operatorname {OS}\) can be defined via its characteristic function:
\[
  \varphi _{\operatorname {OS}}(t) =\prod _{k=1}^\infty \left(1 - \frac{2it}{\pi ^2 k^2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\]




The Cramér-von Mises-Smirnov test of significance level \(\alpha\) is written as follows: \(\left\{ n \omega^2>Q_{\operatorname {OS}}(1-\alpha )\right\}\), where \(Q_{\operatorname {OS}}(\cdot )\) is the quantile function of the omega-squared distribution. The Cramér-von Mises-Smirnov test, like the Kolmogorov test, is asymptotic, since we use not the exact distribution of \(\omega^2\) for each \(n\), but only the limiting distribution.






ProblemProblem 5





Prove the representation \[
  \omega ^2 = \frac{1}{12 n^{2}} + \frac{1}{n} \sum _{k=1}^{n} \left(F_0\left(X_{(k)}\right) - \frac{2k-1}{2n}\right)^2.
\] This representation is often used in practice to compute the value of the statistic \(\omega^{2}\).









ProblemProblem 6





Prove the consistency of the Cramér-von Mises-Smirnov test.

title: Goodness-of-Fit Tests
section: 2.1 A sample from a Bernoulli scheme with known outcomes
text:
2.1 A sample from a Bernoulli scheme with known outcomes
Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be a sample from a Bernoulli scheme with \(m \geq 2\) known outcomes \(A = \left\{ a_1, \ldots , a_m\right\}\). The probability mass function (a generalized density with respect to the counting measure on \(A\)):
\[
  p_j := \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = a_j\right), \;  j = \overline{1,m}
\]
We know the outcomes \(a_1, \ldots , a_m\), but the probabilities \(p_1, \ldots , p_m\) are unknown. Such a distribution is also called categorical and is denoted
\[
  \operatorname {Cat}(A, \overrightarrow {p}), \qquad \overrightarrow {p} = \left(p_1, p_2, \ldots , p_m\right)^T
\]
Let us estimate the unknown distribution by the empirical distribution. In that case the estimator of \(p_j\) equals the sample frequency of hitting \(a_j\):
\[
  \widehat{p_j} = \overline{\; \mathbb {1}_{X = a_j}}, \qquad \widehat{\overrightarrow {p}} = \left(\widehat{p}_1, \widehat{p}_2, \ldots , \widehat{p}_m\right)^T
\]






ExampleExample 3





Prove that \(\widehat{\overrightarrow {p}}\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(\overrightarrow {p}\). Find its asymptotic covariance matrix.






SolutionSolution





Let
\[
  \xi ^{(i)} := \begin{pmatrix}  \; \mathbb {1}_{X_i = a_1} \\ \; \mathbb {1}_{X_i = a_2} \\ \vdots \\ \; \mathbb {1}_{X_i = a_m} \end{pmatrix}
\]
Then \(\xi^{(1)}, \xi^{(2)}, \ldots\) is a sequence of independent identically distributed random vectors, with
\[
  \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n \xi ^{(i)} = \widehat{\overrightarrow {p}}
\]
Next,
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {E}\left[\xi ^{(1)}\right] & = \begin{pmatrix}  \mathbb {P}\left(X_i = a_1\right) \\ \mathbb {P}\left(X_i = a_2\right) \\ \vdots \\ \mathbb {P}\left(X_i = a_m\right) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  p_1 \\ p_2 \\ \vdots \\ p_m \end{pmatrix} = \overrightarrow {p}, \\ \operatorname {Var}\left[\xi ^{(1)}\right] & = \mathbb {E}\left[\xi ^{(1)} \left(\xi ^{(1)}\right)^T\right] - \mathbb {E}\left[\xi ^{(1)}\right]\left(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi ^{(1)}\right]\right)^T = \\ & = \begin{pmatrix}  \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = a_1\right) &  \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = a_1, X_1 = a_2\right) &  \ldots &  \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = a_1, X_1 = a_m\right) \\ \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = a_2, X_1 = a_1\right) &  \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = a_2, X_1 = a_2\right) &  \ldots &  \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = a_2, X_1 = a_m\right) \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = a_m, X_1 = a_1\right) &  \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = a_m, X_1 = a_2\right) &  \ldots &  \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = a_m, X_1 = a_m\right) \end{pmatrix} - \mathbb {E}\left[\xi ^{(1)}\right]\left(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi ^{(1)}\right]\right)^T \end{align}
\]
Since at any given moment \(X_1\) takes exactly one value, the events \(\left\{ X_1=a_i\right\}\) and \(\left\{ X_1=a_j\right\}\) are disjoint for \(i \neq j\) and coincide for \(i=j\); hence \(\mathbb {P}\left(X_1=a_i, X_1=a_j\right) = 0\) for \(i \neq j\) and \(=p_i\) for \(i=j\), i.e. the matrix of joint probabilities is diagonal:
\[
\begin{align}  \operatorname {Var}\left[\xi ^{(1)}\right] & = \begin{pmatrix}  p_1 &  0 &  0 &  \ldots &  0 \\ 0 &  p_2 &  0 &  \ldots &  0 \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ 0 & 0 &  0 &  \ldots &  p_m \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}  p^2_1 &  p_1p_2 &  p_1p_3 &  \ldots &  p_1p_m \\ p_2p_1 &  p^2_2 &  p_2p_3 &  \ldots &  p_2p_m \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ p_mp_1 &  p_mp_2 &  p_mp_3 &  \ldots &  p_m^2 \end{pmatrix} = \\ & = \begin{pmatrix}  p_1(1 - p_1) &  -p_1p_2 &  -p_1p_3 &  \ldots &  -p_1p_m \\ -p_2p_1 &  p_2(1 - p_2) &  -p_2p_3 &  \ldots &  -p_2p_m \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ -p_mp_1 &  -p_mp_2 &  -p_mp_3 &  \ldots &  p_m(1 - p_m) \end{pmatrix} \end{align}
\]
By the CLT we have
\[
  \sqrt{n}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n \xi ^{(i)} - \overrightarrow {p}\right) = \sqrt{n}\left(\widehat{\overrightarrow {p}} - \overrightarrow {p}\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, \operatorname {Var}\left[\xi ^{(1)}\right]\right)
\]







2.1.1 Simple hypothesis
Let \(A\) be a fixed set of outcomes, and consider the following parametric model
\[
  \mathcal{P} = \left\{ \operatorname {Cat}(A, \overrightarrow {p}): \;  \overrightarrow {p}\in [0,1]^m, \sum _{i=1}^m p_i = 1\right\} .
\]
Let \(\overrightarrow {p}^0 \in [0,1]^m\) be a fixed vector such that \(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i = 1\). Consider the parametric hypotheses
\[
  H_0: \mathbb {P} = \mathbb {P}_0 = \operatorname {Cat}(A, \overrightarrow {p}^0), \qquad H_1: \mathbb {P} \in \mathcal{P}\setminus \left\{ \mathbb {P}_0\right\}  = \left\{ \operatorname {Cat}(A, \overrightarrow {p}): \overrightarrow {p} \neq \overrightarrow {p}^0\right\}
\]
Equivalently:
\[
  H_0: \overrightarrow {p} = \overrightarrow {p}_0, \qquad H_1 : \overrightarrow {p} \neq \overrightarrow {p}_0
\]







Definition 3 The chi-squared statistic is defined as \[
  \widehat{\chi ^2} := \sum _{j=1}^{m} \frac{\left(\mu _{j}-n p_{j}^{0}\right)^{2}}{n p_{j}^{0}} = \sum _{j=1}^{m} n\frac{\left(\widehat{p_j} - p_{j}^{0}\right)^{2}}{p_{j}^{0}} = \left\| \eta _n\right\| _{2}^2,
\] where \[
  \mu _{j}=\sum _{i=1}^{n} \; \mathbb {1}_{X_i = a_j}, \qquad \eta _n = \sqrt{n} \begin{pmatrix}  \frac{\widehat{p_1} - p_{1}^{0}}{\sqrt{p_{1}^{0}}} \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\widehat{p_m} - p_{m}^{0}}{\sqrt{p_{m}^{0}}} \end{pmatrix} = \sqrt{n}B \left(\widehat{\overrightarrow {p}} - \overrightarrow {p}^0\right), \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix}  \frac{1}{\sqrt{p_1^0}} &  0 &  0 &  \ldots &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  \frac{1}{\sqrt{p_2^0}} &  0 &  \ldots &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  \frac{1}{\sqrt{p_3^0}} &  \ldots &  0 &  0 \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ 0 &  0 &  0 &  \ldots &  \frac{1}{\sqrt{p_{m-1}^0}} &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  0 &  \ldots &  0 &  \frac{1}{\sqrt{p_m^0}} \\ \end{pmatrix}
\]











Theorem 4 (Pearson) Under the hypothesis \(H_{0}\), the statistic \(\widehat{\chi^2}\) converges in distribution to the chi-squared distribution with \(m-1\) degrees of freedom: \[
  \widehat{\chi ^2} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d_0} \chi _{m-1}^2
\]










ExampleExample 4





Prove Pearson’s theorem.






SolutionSolution





We proved above that \(\sqrt{n}\left(\widehat{\overrightarrow {p}} - \overrightarrow {p}^0\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d_0} \eta \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, \operatorname {Var}\left[\xi^{(1)}\right]\right)\). Hence \(\eta_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d_0} \eta \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, \Sigma \right)\), where \(\Sigma := B\cdot \operatorname {Var}\left[\xi^{(1)}\right] \cdot B^T\). Since \(B\) is diagonal with entries \(1/\sqrt{p_i^0}\), the \((i,j)\)-th entry of \(\Sigma\) equals the \((i,j)\)-th entry of \(\operatorname {Var}\left[\xi^{(1)}\right]\) divided by \(\sqrt{p_i^0p_j^0}\): for \(i=j\) we get \(p_i^0(1-p_i^0)/p_i^0 = 1-p_i^0\), and for \(i \neq j\) we get \(-p_i^0p_j^0/\sqrt{p_i^0p_j^0} = -\sqrt{p_i^0p_j^0}\), i.e.
\[
  \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}  1 - p^0_1 &  -\sqrt{p^0_1p^0_2} &  -\sqrt{p^0_1p^0_3} &  \ldots &  -\sqrt{p^0_1p^0_m} \\ -\sqrt{p^0_2p^0_1} &  1 - p^0_2 &  -\sqrt{p^0_2p^0_3} &  \ldots &  -\sqrt{p^0_2p^0_m} \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ -\sqrt{p^0_mp^0_1} &  -\sqrt{p^0_mp^0_2} &  -\sqrt{p^0_mp^0_3} &  \ldots &  1 - p^0_m \end{pmatrix}
\]
By the theorem on preservation of convergence in distribution we obtain
\[
  \left\| \eta _n\right\| _{2}^2 \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \left\| \eta \right\| _{2}^2
\]
That is, we simply need to understand how \(\left\| \eta \right\|_{2}^2\) is distributed, where \(\eta \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, \Sigma \right)\).
Let us study the matrix \(\Sigma\). The matrix \(\Sigma\) is symmetric, so its singular value decomposition has the form \(\Sigma = U \Lambda U^T\), where \(\Lambda\) is a matrix of dimension \(\operatorname {rk}(\Sigma ) \times \operatorname {rk}(\Sigma )\) with the nonzero real eigenvalues of \(\Sigma\) on the diagonal, and \(U\) is a matrix of dimension \(m \times \operatorname {rk}(\Sigma )\) with orthonormal column vectors.
How do we find the eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \ldots , \lambda_m\) of the matrix \(\Sigma\)? Notice an interesting property of \(\Sigma\): \(\Sigma^2 = \Sigma\) (this property is not hard to show; we leave the proof as an exercise), i.e. \(\Sigma\) is idempotent. At the same time \(\Sigma^2 = U \Lambda U^TU \Lambda U^T = U \Lambda^2 U^T\). Hence the eigenvalues of \(\Sigma\) can only equal \(1\) or \(0\). Moreover, it is known from linear algebra that
\[
  \lambda _1 + \ldots + \lambda _m = \operatorname {tr}(\Sigma ) = m - \sum _{i=1}^m p_i^0 = m-1
\]
Thus, \(\lambda_1 = \ldots = \lambda_{m - 1} = 1, \;  \lambda_m = 0\).
Next, by the properties of Gaussian vectors, \(\eta = U \Lambda^{1/2} \zeta\), where \(\Lambda^{1/2} = I_{m-1}^{1/2} = I_{m-1}\), and \(\zeta \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, I_{m-1}\right)\) is a vector of \(m-1\) independent standard normal random variables. Then
\[
  \left\| \eta \right\| _{2}^2 = \eta ^T \eta = \zeta ^T U^T U \zeta = \zeta ^T \zeta = \left\| \zeta \right\| _{2}^2 \sim \chi ^2_{m-1}
\]






Pearson’s chi-squared test is written as follows: \(\left\{ \widehat{\chi^2}> Q_{\chi^2_{m-1}}(1-\alpha )\right\}\), where \(Q_{\chi^2_{m-1}}(\cdot )\) is the quantile function of \(\chi_{m-1}^{2}\). The chi-squared test is asymptotic; it is customarily applied when \(n \geq 50\) and \(\mu_{j} \geq 5\) for all \(j \in \{ 1, \ldots , m\}\).






ProblemProblem 7





Prove the consistency of the chi-squared test.









ExampleExample 5





According to statistics gathered at a psychiatric hospital over a year, the number of patients admitted to the intensive care unit had the following distribution by day of the week: \[
  \text{Mon} - 36, \text{Tue} - 53, \text{Wed} - 35, \text{Thu} - 26, \text{Fri} - 30, \text{Sat} - 44, \text{Sun} - 28.
\] Are these data consistent with the hypothesis that admission does not depend on the day of the week, at significance levels \(0.05\) and \(0.01\)?






SolutionSolution





Set \(m=7, p_{j}^{0}=\frac{1}{7}, j \in \{ 1, \ldots , m\}\). The total number of observations equals
\[
  n=36+53+35+26+30+44+28=252
\]
Thus \(n p_{j}^{0}=36\) for all \(j \in \{ 1, \ldots , m\}\). The deviations of the observed frequencies from the expected value, by day (Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun), equal
\[
  \mu _j - 36 = 0, \;  17, \;  -1, \;  -10, \;  -6, \;  8, \;  -8,
\]
and the contribution of each day to the statistic, i.e. the term \((\mu_j-36)^2/36\), equals
\[
  0, \quad \frac{17^2}{36} \approx 8.03, \quad \frac{1^2}{36}\approx 0.03, \quad \frac{10^2}{36}\approx 2.78, \quad \frac{6^2}{36}=1, \quad \frac{8^2}{36}\approx 1.78, \quad \frac{8^2}{36}\approx 1.78.
\]
Summing, we get
\[
  \widehat{\chi ^2} = 0+8.03+0.03+2.78+1+1.78+1.78=15.4.
\]

The “move patients” slider lets you redistribute observations between two selected days and live-recomputes \(\chi^2\) and the \(p\)-value; the scale below compares the current \(\chi^2\) with the critical value for the selected significance level. Here \(\chi^2 \sim \chi^2_6\); the \(p\)-value uses the Wilson-Hilferty approximation to the \(\chi^2\) distribution function (a normal approximation), not the exact incomplete gamma function.

The quantiles of the chi-squared distribution with 6 degrees of freedom are: \(u_{0.95} \approx 12.6, u_{0.99} \approx 16.8\). Thus, at significance level \(0.05\) we reject the hypothesis of uniform admission of patients, while at level \(0.01\) we do not reject it (though in the second case the probability of a type II error, of course, increases substantially, so a high significance level is not advisable when there are not so many observations).












ProblemProblem 8





The digits \(0,1,2, \ldots , 9\) among the first 800 decimal digits of \(\pi\) appeared 74, 92, 83, 79, 80, 73, 77, 75, 76, 91 times respectively. Using the chi-squared test, check the hypothesis that these data are consistent with the uniform distribution on the set \(\left\{ 0,1, \ldots , 9\right\}\) at significance level a) \(5\%\), b) \(50\%\), c) \(80\%\).









ProblemProblem 9





A professional dentist has learned to knock out wisdom teeth with a punch. It is known that he knocked out 52 wisdom teeth on the first attempt, 31 on the second, 3 on the third, and needed 4 or more attempts for the remaining 5 teeth. Test the hypothesis that the dentist knocks out an arbitrary wisdom tooth with probability \(\frac{2}{3}\), at significance level \(0.1\).





2.1.2 Composite hypothesis
Pearson’s chi-squared test can also be applied in the case of composite hypotheses
\[
  H_0: \overrightarrow {p} = \overrightarrow {p}^0(\overrightarrow {\theta }), \;  \overrightarrow {\theta } \in \Theta \subset \mathbb {R}^{r}, \;  r < m-1, \qquad H_1: \overrightarrow {p} \neq \overrightarrow {p}^0(\overrightarrow {\theta })
\]
To test such hypotheses one also uses the statistic \(\widehat{\chi^2} = \widehat{\chi^2}(\overrightarrow {\theta })\), in which \(\overrightarrow {\theta }\) is replaced by the maximum likelihood estimator
\[
  \overrightarrow {\theta }^{*} = \operatorname *{arg\, max}_{\overrightarrow {\theta } \in \Theta } \prod _{j=1}^{m}\left(p_{j}^{0}(\overrightarrow {\theta })\right)^{\mu _{j}} .
\]







Theorem 5 (Fisher) Suppose the following conditions hold:

the hypothesis \(H_{0}\) holds;
for every \(\overrightarrow {\theta } \in \Theta\) the equality \(\sum_{j=1}^{m} p_{j}(\overrightarrow {\theta })=1\) holds;
there is a positive number \(c\) such that for all \(j \in \{ 1, \ldots , m\}\) and \(\overrightarrow {\theta } \in \Theta\), \(p_{j}(\overrightarrow {\theta }) \geq c\);
for all \(j \in \{ 1, \ldots , m\} , k, l \in\) \(\{ 1, \ldots , r\}\) the continuous derivatives \(\frac{\partial p_{j}^{0}(\overrightarrow {\theta })}{\partial \theta_{k}}, \frac{\partial^{2} p_{j}^{0}(\overrightarrow {\theta })}{\partial \theta_{k} \partial \theta_{l}}\) exist;
the matrix formed from the partial derivatives \(\frac{\partial p_{j}^{0}(\overrightarrow {\theta })}{\partial \theta_{k}}(j \in \{ 1, \ldots , m\} , k \in\) \(\{ 1, \ldots , r\} )\) has rank \(r\) for all \(\theta \in \Theta\).

Then
\[
  \widehat{\chi ^2}\left(\overrightarrow {\theta }^{*}\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \chi _{m-1-r}^{2}
\]
In the case of composite hypotheses, the chi-squared test is also applied when \(n \geq 50\) and \(\mu_{j} \geq 5\) for all \(j \in \{ 1, \ldots , m\}\).










ExampleExample 6





Test at significance level \(\alpha\) the hypothesis that the measured quantity \(X\) has a binomial distribution with parameters \((2, \theta )\), if, out of \(n=128\) measurements, it took the value \(0, \mu_{1}=n / 4\) times, the value 1 \(\mu_{2}=n / 4\) times, and the value 2 \(\mu_{3}=n / 2\) times.






SolutionSolution





The problem concerns testing the hypothesis \[
  H_{0}: p_{1}^{0}(\theta )=(1-\theta )^{2}, p_{2}^{0}(\theta )=2 \theta (1-\theta ), p_{3}^{0}=\theta ^{2}.
\] Let us find the maximum likelihood estimator: \[
  \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }\left(\ln \prod _{j=1}^{3}\left(p_{j}^{0}(\theta )\right)^{\mu _{j}}\right) = -\frac{2 \mu _{1}}{1-\theta }+\frac{\mu _{2}}{\theta }-\frac{\mu _{2}}{1-\theta }+\frac{2 \mu _{3}}{\theta }.
\] Bringing this to the common denominator \(\theta (1-\theta )\): the numerator equals \(-2\mu_1\theta - \mu_2 \theta + \mu_2(1-\theta ) + 2\mu_3(1-\theta ) = \mu_2 + 2\mu_3 - 2\theta (\mu_1+\mu_2+\mu_3)\), and since \(\mu_1+\mu_2+\mu_3=n\), this equals \(2\mu_3+\mu_2-2n\theta\). So \[
  \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }\left(\ln \prod _{j=1}^{3}\left(p_{j}^{0}(\theta )\right)^{\mu _{j}}\right) = \frac{2 \mu _{3}+\mu _{2}-2 n \theta }{\theta (1-\theta )}.
\] Hence \(\theta^{*}=\frac{2 \mu_{3}+\mu_{2}}{2 n}=\frac{2 \cdot \frac{n}{2}+\frac{n}{4}}{2 n} = \frac{5}{8}\). Then \[
  p^0_1\left(\tfrac {5}{8}\right) = \frac{9}{64}, \quad p^0_2\left(\tfrac {5}{8}\right) = \frac{30}{64}, \quad p^0_3\left(\tfrac {5}{8}\right) = \frac{25}{64}, \qquad np^0_1 = 18, \quad np^0_2 = 60, \quad np^0_3 = 50,
\] and finally we obtain the value of the statistic \[
  \widehat{\chi ^2}(\theta ^*) = \sum _{j=1}^{3} \frac{\left(\mu _{j}-n p_{j}^{0}(5/8)\right)^{2}}{n p_{j}^{0}(5/8)}=\frac{(32-18)^{2}}{18}+\frac{(32-60)^{2}}{60}+\frac{(64-50)^{2}}{50} \approx 10.89 + 13.07 + 3.92 = 27.88
\] Here \(m = 3\), \(r = 1\), i.e. under \(H_0\) the statistic is asymptotically distributed as \(\chi^2_{m-1-r} = \chi^2_1\). Since the 0.99-quantile of \(\chi_{1}^{2}\), to four decimal places, equals \(6.6349 \ll 27.88\), the hypothesis should be rejected even at significance level \(0.01\).












ProblemProblem 10





Among 5000 families with three children, there are exactly 1010 families with three boys, 2200 families with two boys and one girl, and 950 families with one boy and two girls (in all other families, all children are girls). Can we, at significance level \(\alpha =0.02\), consider that the number of boys \(\xi\) in a family with three children has the following distribution: \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\xi = 0\right) = \theta , \quad \mathbb {P}\left(\xi = 1\right) = \theta , \quad \mathbb {P}\left(\xi = 2\right) = 2\theta , \quad \mathbb {P}\left(\xi = 3\right) = 1-4 \theta , \qquad \text{ where } \theta \in \left(0, \frac{1}{4}\right).
\]

title: Goodness-of-Fit Tests
text:
2.2 The general case
The chi-squared test, like the Kolmogorov goodness-of-fit test, is used to test the hypothesis that the distribution from which our sample is drawn coincides with some specific distribution \(\mathbb {P}_0\). Unlike the Kolmogorov test, the chi-squared test does not require heavy computation, but is less “precise.” One can work with the chi-squared test in the case of an arbitrary class of distributions as follows: the range of the sample is partitioned into several intervals, after which the number of sample elements falling into each interval is computed. The resulting values are taken as \(\mu_{j}\). As \(p_{j}^{0}\) one takes the probability that a random variable with distribution \(\mathbb {P}_0\) falls into the \(j\)-th interval. In essence, one compares the histogram of the sample with the theoretical histogram of the distribution \(\mathbb {P}_0\).
On the number of classes, see (Kallenberg et al. 1985).

title: Hypothesis Testing
section: 1.1 Different effects of errors, different hypotheses. Singling out the base hypothesis
text:
1.1 Different effects of errors, different hypotheses. Singling out the base hypothesis
When testing statistical hypotheses one can make 2 different kinds of errors: either claiming that hypothesis \(H_1: \theta \in \Theta_1\) holds when in fact \(H_0: \theta \in \Theta_0\) holds (a type I error), or the reverse (a type II error). As a rule, these errors are not equivalent for the study — one is more dangerous than the other.
For example, in a study of a new drug: at present there is a mass of cold medicines with proven effectiveness, and if the researcher says that the new drug does not work when it actually does, this will not be critical for future patients, since instead of the new medicine they can turn to proven older ones and reliably recover in a short time. But if the researcher claims that a useless drug is effective, and this drug appears on pharmacy shelves, then future patients will be at risk, since they will be buying a useless medicine expecting a quick cure.
Since the errors are not equivalent for the researcher, the hypotheses cannot be equivalent either: we should be inclined to accept the hypothesis whose mistaken rejection would be more critical for us. This hypothesis is usually denoted \(H_0\) and called the null (base) hypothesis, and the opposite one, \(H_1\), the alternative. In the case of medical studies, as a rule, the null hypothesis is that the new drug (or treatment method) is ineffective, and the alternative is that it is effective.

title: Hypothesis Testing
section: 1.2 Significance of data, p-value, significance level
text:
1.2 Significance of data, p-value, significance level
Testing statistical hypotheses proceeds as follows: the researcher initially, before the study, considers the null hypothesis \(H_0\) to be true. Then they obtain data and examine it, trying to answer the question: is the data critical enough for \(H_0\) to reject the null hypothesis \(H_0\) in favor of the alternative \(H_1\)?
How can we numerically assess how critical the data is? Let us consider the example above, about the study of a new drug.






ExampleExample 1





Recovery time is most simply modeled by an exponential distribution. Let \(X_1, \ldots , X_n, \;  n = 100\) be a sample from the exponential distribution \(\operatorname {Exp}\left(\frac{1}{\theta }\right), \;  \theta \in \left\{ 4,6\right\}\) (i.e. \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_1\right] = \theta\)). Suppose a specific experiment \(\omega_0\) was carried out, with \[
  \overline{X}(\omega _0) = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n X_i(\omega _0) = 4.8  
\] Let the null hypothesis be \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0 = 6\), and the alternative \(H_1: \theta = \theta_1 = 4\). Assess how critical the data in experiment \(\omega_0\) is, based on the statistic \(\overline{X}\).






SolutionSolution





Density of the statistic \(\overline{X} \sim \Gamma(n, n/\theta_0)\) under \(H_0\) (\(\theta_0=6\)), the observed value \(\overline{X}(\omega_0)=4.8\) and the p-value \(P(\overline{X}\le 4.8 \mid H_0)\) – the shaded area on the left. Drag the vertical line of the observed value (or move the slider) to see how the p-value changes along with the data; the \(n\) and \(\theta_0\) sliders change the shape of the density.






x̄(ω₀) = 4.8
n = 100
θ₀ = 6.0


p-value $P(\overline{X}\le\text{x̄}(\omega_0)\mid H_0)$ = 





The \(p\)-value itself is a random variable: from experiment to experiment it changes along with the sample. It is useful to think not of a single value of it, but of its distribution over many repetitions of the experiment.
The distribution of the \(p\)-value over many repeated experiments (simulation: on each repetition a new sample, and hence a new \(\overline{X}\), is generated, and the p-value with respect to \(H_0: \theta=\theta_0\) is computed for it). When \(H_0\) is true, it is uniform on \([0,1]\) – this is built into the very definition of the p-value. When \(H_0\) is false (the true value is \(\theta_1 \ne \theta_0\)), the distribution shifts toward zero – the more so, the greater the power of the test (larger \(n\) or larger difference \(|\theta_1-\theta_0|\)). Switch the mode and move the sliders to see this dependence.






H₀ true (θ=θ₀)
H₀ false (θ=θ₁)


n = 30
θ₁ = 4.0


fraction of p ≤ 5%: 





Initially we assume that \(H_0\) is true, i.e. that \(\theta = 6\). We need to understand how critical the data we obtained is — its statistical significance. Let us try to understand this based on the statistic \(\overline{X}\).
\(\theta\) is the expectation. The closer the sample mean is to \(\theta_1\) compared to \(\theta_0\), the more critical the data. In our case the parameter in the alternative hypothesis \(\theta_1\) is smaller than the parameter \(\theta_0\) in the null hypothesis, so the smaller the sample mean, the more critical the data.
Practical meaning: the less time it takes to recover while taking the new drug, the more improbable this is if we assume that the drug does not work.
How can we numerically express how critical the data is? From the properties of the gamma distribution we know that \(\overline{X} \sim \Gamma (n, n/\theta )\), i.e. under \(H_0\) we have \(\overline{X} \sim \Gamma (100, 100/6)\). We have
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{\theta _0}\left(\overline{X} \leq 4.8\right) \approx 1.7\%   
\]
This number is called the p-value of experiment \(\omega_0\). What is its meaning? We obtained a value of the statistic \(\overline{X}\) during the experiment. The p-value is the probability of obtaining, in a copy of the experiment, a value of the statistic that is the same or more critical, given that hypothesis \(H_0\) holds.
The p-value can be used to assess how critical the data is under the assumption of hypothesis \(H_0\).


                                                
Comparison of hypothetical recovery-time distributions: \(H_0\) — \(\operatorname{Exp}(1/\theta_0)\), \(\theta_0=6\) (the drug has no effect), and \(H_1\) — \(\operatorname{Exp}(1/\theta_1)\), \(\theta_1=4\) (the drug is effective). The dashed lines mark the means \(\theta_0\), \(\theta_1\) and the observed sample mean \(\overline{X}(\omega_0)=4.8\).











AnswerAnswer





p-value: \(1.7\%\).






The data of an experiment is said to have statistical significance if obtaining the same data in an independent copy of the experiment would be extremely improbable, under the assumption that the null hypothesis holds. If the data is statistically significant, the null hypothesis must be rejected in favor of the alternative.
We obtained some p-value during the experiment. How can we use it to determine whether the data is significant, whether we need to reject hypothesis \(H_0\)? To resolve this question, before the experiment one sets some threshold for the p-value, called the significance level (notation: \(\alpha\)). The significance level sets the acceptable probability with which we are willing to reject \(H_0\) when it is true. That is, the significance level is the acceptable probability of making a type I error. As a rule, the value \(\alpha = 5\%\) is taken as the significance level, although in medical studies it may also be \(1\%\), \(0.1\%\), or \(0.01\%\).






ExampleExample 2





Under the conditions of example Example 1, test \(H_0\) against \(H_1\) at significance levels \(\alpha_1 = 5\%\), \(\alpha_2 = 1\%\).






SolutionSolution





(via the p-value). p-value: \(1.7\%\).






Enum-item1.



\(1.7\%  < 5\%\), hence the data is significant, critical enough under the assumption of \(H_0\). The variability of the data cannot be attributed to chance. \(H_0\) must be rejected in favor of \(H_1\), and \(H_1\) accepted;








Enum-item2.



\(1.7\%  > 1\%\), hence the data is not significant, not critical enough under the assumption of \(H_0\). Its variability can be attributed to chance. \(H_0\) should not be rejected.


Alternative solution (via critical values). We know the significance levels. Let \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) be the values of the statistic \(\overline{X}\) whose criticality is exactly equal to \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\):
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{\theta _0}\left(\overline{X} \leq q_i\right) = \alpha _i, \quad i \in \left\{ 1,2\right\}   
\]
Given that the null hypothesis holds, \(\overline{X} \sim \Gamma (100,100/6)\). So \(q_i\) is the quantile of level \(\alpha_i\) of this distribution. Let us find them:
\[
  q_1 = 5.05, \quad q_2 = 4.69  
\]
These values are called critical values of the statistic (in this case, of the sample mean). If the statistic is more critical than such a value (in this case, smaller), then \(H_0\) should be rejected.






Enum-item1.



\(\overline{X}(\omega_0) = 4.8 < 5.05 = q_1\), so at significance level \(\alpha_1= 5\%\), \(H_0\) should be rejected;








Enum-item2.



\(\overline{X}(\omega_0) = 4.8 > 4.69 = q_2\), so at significance level \(\alpha_2= 1\%\), \(H_0\) should not be rejected.


Remark. Note that in the second case it is incorrect to say that we accept \(H_0\), since we already accepted it initially, before the experiment. It is more correct to say that we did not reject \(H_0\).









AnswerAnswer





At a significance level of \(5\%\), \(H_0\) should be rejected in favor of \(H_1\). At \(1\%\), \(H_0\) should not be rejected.






Testing statistical hypotheses is similar to a court trial. Practically every judicial system in the modern world follows the principle of presumption of innocence. Before the trial begins, the defendant is considered innocent; this is, one might say, the court’s null hypothesis \(H_0\). Then, during the trial, the prosecutor presents evidence to the court indicating guilt. The judge’s task is to examine the evidence, determine whether the evidence is sufficient to reject the base assumption of the defendant’s innocence and accept the hypothesis of guilt, and render a verdict.
In mathematical statistics, the evidence is the sample, and the researcher must determine whether the evidence is critical enough to reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_1\).






ProblemProblem 1





Let \(X_1, \ldots , X_n, \;  n = 225\) be a sample from the normal distribution \(\mathscr {N}\left(\theta , 1\right), \;  \theta \in \left\{ 5,8\right\}\), where \(\overline{X}(\omega_0) = 5.15\). Let the null hypothesis be \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0 = 5\), and the alternative \(H_1: \theta = \theta_1 = 8\). Find the p-value for experiment \(\omega_0\), and test hypothesis \(H_0\) against \(H_1\) at significance levels \(\alpha_1 = 5\%\), \(\alpha_2 = 2\%\), \(\alpha_3 = 1\%\).






HintHint





Normal distribution.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
2.1 Test, critical region
How can hypothesis testing be formalized in general? Let \(\vec{X} = (X_1, \ldots , X_n)^T\) be a sample from an unknown distribution \(\mathbb {P} \in \mathcal{P}\). Often we have a parametric model, in which case \(\mathcal{P} = \left\{ \mathbb {P}_\theta , \;  \theta \in \Theta \right\}\), although in general \(\mathcal{P}\) can be any family of distributions.
Hypotheses:

in a parametric model
\[
  H_0: \theta \in \Theta _0, \qquad H_1: \theta \in \Theta _1  
\]
where \(\Theta_0 \subset \Theta\), \(\Theta_1 = \Theta_0^{\complement }\)
in general
\[
  H_0: \mathbb {P} \in \mathcal{P}_0, \qquad H_1: \mathbb {P} \in \mathcal{P}_1  
\]
where \(\mathcal{P}_0 \subset \mathcal{P}\), \(\mathcal{P}_1 = \mathcal{P}_0^{\complement }\).

Going forward, for simplicity, we will mostly formulate definitions for the parametric case. But they are easily carried over to the general nonparametric case as well.
If a hypothesis involves only one parameter (one distribution), it is called simple. Otherwise the hypothesis is called composite. So far, in examples (Example 1) and problems (Problem 1) we tested only a simple null hypothesis against a simple alternative. Examples with composite hypotheses are given below.
The decision to reject or not reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_1\) can, as seen in example Example 1, be made in two ways: via the p-value and via critical values. Let us consider the second way, via critical values. We rejected \(H_0\) if the sample mean was less than some value \(q\). This method can also be phrased as follows: let
\[
  S := \left\{ \vec{x} \in \mathbb {R}^{n} \;  : \;  \overline{x} \leq q\right\}   
\]
\(S\) is some subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) (consisting of those column vectors whose arithmetic mean of coordinates does not exceed \(q\)), and we reject \(H_0\) if our sample \(\vec{X}\) falls into \(S\):
\[
  \vec{X} \in S \;  \Rightarrow \;  \text{reject }H_0 \text{ at significance level }\alpha
\]
\(S\) is called the critical set.
In general it is not always clear which statistic to use when testing a hypothesis. Or, even if a statistic has been chosen, it is not always clear what “criticality” of the statistic means. For example, if in the example above we instead had not
\[
  H_0: \theta \in \left\{ 6\right\}  \text{ against } H_1: \theta \in \left\{ 4\right\}
\]
but
\[
  H_0: \theta \in \left\{ 3, 6\right\}  \text{ against } H_1: \theta \in \left\{ 2,4,8\right\}
\]
Which value of the sample mean is more critical here, and which is less? Here “criticality” cannot be defined.
Computing the p-value and the critical value is impossible without the notion of “criticality.” Therefore, in general, hypothesis testing is formalized precisely through critical sets: we reject \(H_0\) if the sample \(\vec{X}\) falls into some subset \(S \subset \mathcal{X}\) of the space \(\mathcal{X}\) of all possible sample values (as a rule, \(\mathcal{X} = \mathbb {R}^{n}\)). Otherwise we do not reject \(H_0\). To reiterate, the region \(S \subset \mathcal{X}\) is called the critical region or simply the test.







Definition 1 Let \(S \subset \mathcal{X}\) be a test.

The power function of the test \(S\) is the function
\[
  \beta (\theta , S) := \mathbb {P}_{\theta }(\vec{X} \in S), \quad \theta \in \Theta  
\]
This is the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) if the true parameter is \(\theta\).
A quantity \(\alpha\) is called a significance level of the test \(S\) if \(\alpha \geq \beta (\theta , S)\) for every \(\theta \in \Theta_{0}\). Note that if \(\theta \in \Theta_0\), then the null hypothesis \(H_0\) holds. In that case \(\beta (\theta , S)\) is the probability of rejecting a true \(H_0\), i.e. of making a type I error. The significance level is thus an upper bound for the possible probabilities of type I errors. These probabilities can differ, since in general \(\Theta_0\) contains several elements.
The minimal significance level under the null hypothesis
\[
  \alpha _{0}=\sup _{\theta \in \Theta _{0}} \beta (\theta , S)  
\]
is called the size of the test \(S\). The size of a test is the exact upper bound for the probabilities of type I errors.
The size of the test is often called the significance level and denoted \(\alpha\).











ExampleExample 3





Let \(X\) be a sample of size 1. Let \(H_0: X \sim U[0,1], \;  H_1: X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1)\). Let \(\alpha \in (0,1)\) be arbitrary. Construct all possible tests \(S\) of significance level (size) \(\alpha \in (0,1)\).






SolutionSolution





Here \(\mathcal{P} = \left\{ U[0,1], \operatorname {Exp}(1)\right\}\), \(\mathcal{P}_0 = \left\{ U[0,1]\right\} , \;  \mathcal{P}_1 = \left\{ \operatorname {Exp}(1)\right\}\). Denote \(\mathbb {P}_0 := U[0,1], \;  \mathbb {P}_1 := \operatorname {Exp}(1)\).
Note that here the range of the sample values is \(\mathcal{X} = \mathbb {R}_+\). Let \(S \subset \mathcal{X}\) be a test. Since \(\mathcal{P}_0 = \left\{ \mathbb {P}_0\right\}\) consists of a single distribution, the supremum over \(\mathcal{P}_0\) is taken trivially: its significance level is
\[
  \alpha = \sup _{\mathbb {P} \in \mathcal{P}_0} \beta (\mathbb {P}, S) = \beta (\mathbb {P}_0, S) = \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(X \in S\right).  
\]
The density of the distribution \(\mathbb {P}_0 = U[0,1]\) equals \(\; \mathbb {1}_{X \in [0,1]}\), so
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(X \in S\right) = \int _S \; \mathbb {1}_{X \in [0,1]}dx = \int _{S \cap [0,1]} dx = \lambda \left(S \cap [0,1]\right),  
\]
where \(\lambda\) is Lebesgue measure.









AnswerAnswer





\(S\) is any set from \(\mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}_+\right)\) such that \(\lambda (S \cap [0,1]) = \alpha\).

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
2.2 Power of a test
If the goal is to constrain the probability of a type I error as much as possible, then, generally speaking, it can be made zero by setting the significance level \(\alpha\) to zero. At such a significance level we would have to stand by \(H_0\) regardless of the data \(\vec{X}\), and we would need to take \(S = \varnothing\). In this case we would never reject \(H_0\), since the sample would never fall into the critical set (as it is empty).
However, in every case where \(H_1\) is actually true, we would be standing by \(H_0\), making a type II error. The probability of a type II error in this case would be \(100\%\).
There is an inverse relationship between the probabilities of type I and type II errors: the smaller one probability, the larger the other, and vice versa. There is no “best” test that would simultaneously minimize both type I and type II errors.
In practice, when searching for the “best” test, one first fixes the significance level (the probability of making a type I error), and then among all tests with the given significance level one searches for the best one from the point of view of the type II error.







Definition 2 The upper bound for the possible values of type II errors is denoted by the letter \(\beta\). The notation coincides with that of the power function, but this usually causes no confusion.
Recall that a type II error occurs when \(H_1\) is true but the researcher does not reject \(H_0\), i.e. when \(\vec{X} \not\in S\):
\[
\begin{align}  \beta & := \sup _{\theta \in \Theta _{1}} \mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(\vec{X} \not\in S\right) = \sup _{\theta \in \Theta _{1}} \left[ 1 - \mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(\vec{X} \in S\right)\right] = \\ & = \sup _{\theta \in \Theta _{1}} \left[ 1 - \beta (\theta , S)\right] \end{align}
\]
The quantity \(1-\beta\) is called the power of the statistical test. Power is the ability of a test to detect an effect (hypothesis \(H_1\)), if that effect really exists. From a statistical point of view, it is the lower bound of the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis:
\[
  1 - \beta = \inf _{\theta \in \Theta _{1}} \mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(\vec{X} \in S\right) = \inf _{\theta \in \Theta _{1}} \beta (\theta , S) \quad \left(1 - \beta = \inf _{\mathbb {P} \in \mathcal{P}_{1}} \beta (\mathbb {P}, S) \text{ in general}\right)
\]

ExampleExample 4





Under the conditions of example Example 3, find the power of each test \(S\). Find the most powerful test of significance level \(\alpha \in (0,1)\).






HintHint





Here \(\mathcal{P}_1 = \left\{ \mathbb {P}_1\right\}\) contains only one distribution. The power computation simplifies: \[
  \beta = \mathbb {P}_{1}\left(X \not\in S\right), \qquad 1 - \beta = \mathbb {P}_{1}\left(X \in S\right)  
\]









SolutionSolution





Let us compute the power of \(S\), i.e. the probability of correctly rejecting \(H_0\). The density of the distribution \(\mathbb {P}_1 = \operatorname {Exp}(1)\) equals \(e^{-x}\) on \(\mathbb {R}_+\), so
\[
  \beta (\mathbb {P}_1, S) = \mathbb {P}_{1}\left(X \in S\right) = \int _S e^{-x} dx.  
\]
The sets \([0,1]\) and \((1, +\infty )\) form a partition of \(\mathcal{X} = \mathbb {R}_+\), so the integral over \(S\) splits into 2 independent terms:
\[
  \int _S e^{-x} dx = \int _{S \cap [0,1]}e^{-x} dx + \int _{S \cap (1, +\infty )}e^{-x} dx.  
\]
Note that the values of these 2 integrals do not depend on each other. Moreover, on \(S \cap (1, +\infty )\) we have no restrictions at all. Hence, to maximize the power, we need to take \(S\) such that \(S \cap (1, +\infty ) = (1, +\infty )\).
Next, consider the integral \(\int_{S \cap [0,1]}e^{-x} dx\). \(e^{-x}\) is strictly decreasing, so, taking into account the constraint \(\lambda (S \cap [0,1]) = \alpha\), the test \(S\) must be taken such that \(S \cap [0,1] = [0, \alpha ]\).


                                                
\(H_0\!:X\sim U[0,1]\) against \(H_1\!:X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\). Most powerful test of significance level \(\alpha\): \(S=[0,\alpha]\cup(1,+\infty)\) (shown for \(\alpha=0.3\)). The violet region is the area under the density of \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) over \(S\), i.e. the power \(1-\beta\) of the most powerful test.











AnswerAnswer





\([0, \alpha ] \cup (1, +\infty )\).












ProblemProblem 2





Let \(X\) be a sample of size 1 from a distribution \(\mathbb {P}\). Let

\(H_0: X \sim U[1,4], \;  H_1: X \sim \mathscr {N}\left(3, 1\right)\);
\(H_0: X \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right), \;  H_1: X \sim \mathscr {N}\left(1, 1\right)\). Let \(\alpha \in (0,1)\) be arbitrary. Find the most powerful test of significance level \(\alpha\).







HintHint





Use the Neyman-Pearson lemma: the critical region should consist of the points where the likelihood ratio \(f_1(x)/f_0(x)\) is largest.






Recall, a hypothesis is called simple if it involves only one parameter or one distribution. So far we have only dealt with testing simple null hypotheses against simple alternatives. In the next problem one must test a simple null hypothesis against a composite alternative.






ProblemProblem 3





Let \(X\) be a sample of size 1 from a distribution \(\mathbb {P}\). Let

\(H_0: X \sim U[-3,3], \;  H_1: \mathbb {P} \in \left\{ \operatorname {TR}[-2,0], \operatorname {TR}[0,2]\right\}\), where \(\operatorname {TR}[a,b]\) is the triangular distribution with density

\[
  p(t) = \begin{cases}  0, & x < a \\ \frac{2(x-a)}{(b-a)\left(\frac{b+a}{2} - a\right)}, & x \in [a, \frac{a+b}{2}), \\ \frac{2(b-x)}{(b-a)\left(b - \frac{b+a}{2}\right)}, & x \in [\frac{a+b}{2}, b), \\ 0, & x \geq b \end{cases}  
\]

\(H_0: X \sim U[-3,3], \;  H_1: \mathbb {P} \in \left\{ \mathscr {N}\left(-1, 1\right), \mathscr {N}\left(1, 1\right)\right\}\). Let \(\alpha \in (0,1)\) be arbitrary. Find the most powerful test of significance level \(\alpha\).

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
2.3 Uniformly most powerful tests
Suppose we have a composite alternative \(H_1\): \(\left|\Theta_1\right| > 1\). Recall that in this situation the power at different parameters \(\theta \in \Theta_1\) from \(H_1\) can turn out to be different. The power of the test itself is then defined as the infimum of these values. Tests of the same significance level can be compared based on this infimum. The best test is the one with the largest power.
In some cases one can find a test with a given significance level whose power is not merely the largest, but is uniformly over \(\theta \in \Theta_1\) the largest.







Definition 3 If \(S\) and \(R\) are two tests of significance level (size) \(\alpha\), then \(S\) is uniformly more powerful than \(R\) if
\[
  \beta (\theta , S) \geq \beta (\theta , R) \quad \forall \theta \in \Theta _1  
\]
This is equivalent to the condition on the probabilities of type II errors
\[
  1 - \beta (\theta , S) \leq 1 - \beta (\theta , R) \quad \forall \theta \in \Theta _1  
\]
In other words, \(S\) is uniformly more powerful than \(R\) if, at every value of the true parameter from hypothesis \(S\), the probability of a type II error for \(H_1\) is smaller. Put differently: the probability of a type II error of test \(S\) is smaller than the probability of a type II error of test \(R\) uniformly over \(\theta \in \Theta_1\).
A test \(S\) is called a uniformly most powerful test (UMP test) of significance level \(\alpha\) if it is uniformly more powerful than any other test of significance level \(\alpha\).




Note that in the case of a simple alternative, speaking of a UMP test is meaningless.






ExampleExample 5





Let \(\vec{X} = \left(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\right)^T\) be a sample from the uniform distribution on the interval \([0, \theta ], \theta >0\). Find a UMP test for testing the hypothesis \(H_{0}: \theta =\theta_{0}\) against the alternative \(H_{1}: \theta <\theta_{0}\), if one exists.






HintHint





Consider tests of the form \(S_c = \left\{ \vec{x} \in \mathbb {R}^{n} \;  : \;  x_{(n)} \leq c \theta_0\right\}\). That is, we reject \(H_0\) when the sample maximum is less than or equal to \(c\theta_0\).









SolutionSolution





Let us find, among the tests \(\left\{ S_c\right\}\), the test \(S_{c_0}\) of the required significance level \(\alpha\). We have
\[
\begin{align}  \alpha & = \mathbb {P}_{\theta _0}\left(\vec{X} \in S_{c_0}\right) = \mathbb {P}_{\theta _0}\left(X_{(n)} \leq c_0\theta _0\right) = \left(\frac{c_0\theta _0}{\theta _0}\right)^n = \\ & = c_0^n \end{align}
\]
Hence \(c_{0}=\sqrt[n]{\alpha }\). The test:
\[
  S_{c_0} = \left\{ \vec{x} \in \mathbb {R}_+^n: x_{(n)} \leq \sqrt[n]{\alpha } \theta _0\right\}   
\]
Let us prove that \(S_{c_0}\) is uniformly more powerful than all other tests of significance level \(\alpha\). Let \(R\) be an arbitrary test of significance level \(\alpha\).

Let the true parameter satisfy \(\theta \leq c_0 \theta_0\). The power of \(S_{c_0}\) equals 1, i.e. is no less than the power of any other test.
Let the true parameter satisfy \(\theta \in (c_0\theta_0, \theta_0)\). The power of \(S_{c_0}\):
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(\vec{X} \in S_{c_0}\right) = \mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(X_{(n)} \leq c_0 \theta _0\right) = \alpha \left(\frac{\theta _0}{\theta }\right)^n  
\]
The power of an arbitrary test \(R \subset \mathbb {R}_+^n\) of significance level \(\alpha\):
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(\vec{X} \in R\right) & = \int _{[0,\theta ]^n} \frac{1}{\theta ^n} \; \mathbb {1}_{R}(\vec{x}) d\vec{x} =\frac{\theta _{0}^{n}}{\theta ^{n}} \int _{\left[0, \theta \right]^{n}} \frac{1}{\theta _{0}^{n}} \; \mathbb {1}_{R}(\vec{x}) d\vec{x} \leq \\ & \leq \frac{\theta _{0}^{n}}{\theta ^{n}} \int _{\left[0, \theta _0\right]^{n}} \frac{1}{\theta _{0}^{n}} \; \mathbb {1}_{R}(\vec{x}) d\vec{x} = \frac{\theta _{0}^{n}}{\theta ^{n}} \mathbb {P}_{\theta _0}\left(\vec{X} \in R\right) \leq \\ & \leq \alpha \frac{\theta _{0}^{n}}{\theta ^{n}} = \mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(\vec{X} \in S_{c_0}\right) \end{align}
\]

Proved.
The power function of the UMP test \(S_{c_0} = \{x_{(n)} \leq c_0\theta_0\}\), \(c_0 = \alpha^{1/n}\), for testing \(H_0: \theta=\theta_0\) against \(H_1: \theta<\theta_0\) from a sample from \(U[0,\theta]\) (\(\theta_0=1\)): \(\beta(\theta, S_{c_0}) = \min\!\big(1, (c_0\theta_0/\theta)^n\big)\). Move the sliders \(n\) for the two curves and the shared \(\alpha\) — both curves are recomputed. For \(\theta \leq c_0\theta_0\) the test rejects \(H_0\) with certainty (power \(=1\)); at the point \(\theta=\theta_0\) the power equals exactly \(\alpha\), regardless of \(n\); the larger \(n\), the sharper the drop of the curve near \(\theta_0\).

\(\left\{ \vec{x} \in \mathbb {R}_+^n: x_{(n)} \leq \sqrt[n]{\alpha } \theta_0\right\}\)

\(X_1, \dots , X_n\) is a sample from \(U[0,\theta ], \;  \theta > 0\). Construct a UMP test of significance level \(\alpha\) for testing \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\) against \(H_1: \theta \neq \theta_0\).
