title: Conditional Expectation
text:
Conditional expectation is the central construction of modern probability theory and, arguably, its most useful export technology. The question it answers is the question behind any forecast: what is the best estimate of a quantity \(\xi\) when only part of the information is available? Tomorrow’s price forecast from today’s data, the estimated position of an object from noisy measurements (the Kalman filter), an insurer’s reserve based on the current loss history — all of these are conditional expectations. Kolmogorov’s key idea: information is a \(\sigma\)-algebra (a collection of events for which we know whether or not they occurred), and conditional expectation is the projection of a quantity onto the available information. On this construction rests the entire theory of martingales (the stochastic processes course: “a martingale is a game in which the conditional expectation of tomorrow’s capital equals today’s”) and the entire theory of regression (the statistics course).
Plan — from the simple to the general, following Shiryaev [@shiryaev2016probability] (Ch. 2, §7) and Klenke [@klenke2020probability] (Ch. 8): elementary conditional probabilities \(\to\) conditional expectation with respect to a partition \(\to\) the general definition via Radon-Nikodym \(\to\) the complete set of properties \(\to\) the geometry of projection \(\to\) Buffon’s needle as a demonstration of the power of the method.

title: Conditional Expectation
text:
2.1 Versions
Conditional expectation is defined up to a set of probability zero; each specific \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable function with these properties is called a version of the conditional expectation. All equalities involving conditional expectation are equalities a.s., even when we do not write this explicitly.

title: Conditional Expectation
text:
2.2 {Conditional expectation at a point: \(\mathbb {E}\left[ \xi \mid \eta = y \right]\)}
By Doob’s factorization lemma, \(\sigma (\eta )\)-measurability means \(\mathbb {E}\left[ \xi \mid \eta \right] = m(\eta )\) for some Borel function \(m\). The function \(m(y) =: \mathbb {E}\left[ \xi \mid \eta = y \right]\) is defined (Shiryaev, Definition 4) by the requirement \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \, \; \mathbb {1}_{\eta \in B}\right] = \int _B m(y)\,  \mathbb {P}_\eta (dy) \qquad \text{for all } B \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right)
\] — this is again Radon-Nikodym, but now on the line, with respect to the distribution \(\mathbb {P}_\eta\). Knowing \(m\), we recover \(\mathbb {E}\left[ \xi \mid \eta \right] = m(\eta )\), and conversely. We will call the function \(m\) the regression function — in topic 12 it becomes the main character.

title: Conditional Expectation
text:
3.1 Caution: projections do not commute
In property 5 the nesting \(\mathcal{G}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{G}_2\) is essential. For arbitrary \(\sigma\)-algebras, in general \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[ \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right][\mathcal{G}_1] \mid \mathcal{G}_2 \right] \neq \mathbb {E}\left[ \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right][\mathcal{G}_2] \mid \mathcal{G}_1 \right]
\] — successive projection onto two non-nested subspaces depends on the order (a counterexample is in the problems). This is a classic mistake in computations with conditional expectation.

title: Conditional Expectation
text:
6.1 Projections do not commute
Construct an example in which \(\mathbb {E}\left[ \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right][\mathcal{G}_1] \mid \mathcal{G}_2 \right] \neq \mathbb {E}\left[ \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right][\mathcal{G}_2] \mid \mathcal{G}_1 \right]\).

title: The Central Limit Theorem
text: The law of large numbers says that \(\frac{S_n}{n} - a \to 0\); the central limit theorem answers the following question: exactly how does this small error fluctuate. The answer is phenomenal in its universality: on the scale \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\) the error is distributed normally — almost regardless of what the distribution of the terms was. Whether you are flipping a coin, summing rounding errors, or adding up measurement errors — the limit is the same. This is precisely the reason for the ubiquity of the Gaussian curve: human height (a sum of many small factors), noise in a communication channel, instrument errors. Confidence intervals for all opinion polls (“\(\pm 3\%\)”), quality control, and the entire statistics course rest on the CLT. The tool for the proof is already at hand — characteristic functions; the missing link is the continuity theorem.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
section: 2.1 De Moivre-Laplace and the Poisson approximation
text:
2.1 De Moivre-Laplace and the Poisson approximation
For the Bernoulli scheme \(S_n \sim \operatorname {Bin}(n, p)\), the CLT gives the integral de Moivre-Laplace theorem: \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(S_n \leq k\right) \approx \Phi \left(\frac{k + \frac12 - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right)
\] (the term \(\frac12\) is the continuity correction: the midpoint between neighboring integers; it noticeably improves accuracy). But for small \(p\) (rare events: \(np\) moderate, \(n\) huge) the normal approximation is poor — the correct limit is Poisson: \[
  \operatorname {Bin}(n, p_n) \xrightarrow {d} \operatorname {Pois}(\lambda ), \qquad n p_n \to \lambda
\] (Poisson’s theorem; instantaneous via the CF: \(\left(1 + p_n(e^{it}-1)\right)^n \to e^{\lambda (e^{it}-1)}\); a quantitative version is Le Cam’s inequality: total variation distance \(\leq \sum p_k^2\)). Rule of thumb: \(np(1-p) \gtrsim 10\) — normal; \(p\) small, \(np\) moderate — Poisson.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
section: 2.2 The law of the iterated logarithm; optional
text:
2.2 The law of the iterated logarithm; optional
For a complete picture of the fluctuations of \(S_n\) (i.i.d., \(a = 0\), \(\sigma = 1\)): \[
  \limsup _{n \to \infty } \frac{S_n}{\sqrt{2 n \ln \ln n}} = 1 \quad \text{a.s.}, \qquad \liminf _{n \to \infty } \frac{S_n}{\sqrt{2n\ln \ln n}} = -1 \quad \text{a.s.}
\] The trajectory of \(S_n\) infinitely often approaches the boundaries \(\pm \sqrt{2n\ln \ln n}\), but a.s. does not asymptotically exceed them. The LIL lives between the LLN (\(S_n = o(n)\)) and the CLT (typical spread \(\sim \sqrt{n}\)): it describes record, rather than typical, fluctuations. The stochastic processes course will refer to it when studying the Wiener process.

title: Weak Convergence of Probability Measures
text:
WarningDraft



This text is still being edited: it may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished spots. If you find something, please let the author know (contact details on the course page).


The second part of the course is about limit theorems for distributions: the central limit theorem asserts that the distribution of a normalized sum is close to normal. For this to become a theorem rather than a slogan, we need a precise notion of closeness of distributions — weak convergence. This notion also underlies all of asymptotic statistics (confidence intervals are statements about weak limits), numerical schemes (binomial trees in finance converge weakly to continuous models), and the theory of stochastic processes (Donsker’s invariance principle: a random walk converges weakly to the Wiener process). Our program: the correct definition (and why the “naive” one does not work), Alexandrov’s theorem on equivalent descriptions, and the pair “tightness + Prokhorov’s theorem” — the compactness tool used to prove existence-of-limit theorems.

1 Definition and first examples







Definition 1 A sequence of probability measures \(\mathbb {P}_n\) on \((\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\) converges weakly to a measure \(\mathbb {P}\) (written \(\mathbb {P}_n \Rightarrow \mathbb {P}\)) if \[
  \int _{\mathbb {R}} f \,  d\mathbb {P}_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \int _{\mathbb {R}} f \,  d\mathbb {P} \qquad \text{for every bounded continuous } f.
\] Random variables \(\xi_n \xrightarrow {d} \xi\) if \(\mathbb {P}_{\xi_n} \Rightarrow \mathbb {P}_\xi\); equivalently (topic 4): \(F_{\xi_n}(x) \to F_\xi (x)\) at every point of continuity of \(F_\xi\) (convergence in the main sense).




Why the definition via the CDF excludes discontinuity points can be seen in the simplest example.






ExampleExample 1 - Why only points of continuity





Let \(\xi_n = \frac{1}{n}\) (degenerate variables). Show that \(\xi_n \xrightarrow {d} 0\), even though \(F_{\xi_n}(0) \not\to F_0(0)\).






SolutionSolution





Common sense demands that “\(\frac1n\) converges to \(0\)” in any reasonable sense. Let us check Definition 1: for bounded continuous \(f\) we have \(\int f \,  d\mathbb {P}_{\xi_n} = f\left(\frac1n\right) \to f(0)\) — weak convergence holds. But the CDF: \[
  F_{\xi _n}(0) = \mathbb {P}\left(\xi _n \leq 0\right) = 0 \quad \not\to \quad F_0(0) = 1.
\] At the point \(x = 0\) — a discontinuity point of the limiting CDF — there is no pointwise convergence, and there should not be: the mass “creeps up” to zero from the right, and any threshold event \(\left\{ \xi \leq 0\right\}\) sees it as a jump. The definition via continuous \(f\) is insensitive to this boundary effect — that is precisely its point. (And if we had required convergence of the CDF everywhere, then \(\frac1n \to 0\) would fail to hold — such a “definition” is useless.)













Theorem 1 (Alexandrov, portmanteau) The following conditions are equivalent:

\(\mathbb {P}_n \Rightarrow \mathbb {P}\);
\(\limsup_n \mathbb {P}_n(C) \leq \mathbb {P}(C)\) for all closed \(C\);
\(\liminf_n \mathbb {P}_n(G) \geq \mathbb {P}(G)\) for all open \(G\);
\(\mathbb {P}_n(A) \to \mathbb {P}(A)\) for all Borel \(A\) with \(\mathbb {P}(\partial A) = 0\);
\(F_n(x) \to F(x)\) at every point of continuity of \(F\).





The asymmetry between items 2 and 3 is the same “mass creeping” phenomenon: a closed set can suddenly gain mass on its boundary in the limit, while an open one can lose it. Item 4 is the practical one: probabilities of sets converge if the limiting measure does not load the boundary. Proof — Shiryaev [@shiryaev2016probability], Ch. 3, §1.






ProblemProblem 1





Let \(\xi_n = \frac1n\) (as in the example). For which of the sets \(A_1 = (0, \infty )\), \(A_2 = [0, \infty )\), \(A_3 = \left\{ 0\right\}\), \(A_4 = [\frac12, 1]\) does \(\mathbb {P}\left(\xi_n \in A_i\right) \to \mathbb {P}\left(0 \in A_i\right)\) hold? Compare with item 4 of Alexandrov’s theorem.









ProblemProblem 2





Let \(\xi_n\) be uniformly distributed on the grid \(\left\{ \frac1n, \frac2n, \ldots , \frac{n}{n}\right\}\). Prove that \(\xi_n \xrightarrow {d} \operatorname {U}[0,1]\).









ProblemProblem 3





Let \(\xi_n\) have density \(p_n(x) = \left(1 + \cos (2\pi n x)\right) \; \mathbb {1}_{[0,1]}(x)\). Prove that \(\xi_n \xrightarrow {d} \operatorname {U}[0,1]\), even though the densities \(p_n\) do not converge to the density \(\; \mathbb {1}_{[0,1]}\) at any point (except points where \(\cos = 0\)).





2 Tightness and Prokhorov’s theorem
A weak limit may fail to exist for a trivial reason: the mass escapes to infinity. Example: \(\xi_n \sim \operatorname {U}[n, n+1]\) — each CDF is honest, but \(F_{\xi_n}(x) \to 0\) for every \(x\): the “limiting function” is identically zero, not a CDF. The condition that forbids the escape of mass:







Definition 2 A family of measures \(\left\{ \mathbb {P}_\alpha \right\}\) is tight if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is a compact \(K = [-C, C]\) with \(\sup_\alpha \mathbb {P}_\alpha (\mathbb {R} \setminus K) \leq \varepsilon\).











Theorem 2 (Prokhorov) A family of probability measures on \(\mathbb {R}\) (and more generally on a Polish space) is relatively compact in the sense of weak convergence (every sequence has a subsequence converging weakly to a probability measure) if and only if it is tight.




The scheme of “\(\Leftarrow\)” on the line: by Helly’s selection theorem, every sequence of CDFs has a pointwise convergent subsequence (diagonal method over rational points); tightness guarantees that the limiting function collects the full unit mass, i.e. is itself a CDF. Prokhorov’s theorem is the probabilistic analogue of compactness: it turns the proof of convergence into two steps — (i) tightness (no escape of mass) + (ii) uniqueness of the limit point (usually via characteristic functions, topic 8). By this scheme we will prove the CLT, and the stochastic processes course will prove the invariance principle. See Shiryaev, Ch. 3, §2 [@shiryaev2016probability].

ProblemProblem 4





Prove: if \(\sup_n \mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi_n\right|\right] = C < \infty\), then the family of distributions \(\left\{ \mathbb {P}_{\xi_n}\right\}\) is tight. Give an example of a tight family for which all expectations are infinite.









ProblemProblem 5





Let \(\xi_n \xrightarrow {d} \xi\) and \(\eta_n \xrightarrow {d} \eta\). Must \(\xi_n + \eta_n \xrightarrow {d} \xi + \eta\) hold? What if additionally \(\xi_n \;  \perp \! \! \! \perp \;  \eta_n\) for each \(n\) and \(\xi \;  \perp \! \! \! \perp \;  \eta\)?

title: The Borel-Cantelli Lemma and the Zero-One Law
text:
WarningDraft



This text is still being edited: it may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished spots. If you find something, please let the author know (contact details on the course page).


Questions about the long-run behavior of random sequences — “will this happen infinitely many more times?”, “will the failures ever stop?”, “will the series converge?” — have a surprising property: their probabilities are almost never “average”. The answer, as a rule, is either \(0\) or \(1\), and this topic is about two tools that compute which one. The Borel-Cantelli lemma is a working countable criterion (“add up the probabilities and see whether the series converges”); Kolmogorov’s zero-one law is the structural reason why intermediate answers never occur. The practical meaning is direct: “an event of positive probability in independent repetitions will occur a.s., and moreover infinitely often” — this is the mathematics of reliability (any failure with nonzero probability will occur regularly — the only question is how often), of cryptography (a random search will sooner or later hit a collision), and of the folkloric “monkey with a typewriter”.

1 The Borel-Cantelli lemma







Definition 1 For a sequence of events \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\) \[
  \limsup _n A_n := \bigcap _{n=1}^\infty \bigcup _{k \geq n} A_k = \left\{ \text{infinitely many of the } A_n \text{ occurred}\right\}  =: \left\{ A_n \text{ i.o.}\right\}
\] (i.o. — “infinitely often”); dually, \(\liminf_n A_n = \left\{ \text{all } A_n \text{ except finitely many}\right\}\).










NoteInteractive illustration placeholder



The interactive illustration has not been created yet. See the source: /home/nedosh/Documents/online_math_notes/math-notes_FPMI_2/courses/nedosh_courses/courses/04-probability/02_PT/contents/specials/050/01_infinitely_often_fig.tex.









Theorem 1 (Borel-Cantelli)  

If \(\sum_{n} \mathbb {P}\left(A_n\right) < \infty\), then \(\mathbb {P}\left(A_n \text{ i.o.}\right) = 0\).
If the events \(A_n\) are independent and \(\sum_{n} \mathbb {P}\left(A_n\right) = \infty\), then \(\mathbb {P}\left(A_n \text{ i.o.}\right) = 1\).





Both parts take one line each. (1): \(\mathbb {P}\left(\limsup A_n\right) \leq \mathbb {P}\left(\bigcup_{k \geq n} A_k\right) \leq \sum_{k \geq n} \mathbb {P}\left(A_k\right) \to 0\) as the tail of a convergent series. (2): by independence and the inequality \(1 - x \leq e^{-x}\)
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\bigcap _{k=n}^{N} A_k^\complement \right) = \prod _{k=n}^N \left(1 - \mathbb {P}\left(A_k\right)\right) \leq \exp \left(-\sum _{k=n}^N \mathbb {P}\left(A_k\right)\right) \xrightarrow [N \to \infty ]{} 0,
\]
hence \(\mathbb {P}\left(\bigcup_{k \geq n} A_k\right) = 1\) for every \(n\), and the intersection over \(n\) also has probability \(1\).
The first part requires no independence whatsoever — it is pure measure theory, and hence foolproof: the overwhelming majority of a.s. convergence proofs in this course and in the stochastic processes course are built as “bound \(\mathbb {P}\left(\left|\xi_n - \xi \right| > \varepsilon \right)\) by a summable sequence — apply Borel-Cantelli”:







Corollary 1 If \(\sum_n \mathbb {P}\left(\left|\xi_n - \xi \right| > \varepsilon \right) < \infty\) for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), then \(\xi_n \to \xi\) a.s.




In the second part independence is essential: take a single coin toss and \(A_n \equiv A = \left\{ \text{heads}\right\}\) — the series diverges, but \(\mathbb {P}\left(A_n \text{ i.o.}\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(A\right) = \frac12\).






ExampleExample 1 - The monkey with a typewriter





A monkey presses equiprobable keys forever and independently (an alphabet of \(K\) symbols). Prove that with probability \(1\) it will type the complete text of “War and Peace” (a string of length \(L\)), and moreover infinitely many times.






SolutionSolution





Split the stream of keystrokes into disjoint blocks of length \(L\): keystrokes \(1, \ldots , L\), then \(L+1, \ldots , 2L\), and so on. Let \(A_n\) be the event “the \(n\)-th block exactly matches the text of the novel”. The blocks do not overlap, so the events \(A_n\) are independent, and \(\mathbb {P}\left(A_n\right) = K^{-L} > 0\) — monstrously small, but the same for every \(n\), so \(\sum_n \mathbb {P}\left(A_n\right) = \infty\). By the second part of Borel-Cantelli, \(\mathbb {P}\left(A_n \text{ i.o.}\right) = 1\).
The trick of “cutting into independent blocks” is the main device for applications of BC2: on their own, the events “the text starts at position \(t\)” are dependent (they overlap), but block by block independence is honest. The engineering moral, without irony: in a sufficiently long series of trials any event of positive probability is guaranteed to occur — rare failures do not “possibly happen”, they happen for certain, and a system must be designed with this in mind.












ProblemProblem 1





Let \(\xi , \xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) be independent identically distributed variables. Prove:

if \(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi \right|\right] < \infty\), then \(\frac{\xi_n}{n} \to 0\) a.s.;
if \(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi \right|\right] = \infty\), then \(\limsup_n \frac{\left|\xi_n\right|}{n} = \infty\) a.s.










ProblemProblem 2





Let \(\left\{ \xi_{n}\right\}\) be an arbitrary (with no assumptions whatsoever!) sequence of random variables. Prove that there exists a non-random sequence \(a_{n} > 0\) for which \(\frac{\xi_{n}}{a_{n}} \to 0\) almost surely.









ProblemProblem 3





A fair coin is tossed. Prove that for any \(k \in \mathbb {N}\) a run of \(k\) consecutive heads will appear infinitely many times a.s. Moreover, show that runs of length \(\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor\) starting no later than toss \(n\) appear i.o. (i.e. record run lengths grow logarithmically).





2 The zero-one law







Definition 2 Let \(\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) be a sequence of random variables. The tail \(\sigma\)-algebra is \[
  \mathcal{T} = \bigcap _{n=1}^{\infty } \sigma \left(\xi _n, \xi _{n+1}, \ldots \right).
\] Tail events are those that do not depend on any finite collection of the first terms: convergence of the series \(\sum \xi_n\), convergence of \(\frac{S_n}{n}\), finiteness of \(\limsup \xi_n\), “\(A_n\) infinitely often”, and so on.











Theorem 2 (Kolmogorov’s zero-one law) If \(\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) are independent, then every tail event has probability \(0\) or \(1\).




The idea of the proof is elegant: a tail event \(A\) does not depend on \(\sigma (\xi_1, \ldots , \xi_n)\) for every \(n\) (it lies in the “tail” \(\sigma\)-algebra); by the criterion via \(\pi\)-systems (topic 1!) \(A\) does not depend on \(\sigma (\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots )\) either — but \(A\) itself lies in this \(\sigma\)-algebra. An event independent of itself: \(\mathbb {P}\left(A\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(A \cap A\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(A\right)^2\), whence \(\mathbb {P}\left(A\right) \in \left\{ 0, 1\right\}\). \(\blacksquare\)
The law explains the “polarization” of all our questions: a random series of independent terms has no scenario “converges with probability \(\frac13\)”. But it does not tell us which of the two alternatives holds — specific criteria settle that. For series, the answer is given by (optional, statement only):







Theorem 3 (Kolmogorov’s three-series theorem) Let \(\xi_n\) be independent, \(c > 0\), \(\xi_n^c := \xi_n \; \mathbb {1}_{\left|\xi_n\right| \leq c}\). The series \(\sum_n \xi_n\) converges a.s. if and only if all three numerical series converge: \[
  \sum _n \mathbb {P}\left(\left|\xi _n\right| > c\right), \qquad \sum _n \mathbb {E}\left[\xi _n^c\right], \qquad \sum _n \operatorname {Var}\left[\xi _n^c\right].
\]










ProblemProblem 4





Let \(\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) be independent. Which of the following events are tail events: (a) \(\left\{ \sum_n \xi_n \text{ converges}\right\}\); (b) \(\left\{ \limsup_n \frac{S_n}{n} > 1\right\}\), where \(S_n = \xi_1 + \ldots + \xi_n\); (c) \(\left\{ \sum_n \xi_n > 1\right\}\); (d) \(\left\{ \xi_n > 0 \text{ i.o.}\right\}\)? For the tail events, draw a conclusion about their probability.









ProblemProblem 5





(Random signs.) Let \(\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \ldots\) be independent, \(\mathbb {P}\left(\varepsilon_n = \pm 1\right) = \frac12\). Prove that the event \(A = \left\{ \sum_n \frac{\varepsilon_n}{n} \text{ converges}\right\}\) has probability \(0\) or \(1\), and determine which one exactly (you may use the three-series theorem or wait for topic 6).

title: Convolution. Covariance and Inequalities
text:
WarningDraft



This text is still being edited: it may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished spots. If you find something, please let the author know (contact details on the course page).


Three storylines of this topic are united by one question: what can be said about the sum of random variables? Sums are the main characters of applied probability: the total loss of an insurance portfolio, the accumulated measurement error, the total demand for a product, the return of a portfolio of assets. Convolution answers the question “what is the distribution of the sum of independent terms”, covariance answers “what happens to the variance of a sum of dependent terms”, and inequalities (Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz, Jensen, Lyapunov) are the working tools we will use to estimate moments for the rest of the course.

1 Convolution







Theorem 1 (The convolution formula) Let \(\xi \;  \perp \! \! \! \perp \;  \eta\). Then the distribution of the sum \(\xi + \eta\) is the convolution of the distributions:

(discrete case) \(\mathbb {P}\left(\xi + \eta = z\right) = \sum_{x} \mathbb {P}\left(\xi = x\right) \mathbb {P}\left(\eta = z - x\right)\);
(continuous case) if \(\xi\) has density \(p_\xi\), then \(\xi + \eta\) has density
\[
  p_{\xi + \eta }(z) = \int _{\mathbb {R}} p_\xi (x) \,  dF_\eta (z - x) \;  \overset {\text{if } p_\eta \text{ exists}}{=} \;  \int _{\mathbb {R}} p_\xi (x) \,  p_\eta (z-x) \,  dx.
\]





The derivation of the continuous case is a textbook application of the technique from topic 2: complete the sum to a full-dimensional change of variables \(\Psi (x, y) = (x + y, y)\) with Jacobian \(1\), obtain \(p_{(\xi +\eta ,\,  \eta )}(z, y) = p_\xi (z - y) p_\eta (y)\), and integrate out the extra coordinate. Note: it suffices for one term to have a density — convolution “smooths out” (the sum of a continuous variable with anything is continuous).






NoteInteractive illustration placeholder



The interactive illustration has not been created yet. See the source: /home/nedosh/Documents/online_math_notes/math-notes_FPMI_2/courses/nedosh_courses/courses/04-probability/02_PT/contents/specials/030/01_uniform_convolution_fig.tex.


It is convenient to collect convolutions into a table of “stable” families — check every row (some are in the problems below, some become trivial in topic 8 via characteristic functions):







\(\operatorname {Bin}(n, p) * \operatorname {Bin}(m, p)\)
\(\operatorname {Bin}(n + m, p)\)




\(\operatorname {Pois}(\lambda _1) * \operatorname {Pois}(\lambda _2)\)
\(\operatorname {Pois}(\lambda _1 + \lambda _2)\)


\(\Gamma (\alpha _1, \lambda ) * \Gamma (\alpha _2, \lambda )\)
\(\Gamma (\alpha _1 + \alpha _2, \lambda )\)


\(\mathscr {N}\left(a_1, \sigma _1^2\right) * \mathscr {N}\left(a_2, \sigma _2^2\right)\)
\(\mathscr {N}\left(a_1 + a_2, \sigma _1^2 + \sigma _2^2\right)\)


\(\operatorname {Cauchy} * \operatorname {Cauchy}\)
\(\operatorname {Cauchy}\) (with summed parameters)









ProblemProblem 1





Let \(\xi \sim \operatorname {Pois}(\lambda_1)\) and \(\eta \sim \operatorname {Pois}(\lambda_2)\) be independent. Prove that \(\xi + \eta \sim \operatorname {Pois}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)\).









ProblemProblem 2





The variables \(\xi_{1} \sim \operatorname {Bern}(0{.}5)\) and \(\xi_{2} \sim \operatorname {U}[0,1]\) are independent. Find the distribution of \(\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}\).









ProblemProblem 3





Let \(\xi_1, \ldots , \xi_n \sim \operatorname {Exp}(\lambda )\) be independent, \(S_n = \xi_1 + \ldots + \xi_n\).

Prove that \(S_n \sim \Gamma (n, \lambda )\).
(Commuter trains.) Trains arrive at independent \(\operatorname {Exp}(\lambda )\)-intervals. Let \(X_T\) be the number of trains that have passed by time \(T\). Prove that \(X_T \sim \operatorname {Pois}(\lambda T)\).










ProblemProblem 4





Let \(\xi , \eta \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\) be independent. Find the distribution of \(\xi /\eta\).









ProblemProblem 5*





\(X, Y, Z \sim \operatorname {U}[0,1]\) are independent. Find the distribution of \(W=(X Y)^{Z}\).





2 Covariance and correlation







Definition 1 For \(\xi , \eta \in L^2\), the covariance and correlation are: \[
  \operatorname {Cov}\left[ \xi , \eta \right] = \mathbb {E}\left[(\xi - \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right])(\eta - \mathbb {E}\left[\eta \right])\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \eta \right] - \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right]\mathbb {E}\left[\eta \right], \qquad \operatorname {Corr}\left[ \xi , \eta \right] = \frac{\operatorname {Cov}\left[ \xi , \eta \right]}{\sqrt{\operatorname {Var}\left[\xi \right]\operatorname {Var}\left[\eta \right]}}.
\]











Proposition 1 (Properties)  

Covariance is bilinear and symmetric; \(\operatorname {Cov}\left[ \xi , \xi \right] = \operatorname {Var}\left[\xi \right]\).
\(\operatorname {Var}\left[\sum_i \xi_i\right] = \sum_i \operatorname {Var}\left[\xi_i\right] + 2\sum_{i < j} \operatorname {Cov}\left[ \xi_i, \xi_j \right]\); for pairwise uncorrelated terms, variances add.
If \(\xi \;  \perp \! \! \! \perp \;  \eta\), then \(\operatorname {Cov}\left[ \xi , \eta \right] = 0\). The converse is false (problem below).
\(\left|\operatorname {Corr}\left[ \xi , \eta \right]\right| \leq 1\), with equality attained if and only if \(\eta = a\xi + b\) a.s. for some constants \(a \neq 0\), \(b\).
The covariance matrix of a vector \(\xi\), \(\Sigma_{ij} = \operatorname {Cov}\left[ \xi_i, \xi_j \right]\), is symmetric and positive semi-definite: for any \(v \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\)
\[
  v^T \Sigma v = \operatorname {Var}\left[v^T \xi \right] \geq 0.
\]





Item 5 is a microscopic formula with large consequences: the variance of any portfolio \(v^T\xi\) (weights \(v\), assets \(\xi\)) is completely determined by the covariance matrix. Markowitz portfolio theory rests on exactly this: diversification works precisely to the extent that covariances are negative (or small); correlation is the language in which finance talks about risk. The flip side (the 2008 lesson from topic 2): correlation measures only linear dependence, and uncorrelatedness is nowhere near independence.






ProblemProblem 6





Let \(X \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\) and \(Y = X^2\). Prove that \(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated but dependent.









ProblemProblem 7





Prove item 4 of proposition Proposition 1: \(\left|\operatorname {Corr}\left[ \xi , \eta \right]\right| \leq 1\), with equality if and only if \(\eta\) is a linear function of \(\xi\) (a.s.).









ProblemProblem 8





(Limiting diversification.) Let \(\xi_1, \ldots , \xi_n\) be variables with unit variances and pairwise correlations all equal to the same number \(\rho\).

Prove that \(\rho \geq -\frac{1}{n-1}\).
Let \(\rho \geq 0\). Show that the variance of the average \(\frac{1}{n}\sum \xi_i\) tends to \(\rho\), not to zero, as \(n \to \infty\).






3 Inequalities







Theorem 2 (Jensen) Let \(g\) be convex and let \(\xi\), \(g(\xi )\) be integrable. Then \[
  g\left(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right]\right) \leq \mathbb {E}\left[g(\xi )\right].
\] For concave functions the inequality is reversed. If \(g\) is strictly convex, equality is attained only for degenerate \(\xi = \operatorname {const}\) a.s.




The proof is one line via a supporting line: a convex \(g\) at the point \(m = \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right]\) has a line \(\ell (x) = g(m) + k(x - m) \leq g(x)\); take the expectation of both sides.






NoteInteractive illustration placeholder



The interactive illustration has not been created yet. See the source: /home/nedosh/Documents/online_math_notes/math-notes_FPMI_2/courses/nedosh_courses/courses/04-probability/02_PT/contents/specials/030/02_jensen_fig.tex.









Corollary 1 (Lyapunov’s inequality) For \(0 < r < s\) \[
  \left(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi \right|^r\right]\right)^{1/r} \leq \left(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi \right|^s\right]\right)^{1/s}.
\] In particular, finiteness of a higher moment implies finiteness of all lower moments.




Indeed, the function \(x \mapsto x^{s/r}\) is convex on \([0, \infty )\), and by Jensen \(\left(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi \right|^r\right]\right)^{s/r} \leq \mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi \right|^s\right]\). Together with the already-used Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz inequality and the Hölder and Minkowski inequalities from ETMT (\(L^p\)-spaces), this is our complete “estimation arsenal” for the semester.






ProblemProblem 9





Let \(\xi > 0\), with \(\xi\) and \(1/\xi\) integrable. Prove that \(\mathbb {E}\left[\frac{1}{\xi }\right] \geq \frac{1}{\mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right]}\), and determine when equality is attained. Give an interpretation: average speed and average time.









ProblemProblem 10





Let \(\xi\) be a non-degenerate random variable with \(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi^2\right] < \infty\), \(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right] = a > 0\). Compare \(\mathbb {E}\left[\ln \xi \right]\) with \(\ln a\) (assuming \(\xi >0\) and \(\ln \xi\) integrable), and prove that \(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi^4\right] \geq \left(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi^2\right]\right)^2 \geq \left(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right]\right)^4\).

title: The Language of Probability Theory
text: In the ETMT course we built measure theory: we learned to extend measures from semirings to \(\sigma\)-algebras, to construct Lebesgue and Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure, and to integrate measurable functions. Let us now move on to obtaining practical results, translating all of elementary probability theory into the language of measure theory.

title: The Language of Probability Theory
text:
1.1 Three reasons
One might object: probabilities were successfully computed even before Kolmogorov — Pascal, Bernoulli, and Laplace managed without \(\sigma\)-algebras. Why do we need this complicated language? There are three fundamental reasons.
Reason 1: continuous variables. Let \(\xi\) be the coordinate of a random point on the interval \([0,1]\). For any point \(x\) it is reasonable to set \(\mathbb {P}\left(\xi = x\right) = 0\). But then “the probability of landing in a set \(B\)” cannot be assembled from the probabilities of individual points: a sum of zeros gives zero, while \(\mathbb {P}\left(\xi \in [0,1]\right) = 1\). Probability in the continuous world is fundamentally not a sum over points, but a measure of a set. Without measure theory we cannot even say which sets \(B\) are allowed to be assigned a probability at all (recall the non-measurable Vitali set from ETMT: there exist sets that cannot be assigned a probability without destroying the axioms).
Reason 2: infinite sequences of experiments. All the main theorems of this course — the laws of large numbers, the Borel-Cantelli lemma, the central limit theorem — are statements about infinite sequences of random variables. For instance, the strong law of large numbers asserts:
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\frac{\xi _1 + \ldots + \xi _n}{n} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \mathbb {E}\left[\xi _1\right]\right) = 1.
\]
The event under the probability is an event about the entire infinite trajectory \((\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots )\); it cannot be expressed through finitely many experiments. For such events to have a probability, we need a \(\sigma\)-algebra (countable operations on events!) and countable additivity of the measure.
Reason 3: a unified language. In elementary probability theory, the discrete and continuous cases are two separate theories: one uses sums, the other integrals; one uses distribution tables, the other densities; every statement is proved twice. Measure theory glues them into a single theory: everything is a Lebesgue integral, and sums and Riemann integrals are its special cases. Moreover, distributions will appear later that are neither discrete nor continuous, and this is not exotica: insurance, for instance, supplies them routinely (see the example with an insurance payout at the end of this topic) — and elementary theory has no tools for them whatsoever.

title: The Language of Probability Theory
text:
1.2 Dictionary
Kolmogorov’s axiomatics (1933) is, in essence, a translation dictionary: probabilistic notions are defined as notions of measure theory. We will use this dictionary throughout the semester:

Dictionary: measure theory \(\leftrightarrow\) probability theory












Measurable space\((\Omega , \mathcal{F})\)
Outcomes and events


Measure\(\mu\) with\(\mu (\Omega ) = 1\)
Probability\(\mathbb {P}\)


Measurable set\(A \in \mathcal{F}\)
Event


Measurable function\(\xi \colon \Omega \to \mathbb {R}\)
Random variable


Pushforward measure\(\mathbb {P} \circ \xi ^{-1}\)
Distribution\(\mathbb {P}_\xi\)


Lebesgue integral\(\int _\Omega \xi \,  d\mathbb {P}\)
Expectation\(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right]\)


Almost everywhere
Almost surely (a.s.)


Convergence in measure
Convergence in probability


\(L^p(\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mathbb {P})\)
Variables with finite\(p\)-th moment


Radon-Nikodym derivative
Density (likelihood)


Fubini’s theorem
Independence, convolution



The right-hand column is not merely a renaming. As the saying goes, “probability theory is measure theory with a soul”: probabilistic notions have substantive interpretations (frequencies, forecasts, risks), and there are concepts of their own that measure theory does not have — above all independence and conditional constructions. It is precisely these that turn measure theory into a working tool: insurance companies compute reserves as expectations, financial mathematics builds prices of derivative instruments via a change of measure (that very Radon-Nikodym derivative), statistics and machine learning maximize likelihood — a density in the Radon-Nikodym sense. All of this is the dictionary above, applied in earnest.

title: The Language of Probability Theory
text:
4.1 Types of distributions
By the Lebesgue decomposition theorem, every CDF can be represented as a mixture \[
  F = \alpha _1 F_{\text{d}} + \alpha _2 F_{\text{ac}} + \alpha _3 F_{\text{sing}}, \qquad \alpha _i \geq 0, \quad \alpha _1 + \alpha _2 + \alpha _3 = 1,
\] where \(F_{\text{d}}\) is discrete (step-like), \(F_{\text{ac}}\) is absolutely continuous (has a density), and \(F_{\text{sing}}\) is singular (continuous, but increasing on a set of Lebesgue measure zero; the standard example is the Cantor staircase from ETMT). The discrete and absolutely continuous distributions of the elementary course are only the extreme cases.

title: Foundations of Probability and Measure Theory
text:
The course is designed for third-semester students at MIPT and consists of two parts. The first part is a classical introduction to probability theory (probability space, random variables, independence, expectation and variance). The second part is a rigorous construction of Lebesgue measure and the Lebesgue integral, on which all further, “genuine” probability theory rests: sigma-algebras, Carathéodory’s extension theorem, measurable functions and their modes of convergence, the Lebesgue integral and its properties, products of measures, signed measures, and the Radon-Nikodym theorem.
For the full program broken down by session, see the program page.

title: Signed measures, densities
text:
1.1 Introduction
We want to understand what kinds of signed measures exist and how to decompose them into simple pieces. First we decompose into a positive/negative part (Jordan), then, relative to a reference measure, into a singular/absolutely continuous part (Lebesgue), and then for the absolutely continuous part we find a density (Radon-Nikodym).
Let \((X, \mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space.







Definition 1 We call a function \(\nu : \mathcal{F} \to [-\infty , +\infty ]\) a real measure, a signed measure, or a charge if

\(\nu (\varnothing ) = 0\);
\(+\infty \not\in \operatorname {Im}\nu\) or \(-\infty \not\in \operatorname {Im}\nu\). In other words: \(\nu\) cannot take the values \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\) simultaneously. That is, if \(\nu\) takes the value \(+\infty\) on some set, then it does not take the value \(-\infty\) on any other set, and vice versa.
\(\nu\) is countably additive: if \(E_1, E_2, \ldots \in \mathcal{F}\) is a sequence of pairwise disjoint sets from the sigma-algebra, then
\[
  \nu \left(\bigsqcup _{n=1}^{+\infty }E_n\right) = \sum _{n=1}^{+\infty }\nu \left(E_n\right)
\]





Condition 2 is needed so that no indeterminate form \(+\infty + (-\infty )\) arises in additivity.
The meaning of the word “measure” varies across the mathematical literature. As a rule, a “measure” is a countably additive function on a sigma-algebra \(\mu : \mathcal{F} \to [0,+\infty ]\) such that \(\mu (\varnothing ) = 0\) (this is how we defined “measure” at the very beginning). However, some authors use the word “measure” to refer to what we have just introduced under the name “real measure”; in that case they use the expression “positive measure” or “nonnegative measure” for what we defined as a “measure.” To remove this ambiguity, in this chapter we will call a “measure” a “(nonnegative) measure.” A (nonnegative) measure is a special case of a real measure (in our terminology).
As a rule, we will denote a (nonnegative) measure by the letter \(\mu\), and a real measure by the letter \(\nu\).
Some authors use the term “signed measure” instead of “real measure”; some authors do not allow a real measure to take the value \(+\infty , -\infty\).
Let us examine countable additivity of a real measure in more detail.






ExampleExample 1





Let \(E_1, E_2, \ldots \in \mathcal{F}\) be an arbitrary pairwise disjoint collection of sets. Investigate the convergence of the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{+\infty }\nu (E_n)\).
Notice that now the terms of the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{+\infty }\nu (E_n)\) may be negative.






SolutionSolution






Can this series diverge? (Diverge in the sense that it has several limit points, including infinities.) No! Indeed, this series must equal \(\nu (E) \in [-\infty , +\infty ]\), where \(E =\bigsqcup_{n=1}^{+\infty }E_n\). That is, the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{+\infty }\nu (E_n)\) either converges to a finite number or to one of the infinities.
Suppose \(\sum_{n=1}^{+\infty }\nu (E_n)\) converges to a finite number. Can it converge conditionally? Also no! Indeed, if \(p: \mathbb {N} \to \mathbb {N}\) is some permutation of the natural numbers, then \(\bigsqcup_{n=1}^{+\infty }E_n = \bigsqcup_{n=1}^{+\infty }E_{p_n}\). That is, it does not matter in what order we take the union of the sets. By the definition of countable additivity we obtain
\[
  \sum _{n=1}^{+\infty } \nu \left(E_{n}\right)=\nu \left(\bigsqcup _{n=1}^{+\infty }E_n \right) = \nu \left( \bigsqcup _{n=1}^{+\infty }E_{p_n}\right) = \sum _{n=1}^{+\infty } \nu \left(E_{p_n}\right)
\]
It follows that the sum of the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{+\infty } a_n\) (where \(a_n = \nu \left(E_{p_n}\right)\)) does not depend on the permutation of its terms. By the Riemann series theorem, a series of real numbers converges (to a finite number) with its sum independent of the permutation of its terms (such convergence is called unconditional) if and only if it converges absolutely, i.e. the series of its absolute values converges.







Let us state the resulting lemma.







Lemma 1 Let \(\nu\) be a real measure on \((X,\mathcal{F})\), and let \(E_1, E_2, \ldots \in \mathcal{F}\) be a pairwise disjoint collection of sets. Then the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{+\infty } \nu (E_n)\) converges unconditionally (to a finite number or to one of the infinities).
Moreover, if it converges to a finite number, then it converges absolutely.




How can real measures be obtained? Via the Lebesgue integral with respect to some (nonnegative) measure.







Lemma 2 Let \(\mu\) be a (nonnegative) measure on \((X,\mathcal{F})\). Let \(h: X \to \overline{\mathbb {R}}\) be a measurable function. Denote \[
  \nu _h(E) := \int _{E} h \;  d\mu
\] (if the integral exists).

If \(h\) is nonnegative (i.e. \(\operatorname {Im}h \subset [0, +\infty ]\)), then \(\nu_h\) is a (nonnegative) measure;
If at least one of the functions \(h^+\), \(h^-\) is integrable, then \(\nu_h\) is a real measure.





For \(\nu_h\) one also uses the notation \(\nu_h = h \;  d\mu\), to emphasize the role of \(\mu\).
In what cases is \(\nu = \nu_h\) for some function \(h\)? See the Radon-Nikodym theorem below.

title: Signed measures, densities
section: 1.2 The Hahn theorem and the Jordan theorem: decomposing a real measure into positive and negative parts
text:
1.2 The Hahn theorem and the Jordan theorem: decomposing a real measure into positive and negative parts







Theorem 1 (Hahn decomposition, without proof) Let \(\nu\) be a real measure on \((X, \mathcal{F})\). Then there exists a partition of \(X\) into \(X^+, X^- \in \mathcal{F}\) (i.e. \(X = X^+ \sqcup X^-\)) such that

\(\nu (E) \geq 0\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\), \(E \subset X^{+}\)
\(\nu (E) \leq 0\) for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\), \(E \subset X^{-}\)





Real or (nonnegative) measures \(\nu_1\), \(\nu_2\) are called singular if they “live” on disjoint sets, i.e. there exists a partition of \(X\) into \(X_1, X_2 \in \mathcal{F}\) (\(X = X_1 \sqcup X_2\)) such that
\[
  \nu _1 (E) = \nu _1\left(E \cap X_1\right), \quad \nu _2(E) = \nu _{2}\left(E \cap X_2\right) \qquad \text{for all } E\in \mathcal{F}
\]






ExampleExample 2





Show that \(\lambda\) and \(\#_{\mathbb {Z}}\) (counting measure on \(\mathbb {Z}\)) are singular (nonnegative) measures on \((\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\).






SolutionSolution





Let \(X_1 = \mathbb {R} \setminus \left\{ \mathbb {Z}\right\}\), \(X_2 = \mathbb {Z}\).






Note that if in the Hahn theorem we define
\[
  \nu ^+(E) := \nu (E \cap X^+), \qquad \nu ^{-}(E) := -\nu (E \cap X^-),
\]
then \(\nu^+\) and \(\nu^-\) are exactly the singular (nonnegative) measures we wanted. Moreover \(\nu = \nu^+ - \nu^-\). We have essentially proved







Theorem 2 (Jordan decomposition) Every real measure is the difference of two (nonnegative) singular measures, at least one of which is finite. Namely, if \(\nu\) is a real measure on \((X, \mathcal{F})\), then there exist (nonnegative) singular measures \(\nu^+\) and \(\nu^-\) such that \(\nu = \nu^+ - \nu^-\).




\(\nu\) may take the value \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\), but not both. Hence, among the (nonnegative) measures \(\nu^+\), \(\nu^-\) at least one is finite. Moreover, they are both finite (do not take the value \(+\infty\)) if and only if \(\nu\) is finite (\(+\infty , -\infty \not\in \operatorname {Im}\nu\)).
The (nonnegative) measure \(\left|\nu \right| := \nu^+ + \nu^{-}\) is called the total variation measure of \(\nu\).
If \(d\nu = h \;  d\mu\) for some measurable \(h\), then it is not hard to show that
\[
  d\nu ^+ = h^+ \;  d\mu , \qquad d\nu ^- = h^- \;  d\mu , \qquad d\left|\nu \right| = \left|h\right| \;  d\mu
\]
That is,
\[
  \nu ^+(E) = \int _{E} h^{+} \;  d\mu , \qquad \nu ^-(E) = \int _{E} h^{-} \;  d\mu , \qquad \left|\nu \right|(E) = \int _{E} \left|h\right| \;  d\mu
\]
for all \(E \in \mathcal{F}\).






ProblemProblem 1





On the measurable space \((\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\) let

\(d\nu_1 = f \;  d\lambda\), where \(f_1(x) = x^2 - 4\)
\(\nu_2 = \sum_{k=-3}^{3}(-1)^k\cdot k \cdot \delta_{k}\)

Let \(\nu = \nu_1 + \nu_2\).

Find the Jordan decomposition \(\nu = \nu^+ - \nu^-\) of the real measure \(\nu\).
Find the integral \(\int_{[-2,0]} f \;  d\left|\nu \right|\), where \(f(x) = x^2\).










ProblemProblem 2





On the measurable space \((\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\) let

\(d\nu_1 = h_1\;  d\lambda\), where \(h_1(x) = x^2 - 4\)
\(d\nu_2 = h_2 \;  d\lambda\), where \(h_2(x) = (x-2)^2 - 5\)

Let \(\nu = \nu_1 + \nu_2\).

Find the Jordan decomposition \(\nu = \nu^+ - \nu^-\) of the real measure \(\nu\).
Find the integral \(\int_{[-2,0]} f \;  d\left|\nu \right|\), where \(f(x) = x^2\).

title: Signed measures, densities
section: 2.1 The Radon-Nikodym theorem: characterizing measures obtained via the integral of another measure
text:
2.1 The Radon-Nikodym theorem: characterizing measures obtained via the integral of another measure
\(\mu\) will everywhere be a (nonnegative) measure, while \(\nu\) will first be (nonnegative), then a real measure. Both will be \(\sigma\)-finite. Without the sigma-finiteness condition, various pathological counterexamples to the theorem below arise.

2.1.1 The case of a (nonnegative) measure \(\nu\)
Recall that if \((X,\mathcal{F}, \mu )\) is a space with a (nonnegative) measure and \(h: X \to [0,+\infty ]\) is a nonnegative function, then
\[
  \nu _h(E) := \int _E h \;  d\mu
\]
is also a (nonnegative) measure. Moreover, if \(\mu (E) = 0\), then \(\nu_h(E) = 0\). This property is called absolute continuity. Namely, if \(\mu\), \(\nu\) are two (nonnegative) measures, one says that \(\nu\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(\mu\), or \(\nu\) is dominated by \(\mu\), and writes \(\nu \ll \mu\), if \(\nu (E) = 0\) for all sets of \(\mu\)-measure zero.
Let us connect this definition with the more familiar \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) construction.







Lemma 3 (An equivalent condition for absolute continuity of a finite (nonnegative) measure) Let \(\nu\) be a finite (nonnegative) measure, and \(\mu\) an arbitrary (nonnegative) measure. The following conditions are equivalent:

\(\nu \ll \mu\)
For every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that \(\nu (E) < \varepsilon\) for all measurable \(E\) such that \(\mu (E) < \delta\).





It turns out that in the sigma-finite case, absolute continuity is equivalent to the measure being representable via an integral!







Theorem 3 (Radon-Nikodym) Let \(\mu\), \(\nu\) be (nonnegative) \(\sigma\)-finite measures on \((X,\mathcal F)\). The following conditions are equivalent:

\(\nu \ll \mu\);
\(d\nu = h \;  d\mu\) for some nonnegative measurable \(h: X \to [0,+\infty ]\)

Moreover, \(h\) is unique up to agreement \(\mu\)-a.e. That is, if \(g\) is another function such that \(\nu (E) = \int_E g \;  d\mu\), then \(h = g\) \(\mu\)-a.e.










Mn-proofProof







\(\Rightarrow\) (i) is obvious: if \(d\nu = h\, d\mu\) and \(\mu (E)=0\), then \(\nu (E) = \int_E h\, d\mu = 0\).

Let us prove (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii). The idea (due to J. von Neumann) is to apply the Riesz representation theorem for the Hilbert space \(L^2(\mu +\nu )\) (the Riesz representation theorem, the chapter on the Hilbert space \(L^2(\mu )\)); this is exactly the point in the course where the study of Hilbert spaces pays off.
Step 1 (existence, finite measures). Suppose first that \(\mu (X), \nu (X) < \infty\). Then \(\mu +\nu\) is a finite measure, and \(L^2(\mu +\nu )\) is a Hilbert space with inner product \(\left\langle f, g \right\rangle = \int fg \;  d(\mu +\nu )\) (the Riesz-Fischer theorem, the seminar on \(L^p\)-spaces). Define the linear functional
\[
  \varphi (f) := \int f \;  d\nu , \qquad f \in L^2(\mu +\nu ).
\]
It is well defined: since \(\nu \ll \mu\), and hence also \(\nu \ll \mu +\nu\), functions that agree \((\mu +\nu )\)-a.e. also agree \(\nu\)-a.e., so the value \(\varphi (f)\) does not depend on the choice of representative of the equivalence class. It is bounded: applying the Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz inequality (theorem the Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz inequality) to the functions \(\left|f\right|\) and \(\mathbb 1\) (the latter lies in \(L^2(\mu +\nu )\), since the measure \(\mu +\nu\) is finite),
\[
  \left|\varphi (f)\right| \;  \leq \;  \int \left|f\right| \;  d\nu \;  \leq \;  \int \left|f\right| \;  d(\mu +\nu ) \;  \leq \;  \left(\mu (X)+\nu (X)\right)^{1/2} \cdot \left\| f\right\| _{2} \;  < \;  \infty
\]
(the step \(\int \left|f\right| \,  d\nu \leq \int \left|f\right| \,  d(\mu +\nu )\) holds because \(\mu \geq 0\)). Hence \(\varphi\) is a bounded linear functional on \(L^2(\mu +\nu )\). By the Riesz representation theorem there is \(g \in L^2(\mu +\nu )\) such that
\[
  \int f \;  d\nu \;  = \;  \int fg \;  d(\mu +\nu ), \qquad \forall f \in L^2(\mu +\nu ),
\]
that is,
\[
  \int f(1-g) \;  d\nu \;  = \;  \int fg \;  d\mu , \qquad \forall f \in L^2(\mu +\nu ). \tag {$*$}
\]
Substitute into (\(*\)) \(f = \; \mathbb {1}_{g \geq 1}\): on the left \(\int_{\left\{ g\geq 1\right\} }(1-g)\, d\nu \leq 0\) (since \(1-g\leq 0\) on \(\left\{ g\geq 1\right\}\), \(\nu \geq 0\)), on the right \(\int_{\left\{ g\geq 1\right\} } g\, d\mu \geq 0\) (since \(g\geq 1>0\) there, \(\mu \geq 0\)). Both sides are equal and are sandwiched between \(\leq 0\) and \(\geq 0\), so both are zero; from the right-hand side being zero and \(g\geq 1\) on \(\left\{ g\geq 1\right\}\), it follows that \(\mu (\left\{ g\geq 1\right\} )=0\). Similarly, substituting \(f=\; \mathbb {1}_{g<0}\): on the left \(\int_{\left\{ g<0\right\} }(1-g)\, d\nu \geq 0\) (since \(1-g>1>0\) there), on the right \(\int_{\left\{ g<0\right\} }g\, d\mu \leq 0\) (since \(g<0\) there); the same reasoning gives \(\mu (\left\{ g<0\right\} )=0\).
Since \(\nu \ll \mu\), from \(\mu (\left\{ g\geq 1\right\} ) = \mu (\left\{ g<0\right\} ) = 0\) it also follows that \(\nu (\left\{ g\geq 1\right\} ) = \nu (\left\{ g<0\right\} ) = 0\). Redefine \(g\), setting it equal to \(\tfrac 12\) on the set \(\left\{ g\geq 1\right\} \cup \left\{ g<0\right\}\) — this set has zero \((\mu +\nu )\)-measure, so the identity (\(*\)) does not change — and now \(0\leq g < 1\) everywhere on \(X\). Set
\[
  h := \frac{g}{1-g} \;  \geq \;  0
\]
(the denominator is strictly positive everywhere), and let us prove that \(d\nu =h\, d\mu\). Fix \(E\in \mathcal F\) and for \(k\in \mathbb {N}\) set
\[
  f_k(x) := \begin{cases}  \dfrac {\; \mathbb {1}_{E}(x)}{1-g(x)}, &  \text{if } \dfrac {\; \mathbb {1}_{E}(x)}{1-g(x)} \leq k, \\ 0, &  \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
\]
The function \(f_k\) is bounded by \(k\), hence \(f_k \in L^2(\mu +\nu )\) (the measure \(\mu +\nu\) is finite). Substituting \(f_k\) into (\(*\)): \(\int f_k(1-g)\, d\nu = \int f_k g \,  d\mu\). For fixed \(x\) the sequence \(f_k(x)\) is nondecreasing in \(k\) (from \(0\) up to the value \(\tfrac {\; \mathbb {1}_{E}(x)}{1-g(x)}\), at which it stays for all further \(k\)); hence \(f_k(1-g) \uparrow \; \mathbb {1}_{E}\) and \(f_kg \uparrow \; \mathbb {1}_{E} \cdot h\) pointwise and monotonically. By Levi’s monotone convergence theorem, passing to the limit as \(k\to \infty\):
\[
  \nu (E) \;  = \;  \int _E 1 \;  d\nu \;  = \;  \int _E h \;  d\mu .
\]
Since \(E\in \mathcal F\) was arbitrary, \(d\nu = h\, d\mu\). This completes Step 1.
Uniqueness. Let \(h,\widetilde h : X \to [0,+\infty ]\) both be measurable and \(\nu (E) = \int_E h\, d\mu = \int_E \widetilde h\, d\mu\) for all \(E\in \mathcal F\). Since \(\mu\) is \(\sigma\)-finite, there exist \(X_1\subseteq X_2\subseteq \cdots \in \mathcal F\), \(\bigcup_k X_k = X\), \(\mu (X_k)<\infty\). Fix \(k\) and set \(E := \left\{ h>\widetilde h\right\} \cap X_k\); then \(\int_E (h-\widetilde h)\, d\mu = \nu (E)-\nu (E) = 0\), and the integrand is strictly positive on \(E\) with \(\mu (E)\leq \mu (X_k)<\infty\) — a standard fact about the Lebesgue integral gives \(\mu (E)=0\). Similarly \(\mu (\left\{ h<\widetilde h\right\} \cap X_k)=0\). Letting \(k\to \infty\) (continuity of the measure from below): \(\mu (\left\{ h>\widetilde h\right\} ) = \mu (\left\{ h<\widetilde h\right\} ) = 0\), i.e. \(h=\widetilde h\) \(\mu\)-a.e.
Step 2 (existence, \(\sigma\)-finite measures). Now suppose \(\mu ,\nu\) are only \(\sigma\)-finite. Since both are \(\sigma\)-finite, one can choose (by intersecting exhausting sequences for \(\mu\) and for \(\nu\)) a single increasing sequence \(X_1\subseteq X_2\subseteq \cdots \in \mathcal F\) such that \(\bigcup_k X_k = X\) and \(\mu (X_k), \nu (X_k) < \infty\) for each \(k\). Let \(\mathcal F_k := \left\{ E \cap X_k \;  : \;  E \in \mathcal F\right\}\), and let \(\mu_k, \nu_k\) be the restrictions of \(\mu , \nu\) to \((X_k, \mathcal F_k)\); these are finite measures, and \(\nu_k \ll \mu_k\) (immediately from \(\nu \ll \mu\)). By Step 1 there is a nonnegative measurable \(h_k : X_k \to [0,+\infty )\) such that \(\nu_k(E) = \int_E h_k \,  d\mu_k\) for all \(E \in \mathcal F_k\). By the already-established uniqueness, for \(j<k\) the functions \(h_j\) and \(h_k\) both represent \(\nu_j = \nu_k|_{\mathcal F_j}\) with respect to \(\mu_j = \mu_k|_{\mathcal F_j}\), so \(h_j = h_k\) \(\mu\)-a.e. on \(X_j\).
Define \(h: X \to [0,+\infty )\) as follows: \(h(x) := h_k(x)\) for \(x \in X_k\) (this definition is consistent \(\mu\)-a.e. by what was just said; on the remaining set of \(\mu\)-measure \(0\), define \(h\) to be zero). For an arbitrary \(E \in \mathcal F\), by continuity of the measure from below (\(E = \bigcup_k (E\cap X_k)\), the sets increasing) and Levi’s monotone convergence theorem,
\[
  \nu (E) \;  = \;  \lim _{k\to \infty } \nu (E \cap X_k) \;  = \;  \lim _{k\to \infty }\int _{E\cap X_k} h_k \;  d\mu \;  = \;  \lim _{k\to \infty }\int _E h \cdot \; \mathbb {1}_{X_k} \;  d\mu \;  = \;  \int _E h \;  d\mu .
\]
Hence \(d\nu = h\, d\mu\). This completes the proof of existence, and hence of the whole theorem (uniqueness in the general \(\sigma\)-finite case was already established above).










Mn-remarkRemark




2.2 a preview: change of density on path space — the Cameron-Martin and Girsanov theorems
The Radon-Nikodym theorem is proved for an arbitrary measurable space \((X,\mathcal F)\). As \(X\) one may also take the space of continuous functions \(C[0,1]\) with the uniform metric (see the chapter on the Lebesgue spaces \(L^p\), where it was discussed that \(C[0,1]\) is the natural phase space for the paths of random processes) — and then the Radon-Nikodym theorem becomes a substantive tool of the theory of random processes, not just of analysis on \(\mathbb {R}^n\).
Let \(\mathbb {P}\) be the Wiener measure on \(C[0,1]\), i.e. the distribution of the path of standard Brownian motion \((W_t)_{t\in [0,1]}\), \(W_0=0\). Fix a constant \(c\in \mathbb {R}\) and consider the “drifted” Brownian motion \(W_t + ct\); let \(\mathbb {Q}\) be its distribution (also a measure on \(C[0,1]\)). The simplest special case of Girsanov’s theorem is the Cameron-Martin theorem: \(\mathbb {Q} \ll \mathbb {P}\), and moreover
\[
  \frac{d\mathbb {Q}}{d\mathbb {P}}(\omega ) = \exp \left(c\, \omega (1) - \frac{c^2}{2}\right), \qquad \omega \in C[0,1].
\]
In other words, to compute the probability of any event concerning the drifted Brownian motion, it suffices to take the same event for ordinary Brownian motion and multiply the integrand by the explicit, computable density \(\exp (c\, \omega (1)-c^2/2)\), which depends only on the value of the path \(\omega (1)\) at the final time. The formula can plausibly be checked on finite-dimensional distributions: the vector \((W_{t_1},\ldots ,W_{t_n})\) has a multivariate Gaussian density, and by direct computation (shifting the mean in the Gaussian density) the density of the shifted vector relative to the ordinary one indeed turns out to be the exponential of a linear function of the values.
The general Girsanov theorem replaces the constant drift \(ct\) by the drift \(\int_0^t \theta_s\, ds\) for an arbitrary (adapted) random process \(\theta\), and the density formula turns into the exponential martingale \(\exp \left(\int_0^1 \theta_s\, dW_s - \frac12\int_0^1\theta_s^2\, ds\right)\) instead of the simple \(c\, \omega (1)-c^2/2\). To make sense of this integral with respect to Brownian motion (\(dW_s\), rather than \(ds\)) one needs the Itô stochastic integral — the subject of a separate course on random processes. But the principle behind this preview is exactly the one we have already proved: the Radon-Nikodym theorem, applied not to \(\mathbb {R}^n\) but to path space.



Notation: \(h = \frac{d\nu }{d\mu }\). \(h\) is called the Radon-Nikodym derivative.







Lemma 4 (Properties of the Radon-Nikodym derivative) Let \(\mu\) be a (nonnegative) \(\sigma\)-finite measure, and let \(\nu_1\), \(\nu_2\) also be (nonnegative) \(\sigma\)-finite measures. Then

if \(\nu_1 \ll \mu\) and \(\nu_2 \ll \mu\), then
\[
  \frac{d(\nu _1 + \nu _2)}{d\mu } = \frac{d\nu _1}{d\mu } + \frac{d\nu _2}{d\mu } \qquad \mu \text{-a.e.}
\]
if \(\nu_1 \ll \nu_2 \ll \mu\), then
\[
  \frac{d\nu _1}{d\mu } = \frac{d\nu _1}{d\nu _2} \cdot \frac{d\nu _2}{d\mu } \qquad \mu \text{-a.e.}
\]
if \(\nu_1 \ll \nu_2\) and \(\nu_2 \ll \nu_1\), then
\[
  \frac{d\nu _2}{d\nu _1} = \left(\frac{d\nu _1}{d\nu _2}\right)^{-1} \qquad \nu _1\text{-a.e.}
\]











ProblemProblem 3





Consider on \((\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\) the following (nonnegative) measures:

\(\lambda\) (Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb {R}\));
\(\frac{1}{3} \cdot \lambda_{[-1,1]}\) (Lebesgue measure on \([-1,1]\) with a coefficient);
\(f \;  d\lambda\), where \(f(x) = x^{2}I_{[0,1]}(x)\);
\(f \;  d\lambda + 3\delta_{7}\), where \(f(x) = x^{2}I_{[0,1]}(x)\);
\(f \;  d\lambda\), where \(f(x) = e^{-3\left|x\right|}I_{[-1,1]}(x)\);
\(f \;  d\lambda\), where \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x} \cdot I_{(0,1]}(x)\);
\(\#_{\mathbb {N}}\);
\(\#_{\mathbb {Z}}\);
\(\#_{\mathbb {Q}}\);
\(\delta_0\);
\(7\cdot \delta_{-3} + \frac{1}{3}\delta_{2}\); Check that they are sigma-finite. Then go through all possible pairs \(\nu , \mu\) among them and check whether \(\nu \perp \mu\) or \(\nu \ll \mu\) holds. If the latter holds, find \(\frac{d\nu }{d\mu }\).




The same question makes sense not only on \(\mathbb {R}\): any measurable (in particular, continuous) injection \(\varphi : \mathbb {R}^n \to X\) from a finite-dimensional space into an arbitrary measurable space \((X, \mathcal F)\) allows one to transport a measure from \(\mathbb {R}^n\) to \(X\) — in exactly the same way that the distribution of a random variable transports the probability measure from \(\Omega\) to \(\mathbb {R}\). The following problem carries this out for \(X = C[0,1]\) (with the Borel sigma-algebra with respect to the uniform metric, the chapter on the Lebesgue spaces \(L^p\)) — an infinite-dimensional space — but all the computations in it are arranged so as to reduce to the already familiar one- and two-dimensional Lebesgue measure.






ProblemProblem 4





Let \(X = C[0,1]\). Denote by \(\mathbf{0} \in X\) the identically zero function, and for \(n \in \mathbb {N}\) let \(f_n(x) := x^n\) (so that \(f_1(x)=x\)). Let \(\varphi : \mathbb {R} \to X\), \(\varphi (a) :=\) (the constant function \(\equiv a\)), and \(\psi : \mathbb {R}^2 \to X\), \(\psi (a,b) := \left(x \mapsto a + bx\right)\) (both are continuous, and hence measurable, injections). Consider on \((X, \mathcal B)\) the following (nonnegative) measures:

\(\delta_{\mathbf0}\);
\(\mu_1(A) := \lambda \left(\varphi^{-1}(A) \cap [0,1]\right)\) (transport of Lebesgue measure onto the line of constants);
\(\mu_2(A) := \lambda_2\left(\psi^{-1}(A) \cap [0,1]^2\right)\) (transport of two-dimensional Lebesgue measure onto the plane of affine functions);
\(\mu_3(A) := \int_{\psi^{-1}(A) \cap [0,1]^2} (a+b) \;  d\lambda_2(a,b)\) (the same plane, but with density \((a+b)\));
\(\mu_5(A) := \lambda_2\left(\psi^{-1}(A) \cap [0,\tfrac 12]^2\right)\) (the same plane, but with a truncated parameter domain);
\(\mu_4 := \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n}\delta_{f_n}\) (a weighted sum of point masses at monomials);
\(\#\) — counting measure on the countable set \(\left\{ f_n \;  : \;  n \in \mathbb {N}\right\}  \subset X\);
\(\delta_g\), where \(g(x) := \sin \left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)\). Go through all pairs \(\nu , \mu\) from this list and check whether \(\nu \perp \mu\) or \(\nu \ll \mu\) holds; if the latter holds, find \(\frac{d\nu }{d\mu }\) — if possible not in terms of the parameters \((a,b)\), but intrinsically, via the function \(f \in X\) itself (say, via \(f(0)\), \(f(1)\), or the index \(n\), if \(f=f_n\)).

To check that \(\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3, \mu_5\) are indeed well-defined measures on \(\mathcal B\), it suffices to note that countable additivity transfers one-to-one through an injective preimage from \(\lambda\) (resp. \(\lambda_2\)) — this is the same fact you used when checking that the distribution of a random variable is a measure. For comparing measures “along the same \(\psi\)” (the pairs \(\mu_2,\mu_3,\mu_5\)), the comparison reduces to comparing densities/regions on \(\mathbb {R}^2\) — just as in ordinary \(\mathbb {R}^n\). A single point \(\left\{ f\right\}\) always has zero \(\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3,\mu_5\)-measure (the preimage of a point under an injection is a point, which has \(\lambda\)- or \(\lambda_2\)-measure zero) — use this for all pairs involving a point mass. Also note that \(a = f(0)\), \(b = f(1)-f(0)\) for \(f = \psi (a,b) = a+bx\) — this allows any answer using \((a,b)\) to be rewritten in terms of the values of \(f\) at the points \(0\) and \(1\).





2.2.1 The case of a real measure \(\nu\)
Recall that if \((X,\mathcal{F}, \mu )\) is a space with a (nonnegative) measure and \(h: X \to \mathbb {R}\) is a function such that at least one of \(h^+\) and \(h^-\) is integrable, then
\[
  \nu _h(E) := \int _E h \;  d\mu
\]
is a real measure. Moreover, if \(\mu (E) = 0\), then \(\left|\nu_h\right|(E) = \int_E \left|h\right| \;  d\mu = 0\).
If \(\mu\) is a nonnegative measure and \(\nu\) is a real measure, one says that \(\nu\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(\mu\), or \(\nu\) is dominated by \(\mu\), and writes \(\nu \ll \mu\), if \(\left|\nu \right| \ll \mu\) in the sense of the definition above, i.e. if \(\left|\nu \right|(E) = 0\) for all sets of \(\mu\)-measure zero. It is not hard to show that this is equivalent to \(\nu^+ \ll \mu\) and \(\nu^- \ll \mu\).
In summary, briefly
\[
  \nu \ll \mu \quad \stackrel{\text{def}}{\iff } \quad \left|\nu \right| \ll \mu \quad \iff \quad \begin{cases}  \nu ^+ \ll \mu \\ \nu ^- \ll \mu \end{cases}
\]
It turns out that, again in the sigma-finite case, absolute continuity is equivalent to the measure being representable via an integral! Indeed, if \(\nu \ll \mu\), then \(\nu^+ \ll \mu\) and \(\nu^- \ll \mu\), and hence by the Radon-Nikodym theorem for the previous case there are densities \(h^+\), \(h^-\).







Theorem 4 (Radon-Nikodym) Let \(\mu\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite (nonnegative) measure, \(\nu\) a real \(\sigma\)-finite measure, \(\nu \ll \mu\). Then there exists a measurable function \(h: X \to \overline{\mathbb {R}}\) such that \[
  \nu (E) = \int _E h \;  d\mu , \qquad \forall E \in \mathcal{F}
\]

section: 2.3 The Lebesgue theorem: decomposing a measure into an absolutely continuous and a singular part
text:
2.3 The Lebesgue theorem: decomposing a measure into an absolutely continuous and a singular part
\(\mu\) will everywhere be a (nonnegative) measure, while \(\nu\) will first be (nonnegative), then a real measure. Both will be \(\sigma\)-finite.

2.3.1 The case of a (nonnegative) measure \(\nu\)







Theorem 5 (Lebesgue) Let \(\mu\) be a (nonnegative) \(\sigma\)-finite measure on \((X, \mathcal{F})\). Then for any (nonnegative) \(\sigma\)-finite measure \(\nu\) on \((X, \mathcal{F})\) there exist unique (nonnegative) measures \(\nu_{a}\), \(\nu_{s}\) such that \(\nu = \nu_{a} + \nu_{s}\) and \[
  \nu _a \ll \mu , \qquad \nu _s \perp \mu
\]






2.3.2 The case of a real measure \(\nu\)
Now let \(\nu\) be a real \(\sigma\)-finite measure. Let \(\nu = \nu^+ - \nu^-\) be its Jordan decomposition, consisting of \(\sigma\)-finite (nonnegative) measures. Each of \(\nu^+\) and \(\nu^-\) can be decomposed, by the Lebesgue theorem above, into an absolutely continuous and a singular component with respect to \(\mu\):
\[
  \nu ^+ = \nu ^+_a + \nu ^+_{s}, \qquad \nu ^- = \nu ^-_a + \nu ^-_{s}
\]
Let
\[
  \nu _a := \nu ^+_a - \nu ^-_a, \qquad \nu _{s} := \nu ^+_{s} - \nu ^-_{s}
\]
What can be said about the real measures \(\nu_a\), \(\nu_{s}\)?

\(\left|\nu_a\right| = \nu^+_a + \nu^-_a \ll \mu\). That is, the real measure \(\nu_a\) is absolutely continuous with respect to the (nonnegative) measure \(\mu\).
\(\nu^+_{s}\), \(\nu^-_{s}\) are (nonnegative) measures, singular with respect to \(\mu\). That is, there exist \(A_1, B_1, A_2, B_2\in \mathcal{F}\): \(X = A_1 \sqcup B_1 = A_2 \sqcup B_2\), with \(\nu^+_{s}\) “living” on \(A_1\) (in the sense that \(\nu^+_{s}(E) = \nu^+_{s}(E \cap A_1)\) for any \(E \in \mathcal{F}\)), \(\nu^-_{s}\) “living” on \(A_2\), \(\mu\) “living” on \(B_1\) and \(B_2\). Hence \(\mu\) “lives” on \(B_1 \cap B_2\), and \(\nu_{s} = \nu^+_{s} - \nu^-_{s}\) “lives” on \(A_1 \cup A_2\). Moreover
\[
  X = \left(A_1 \cup A_2\right) \sqcup \left(B_1 \cap B_2\right)
\]
In summary, \(\nu_{s}\) and \(\mu\) are singular.








Theorem 6 (Lebesgue) Let \(\mu\) be a (nonnegative) \(\sigma\)-finite measure on \((X, \mathcal{F})\). Then for any real \(\sigma\)-finite measure \(\nu\) on \((X, \mathcal{F})\) there exist unique real measures \(\nu_{a}\), \(\nu_{s}\) such that \(\nu = \nu_{a} + \nu_{s}\) and \[
  \nu _a \ll \mu , \qquad \nu _s \perp \mu
\]










Mn-remarkRemark




Everything we have discussed in this chapter is abstract and applies to arbitrary measurable spaces. The application of this theory to the concrete case \(X=\mathbb {R}\) with Lebesgue measure — the relationship between absolute continuity of measures and absolute continuity of functions, and differentiation of a distribution’s density — is deferred to a separate chapter on differentiation of the Lebesgue integral, since that is also where all the analytic machinery naturally belongs (the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function, the Lebesgue differentiation theorem) needed for an honest proof.

title: Products of measures
text:
1.1 The product of \(\sigma\)-algebras
Let \((X,\mathcal{F}_{X})\), \((Y,\mathcal{F}_{Y})\) be measurable spaces. Then the product of measurable spaces is the set \(X \times Y\) together with the sigma-algebra
\[
  \mathcal{F}_{X} \otimes \mathcal{F}_{Y} := \sigma \left(\left\{ A \times B \;  : \;  A \in \mathcal{F}_{X}, B \in \mathcal{F}_{Y}\right\} \right)
\]
That is, this is the Cartesian product of \(X\) and \(Y\) together with the minimal sigma-algebra on the rectangles \(A \times B\).
Let \(E \subset X \times Y\). Let \(a \in X\). The vertical section (cut) of the set \(E\) at the point \(a\) is the set
\[
  [E]_{a} := \left\{ y \in Y \;  : \;  (a, y) \in E\right\}
\]
The set \([E]^b\), \(b \in Y\), is defined analogously.


                                                
The vertical section \([E]_a\) and the horizontal section \([E]^b\) of the set \(E \subset X \times Y\) — both are measurable.









Lemma 1 (Sections of measurable sets are measurable) If \(E \in \mathcal{F}_{X} \otimes \mathcal{F}_{Y}\), then \([E]_{a} \in \mathcal{F}_{Y}\) for every \(a \in X\), and \([E]^{b} \in \mathcal{F}_{X}\) for every \(b \in X\).




Sections of a function are defined analogously. If \(f: X \times Y \to \mathbb {R}\) is a function and \(a \in X\), then \([f]_{a}: Y \to \mathbb {R}\) is defined by
\[
  [f]_{a}(y) := f(a, y), \quad y \in Y
\]
Similarly for \([f]^b\).







Lemma 2 (Sections of measurable functions are measurable) Let \(f: X \times Y \to \mathbb {R}\) be an \(\mathcal{F}_{X} \otimes \mathcal{F}_{Y}\)-measurable function. Then for every point \(a \in X\) the section \([f]_a\) is an \(\mathcal{F}_Y\)-measurable function.
Similarly for \([f]^b\).










ProblemProblem 1





Suppose \((X, \mathcal{F}_{X})\) and \((Y, \mathcal{F}_{Y})\) are measurable spaces. Prove that every rectangle in \(\mathcal{F}_{X} \otimes \mathcal{F}_{Y}\) can be obtained only as the Cartesian product of elements of \(\mathcal{F}_{X}\) and \(\mathcal{F}_{Y}\). That is, if \(A\) is a nonempty subset of \(X\) and \(B\) is a nonempty subset of \(Y\) such that \(A \times B \in \mathcal{F}_{X} \otimes \mathcal{F}_{Y}\), then necessarily \(A \in \mathcal{F}_{X}\) and \(B \in \mathcal{F}_{Y}\).









ProblemProblem 2





Suppose \((X, \mathcal{F}_{X})\) is a measurable space. Prove that if \(E \in \mathcal{F}_{X} \otimes \mathcal{F}_{X}\), then \[
  \left\{ x \in X:(x, x) \in E\right\}  \in \mathcal{F}_{X} .
\]

title: Products of measures
text:
1.2 The product of measures
The following result will let us introduce the product of \(\sigma\)-finite measures.







Lemma 3 (The measure of a section is a measurable function) Let \((X, \mathcal{F}_{X}, \mu )\), \((Y, \mathcal{F}_{Y}, \nu )\) be two spaces with \(\sigma\)-finite measures. Let \(E \in \mathcal{F}_{X} \otimes \mathcal{F}_{Y}\). Then the function \[
  x \mapsto \nu \left([E]_{x}\right)
\] is \(\mathcal{F}_{X}\)-measurable. Similarly for \(y \mapsto \mu \left([E]^{y}\right)\).




Suppose \((X, \mathcal{F}_{X}, \mu )\) and \((Y, \mathcal{F}_{Y}, \nu )\) are measure spaces, and \(f: X \times Y \rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) is a function. Then
\[
  \int _{X} \int _{Y} \;  f(x, y) d \nu (y) d \mu (x) \quad \text{ means } \quad \int _{X}\left(\int _{Y} f(x, y) d \nu (y)\right) d \mu (x) .
\]
In other words, to compute \(\int_{X} \int_{Y} f(x, y) d \nu (y) d \mu (x)\), first (temporarily) fix \(x \in X\) and compute the integral \(\int_{Y} [f]_x(y) \;  d \nu (y)\) of the section \([f]_x\) (if this integral makes sense). Then compute the integral with respect to \(\mu\) of the function
\[
x \mapsto \int _{Y} [f]_x(y) d \nu (y)
\]
(if this integral makes sense).






ExampleExample 1





Compute \[
  \int _{[0,4]}\int _{[0,4]}f(x,y)\;  d\lambda (x) \;  d\lambda (y), \qquad \int _{[0,4]}\int _{[0,4]}f(x,y)\;  d\lambda (y) \;  d\lambda (x)
\] where \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y\).






SolutionSolution





\([f]_x(y)\) is a continuous function on \([0,4]\) (as a function of \(y\)) for every \(x\). Hence it is Riemann integrable in the proper sense, and the Riemann integral equals the Lebesgue integral, so we may freely pass to the Riemann integral. Similarly for \([f]^y\). In that case we obtain \[
\begin{align}  \int _{[0,4]} \int _{[0,4]}\left(x^2+y\right) d \lambda (y) d \lambda (x) &  =\int _{[0,4]}\left(4 x^2+8\right) d \lambda (x) =\frac{352}{3} \\ \int _{[0,4]} \int _{[0,4]}\left(x^2+y\right) d \lambda (x) d \lambda (y) &  =\int _{[0,4]}\left(\frac{64}{3}+4 y\right) d \lambda (y) =\frac{352}{3} \end{align}
\] The two iterated integrals in this example turned out to be equal to \(\frac{352}{3}\), even though at the intermediate stage of the computation they look different. As we shall see in the next section, this equality of integrals under a change of the order of integration is not a coincidence.









AnswerAnswer





In both cases, \(\frac{352}{3}.\)













Definition 1 (The product of two measures: \(\mu \times \nu\)) Suppose \((X, \mathcal{F}_{X}, \mu )\) and \((Y, \mathcal{F}_{Y}, \nu )\) are spaces with \(\sigma\)-finite measures. For \(E \in \mathcal{F}_{X} \otimes \mathcal{F}_{Y}\) define the value of the measure \((\mu \times \nu )(E)\) as the iterated integral of the indicator: \[
  (\mu \times \nu )(E) := \int _{X} \int _{Y} I_E \;  d \nu \,  d \mu
\]




As we shall prove later (see Tonelli’s theorem), it does not matter in which order we integrate in the definition above.
The definition of \((\mu \times \nu )(E)\) given above makes sense because the inner integral equals \(\nu \left([E]_x\right)\), and above we stated that sections of measurable sets are measurable (i.e. we may “plug” \([E]_x\) into \(\nu\)). Furthermore, the outer integral makes sense because above we showed that \(x \mapsto \nu ([E]_x)\) is a measurable function.







Lemma 4 (The product of two sigma-finite measures is a measure) Suppose \((X, \mathcal{F}_{X}, \mu )\) and \((Y, \mathcal{F}_{Y}, \nu )\) are spaces with \(\sigma\)-finite measures. Then \(\mu \times \nu\) is a measure on \((X \times Y, \mathcal{F}_{X} \otimes \mathcal{F}_{Y})\).




We restrict the definition above to \(\sigma\)-finite measures because the main results we will obtain fail without \(\sigma\)-finiteness (see Example Example 3 in the next section).






ExampleExample 2





Prove that under the conditions above, the measure of a rectangle is the product of the measures of its sides.






SolutionSolution





Suppose \((X, \mathcal{F}_{X}, \mu )\) and \((Y, \mathcal{F}_{Y}, \nu )\) are spaces with a \(\sigma\)-finite measure. If \(A \in \mathcal{F}_{X}\) and \(B \in \mathcal{F}_{Y}\), then \[
  \begin{aligned}  (\mu \times \nu )(A \times B) &  =\int _{X} \underbrace{\left(\int _{Y} I_{A \times B}(x, y) d \nu (y)\right)}_{=\nu ([A \times B]_x) = \nu (B) \cdot I_{A}(x)} d \mu (x) \\ &  =\int _{X} \nu (B) I_A(x) d \mu (x) = \nu (B) \cdot \int _{X} I_A(x) d \mu (x) =\\ &  =\nu (B) \cdot \mu (A) \end{aligned}
\]












ProblemProblem 3





Suppose \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are \(\sigma\)-finite measures. Prove that \(\mu \times \nu\) is \(\sigma\)-finite.

section: 2.1 Equality of multiple and iterated integrals: Tonelli’s and Fubini’s theorems
text:
2.1 Equality of multiple and iterated integrals: Tonelli’s and Fubini’s theorems
The conclusion of Tonelli’s theorem and of Fubini’s theorem is (almost) the same, but the hypotheses differ slightly: in Tonelli’s theorem \(f\) is nonnegative, whereas in Fubini’s theorem \(f\) has arbitrary sign but is integrable.






NoteTonelli’s theorem and Fubini’s theorem



Let

\((X, \mathcal{F}_{X}, \mu)\) and \((Y, \mathcal{F}_{Y}, \nu)\) be spaces with \(\sigma\)-finite measures,
\(f: X\times Y \to \bar{\mathbb{R}}\) be an \(\mathcal{F}_{X} \otimes \mathcal{F}_{Y}\)-measurable function.








Tonelli’s theorem
Fubini’s theorem




Let \(f\) be nonnegative: \(f: X \times Y \to [0,+\infty]\)
\(f\) is integrable: \(\int_{X \times Y} \|f\| \, d(\mu \times \nu) < \infty\)



Then:

The function \(x \mapsto \int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_{X}\)-measurable. Similarly for \(y \mapsto \int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\).
The multiple integral equals the iterated integrals:

\[
\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_Y \left(\int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\right)d\nu(y) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)\right)d\mu(x)
\]

P.S. Fubini’s theorem additionally asserts that for \(\mu\)-almost all \(x \in X\) the section \([f]_x\) is \(\nu\)-integrable. Similarly for \([f]^y\).








ExampleExample 3





Show that Tonelli’s theorem can fail without the hypothesis of \(\sigma\)-finiteness.






SolutionSolution






Let the 1st space be the space \(([0,1], \mathscr {B}\left([0,1]\right), \lambda )\), where \(\lambda\) is Lebesgue measure on \([0,1]\).
Let the 2nd space be the space \(([0,1], \mathscr {B}\left([0,1]\right), \# )\), where \(\#\) is counting measure. This space is not sigma-finite.
We showed earlier in a problem that \(\mathscr {B}\left([0,1]\right) \otimes \mathscr {B}\left([0,1]\right)\) is the Borel sigma-algebra on the square \([0,1]^2\). Hence the diagonal \(D = \left\{ (x,x) \;  : \;  x \in [0,1]\right\}\) lies in the product of these sigma-algebras: the diagonal is a closed set, and hence Borel.
Consider the indicator function of the diagonal \(f = I_{D}: [0,1]^2 \to \overline{\mathbb {R}}\). It is measurable, being the indicator of a measurable set. It is nonnegative. Hence the hypotheses of Tonelli’s theorem are satisfied.
Note that
\[
  I_{D}(x,y) = \begin{cases}  1, &  x = y \\ 0, &  x \neq y \end{cases}
\]
Let us compute the first iterated integral: for fixed \(y\), the function \([f]^y(x)\) equals \(1\) at only one point, namely \(y = x\). Hence it is equal to zero Lebesgue-almost everywhere, and \(\int_{[0,1]} [f]^y(x) \;  d\lambda (x) = 0\) for all \(y \in [0,1]\). Hence,
\[
  \int _{Y} \left(\int _{X} f(x,y) \;  d\lambda (x)\right) \;  d\# (y) = \int _{Y} 0 \;  d\# (y) = 0
\]
Let us compute the second iterated integral: for fixed \(x\), the function \([f]_x(y)\) equals \(0\) everywhere except at the point \(y = x\), where it equals \(1\). The integral with respect to counting measure is simply the sum of the values of the function at all nonzero points. Hence \(\int_{[0,1]} [f]_x(y) \;  d\# (y) = 1\) for all \(x \in [0,1]\), and
\[
  \int _{X} \left(\int _{Y} f(x,y) \;  d\# (y)\right) \;  d\lambda (x) = \int _{X} 1 \;  d\lambda (x) = 1
\]

The two iterated integrals turned out to be different.












ProblemProblem 4






Let \(\lambda\) denote Lebesgue measure on \([0,1]\). Show that

\[
  \int _{[0,1]} \int _{[0,1]} \frac{x^{2}-y^{2}}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}} d \lambda (y) d \lambda (x) = \frac{\pi }{4}
\]
and
\[
  \int _{[0,1]} \int _{[0,1]} \frac{x^{2}-y^{2}}{\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}} d \lambda (x) d \lambda (y) = -\frac{\pi }{4}
\]

Explain why the previous part does not contradict either Tonelli’s theorem or Fubini’s theorem.







HintHint











Enum-item(1)



Fix \(x \in [0,1]\). Polar substitution: \(\theta = \arctan \frac{y}{x}\), \(y = x\tan \theta\), \(dy = \frac{x}{\cos^2 \theta } d\theta\), \(x^2+y^2 = \frac{x^2}{\cos^2 \theta }\). Then
\[
\begin{align}  \int _0^1 \frac{x^2-y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2} dy & = \int _{0}^{\arctan (1/x)}\frac{x^2 - x^2\tan ^2\theta }{\left(\frac{x^2}{\cos ^2\theta }\right)^2} \cdot \frac{x}{\cos ^2 \theta } \;  d\theta = \frac{1}{x} \cdot \int _0^{\arctan (1/x)} \cos ^2\theta - \sin ^2\theta \;  d\theta = \\ & = \int _0^{\arctan (1/x)} \cos 2\theta \;  d\theta = \frac{1}{2x} \sin (2\arctan (1/x)) \end{align}
\]
where \(\sin (2\arctan 1/x) = \frac{2x}{1+x^2}\).








Enum-item(2)



On which part of the square \([0,1]^2\) is the integrand nonnegative? On which part is it negative?
