2.2 The area under a graph
Suppose \(X\) is a set (of arbitrary nature, in general) and \(f: X \to [0, +\infty ]\) is a function. Then the region under the graph of the function \(f\), denoted \(U_f\), is defined as follows:
\[
  U_f=\{ (x, t) \in X \times (0, +\infty ): 0<t<f(x)\}  .
\]
We call \(U_f\) the region under the graph of \(f\) even when \(X\) is not a subset of \(\mathbb {R}\). The term “area” in the next paragraph should remind you of the ordinary notion of area, although what we are actually dealing with is the measure of \(U_f\) in the product space.
The first equality in the result below can be viewed as a reminder of Riemann’s concept of the integral as the area under a graph (though now in a far more general context, with arbitrary \(\sigma\)-finite measures). The second equality in the result below can be viewed as a strengthening of Lebesgue’s concept of computing the area under a graph by integrating in the direction perpendicular to Riemann’s direction.







Lemma 5 (The area under the graph of a function equals the integral) Suppose \((X, \mathcal{F}_{X}, \mu )\) is a space with a \(\sigma\)-finite measure, and \(f: X \to [0, +\infty ]\) is a function measurable with respect to \(\mathcal{F}_{X}\). Then the region under the graph is measurable (\(U_f \in \mathcal{F}_{X} \otimes \mathscr {B}\left([0,+\infty )\right)\)) and \[
  (\mu \times \lambda )\left(U_f\right)=\int _{X} f d \mu = \int _{0}^{+\infty } \mu (f > t) \;  d t
\]




It follows from Markov’s inequality that if \(f\) and \(\mu\) are as in the result above, then
\[
  \mu (\{ x \in X: f(x)>t\} ) \leq \frac{\int _{X} f d \mu }{t}
\]
for all \(t>0\). Thus, if \(\int_{X} f d \mu <\infty\), the result above should be regarded as somewhat stronger than Markov’s inequality (since \(\int_{(0, \infty )} \frac{1}{t} d \lambda (t)=\infty\)).

3.1 Lebesgue measure and the Borel sigma-algebra in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\)
Recall that a set in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) is called open if every point in it belongs together with some open ball around it. The Borel sigma-algebra in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) is the minimal sigma-algebra containing all open sets.







Lemma 6 Let \(m,n\in \mathbb {N}\).

If \(G_1\), \(G_2\) are open subsets of \(\mathbb {R}^{m}\), \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\), then \(G_1 \times G_2\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{m + n}\);
\(\mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{m}\right) \otimes \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{n}\right) = \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{m +n}\right)\);
\(\mathcal{M}(\lambda_m) \otimes \mathcal{M}(\lambda_n) \subsetneq \mathcal{M}(\lambda_{m+n})\);
If \(\lambda_{m}\), \(\lambda_n\) are Lebesgue measures on \((\mathbb {R}^{m}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{m}\right))\) and \((\mathbb {R}^{n}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{n}\right))\), then
\[
  \lambda _{m+n} = \lambda _m \times \lambda _n
\]
where \(\lambda_{m + n}\) is Lebesgue measure on \((\mathbb {R}^{m+n}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{m+n}\right))\).











ProblemProblem 5





Let \(X = Y = \mathbb {R}\). Prove that

\(\mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right) \otimes \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right) = \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{2}\right)\);
\(\mathcal{M}(\lambda ) \otimes \mathcal{M}(\lambda ) \subsetneq \mathcal{M}(\lambda_2)\), where \(\lambda_2\) is Lebesgue measure in \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\), and \(\mathcal{M}(\lambda_2)\) is the sigma-algebra of Lebesgue-measurable subsets of \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\)?










ProblemProblem 6





Show that there exists a set \(E \subseteq \mathbb {R}^{2}\) such that the sections \([E]_{a}\) and \([E]^{a}\) are open subsets of \(\mathbb {R}\) for every \(a \in \mathbb {R}\), but \(E \notin \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{2}\right)\).









ProblemProblem 7





Suppose \(G_{1}\) is a nonempty subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{m}\) and \(G_{2}\) is a nonempty subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\). Prove that \(G_{1} \times G_{2}\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{m} \times \mathbb {R}^{n}\) if and only if \(G_{1}\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{m}\) and \(G_{2}\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\).









ProblemProblem 8





Suppose \(E\) is a subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{m} \times \mathbb {R}^{n}\) and \[
  A = \left\{ x \in \mathbb {R}^{m}:(x, y) \in E \text{ for some } y \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\right\}
\]

Prove that if \(E\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{m} \times \mathbb {R}^{n}\), then \(A\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{m}\).
Prove or give a counterexample: if \(E\) is a closed subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{m} \times \mathbb {R}^{n}\), then \(A\) is a closed subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{m}\).

text:
3.2 The volume of the unit ball in \(\mathbb {R}^n\)







Lemma 7 (The scaling measure) Suppose \(t>0\). If \(E \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{n}\right)\), then \(t E \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{n}\right)\) and \(\lambda_n(t E)=t^n \lambda_n(E)\).




Denote the open unit ball in \(\mathbb {R}^n\) by:
\[
  \mathbf{B}_n := \left\{ \left(x, \ldots , x_n\right) \in \mathbb {R}^n: x^2+\cdots +x_n^2<1\right\}  .
\]
The open unit ball \(\mathbf{B}_n\) is open in \(\mathbb {R}^n\) (you should convince yourself of this) and therefore belongs to the family of Borel sets \(\mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{n}\right)\).







Theorem 1 (The volume of the unit ball in \(\mathbb {R}^n\)) The volume of the \(n\)-dimensional unit ball equals \[
  \lambda _n\left(\mathbf{B}_n\right) = \frac{\pi ^{n / 2}}{\Gamma \left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right)}= \begin{cases}  \dfrac {\pi ^{n / 2}}{(n / 2)!} &  \text{ if } n \text{ is even, } \\ \dfrac {2^{(n+1) / 2} \pi ^{(n-1) / 2}}{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots \cdot n} &  \text{ if } n \text{ is odd. } \end{cases}
\]










ProblemProblem 9





Prove the formula for the volume of the unit ball.






HintHint





Prove that \(\lambda_n\left(\mathbf{B}_n\right) = \frac{2\pi }{n}\lambda_{n-2}\left(\mathbf{B}_{n-2}\right)\) for \(n \geq 3\). Use a change to polar coordinates in the integral.












ProblemProblem 10






Prove that \(\lambda_{n}\left(\mathbf{B}_{n}\right) \to 0\) as \(n \to +\infty\).
Find the value of \(n\) that maximizes \(\lambda_{n}\left(\mathbf{B}_{n}\right)\).

3.3 The curse of dimensionality






ExampleExample 4





er






SolutionSolution





Let \(X_1, \ldots , X_n\), \(Y_1, \ldots , Y_n\), \(\xi_{i} = X_{i} - Y_{i}\). The central moments of \(\xi_i\)
\[
\begin{align}  \mu _1 = 0, \quad \mu _2 = 2\int _0^1x^2(1-x)dx = 2 \left(\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{6} \\ \mu _3 = 0, \quad \mu _4 = 2\int _{0}^1x^4(1-x)dx = 2 \left(\frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{6}\right) = \frac{1}{15} \end{align}
\]
Then
\[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\xi _i^2\right] = \frac{1}{6}, \quad \operatorname {Var}\left[\xi _i^2\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[\xi _i^4\right] - \left(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi _i^2\right]\right)^2 = \frac{1}{15} - \frac{1}{36} = \frac{12 - 5}{180} = \frac{7}{180}
\]
Then
\[
  D^2 = \xi _1^2 + \ldots + \xi _n^2 \approx N\left(na, n\sigma ^2\right)
\]
\(a = \frac{1}{6}\), \(\sigma^2 = \frac{7}{180}\).
We have
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(D \leq t\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(D^2 \leq t^2\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(\frac{D^2 - an}{\sqrt{n}\sigma } \leq \frac{t^2 - an}{\sqrt{n}\sigma }\right) = \Phi \left(\frac{t^2 - an}{\sqrt{n}\sigma }\right)
\]
Density:
\[
  f\left(\frac{t^2 - an}{\sqrt{n}\sigma }\right) \cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{n}\sigma }t
\]
We have
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {E}\left[D\right] \approx \sqrt{na} \\ \operatorname {Var}\left[D\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[D^2\right] - \mathbb {E}\left[D\right]^2 = na - \end{align}
\]

text:
3.4 Equality of mixed partial derivatives







Definition 2 Suppose \(G\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb {R}^2\) and \(f: G \rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) is a function. For \((x, y) \in G\) the partial derivatives \(\left(D_1 f\right)(x, y)\) and \(\left(D_2 f\right)(x, y)\) are defined as follows: \[
  \left(D_1 f\right)(x, y)=\lim _{t \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+t, y)-f(x, y)}{t}
\] and \[
  \left(D_2 f\right)(x, y)=\lim _{t \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x, y+t)-f(x, y)}{t}
\] if these limits exist.




Using the notation for the section of a function (see 5.7), we can write the definitions of \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) as follows:
\[
  \left(D_1 f\right)(x, y)=\left([f]^y\right)^{\prime }(x) \quad \text{ and } \quad \left(D_2 f\right)(x, y)=\left([f]_x\right)^{\prime }(y) .
\]






ExampleExample 5





Examples of partial derivatives of \(x^y\)






SolutionSolution





Let \(G=\left\{ (x, y) \in \mathbb {R}^2: x>0\right\}\) and define \(f: G \rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) by \(f(x, y)=x^y\). Then \[
  \left(D_1 f\right)(x, y)=y x^{y-1} \quad \text{ and } \quad \left(D_2 f\right)(x, y)=x^y \ln x,
\] (check this yourself). Taking partial derivatives of these partial derivatives, we have \[
  \left(D_2\left(D_1 f\right)\right)(x, y)=x^{y-1}+y x^{y-1} \ln x
\] and \[
  \left(D_1\left(D_2 f\right)\right)(x, y)=x^{y-1}+y x^{y-1} \ln x,
\] (check this yourself). We obtain \(D_1\left(D_2 f\right)=D_2\left(D_1 f\right)\) as functions on \(G\).






In the example above, the two mixed partial derivatives turn out to be equal, even though the intermediate results look completely different. The following result shows that the behavior in the example above is typical rather than a coincidence.
Some proofs of the result below do not use Fubini’s theorem. However, Fubini’s theorem leads to an elegant proof below.
The integrals appearing in the proof below make sense because continuous real-valued functions on \(\mathbb {R}^2\) are measurable (since for a continuous function the preimage of every open set is open), and also because continuous real-valued functions on closed bounded subsets of \(\mathbb {R}^2\) are bounded.
Although the continuity hypotheses in the result below can be weakened somewhat, they cannot be dropped entirely, as shown in Exercise 14 of this section.







Theorem 2 (Equality of mixed partial derivatives) Suppose \(G\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb {R}^2\), and \(f: G \rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) is a function such that \(D_1 f\), \(D_2 f, D_1\left(D_2 f\right)\), and \(D_2\left(D_1 f\right)\) exist and are continuous functions on \(G\). Then \[
  D_1\left(D_2 f\right)=D_2\left(D_1 f\right)
\] on \(G\).










Mn-proofProof






Fix \((a, b) \in G\). For \(\delta >0\) let \(S_\delta =[a, a+\delta ] \times [b, b+\delta ]\). If \(S_\delta \subseteq G\), then
\[
  \begin{aligned}  \int _{S_\delta } D_1\left(D_2 f\right) d \lambda _2 &  =\int _b^{b+\delta } \int _a^{a+\delta }\left(D_1\left(D_2 f\right)\right)(x, y) d x d y \\ &  =\int _b^{b+\delta }\left[\left(D_2 f\right)(a+\delta , y)-\left(D_2 f\right)(a, y)\right] d y \\ &  =f(a+\delta , b+\delta )-f(a+\delta , b)-f(a, b+\delta )+f(a, b) \end{aligned}
\]
where the first equality follows from Fubini’s theorem, and the second and third equalities follow from the fundamental theorem of calculus.
An analogous computation of \(\int_{S_\delta } D_2\left(D_1 f\right) d \lambda_2\) gives the same result. Thus,
\[
  \int _{S_\delta }\left[D_1\left(D_2 f\right)-D_2\left(D_1 f\right)\right] d \lambda _2=0
\]
for all \(\delta\) such that \(S_\delta \subseteq G\). If \(\left(D_1\left(D_2 f\right)\right)(a, b)>\left(D_2\left(D_1 f\right)\right)(a, b)\), then by continuity of \(D_1\left(D_2 f\right)\) and \(D_2\left(D_1 f\right)\) the integrand in the equation above is positive on \(S_\delta\) for sufficiently small \(\delta\), contradicting the fact that the integral above equals 0. Similarly, the inequality \(\left(D_1\left(D_2 f\right)\right)(a, b)<\left(D_2\left(D_1 f\right)\right)(a, b)\) also contradicts the equation above for small \(\delta\). We thus conclude that
\[
  \left(D_1\left(D_2 f\right)\right)(a, b)=\left(D_2\left(D_1 f\right)\right)(a, b),
\]
as required.










ProblemProblem 11





Define \(f: \mathbb {R}^{2} \rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) by the formula \[
  f(x, y) = \begin{cases} \frac{x y\left(x^{2}-y^{2}\right)}{x^{2}+y^{2}} &  \text{ if }(x, y) \neq (0,0) \\ 0 &  \text{ if }(x, y) = (0,0)\end{cases}
\]

Prove that \(D_{1}\left(D_{2} f\right)\) and \(D_{2}\left(D_{1} f\right)\) exist everywhere on \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\).
Show that \(\left(D_{1}\left(D_{2} f\right)\right)(0,0) \neq \left(D_{2}\left(D_{1} f\right)\right)(0,0)\).
Explain why the previous part does not contradict the theorem on equality of partial derivatives.










ProblemProblem 12





Let \(\mu_1\), \(\mu_2\) be measures on \((\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\), where \(\mu_1\) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure with density \(f_1(x) = e^{-2x} \cdot I_{[0,+\infty )}(x)\), and \(\mu_2 = \sum_{k=1}^{+\infty }\frac{1}{3^k}\delta_k\). Let \(\mu = \mu_1 \otimes \mu_2\). Find \(\int_{\mathbb {R}^{2}} g \;  d\mu\) for the following functions:

title: Measurable functions and their modes of convergence
text:
WarningDraft



This lecture note is still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished spots. If you find something, please let the author know (contact info on the course page).


\((\Omega , \mathcal{F})\) will denote a space together with a sigma-algebra on it (a measurable space).

1 Definitions







Definition 1 Let \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}), \;  (\Omega^\prime , \mathcal{F}^\prime )\) be two arbitrary measurable spaces. A map \(f: \Omega \to \Omega^\prime\) is called \(\mathcal{F} | \mathcal{F}^\prime\)-measurable (or simply measurable, if it is clear from context which sigma-algebras are meant) if the preimages of all elements of \(\mathcal{F}'\) lie in \(\mathcal{F}\):
\[
  f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{F}, \qquad \forall B \in \mathcal{F}^\prime  
\]
This condition can be rewritten as \(f^{-1}(\mathcal{F}^\prime ) \subseteq \mathcal{F}\). The following notation is also used for \(f^{-1}(B)\): \(\left\{ f \in B\right\}\). A measurable function is also written as:
\[
  f: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\Omega ^\prime , \mathcal{F}^\prime )  
\]











Lemma 1 (Measurability criterion) Suppose the sigma-algebra \(\mathcal{F}'\) on the codomain \(\Omega '\) is generated by some family \(\mathcal{A} \subset 2^{\Omega '}\): \(\mathcal{F}' = \sigma (\mathcal{A})\). Then \(f: \Omega \to \Omega '\) is measurable if and only if the preimages of the sets in \(\mathcal{A}\) lie in \(\mathcal{F}\): \(f^{-1}(\mathcal{A}) \subset \mathcal{F}\).




As a rule, we will be interested in numerical measurable maps, i.e., measurable functions. In this case \((\Omega^\prime , \mathcal{F}^\prime ) = (\overline{\mathbb {R}}, \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right))\). It is convenient to take the extended real line as the codomain right away, since later on we will need, for example, to prove that the supremum of a collection of measurable functions is itself measurable. The open sets in \(\overline{\mathbb {R}} = [-\infty , +\infty ]\) are taken to be sets of the form
\[
  A, \quad A \cup [-\infty , x), \quad A \cup (y, +\infty ], \quad A \cup [-\infty ,x) \cup (y, +\infty ]  
\]
where \(A \subset \mathbb {R}\) is open, \(x, y \in \mathbb {R}\). \(\mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right)\) is the Borel sigma-algebra on \(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\), i.e., the minimal sigma-algebra containing all open subsets of \(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\). It is not hard to prove that
\[
\begin{align}  \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right) = \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right) & \cup \left\{ B \cup \left\{ +\infty \right\} , B \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right)\right\}  \cup \\ & \cup \left\{ B \cup \left\{ -\infty \right\} , B \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right)\right\}  \cup \\ & \cup \left\{ B \cup \left\{ -\infty , +\infty \right\} , B \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right)\right\}  \end{align}
\]
From the measurability criterion and the properties of the Borel sigma-algebra on \(\mathbb {R}\) the following lemma follows.







Lemma 2 (measurability criterion for a function (a numerical map)) Let \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb {R}\), let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a sigma-algebra on \(\Omega\). Let \(D\) be a dense subset of \(\mathbb {R}\). The following conditions are equivalent:

\(f\) is \(\mathcal{F}\mid \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right)\)-measurable;
\(f^{-1}((x, +\infty ]) \in \mathcal{F}, \quad \forall x \in D\)
\(f^{-1}([x, +\infty ]) \in \mathcal{F}, \quad \forall x \in D\)
\(f^{-1}([-\infty , x)) \in \mathcal{F}, \quad \forall x \in D\)
\(f^{-1}([-\infty , x]) \in \mathcal{F}, \quad \forall x \in D\)
\(f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{F} \;  \forall B \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right)\) and \(f^{-1}(\left\{ -\infty \right\} ), f^{-1}(\left\{ +\infty \right\} ) \in \mathcal{F}\).












Definition 2 A measurable function \(f: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\overline{\mathbb {R}}, \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right))\) is called Borel measurable if its domain \((\Omega , \mathcal{F})\) is a Borel subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{k}\) with the Borel sigma-algebra: \(\left(\Omega , \mathcal{F}\right) = \left(B, \mathscr {B}\left(B\right)\right)\), \(B \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{k}\right)\).
A measurable function \(f: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\overline{\mathbb {R}}, \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right))\) is called Lebesgue measurable if its domain is a Lebesgue measurable subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{k}\) with the sigma-algebra of its Lebesgue measurable subsets, i.e., \(\Omega = A \in \mathcal{M}(\lambda_k^*) \subset 2^{\mathbb {R}^{k}}\), \(\mathcal{F} = A \cap \mathcal{M}(\lambda^*_k)\).










ProblemProblem 1





Prove that the function \(f = \; \mathbb {1}_{A}\) is \(\mathcal{F}|\mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right)\)-measurable if and only if \(A \in \mathcal{F}\).









ProblemProblem 2





Let \(B \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{k}\right)\) be an arbitrary Borel subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{k}\). Prove that a continuous function \(f: B \to \overline{\mathbb {R}}\) is Borel measurable.






HintHint





A function is continuous (i.e., continuous at every point of its whole domain) if and only if the preimage of every open subset of the codomain is open in the domain.












ProblemProblem 3





Construct on \([0,1]\) a Lebesgue measurable function that is discontinuous at every point.









ProblemProblem 4





Let \(A_1, \dots , A_n\) be a partition of \(\Omega\) and let \(\mathcal{F} = \sigma (\left\{ A_1, \dots , A_n\right\} )\). Characterize all measurable functions from \((\Omega , \mathcal{F})\) in this case.









ExampleExample 1





Let \(f: [0,1] \to \overline{\mathbb {R}}\) be a function monotone on \([0,1]\). Prove that \(f\) is Borel measurable.






SolutionSolution





Without loss of generality, let \(f\) be increasing. … to be completed












ProblemProblem 5





Prove that \(\mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right) \subsetneq \mathcal{M}(\lambda )\). Namely, construct a Lebesgue measurable set that is not Borel.






HintHint











Enum-item(1)



Give an example of a continuous function \(f: [0,1] \to [0,1]\) and a set \(C \in \mathcal{M}(\lambda^*)\) such that \(C \subset [0,1], \lambda (C) = 0\), but \(\lambda (f(C)) > 0\) (for this, of course, we must require that \(f(C) \in \mathcal{M}(\lambda^*)\)). Namely, let \(f\) be the Cantor staircase (function), and let \(C\) be the Cantor set. Characterize the sets \(f\left(C^{\complement }\right)\) and \(f(C)\).








Enum-item(2)



Consider the function \(g(x) = \frac{f(x) + x}{2}\). Prove that \(g\) satisfies the previous item, but is additionally strictly increasing, i.e., bijective on \([0,1]\).








Enum-item(3)



Prove that the function \(h = g^{-1}\), where \(g\) is obtained in the previous item, is continuous and strictly increasing.








Enum-item(4)



Use Vitali’s construction to prove that there exists a non-Lebesgue-measurable \(B \subset g(C)\).








Enum-item(5)



Let \(A := h(B) = g^{-1}(B)\), where \(B, h, g\) are as in the previous items. Prove that \(A\) is Lebesgue measurable.








Enum-item(6)



Prove that \(A\) from the previous item is not Borel. Hint: a continuous strictly increasing function maps Borel sets to Borel sets.










2 Measurable functions and arithmetic operations






ProblemProblem 6





Let \(f: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\overline{\mathbb {R}}, \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right))\) be a measurable function. Prove that \[
  h(\omega ) = \begin{cases}  \frac{1}{f(\omega )}, &  f(\omega ) \neq 0 \\ c, &  f(\omega ) = 0 \end{cases}  
\] is measurable. Here \(c \in \mathbb {R}\) is an arbitrary constant.









ExampleExample 2





Let \(f,g: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\overline{\mathbb {R}}, \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right))\) be measurable functions. Prove that the event \(\left\{ f > g\right\}\) is measurable, i.e., that \[
\left\{ f > g\right\}  = \left\{ \omega \;  : \;  f(\omega ) > g(\omega )\right\}  \in \mathcal{F}
\]






SolutionSolution







                                                
The set {f>g} as a countable union ⋃_{q∈ℚ}({f>q}∩{g<q}): move the slider q₀ and find a rational q₀ for which the point (f(ω₀),g(ω₀)) falls into the rectangle {f>q₀}∩{g<q₀} (it and the point turn green) — such a q₀ must exist, since the point lies above the diagonal f>g.


Note that
\[
  \left\{ f > g\right\}  = \left\{ \omega \;  : \;  f(\omega ) > g(\omega )\right\}  = \bigcup _{q \in \mathbb {Q}} \bigg[\left\{ \omega \;  : \;  f(\omega ) > q\right\}  \cap \left\{ \omega \;  : \;  q > g(\omega )\right\}  \bigg]  
\]
Indeed, for an arbitrary \(\omega_0 \in \left\{ f > g\right\}\) there is a rational number \(q_0 = q(\omega_0)\) such that \(f(\omega_0) > q_0 > g(\omega_0)\) (since the rational numbers are dense in \(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\)). Hence
\[
  \left\{ f > g\right\}  \subset \bigcup _{q \in \mathbb {Q}} \bigg[\left\{ \omega \;  : \;  f(\omega ) > q\right\}  \cap \left\{ \omega \;  : \;  q > g(\omega )\right\}  \bigg]  
\]
The reverse inclusion
\[
  \left\{ f > g\right\}  \supset \bigcup _{q \in \mathbb {Q}} \bigg[\left\{ \omega \;  : \;  f(\omega ) > q\right\}  \cap \left\{ \omega \;  : \;  q > g(\omega )\right\}  \bigg]  
\]
is obvious.
We have
\[
\begin{align}  \left\{ f > g\right\}  & = \bigcup _{q \in \mathbb {Q}} \bigg[\left\{ \omega \;  : \;  f(\omega ) > q\right\}  \cap \left\{ \omega \;  : \;  q > g(\omega )\right\}  \bigg] = \\ & = \bigcup _{q \in \mathbb {Q}}\bigg[\underbrace{f^{-1}\left((q, +\infty ]\right)}_{\in \mathcal{F}} \cap \underbrace{g^{-1}\left([-\infty ,q)\right)}_{\in \mathcal{F}} \bigg] \in \mathcal{F} \end{align}
\]
We used the measurability of \(f\), \(g\), as well as the closedness of the sigma-algebra under countable intersections.












ProblemProblem 7





Let \(f,g: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\overline{\mathbb {R}}, \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right))\) be measurable functions. Let \[
  h(\omega ) = \begin{cases}  f(\omega ) + g(\omega ), &  f(\omega ) + g(\omega ) \text{ is defined} \\ c, &  \text{ otherwise}\end{cases}  
\] where \(c\in \overline{\mathbb {R}}\) is an arbitrary fixed number. Prove that \(h\) is measurable.
An indeterminacy can arise when \(f(\omega ) = +\infty\), \(g(\omega ) = -\infty\).









ProblemProblem 8





Let \(f,g: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\overline{\mathbb {R}}, \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right))\) be measurable functions. Prove that \(\min (f,g), \max (f,g)\) are measurable functions.



The following problem shows that if \(f\) is measurable, \(g = f\) almost everywhere (i.e., the set of \(\omega\) where they are not equal has measure zero), and the space is complete, then \(g\) is also measurable.






ProblemProblem 9





Let \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mu )\) be a measurable space with a complete measure \(\mu\). Let \(f: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\overline{\mathbb {R}}, \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right))\) be a measurable function, and let \(g: \Omega \to \mathbb {R}\) be a function such that \(\left\{ f\neq g\right\}  = \left\{ \omega \in \Omega : f(\omega ) \neq g(\omega )\right\}  \in \mathcal{F}\) and \(\mu (\left\{ f \neq g\right\} ) = 0\). Prove that \(g\) is an \(\mathcal{F}|\mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right)\)-measurable function.









ProblemProblem 10





Show that the completeness condition on the measure cannot be dropped in the previous problem. That is, give an example of a measure space \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mu )\) and functions \(f,g: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\overline{\mathbb {R}}, \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right))\) such that \(f=g\) a.e., while \(f\) is measurable but \(g\) is not.





3 Sequences of measurable functions







Theorem 1 Let \(f_n: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\overline{\mathbb {R}}, \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right)), n \in \mathbb {N}\) be a sequence of \(\mathcal{F}|\mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right)\)-measurable functions. Then

The functions

\[
  \sup _n f_n, \quad \inf _n f_n, \quad \varliminf _{n \to \infty } f_n, \quad \varlimsup _{n \to \infty } f_n  
\]
are \(\mathcal{F}|\mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right)\)-measurable;

\(\left\{ \exists \lim_{n \to \infty }f_n\right\}  = \left\{ \omega \in \Omega : \lim_{n\to \infty }f_n(\omega ) \text{ exists}\right\}  \in \mathcal{F}\);
Let

\[
  h(\omega ) := \begin{cases}  \lim \limits _{n\to \infty }f_n(\omega ), &  \lim \limits _{n\to \infty }f_n(\omega )\text{ exists} \\ c, &  \text{ otherwise}\end{cases}  
\]
where \(c \in \overline{\mathbb {R}}\) is an arbitrary fixed number. Then the function \(h\) is \(\mathcal{F}|\mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right)\)-measurable.










ExampleExample 3





Prove item 2 of the theorem.






HintHint





Use the Cauchy criterion.









SolutionSolution





We have
\[
\begin{align}  \left\{ \exists \lim \limits _{n \to \infty } f_n\right\}  & = \left\{ \omega \in \Omega : \lim _{n\to \infty }f_n(\omega ) \text{ exists}\right\}  = \\ & = \left\{ \forall k \in \mathbb {N} \;  \exists N \in \mathbb {N}\;  :\;  \forall m,n \geq N \hookrightarrow \left|f_n - f_m\right| < \frac{1}{k}\right\}  = \\ & =\bigcap _{k=1}^{\infty }\left\{ \exists N\;  :\;  \forall m,n \geq N \hookrightarrow \left|f_n - f_m\right| < \frac{1}{k}\right\}  = \\ & = \bigcap _{k=1}^{\infty } \bigcup _{N=1}^{\infty } \bigcap _{m,n = N}^{\infty } \left\{ \left|f_n - f_m\right| < \frac{1}{k}\right\}  = \\ & = \bigcap _{k=1}^{\infty } \bigcup _{N=1}^{\infty } \bigcap _{m,n = N}^{\infty } \left(\left\{ f_{n} - f_{m} < \frac{1}{k}\right\}  \cap \left\{ f_{n} - f_{m} > -\frac{1}{k}\right\} \right) \end{align}
\]
(a universal quantifier turns into an intersection, an existential quantifier turns into a union). Next, the sets
\[
  \left\{ f_{n} - f_{m} < \frac{1}{k}\right\} , \left\{ f_{n} - f_{m} > -\frac{1}{k}\right\}  \in \mathcal{F}  
\]
i.e., they are measurable (see Example 2, where this is proved). \(\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty } \bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty } \bigcap_{m,n = N}^{\infty }\) are countable intersections and unions. Hence,
\[
  \left\{ \exists \lim \limits _{n \to \infty } f_n\right\}  \in \mathcal{F}  
\]
It is important that all unions and intersections range over at most countable collections of events.












ProblemProblem 11





Using the first 2 items, prove item 3 of the theorem.









ProblemProblem 12





Give an example of an uncountable collection \(f_e: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\overline{\mathbb {R}}, \mathscr {B}\left(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\right)), e \in E\) of measurable functions such that the function \(\sup_{e \in E}f_e\) is not measurable.





4 “Almost everywhere”







Definition 3 Let \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mu )\) be a measure space. We say that some property holds for almost all outcomes \(\omega\) (also said to hold \(\mu\)-almost everywhere, abbreviated \(\mu\)-a.e. or simply a.e.), if the measure of the outcomes where the property fails is zero. For example, one can say that almost all numbers in \(\mathbb {R}\) (taking Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb {R}\) unless stated otherwise) are irrational, since the measure of the rational numbers is zero.










ProblemProblem 13





Define a function \(f(x)\) on the interval \([0, 1]\) (with Lebesgue measure) as follows. If \(x=\) \(\overline{0, n_{1} n_{2} n_{3} \cdots }\) is the decimal expansion of \(x\), let \(f(x)=\max_{i} n_{i}\). Prove that \(f(x)\) is measurable and is almost everywhere constant.









ProblemProblem 14





Let \(f : \mathbb {R} \to \overline{\mathbb {R}}\). On the domain we take Lebesgue measure. Consider 2 conditions:

\(f\) is continuous almost everywhere;
there exists a continuous function \(g: \mathbb {R} \to \overline{\mathbb {R}}\) such that \(f=g\) almost everywhere. Give examples showing that neither condition follows from the other.






5 2 new modes of convergence for functions: almost everywhere and in measure
In this section, instead of the extended real line \(\overline{\mathbb {R}}\) the functions will take values in \(\mathbb {R}\), in order to avoid indeterminate forms such as \(+\infty - (+\infty )\).







Definition 4 Let \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mu )\) be a measure space. Let \(f, f_1, f_2, \dots : (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\) be a collection of \(\mathcal{F}|\mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right)\)-measurable functions. We say that \(f_n\) converges to \(f\) almost everywhere with respect to the measure \(\mu\), or \(\mu\)-a.e. (or simply a.e., if it is clear which measure is meant), if \[
  \mu \left(\left\{ \lim f_n \neq f\right\} \right) = \mu \left(\left\{ \omega \in \Omega : \lim _{n \to \infty } f_n(\omega ) \neq f(\omega )\right\} \right) = 0  
\] The notation “\(\lim_{n \to \infty } f_n(\omega ) \neq f(\omega )\)” means that either the limit does not exist, or it exists but is not equal to \(f(\omega )\).




For this definition to be well posed we need the measurability of \(\left\{ \lim f_n \neq f\right\}\), i.e., we need \(\left\{ \omega \in \Omega : \lim_{n \to \infty } f_n(\omega ) \neq f(\omega )\right\}  \in \mathcal{F}\). Note that
\[
\begin{align}  \left\{ \omega \in \Omega : \lim _{n \to \infty } f_n(\omega ) = f(\omega )\right\}  & = \left\{ \omega \in \Omega : \;  \forall m \in \mathbb {N} \,  \exists N \in \mathbb {N} \,  \forall n \geq N \,  \hookrightarrow \,  \left|f(\omega ) - f_{n}(\omega )\right| \leq \frac{1}{m}\right\}  = \\ & = \bigcap _{m=1}^\infty \bigcup _{N=1}^\infty \bigcap _{n=N}^\infty \underbrace{\left\{ \omega : \left|f(\omega ) - f_n(\omega )\right| \leq \frac{1}{m}\right\} }_{\in \mathcal{F}} \in \mathcal{F} \end{align}
\]
Hence,
\[
  \left\{ \lim f_n \neq f\right\}  = \left\{ \lim f_n = f\right\} ^{\complement } \in \mathcal{F}  
\]







Definition 5 Let \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mu )\) be a measure space. Let \(f, f_1, f_2, \dots : (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\) be a collection of \(\mathcal{F}|\mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right)\)-measurable functions. We say that \(f_n\) converges to \(f\) in measure \(\mu\) if \[
  \mu \left(\omega : \left|f_n(\omega ) - f(\omega )\right| > \varepsilon \right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} 0, \quad \forall \varepsilon > 0  
\]




In probability theory, as you may recall, convergence in measure was called convergence in probability. Convergence in probability is a special case of convergence in measure, in which the measure is a probability measure.






ProblemProblem 15





Let \[
  f_n(x) = \frac{nx}{1 + n^2x^2}, \qquad g_n(x) = \frac{n^2x}{n^4 + x^2}  
\] Do the function sequences below converge with respect to Lebesgue measure, or almost everywhere, on the interval \(I\)?

\(f_n, \quad I = (0,1)\)
\(f_n, \quad I = (1,+\infty )\)
\(g_n, \quad I = (0,1)\)
\(g_n, \quad I = (1,+\infty )\)







HintHint





Link to the plot.












ProblemProblem 16






Let \(f_n \to f\) almost everywhere, \(f_n \to g\) almost everywhere. Prove that then \(f=g\) almost everywhere.
Let \(f_n \to f\) in measure, \(f_n \to g\) in measure. Prove that then \(f=g\) almost everywhere.










ProblemProblem 17





Construct a sequence \((f_n)\) of functions on \([0,1]\) such that \(f_n \to 0\) in (Lebesgue) measure, but \(\varlimsup_{n \to \infty } f_n = +\infty\) almost everywhere and \(\varliminf_{n \to \infty } f_n = -\infty\) almost everywhere.









ProblemProblem 18





Let a sequence of nonnegative functions \(\left\{ f_{n}(x)\right\}_{n=1}^{\infty }\) converge in measure to \(f(x)\) on \(A\). Prove that \(f(x) \geqslant 0\) a.e. on \(A\).










Theorem 2 (F. Riesz) If \((f_n)\) converges to \(f\) in measure, then there is a subsequence \((f_{n_k})_{k=1}^\infty\) that converges to \(f\) almost everywhere.











Theorem 3 (H. Lebesgue) If \(\mu \left(\Omega \right) < +\infty\), then convergence a.e. implies convergence in measure.










ProblemProblem 19





Show that, in general, convergence a.e. does not imply convergence in measure when the measure is \(\sigma\)-finite.





6 Egorov’s theorem
A pointwise convergent sequence of functions need not converge uniformly. However, the following result asserts that a pointwise convergent sequence of functions on a measure space of finite total measure converges almost uniformly, in the sense that it converges uniformly except on a set that can be made to have arbitrarily small measure.







Theorem 4 (D. Egorov) Let \(\mu \left(\Omega \right) < +\infty\) and let \(f_n\) converge to \(f\) almost everywhere. Then \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\) there exists \(B_\varepsilon \in \mathcal{F}\) such that \(f_n \to f\) uniformly on \(B_\varepsilon\) and \(\mu \left(B_\varepsilon^\complement \right) < \varepsilon\).










ProblemProblem 20





Show that the condition \(\mu \left(\Omega \right) < +\infty\) cannot be dropped in Egorov’s theorem. Show, for example, that the conclusion of Egorov’s theorem fails for Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb {R}\).





7 Lebesgue measurable functions

The passage from Borel measurable functions to Lebesgue measurable functions is the work of the devil. Don’t even think about it!
— Barry Simon (winner of the American Mathematical Society’s Steele Prize) in his five-volume “A Comprehensive Course in Analysis”

Although there exist Lebesgue measurable sets that are not Borel, you are unlikely to encounter them. Likewise, a Lebesgue measurable function that is not Borel measurable is unlikely to arise in your work. An excellent way to avoid potential confusion is to consider only Borel measurable functions.
The following result asserts that if we adhere to the philosophy that what happens on a set of outer measure \(0\) does not matter much, then we may restrict our attention to Borel measurable functions.







Theorem 5 (every Lebesgue measurable function is almost Borel measurable.) Suppose \(f: \mathbb {R} \rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) is a Lebesgue measurable function. Then there exists a Borel measurable function \(g: \mathbb {R} \rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) such that \[
  \lambda \left(g \neq f\right) = \lambda \left(\left\{ x \in \mathbb {R} \;  : \;  g(x) \neq f(x)\right\} \right) = 0  
\]

title: Outer measure, Carathéodory’s extension theorem
text:
The material of this chapter is abstract: \(X\) is an arbitrary set, and the outer measure and Carathéodory’s extension theorem are formulated and proved for an arbitrary space, with no connection to \(\mathbb {R}\) whatsoever (Lebesgue measure will appear only as a special case of this construction in the next chapter).
Extending premeasures from semirings to the generated sigma-algebras is needed not only when constructing measures on finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces \(\mathbb {R}^{k}\), but also, for example, in the theory of random functions (random processes), where the function spaces are typically infinite-dimensional (\(C[0,1]\), for instance). For this reason we will formulate Carathéodory’s theorem for an arbitrary space. To do this, let us first discuss what an outer measure is in the general case.

title: Outer measure, Carathéodory’s extension theorem
section: 2.1 Carathéodory’s theorem works not only for \(\mathbb {R}^n\)
text:
2.1 Carathéodory’s theorem works not only for \(\mathbb {R}^n\)
So far, everywhere, \(X\) has been a subset of \(\mathbb {R}\) or \(\mathbb {R}^n\). But Theorem Theorem 2 is proved for an arbitrary set \(X\) — and this is not a mere formality: this is exactly how probabilistic models are built for infinite sequences of trials, where \(X\) is not a subset of a Euclidean space at all.

title: Outer measure, Carathéodory’s extension theorem
text:
3.1 The good sets method
The \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem (or the monotone class theorem) is very convenient when one needs to prove that some condition \(P\) holds for all elements of some sigma-algebra \(\mathcal{F}\). Denote by \(\mathcal{S}_P \subset 2^\Omega\) those subsets of \(\Omega\) (not necessarily lying in \(\mathcal{F}\)) for which condition \(P\) holds. These are the so-called good sets. We need to prove that \(\mathcal{F} \subset \mathcal{S}_P\). The proof proceeds in 2 stages. First, we need to find a \(\pi\)-system (or algebra) \(\mathcal{I}\) such that \(\sigma (\mathcal{I}) = \mathcal{F}\), and for which condition \(P\) holds, i.e., \(\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{S}_P\). Next, we need to prove that \(\mathcal{S}_P\) is a \(\lambda\)-system (or, respectively, a monotone class). As a result, by the theorem, we obtain \(\mathcal{F} = \sigma (\mathcal{I}) = \lambda (\mathcal{I}) \subset \mathcal{S}_P\) (respectively, \(\mathcal{F} = \sigma (\mathcal{I}) = M(\mathcal{I}) \subset \mathcal{S}_P\)).







Theorem 6 (For probability measures to coincide, it suffices that they coincide on a generating \(\pi\)-system) Let \(\mathbb {P}_{1}, \mathbb {P}_{2}\) be 2 probability measures on \((\Omega , \mathcal{F})\), where \(\mathcal{F}\) is a sigma-algebra on \(\Omega\). Suppose their values coincide on some \(\pi\)-system \(\mathcal{I}\), i.e., \(\mathbb {P}_{1}|_{\mathcal{I}} \equiv \mathbb {P}_{2}|_{\mathcal{I}}\), and moreover this \(\pi\)-system generates the sigma-algebra: \(\sigma (\mathcal{I}) = \mathcal{F}\). Prove that \(\mathbb {P}_{1} \equiv \mathbb {P}_{2}\), i.e., that they coincide on all of \(\mathcal{F}\).
In other words, for 2 probability measures to coincide (on some sigma-algebra), it suffices that they coincide on some pi-system that generates the sigma-algebra.










ExampleExample 5





Prove theorem Theorem 6.






SolutionSolution






Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be our good sets, i.e., all those sets on which \(\mathbb {P}_{1}, \mathbb {P}_{2}\) coincide:
\[
  \mathcal{S} = \left\{ B \in \mathcal{F} \;  : \;  \mathbb {P}_{1}\left(B\right) = \mathbb {P}_{2}\left(B\right)\right\}   
\]
We know that \(\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{S}\). We want to show that \(\mathcal{F} \subset \mathcal{S}\). Suppose we have managed to prove that \(\mathcal{S}\) is a \(\lambda\)-system. Then, by the \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem, \(\mathcal{F} = \sigma (\mathcal{I}) = \lambda (\mathcal{I}) \subset \mathcal{S}\), and the proof is complete.
It remains to prove that \(\mathcal{S}\) is a \(\lambda\)-system.






Enum-item1.



\(\Omega \in \mathcal{S}\)? We are working with probability measures, so \(1 = \mathbb {P}_{1}\left(\Omega \right) = \mathbb {P}_{2}\left(\Omega \right)\). Hence \(\Omega \in \mathcal{S}\).








Enum-item2.



If \(A, B \in \mathcal{S}, A \subset B\), is \(B \setminus A \in \mathcal{S}\)? We have \(B = A \sqcup (B \setminus A)\). By additivity of measure we get
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{1}\left(A\right) + \mathbb {P}_{1}\left(B \setminus A\right) = \mathbb {P}_{1}\left(B\right) = \mathbb {P}_{2}\left(B\right) = \mathbb {P}_{2}\left(A\right) + \mathbb {P}_{2}\left(B \setminus A\right)  
\]
Since the measures are finite, \(\mathbb {P}_{1}\left(A\right), \mathbb {P}_{2}\left(A\right) < \infty\), so we can cancel them and are left with
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{1}\left(B \setminus A\right) = \mathbb {P}_{2}\left(B \setminus A\right)  
\]








Enum-item3.



Is there closure under increasing countable unions, i.e., if \(A_1, A_2, \dots \in \mathcal{S}\) and \(A_1 \subset A_2 \subset A_3 \subset \dots\), is \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \in \mathcal{S}\)? By continuity from below for measures we get
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{1}\left(\bigcup _{n=1}^\infty A_n\right) = \lim _{n \to \infty }\mathbb {P}_{1}\left(A_n\right) = \lim _{n \to \infty }\mathbb {P}_{2}\left(A_n\right) = \mathbb {P}_{2}\left(\bigcup _{n=1}^\infty A_n\right)  
\]
Hence \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n \in \mathcal{S}\).


Proved.







A more general case: we weaken the requirement on the measures, allowing them to be non-probability measures as well. But we are forced to strengthen the requirements on the \(\pi\)-system.







Theorem 7 (For \(\sigma\)-finite measures to coincide, it suffices that they coincide on a generating \(\pi\)-system that also contains sets covering the whole space, on which the measures are finite) Let \(\mu_{1}, \mu_{2}\) be 2 \(\sigma\)-finite measures on a measurable space \((\Omega , \mathcal{F})\). Suppose their values coincide on some \(\pi\)-system \(\mathcal{I}\), i.e., \(\mu_{1}|_{\mathcal{I}} \equiv \mu_{2}|_{\mathcal{I}}\), and moreover

this \(\pi\)-system generates the sigma-algebra: \(\sigma (\mathcal{I}) = \mathcal{F}\);
there exist \(\Omega_1, \Omega_2, \ldots \in \mathcal{I}\) such that \(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty } \Omega_n = \Omega\) and \(\mu_{1}(\Omega_n) = \mu_2(\Omega_n) < \infty\) for every \(n \in \mathbb {N}\).

Prove that then \(\mu_{1} \equiv \mu_{2}\), i.e., that they coincide on all of \(\mathcal{F}\).










ProblemProblem 6





Prove theorem Theorem 7.









ProblemProblem 7





What happens if we drop condition  from theorem Theorem 7? Namely, let \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}) = (\mathbb {Z}, 2^{\mathbb {Z}})\), and let \[
  \mathcal{I} = \left\{ [-n,n] \cap \mathbb {Z} \;  : \;  n \in \mathbb {N}\right\}   
\]

Prove that \(\mathcal{I}\) is a \(\pi\)-system.
Come up with different probability measures on \((\mathbb {Z}, 2^{\mathbb {Z}})\) that coincide on \(\mathcal{I}\).
What sigma-algebra does \(\mathcal{I}\) generate?










ProblemProblem 8





What happens if we drop condition  from theorem Theorem 7? Namely, let \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}) = (\mathbb {Z}, 2^{\mathbb {Z}})\), and let \[
  \mathcal{I} = \left\{ (-\infty ,n] \cap \mathbb {Z} \;  : \;  n \in \mathbb {Z}\right\}   
\]

Prove that \(\mathcal{I}\) is a \(\pi\)-system.
Prove that \(\mathcal{I}\) generates \(2^{\mathbb {Z}}\): \(\sigma (\mathcal{I}) = 2^{\mathbb {Z}}\).
Come up with different \(\sigma\)-finite measures on \((\mathbb {Z}, 2^{\mathbb {Z}})\) that coincide on \(\mathcal{I}\).

title: Systems of sets. The Borel sigma-algebra
text:
@debt:borel-lebesgue (first half), @debt:measurability (partially) This chapter begins repaying the debts accumulated in the chapters on the probability space–on limit theorems (their complete list is at the end of the chapter on limit theorems). We already defined the abstract notion of a sigma-algebra back in week 1, when we needed it for geometric probability. Here we will complete the full picture around it: simpler and more visual systems of sets — semirings, rings, algebras — from which it is convenient to generate sigma-algebras, and, most importantly, we will finally give a rigorous definition of a specific, canonical sigma-algebra \(\mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{n}\right)\) — the Borel sigma-algebra — which we have been using in geometric models and in the definition of a random variable while knowing only its name. The second half of debt @debt:borel-lebesgue — Lebesgue measure — will be repaid in the chapters on Carathéodory’s theorem–on Lebesgue measure.
Measure theory is concerned with computing lengths, areas, volumes, and so on. All these numerical characteristics — length (of a linear set), area (of a planar set), and volume (of a set in three-dimensional space) — are known as measures, defined on (suitable) subsets of an ambient space, usually denoted \(\Omega\). In the examples above, \(\Omega\) equals the one-, two-, or three-dimensional space \(\mathbb {R}^{1}, \mathbb {R}^{2}, \mathbb {R}^{3}\), respectively.
The advantage of this abstraction is that the notion of measure can be applied to a wide range of situations, from discrete spaces (the familiar high-school models with a finite or countable number of possible outcomes of a random experiment) to finite-dimensional spaces \(\mathbb {R}^n, n \geq 1\), where the famous Lebesgue measure is \(n\)-dimensional volume (in particular, this is length for \(n=1\), area for \(n=2\), ordinary volume for \(n=3\)), and even to infinite-dimensional spaces (such as \(C[0,1]\) or \(C[0, \infty )\), where, for instance, Wiener measure of the corresponding set of functions is the probability that a random trajectory undergoing Brownian motion belongs to that set).
To begin, let us consider the natural choice of the sample space \(\Omega\) when we need to address probabilistic questions concerning simple experiments with various possible outcomes.
More general experiments will lead to various sets of outcomes \(\Omega\). Given an experiment with the set of all outcomes denoted \(\Omega\), one is interested in specific events. For example,
As seen above, each such event is typically a subset of \(\Omega\). In experiments 1, 2, and 3, we were able to enumerate the set of outcomes, so we could take the set of all subsets of \(\Omega\), i.e., the set of all events, equal to the power set \(\mathcal{P}(\Omega )\). However, when the set \(\Omega\) is infinite, as in experiment 4, a problem arises in defining the probability of arbitrary subsets of \(\Omega\). To understand precisely the nature of this problem, consider the following question.
Question: given a set \(A \subset \mathbb {R}^3\), can we measure the volume of \(A\)?
Let us examine the “reasonable requirements” that a procedure for assigning volumes to sets should satisfy. In particular, if \(|S|\) denotes the volume of a set \(S \subseteq \mathbb {R}^3\), then it seems natural to require that the assignment \(S \mapsto |S|\) satisfy the following conditions:
Unfortunately, it is impossible to define \(|S|\) for all subsets \(S\) of \(\mathbb {R}^3\) in such a way that all the conditions (1)–(5) above are satisfied. This problem is caused by the existence of certain very strange “nonmeasurable” sets.
Consequently, whether the motivation comes from computing the probabilities of certain events of an experiment with sample space \(\Omega\), or from computing the lengths of subsets of a space \(\Omega\), one must first come to grips with the notion of events or subsets. This is exactly what we do in the next section.
Why do we need systems of sets?

title: Mathematical Logic and Theory of Algorithms
text:
Contents of the published program
Below is the complete list from the available 2022 program “Mathematical Logic”, lecturer E. V. Dashkov. It contains 24 topics and is published as a historical version, not as a fixed program for the 2025 intake.

The intuitive notion of a set, elements, inclusion, equality, ways of forming sets, the empty set and Russell’s paradox.
Union, intersection, complement and their identities; Kuratowski pairs, Cartesian product, ordered \(n\)-tuples and powers of a set.
Binary relations, inverse and composition, relations on a set, images and preimages.
Functionality, injectivity, surjectivity and totality of relations; partial functions and functions of several arguments.
Injections, surjections, bijections, equinumerosity, comparison of cardinalities, Cantor’s theorem and the Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder theorem, the axiom of choice and indexed families.
Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity; partial and linear orders, bounds, supremum, infimum, lattices, chains and antichains.
Equivalence relations, equivalence classes, quotient sets and partitions.
Finite sets, induction, the pigeonhole principle, cardinality and the recursion theorem.
Cardinality properties of finite and countable sets, the sum and product rules, countable unions.
Words and formal languages, concatenation, prefixes and suffixes, inductive definitions and structural induction.
Well-founded and well-ordered sets, the induction principle, limit elements.
The structure of well-ordered sets, addition and multiplication of them.
Initial segments, isomorphism and comparison of well-ordered sets.
Comparing a well-ordered set with its subset, subtraction and division with remainder.
Chains in a partially ordered set, Zorn’s lemma, Zermelo’s theorem and their relation to the axiom of choice.
Algorithms, computable functions, decidable and computably enumerable sets, Post’s theorem.
The \(T\)-predicate of an algorithm, the graph theorem for computable functions, images and preimages, the semicharacteristic function.
The universal computable function, the self-applicability and halting problems, examples of enumerable and undecidable sets.
The principal universal function, coding of pairs, Kleene’s fixed point theorem, the recursion theorem and mutual recursion.
Index sets, the Rice–Uspensky and Rice–Shapiro theorems, \(m\)-reducibility.
Turing machines and the realization of properties of algorithms in the models of Turing machines and partial recursive functions.
The untyped \(\lambda\)-calculus: terms, combinators, \(\beta\)- and \(\eta\)-reductions, normal form and the Church–Rosser theorem.
Representability of partial functions in the \(\lambda\)-calculus, encoding of logic and natural numbers, composition and primitive recursion.
Fixed-point combinators, recursion and minimization, equivalence of the models of partial recursive functions and the \(\lambda\)-calculus, undecidability of the \(\lambda\)-calculus and Scott’s theorem.

title: Discrete Analysis 1
text:
Contents of the published program
The title “Discrete Analysis 1” is this site’s editorial division; below is the complete list of the main (pass/fail test, or zachet) questions from the FPMI fall 2022 program for 2nd-year Applied Mathematics and Informatics students, Informatics track. The document also contains 16 separate questions “for an excellent grade”; they are listed after the main program.

Graphs with loops and multiple edges, digraphs, the handshaking lemma, paths, cycles and criteria for Eulerian graphs.
De Bruijn sequences and graphs; the binary alphabet, subwords and the “0 is better than 1” rule.
Plane and planar graphs, Euler’s formula, non-planar graphs and the Pontryagin–Kuratowski criterion.
Hamiltonian paths and cycles, Dirac’s sufficient condition.
The chromatic number, the independence number and the clique number, relations between them.
Turán’s theorem, the asymptotics of the maximum number of edges without \(k\)-cliques and its refinement for the distance graph.
Estimates of factorials and binomial coefficients, Stirling’s formula and the asymptotics of the central binomial coefficient.
The asymptotics of \(\ln n!\) and \(\sqrt[n]{n!}\) without Stirling’s formula.
Asymptotic estimates of binomial and multinomial coefficients.
The asymptotics of \(\binom nk\) for \(k^2=o(n)\) and for large \(k\).
Random graphs, Markov’s and Chebyshev’s inequalities, random walk.
Connectivity of a random graph for \(p=c\ln n/n\), the giant component.
Bollobás’s theorems on the chromatic number of a random graph and special regimes of \(p\).
Comparison of bounds on the chromatic number via the clique number and the independence number.
Kneser graphs, bounds on the chromatic and clique numbers, independent sets.
Lovász’s theorem on the chromatic number of the Kneser graph.
Intersecting hypergraphs and the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem.
Subsequent generalizations: the theorems of Frankl, Wilson and Ahlswede–Khachatrian.
The quantity \(m(n,k,t)\), the exact value of \(m(n,3,1)\) and the linear-algebraic bound.
The bound on \(m(n,5,2)\) and its asymptotic sharpness.
The Frankl–Wilson theorem for \(m(n,k,k-p)\) with \(k<2p\).
The chromatic number of space and its relation to distance graphs.


Questions “for an excellent grade” in the 2022 program

The exact formula and asymptotics for the number of unicyclic graphs.
The graph isomorphism problem and an algorithm that works on almost all graphs.
Connectivity of a random graph for \(p=c\ln n/n\), \(c>1\).
Deviations of Lipschitz random variables and Bollobás’s theorem for \(p=n^{-\alpha}\).
Another derivation of Bollobás’s theorem for \(p=n^{-\alpha}\).
Edge deviations and a technical estimate for Bollobás’s theorem for \(p=1/2\).
The full version of Bollobás’s theorem for \(p=1/2\).
Accuracy of the greedy coloring of a random graph and Kučera’s theorem.
Erdős’s theorem on a graph with large girth and large chromatic number.
The Borsuk–Ulam–Lyusternik–Schnirelmann theorem and Lovász’s theorem.
Special cases of the Borsuk–Ulam–Lyusternik–Schnirelmann theorem for closed sets.
The Frankl–Wilson theorem for \(k\geq2p\).
Sharpness of the Frankl–Wilson theorems, the quantity \(h(n,k,t)\), the connection with coding and Rödl’s theorem.
An exponential lower bound on the chromatic number of space.
Borsuk’s problem on the line and in the plane.
An exponential lower bound on the Borsuk number.

title: Discrete Analysis 1
text:
Grading
The fall 2022 program publishes the rules of the pass/fail test (zachet); this is a historical grading scheme, not a guarantee for the 2025 intake. The seminar grade \(S\) ranges from 0 to 10. The zachet grade \(E\) ranges from 2 to 10; if \(E=2\), the final grade is immediately 2, otherwise \(I=0.5S+0.5E\), rounded to the nearest integer, with halves rounded up.
Each exam card contained two theory questions and a problem, 18 points in total, with 100 minutes allowed for the answer. After the first part: up to 7 points gives \(E_1=2\), 8–9 gives 3, 10–11 gives 4, 12–14 gives 5, 15–16 gives 6, 17–18 gives 7. With 15–18 points one could take an additional question “for an excellent grade” and receive \(E_2\) from 0 to 3; then \(E=E_1+E_2\).

title: Computational Complexity 2
text:
Contents
No primary program was found for the title “Computational Complexity 2”. However, the full plan of the related elective course “Computational Complexity: Additional Chapters”, semester VI, version of February 1, 2024, is published. It does not stand in for a separate discipline that does not exist in the curriculum, but it is given here in full as the available material:

Interactive protocols, the classes \(dIP\) and \(IP\), completeness and soundness, the examples of graph isomorphism and quadratic non-residues; the inclusion \(IP\subseteq PSPACE\).
Public coins, Arthur–Merlin games, the classes \(AM\) and \(MA\), pairwise independent hash functions and the Goldwasser–Sipser protocol.
Shamir’s theorem \(IP=PSPACE\): arithmetization, protocols for \(\#SAT\) and \(TQBF\).
Perfect, statistical and computational zero knowledge; the classes \(PZK\), \(SZK\), \(CZK\) and the example of graph isomorphism.
One-way functions, commitment schemes, zero knowledge for 3-coloring, the ideas behind the inclusions \(NP\subseteq CZK\) and \(IP\subseteq CZK\).
Probabilistically checkable proofs, the class \(PCP\), approximation of NP-complete problems, the PCP theorem and Khot’s conjecture.
Multi-prover protocols, the class \(MIP\) and the equality \(MIP=MIP2=PCP(poly,poly)=NEXP\).
Rational interactive proofs, the classes \(FRMA\), \(DRMA\), \(RIP\), the counting hierarchy.
Complexity of total search problems: \(TFNP\), the classes \(PLS\), \(PPP\), \(PPA\), \(PPAD\) and complete problems.

The program also states that materials, assignments, partial solutions, individual homework assignments and a practice version were to be published in a Telegram channel and a shared folder. The grading section of the document says only “to be added”: no numerical grading scheme has been published.

Reading list in the 2024 program
D. V. Musatov, Computational Complexity: Classics and Modern Times (draft); S. Arora, B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach; O. Goldreich, Foundations of Cryptography, Vol. I and Computational Complexity: A Conceptual Perspective; C. Moore, S. Mertens, The Nature of Computation; J. Katz, Notes on Complexity Theory; C. Papadimitriou, Computational Complexity. The online resources named are the Complexity Zoo, Dick Lipton’s blog, Shtetl-Optimized, the Computational Complexity Blog and question-and-answer sites on theoretical computer science.

Semester I: fall 2022 program

Sets, subsets, operations, tuples and the Cartesian product.
Maps, images and preimages, composition, the inverse map and Cartesian powers of a set.
Equinumerosity, the Cantor–Bernstein theorem, countable and uncountable sets, Cantor’s theorem.
Binary relations, equivalence, partial and linear orders, extremal elements.
Operations, properties and isomorphisms of ordered sets.
Preorders, total preorders, quasi-transitivity, acyclicity and lattices.
The sum and product rules, the pigeonhole principle, two-colorings and the problem of pairwise non-orthogonal \((-1,0,1)\)-vectors.
Arrangements, permutations, combinations with and without repetition; the binomial and multinomial formulas, identities and sums of powers.
The inclusion–exclusion formula and alternating identities.
Prime numbers, the infinitude of primes and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.
Divisor sums and the Möbius function.
The Möbius inversion formula.
Counting cyclic sequences via Möbius inversion.
General Möbius inversion for partially ordered sets.
Linear recurrence relations with constant coefficients.
Integer partitions, Young diagrams, Euler’s theorems, the Hardy–Ramanujan formula.
Formal power series and generating functions; Fibonacci and Catalan numbers and taking roots of series.
The theory of congruences and residue systems.
Binomial coefficients modulo a number.
The Chevalley theorem.
The Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv problem.



Semester II: spring 2023 program

The Euclidean algorithm, the fundamental theorem of arithmetic and Euclid’s lemma.
Congruences, residue systems, Euler’s and Fermat’s theorems.
Linear congruences, the Chinese remainder theorem and Euler’s totient function.
The number of roots of a polynomial modulo a prime and Wilson’s theorem.
Quadratic congruences, quadratic residues and non-residues.
The Legendre symbol and the law of quadratic reciprocity.
Hadamard matrices, their constructions and the Hadamard conjecture.
Binary codes, Hamming distance, the Hamming and Plotkin bounds, codes from Hadamard matrices.
Coloring problems in terms of discrepancy and Hadamard matrices.
Distribution of primes: the functions \(\pi(x)\), \(\theta(x)\), \(\psi(x)\) and Chebyshev’s theorem.
The asymptotic law of distribution of primes and gaps between consecutive primes.
Primitive roots, indices and algorithmic problems of the discrete logarithm.
Dirichlet’s theorem on Diophantine approximation and Minkowski’s theorem.
Finite continued fractions and convergents.
Infinite continued fractions, quality of approximation and periodicity for quadratic irrationals.
Algebraic and transcendental numbers, Liouville’s theorem and Gelfond’s theorem.
Irrationality and transcendence of \(e\).
Lattices, the determinant, the multidimensional Minkowski theorem and the Minkowski–Hlawka theorem.
Sequences uniformly distributed modulo 1.
Trigonometric sums, Weyl’s criterion, Gauss sums.
The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena primality test and its polynomiality.

title: Shortest common superstring
text:
Let \(\Sigma\) be an arbitrary set, which we call an alphabet. Denote by \(\Sigma^{*}\) the set of all finite tuples of elements of the alphabet \(\Sigma\). We call them strings or words. Denote by \(\Sigma^{+}\) the set of all strings over the alphabet \(\Sigma\) that does not contain the empty word \(\varepsilon\).
If some string \(s\) in \(U\) is a substring of another string \(t\), then instead of \(U\) we can solve the problem for \(U' = U \setminus \left\{ s\right\}\). Clearly the optimal solution is the same for both problems. Hence, without loss of generality, we will henceforth assume that every string in \(U\) is “unique,” i.e., no string \(t\) contains another string \(s\) as a substring.
The shortest common superstring problem is \(NP\)-hard. We consider several approximation algorithms.

title: Shortest common superstring
section: 2.1 Reduction to the set cover problem
text:
2.1 Reduction to the set cover problem

2.1.1 Constructing the instance
Using the original set of strings \(U\) from the shortest common superstring problem, we construct a corresponding instance of the set cover problem, which we denote \(\mathcal{S}\). For each pair of strings \(s_{i}, s_{j} \in U\) and for some \(k \geq 1\), if the last \(k\) characters of the string \(s_{i}\) coincide with the first \(k\) characters of the string \(s_{j}\), we can construct a new string \(\sigma_{ijk}\) as the overlap-merge of \(s_{i}\) and \(s_{j}\) at \(k\) positions. Formally:
\[
  \sigma _{ijk} = s_i[:-k] \;  s_j
\]
(the first \(\left|s_i\right| - k\) characters of the string \(s_i\), followed by the entire string \(s_j\)).
For example, if \(s_i = \text{cabab}\) and \(s_j = \text{ababc}\), we get:
\[
  \sigma _{ij2} = \text{cabababc}, \qquad \sigma _{ij4} = \text{cababc}.
\]
Here \(\sigma_{ij1}, \sigma_{ij3}, \ldots\) do not exist.
Each string \(\sigma_{ijk}\) corresponds to the set of original strings of \(U\) that it covers (i.e., that are substrings of it). We thus obtain an instance of the set cover problem: the set of all such \(\sigma_{ijk}\) covers the original set \(U\). Constructing an approximate solution to the superstring problem then reduces to finding a small subset of the strings \(\sigma_{ijk}\) that covers all the strings of \(U\).


  Constructing the merge string \(\sigma_{ijk}\)
  The last \(k\) characters of \(s_i\) match the first \(k\) characters of \(s_j\); the result of the merge \(\sigma_{ijk}=s_i[:-k]\,s_j\) is the whole string shown below. Move the slider: the larger the overlap, the shorter the merge.

Let the set \(\mathcal{F}\) consist of all possible admissible strings \(\sigma_{i j k}\). For each string \(\pi \in \Sigma^{+}\) define the set \(\operatorname {set}(\pi )=\{ s \in U \mid s\) is a substring of \(\pi \}\). We must cover the elements of \(U\) with the subsets \(\operatorname {set}(\pi )\), where \(\pi \in U \cup \mathcal{F}\). Set the weight of the set \(\operatorname {set}(\pi )\) equal to \(|\pi |\), i.e., the length of the string \(\pi\).


2.1.2 Accuracy of the reduction
Let \(\operatorname {OPT}_{\mathcal{S}}\) and \(\operatorname {OPT}\) denote the cost of an optimal solution of the cover instance \(\mathcal{S}\) and the length of the shortest common superstring, respectively. We show that these quantities can differ from each other by at most a factor of 2.







Lemma 1 \(\operatorname {OPT} \leq \operatorname {OPT}_{\mathcal{S}} \leq 2 \cdot \operatorname {OPT}\).










Mn-proofProof







\(\operatorname {OPT} \stackrel{?}{\leq } \operatorname {OPT}_{\mathcal{S}}\).
Consider an optimal cover \(\left\{ \operatorname {set}\left(\pi_{i}\right) \mid 1 \leq i \leq l\right\}\) and obtain a string \(s\) by concatenating the strings \(\pi_{i}, 1 \leq i \leq l\), in an arbitrary order. Clearly \(|s|=\operatorname {OPT}_{\mathcal{S}}\). Since every string of \(U\) is a substring of some string \(\pi_{i}\), it is also a substring of \(s\). Hence the resulting string is a superstring, and \(\operatorname {OPT}_{\mathcal{S}}=|s| \geq \operatorname {OPT}\).
\(\operatorname {OPT}_{\mathcal{S}} \stackrel{?}{\leq } 2 \cdot \operatorname {OPT}\).
To prove the second inequality, consider a shortest common superstring \(s^{*}\) for the strings \(s_{1}, \ldots , s_{n},\left|s^{*}\right|=\operatorname {OPT}\). We show that for the cover instance \(\mathcal{S}\) there exists a cover of weight at most \(2 \cdot \operatorname {OPT}\).
Consider the leftmost occurrence of the strings \(s_{1}, \ldots , s_{n}\) in the string \(s^{*}\). Since none of the strings \(s_{1}, \ldots , s_{n}\) is a substring of another, the leftmost occurrences of the \(n\) strings begin at distinct positions. For the same reason, they end at distinct positions. Renumber the strings in the order of their occurrence. Since none of the strings is a substring of another, they will also end in the same order.
Split the ordered list of strings \(s_{1}, \ldots , s_{n}\) into groups, as shown in the figure below. Each group will consist of a set of pairwise-overlapping strings. Denote by \(b_{i}\) and \(e_{i}\) the indices of the first and last string in the \(i\)-th group. If group \(i\) consists of a single string, then \(b_{i}=e_{i}\). Set \(b_{1}=1\). Let \(e_{1}\) be the largest index of a string overlapping with the string \(s_{1}\) (there is at least one such string — \(s_{1}\) itself). In general: if \(e_{i}<n\), set \(b_{i+1}=e_{i}+1\) and define \(e_{i+1}\) as the largest index of a string overlapping with the string \(s_{b_{i+1}}\). At the end of this process we get \(e_{t}=n\) for some \(t \leq n\).
