For each pair of strings \(\left(s_{b_{i}}, s_{e_{i}}\right)\) there is some \(k_{i}>0\) giving the length of the overlap of these strings within the string \(s\) (which may differ from their maximal overlap). Let \(\pi_{i}=\sigma_{b_{i} e_{i} k_{i}}\). Then the collection of subsets \(\left\{ \operatorname {set}\left(\pi_{i}\right) \mid 1 \leq i \leq t\right\}\) is a feasible solution of the instance \(\mathcal{S}\), with cost \(\sum_{i}\left|\pi_{i}\right|\).
Now note that \(\pi_{i}\) does not overlap with \(\pi_{i+2}\). We prove this claim for \(i=1\). Suppose the strings \(\pi_{1}\) and \(\pi_{3}\) overlap. Then \(s_{b_{3}}\) overlaps with \(s_{e_{1}}\) in the string \(s^{*}\). However, by construction \(s_{b_{3}}\) does not overlap with \(s_{b_{2}}\) (since \(s_{b_{3}}\) belongs to the next group). Hence \(s_{e_{1}}\) ends later than \(s_{b_{2}}\). This contradicts the fact that the strings must end in the same order in which they begin. The proof for other values of \(i\) is analogous.
We thus find that each character of the string \(s^{*}\) belongs to at most two strings \(\pi_{i}\). From this we get \(\operatorname {OPT}_{\mathcal{S}} \leq \sum_{i}\left|\pi_{i}\right| \leq 2 \cdot \operatorname {OPT}\).

title: Shortest common superstring
text:
2.2 Applying set-cover algorithms
After the reduction, we can use some algorithm for the set cover problem. Consider, for example, applying the greedy algorithm.







Algorithm 2 Building a superstring via the greedy set-cover algorithm

 a set of strings \(U = \{s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\}\).
 an approximate superstring \(s\) containing every string of \(U\) as a substring. 
Over all pairs of strings in \(U\) and all admissible overlaps, build the strings \(\sigma_{ijk}\) and the family of sets \(\left\{\operatorname{set}(\pi) \mid \pi \in U \cup \mathcal{F}\right\}\) with weights \(\left|\pi\right|\).
Obtain an instance of the set cover problem: cover \(U\) with sets \(\operatorname{set}(\pi)\) of minimum total weight.
Using Chvátal’s greedy algorithm, find an approximate cover \(C = \{\operatorname{set}(\pi_{1}), \ldots, \operatorname{set}(\pi_{l})\}\).
Concatenate the strings \(\pi_{1}, \ldots, \pi_{l}\) in an arbitrary order, forming the superstring \(s = \pi_{1} \pi_{2} \ldots \pi_{l}\).
return \(s\)





The number of elements of \(U\) in the instance \(\mathcal{S}\) equals \(n\), i.e., the number of strings in the superstring problem.







Theorem 2 Algorithm @SSP:SetCov:GrAlg is a \(2 H_{n}\)-approximation algorithm for the superstring problem, where \(n\) is the number of strings in the given instance.










Mn-proofProof






The length of the constructed superstring equals \(\sum_{i=1}^{l} \left|\pi_i\right|\), i.e., the weight of the cover found. Chvátal’s greedy algorithm on a universe of \(n\) elements produces a cover of weight at most \(H_n \cdot \operatorname {OPT}_{\mathcal{S}}\), and by the reduction accuracy lemma \(\operatorname {OPT}_{\mathcal{S}} \leq 2 \cdot \operatorname {OPT}\). Altogether the length of the superstring does not exceed \(2 H_n \cdot \operatorname {OPT}\).

title: Metric problems
text:
In this chapter we present approximation algorithms for the metric Steiner tree problem and the metric traveling salesman problem. The reasons for considering the metric variants of these problems differ. For the Steiner tree problem, the metric case is the core of the general problem, and the general problem can be reduced to the metric one. For the traveling salesman problem, without this restriction no “good” approximation algorithms exist, assuming \(P \neq N P\). Nevertheless, the approximation algorithms for these problems share a common idea, which we develop in this chapter.
The shortest common superstring problem (chapter “Shortest common superstring” in the “Miscellaneous topics” part) can also be reduced to the traveling salesman problem with a special metric, and a 4-approximation algorithm exists for it.

title: Metric problems
section: 2.1 The general traveling salesman problem is inapproximable
text:
2.1 The general traveling salesman problem is inapproximable
The traveling salesman problem is one of the best-known problems in combinatorial optimization: find the cheapest route that visits each of the given cities exactly once and then returns to the starting city.


The traveling salesman problem


A complete graph \(G=(V, E)\), edge costs \(\operatorname {cost}: E \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}^{+}\).


A Hamiltonian cycle \(C\) of minimum cost.


A cycle that contains all vertices is called Hamiltonian.







Theorem 3 For any polynomially computable function \(\alpha (n)\), there is no \(\rho\)-approximation algorithm with \(\rho =\alpha (n)\) for the traveling salesman problem, unless \(P = N P\).










Mn-proofProof






We argue by contradiction. Suppose a \(\rho\)-approximation algorithm \(\mathcal{A}\) with \(\rho =\alpha (n)\) exists for the traveling salesman problem. We show that the polynomial-time algorithm \(\mathcal{A}\) could then be used to solve the NP-hard Hamiltonian cycle problem. This would imply \(P=N P\).
The basic idea of the reduction is to construct, from the graph \(G\), a complete weighted graph \(G^{\prime }\) such that:

if \(G\) has a Hamiltonian cycle, then the cost of an optimal solution of the traveling salesman problem on \(G^{\prime }\) equals \(n\), and
if \(G\) has no Hamiltonian cycle, then the optimal solution of the traveling salesman problem for \(G^{\prime }\) has cost greater than \(\alpha (n) \cdot n\).

Note that on the graph \(G^{\prime }\) the algorithm \(\mathcal{A}\) must find a solution of cost \(\operatorname {cost} \leq \alpha (n) \cdot n\) in the first case and of cost \(\operatorname {cost} > \alpha (n) \cdot n\) in the second case.
From the graph \(G\) construct a complete weighted graph \(G^{\prime }\). Assign cost 1 to the edges present in \(G\), and cost \(\alpha (n) \cdot n\) to the edges absent from \(G\). If \(G\) has a Hamiltonian cycle, then the corresponding tour in \(G^{\prime }\) has cost \(n\). On the other hand, if \(G\) has no Hamiltonian cycle, then any tour in \(G^{\prime }\) must use an edge of cost \(\alpha (n) \cdot n\), so the cost of the tour will be \(\operatorname{cost} >\alpha (n) \cdot n\).




Note that this proof of strong inapproximability uses edge costs that violate the triangle inequality. If we restrict attention to graphs on which this inequality holds, i.e., to the metric traveling salesman problem, the problem remains NP-hard but is no longer as hard to approximate.


The metric traveling salesman problem


A complete graph \(G=(V, E)\), edge costs \(\operatorname {cost}: E \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}^{+}\) such that for any three vertices \(u, v\) and \(w\) \[
  \operatorname {cost}(u, v) \leq \operatorname {cost}(u, w)+\operatorname {cost}(w, v)
\]


A Hamiltonian cycle \(C\) of minimum cost.

title: Metric problems
text:
2.2 A \(2\)-approximation algorithm
We present a simple 2-approximation algorithm for the metric traveling salesman problem. As a lower bound we use the optimal solution of the minimum spanning tree problem on the graph \(G\). This solution is a lower bound for the optimal solution of the traveling salesman problem, since removing any edge from a Hamiltonian cycle yields a spanning tree of \(G\).







Algorithm 2 Double Spanning Tree algorithm (\(G=(V, E), \operatorname {cost} : E \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}^{+}\))

Find a minimum spanning tree \(T\) in the graph \(G\).
Double every edge of the tree \(T\) to obtain an Eulerian graph \(H\).
Find an Eulerian tour \(R\) in the graph \(H\).
Build a Hamiltonian cycle \(C\) by visiting the vertices of \(G\) in the order in which they occur in \(R\).
return \(C\).





Note that step 4 amounts to the shortcutting technique used in the theorem above.

  The "double tree" algorithm for the metric traveling salesman problem
  1) build an MST; 2) double its edges — this gives an Eulerian graph — and traverse it; 3) "shortcut," skipping already-visited vertices, to get a Hamiltonian cycle of cost \(\le 2\cdot\mathrm{MST}\le 2\cdot\mathrm{OPT}\). On steps 3 and 4 the tour is animated as it is traced.
  
  
  









Theorem 4 The Double Spanning Tree algorithm is a \(2\)-approximation algorithm for the metric traveling salesman problem.










Mn-proofProof






As noted above, \(\operatorname {cost}(T) \leq \operatorname {OPT}\). Since the graph \(H\) contains every edge of the tree \(T\) twice, \(\operatorname {cost}(R)=2 \cdot \operatorname {cost}(T)\). Then by the triangle inequality, after shortcutting we get \(\operatorname {cost}(C) \leq \operatorname {cost}(R)\) and \(\operatorname {cost}(C) \leq 2 \cdot \operatorname {OPT}\).





  Tightness of the factor-2 bound for the "double tree" algorithm
  A complete graph on \(n\) vertices (here \(n=6\)) with edges of cost \(1\) and \(2\): the bold cost-\(1\) edges form a star \(K_{1,n-1}\) and a cycle on the remaining \(n-1\) vertices. Hover over an edge to see its cost; the button on the right traces a bad tour.
  Show the bad tourHide
  
    
    
  
  (a) The optimal traveling-salesman tour, of cost \(n=6\): a cycle along the cheap edges (center \(\to\) outer vertex \(\to\) around the cycle \(\to\) center). (b) If the algorithm finds an MST shaped like a star, and the Eulerian tour visits the vertices in the order \(5,3,2,1,4,6\), then after shortcutting the cycle contains \(n-2\) edges of cost \(2\) — cost \(2n-2\), twice the optimum as \(n\to\infty\).

title: Metric problems
text:
2.3 A \(1.5\)-approximation algorithm
The Double Spanning Tree algorithm first finds a cheap Eulerian tour from a spanning tree of the graph \(G\), and then turns it into a traveling-salesman tour by shortcutting. Is there an Eulerian tour other than the one found via the double spanning tree? Recall that a graph has an Eulerian tour if and only if every vertex has even degree. Let \(V^{\prime }\) be the set of all vertices of odd degree in the spanning tree. Then the number of such vertices \(\left|V^{\prime }\right|\) must be even, since the sum of the degrees of all vertices in any graph is even. If we add to the minimum spanning tree a minimum-weight perfect matching on the set \(V^{\prime }\), then every vertex will have even degree, and we obtain an Eulerian graph. Recall that the minimum-cost perfect matching problem can be solved in polynomial time.







Algorithm 3 Christofides–Serdyukov algorithm (\(G=(V, E), \operatorname {cost} : E \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}^{+}\))

Find a minimum spanning tree \(T\) in the graph \(G\).
Find a minimum-cost matching \(M\) on the set of vertices of \(T\) having odd degree.
Add the edges of \(M\) to \(T\) to obtain an Eulerian graph \(H\).
Find an Eulerian tour \(R\) in the graph \(H\).
Build a Hamiltonian cycle \(C\) by visiting the vertices of \(G\) in the order in which they occur in \(R\).
return \(C\).






  The Christofides-Serdyukov algorithm
  The same graph \(v_1,\ldots,v_9\) as in the "double tree" algorithm. Instead of doubling the whole tree, we add only a minimum perfect matching on the odd-degree vertices — the tour is cheaper: \(\le\frac32\cdot\mathrm{OPT}\). Hover over a vertex to see its degree.
  
  
  


To bound the accuracy of this algorithm, we present a new lower bound on the cost of an optimal solution of the traveling salesman problem.







Lemma 1 Let \(V^{\prime } \subseteq V\) with \(\left|V^{\prime }\right|\) even, and let \(M\) be a minimum-cost perfect matching for \(V^{\prime }\). Then \(\operatorname {cost}(M) \leq \operatorname {OPT} / 2\).










Mn-proofProof






Consider an optimal cycle \(\tau\) for the traveling salesman problem on the graph \(G\). Let the cycle \(\tau^{\prime }\) be obtained from \(\tau\) on the vertex set \(V^{\prime }\) by shortcutting. By the triangle inequality, \(\operatorname {cost}\left(\tau^{\prime }\right) \leq \operatorname {cost}(\tau )\). But \(\tau^{\prime }\) is the union of two perfect matchings on \(V^{\prime }\), formed from the alternating edges of the cycle \(\tau^{\prime }\). Hence the smaller of the two matchings has cost at most \(\operatorname {cost}\left(\tau^{\prime }\right) / 2 \leq \operatorname {OPT} / 2\). Consequently, the optimal matching also has cost at most \(\operatorname {OPT} / 2\).











Theorem 5 The Christofides–Serdyukov algorithm is a \(\frac{3}{2}\)-approximation algorithm for the metric traveling salesman problem.










Mn-proofProof






We bound the cost of the Eulerian tour \(R\): \[
  \operatorname {cost}(R) \leq \operatorname {cost}(T)+\operatorname {cost}(M) \leq \operatorname {OPT}+\frac{1}{2} \operatorname {OPT}=\frac{3}{2} \operatorname {OPT}
\] Using the triangle inequality, we get \(\operatorname {cost}(C) \leq \operatorname {cost}(R)\). This proves the theorem.





  Tightness of the \(3/2\) bound for the Christofides-Serdyukov algorithm
  A zigzag chain of \(m=\lceil n/2\rceil\) triangles, all edges shown have cost \(1\). The bold edges are the MST \(T\) (a zigzag path): it has exactly two odd-degree vertices — the endpoints — and the matching on them is a single edge between the endpoints, whose cost (under the shortest-path metric) equals \(\lceil n/2\rceil\). The button traces the algorithm's tour.
  
    \(m=\lceil n/2\rceil=\)4
    Show the algorithm's tour
  
  
  


Can one find an algorithm with better accuracy? Yes! In 2020 an algorithm with accuracy \(\alpha < 1.5 - 10^{-36}\) was obtained. As one can see, the improvement is not very substantial. The search for better approximation algorithms with guaranteed accuracy bounds for the metric traveling salesman problem continues. Many researchers believe that a \(\frac{4}{3}\)-approximation algorithm ought to exist.
The metric traveling salesman problem cannot be approximated within a factor smaller than \(\frac{123}{122} \approx 1.008\) (assuming \(\operatorname {P} \neq \operatorname {NP}\)).
For the Euclidean traveling salesman problem (the case where the vertices of the graph are points in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) and the edge cost equals the Euclidean distance), there exists an approximation algorithm with factor \((1+\varepsilon )\) for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), i.e., a polynomial-time approximation scheme exists. However, it is not fully polynomial: the dependence on \(\frac{1}{\varepsilon }\) is not polynomial.

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
text:
Combinatorial optimization is one of the youngest and most actively developing areas of discrete mathematics. Optimization problems arise in scheduling theory, facility location, network design, database management, information transmission, and also in economics and finance — from investment to auction and marketing strategies.
Unfortunately, most such problems are \(\operatorname {NP}\)-hard, and it is believed that no efficient algorithms exist for solving them exactly. The main goal of our course is therefore to study methods for constructing approximation algorithms and approximation schemes. To do this we must first formally define the problems under consideration and the properties of the algorithms.

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
section: 4.1 An algorithm for vertex cover via matchings
text:
4.1 An algorithm for vertex cover via matchings







Algorithm 2 Algorithm for the vertex cover problem via matchings

\(G' \gets G\), \(\operatorname{Sol} \gets \varnothing\)
while \(E(G') \neq \varnothing\) do

find an arbitrary edge \(e \in E(G')\), let \(e = \left\{v_1,v_2\right\}\)
\(\operatorname{Sol} \gets \operatorname{Sol} \cup \{v_1,v_2\}\)
remove \(v_1\), \(v_2\), and all edges incident to \(v_1\), \(v_2\) from \(G'\)

return \(\operatorname{Sol}\)






  The matching-based algorithm for vertex cover
  The algorithm builds a maximal (by inclusion) matching — a set of edges with no shared vertices — and outputs all vertices incident to its edges. Red edges form the matching; hover over an edge to see whether it can still be added.
  
  
  


At first glance this algorithm may seem less efficient than the greedy one. However, as we will show, it has a constant accuracy guarantee: its solution is at most twice as bad as the optimum. The greedy algorithm, on the other hand, as we will see in the next chapter, can in the worst case perform arbitrarily worse than the optimum.
Moreover, the output of the matching-based algorithm is often easy to improve by postprocessing: one can try removing from the resulting set any vertices whose removal does not break the covering of all edges. This brings the solution closer to optimal. This simple trick generally does not work for the output of the greedy algorithm.

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
text:
4.2 Accuracy of the algorithm
Key fact: the size of a maximal (with respect to inclusion) matching is a lower bound on the size of any vertex cover. Indeed, for every edge of the matching, at least one of its endpoints must belong to the cover. Since the edges of a matching share no vertices, the number of vertices in any cover cannot be smaller than the number of edges in the matching. This simple fact shows how lower bounds are naturally connected to the construction of approximate solutions.







Theorem 1 The matching-based algorithm is a 2-approximation algorithm for the minimum-cardinality vertex cover problem.










Mn-proofProof






Let \(M \subset E\) be a maximal (with respect to inclusion) matching in the graph. The algorithm selects two vertices for each edge of \(M\), so \(\left|\sigma_{\mathrm{matching}}\right| = 2\left|M\right|\). Since \(|M|\) is a lower bound on the size of any vertex cover, we get \[
  \left|\sigma _{\mathrm{matching}}\right| = 2\left|M\right| \leq 2 \cdot \left|\sigma ^*\right|,
\] where \(\sigma^*\) is an optimal cover.




We have obtained our first approximation algorithm. The main questions for improving the result are:

Can the quality analysis of the algorithm be sharpened? Is the bound of 2 given above tight?
Does there exist an algorithm with approximation factor \(\rho <2\) that always produces a solution no worse than \(\rho\) times the lower bound?
Can other lower bounds be used to construct a \(\rho\)-approximation algorithm with \(\rho <2\)?

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
text:
4.3 Is the algorithm’s bound tight?
The following example shows that the quality analysis of the matching-based algorithm cannot be improved. We construct an infinite family of examples on which it is off by a factor of two. Consider the complete bipartite graph \(K_{n, n}\) shown in the figure below. The matching-based algorithm will select all \(2 n\) vertices into the solution on this graph, whereas the optimal solution consists of the \(n\) vertices of one side.

  Tightness of the matching-based algorithm's bound: \(K_{n,n}\)
  In the complete bipartite graph \(K_{n,n}\), any perfect matching is already maximal by inclusion, so the algorithm selects all \(2n\) vertices, whereas the optimal cover is a single side of \(n\) vertices: the ratio tends to \(2\).
  
    \(n=\)3
    Algorithm: matchingOptimum: one side

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
section: 4.4 Is there another algorithm that improves on the lower bound we obtained via the size of a maximal matching?
text:
4.4 Is there another algorithm that improves on the lower bound we obtained via the size of a maximal matching?
Suppose the lower bound via the size of a matching is used to assess solution quality. Let us give an example on which the value of this lower bound differs from the optimum by a factor of two. Consider the complete graph on \(n\) vertices, where \(n\) is odd. The size of a maximum matching equals \((n-1) / 2\), while the size of an optimal vertex cover is \(n-1\). Hence the cost of the solution produced by any algorithm (even a non-polynomial one) can be almost twice as bad as the lower bound.

  The complete graph \(K_5\): a 2-edge matching versus a 4-vertex cover
  In \(K_5\) (an odd number of vertices), a maximum matching contains only 2 edges, e.g. \(\{v_1,v_2\}\) and \(\{v_3,v_4\}\) — the matching-based algorithm will return 4 vertices. But the optimal cover also consists of 4 vertices (any 4 out of 5): here the algorithm happens to be exact.
  
    Matching → 4 verticesOptimal cover

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
section: 4.5 Is there another algorithm that is better overall, perhaps using some other lower bound?
text:
4.5 Is there another algorithm that is better overall, perhaps using some other lower bound?
The question of whether a \(\rho\)-approximation algorithm with \(\rho <2\) exists, using some other lower bound, is much harder. Recently Subhash Khot put forward a plausible conjecture [7], [8], according to which the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm for the vertex cover problem with a guaranteed bound of \(2-\varepsilon\) for any fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) would imply that the classes \(\operatorname {P}\) and \(\operatorname {NP}\) coincide.

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
text:
6.1 Minimum spanning tree
The minimum-weight spanning tree problem (minimum spanning tree, MST). A spanning tree of a connected graph \(G = (V,E)\) is a tree containing all the vertices of the graph. Weights are assigned to the edges, and we must find a spanning tree of minimum total weight.
Classical polynomial-time algorithms exist for this problem: Kruskal’s algorithm, Prim’s algorithm, and also faster algorithms based on modern data structures.

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
text:
6.2 Shortest paths
One of the fundamental problems is finding shortest paths in a graph.

From a single source (single-source shortest paths): Dijkstra’s algorithm (for nonnegative weights), the Bellman–Ford algorithm (also works with negative edge weights).
Between all pairs of vertices: the Floyd–Warshall algorithm and Johnson’s algorithm.

All of these problems can be solved in polynomial time and are widely used in practice.

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
text:
6.3 Maximum flow
The maximum flow problem in a transportation network. Given a directed network \(G = (V,E)\) with capacities \(c : E \to \mathbb {R}_+\), we must find the largest flow from a source \(s\) to a sink \(t\) satisfying the edge constraints and conservation laws.
Known algorithms: the Ford–Fulkerson algorithm, the Edmonds–Karp algorithm, Dinic’s algorithm, and various modern refinements. Closely related is the minimum cut problem, which is equivalent to the maximum flow problem (the max-flow min-cut theorem).

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
text:
6.4 Minimum-cost flow
A generalization of the maximum flow and assignment problems. Given a network with capacities \(c : E \to \mathbb {R}_+\) and costs \(w : E \to \mathbb {R}\), we must find a flow of a given value with minimum cost.
Exact polynomial-time algorithms are known for this problem, for example based on potential (successive shortest paths) algorithms.

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
text:
6.5 Maximum matching
A subset of edges \(M \subseteq E\) is called a matching if no two edges of \(M\) share a vertex.

A maximum matching is a matching with the largest possible number of edges.
A maximal matching is a matching to which no edge can be added.

Every maximum matching is maximal, but not conversely.
For bipartite graphs the problem is solved by the Hungarian algorithm (Kuhn’s algorithm). For general graphs, Edmonds’ algorithm (the blossom algorithm) is used.

title: Combinatorial optimization: an introduction
text:
6.6 Minimum-weight \(k\)-factor
A spanning subgraph is a subgraph containing all the vertices of the original graph.
A graph is called \(k\)-regular if all of its vertices have degree \(k\).
A \(k\)-factor of a graph \(G\) is a \(k\)-regular spanning subgraph of \(G\). In particular:

a \(1\)-factor is a perfect matching, i.e., a matching covering all vertices of the graph;
a \(2\)-factor is a collection of cycles covering all vertices of the graph.

Exact polynomial-time algorithms exist for the minimum-weight \(k\)-factor problem, including ones based on a reduction to the perfect matching problem.
Thus, although many combinatorial optimization problems are \(\operatorname {NP}\)-hard, there is a broad class of fundamental problems for which efficient polynomial-time algorithms have been developed. These problems and methods serve as building blocks for more complex algorithms and approximation schemes.

Contents of the published program
Below is the complete list from the available program of the Department of Discrete Mathematics for spring 2023. This is not a claim that the 2025/26 program is unchanged, but it is the most detailed open primary document for the course.

Rings, divisibility properties and Euclidean rings.
Unique factorization in a Euclidean ring; primes in the Gaussian and Eisenstein integers.
Pythagorean triples and the special case \(n=3\) of Fermat’s Last Theorem.
Subrings, ideals, principal ideal rings, maximal and prime ideals, Noetherian rings and Hilbert’s basis theorem.
The field of fractions, unique factorization in a polynomial ring over an integral domain, and Eisenstein’s criterion.
Extensions of rings and fields, finite extensions and adjoining a root of an irreducible polynomial.
Algebraic closure and the primitive element theorem.
Ruler-and-compass constructions.
Field homomorphisms and normal extensions.
Galois extensions and the correspondence between subgroups and intermediate fields.
Finite fields: uniqueness, subfields and the number of irreducible polynomials of a given degree.

E. B. Vinberg, A Course in Algebra, 2nd ed., 2001.
A. I. Kostrikin, Introduction to Algebra, in three parts, 2001.
M. Artin, Algebra, 2011.
R. B. J. T. Allenby, Rings, Fields and Groups, 1991.

title: Group Theory
text:
Contents of the published program
Below are all 24 items of V. V. Shtepin’s exam program for 2025. It belongs specifically to this course; sections on rings and fields from adjacent materials are not carried over here.

Groups, examples, cyclic groups and their subgroups.
Cosets, the index of a subgroup and Lagrange’s theorem.
Normal subgroups, the quotient group, homomorphisms, kernel and image; the fundamental homomorphism theorem.
The product of a normal subgroup and a subgroup, and the first isomorphism theorem.
Subgroups of a quotient group and the correspondence theorem.
Group actions, orbits, stabilizers and the orbit formula.
Examples of actions, Cayley’s theorem, the centralizer of an element and the normalizer of a subgroup.
Automorphisms and the group of inner automorphisms \(\operatorname{Inn}(G)\).
The class equation and Burnside’s lemma on the average number of fixed elements.
External and internal direct products, a criterion of decomposability into a direct product.
The semidirect product and a criterion for the corresponding decomposition.
The center of a group, the quotient by the center, and the center of a \(p\)-group.
Solvable and nilpotent groups, equivalent definitions, and relations with subgroups and quotient groups.
Simple groups and a lemma on conjugacy classes in a subgroup of index 2.
Simplicity of the group \(A_n\) for \(n\geq5\).
The free group, its quotient groups, and presentation of a group by generators and defining relations.
Existence in a \(p\)-group of subgroups of all admissible orders.
Existence and number of Sylow subgroups: the first and third Sylow theorems.
Conjugacy of Sylow subgroups and embedding of a \(p\)-subgroup into a Sylow subgroup: the second Sylow theorem.
Decomposition of a finite group into a direct product of Sylow subgroups; decomposition of a group of order \(pq\).
Free abelian groups, bases, rank, subgroups of free abelian groups.
The Smith normal form and existence of a decomposition of a finitely generated abelian group.
The torsion part of an abelian group and uniqueness of its classification decomposition.
Rings and algebras, ideals, the quotient ring, and the fundamental homomorphism theorem for rings.

title: Bilinear and Quadratic Forms
text:
1.1 Bilinear forms







Definition 1 Let \(V\) be a vector space over a field \(\mathbb {F}\) (typically, \(\mathbb {F}\) is either the real or the complex numbers). A bilinear function (or bilinear form) on \(V\) is a map \(b : V \times V \to \mathbb {F}\) that is linear in each argument. That is,
\[
\begin{align}  b(\alpha \overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}) & = \alpha \cdot b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}), &  b(\overrightarrow {x}_1 + \overrightarrow {x}_2, \overrightarrow {y}) = b(\overrightarrow {x}_1, \overrightarrow {y}) + b(\overrightarrow {x}_2, \overrightarrow {y}) \\ b(\overrightarrow {x}, \beta \overrightarrow {y}) & = \beta b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}), &  b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}_1 + \overrightarrow {y}_2) = b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}_1) + b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}_2) \end{align}
\]
for any \(\alpha , \beta \in \mathbb {F}\), \(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {x}_1, \overrightarrow {x}_2, \overrightarrow {y}, \overrightarrow {y}_1, \overrightarrow {y}_2 \in V\).
We denote the set of all bilinear forms on \(V\) by \(V^{(2)}\).




If \(V\) is equipped with a basis \((\overrightarrow {e}_i)_1^n\), then the value of a bilinear function on an arbitrary pair of vectors \(\overrightarrow {x}\), \(\overrightarrow {y}\) is completely determined by their coordinates in the basis \((\overrightarrow {e}_i)_1^n\) and by the values of the bilinear function \(b\) on the basis vectors \(b(\overrightarrow {e}_i, \overrightarrow {e}_j) =: b_{ij}\), \(i,j \in \left\{ 1, \ldots , n\right\}\). Indeed, if \([\overrightarrow {x}]^T = (x_1, \ldots , x_n)^T\), \([\overrightarrow {y}]^T = (y_1, \ldots , y_n)^T\) are the coordinates of \(\overrightarrow {x}\), \(\overrightarrow {y}\) in this basis, then by linearity we have
\[
\begin{align}  b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}) & = b\left(\sum _{i=1}^n x_i \overrightarrow {e}_i, \;  \sum _{j=1}^n y_j \overrightarrow {e}_j\right) = \sum _{i,j=1}^n x_iy_j \cdot b(\overrightarrow {e}_i, \overrightarrow {e}_j) = \\ & = \begin{pmatrix}  x_1 &  x_2 &  \cdots &  x_n \end{pmatrix} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}  b(\overrightarrow {e}_1, \overrightarrow {e}_1) &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_1, \overrightarrow {e}_2) &  \cdots &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_1, \overrightarrow {e}_n) \\ b(\overrightarrow {e}_2, \overrightarrow {e}_1) &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_2, \overrightarrow {e}_2) &  \cdots &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_2, \overrightarrow {e}_n) \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ b(\overrightarrow {e}_n, \overrightarrow {e}_1) &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_n, \overrightarrow {e}_2) &  \cdots &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_n, \overrightarrow {e}_n) \end{pmatrix}}_{=: B} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{pmatrix} = \\ & = [\overrightarrow {x}]^T \cdot B \cdot [\overrightarrow {y}] \end{align}
\]
The matrix \(B \in \mathbf{F}^{n \times n}\) is called the matrix of the bilinear form \(b\) in the basis \((\overrightarrow {e}_i)_1^n\). Note that once a basis is fixed, a bilinear form is expressed as a polynomial in the coordinates of the vectors, and every monomial has degree exactly \(2\).






ExampleExample 1





Let \(V = \mathbf{F}^3\). Define a map \(b: V \times V \to \mathbb {R}\) as follows: \[
  b\left(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}\right) = b\left(\begin{bmatrix}  x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}  y_1 \\ y_2 \\ y_3 \end{bmatrix}\right) : = x_1y_2 - 5x_2y_3 + 2x_3y_1
\]

Check that \(b\) is a bilinear form.
Write down the matrix of \(b\) in the standard basis.







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)



A simple exercise …








Enum-item(2)



\[
  B = \begin{pmatrix}  b(\overrightarrow {e}_1, \overrightarrow {e}_1) &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_1, \overrightarrow {e}_2) &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_1, \overrightarrow {e}_3) \\ b(\overrightarrow {e}_2, \overrightarrow {e}_1) &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_2, \overrightarrow {e}_2) &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_1, \overrightarrow {e}_3) \\ b(\overrightarrow {e}_3, \overrightarrow {e}_1) &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_3, \overrightarrow {e}_2) &  b(\overrightarrow {e}_1, \overrightarrow {e}_3) \\ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  1 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  -5 \\ 2 &  0 &  0 \end{pmatrix}
\]














ExampleExample 2





Let \(V = \mathcal{P}^{(n)}(\mathbb {R})\) for some \(n \in \mathbb {N}\). Define a map \(b: V \times V \to \mathbb {R}\) as follows: \(b(p, q) = p(2) \cdot q'(3)\).

Check that \(b\) is a bilinear form.
Let \(n=2\). Write down its matrix in the basis \(1, x, x^2\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)



A simple exercise …








Enum-item(2)



\[
  B = \begin{pmatrix}  b(1,1) &  b(1,x) &  b(1,x^2) \\ b(x,1) &  b(x,x) &  b(x,x^2) \\ b(x^2,1) &  b(x^2,x) &  b(x^2,x^2) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  1 &  6 \\ 0 &  2 &  12 \\ 0 &  4 &  24 \end{pmatrix}
\]















Theorem 1 Let \(\overrightarrow {e}_1, \ldots , \overrightarrow {e}_n\) be a basis of \(V\). Then the map \(V^{(2)} \to \mathbf{F}^{n\times n}\) sending a bilinear form to its matrix is an isomorphism of vector spaces.




As a corollary of the theorem above we get
\[
  \operatorname {dim}V^{(2)} = \operatorname {dim}\mathbf{F}^{n\times n} = n^2 = \left(\operatorname {dim}V\right)^2
\]
If \((\overrightarrow {e}'_i)_1^n\) is another basis of \(V\), and \(S\) is the change-of-basis matrix from \((\overrightarrow {e}_i)_1^n\) to \((\overrightarrow {e}'_i)_1^n\), then the matrix of \(b\) in the new basis can be found as follows:
\[
  B' = S^T \cdot B \cdot S
\tag{1}\]
Note that, unlike the matrix of an operator, which transforms as \(A' = S^{-1}AS\), the old matrix of a bilinear form is multiplied on the left not by \(S^{-1}\), but by \(S^T\). In particular, the determinant of the matrix \(B\) is no longer an invariant, unlike the determinant of \(A\), since
\[
  \left|B'\right| = \left|S^T\right|\left|B\right|\left|S\right| = \left|S\right|^2 \cdot \left|B\right|
\]
and \(\left|S\right|\) may be different from \(1\) and \(-1\).
On the other hand, the following are invariants:

the rank \(\operatorname {rk}\left(B\right)\),
the sign of the determinant \(\operatorname {sgn}(\left|B\right|)\), if the field \(\mathbb {F}\) is the field of real numbers.







ExampleExample 3





Consider the bilinear form from example Example 2.

Write down its matrix in the basis \(\overrightarrow {e}'_1 = 1\), \(\overrightarrow {e}'_2 = x-2\), \(\overrightarrow {e}'_3 = (x-3)^2\), without using the change-of-basis formula Equation 1.
Check that the change-of-basis formula Equation 1 holds.







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)



\[
  B' = \begin{pmatrix}  b(1,1) &  b(1,x-2) &  b(1,(x-3)^2) \\ b(x-2,1) &  b(x-2,x-2) &  b(x-2,(x-3)^2) \\ b((x-3)^2,1) &  b((x-3)^2,x-2) &  b((x-3)^2,(x-3)^2) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  1 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 &  0 \end{pmatrix}
\]








Enum-item(2)



Change-of-basis matrix:
\[
  S = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  -2 &  9 \\ 0 &  1 &  -6 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
We have
\[
\begin{align}  S^T \cdot B \cdot S & = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  0 \\ -2 &  1 &  0 \\ 9 &  -6 &  1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  1 &  6 \\ 0 &  2 &  12 \\ 0 &  4 &  24 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  -2 &  9 \\ 0 &  1 &  -6 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  1 &  6 \\ 0 &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 &  6 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  -2 &  9 \\ 0 &  1 &  -6 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 \end{pmatrix} = \\ & = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  1 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 &  0 \\ \end{pmatrix} \end{align}
\]

title: Bilinear and Quadratic Forms
text:
1.2 Symmetric bilinear forms
A bilinear function \(b\) is called symmetric if \(b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}) = b(\overrightarrow {y}, \overrightarrow {x})\) for any \(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y} \in V\).






ExampleExample 4





Prove that a bilinear form is symmetric if and only if its matrix \(B\) in some (and hence in every) basis is symmetric: \(B^T = B\).






SolutionSolution





If \(b\) is symmetric, then \(b_{i,j} = b(\overrightarrow {e}_i, \overrightarrow {e}_j) = b(\overrightarrow {e}_j, \overrightarrow {e}_i) = b_{j,i}\), i.e., \(B^T = B\) in every basis. Conversely, suppose \(B = B^T\) in some basis. A number can be viewed as a \(1 \times 1\) matrix, which coincides with its own transpose, hence \[
  b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}) = [\overrightarrow {x}]^T B [\overrightarrow {y}] = \left([\overrightarrow {x}]^T B [\overrightarrow {y}]\right)^T = [\overrightarrow {y}]^T B^T [\overrightarrow {x}] = [\overrightarrow {y}]^T B [\overrightarrow {x}] = b(\overrightarrow {y}, \overrightarrow {x})
\]

title: Bilinear and Quadratic Forms
text:
1.3 Quadratic forms







Definition 2 A quadratic function on \(V\) is a function \(q: V \to \mathbb {F}\) for which there exists a symmetric bilinear function \(b: V \times V \to \mathbb {F}\) such that
\[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) = b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {x}), \quad \forall \overrightarrow {x} \in V
\]
A quadratic function is sometimes called a quadratic form.










Mn-remarkRemark




A symmetric bilinear function \(b\) is uniquely recovered from its quadratic function \(q\) by the polarization formula: \[
  b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}) = \frac{1}{2}\bigg(q(\overrightarrow {x} + \overrightarrow {y}) - q(\overrightarrow {x}) - q(\overrightarrow {y})\bigg)
\] (expand \(q(\overrightarrow {x} + \overrightarrow {y}) = b(\overrightarrow {x} + \overrightarrow {y}, \overrightarrow {x} + \overrightarrow {y})\) using bilinearity and use symmetry). In practice this amounts to a simple rule: in the matrix \(B\), the coefficient of \(x_i^2\) goes on the diagonal, while the coefficient of \(x_i x_j\) (\(i \neq j\)) is split evenly between positions \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\).









ExampleExample 5





Write down the matrix of the bilinear function \[
  b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}) = 2 x_1 y_1 - x_1 y_2 - x_2 y_1 - 5 x_2 y_2
\] in a two-dimensional vector space and write down the corresponding quadratic function.






SolutionSolution





We assume that some basis \((\overrightarrow {e}_1, \overrightarrow {e}_2)\) of the 2-dimensional space \(V\) is given, and \(x_1, x_2, y_1,y_2\) are the coordinates of the vectors \(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y} \in V\) in this basis. The matrix of \(b\) in this basis:
\[
  B = \begin{pmatrix}  2 &  -1 \\ -1 &  -5 \end{pmatrix}
\]
The bilinear function in matrix form:
\[
  b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}) = \begin{pmatrix}  x_1 &  x_2 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  2 &  -1 \\ -1 &  -5 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}  y_1 \\ y_2 \end{pmatrix}
\]
The quadratic function \(q\) corresponding to \(b\):
\[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) = b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {x}) = \begin{pmatrix}  x_1 &  x_2 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  2 &  -1 \\ -1 &  -5 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}  x_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix} = 2x_1^2 - 2x_1x_2 - 5x_2^2
\]












ExampleExample 6





Recover the symmetric bilinear function in a two-dimensional vector space from the quadratic function \[
  q(\overrightarrow {x})=-18 x_1 x_2+9 x_2^2
\] and write down its matrix.






SolutionSolution





By the polarization rule, the coefficient of \(x_1 x_2\) is split evenly between the symmetric positions: \[
  b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y}) = -9 x_1y_2 - 9x_2y_1 + 9x_2y_2, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  -9 \\ -9 &  9 \end{pmatrix}
\] Check: \(b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {x}) = -9x_1x_2 - 9x_2x_1 + 9x_2^2 = -18x_1x_2 + 9x_2^2 = q(\overrightarrow {x})\).












ExampleExample 7





The quadratic function \[
  q(\overrightarrow {x})=25 x_1^2-14 x_1 x_2+2 x_2^2
\] is given in the basis \(\left\{ \overrightarrow {e}_1, \overrightarrow {e}_2\right\}\). Write down this quadratic function in the basis \(\left\{ \overrightarrow {e}_1^{\prime }, \overrightarrow {e}_2^{\prime }\right\}\), where \[
  \overrightarrow {e}_1^{\prime }=\overrightarrow {e}_1+\overrightarrow {e}_2, \overrightarrow {e}_2^{\prime }=-\overrightarrow {e}_1+\overrightarrow {e}_2
\]






SolutionSolution





Let \(b\) be the bilinear function corresponding to the quadratic function \(q\). Then its matrix in the basis \((\overrightarrow {e}_1, \overrightarrow {e}_2)\):
\[
  B = \begin{pmatrix}  25 &  -7 \\ -7 &  2 \end{pmatrix}
\]
The change-of-basis matrix to the primed basis, and the matrix of the quadratic function \(b\) in the primed basis:
\[
  S = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  -1 \\ 1 &  1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad B' = S^TBS = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  1 \\ -1 &  1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}  25 &  -7 \\ -7 &  2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  -1 \\ 1 &  1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  13 &  -23 \\ -23 &  41 \end{pmatrix}
\]
Let \(\overrightarrow {x} = x_1'\overrightarrow {e}_1' + x_2'\overrightarrow {e}_2'\), i.e., \(x_1', x_2'\) are the coordinates of \(\overrightarrow {x}\) in the new, primed basis. Then
\[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) = b(\overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {x}) = \begin{pmatrix}  x'_1 &  x'_2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}  13 &  -23 \\ -23 &  41 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}  x'_1 \\ x'_2 \end{pmatrix} = 13(x'_1)^2 - 46x_1'x_2' + 41(x_2')^2
\]

title: Bilinear and Quadratic Forms
section: 2.1 Positive and negative definite quadratic functions
text:
2.1 Positive and negative definite quadratic functions







Definition 3 A quadratic form \(q\) on the space \(V\) is called positive definite if
\[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) > 0, \qquad \forall \overrightarrow {x} \in V, \;  \overrightarrow {x} \neq \overrightarrow {0}
\]
\(q\) is called positive semidefinite (also called nonnegative definite) if the strict inequality above is replaced by a non-strict one:
\[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) \geq 0, \qquad \forall \overrightarrow {x} \in V, \;  \overrightarrow {x} \neq \overrightarrow {0}
\]
The notions of negative definiteness and negative semidefiniteness are introduced analogously.

title: Bilinear and Quadratic Forms
section: 2.2 The law of inertia, and reduction of a form to canonical form
text:
2.2 The law of inertia, and reduction of a form to canonical form







Theorem 2 (Sylvester’s law of inertia) Let \(q: V \to \mathbb {R}\) be a quadratic form. Then there exists a basis \((\overrightarrow {e}_i)_1^n\) of \(V\) in which the form takes the diagonal form
\[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) = x_1^2 + \cdots + x_{r_+}^2 - x_{r_+ + 1}^2 - \cdots - x_{r_++r_-}^2 = \sum _{i=1}^{r_+} x_i^2 - \sum _{j=r_++1}^{r_++r_-}x_j^2,
\tag{2}\]
where \((x_i)_1^n\) are the coordinates of the vector \(\overrightarrow {x}\) in this basis and \(r_+ \leq r_++r_- \leq \operatorname {dim}(V) = n\). Equivalently, one can say that the matrix of the bilinear form \(b\) corresponding to \(q\) takes, in this basis, the form
\[
  B = \left(\begin{array}{cccc|cccc|ccc}&  1 &  2 &  \cdots &  r_+ &  r_++1 &  r_++2 &  \cdots &  r_++r_- &  r_++r_-+1 &  \cdots &  n \\ 1 &  1 &  0 &  \cdots &  0 &  0 & & & &  0 & & \\ 2 &  0 &  1 &  \cdots &  0 & & & & & & & \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \ddots &  \vdots \\ r_+ &  0 &  0 &  \cdots &  1 & \\ \hline r_++1 &  0 & & & &  -1 &  0 &  \cdots &  0 &  0 & & \\ r_++2 & & & & &  0 &  -1 &  \cdots &  0 & & & \\ \vdots & & & & &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \ddots &  \vdots \\ r_++r_- & & & & &  0 &  0 &  \cdots &  -1 & & & \\ \hline r_++r_- + 1 &  0 & & & &  0 & & & &  0 \\ \vdots & \\ n \\ \end{array}\right)= \left(\begin{array}{cccc|cccc|ccc}I_{r_+} & & & &  0 & & & &  0 \\ \hline 0 & & & &  -I_{r_-} & & & &  0 & & \\ \hline 0 & & & &  0 & & & &  0 & & \\ \end{array}\right)
\]
Moreover, the numbers \(r_+, r_- \in \mathbb {N}\) do not depend on the choice of the basis \((\overrightarrow {e}_i)_1^n\) diagonalizing the form \(q\) (there may be many such bases). That is, \(r_+\), \(r_-\) are invariants of the quadratic form, on a par with its rank or the sign of its determinant.




The form Equation 2 of a quadratic form is called canonical. The numbers \(r_+\) and \(r_-\) from the theorem are called the positive and negative indices of inertia, respectively, of the quadratic form \(b\). This is where the theorem gets its name.
It turns out that \(r_+\), \(r_-\) are the dimensions of the maximal subspaces \(U\), \(W\) of \(V\) on which the form \(q\) is positive definite and negative definite, respectively. That is,
\[
\begin{align}  q(\overrightarrow {y}) & > 0, \quad \forall \overrightarrow {y} \in U, \;  \overrightarrow {y} \neq \overrightarrow {0} \\ q(\overrightarrow {w}) & < 0, \quad \forall \overrightarrow {w} \in W, \;  \overrightarrow {w} \neq \overrightarrow {0} \end{align}
\]
Note that \(r_+ + r_- = \operatorname {rk}\left(B\right)\), i.e., the sum of the positive and negative indices of inertia equals the rank of the quadratic form. The difference \(r_+ - r_-\) is called the signature of the quadratic form \(q\).






ExampleExample 8





Reduce the given quadratic form to canonical form using either Lagrange’s method or elementary transformations of its matrix. Find the rank, the positive and negative indices of inertia, and the signature of this form: \[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_3 + x_2^2 + 2x_2x_3 + 4x_3^2
\]






SolutionSolution





There are 2 main methods.

Lagrange’s method for reducing a quadratic form to canonical form consists in successively completing the square. Namely, if the form contains the square of some coordinate, then we must complete the square using all the terms involving that coordinate. In our case we have \(x_1^2\). Write out all the terms containing \(x_1\): \(x_1^2 + 4x_1x_3\). Complete the square:
\[
  x_1^2 + 4x_1x_3 = (x_1 + 2x_3)^2 - 4x_3^2
\]
The form becomes:
\[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) = (x_1 + 2x_3)^2 - 4x_3^2 + x_2^2 + 2x_2x_3 + 4x_3^2 = (x_1 + 2x_3)^2 + x_2^2 + 2x_2x_3
\]
Consider the part of the form remaining after completing the square with \(x_1\): \(x_2^2 + 2x_2x_3\). We have \(x_2^2\), so let us complete the square with leading term \(x_2\):
\[
  x_2^2 + 2x_2x_3 = (x_2 + x_3)^2 - x_3^2
\]
We obtain
\[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) = (x_1 + 2x_3)^2 + (x_2 + x_3)^2 - x_3^2
\]
Introduce new coordinates by the formula:
\[
  x'_1 = x_1 + 2x_3, \qquad x'_2 = x_2 + x_3, \qquad x'_3 = x_3
\]
The matrix \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}  1 &  0 &  2 \\ 0 &  1 &  1 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) is nonsingular, so this is indeed a change of coordinates. In the new coordinates the form takes the canonical form
\[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) = \left(x'_1\right)^2 + \left(x'_2\right)^2 -\left(x'_3\right)^2
\]
We have
\[
  r_+ = 2, \quad r_- = 1, \quad \operatorname {rk}\left(q\right) = r_+ + r_- = 3, \quad r_+ - r_- = 1
\]
Note that
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}  x'_1 \\ x'_2 \\ x'_3 \end{pmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  2 \\ 0 &  1 &  1 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 \end{pmatrix}}_{ =: C} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{pmatrix}
\]
The matrix \(C\) lets us pass from the old coordinates to the new ones. That is, it is the change-of-basis matrix from the new (canonical) basis to the old (original) one (don’t get confused!). To obtain the change-of-basis matrix from the original basis to the canonical one, we need to find the inverse matrix:
\[
  S = C^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  2 \\ 0 &  1 &  1 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 \end{pmatrix}^{-1}= \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  -2 \\ 0 &  1 &  -1 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
We have
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  -1 \end{pmatrix} = B' = S^TBS = S^T \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  2 \\ 0 &  1 &  1 \\ 2 &  1 &  4 \end{pmatrix} \cdot S
\]
where \(B'\) is the matrix of the bilinear form in the canonical basis, and \(B\) is the matrix \(B\) in the original basis.
The method of elementary transformations of the matrix. Note that to obtain the canonical form, it suffices to find the change-of-basis matrix \(S\) to the new basis. Indeed, \(B' = S^T BS\). Here \(S\) is a nonsingular square matrix, so it can be obtained from the identity matrix by elementary column transformations.
Every elementary column transformation of a matrix corresponds to multiplying the matrix on the right by some matrix. For example, adding to the first column of an arbitrary matrix \(A\) its third column with coefficient \(-5\) corresponds to multiplying on the right by the matrix
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 &  0 \\ -5 &  0 &  1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
That is, \(S = S_1 \cdot S_2 \cdot \cdots \cdot S_p\), where \(S_i\) is the matrix of an elementary column transformation. Then
\[
\begin{align}  B' & = S^TBS = S_p^T \cdot \cdots \cdot S_2^T \cdot S_1^T \cdot B \cdot S_1 \cdot S_2 \cdot \cdots \cdot S_p = \\ & = S^T_p \cdot \left(S_{p-1}^T\cdot \cdots \cdot \left(S_2^T \cdot \left(S_1^T \cdot B \cdot S_1\right) \cdot S_2\right) \cdot \cdots \cdot S_{p-1}\right) \cdot S_p \end{align}
\]
If the matrix \(S_i\) corresponded to an elementary column transformation, then \(S_i^T\) corresponds to the analogous elementary row transformation. Finding the diagonal matrix \(B'\) with \(1\), \(-1\) and \(0\) on the diagonal amounts to successively performing symmetric elementary transformations on the rows and columns.
We have
\[
  \begin{aligned}  B &  = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  2 \\ 0 &  1 &  1 \\ 2 &  1 &  4 \end{pmatrix} \sim \\ &  \sim \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  2 \\ 0 &  1 &  1 \\ 0 &  1 &  0 \end{pmatrix} \sim \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 &  1 \\ 0 &  1 &  0 \end{pmatrix} \sim \\ &  \sim \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 &  1 \\ 0 &  0 &  -1 \end{pmatrix} \sim \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  -1 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}
\]
We have arrived at the canonical form! Here
\[
  S_1 = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  -2 \\ 0 &  1 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 \\ \end{pmatrix}, \quad S_2 = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 &  -1 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 \\ \end{pmatrix}, \quad S = S_1S_2 = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  -2 \\ 0 &  1 &  -1 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
We obtained the same change-of-basis matrix as in Lagrange’s method.










AnswerAnswer






Canonical form: \(q(\overrightarrow {x}) = \left(x'_1\right)^2 + \left(x'_2\right)^2 -\left(x'_3\right)^2\);
Positive index of inertia: \(2\);
Negative index of inertia: \(1\);
Rank: \(3\);
Signature: \(1\).













ExampleExample 9





Reduce the given quadratic form to canonical form using either Lagrange’s method or elementary transformations of its matrix. Find the rank, the positive and negative indices of inertia, and the signature of this form: \[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) = x_1x_2 + x_2x_3 + x_1x_3
\]






SolutionSolution






Lagrange’s method. In this case there are no squares in the form. In such a case the following intermediate substitution can help:
\[
  x_1 = \tilde{x}_1 + \tilde{x}_2, \quad x_2 = \tilde{x}_1 - \tilde{x}_2, \quad x_3 = \tilde{x}_3
\]
Then
\[
\begin{align}  q(\overrightarrow {x}) & = \left(\tilde{x}_1 + \tilde{x}_2\right)\left(\tilde{x}_1 - \tilde{x}_2\right) + \left(\tilde{x}_1 - \tilde{x}_2\right)\tilde{x}_3 + \left(\tilde{x}_1 + \tilde{x}_2\right)\tilde{x}_3 = \\ & = \tilde{x}_1^2 - \tilde{x}_2^2 + 2\tilde{x}_1\tilde{x}_3 \end{align}
\]
Complete the square with leading term \(\tilde{x}_1\):
\[
  \tilde{x}_1^2 + 2\tilde{x}_1\tilde{x}_3 = \left(\tilde{x}_1 + \tilde{x}_3\right)^2 - \tilde{x}_3^2
\]
We have
\[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) = \left(\tilde{x}_1 + \tilde{x}_3\right)^2 - \tilde{x}_2^2 - \tilde{x}_3^2
\]
New substitution:
\[
  \begin{cases}  x'_1 = \tilde{x}_1 + \tilde{x}_3 \\ x'_2 = \tilde{x}_2 \\ x'_3 = \tilde{x}_3 \\ \end{cases}
\]
In the new coordinates the quadratic form takes the canonical form:
\[
  q(\overrightarrow {x}) = \left(x'_1\right)^2 - \left(x'_2\right)^2 - \left(x'_3\right)^2
\]
Indices of inertia, rank, signature:
\[
  r_+ = 1, \quad r_- = 2, \quad \operatorname {rk}\left(q\right) = r_+ + r_- = 3, \quad r_+ - r_- = -1
\]
The method of elementary transformations of the matrix. We have
\[
  \hspace{-20em}\begin{aligned}  B &  = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  1/2 &  1/2 \\ 1/2 &  0 &  1/2 \\ 1/2 &  1/2 &  0 \end{pmatrix} \sim \\ &  \sim \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  \sqrt{2}/2 &  \sqrt{2}/2 \\ \sqrt{2}/2 &  0 &  \sqrt{2}/2 \\ \sqrt{2}/2 &  \sqrt{2}/2 &  0 \end{pmatrix} \sim \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  1 &  1 \\ 1 &  0 &  1 \\ 1 &  1 &  0 \end{pmatrix} \sim \\ &  \sim \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  1 &  2 \\ 1 &  0 &  1 \\ 1 &  1 &  0 \end{pmatrix} \sim \begin{pmatrix}  2 &  1 &  2 \\ 1 &  0 &  1 \\ 2 &  1 &  0 \end{pmatrix} \sim \\ &  \sim \begin{pmatrix}  2 &  1 &  2 \\ 0 &  -1/2 &  0 \\ 2 &  1 &  0 \end{pmatrix} \sim \begin{pmatrix}  2 &  0 &  2 \\ 0 &  -1/2 &  0 \\ 2 &  0 &  0 \end{pmatrix} \sim \\ &  \sim \begin{pmatrix}  2 &  0 &  2 \\ 0 &  -1/2 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  -2 \end{pmatrix} \sim \begin{pmatrix}  2 &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  -1/2 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  -2 \end{pmatrix} \sim \\ &  \sim \begin{pmatrix}  2/\sqrt{2} &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  -\sqrt{2}/2 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  -2/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \sim \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  -1 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  -1 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}
\]










AnswerAnswer






Canonical form: \(q(\overrightarrow {x}) = \left(x'_1\right)^2 - \left(x'_2\right)^2 -\left(x'_3\right)^2\);
Positive index of inertia: \(1\);
Negative index of inertia: \(2\);
Rank: \(3\);
Signature: \(-1\).
