title: Weak convergence in a Banach space
text:
1.1 Weak convergence







Definition 1 Let \(V\) be a normed space.

A sequence \(\left\{ f_n: n \geq 1\right\}\) of elements of the normed space \(V\) is said to converge weakly to an element \(f \in V\) if the action of every continuous linear functional on \(f_n\) converges to its action on \(f\):
\[
  \varphi \left(f_n\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \varphi (f), \qquad \forall \varphi \in V^*
\]
Notation: \(f_n \xrightarrow {w} f\).
A sequence \(\left\{ f_n: n \geq 1\right\}  \subset V\) is said to converge strongly to \(f \in V\) if \(f_n\) converges to \(f\) in \(V\) in the usual sense, i.e., in norm.
A sequence of vectors \(\left\{ f_n: n \geq 1\right\}  \subset V\) is called weakly bounded if, for every bounded linear functional \(\varphi \in V^*\), the sequence of numbers \(\left\{ \varphi \left(f_n\right): n \geq 1\right\}\) is bounded.
A sequence of vectors \(\left\{ f_n: n \geq 1\right\}  \subset V\) is called a weak Cauchy sequence if, for every bounded functional \(\varphi \in V^*\), the sequence of numbers \(\left\{ \varphi \left(f_n\right): n \geq 1\right\}\) is a Cauchy sequence.





Strong convergence of a sequence of vectors in a normed space implies weak convergence:
\[
  f_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} f \quad \;  \Rightarrow \;  \quad f_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{w} f
\]
The converse is not true in general.






ExampleExample 1





Prove that every strongly convergent sequence in a normed space converges weakly. Is the converse true?






SolutionSolution






Any element \(\varphi\) of \(V^*\) is bounded by definition, which is equivalent to continuity (for linear maps). That is, if \(f_n \to f\), then
\[
  \varphi (f_n) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \varphi (f)
\]
The converse is false; let us give a counterexample. Let \(V = \ell^{2}\), and consider the sequence of vectors \(e^{(n)}, \  n \geq 1\). Since \(\left\| e^{(n)}-e^{(m)}\right\|  = \sqrt{2}\) for all \(n \neq m\), the sequence \(\left\{ f^{(n)}: n \geq 1\right\}\) is not Cauchy, and hence does not converge (strongly) in \(\ell^{2}\).
We now show that \(f^{(n)} \xrightarrow {w} 0, \  n \rightarrow \infty\).
Recall that \(\left(\ell^{2}\right)^{*}\) can be identified with \(\ell^{2}\) itself: if \(\varphi \in \left(\ell^{2}\right)^{*}\), then there exists \(g \in \ell^{2}\) such that \(\varphi (f) = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty } f_{n} \overline{g_{n}}, \  f \in \ell^{2}\). In our case
\[
  \varphi \left(e^{(n)}\right) = \overline{a_{n}} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} 0 = \varphi (0)
\]
since the series \(\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty }\left|a_{n}\right|^{2}\) converges. Hence \(e^{(n)} \xrightarrow {w} 0, \  n \rightarrow \infty\).














Lemma 1 Let \(V\) be a Banach space, and let \(f_n \xrightarrow {w}f\). Then \((f_n)\) is a bounded sequence (i.e., \(\left\{ \left\| f_n\right\| \right\}\) is a bounded set), and moreover \[
  \left\| f\right\|  \leq \varliminf _{n \to \infty }\left\| f_n\right\|
\]











Theorem 1 (Criterion for weak convergence in an arbitrary Banach space) Let \(V\) be a Banach space, and let \(f, f_1, f_2, \ldots \in V\). Then \(f_n \xrightarrow {w} f\) if and only if the following conditions hold:

the sequence \(f_n\) is uniformly bounded: there exists \(C > 0\) such that \(\left\| f_n\right\|  \leq C\) for all \(n\);
there is a total set of functionals \(M\) in \(V^*\) (i.e., \(\overline{\operatorname {span}M} = V^*\)) on which \(f_n\) converges to \(f\):

\[
  \varphi (f_n) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{}f \qquad \forall \varphi \in M
\]




In other words, to establish weak convergence of \(f_n\) to \(f\), one does not need to check the convergence of \(\varphi (f_n)\) to \(\varphi (f)\) for every possible continuous functional \(\varphi \in V^*\). It suffices to check the convergence of \(\varphi (f_n)\) to \(\varphi (f)\) for all \(\varphi\) from some total subset of \(V^*\) (plus checking the technical condition of uniform boundedness of \(\left\{ f_n\right\}_{n \in \mathbb {N}}\)).







Lemma 2 (Criterion for weak convergence in \(C[ a, b]\)) A sequence \(f_1, f_2, \ldots \in C[0,1]\) converges weakly to \(f \in C[a, b]\) if and only if the following conditions hold:

the sequence \(f_n\) is uniformly bounded;
\(f_n(t) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} f(t)\) for every \(t \in [a,b]\)












Lemma 3 (Criterion for weak convergence in \(l^{p}, 1 < p < +\infty\)) Let \(1 < p < +\infty\). A sequence \(\left\{ f^{(n)} = \left(f_{1}^{(n)}, f_{2}^{(n)}, \ldots \right): n \geq 1\right\}  \subset \ell^{p}\) converges weakly to an element \(f = \left(f_{1}, f_{2}, \ldots \right) \in \ell^{p}\) if and only if the following conditions hold:

the sequence \(f_n\) is uniformly bounded;
\(f^{(n)}_k \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} f_k\) for every \(k \in \mathbb {N}\)












Lemma 4 (Criterion for weak convergence of elements in \(L^{p}[ a, b], 1 < p < +\infty\)) Let \(1 < p < +\infty\). A sequence \(\left\{ f_{n}: n \geq 1\right\}  \subset L^{p}[a,b]\) converges weakly to an element \(f \in L^{p}[a,b]\) if and only if the following conditions hold:

the sequence \(f_n\) is uniformly bounded;
\(\int_a^t f_n(s)ds \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \int_a^t f(s)ds\) for every \(t \in [a,b]\)












Theorem 2 (Schur) In \(\ell^1\), strong and weak convergence coincide.










ExampleExample 5.1





Prove the following statements:

(Criterion for weak convergence of elements in \(C[a, b]\).)
(Criterion for weak convergence of elements in \(\ell^{p}, 1 < p < +\infty\).)
(Criterion for weak convergence of elements in \(L^{p}[a, b], 1 < p < +\infty\).)







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Necessity. Condition (a) holds by the criterion for weak convergence (Theorem 5.5). For any fixed \(t \in [a, b]\) consider the functional \(\varphi (f) = f(t), \  \varphi \in (C[a, b])^{*}\). Since
\[
  \varphi \left(f_{n}\right) = f_{n}(t) \rightarrow \varphi (f) = f(t), \quad n \rightarrow \infty ,
\]
condition (b) also holds. Sufficiency. By Theorem 3.4, every functional \(\varphi \in (C[a, b])^{*}\) has the form \(\varphi (f) = \int_{a}^{b} f(t) d g(t)\), where \(g \in B V_{0}[a, b]\). Let \(\lambda_{v}\) be the Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure corresponding to the function \(v(t) = V(g,[a, t], \  t \in [a, b]\). Then
\[
  \begin{aligned}  \left|\varphi \left(f_{n}\right)-\varphi (f)\right| &  = \left|\int _{a}^{b}\left(f_{n}(t)-f(t)\right) d g(t)\right| \leq \\ &  \leq \int _{a}^{b}\left|f_{n}(t)-f(t)\right| d v(t) = \int _{[a, b]}\left|f_{n}(t)-f(t)\right| d \lambda _{v}(t) \end{aligned}
\]
From conditions (a), (b) and Lebesgue’s dominated convergence theorem it follows that \(\varphi \left(f_{n}\right) \rightarrow \varphi (f), \  n \rightarrow \infty\).








Enum-item2.



We apply the criterion for weak convergence (Theorem 5.5). Consider the functionals \(\varphi_{k}(f) = f_{k}, \  f = \left(f_{1}, f_{2}, \ldots \right) \in \ell^{p}, \  k \geq 1\). Condition (b) of part (2) means that \(\varphi_{k}\left(f^{(n)}\right) \rightarrow \varphi_{k}(f), \  n \rightarrow \infty\). It therefore suffices to check that the set \(M = \left\{ \varphi_{k}: k \geq 1\right\}\) is total in \(\left(\ell^{p}\right)^{*}\). This is true because the spaces \(\left(\ell^{p}\right)^{*}\) and \(l_{q}\), where \(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q} = 1\), are isometrically isomorphic (see Corollary 3.1 to Theorem 3.3), and the image of the set \(M\) under this isomorphism is the set \(\left\{ e_{k}: k \geq 1\right\}\), which is total in \(l_{q}\).








Enum-item3.



We apply the criterion for weak convergence (Theorem 5.5). Consider the functionals \(\varphi_{\tau }(f) = \int_{a}^{\tau } f(t) d t, \  f \in L^{p}[a, b], \  \tau \in (a, b]\). Condition (b) of part (3) means that \(\varphi_{\tau }\left(f_{n}\right) \rightarrow \varphi_{\tau }(f), \  n \rightarrow \infty\). It therefore suffices to check that the set \(M = \left\{ \varphi_{\tau } \mid \tau \in (a, b]\right\}\) is total in \(\left(L^{p}[a, b]\right)^{*}\). This is true because the spaces \(\left(L^{p}[a, b]\right)^{*}\) and \(L_{q}[a, b]\), where \(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q} = 1\), are isometrically isomorphic (see Theorem 3.3), and the image of the set \(M\) under this isomorphism is the set \(\left\{ \chi_{[a, \tau ]} \mid \tau \in (a, b]\right\}\), which is total in \(L_{q}[a, b]\).


Remark. The criterion for weak convergence in \(L^{p}(\mathbb {R}), 1 < p < +\infty\), is analogous (see Problem 5.7).












ExampleExample 5.3





Investigate the following sequences for strong and weak convergence in the normed space \(V\). For convergent sequences, find their limits.

\(V = \ell^{p}, 1 \leq p < +\infty , \  f^{(n)} = (0, \ldots , 0, \underbrace{\frac{n}{n+1}}_{n}, 0, \ldots )\);
\(V = \ell^{p}, 1 \leq p \leq +\infty , \  f^{(n)} = \left(1, \frac{1}{2}, \ldots , \frac{1}{n}, 0, \ldots \right)\);
\(V = L^{p}[0,1], 1 \leq p \leq +\infty , \  f_{n}(t) = \begin{cases}  n, &  t \in \left[0, \frac{1}{n^{2}}\right], \\ 0, &  t \in \left(\frac{1}{n^{2}}, 1\right]; \end{cases}\)
\(V = L^{p}[0,1], 1 < p < +\infty , \  f_{n}(t) = \sin \pi n t, \  t \in [0,1]\);
\(V = C[0,1], \  f_{n}(t) = \frac{n t^{2}}{1+n^{2} t^{4}}, \  t \in [0,1]\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



If a sequence converges weakly (in particular, if it converges strongly) in \(\ell^{p}\), \(1 \leq p < +\infty\), then it converges coordinatewise. For \(1 < p < +\infty\) this follows from Problem 5.1, part (2), and for \(p = 1\) one may directly consider the functionals \(\varphi_{k}(f) = f_{k}, \  f \in \ell^{1}, \  k \geq 1\). Hence the coordinatewise limit of the sequence is the only “candidate” for a weak or strong limit. For each \(k \geq 1\) we have \(f_{k}^{(n)} = 0, \  n \geq k+1\), so \(f_{k}^{(n)} \rightarrow 0, \  n \rightarrow \infty\). We now investigate the sequence for strong and weak convergence to \(f = 0\).
For all \(1 \leq p < +\infty\) we have
\[
  \left\| f^{(n)}-0\right\| _{p}^{p} = \sum _{k = 1}^{\infty }\left(f_{k}^{(n)}-0\right)^{p} = \left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^{p} \rightarrow 1 \neq 0, \quad n \rightarrow \infty ,
\]
so there is no strong convergence.
Let \(1 < p < +\infty\). We apply the criterion for weak convergence in \(\ell^{p}\). (a) We have \(\left\| f^{(n)}\right\|  = \frac{n}{n+1} \leq 1, \  n \geq 1\). (b) Coordinatewise convergence to zero has already been established. Hence \(f^{(n)} \xrightarrow {w} 0, \  n \rightarrow \infty\).
It remains to consider the case \(p = 1\). Take the functional
\[
  \varphi (f) = \sum _{n = 1}^{\infty } f_{n}, \quad f \in \ell ^{1}.
\]
Then \(\varphi \in \left(\ell^{1}\right)^{*}\), since \((1,1,\ldots ) \in \ell^{\infty }\), and
\[
  \varphi \left(f^{(n)}\right) = \frac{n}{n+1} \rightarrow 1 \neq 0 = \varphi (0), \quad n \rightarrow \infty .
\]
Hence \(f^{(n)} \xrightarrow {w} 0\) fails in \(\ell^{1}\).
Remark. For \(p = +\infty\) the sequence does not converge strongly. Since both the terms of the sequence and the “candidate” limit belong to the subspace \(c_{0}\) of \(\ell^{\infty }\), the sequence converges weakly in \(\ell^{\infty }\) if and only if it converges weakly in \(c_{0}\). One can apply the criterion for weak convergence in \(c_{0}\) (see part (1) of Problem 5.8) to check that this sequence converges weakly.








Enum-item2.



Let us find the coordinatewise limit. For each \(k \geq 1\) we have \(f_{k}^{(n)} = \frac{1}{k}, \  n \geq k+1\), so \(f_{k}^{(n)} \rightarrow \frac{1}{k}, \  n \rightarrow \infty\). Set \(f = \left(1, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{3}, \ldots \right)\) and check whether \(f^{(n)} \rightarrow f\) in \(\ell^{p}\).
For \(p = 1\) we have \(f \notin \ell^{1}\), since the series \(\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty } \frac{1}{n}\) diverges. Hence for \(p = 1\) the sequence converges neither weakly nor strongly.
Let \(1 < p < +\infty\). Then \(f \in \ell^{p}\), since the series \(\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty } \frac{1}{n^{p}}\) converges. We have
\[
  \left\| f^{(n)}-f\right\| _{p}^{p} = \sum _{k = n+1}^{\infty } \frac{1}{k^{p}} \rightarrow 0, \quad n \rightarrow \infty ,
\]
as the tail of a convergent series. Hence \(f^{(n)} \rightarrow f\) in \(\ell^{p}\), and therefore \(f^{(n)} \xrightarrow {w} f\).
For \(p = +\infty\) we have \(f \in \ell^{\infty }\), since the sequence \(\left\{ \frac{1}{k}\right\}\) is bounded. Since
\[
  \left\| f^{(n)}-f\right\| _{\infty } = \sup _{k \geq n+1} \frac{1}{k} = \frac{1}{n+1} \rightarrow 0,
\]
we get \(f^{(n)} \rightarrow f\) in \(\ell^{\infty }\), and hence \(f^{(n)} \xrightarrow {w} f\).








Enum-item3.



Neither strong nor weak convergence in \(L^{p}[0,1]\) generally implies convergence almost everywhere. However, if a limit almost everywhere exists for a given sequence, it is natural to view it as a “candidate” for the limit.
For each \(t \in (0,1]\) there exists \(N\) such that \(\frac{1}{n^{2}} < t\) for \(n \geq N\), so \(f_{n}(t) = 0\) for \(n \geq N\). Hence \(f_{n}(t) \rightarrow 0 = f_{0}(t)\) almost everywhere.
Let \(1 \leq p < +\infty\). Then
\[
  \left\| f_{n}-f_{0}\right\| _{p}^{p} = \int _{0}^{1/n^{2}} n^{p} dt = \frac{1}{n^{2-p}}.
\]
Hence \(f_{n} \rightarrow f_{0}\) in \(L^{p}\) if and only if \(p < 2\).
For \(p = 2\) there is weak but not strong convergence. For \(p > 2\) the sequence is unbounded and hence converges neither weakly nor strongly.








Enum-item4.



Set \(f_{0}(t) = 0\). Then by the criterion for weak convergence we have \(f_{n} \xrightarrow {w} f_{0}\), but
\[
  \left\| f_{n}\right\| _{p}^{p} = \frac{1}{\pi }\int _{0}^{\pi }|\sin s|^{p} ds \nrightarrow 0,
\]
so there is no strong convergence.






Note



Figure under development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: : \(f_n(t)=\sin(\pi n t)\) on \([0,1]\) for \(n=2,5,15\) (numpy, step depends on \(n\) to avoid aliasing when drawing, deterministic, no seed needed). The amplitude/norm does not change as \(n\) grows (\(\|f_n\|_p\) does not depend on \(n\), see the solution in the text), but \(f_n \to 0\) weakly: the integral against any smooth/continuous “test” function is damped by the fast sign-alternating oscillations (a Riemann-Lebesgue-lemma-type effect). Interactive: slider over \(n\) (non-integer values allowed via frequency interpolation), with a running plot of \(\int_0^t f_n\) and a visual “damping” of the area as \(n\) grows.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/FA/contents/specials/080/010_weak_oscillation_fig.tex










Enum-item5.



By the criterion for weak convergence in \(C[0,1]\), the coordinatewise limit is \(f_{0}(t)=0\). However
\[
  \left\| f_{n}\right\|  = \frac{1}{2},
\]
so there is no strong convergence, but there is weak convergence: \(f_{n} \xrightarrow {w} f_{0}\).
crumbs: 8. Weak convergence in a Banach space

title: Weak convergence in a Banach space
text:
1.2 Weak-* convergence
Let us recall a fundamental theorem.







Theorem 3 (Banach–Steinhaus; the uniform boundedness principle) Let \(V\) be a Banach space, and let \(\left\{ \varphi_\alpha : \alpha \in A\right\}\) be a family of functionals from \(V^*\) that is bounded at every point. Then this family is bounded (uniformly, in the norm of \(V^*\)): there exists \(C>0\) such that \[
  \left\| \varphi _{\alpha }\right\|  \leq C \qquad \forall \alpha \in A
\]











Definition 2 Let \(V\) be a normed space.

A sequence \(\left\{ \varphi_n: n \geq 1\right\}\) of functionals from \(V^*\) is said to converge weak-* to a functional \(\varphi \in V\) if its action on every vector of \(V\) converges:
\[
  \varphi _n\left(f\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \varphi (f), \qquad \forall f \in V
\]
Notation: \(\varphi_n \xrightarrow {w-*} \varphi\).
A sequence \(\left\{ \varphi_n: n \geq 1\right\}  \subset V^*\) is said to converge strongly to \(\varphi \in V^*\) if \(\varphi_n\) converges to \(\varphi\) in \(V^*\) in the usual sense, i.e., in norm.












Theorem 4 (Criterion for weak-* convergence of functionals) Let \(V\) be a Banach space, \(\left\{ \varphi_n: n \geq 1\right\}  \subset V^*, \varphi \in V^*\). Then \(\varphi_n \xrightarrow {w-*} \varphi\) if and only if the following conditions hold:

\(\left\{ \varphi_n\right\}\) is bounded in \(V^*\): the set of norms \(\left\{ \left\| \varphi_n\right\| \right\}\) is bounded;
there is a total set \(M\) in \(V\) such that \(\varphi_n(f) \rightarrow \varphi (f)\) for all \(f \in M\).












Theorem 5 (The dual space of a Banach space is weak-* complete) Let \(V\) be a Banach space, and let a sequence of functionals \(\left\{ \varphi_n: n \geq 1\right\}  \subset V^*\) be a weak-* Cauchy sequence, i.e., for every \(f \in V\) the sequence \(\left\{ \varphi_n(f): n \geq 1\right\}\) is a Cauchy sequence. Then there exists a functional \(\varphi \in V^*\) such that \(\varphi_n \xrightarrow {w-*} \varphi , n \rightarrow \infty\).











Theorem 6 (Banach–Alaoglu; weak-* compactness of the ball in the dual space) Let \(V\) be a separable normed space, \(R>0\). Then every sequence of functionals from the ball \(\bar{B}(0, R)= \left\{ \varphi \in V^* \mid \| \varphi \|  \leq R\right\}\) in \(V^*\) has a subsequence that converges weak-* to some functional in \(V^*\).










ExampleExample 5.4





Prove that the sequence of functionals \(\left\{ \varphi_{n}: n \geq 1\right\}  \subset V^{*}\) converges weak-*, if

\(V = L^{1}[a, b], \  \varphi_{n}(f) = \int_{a}^{b} f(t) e^{i n t} d t ;\)
\(V = L^{p}[0,1], \  2 \leq p < +\infty , \  \varphi_{n}(f) = \int_{0}^{1 / n^{2}} n f(t) d t\);
\(V = C[0,1], \  \varphi_{n}(f) = \sqrt{n} \int_{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}}^{1} f(t) d t\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



We apply the criterion for weak-* convergence of functionals. Let us verify its conditions.

Boundedness? Set \(h_{n}(t) = e^{i n t}, \  t \in [a, b]\). Since \(h_{n} \in L^{\infty }[a, b]\), Theorem 3.3 gives \(\varphi_{n} \in V^{*}\) and

\[
  \left\| \varphi _{n}\right\|  = \left\| h_{n}\right\| _{\infty } = 1.
\]

Convergence on some total set? The set \(M = \left\{ \; \mathbb {1}_{[a, s]} \mid s \in [a, b]\right\}\) of indicators of intervals is total in \(L^{1}[a, b]\). For an arbitrary \(f = \; \mathbb {1}_{[a, s]} \in M\) we have

\[
  \left|\varphi _{n}(f)\right| = \left|\int _{a}^{s} e^{i n t} d t\right| = \left|\frac{e^{i n s}-e^{i n a}}{i n}\right| \leq \frac{2}{n} \rightarrow 0, \quad n \rightarrow \infty .
\]
Hence \(\varphi_{n} \xrightarrow {w-*} 0, \  n \rightarrow \infty\), in \(\left(L^{1}[a, b]\right)^{*}\).
Remark. This convergence means that
\[
  \int _{a}^{b} f(t) e^{i n t} d t \rightarrow 0, \quad n \rightarrow \infty ,
\]
for all \(f \in L^{1}[a, b]\) (the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma).








Enum-item2.



If \(\left\{ \varphi_{n}: n \geq 0\right\}  \subset \left(L^{p}[a, b]\right)^{*}\), then
\[
  \varphi _{n}(f) = \int _{a}^{b} h_{n}(t) f(t) d t, \quad n \geq 0,
\]
where \(h_{n} \in L^{q}[a, b]\) and \(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q} = 1\). By definition, \(\varphi_{n} \xrightarrow {w-*} \varphi_{0}, \  n \rightarrow \infty\), if and only if
\[
  \forall f \in L^{p}[a, b]: \int _{a}^{b} h_{n}(t) f(t) d t \rightarrow \int _{a}^{b} h_{0}(t) f(t) d t, \quad n \rightarrow \infty .
\]
This is equivalent to weak convergence \(h_{n} \xrightarrow {w} h_{0}, \  n \rightarrow \infty\), in \(L^{q}[a, b]\). In our case \([a, b] = [0,1]\) and
\[
  h_{n}(t) = \begin{cases}  n, &  t \in \left[0, \frac{1}{n^{2}}\right], \\ 0, &  t \in \left(\frac{1}{n^{2}}, 1\right], \end{cases} \quad n \geq 1.
\]
One can show that \(h_{n} \xrightarrow {w} 0 = h_{0}, \  n \rightarrow \infty\), in \(L^{q}[0,1]\) for \(1 < q \leq 2\). Hence \(\varphi_{n} \xrightarrow {w-*} 0, \  n \rightarrow \infty\), in \(\left(L^{p}[0,1]\right)^{*}\) for \(2 \leq p < +\infty\).








Enum-item3.



Set \(\varphi (f) = f(1), \  f \in C[0,1]\). We show that \(\varphi_{n} \xrightarrow {w-*} \varphi , \  n \rightarrow \infty\). First consider the space of real-valued functions \(C[0,1]\). By the mean value theorem for the Riemann integral, for every function \(f \in C[0,1]\) and every \(n \geq 1\) there exists \(\theta_{n} \in \left[1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}, 1\right]\) such that
\[
  \varphi _{n}(f) = f\left(\theta _{n}\right), \quad n \geq 1.
\]
Since \(\theta_{n} \rightarrow 1\), \(n \rightarrow \infty\), and \(f \in C[0,1]\), we get
\[
  \varphi _{n}(f) = f\left(\theta _{n}\right) \rightarrow f(1) = \varphi (f), \quad n \rightarrow \infty .
\]
Similarly, in the complex space \(C[0,1]\), for every function \(f \in C[0,1]\) there exist \(\theta_{n}^{\prime }, \theta_{n}^{\prime \prime } \in \left[1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}, 1\right]\) such that
\[
  \varphi _{n}(f) = \operatorname {Re} f\left(\theta _{n}^{\prime }\right) + i \operatorname {Im} f\left(\theta _{n}^{\prime \prime }\right) \rightarrow f(1) = \varphi (f), \quad n \rightarrow \infty .
\]
By definition this means that \(\varphi_{n} \xrightarrow {w-*} \varphi , \  n \rightarrow \infty\), in \((C[0,1])^{*}\).














ProblemProblem 1





Find the closure of the unit sphere of the space \(\ell^{2}\) in the sense of weak convergence.
[@VKK, Problem  10.1]









ProblemProblem 2





Is a Hilbert space (an arbitrary Banach space) complete in the sense of weak convergence?
[@VKK, Problem  10.2]









ExampleExample 5





The spaces \(C[0,1]\), \(c_0\), \(c\) are not complete in the sense of weak convergence. Show this.






SolutionSolution






\(c_0\). Let \(f^{(n)} = (\underbrace{1,\ldots ,1}_{n},0,0,\ldots )\). Since \((c_0)^* \cong \ell^1\), for any \(g \in \ell^1\) we have \(\varphi_g(f^{(n)}) = \sum_{k=1}^n g_k \to \sum_{k=1}^\infty g_k\) (the series converges absolutely) — so \((f^{(n)})\) is weakly Cauchy. If it converged weakly to some \(f \in c_0\), then applying \(\varphi_g\) with \(g=e_k\) (the coordinate functional) would give \(f_k = \lim_n f^{(n)}_k = 1\) for every \(k\), i.e., \(f=(1,1,\ldots )\) — but this is not an element of \(c_0\) (it does not tend to \(0\)). Hence there is no weak limit in \(c_0\).
\(c\). The same sequence \(f^{(n)}\): it is weakly Cauchy in \(c\) as well (this follows from the representation \(c^* \cong \mathbb {R} \oplus \ell^1\): a functional has the form \(\varphi (x) = \alpha \lim_k x_k + \sum_k \beta_k x_k\), \((\beta_k)\in \ell^1\); then \(\varphi (f^{(n)}) = \alpha \cdot 0 + \sum_{k=1}^n\beta_k \to \sum_k\beta_k\), since \(\lim_kf^{(n)}_k=0\) for every finite \(n\)). If a limit \(f\in c\) existed, then the coordinate functionals (\(\alpha =0,\beta =e_k\)) would again give \(f_k=1\) for all \(k\), i.e., \(f=(1,1,\ldots )\); but the “limit” functional (\(\alpha =1,\beta =0\)) gives a contradiction: \(\varphi (f^{(n)}) = 0 \to 0\), whereas it should converge to \(\varphi (f)=\lim_kf_k=1\). Hence there is no weak limit in \(c\) either.
\(C[0,1]\). Let \(f_n(t) = t^n\). For any finite Borel measure \(\mu\) on \([0,1]\) (by the Riesz representation theorem, \(C[0,1]^*\) consists of such measures), the dominated convergence theorem (\(|t^n|\leq 1\)) gives \(\int_0^1 t^n\, d\mu (t) \to \mu (\left\{ 1\right\} )\) — the limit exists, i.e., \((f_n)\) is weakly Cauchy. If \(f_n \xrightarrow {w} f\) for some \(f \in C[0,1]\), then in particular the point-evaluation functionals \(\varphi_t(g)=g(t)\) would give \(f(t) = \lim_n t^n = 0\) for \(t<1\) and \(f(1)=1\) — a discontinuous function, not lying in \(C[0,1]\). Contradiction; there is no weak limit.













ProblemProblem 3





Let \(V\) be a Hilbert space, \(f_n \xrightarrow {} f\), \(g_{n} \xrightarrow {w} g\). Prove that \[
  \left\langle f_n, g_n \right\rangle \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \left\langle f, g \right\rangle
\] Can the strong convergence condition \(f_n \xrightarrow {} f\) be replaced by the weaker one \(f_{n} \xrightarrow {w} f\)?
[@VKK, Problem  10.8]









ProblemProblem 4





Let a sequence \(f_{n}\) in a Hilbert space \(V\) converge weakly to \(f\), with the norms also converging: \[
  \left\| f_n\right\|  \xrightarrow [n\to \infty ]{}\left\| f\right\|
\] Prove that \(f_n \xrightarrow {} f\). Is this statement true for an arbitrary Banach space?
[@VKK, Problem  10.9]

title: Weak convergence in a Banach space
text:
1.3 Compact operators and weak convergence







Lemma 5 Let \(V\) and \(W\) be Banach spaces, and let \(T: V \rightarrow W\) be a compact operator. If \(f_{n} \xrightarrow {w} f\), then \(T f_{n} \rightarrow T f\).











Lemma 6 Let \(V\) and \(W\) be Hilbert spaces and \(T \in \mathcal{B}(H, K)\). Then \(T\) is compact if and only if, for every sequence \(\left(f_{n}\right) \subset V\) converging weakly to \(f\), the sequence \((T f_{n})\) converges (strongly) to \(Tf\) in \(W\).

title: Generalized functions
text:
2.1 Regular distributions
A Lebesgue measurable function \(T: \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {C}\) is called locally integrable if \(T \in L^1([a,b])\) for all \(a<b\). The set of such functions is denoted \(L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb {R})\).
A regular generalized function in \(\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\) is a functional of the form
\[
  \langle T, f\rangle = \int _{\mathbb {R}} T(x)f(x)\, dx,
\]
where \(T \in L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb {R})\). The following statement holds.
Lemma 14.1 (du Bois-Reymond). Let \(G\) be an open subset of \(\mathbb {R}\), and let the function \(T: G \to \mathbb {C}\) be locally integrable on \(G\). If, for every \(f \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R})\) with support in \(G\),
\[
  \int _{\mathbb {R}} T(x)f(x)\, dx = 0,
\]
then \(T(x)=0\) almost everywhere in \(G\).
It follows from this lemma that there is a one-to-one correspondence between the space \(L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb {R})\) and the space of regular generalized functions. Thus a function \(T \in L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb {R})\) can be identified with the corresponding regular generalized function. For example:
\[
  \langle 1, f\rangle = \int _{\mathbb {R}} 1 \cdot f(x)\, dx = \int _{\mathbb {R}} f(x)\, dx, \quad f \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R}).
\]
If \(T \in C(\mathbb {R})\), then \(\operatorname {supp} T\) as the support of the generalized function coincides with \(\operatorname {supp} T\) as the support of the classical function.

title: Generalized functions
text:
2.2 Singular distributions
Every generalized function that is not regular is called singular. For example, the Dirac delta function \(\delta\), defined by \(\langle \delta , f\rangle = f(0)\), \(f \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R})\), is singular. The shifted delta function \(\delta_a\), \(a \in \mathbb {R}\), is defined by \(\langle \delta_a, f \rangle = f(a)\), and is also singular. In particular, \(\delta_0 = \delta\).






ExampleExample 1





Prove that the series \(\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty } a_n \delta_n\) converges in the space \(\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\) for any \(a_n \in \mathbb {C}\).






SolutionSolution





For each \(N \in \mathbb {N}\), the partial sum \(S_N = \sum_{n = 1}^{N} a_n \delta_n\) belongs to the space \(\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\), since it is a linear combination of shifted delta functions. Let \(\varphi \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R})\). There exists \(m \in \mathbb {N}\) such that \(\varphi (x) = 0\) for \(|x| > m\). Then for all \(N \ge m\) we have
\[
  \left\langle S_N, \varphi \right\rangle = \sum _{n = 1}^{N} a_n \varphi (n) = \sum _{n = 1}^{m} a_n \varphi (n) \rightarrow \sum _{n = 1}^{m} a_n \varphi (n) \in \mathbb {C}, \quad N \to \infty .
\]
By the completeness of the space \(\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\), there exists \(S \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\) such that \(S_N \xrightarrow {\mathcal{D}’(\mathbb {R})} S\), so the series converges to \(S\) in \(\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\).












ExampleExample 2





Prove that the functional \(\mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}\), defined by \[
  \left(\mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}\right)(\varphi ) = \text{p.v.} \int _{\mathbb {R}} \frac{\varphi (x)}{x} \,  dx := \lim _{\varepsilon \to 0+} \int _{\mathbb {R} \setminus (-\varepsilon , \varepsilon )} \frac{\varphi (x)}{x} \,  dx, \quad \varphi \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R}),
\] is a singular generalized function.






SolutionSolution





First we show that the limit exists. For \(0 < \varepsilon < 1\) and \(\varphi \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R})\) we have
\[
  \int _{\mathbb {R} \setminus (-\varepsilon , \varepsilon )} \frac{\varphi (x)}{x} \,  dx = \int _{\mathbb {R} \setminus (-1,1)} \frac{\varphi (x)}{x} \,  dx + \int _{[-1,1] \setminus (-\varepsilon , \varepsilon )} \frac{\varphi (x) - \varphi (0)}{x} \,  dx.
\]
The limit \(\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\varphi (x) - \varphi (0)}{x} = \varphi '(0)\) exists, so the integral \(\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{\varphi (x) - \varphi (0)}{x} \,  dx\) exists as a Riemann integral. Therefore,
\[
  \lim _{\varepsilon \to 0+} \int _{\mathbb {R} \setminus (-\varepsilon , \varepsilon )} \frac{\varphi (x)}{x} \,  dx = \int _{\mathbb {R} \setminus (-1,1)} \frac{\varphi (x)}{x} \,  dx + \int _{-1}^{1} \frac{\varphi (x) - \varphi (0)}{x} \,  dx,
\]
that is, the functional \(\mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}\) is well-defined. Linearity of \(\mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}\) is clear from its representation. Let us prove its continuity by estimating \(\left|\left\langle \mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}, \varphi \right\rangle \right|\) for \(\operatorname {supp} \varphi \subset [-a, a]\), where \(a > 1\). We have
\[
  \left|\left\langle \mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}, \varphi \right\rangle \right| \le \int _{[-a,a] \setminus (-1,1)} |\varphi (x)| \,  dx + \int _{-1}^{1} \frac{|\varphi (x) - \varphi (0)|}{|x|} \,  dx.
\]
Further, for \(x \ne 0\), by the mean value theorem,
\[
  \left|\frac{\varphi (x) - \varphi (0)}{x}\right| = |\varphi '(\theta _x)| \le \max _{x \in \mathbb {R}} |\varphi '(x)|,
\]
where \(\theta_x\) is an intermediate point between \(0\) and \(x\). Then
\[
  \left|\left\langle \mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}, \varphi \right\rangle \right| \le 2a \cdot \max _{x \in \mathbb {R}} |\varphi (x)| + 2 \max _{x \in \mathbb {R}} |\varphi '(x)|.
\]
It suffices to prove continuity of the functional at zero. Let \(\varphi_n \xrightarrow {\mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R})} 0\), \(n \to \infty\). Then there exists \(a > 1\) such that \(\operatorname {supp} \varphi_n \subset [-a,a]\) for all \(n \ge 1\). Since \(\varphi_n \rightrightarrows 0\) and \(\varphi_n' \rightrightarrows 0\) on \(\mathbb {R}\) as \(n \to \infty\), we have
\[
  \left|\left\langle \mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}, \varphi _n \right\rangle \right| \le 2a \cdot \max _{x \in \mathbb {R}} |\varphi _n(x)| + 2 \max _{x \in \mathbb {R}} |\varphi _n'(x)| \to 0, \quad n \to \infty .
\]
Therefore,
\[
  \left|\left\langle \mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}, \varphi _n \right\rangle \right| \to 0 = \left|\left\langle \mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}, 0 \right\rangle \right|, \quad n \to \infty .
\]
This means that \(\mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}\) is a continuous linear functional, that is, \(\mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x} \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\).
Suppose that \(\mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}\) is a regular distribution, that is, \(\exists f \in L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb {R})\) such that for all \(\varphi \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R})\)
\[
  \left\langle \mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}, \varphi \right\rangle = \lim _{\varepsilon \to 0+} \int _{\mathbb {R} \setminus (-\varepsilon , \varepsilon )} \frac{\varphi (x)}{x} \,  dx = \int _{\mathbb {R}} f(x) \varphi (x) \,  dx.
\]
If \(\operatorname {supp} \varphi \subset \mathbb {R} \setminus \{ 0\}\), then \(\int_{\mathbb {R} \setminus (-\varepsilon , \varepsilon )} \frac{\varphi (x)}{x} \,  dx = \int_{\mathbb {R}} \frac{\varphi (x)}{x} \,  dx\) for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon > 0\). Then \(\int_{\mathbb {R}} \left(\frac{1}{x} - f(x)\right)\varphi (x) \,  dx = 0\), and by the du Bois-Reymond lemma we get \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\) almost everywhere on \(\mathbb {R} \setminus \{ 0\}\). But \(f \notin L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb {R})\) — a contradiction. Therefore \(\mathcal{P} \frac{1}{x}\) is a singular distribution.












ExampleExample 3





Let, for \(n \in \mathbb {N}\), the function \(\mathcal{P} \frac{\cos nx}{x}\) be defined by \[
  \left\langle \mathcal{P} \frac{\cos nx}{x}, \varphi \right\rangle = \text{p.v.} \int _{\mathbb {R}} \frac{\cos nx}{x} \varphi (x) \,  dx := \lim _{\varepsilon \to 0+} \int _{\mathbb {R} \setminus (-\varepsilon , \varepsilon )} \frac{\cos nx}{x} \varphi (x) \,  dx, \quad \varphi \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R}).
\] Prove that \(\mathcal{P} \frac{\cos nx}{x} \xrightarrow {\mathcal{D}’(\mathbb {R})} 0\) as \(n \to \infty\).






SolutionSolution





As in the solution of the previous example, we have
\[
  \left\langle \mathcal{P} \frac{\cos nx}{x}, \varphi \right\rangle = \int _{\mathbb {R} \setminus (-1,1)} \frac{\cos nx}{x} \varphi (x) \,  dx + \int _{-1}^{1} \frac{\cos nx}{x} (\varphi (x) - \varphi (0)) \,  dx.
\]
Let \(\varphi \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R})\) with \(\varphi (x) = 0\) for \(|x| > a\), where \(a > 1\). Then
\[
  \left\langle \mathcal{P} \frac{\cos nx}{x}, \varphi \right\rangle = \int _{-a}^{-1} \cos nx \,  \frac{\varphi (x)}{x} \,  dx + \int _{-1}^{1} \cos nx \,  \frac{\varphi (x) - \varphi (0)}{x} \,  dx + \int _{1}^{a} \cos nx \,  \frac{\varphi (x)}{x} \,  dx.
\]
Define the function \(\frac{\varphi (x) - \varphi (0)}{x}\) continuously at \(x=0\) by setting it equal to \(\varphi '(0)\). Then each of the integrands is a product of \(\cos nx\) and some continuous function. By the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma, each of the three integrals tends to zero as \(n \to \infty\). Therefore \(\left\langle \mathcal{P} \frac{\cos nx}{x}, \varphi \right\rangle \to 0 = \langle 0, \varphi \rangle\), \(n \to \infty\). Thus \(\mathcal{P} \frac{\cos nx}{x} \xrightarrow {\mathcal{D}’(\mathbb {R})} 0\), \(n \to \infty\).












ExampleExample 4





Find the limit in \(\mathcal{D}^{\prime }\) of the following sequences:

\(\frac{1}{\varepsilon } e^{-|x| / \varepsilon }\) as \(\varepsilon \rightarrow +0\);
\(\frac{1}{\pi } \frac{\sin n x}{x}\) as \(n \rightarrow +\infty\).

[@BSSH, Problem  16.21]






SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Let us split the integral:
\[
\begin{align}  \left\langle \frac{1}{\varepsilon } e^{-|x|/\varepsilon }, \varphi \right\rangle & = \frac{1}{\varepsilon } \int _{-\infty }^{0} e^{x/\varepsilon } \varphi (x) dx + \frac{1}{\varepsilon } \int _{0}^{\infty } e^{-x/\varepsilon } \varphi (x) dx \\ & = \int _{-\infty }^{0} e^{y} \varphi (\varepsilon y) dy + \int _{0}^{\infty } e^{-y} \varphi (\varepsilon y) dy \to \varphi (0) \int _{-\infty }^{0} e^{y} dy + \varphi (0) \int _{0}^{\infty } e^{-y} dy \\ & = \varphi (0)(1 + 1) = 2\varphi (0). \end{align}
\]
The limit is \(2\delta (x)\).








Enum-item2.



This is the Dirichlet kernel. For every \(\varphi \in \mathcal{D}\):
\[
  \left\langle \frac{1}{\pi } \frac{\sin nx}{x}, \varphi \right\rangle = \frac{1}{\pi } \int _{-\infty }^{\infty } \frac{\sin nx}{x} \varphi (x) dx = \frac{1}{\pi } \int _{-\infty }^{\infty } \frac{\sin y}{y} \varphi \left(\frac{y}{n}\right) dy \to \varphi (0) \frac{1}{\pi } \int _{-\infty }^{\infty } \frac{\sin y}{y} dy = \varphi (0).
\]
The limit is \(\delta (x)\).











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(2 \delta_{0}\);








Enum-item2.



\(\delta_{0}\).

\(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon }} e^{-x^{2} / \varepsilon }\) as \(\varepsilon \rightarrow +0\);

title: Generalized functions
text:
2.3 Multiplication by smooth functions
The product of a function \(\alpha (x) \in C^{\infty }(\mathbb {R})\) and a generalized function \(T \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\) is defined as the generalized function \(\alpha T\), given by the rule \(\langle \alpha T, f \rangle = \langle T, \alpha f \rangle\), \(f \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R})\).

title: Generalized functions
text:
2.4 Change of variables
Let \(T \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\), \(a, b \in \mathbb {R}\), \(a \ne 0\). Then the generalized function \(T(a x + b)\) is defined by
\[
  \langle T(a x + b), f(x)\rangle = \frac{1}{|a|}\left\langle T(t), f\left(\frac{t - b}{a}\right)\right\rangle , \quad f \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R}).
\]
For \(a=1\) we have \(\langle T(x+b), f(x)\rangle = \langle T(t), f(t - b)\rangle\), which corresponds to a shift of the generalized function \(T\) by \((-b)\). In particular,
\[
  \langle \delta (x - x_0), f(x)\rangle = \langle \delta (t), f(t + x_0)\rangle = f(x_0) = \langle \delta _{x_0}, f\rangle ,
\]
hence \(\delta (x - x_0) = \delta_{x_0}\) is the shifted delta function.
Let \(T \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R}^{m})\), let \(A\) be a nonsingular \(m \times m\) matrix, and \(b \in \mathbb {R}^{m}\). Then
\[
  \langle T(Ay + b), f(y)\rangle = \left\langle T(x), \frac{f(A^{-1}(x - b))}{|\det A|} \right\rangle , \quad f \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R}^{m}).
\]
In particular, if \(A = aI\), \(a \ne 0\), then
\[
  \langle T(a y + b), f(y)\rangle = \left\langle T(x), \frac{f\left(\frac{x - b}{a}\right)}{a^m} \right\rangle .
\]

title: Generalized functions
text:
3.1 Differential equations
If a generalized function \(T\) satisfies the equation \(T' = 0\), then \(T = \text{const}\), that is, there exists \(C \in \mathbb {C}\) such that
\[
  \langle T, f\rangle = \langle C, f\rangle = C \int _{\mathbb {R}} f(x)\, dx, \quad \forall f \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R}).
\]
Let \(a_k \in C^{\infty }(\mathbb {R})\), \(0 \le k \le m\). Consider the differential operator
\[
  L y = \sum _{k=0}^{m} a_k(x) y^{(k)}, \quad y \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R}).
\]
Let \(T \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\). A generalized solution of the equation \(L y = T\) is a generalized function \(y \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\) satisfying this equation in the space \(\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\), that is,
\[
  \left\langle \sum _{k=0}^{m} a_k y^{(k)}, f \right\rangle = \left\langle y, \sum _{k=0}^{m} (-1)^k (a_k f)^{(k)} \right\rangle = \langle T, f \rangle , \quad \forall f \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R}).
\]
Any solution can be represented as the sum of a particular solution and the general solution of the homogeneous equation \(L y = 0\).
Let \(T, g: \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {C}\), \(T, g \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\). The function
\[
  h(x) = \int _{\mathbb {R}} T(t) g(x - t)\, dt, \quad x \in \mathbb {R},
\]
is called the convolution of the functions \(T\) and \(g\) and is denoted \(T * g\). Then \(h \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\).
Let \(T \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb {R})\), \(f \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R})\). Their convolution is defined as
\[
  (T * f)(x) = \langle T(y), f(x - y)\rangle , \quad x \in \mathbb {R}.
\]
On the right-hand side the generalized function \(T(y)\) acts on the test function \(\psi (y) = f(x - y)\), where \(x\) is regarded as a parameter. If \(T \in L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb {R})\), then
\[
  (T * f)(x) = \int _{\mathbb {R}} T(y) f(x - y)\, dy, \quad x \in \mathbb {R}.
\]

title: Generalized functions
text:
3.2 Fundamental solution
Consider the differential operator with constant coefficients
\[
  L = D^n + a_1 D^{n-1} + \ldots + a_{n-1} D + a_n I, \quad n \ge 1, \quad a_1, \ldots , a_n \in \mathbb {C}.
\]
A generalized function \(\mathcal{E}\) is called a fundamental solution of the operator \(L\) if \(L \mathcal{E} = \delta_0\). Let \(z\) be the solution of the Cauchy problem
\[
  L z = 0, \quad z(0)=z'(0)=\ldots =z^{(n-2)}(0)=0, \quad z^{(n-1)}(0)=1.
\]
Then the fundamental solution of the operator \(L\) is the locally integrable function
\[
  \mathcal{E}(x) = \theta (x) z(x), \quad x \in \mathbb {R},
\]
where \(\theta (x) = \chi_{[0, +\infty )}(x)\) is the Heaviside function. For \(f \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb {R})\), the linear inhomogeneous differential equation \(L u = f\), \(u \in C^{\infty }(\mathbb {R})\), has a particular solution \(u(x) = (\mathcal{E} * f)(x)\).






ExampleExample 6





Solve the following differential equations in \(\mathcal{D}^{\prime }\):

\(F^{\prime }+F = \delta_{0}\);
\(F^{\prime \prime }+F = \delta_{0}\);
\(x F^{\prime } = 1\);

[@BSSH, Problem  16.44]






SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



The equation \(F' + F = \delta_0\). The homogeneous equation \(F' + F = 0\) has the solution \(Ce^{-x}\). A particular solution: \(H(x)e^{-x}\), where \(H(x)\) is the Heaviside function. Let us check:
\[
  (H(x)e^{-x})' + H(x)e^{-x} = \delta (x)e^{-x} - H(x)e^{-x} + H(x)e^{-x} = \delta (x).
\]
General solution: \(F(x) = Ce^{-x} + H(x)e^{-x}\).








Enum-item2.



The equation \(F'' + F = \delta_0\). Homogeneous solution: \(C_1 \cos x + C_2 \sin x\). A particular solution: \(H(x)\sin x\). Let us check (using \(\delta (x)g(x)=g(0)\delta (x)\) for continuous \(g\)):
\[
\begin{align}  (H(x)\sin x)' & = \delta (x)\sin x + H(x)\cos x = \sin (0)\delta (x) + H(x)\cos x = H(x)\cos x, \\ (H(x)\sin x)'' & = \delta (x)\cos x - H(x)\sin x = \cos (0)\delta (x) - H(x)\sin x = \delta (x) - H(x)\sin x, \\ (H(x)\sin x)'' + H(x)\sin x & = \delta (x). \end{align}
\]
So \(H(x)\sin x\) is indeed a particular solution. General solution:
\[
  F(x) = C_1 \cos x + C_2 \sin x + H(x)\sin x.
\]








Enum-item3.



The equation \(xF' = 1\). In the classical sense on \(\mathbb {R}\setminus \{ 0\}\), the solution is: \(F(x) = \ln |x| + C\); indeed, \(x \cdot (\ln |x|)' = x \cdot \mathcal P\frac1x = 1\) (with no p.v. effects, since \(x\cdot \frac{\varphi (x)}{x}=\varphi (x)\) is already regular). The homogeneous equation \(xG'=0\) means \(G' = c_1\delta_0\) (the general solution of \(xf=0\) in \(\mathcal D'\) is \(f=c\delta_0\)), whence \(G = c_1\theta (x) + c_2\) (since \(\theta '=\delta_0\), and two solutions with the same derivative differ by a constant). Altogether, in \(\mathcal{D}'\):
\[
  F(x) = \ln |x| + c_1\theta (x) + c_2.
\]
(The term \(c_2\delta (x)\) cannot be added here: \(x\left(\ln |x|+c_2\delta (x)\right)' = 1 + c_2\, x\delta '(x) = 1 - c_2\delta (x) \neq 1\) for \(c_2\neq 0\), since \(x\delta '(x)=-\delta (x)\).)











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(e^{-x}(\theta (x)+C)\), where \(C\) is an arbitrary number;








Enum-item2.



\(\theta (x) \sin x+A \cos x+B \sin x\), where \(A\) and \(B\) are arbitrary numbers;








Enum-item3.



\(\ln |x|+c_{1} \theta (x)+c_{2}\), where \(c_{j} \in \mathbb {C}\);

\(F^{(n)} = 0\);

title: Lebesgue spaces
text:
WarningDraft



This set of notes is still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished spots. If you find any, please let the author know (contact information on the course page).



1 \(\mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\)
Our next main goal is to define an important class of vector spaces generalizing the spaces \(\ell^p\) defined earlier.
Let \((X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\) be a measure space, \(0 < p < \infty\), and let \(f: X \to \mathbb {F}\) be \(\mathcal{S}\)-measurable. Then the \(p\)-norm of \(f\) is denoted \(\left\| f\right\|_{p}\) and is defined as
\[
  \left\| f\right\| _{p} = \left( \int |f|^p d\mu \right)^{1/p}.
\]
where the integral in parentheses is the Lebesgue integral. Also, \(\left\| f\right\|_{\infty }\), called the essential supremum of \(f\), is defined as
\[
  \left\| f\right\| _{\infty } = \inf \{  t > 0 : \mu (\{ x \in X : |f(x)| > t\} ) = 0 \} .
\]
For \(0 < p < \infty\), the \(p\)-norm \(\left\| f\right\|_{p}\) does not change if \(f\) is altered on a set of \(\mu\)-measure zero. By using the essential supremum instead of the ordinary supremum in the definition of \(\left\| f\right\|_{\infty }\), we ensure that the \(\infty\)-norm has the same property. Think of \(\left\| f\right\|_{\infty }\) as the smallest value that can be obtained for the supremum of \(\left|f\right|\) after modifications on sets of measure zero.







Definition 1 Let \((X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\) be a measure space and \(0 < p \leq \infty\). The Lebesgue space \(\mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\), sometimes denoted \(\mathcal{L}^p(X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\), is defined as the set of \(\mathcal{S}\)-measurable functions \(f: X \to \mathbb {F}\) such that \(\left\| f\right\|_{p} < \infty\).










ExampleExample 1





Show that the previously introduced sequence spaces \(\ell^{p}\) and \(\ell^{\infty }\) are special cases of Lebesgue spaces.
Show that the previously introduced spaces \(\mathbb {F}^{n}\) with the norm \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{p}\) are also special cases of Lebesgue spaces.






SolutionSolution






\(\ell^{p}\) and \(\ell^{\infty }\) are sequence spaces, i.e., spaces of functions from \(\mathbb {N}\) into the field \(\mathbb {F}\). So here \(X = \mathbb {N}\), \(\mathcal{S} = 2^{\mathbb {N}}\).
Next, we need to define the measure. In which case does the Lebesgue integral simply turn into a sum over all values? This is the case if \(\mu\) is the counting measure \(\#\):
\[
  \# (A) = \begin{cases}  \left|A\right|, &  A \text{ is finite} \\ +\infty , &  \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \qquad A \subset \mathbb {N}
\]
Hence,
\[
  \ell ^{p} = \mathcal{L}^{p}(\mathbb {N}, 2^{\mathbb {N}}, \# )
\]
for \(0 < p \leq +\infty\).
The vector space \(\mathbb {F}^{n}\) of tuples of length \(n\) of scalars from the field \(\mathbb {F}\) can be identified with \(\mathbb {F}^{\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\} }\), i.e., the space of functions from \(\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\}\) into \(\mathbb {F}\). For example, for \(n=4\) the tuple \((-2, \pi , 5.4, 0)\) corresponds to the function
\[
  f(k) = \begin{cases}  -2, & k = 1 \\ \pi , &  k = 2\\ 5.4, &  k = 3 \\ 0, &  k = 4 \end{cases}
\]
The vector spaces \(\mathbb {F}^{n}\) and \(\mathbb {F}^{\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\} }\) are isomorphic, so we will often use them interchangeably. The norm
\[
  \left\| x\right\| _{p} = \begin{cases}  \left(\sum _{k=1}^{n}\left|x_k\right|^p\right)^{1/p}, &  p < +\infty \\ \max _{k \in \left\{ 1,\ldots , n\right\} }\left|x_k\right|, &  p = +\infty \end{cases}
\]
carries over under this isomorphism from \(\mathbb {F}^{n}\) to \(\mathbb {F}^{\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\} }\), and moreover, up to an isometric (i.e., norm-preserving) isomorphism of normed spaces we may write
\[
  \left(\mathbb {F}^{n}, \left\| \cdot \right\| _{p}\right) = \left(\mathbb {F}^{\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\} }, \left\| \cdot \right\| _{p}\right) = \mathcal{L}^p\left(\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\} , 2^{\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\} }, \# \right)
\]
again with the counting measure.
In general, \(\ell^p(X)\) denotes the space of functions on \(X\) with the counting measure:
\[
  \ell ^p(X) := \mathcal{L}^p\left(X, 2^{X}, \# \right)
\]
In particular,
\[
  \ell ^{p} = \ell ^{p}(\mathbb {N}), \qquad \left(\mathbb {F}^n, \left\| \cdot \right\| _{p}\right) = \ell ^p(\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\} )
\]
(up to isomorphism of normed spaces).














Theorem 1 (\(\mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\) is a vector space) Let \((X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\) be a measure space and \(0 < p < \infty\). Then

\(\| f + g\|_p^p \leq 2^p (\left\| f\right\|_{p}^p + \| g\|_p^p)\)
\(\| af\|_p = |a| \left\| f\right\|_{p}\) for all \(f, g \in \mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\) and all \(a \in \mathbb {F}\). Moreover, with the usual operations of addition and scalar multiplication of functions, \(\mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\) is a vector space.





For \(1 \leq p \leq +\infty\), the conjugate exponent of \(p\) is denoted \(p'\) or \(q\) and is the element of \([1, +\infty ]\) such that
\[
  \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q} = 1.
\]






ExampleExample 2





Find the conjugate exponents for \(1, \infty , 2, 4, \frac{5}{3}\).






SolutionSolution





\[
  1' = \infty , \quad \infty ' = 1, \quad 2' = 2, \quad 4' = \frac{4}{3}, \quad \left(\frac{5}{3}\right)' = \frac{5}{2} = 2.5
\]













Lemma 1 (Young’s inequality) Let \(1 < p < \infty\). Then \[
  ab \leq \frac{a^p}{p} + \frac{b^{q}}{q}
\] for all \(a \geq 0\) and \(b \geq 0\).











Theorem 2 (Hölder’s inequality) Let \((X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\) be a measure space, \(1 \leq p \leq \infty\), and let \(f, h: X \to \mathbb {F}\) be \(\mathcal{S}\)-measurable. Then \[
  \| fh\| _1 \leq \left\| f\right\| _{p} \left\| h\right\| _{q}.
\]











Corollary 1 (Lyapunov’s inequality: inclusion of \(\mathcal{L}^p\) spaces for finite measure) Let \((X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\) be a measure space with \(\mu (X) < \infty\). Suppose \(0 < p < q \leq \infty\). Then \(\mathcal{L}^q(\mu ) \subset \mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\). Moreover, if \(0 < p < q < \infty\), then
\[
  \left\| f\right\| _{p} \leq \mu (X)^{\frac{1}{p} - \frac{1}{q}} \| f\| _q
\]
for all \(f \in \mathcal{L}^q(\mu )\).
In particular, if \(\mu\) is a probability measure (i.e., \(\mu (X) = 1\)), then every random variable in \(\mathcal{L}^p\) also lies in \(\mathcal{L}^q\) for \(0 < p < q \leq +\infty\), and
\[
  \left(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi \right|^p\right]\right)^{1/p} = \left\| \xi \right\| _{p} \leq \left\| \xi \right\| _{q} = \left(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi \right|^q\right]\right)^{1/q}
\]
for an arbitrary random variable \(\xi\) in \(\mathcal{L}^q\).










ProblemProblem 1





Prove Corollary Corollary 1.






HintHint





We need to prove \[
  \int _{X} \left|f\right|^p \;  d\mu = \left\| f\right\| _{p}^p \leq \mu (X)^{1 - \frac{p}{q}} \cdot \left\| f\right\| _{q}^{p}
\] Use Hölder’s inequality for \(\tilde{f} = \left|f\right|^p\), \(\tilde{h} = 1\), \(\tilde{p} = \ldots\).












ExampleExample 3





Describe the Lebesgue spaces on Borel subsets of \(\mathbb {R}\) with Lebesgue measure.






SolutionSolution





We adopt the standard convention: if \(E\) is a Borel subset of \(\mathbb {R}\) and \(0 < p \leq \infty\), then \(\mathcal{L}^p(E)\) means \(\mathcal{L}^p(E, \mathscr {B}\left(E\right), \lambda_E)\), where \(\lambda_E\) is Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\) restricted to the Borel subsets of \(\mathbb {R}\) contained in \(E\).
For example, \(\mathcal{L}^p[0,1]\) is the space of Borel-measurable functions from \([0,1]\) into \(\mathbb {F}\) with finite \(p\)-norm integral. From what was proved above it follows that if \(0 < p < q < \infty\), then \(\mathcal{L}^q([0,1]) \subset \mathcal{L}^p([0,1])\) and \(\left\| f\right\|_{p} \leq \| f\|_q\) for \(f \in \mathcal{L}^q([0,1])\).












ProblemProblem 2





Let \(0 < p < q \leq \infty\).

Prove that \(\ell^{p} \subseteq \ell^{q}\).
Prove that \(\ell^{p} \subsetneq \bigcap_{r > p} \ell^{r}\).
Prove that \(\left\| a\right\|_{p} \geq \left\| a\right\|_{q}\) for every sequence \(a = (a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots )\) of elements of \(\mathbb {F}\).

Theorem 3 (Formula for \(\| f\|_p\) in terms of functions from \(\mathcal{L}^q\)) Let \((X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\) be a measure space. Suppose

either \(1 \leq p < \infty\),
or \(p = +\infty\) and \(\mu\) is a sigma-finite measure.

Then \[
  \left\| f\right\| _{p} = \sup _{\substack {h \in \mathcal{L}^q \\ \left\| h\right\| _{q} \leq 1}}\left|\varphi _{h}(f)\right|
\] where \(\varphi_h(f) := \int fh \;  d\mu\) is a linear functional on \(\mathcal{L}^p\) (more on this below).










ProblemProblem 3





Show that the formula above may fail if \(p = +\infty\) and \(\mu\) is not sigma-finite.






HintHint





Let \(X = \left\{ b\right\}\) be a set consisting of exactly one element \(b\), \(\mathcal{S} = 2^{X}\), and let \(\mu\) be the measure such that \(\mu (\varnothing ) = 0\) and \(\mu (\{ b\} ) = +\infty\).













Theorem 4 (Minkowski’s inequality) Let \((X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\) be a measure space, \(1 \leq p \leq \infty\), and \(f, g \in \mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\). Then \[
  \| f + g\| _p \leq \left\| f\right\| _{p} + \| g\| _p.
\]






2 \(L^p(\mu )\)
Suppose \((X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\) is a measure space and \(1 \leq p \leq \infty\). If there exists a nonempty set \(E \in \mathcal{S}\) such that \(\mu (E)=0\), then the \(p\)-norm of the characteristic function \(I_{E}\) is zero, while the characteristic function itself is nonzero. Hence in this case the expression \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{p}\) is not positive definite (the condition \(\left\| f\right\|_{p} = 0 \iff f = 0_{V}\) fails), i.e., it is not a norm on \(V = \mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\). The standard way to fix this problem is to identify functions that differ only on a set of \(\mu\)-measure \(0\).







Definition 2 Suppose \((X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\) is a measure space and \(0<p \leq \infty\).

\(\mathcal{Z}(\mu )\) denotes the set of \(\mathcal{S}\)-measurable functions from \(X\) into \(\mathbb {F}\) that are equal to 0 almost everywhere.
For \(f \in \mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\), let \([f]\) be the subset of \(\mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\) defined by
\[
  [f] = \left\{ f + z \;  : \;  z \in \mathcal{Z}(\mu )\right\}
\]





The set \(\mathcal{Z}(\mu )\) is closed under scalar multiplication. Moreover, \(\mathcal{Z}(\mu )\) is closed under addition, since the union of two sets of \(\mu\)-measure \(0\) is again a set of \(\mu\)-measure \(0\). Thus \(\mathcal{Z}(\mu )\) is a subspace of \(\mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\).
Note that if \(f, g \in \mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\), then \([f] = [g]\) if and only if \(f(x)=g(x)\) for almost every \(x \in X\).
Suppose \(\mu\) is a measure and \(0<p \leq \infty\).

Let \(L^p(\mu )\) denote the collection of subsets of \(\mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\) defined by
\[
  L^p(\mu )=\left\{  [f] \;  : \;  f \in \mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\right\}  .
\]
For \([f], [g] \in L^p(\mu )\) and \(\alpha \in \mathbb {F}\), define \([f]+[g]\) and \(\alpha [f]\) as follows:
\[
  [f]+[g]=[f + g] \quad \text{ and } \quad \alpha [f]= [\alpha f].
\]

Elements of \(L^p(\mu )\) can be regarded as equivalence classes of functions in \(\mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\), where two functions are equivalent if they agree almost everywhere.
In functional analysis, elements of \(L^p(\mu )\) are often called functions, where two functions are considered equal if they differ only on a set of \(\mu\)-measure \(0\). This abuse of notation is harmless provided that operations performed on such “functions” give the same results when the functions are modified on a set of measure \(0\).
Note the typographical distinction between \(\mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\) and \(L^p(\mu )\). An element of the calligraphic \(\mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\) is a function; an element of \(L^p(\mu )\) is a set of functions, any two of which agree almost everywhere.
Suppose \(\mu\) is a measure and \(0<p \leq \infty\). Define \(\| \cdot \|_p\) on \(L^p(\mu )\) as follows:
\[
  \| [f]\| _p=\| f\| _p
\]
where \(f \in \mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\) is an arbitrary representative of \([f]\). Note that if \(f, g \in \mathcal{L}^p(\mu )\) and \([f] = [g]\), then \(\left\| f\right\|_{p} = \left\| g\right\|_{p}\). Thus the definition above is well-posed: it does not depend on the choice of representative.







Lemma 2 (\(L^p(\mu )\) is a normed space) Suppose \(\mu\) is a measure and \(1 \leq p \leq \infty\). Then \(L^p(\mu )\) is a vector space, and \(\| \cdot \|_p\) is a norm on \(L^p(\mu )\).




For readers familiar with quotient spaces: you may notice that \(L^p(\mu )\) is the quotient space
\[
  \mathcal{L}^p(\mu ) / \mathcal{Z}(\mu ).
\]
If \(\mu = \#\) is the counting measure on \(\mathbb {N}\), then
\[
  \mathcal{L}^p(\# )=L^p(\# )=\ell ^p
\]
since the counting measure has no sets of measure \(0\) other than the empty set.






ProblemProblem 4






Prove that if \(\mu\) is a measure, \(1 < p < \infty\), and \(f, g \in L^{p}(\mu )\) are such that
\[
  \left\| f\right\| _{p} = \left\| g\right\| _{p} = \left\| \frac{f+g}{2}\right\| _{p}
\]
then \(f = g\).
Give an example showing that the result of part (a) may fail for \(p = 1\).
Give an example showing that the result of part (a) may fail for \(p = \infty\).






3 Dual spaces: \(\left(L^p\right)' \cong L^{q}\) almost always
Recall that the dual space of a normed vector space \(V\) is denoted \(V^{\prime }\) and is defined as the Banach space of bounded linear functionals on \(V\).
Let \((X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\) be a measure space, and let \(1 \leq p \leq +\infty\). What does the dual space of \(V = L^{p}(\mu )\) look like? Recall Hölder’s inequality: if \(f \in L^p\), \(h \in L^{q}\), then
\[
  \int \left|fh\right| \;  d\mu = \left\| fh\right\| _{1} \leq \left\| f\right\| _{p} \cdot \left\| h\right\| _{q}
\]
So, if we take an arbitrary function \(h \in L^q\) and define on \(L^p\) the functional
\[
  \varphi _{h}(f) = \int fh \;  d\mu ,
\]
equal to the integral of the product with \(h\), then it will be linear (since the Lebesgue integral is linear). But will it be bounded? We have
\[
  \left|\varphi _{h}(f)\right| = \left|\int fh \;  d\mu \right| \leq \int \left|fh\right| \;  d\mu \leq C_{h}\left\| f\right\| _{p}
\]
where \(C_{h} = \left\| h\right\|_{q} \in [0,+\infty )\). In other words, the norm of the linear functional \(\varphi_{h}: L^{p} \to \mathbb {F}\) is bounded:
\[
  \left\| \varphi _{h}\right\|  \leq \left\| h\right\| _{q}
\]
Thus, \(\varphi_h\) is a bounded linear functional (\(\varphi_{h} \in \left(L^p(\mu )\right)'\)), and hence \(h \mapsto \varphi_{h}\) is a map from \(L^q\) into \(\left(L^p(\mu )\right)'\).
Moreover, this map itself is linear, owing to linearity of the Lebesgue integral:
\[
  \varphi _{h_1 +h_2}(f) = \int f \cdot \left(h_{1} + h_{2}\right) \;  d\mu = \int f \cdot h_{1} \;  d\mu + \int f \cdot h_{2} \;  d\mu = \varphi _{h_1}(f) + \varphi _{h_2}(f)
\]
(likewise for scalar multiplication: \(\varphi_{\alpha h} = \alpha \varphi_{h}\)). Hence \(h \mapsto \varphi_{h}\) is a homomorphism of the vector spaces \(L^{q}\) and \(\left(L^p\right)'\). When is it an isomorphism? When does it preserve norms: \(\left\| \varphi_{h}\right\|  = \left\| h\right\|_{q}\)? As follows from the theorem below, this holds almost always — almost always \(L^q\) will be isometrically (i.e., norm-preservingly) isomorphic to \(\left(L^p\right)'\).







Theorem 5 (On the dual space of \(L^{p}\)) Consider the map \(h \to \varphi_{h}\) defined above, from \(L^{q}(\mu )\) into \(\left(L^p(\mu )\right)'\). It is always a homomorphism (see the justification above). Further, suppose that

either \(1 < p \leq +\infty\),
or \(1 = p\) and \(\mu\) is a \(\sigma\)-finite measure.

Then

\(h \mapsto \varphi_h\) preserves norms: \(\left\| \varphi_h\right\| =\left\| h\right\|_{q}\) for all \(h \in L^{q}(\mu )\);
\(h \mapsto \varphi_h\) is injective;
if \(p \neq +\infty\), then \(h \mapsto \varphi_h\) is surjective.





In practice, measures that are not \(\sigma\)-finite are rare. As a rule, a measure \(\mu\) on \((X,\mathcal{S})\) will be, if not finite (as in probability theory), then at least sigma-finite (as, for example, Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\)). Therefore (in the case of a sigma-finite measure)
\[
  L^q = \left(L^p\right)' \qquad \text{ for } \quad 1 \leq p < +\infty
\] (up to isometric isomorphism). Further, (up to isometric isomorphism) \[
  L^{1} \subset \left(L^{\infty }\right)'\text{, but, as a rule, } L^{1} \neq \left(L^{\infty }\right)'
\]
The hardest part of the theorem above is proving surjectivity, i.e., proving that an arbitrary functional in \(\left(L^p\right)'\) can be represented as \(\varphi_{h}\). The remaining parts are fairly easy to prove.






ProblemProblem 5





Consider Theorem Theorem 5 on the map \(h \mapsto \varphi_{h}\). Prove norm preservation (part ) in the case where

\(1 < p \leq +\infty\)
\(p = 1\) and \(\mu\) is sigma-finite.







HintHint











Enum-item(i)



Use Theorem Theorem 3.








Enum-item(ii)



By contradiction: suppose \(\left\| \varphi_{h}\right\|  < \left\| h\right\|_{\infty }\). Then there is \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that the set
\[
  E_{\varepsilon } = \left\{ x \in E \;  : \;  \left|h(x)\right| > \left\| \varphi _{h}\right\|  + \varepsilon \right\}
\]
has nonzero measure.














ProblemProblem 6





Consider Theorem Theorem 5 on the map \(h \mapsto \varphi_{h}\). Prove injectivity of the map \(h \mapsto \varphi_{h}\) (part ).



In the following problem, among other things, you are asked to actually prove surjectivity in the theorem above for a particular case — for the counting measure on \(\mathbb {N}\).






ProblemProblem 7






Prove that \(\left(\ell^{p}\right)' \cong \ell^{q}\) for \(1 \leq p < +\infty\);
Prove that \(\left(c_{0}\right)' \cong \ell^{1}, c' \cong \ell^{1}\);
Is it true that \(\left(\ell^{\infty }\right)' \cong \ell^{1}\)?

[@VKK, Problem  9.1]
Here \(V \cong W\) means that there is an isometric isomorphism between \(V\) and \(W\), i.e., an isomorphism preserving norms. The spaces \(c\), \(c_0\) are subspaces of \(\ell^{\infty }\) consisting of sequences that converge (to something) and sequences converging to zero, respectively. The norms on \(c\), \(c_0\) are inherited from \(\ell^{\infty }\).






HintHint





For part (3): consider the functional constructed in the problem about a functional on \(\ell^\infty\) extending the limit.












ProblemProblem 8





Prove that the following operators are bounded linear operators, and find their norms:

\(A: L^{1}[0,1] \rightarrow L^{1}[0,1], \quad (A f)(t) = f(\sqrt{t})\);
\(L^{2}[0,1] \rightarrow L^{2}[0,1], \quad (A f)(t) = t \int_{0}^{1} f(s) d s\).

[@VKK, Problem  6.6]
\(L^{p}[0,1] = L^{p}\left([0,1], \mathscr {B}\left([0,1]\right), \lambda \right)\), where \(\lambda\) is Lebesgue measure.

title: Topological spaces
text:
WarningDraft



This text is still being edited: it may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally underdeveloped passages. If you find something, please let the author know (contact information on the course page).


In the previous chapters we considered metric spaces. There, the metric was used to define an open ball, and an open set was defined as a union of open balls. A number of notions, such as the continuity of maps, were expressed exclusively in terms of open sets associated with the metric. Here we consider spaces in which the notion of an open set is fundamental. Such spaces are called topological spaces. They are more general than metric spaces. On a normed linear space \(X\) there are important notions, such as weak convergence, which, as we will prove, cannot be formulated within the framework of a metric, but can be treated with respect to the weak topology. Likewise, pointwise convergence of functions can be treated with respect to a product topology, but is not a metric notion. Beyond greater generality, new notions — such as the compactness of an arbitrary product of compact metric spaces — reveal properties of normed linear spaces that are not obvious in the metric setting.

1 Open sets, closed sets, bases, subbases
Definition: Let \(X\) be a nonempty set. A topology \(T\) on \(X\) is a family of subsets of \(X\), called open sets, having the following properties:

The whole set \(X\) and the empty set \(\emptyset\) are open.
The intersection of any finite collection of open sets is open.
The union of any collection of open sets is open.

A nonempty set \(X\) together with a topology on \(X\) is called a topological space. For a point \(x\) in \(X\), an open set containing \(x\) is called a neighborhood of \(x\).
The metric topology: Consider a metric space \((X, \rho )\). Define a subset \(\mathcal{O}\) of \(X\) to be open if for every point \(x \in \mathcal{O}\) there is an open ball centered at \(x\) contained in \(\mathcal{O}\). This collection of open sets is a topology for \(X\), called the metric topology induced by the metric \(\rho\). A particular case is the Euclidean topology on \(\mathbb {R}^n\) induced by the Euclidean metric.
The discrete topology: Let \(X\) be any nonempty set. Define \(\mathcal{T}\) to be the collection of all subsets of \(X\). Then \(\mathcal{T}\) is a topology for \(X\), called the discrete topology. For the discrete topology, every set containing a point is a neighborhood of it. The discrete topology is induced by the discrete metric.
The trivial topology: Let \(X\) be any nonempty set. Define \(\mathcal{T}\) to be the collection of subsets of \(X\) consisting of \(\emptyset\) and \(X\). Then \(\mathcal{T}\) is a topology for \(X\), called the trivial topology. For the trivial topology, the only neighborhood of a point is the whole set \(X\).
Topological subspaces: Given a topological space \((X, \mathcal{T})\) and a nonempty subset \(E\) of \(X\), we define the inherited topology \(\mathcal{S}\) for \(E\) to be the collection of all sets of the form \(E \cap \mathcal{O}\), where \(\mathcal{O}\) belongs to \(\mathcal{T}\). The topological space \((E, \mathcal{S})\) is called a subspace of \((X, \mathcal{T})\).
Base of a topology: A collection of open sets \(\mathcal{B}\) is called a base for the topology \(\mathcal{T}\) if every nonempty open set is a union of some subcollection of \(\mathcal{B}\). A collection of subsets \(\mathcal{S}\) of a space \(X\) that covers \(X\) is called a subbase for the topology \(\mathcal{T}\) if the collection of all finite intersections of sets from \(\mathcal{S}\) forms a base for \(\mathcal{T}\).
Closure: For a subset \(E\) of a topological space \(X\), a point \(x \in X\) is called a point of closure of the set \(E\) if every neighborhood of \(x\) contains a point of \(E\). The collection of points of closure of \(E\) is called the closure of \(E\) and is denoted \(\overline{E}\). A set \(E\) is called closed if it contains all its points of closure, i.e., \(E = \overline{E}\).






ExampleExample 1





Show that the discrete topology on a nonempty set \(X\) is a metric topology.






SolutionSolution





The discrete topology is generated by the discrete metric: \[
  d(x, y) = \begin{cases}  0, &  \text{if } x = y, \\ 1, &  \text{if } x \neq y. \end{cases}
\] With this metric, every singleton \(\{ x\}\) is an open ball of radius \(1/2\), so every subset is open.












ExampleExample 2





Show that the trivial topology on a set has a unique base.






SolutionSolution





The trivial topology on a set \(X\) consists only of \(\emptyset\) and \(X\). The only possible base is \(\{ X\}\), since any base must contain a set whose union equals \(X\), and \(\emptyset\) cannot belong to the base (since bases are usually taken to consist of nonempty open sets).












ExampleExample 3





Let \(E\) be a subset of a topological space \(X\).

A point \(x \in X\) is called an interior point of the set \(E\) if there is a neighborhood of \(x\) contained in \(E\): the collection of interior points of \(E\) is called the interior of \(E\) and is denoted \(\operatorname {int} E\). Show that \(\operatorname {int} E\) is always open, and \(E\) is open if and only if \(E = \operatorname {int} E\).
A point \(x \in X\) is called an exterior point of the set \(E\) if there is a neighborhood of \(x\) contained in \(X \setminus E\): the collection of exterior points of \(E\) is called the exterior of \(E\) and is denoted \(\operatorname {ext} E\). Show that \(\operatorname {ext} E\) is always open, and \(E\) is closed if and only if \(\bar{E} \setminus E \subseteq \operatorname {ext} E\).
A point \(x \in X\) is called a boundary point of the set \(E\) if every neighborhood of \(x\) contains points of \(E\) and points of \(X \setminus E\): the collection of boundary points of \(E\) is called the boundary of \(E\) and is denoted \(\operatorname {bd} E\). Show that (i) \(\operatorname {bd} E\) is always closed, (ii) \(E\) is open if and only if \(E \cap \operatorname {bd} E = \emptyset\), and (iii) \(E\) is closed if and only if \(\operatorname {bd} E \subseteq E\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



For every \(x \in \text{int } E\) there is an open set \(U_x\) such that \(x \in U_x \subseteq E\). Then \(\text{int } E = \bigcup_{x \in \text{int } E} U_x\) is open. If \(E\) is open, then for every \(x \in E\), \(E\) itself is a neighborhood of \(x\) contained in \(E\), so \(x \in \text{int } E\). Thus \(E = \text{int } E\). Conversely, if \(E = \text{int } E\), then \(E\) is open.








Enum-item2.



\(\operatorname {ext} E = \operatorname {int} (X \setminus E)\), so it is open. \(E\) is closed \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(X \setminus E\) is open \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(X \setminus E = \operatorname {int} (X \setminus E) = \operatorname {ext} E\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(\bar{E} \setminus E \subseteq \operatorname {ext} E\) (since \(\bar{E} \setminus E\) is the set of limit points of \(E\) that do not belong to \(E\)).








Enum-item3.




\(\operatorname {bd} E = X \setminus (\operatorname {int} E \cup \operatorname {ext} E)\), and since \(\operatorname {int} E\) and \(\operatorname {ext} E\) are open, their union is open, so \(\operatorname {bd} E\) is closed.
\(E\) is open \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(E = \operatorname {int} E\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(E \cap \operatorname {bd} E = \emptyset\).
\(E\) is closed \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(X \setminus E\) is open \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(X \setminus E = \operatorname {int} (X \setminus E) = \operatorname {ext} E\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(\operatorname {bd} E = \bar{E} \setminus \operatorname {int} E \subseteq E\).















ProblemProblem 1 - The Sorgenfrey line





Show that the collection of intervals of the form \([a, b)\), where \(a < b\), is a base for a topology on the set of real numbers \(\mathbf{R}\). The set of real numbers \(\mathbf{R}\) with this topology is called the Sorgenfrey line.









ProblemProblem 2 - The Moore plane





Consider the upper half-plane, \(\mathbf{R}^{2,+} = \left\{ (x, y) \in \mathbf{R}^{2} \mid y \geq 0\right\}\). For points \((x, y)\) with \(y > 0\), take as a basic open neighborhood the ordinary Euclidean open ball centered at \((x, y)\) contained in the upper half-plane. As a basic open neighborhood of a point \((x, 0)\), take the set consisting of the point itself together with all points of an open Euclidean ball in the upper half-plane that is tangent to the real line at the point \((x, 0)\). Show that this collection of sets is a base. The set \(\mathbf{R}^{2,+}\) with this topology is called the Moore plane.





2 Separation axioms


  Hierarchy of separation axioms
  An arrow \(A \to B\) means: every space of class \(A\) lies in class \(B\). All inclusions are strict: next to each arrow is a note on why the converse implication fails. Every metric space lies in the topmost class of the diagram, i.e., it satisfies all the axioms simultaneously.
  

    
      T4normal Hausdorff
      
        \(X\in T_1\) (equivalently, \(X\in T_2\)) and \(X\) is normal: any two disjoint closed sets \(A,B\subset X\) are separated by disjoint neighborhoods.
        Urysohn's lemma: normality is equivalent to functional separation of closed sets: there exists a continuous \(f:X\to[0,1]\) with \(f|_A\equiv0\), \(f|_B\equiv1\). A normal space need not itself be Hausdorff (for example, the indiscrete topology).
      
    

    
      
      The converse fails: the Moore plane and the Sorgenfrey plane (the product of two Sorgenfrey lines) are Tychonoff but not normal.
    

    
      T3½Tychonoff
      
        \(X\in T_1\) (equivalently, \(X\in T_2\)) and \(X\) is completely regular: any closed \(C\subset X\) and point \(p\notin C\) are functionally separated: there exists a continuous \(f:X\to[0,1]\) with \(f(p)=0\), \(f|_C\equiv1\).
        Tychonoff spaces are exactly the subspaces of compact Hausdorff spaces (Tychonoff cubes \([0,1]^{\mathcal A}\)).
      
    

    
      
      \(T_{3\frac12}\Rightarrow T_3\). The preimages of \([0,\tfrac12)\) and \((\tfrac12,1]\) are the desired neighborhoods. The converse fails, but the counterexamples are elaborate (the Tychonoff corkscrew).
    
    
    
      
      \(T_{3\frac12}\Rightarrow\) completely \(T_2\). The point \(y\) is a closed set; we separate \(x\) from it functionally. The converse fails: \(\mathbb R_K\) (see below) is completely \(T_2\) but not regular.
    

    
      T3regular Hausdorff
      
        \(X\in T_1\) (equivalently, \(X\in T_2\)) and \(X\) is regular: any closed \(C\subset X\) and point \(p\notin C\) are separated by disjoint neighborhoods.
        A regular space need not itself be Hausdorff.
      
    
    
      ⇍ ⇏
      classes not comparable
    
    
      completely T2functionally Hausdorff
      
        Any two points \(x\ne y\) are separated functionally: there exists a continuous \(f:X\to[0,1]\) with \(f(x)=0\), \(f(y)=1\).
        In other words, continuous functions \(X\to\mathbb R\) separate the points of \(X\).
      
    

    
      
      \(T_3\Rightarrow T_2\). The converse fails: \(\mathbb R_K\) — the line with a base of intervals \((a,b)\) and sets \((a,b)\setminus K\), \(K=\{1/n\}\). It is Hausdorff, but the point \(0\) and the closed set \(K\) cannot be separated by neighborhoods.
    
    
    
      
      Completely \(T_2\Rightarrow T_2\). The preimages of \([0,\tfrac12)\) and \((\tfrac12,1]\) are disjoint neighborhoods of \(x\) and \(y\). The converse fails.
    

    
      T2Hausdorff
      
        Equivalent formulations:
        
          any two points \(x\ne y\) are separated by disjoint neighborhoods;
          the limit of any net (in particular, of any sequence) is unique;
          the diagonal \(\Delta=\{(x,x)\}\) is closed in \(X\times X\).
        
      
    

    
      
      The converse fails: the Zariski topology (the cofinite topology) on an infinite set is \(T_1\), but any two nonempty open sets intersect (see the problem on the Zariski topology below).
    

    
      T1the Fréchet axiom
      
        Equivalent formulations:
        
          for any \(x\ne y\) there is a neighborhood of \(x\) not containing \(y\) (and vice versa);
          all singletons are closed;
          every subset of \(X\) is the intersection of all open sets containing it.
        
      
    

    
      
      The converse fails: the connected two-point space (the Sierpiński space) \(\{a,b\}\) with open sets \(\varnothing,\{a\},\{a,b\}\) is \(T_0\), but the point \(a\) is not closed.
    

    
      T0Kolmogorov space
      
        Any two distinct points are topologically distinguishable: for \(x_1\ne x_2\) there is an open set \(A\) containing exactly one of them.
      
    

  
  
    \(T_3\) and completely \(T_2\) are not comparable: \(\mathbb R_K\) is completely \(T_2\) (it is finer than the usual topology, so all ordinary continuous functions remain continuous) but not regular; on the other hand, there exist regular Hausdorff spaces on which every continuous function \(X\to\mathbb R\) is constant (Hewitt) — these are not completely \(T_2\).
    Metric spaces: \(A\) and \(B\) are closed and disjoint \(\Rightarrow\) the function \(f(x)=\dfrac{\rho(x,A)}{\rho(x,A)+\rho(x,B)}\) is continuous and separates them, so \(X\in T_4\).
  







ProblemProblem 3





Consider the set of real numbers with the topology having as a subbase the sets of the form \((-\infty , c), c \in \mathbf{R}\). Show that this space is not Tychonoff.









ProblemProblem 4 - The Zariski topology





In \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\), let \(\mathcal{B}\) be the family of sets \(\left\{ x \in \mathbf{R}^{n} \mid p(x) \neq 0\right\}\), where \(p\) is a polynomial in \(n\) variables. Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the topology on \(X\) having \(\mathcal{B}\) as a subbase. Show that \(\mathcal{T}\) is a topology on \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\) that is \(T_1\) but not Hausdorff.









ProblemProblem 5





Show that the Sorgenfrey line and the Moore plane are Hausdorff (see the previous problems).





3 Countability and separability
Convergence of a sequence: A sequence \(\{ x_n\}\) in a topological space \(X\) converges to a point \(x \in X\) if for every neighborhood \(\mathcal{U}\) of \(x\) there is an index \(N\) such that if \(n \geq N\), then \(x_n\) belongs to \(\mathcal{U}\). In a Hausdorff space, the limit of a sequence is unique.
Definitions:

A space \(X\) satisfies the first axiom of countability if every point has a countable neighborhood base.
A space \(X\) satisfies the second axiom of countability if the whole topology has a countable base.
A subset \(E\) of a space \(X\) is called dense if every open set in \(X\) contains a point of \(E\). A space \(X\) is called separable if it has a countable dense subset.

Example: Every metric space satisfies the first axiom of countability, since the open balls with rational radii form a countable base at a point.
Metrizability: A topological space is called metrizable if its topology is generated by some metric. Not every topology is metrizable (for example, the trivial topology on a set with more than one point).
Urysohn’s metrization theorem: A topological space with a countable base is metrizable if and only if it is \(T_1\) and normal (which, for spaces with a countable base, is equivalent to \(T_3\), i.e., regularity \(+\) \(T_1\): without the \(T_1\) condition the statement fails — for example, the indiscrete topology on a set with \(\geq 2\) points is normal and has a finite base, but is not metrizable, since it is not Hausdorff).


4 Continuous maps, weak topologies, metrizability
Definition: A map \(f: X \to Y\) between topological spaces is called continuous at a point \(x_0 \in X\) if for every neighborhood \(\mathcal{O}\) of \(f(x_0)\) in \(Y\) there is a neighborhood \(\mathcal{U}\) of \(x_0\) in \(X\) such that \(f(\mathcal{U}) \subseteq \mathcal{O}\). A map is continuous if it is continuous at every point.
Criterion: A map \(f: X \to Y\) is continuous if and only if the preimage of every open set in \(Y\) is open in \(X\).
Homeomorphism: A bijective continuous map \(f: X \to Y\) from a space \(X\) onto a space \(Y\) whose inverse is also continuous is called a homeomorphism. Spaces \(X\) and \(Y\) are called homeomorphic if there exists a homeomorphism between them.
Example: Any bounded open interval of the real line is homeomorphic to \(\mathbb {R}\).






ProblemProblem 6





Prove that a segment and a circle are not homeomorphic.
[@VKK, Problem  1.10]

5 Compactness


  Relations among the various notions of compactness
  Solid arrows are unconditional implications. Dashed arrows are converse implications, valid under the condition on \(X\) noted alongside. If \(X\) is metrizable, all five notions are equivalent.
  

    
      Compactness
      Every open cover of \(X\) has a finite subcover.
    
    
      Sequential compactness
      Every sequence in \(X\) has a subsequence converging to an element of \(X\).
    

    
      
        
        always
      
      
        
        if \(X\) is Lindelöf (for example, \(X\) has a countable base) or \(X\) is metrizable
      
    
    
      
        
        always
      
      
        
        if \(X\) is sequential; in particular, if \(X\) is first-countable (for example, metrizable)
      
    

    
      Countable compactness
      Every countable open cover of \(X\) has a finite subcover. Equivalently: every infinite \(A\subset X\) has a complete accumulation point \(p\) (every neighborhood of \(p\) contains infinitely many points of \(A\)).
    

    
      
        
        always
      
      
        
        if \(X\) is normal (\(X\in T_4\))
      
    
    
      
        
        always
      
      
        
        if \(X\in T_1\)
      
    

    
      Pseudocompactness
      Every continuous function \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is bounded.
    
    
      Limit point compactness
      Every infinite subset of \(X\) has a limit point in \(X\).
    

  
  
    Compactness \(\Rightarrow\) countable compactness \(\Rightarrow\) pseudocompactness and limit point compactness; sequential compactness \(\Rightarrow\) countable compactness. All other implications among these notions either follow from the ones listed by transitivity, or fail without additional conditions.
    Metrizable \(X\): it is normal, \(T_1\), and first-countable, so all dashed arrows become solid and the five notions coincide.
  

Properties:

A continuous image of a compact space is compact.
A closed subset of a compact space is compact.
In a Hausdorff space, every compact subset is closed.
A compact Hausdorff space is normal.
A continuous real-valued function on a compact space attains its maximum and minimum.

Theorem: A continuous bijective map from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.
