Contents of the published program
Below is the complete list of sections of E. S. Polovinkin’s program for 2025. The wording is condensed, but all 36 exam items are kept.

The complex derivative and differentiability; a criterion of regularity.
Integral along a curve.
Antiderivative, total differential and path independence of the integral.
Goursat’s theorem and Cauchy’s theorem in a simply connected domain.
Cauchy’s integral formula.
Differentiation of the Cauchy integral and infinite differentiability of an analytic function.
Power series and Taylor series in a disk.
Weierstrass’s theorem on locally uniformly convergent series.
Laurent series in an annulus.
The identity theorem.
Morera’s theorem and removable singularities.
Classification of isolated singular points.
Residues, the residue theorem and the computation of residues.
Computation of improper integrals of rational functions and of expressions with \(e^{iax}\); Jordan’s lemma.
Increment of the argument along a curve.
The inverse function and the principal branches of the logarithm and the root.
Regular branches of \(\log f(z)\).
Regular branches of a root of \(f(z)\).
Growth of entire functions and Liouville’s theorem.
Sokhotski’s theorem for an entire function.
The argument principle, Rouché’s theorem and the fundamental theorem of algebra.
Meromorphic functions and partial fraction expansion.
The open mapping principle, preservation of domains and local univalence.
Conformality in a domain and a criterion of conformality at a point.
Conformal maps on the Riemann sphere, passing between the half-plane and the disk, examples of maps of the disk onto itself.
Linear fractional transformations and their properties.
The power and exponential maps.
The Zhukovsky transform.
Harmonic functions on \(\mathbb R^2\) and the minimum–maximum principle.
The maximum modulus principle and the Schwarz lemma.
The general form of maps of the disk onto itself.
The Riemann mapping theorem and uniqueness of the normalized map.
Invariance of harmonicity, the Dirichlet problem in the plane and uniqueness of the bounded solution.
The Poisson integral in the disk and existence of a solution of the Dirichlet problem.
Analytic continuation along a chain of domains and along a curve; complete analytic functions, the Riemann surface and the logarithm.
Branch points and the Cauchy–Hadamard formula.

title: Conformal maps by elementary functions
text:
4.1 Conformality
On which domains is it conformal? Injectivity: for \(z_1 \neq z_2\) we have \(\operatorname {Zh}(z_1) = \operatorname {Zh}(z_2)\) \(\iff\) \(z_1z_2 = 1\). A domain of conformality cannot contain \(\pm 1\), since a neighborhood of either point will always contain points that break injectivity. Also, \(0\) and \(\infty\) cannot both be present at once.
Regularity? \(\operatorname {Zh}'(z)\neq 0\), so \(z \neq \pm 1\).
It suffices for the function to be univalent and regular at every point. On the whole sphere, the Zhukovsky function has only 2 poles of the first order.
In total: \(\operatorname {Zh}\) is conformal on \(D \subset \overline{\mathbb {C}}\) \(\iff\) \(\forall z \in D\) \(\frac{1}{z}\not\in D\).

title: The geometric meaning of the modulus and argument of the derivative
text:
WarningDraft



These notes are still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and places that have not been fully worked out locally. If you find something, please let the author know (contact info on the course page).


Differentiability of a function at a point \(z_0\) means that, locally near \(z_0\), the increment \(\Delta f_{z_0}\) is approximately equal to the product of \(\Delta z\) and a constant:
\[
  \Delta f_{z_0} = \Delta f_{z_0}(\Delta z) = f(z_0 + \Delta z) - f(z_0) \approx A \cdot \Delta z
\]
with \(A = f'(z_0)\). Note that multiplying the complex argument \(\Delta z\) by the complex constant \(A\) geometrically means a rotation by \(\operatorname {arg}A\) and a scaling by \(\left|A\right|\). That is, if a smooth curve \(\gamma\) passes through the point \(z_0\), with slope \(\varphi\) at \(z_0\) (the angle between the tangent vector to \(\gamma\) at \(z_0\) and the axis \(\operatorname {Re}z\) equal to \(\varphi\)), then the angle of the image curve \(f(\gamma )\) at the point \(f(z_0)\) will equal \(\varphi + \operatorname {arg}A\). The angle-preservation property: if \(f\) is differentiable at \(z_0\) and the smooth curves \(\gamma_1\), \(\gamma_2\) intersect at \(z_0\) at some angle, then \(f(\gamma_1)\) and \(f(\gamma_2)\) will intersect at \(f(z_0)\) at the same angle.
What is the geometric meaning of \(\left|A\right| = \left|f'(z_0)\right|\)? If we draw a circle of small radius \(\rho\) around \(z_0\), its image will approximately correspond to a circle of radius \(\left|A\right| \cdot \rho\) around \(f(z_0)\). The smaller \(\rho\) is, the more the resulting figure will resemble a circle. \(\left|f'(z_0)\right|\) is also called the coefficient of linear dilation at the point \(z_0\).

ProblemProblem 25.2





Find the set of all points \(z_{0}\) at which the coefficient of linear dilation for the following maps equals one:

\(w = \frac{1+i z}{1-i z}\).










ProblemProblem 25.3





Find the set of all points \(z_{0}\) at which the angle of rotation for the following maps equals zero:

\(w = z^{2}-2 z\);
\(w = \frac{i}{z}\);





1 Lengths of curves
If a regular function \(f\) maps a curve \(\gamma = \gamma (t)\) bijectively (injectively) onto a curve \(f \circ \gamma\), their lengths can be computed by the formulas
\[
  \left|\gamma \right| = \int _{\gamma }\left|dz\right|, \quad \left|f \circ \gamma \right| = \int _{f \circ \gamma }\left|dw\right| = \int _{\gamma } \left|f'(z)\right| \;  \left|dz\right|
\]






ExampleExample 25.6





Find the lengths of the images of the following curves \(\Gamma\) under the given maps:

\(\Gamma = \left\{ z: z = i t+1,0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1\right\} , w = z^{2}\);
\(\Gamma = \left\{ z: z = (1+i) t, 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2 \pi \right\} , w = e^{z}\);







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\(f(z) = z^2\) is an entire function. Let us check injectivity: suppose \(f(it_1 + 1) = f(it_2 + 1)\). I.e.
\[
  1 - t_1^2 + 2it_1 = 1 - t_2^2 + 2it_2
\]
In particular, the imaginary parts are equal: \(2t_1 = 2t_2\). Hence, \(t_1 = t_2\). We have proved injectivity.
We have
\[
\begin{align}  \left|f \circ \Gamma \right| & = \int _{\Gamma }\left|f'(z)\right| \;  \left|dz\right| = \int _{\Gamma } \left|2z\right| \;  \left|dz\right| = \int _0^1 \left|2(it + 1)\right| \cdot \left|i\right| \;  dt = \\ & = 2 \int _0^1 \sqrt{1 + t^2}\, dt = 2 \cdot \left[\frac{t\sqrt{1+t^2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\ln \left(t + \sqrt{1+t^2}\right)\right]_{0}^{1} = \sqrt{2} + \ln \left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right) \end{align}
\]








Enum-item2.



We have
\[
\begin{align}  \left|f \circ \Gamma \right| & = \int _{\Gamma }\left|f'(z)\right| \;  \left|dz\right| = \int _{\Gamma } \left|e^{z}\right| \;  \left|dz\right| = \int _0^{2\pi } \left|e^{(1+i)t}\right| \cdot \left|1 + i\right| \;  dt = \\ & = \sqrt{2}\int _0^{2\pi }e^{t} dt = \sqrt{2}(e^{2\pi } - 1) \end{align}
\]











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(\sqrt{2}+\ln (1+\sqrt{2})\);








Enum-item2.



\(\sqrt{2}\left(e^{2 \pi }-1\right)\);














ProblemProblem 25.6





Find the lengths of the images of the following curves \(\Gamma\) under the given maps:

\(\Gamma = \left\{ z: z = i t, 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2 \pi \right\} , w = e^{z}\);
\(\Gamma = \left\{ z: z = (1+i) t, 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1\right\} , w = z^{m}(m = 1,2, \ldots )\).






2 Dilation of areas
\(f\) is called univalent if it is injective on its domain of definition. That is, it does not glue points together. Let \(f: D \to f(D) =: G\) be holomorphic and univalent. How do we compute the area of \(G\)? We have
\[
  S(G) = \iint _G dudv \enclose {circle}{=}
\]
Note that \(f: (x,y) \mapsto (u,v)\),
\[
  \mathbf{J}_f = \begin{pmatrix}  u_x &  u_y \\ v_x &  v_y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  A &  -B \\ B &  A \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \operatorname {det}\mathbf{J}_f = A^2 + B^2 = \left|f'\right|^2
\]
where \(u_x = v_y = A\), \(v_x = -u_y = B\). Then
\[
  \enclose {circle}{=} \iint _{D} \left|\operatorname {det}\mathbf{J}_f\right| \;  dxdy = \iint _{D} \left|f'(z)\right|^2 \;  dx dy
\]






ExampleExample 2





Let \(f(z) = z^2\), \[
  D = \left\{ z \in \mathbb {C} \;  : \;  2 < \left|z\right| < 3, \;  \left|\arg z\right| < \frac{\pi }{4}\right\}
\] \(G := f(D)\). Find \(S(G)\).






SolutionSolution





We must first check whether \(f\) is univalent on \(D\). Suppose \(z_1^2 = z_2^2\). Then \(z_1 = z_2\) or \(z_1 = -z_2\). There are no antipodal points in the domain. I.e. \(z_1 = z_2\), so the function is univalent.
We have
\[
\begin{align}  S(G) & = \iint _{D} \left|f'(z)\right|^2 \;  dxdy = \iint _{D} 4\left|z\right|^2 \;  dxdy = 4 \cdot \int _{2}^3 \left(\int _{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} r^2 \;  d\varphi \right) \cdot r \cdot dr =\\ & = 4 \cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \cdot \int _2^3 r^3 \;  dr = 2\pi \cdot \frac{3^4 - 2^4}{4} = \frac{65}{2}\pi \end{align}
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(S(G) = 2\pi \cdot \frac{3^4 - 2^4}{4} = \frac{65}{2}\pi\).












ExampleExample 25.7





Find the areas of the images of the domains \(D\) under the given maps:

\(D = \left\{ z: 0 < \operatorname {Re} z < 1,\;  |\operatorname {Im} z| < \pi \right\} , w = e^{z}\);
\(D = \left\{ z: -1 < \operatorname {Re} z < 0,\;  1 < \operatorname {Im} z < 2\right\}\), \(w = \frac{z-1}{z+1}\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



The function \(e^{z}\) is injective on the open strip \(\left|\operatorname {Im}z\right| < \pi\) (width exactly \(2\pi\), boundary excluded). We have \(\left|\left(e^{z}\right)'\right|^{2} = \left|e^{z}\right|^{2} = e^{2x}\), hence
\[
  S = \iint _{D} e^{2x} \,  dxdy = 2\pi \int _{0}^{1}e^{2x}\, dx = 2\pi \cdot \frac{e^{2}-1}{2} = \pi \left(e^{2} - 1\right)
\]








Enum-item2.



A fractional-linear (Möbius) map is injective (globally on \(\bar{\mathbb {C}}\)), so there is nothing to check. We have \(w' = \frac{2}{(z+1)^{2}}\), i.e., denoting \(u := x + 1 \in (0, 1)\):
\[
  S = \iint _{D}\frac{4}{\left|z+1\right|^{4}}\, dxdy = \int _{1}^{2}\left(\int _{0}^{1} \frac{4\, du}{\left(u^{2}+y^{2}\right)^{2}}\right) dy = \int _{1}^{2}\left[\frac{2}{y^{2}\left(1+y^{2}\right)} + \frac{2}{y^{3}}\operatorname {arctg}\frac{1}{y}\right]dy
\]
The first term is integrated using the decomposition \(\frac{1}{y^2(1+y^2)} = \frac{1}{y^2} - \frac{1}{1+y^2}\):
\[
  2\int _{1}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{y^{2}} - \frac{1}{1+y^{2}}\right)dy = 2\left[-\frac{1}{y} - \operatorname {arctg}y\right]_{1}^{2} = 1 + \frac{\pi }{2} - 2\operatorname {arctg}2
\]
The second, by parts, using \(\left(\operatorname {arctg}\frac{1}{y}\right)' = -\frac{1}{1+y^{2}}\):
\[
  2\int _{1}^{2}\frac{\operatorname {arctg}\frac{1}{y}}{y^{3}}\, dy = \left[-\frac{\operatorname {arctg}\frac{1}{y}}{y^{2}} + \frac{1}{y} + \operatorname {arctg}y\right]_{1}^{2} = \operatorname {arctg}2 - \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4}\operatorname {arctg}\frac{1}{2}
\]
Adding and using \(\operatorname {arctg}2 + \operatorname {arctg}\frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi }{2}\), we obtain
\[
  S = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\pi }{2} - \operatorname {arctg}2 - \frac{1}{4}\operatorname {arctg}\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{4} \operatorname {arctg} \frac{1}{2}
\]











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(\pi \left(e^{2}-1\right)\);








Enum-item2.



\(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{4} \operatorname {arctg} \frac{1}{2}\).














ProblemProblem 25.7





Find the areas of the images of the domains \(D\) under the given maps:

\(D = \left\{ z: 2 < |z| < 3,|\arg z| < \frac{\pi }{4}\right\} , w = z^{2} ;\)

title: The argument principle and Rouché’s theorem
text:
1.1 Mapping curves: \(f \circ \gamma\)
One of the key notions in this topic is the image of one curve under a map to another. That is, if \(z=\gamma (t)\) is a curve and \(w=f(z)\) is a function, then \(w=f \circ \gamma (t)=f(\gamma (t))\) is another curve. We say that \(f\) maps \(\gamma\) to \(f \circ \gamma\).






ExampleExample 1





Let \(\gamma (t)=\mathrm{e}^{i t}\), where \(0 \leq t \leq 2 \pi\) (the unit circle). Let \(f(z)=z^{2}\). Describe the curve \(f \circ \gamma\).






SolutionSolution





\(f \circ \gamma (t)=\mathrm{e}^{2 i t}\) traces the unit circle twice as \(t\) ranges from 0 to \(2 \pi\).












ExampleExample 2





Let \(\gamma (t)=\) it, where \(-\infty <t<\infty\) (the \(y\)-axis). Let \(f(z)=1 /(z+1)\). Describe the curve \(f \circ \gamma (t)\).






SolutionSolution





\(f(z)\) is a fractional-linear (Möbius) transformation, which maps the line given by \(\gamma\) to a circle passing through the origin, centered at the point \(1 / 2\). Checking at several points: \[
  f(-i)=\frac{1}{-i+1}=\frac{1+i}{2}, \quad f(0)=1, \quad f(i)=\frac{1}{i+1}=\frac{1-i}{2}, \quad f(\infty )=0.
\] We see that the circle is traversed clockwise as \(t\) ranges from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\).

title: Residues
text:
2.1 Quick computation of the residue
If \(f\) is holomorphic in \(\dot{U}_{\varepsilon }(z_0)\), then it expands there into a Laurent series:
\[
  f(z) = \sum _{n=-\infty }^{+\infty }c_n(z - z_0)^{n}
\]
This series converges on every compact subset within the punctured neighborhood, so when integrating over the contour \(\gamma_{\rho }\), \(\rho < \varepsilon\), we may interchange integration and summation:
\[
  \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z = z_0}f(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint _{\gamma _{\rho }}f(z) dz = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint _{\gamma _{\rho }} \sum _{n=-\infty }^{+\infty }c_n(z - z_0)^{n} dz = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \sum _{n=-\infty }^{+\infty }c_n\oint _{\gamma _{\rho }}(z - z_0)^{n} dz
\]
Further, recall that \(\oint_{\gamma_{\rho }}(z - z_0)^{n} dz = 2\pi i\) if \(n = -1\). In every other case this integral equals zero. In total,
\[
  \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z = z_0}f(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \cdot c_{-1} \cdot 2\pi i = c_{-1},
\]

i.e. the residue simply equals the coefficient of the Laurent series at the power \(-1\).

Computing residues








ExampleExample 1





Find the residue at the point \(z_0\) for the function \(f\):

\(f(z) = \dfrac {e^{3z}}{(z-1)^2}\), \(z_0 = 1\);
\(f(z) = z^3\cos \left(\frac{1}{z} - \frac{1}{z^2}\right)\), \(z_0 = 0\).
\(f(z) = \dfrac {\operatorname {tg}z - z}{(1 - \cos z)^2}\), \(z_0 = 0\);
\(f(z) = z \cos \dfrac {z}{z-2}\), \(z_0 = 2\)
\(f(z) = \sin z \sin \frac{1}{z}\), \(z_0 = 0\);







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)



This is a pole of order \(2\) for \(f\). We have
\[
  \bigg((z-1)^2f(z)\bigg)' = 3e^{3z}
\]
The limit as \(z \to 1\): \(3e^{3}\).








Enum-item(2)



Let us expand \(f\) into a Laurent series in a punctured neighborhood of zero. Remember that we only care about the coefficient of \(\frac{1}{z}\). We have
\[
\begin{align}  \cos \left(\frac{1}{z} - \frac{1}{z^2}\right) & = 1 - \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{z} - \frac{1}{z^2}\right)^2 + \frac{1}{4!}\left(\frac{1}{z} - \frac{1}{z^2}\right)^4 - \ldots = \\ & = 1 - \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{z^2} + \frac{1}{z^3} - \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{24}\right)}_{=11/24}\frac{1}{z^4} + \ldots \\ f(z) & = z^3 - \frac{1}{2}z + 1 - \frac{11}{24}\frac{1}{z} + \ldots \end{align}
\]








Enum-item(3)



For the numerator, \(z_0 = 0\) is a zero of order \(3\); for the denominator, a zero of order \(4\). I.e. \(z_0 = 0\) is a pole of order \(1\) for \(f(z)\). Then
\[
  \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_0 f(z) = \lim _{z \to 0}z \cdot f(z) = \frac{4}{3}
\]








Enum-item(4)



This is an essential singularity. Let \(z-2 = w\),
\[
\begin{align}  f(z) & = f(z(w)) = (2 + w)\cos \left(1 + 2\frac{1}{w}\right) = (2+w) \cdot \left(\cos (1)\cos \frac{2}{w} - \sin (1)\sin \frac{2}{w}\right) = \\ & = (2 +w) \left(\cos (1) \cdot \left(1 - \frac{2}{w^2} + \ldots \right) - \sin (1) \cdot \left(\frac{2}{w} - \frac{8}{6w^3} + \ldots \right)\right) = \\ & = \left(-4\sin (1) - 2\cos (1)\right)\frac{1}{w} + \ldots \end{align}
\]








Enum-item(5)



\[
  \sin z \sin \frac{1}{z} = \left(\sum _{n=0}^{\infty } \frac{(-1)^n}{(2n+1)!}z^{2n + 1}\right) \cdot \left(\sum _{m=0}^{\infty } \frac{(-1)^m}{(2m+1)!}\frac{1}{z^{2m + 1}}\right) = \ldots + 0 \cdot \frac{1}{z} + \ldots
\]
(multiplying out gives only even powers \(z^{2(n-m)}\), so the coefficient of \(\frac{1}{z}\) is zero).











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item(1)



\(\mathop{\mathrm{res}}_1 \frac{e^{3z}}{(z-1)^2} = 3e^{3}\);








Enum-item(2)



\(\mathop{\mathrm{res}}_0 z^3\cos \left(\frac{1}{z} - \frac{1}{z^2}\right) = -\frac{11}{24}\).








Enum-item(3)



\(\frac{4}{3}\)








Enum-item(4)



\(-4\sin (1) - 2\cos (1)\)








Enum-item(5)



\(0\)














ExampleExample 2





\(f(z) = \dfrac {1}{\sin \pi z}\). Find the residues at all isolated singular points.






SolutionSolution





Singular points: \(z_k = k\), \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\), and also \(\infty\), though it is not isolated. At the points \(z_k\) the numerator is holomorphic and nonzero, while the denominator has a zero of order \(1\). Using the formula:
\[
  \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z_k}f = \frac{1}{\sin '(\pi z)}\bigg|_{z = z_k} = \frac{1}{\pi \cos (\pi z_{k})} = \frac{1}{\pi \cos (\pi k)} = \frac{1}{\pi \cdot (-1)^k}
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(\mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{k}\frac{1}{\sin \pi z} = \frac{(-1)^k}{\pi }\), \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\).












ProblemProblem 13.2





Find the residues of the following functions at all their finite singular points:

\(\frac{\sin \pi z}{(z-1)^{3}}\);










ProblemProblem 13.3





Find \(\underset {z = a}{\mathop{\mathrm{res}}} f(z)\), if:

\(f(z) = z^{2} \sin \frac{z}{z-1}, \quad a = 1\);

title: Residues
text:
3.1 Quick computation of the residue

3.1.1 Reduction to the residue at zero
We use the substitution \(w = \frac{1}{z} = \frac{1}{\left|z\right|}e^{-i\operatorname {arg}z}\). Note that under this substitution the circle of radius \(\frac{1}{\rho }\) about zero maps to the circle of radius \(\rho\) about zero. Further, note that under this substitution the orientation of traversal reverses (the angle used to be \(\operatorname {arg}z\), and becomes \(-\operatorname {arg}z\)). Also note that if \(f(z)\) was holomorphic in \(\dot{U}_{\varepsilon }(\infty )\), then \(g(w) = f\left(\frac{1}{w}\right)\) will be holomorphic in \(\dot{U}_{\varepsilon }(0) = \left\{ z \;  : \;  0 < \left|z\right| < \varepsilon \right\}\), with \(\rho < \varepsilon\). Then
\[
  \oint ^{\curvearrowright }_{\gamma _{1/\rho }}f(z) dz = \oint _{\gamma _{\rho }}f\left(\frac{1}{w}\right) d\frac{1}{w} = -\oint _{\gamma _{\rho }}\frac{1}{w^2}f\left(\frac{1}{w}\right) dw
\]
Consequently,
\[
  \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{\infty }f(z) = -\mathop{\mathrm{res}}_0\left(\frac{1}{w^2}f\left(\frac{1}{w}\right)\right)
\]


3.1.2 Via the Laurent series
If \(f\) is holomorphic in \(\dot{U}_{\varepsilon }(\infty )\), then it expands there into a Laurent series:
\[
  f(z) = \sum _{n=-\infty }^{+\infty }c_n\left(z^{-1}\right)^{n}
\]
We may interchange integration and summation (for justification see above, for the finite point):
\[
\begin{align}  \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{\infty }f(z) & = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint ^{\curvearrowright }_{\gamma _{1/\rho }}f(z) dz = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint ^{\curvearrowright }_{\gamma _{1/\rho }} \sum _{n=-\infty }^{+\infty }c_nz^{-n} dz = \\ & = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \sum _{n=-\infty }^{+\infty }c_n \cdot \oint ^{\curvearrowright }_{\gamma _{1/\rho }}z^{-n} dz = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \sum _{n=-\infty }^{+\infty }c_n\cdot \left(-\oint _{\gamma _{1/\rho }}z^{-n} dz\right) = \\ & =-c_{1} \end{align}
\]
i.e. the residue simply equals the coefficient of the Laurent series at \(\frac{1}{z} = \left(z^{-1}\right)^1\), taken with a minus sign. The minus sign appears because the circle is traversed clockwise in the definition.


3.1.3 General table
: Computing residues at infinity
Be careful when using the substitution \(w = \frac{1}{z}\): \[
  \boxed {\mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z = \infty } f(z) \neq \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{w = 0}f\left(\frac{1}{w}\right)}
\] In fact: \[
  \boxed {\mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z = \infty } f(z) = -\mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{w = 0}\frac{1}{w^2}f\left(\frac{1}{w}\right)}
\]






ExampleExample 13.4





Find the residues of the following functions at infinity:

\(\dfrac {z^{4}+1}{z^{6}-1}\);
\(\dfrac {\cos^{2} \frac{\pi }{z}}{z+1}\);
\(z \cos^{2} \frac{\pi }{z}\).







SolutionSolution





All equivalences and limits are written as \(z \to \infty\).






Enum-item1.



\[
f(z) = \frac{1 + \frac{1}{z^4}}{z^2 - \frac{1}{z^4}} \sim \frac{1}{z^2}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
  \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{\infty }f(z) = 0
\]








Enum-item2.



We have \(\frac{\pi }{z} \to 0\), hence \(\cos^2\frac{\pi }{z} \to 1\) and
\[
  \frac{\cos ^{2} \frac{\pi }{z}}{z+1} \sim \frac{1}{z}
\]
as \(z \to \infty\). Hence the residue equals \(-1\).








Enum-item3.



Let us expand into a Laurent series (in a punctured neighborhood of infinity). Remember that we only care about the coefficient of \(\frac{1}{z}\):
\[
  z\cos ^2\frac{\pi }{z} = \frac{z}{2}\left(1 + \cos \frac{2\pi }{z}\right) = \frac{z}{2} \left(1 + 1 - \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2\pi }{z}\right)^2 + \ldots \right) = -\pi ^2\cdot \frac{1}{z} + \ldots
\]
Consequently, \(\mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{\infty }f(z) = \pi^2\).











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(0\);








Enum-item2.



\(-1\);








Enum-item3.



\(\pi^{2}\).














ProblemProblem 13.4





Find the residues of the following functions at infinity:

\(\dfrac {\sin \frac{1}{z}}{z-1}\);
\(\dfrac {\left(z^{10}+1\right) \cos \frac{1}{z}}{\left(z^{5}+2\right)\left(z^{6}-1\right)}\);

title: Laurent series
text:
WarningDraft



These notes are still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and places that have not been fully worked out locally. If you find something, please let the author know (contact info on the course page).
Let us define
\[
  \sum _{n=-\infty }^{+\infty } c_n (z-z_0)^n := \sum _{n=0}^{+\infty } c_n(z - z_{0})^n + \sum _{n=-1}^{-\infty }c_n(z - z_{0})^n
\]
The series on the left converges if each of the two series converges.
In total, the series \(\sum_{n=-\infty }^{+\infty } c_n (z-z_0)^n\) converges in the annulus \(r < \left|z - z_{0}\right| < R\). If \(r > R\), the series converges nowhere (and for \(r = R\) convergence is possible at best at isolated points of the circle \(\left|z - z_{0}\right| = r\)).
Properties:
We will discuss the meaning of the integral in the theorem above a bit later.
The series from the theorem is called the Laurent series of the function \(f\). The part of the Laurent series with nonnegative powers is called the regular part, and the part with negative powers is called the principal part.
The Taylor series of a function is a special case of a Laurent series.
In practice, when expanding a function into a Laurent series, the integral from the theorem above is rarely used. More often one uses known expansions (the best known being the sum of a geometric series) together with the uniqueness theorem.

title: Laurent series
section: 2.1 The line integral of the second kind
text:
2.1 The line integral of the second kind
Let \(\gamma\) be a rectifiable piecewise-smooth curve in \(\mathbb {C}\), and let \(z(t)\), \(t \in [\alpha ,\beta ]\), be some (good) parametrization of it. Let \(f: \gamma \to \mathbb {C}\) be some continuous function. Then
\[
  \int _{\gamma }f(z) dz := \lim _{\left|T\right| \to 0} \sigma \left(f, \gamma , T, \xi \right) = \lim _{\left|T\right| \to 0} \sum _{k=1}^{n}f\left(z(\xi _k)\right) \cdot \left(z(t_k) - z(t_{k-1})\right)
\]
where \(T\) is a partition of \([\alpha , \beta ]\), and \((T,\xi )\) is a tagged partition.
Further, (informally) \(f = u + iv\), \(dz = dx + idy\),
\[
  \int _{\gamma }f(z) dz = \int _{\gamma }\left(u + iv\right) \left(dx + idy\right) = \int _{\gamma }\left(udx - vdy\right) + i \cdot \int _{\gamma } \left(vdx + udy\right)
\]
where the last 2 integrals are line integrals of the second kind.
How to compute it? By change of variable:
\[
  \int _{\gamma } f(z) \;  dz = \int _{\alpha }^{\beta } f(z(t)) \cdot z'(t) \cdot dt
\]

title: Laurent series
section: 2.2 The line integral of the first kind
text:
2.2 The line integral of the first kind
Next, another complex integral:
\[
  \int _{\gamma }f(z) \left|dz\right| := \lim _{\left|T\right| \to 0} \tilde{\sigma }\left(f, \gamma , T, \xi \right) = \lim _{\left|T\right| \to 0} \sum _{k=1}^{n}f\left(z(\xi _k)\right) \cdot \left|z(t_k) - z(t_{k-1})\right|
\]
Informally: \(\left|dz\right| = \sqrt{(dx)^2 + (dy)^2} = ds\) is the element of arc length of the curve. Then
\[
  \int _{\gamma }f(z) \left|dz\right| = \int _{\gamma } u \; ds + i \cdot \int _{\gamma } v \; ds
\]
where the last 2 integrals are line integrals of the first kind.
How to compute it? By change of variable:
\[
  \int _{\gamma } f(z) \;  \left|dz\right| = \int _{\alpha }^{\beta } f(z(t)) \cdot \left|z'(t)\right| \cdot dt
\]
since \(\left|dz\right| = ds = \left|z'(t)\right| dt\).

title: Laurent series
text:
2.3 Estimates
\[
\begin{align}  \left|\int _{\gamma } f(z) dz\right| & \leq \int _{\gamma } \left|f(z)\right| \cdot \left|dz\right| \leq \int _{\gamma } \left\| f\right\|  \cdot ds = \left\| f\right\|  \cdot \left|\gamma \right| \\ \left|\int _{\gamma } f(z) \left|dz\right|\right| & \leq \int _{\gamma } \left|f(z)\right| \left|dz\right| \end{align}
\]
where \(\left\| f\right\|  = \max_{z \in \gamma }\left|f(z)\right|\) (we assume \(f\) is continuous).






ExampleExample 5





Let \(\gamma = \left\{ z \in \mathbb {C} \;  : \;  \left|z - a\right| = \rho \right\}\) be the circle centered at \(a\) with radius \(\rho\). Compute

\(\int_{\gamma } (z-a)^n \;  \left|dz\right|\);
\(\int_{\gamma } (z-a)^n \;  dz\).







SolutionSolution





\(\gamma\): \(z(\varphi ) = a + \rho e^{i\varphi }\), \(\varphi \in [0,2\pi ]\), \(z'(\varphi ) = i\rho e^{i\varphi } = \rho e^{i\left(\varphi + \frac{\pi }{2}\right)}\).






Enum-item1.



If \(n \neq 0\), then
\[
\begin{align}  \int _{\gamma } (z-a)^n \;  \left|dz\right| & = \int _{0}^{2\pi } \rho ^n e^{i n\varphi } \cdot \rho \cdot d\varphi = \frac{\rho ^{n+1}}{in} \cdot e^{in\varphi }\bigg\rvert _{0}^{2\pi } = \\ & = \frac{\rho ^{n+1}}{in} \cdot \left(\underbrace{e^{i n 2\pi }}_{=1} - 1\right) = 0 \end{align}
\]
If \(n = 0\), then \(\int_{\gamma } (z-a)^n \;  \left|dz\right| = \int_{\gamma } 1 \;  ds = 2 \pi \rho\).








Enum-item2.



If \(n \neq -1\), then
\[
\begin{align}  \int _{\gamma } (z-a)^n \;  dz & = \int _{0}^{2\pi } \rho ^n e^{i n\varphi } \cdot i \rho e^{i\varphi } \cdot d\varphi = i \rho ^{n+1}\int _{0}^{2\pi } e^{i(n+1)\varphi } \;  d\varphi = \frac{\rho ^{n+1}}{n+1} \cdot e^{i(n+1)\varphi }\bigg\rvert _{0}^{2\pi } = 0 \end{align}
\]
If \(n = -1\), then \(\int_{\gamma } (z-a)^n \;  dz = i \rho^{n+1} \cdot 2 \pi = 2 \pi i\).











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(2 \pi \rho\) if \(n = 0\), \(0\) if \(n \neq 0\);








Enum-item2.



\(2 \pi i\) if \(n = -1\), \(0\) if \(n \neq -1\).














ExampleExample 6





Prove: \(\left|\sin (z)\right| \leq \operatorname {ch}1 \cdot \left|z\right|\), \(\left|z\right| \leq 1\).






SolutionSolution





We have \(\sin (z) = \int_{[0,z]} \cos (\zeta ) d\zeta\) (\(\zeta\) is a complex argument), \[
\begin{align}  \left|\sin (z)\right| & \leq \left|\int _{[0,z]} \cos (\zeta ) d\zeta \right| \leq \int _{[0,z]} \left|\cos (\zeta )\right| \;  \left|d\zeta \right| \leq \left(\max _{\left|\zeta \right|\leq 1 } \left|\cos \zeta \right|\right) \cdot \int _{[0,z]} 1 \;  \left|d\zeta \right| = \\ & = \left(\max _{\left|\zeta \right|\leq 1 } \left|\cos \zeta \right|\right) \cdot \left|z\right| \end{align}
\] Further, recall the formula from 3.13(2): \(\left|\cos \zeta \right| = \sqrt{\operatorname {ch}^2 y - \sin^2 x}\), \(\zeta = x + iy\). It is not hard to show that \[
  \max _{x^2 + y^2 \leq 1}\sqrt{\operatorname {ch}^2 y - \sin ^2(x)} = \sqrt{\operatorname {ch}^2 1 - \sin ^2 0} = \operatorname {ch} 1
\]













Theorem 3 (Cauchy’s integral theorem, 1st formulation) Let \(D\) be a simply connected domain (i.e. any closed curve in the domain can be contracted to a point). Let \(\gamma \subset D\) be a piecewise-smooth closed curve in \(D\), and \(f: D \to \mathbb {C}\) holomorphic. Then \[
  \int _{\gamma } f(z) \;  dz = 0
\]











Theorem 4 (Cauchy’s integral theorem, 2nd formulation) Let \(D\) be an arbitrary domain. Let \(\gamma \subset D\) be a piecewise-smooth closed curve in \(D\) that can be contracted to a point within \(D\). Let \(f: D \to \mathbb {C}\) be holomorphic. Then \[
  \int _{\gamma } f(z) \;  dz = 0
\]











Theorem 5 (Cauchy’s integral theorem, 3rd formulation) Let \(D\) be an arbitrary domain, and let \(\partial D\) be the union of finitely many closed piecewise-smooth curves. Let \(f: \overline{D} \to \mathbb {C}\) be holomorphic in \(D\) and continuous on \(\overline{D}\). Then \[
  \int _{\partial D} f(z) \;  dz = 0
\] where \(\partial D\) is the union of several curves, which must be correctly oriented, i.e. oriented so that the domain \(D\) stays on the left as it is traversed.











Theorem 6 (Cauchy’s integral theorem, 4th formulation) Let \(D\) be a simply connected domain. Let \(f: D \to \mathbb {C}\) be holomorphic in \(D\). Let \(z_1, z_2 \in D\). Then the integral from \(z_1\) to \(z_2\) does not depend on the curve along which it is taken. I.e. if \(\gamma_1\), \(\gamma_2\) are 2 piecewise-smooth curves with \(z_1\), \(z_2\) as their endpoints, then \[
  \int _{\gamma _1} f(z) \;  dz = \int _{\gamma _2} f(z) \;  dz
\]










ExampleExample 7





Let \[
  \gamma = \left\{ z \in \mathbb {C} \;  : \;  \left|z-i\right| = 1, \;  \operatorname {Re}z \geq 0\right\}
\] Find \(\int_{\gamma } \frac{1}{z^2 -1 }dz\).






SolutionSolution





Strictly speaking, the problem is not well posed, since the orientation of the curve is not specified. Let us assume the orientation from the point \(0\) to the point \(2i\) (otherwise the answer will have the opposite sign). Note that the function \(\frac{1}{z^2 - 1}\) is holomorphic in the domain \(\mathbb {C} \setminus \left\{ 1, -1\right\}\). By Cauchy’s integral theorem we have
\[
\begin{align}  \int _{\gamma } \frac{1}{z^2 -1 }dz & = \int _{[0, 2i]} \frac{1}{z^2 - 1} dz = \int _{0}^2 \frac{1}{(it)^2 - 1} \cdot i \cdot dt = -i \int _{0}^2 \frac{1}{t^2 + 1} dt = \\ & = -i \arctan (t) \bigg\rvert _{0}^2 = -i \arctan (2) \end{align}
\]






Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: the arc gamma (the right half of the circle |z-i|=1), the segment [0,2i], the singular points +-1, the shaded half-disk between the arc and the segment. Interactive: a slider for the homotopy parameter t in [0,1] that continuously deforms the arc into the segment (the family of curves (1-t)arc + tsegment), with the numerical value of the integral shown alongside (the constant -i*arctan(2)); the ability to drag the singular points +-1 to see when the deformation stops being legitimate.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/140/060_contour_deformation_fig.tex


Method 2, via multivalued functions
\[
\begin{align}  2\int _{\gamma } \frac{1}{z^2 -1 }dz & = 2\int _{[0, 2i]} \frac{1}{z^2 - 1} dz = \int _{[0,2i]}\frac{dz}{z - 1} - \int _{[0,2i]}\frac{dz}{z+1} = \ln (z-1) \bigg\rvert _0^{2i} - \ln (z+1)\bigg\rvert _0^{2i} = \\ & = \ln (2i - 1) - \ln (-1) - \ln (2i+1) + \ln (1) = \\ & = \underbrace{\ln \left|2i-1\right| - \ln \left|-1\right| - \ln \left|2i+1\right| + \ln \left|1\right|}_{=0} + i \left(\operatorname {arg}(2i-1) - \operatorname {arg}(-1)- \operatorname {arg}(2i+1) + \operatorname {arg}(1)\right) \end{align}
\]
Note that here \(\ln\) and \(\arg\) denote single-valued branches. They must be chosen from the same branches of \(\operatorname {Ln}\) and \(\operatorname {Arg}\). It is convenient to take the branch for which \(\operatorname {arg}(1) = 0\). Then (it is best to draw a picture with the points here) \(\operatorname {arg}(-1) = \pi\), \(\operatorname {arg}(2i + 1) = \alpha\), \(\operatorname {arg}(2i-1)= \pi - \alpha\), where \(\alpha = \arctan (2)\).






Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: the points 1, -1, 2i+1, 2i-1, the paths of the points z+1 and z-1 as z moves along the segment [0,2i], the angles alpha and pi-alpha at the origin. Interactive: a slider for the position of z on the segment [0,2i] (or a free endpoint of the path), a dynamic display of arg(z-1) and arg(z+1), the accumulated increments of the argument, and the value of the integral assembled from these increments.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/140/070_argument_choice_fig.tex


In total
\[
  2\int _{\gamma } \frac{1}{z^2 -1 }dz = i \left((\pi - \alpha ) - \pi - \alpha + 0\right) = -2i\alpha , \qquad \text{i.e.} \quad \int _{\gamma } \frac{1}{z^2 -1 }dz = -i\arctan (2)
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(-i \arctan (2)\) or \(i \arctan (2)\).













Theorem 7 (Cauchy’s integral FORMULA) Let \(D \subset \mathbb {C}\) be a domain, \(f: D \to \mathbb {C}\) holomorphic. Let \(a \in \operatorname {int}D\), i.e. there is \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that \(\overline{U_{\varepsilon }(a)} \subset D\). Then for every \(z \in U_{\varepsilon }(a)\) we have \[
  f(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint _{\partial U_{\varepsilon }(a) } \frac{f(\zeta )}{\zeta - z} d\zeta
\]











Corollary 1 Under the assumptions of the previous theorem, if we differentiate the expression (it can be shown that this is legitimate), we obtain \[
  f^{(n)}(z) = \frac{n!}{2\pi i } \oint _{\partial U_{\varepsilon }(a) } \frac{f(\zeta )}{(\zeta - z)^{n+1}} d\zeta
\] That is, a holomorphic function is infinitely differentiable!










ExampleExample 8





Compute \[
  \oint _{\left|\zeta -i\right|=1} \frac{\cos \zeta }{(\zeta -i)^3} d\zeta
\]






SolutionSolution





The function \(f(z) = \cos z\) is holomorphic everywhere. We have \[
\begin{align}  f^{(2)}(i) & = \frac{2!}{2\pi i} \oint _{\left|\zeta -i\right|=1} \frac{\cos \zeta }{(\zeta -i)^3} d\zeta \\ f^{(2)}(i) & = -\cos (i) = -\frac{e^{i \cdot i} + e^{-i \cdot i}}{2} = -\frac{e + \frac{1}{e}}{2} \end{align}
\] In total \[
  \oint _{\left|\zeta -i\right|=1} \frac{\cos \zeta }{(\zeta -i)^3} d\zeta = \frac{2\pi i}{2!} \cdot f^{(2)}(i) = -\frac{\pi }{2} \left(e + \frac{1}{e}\right) i
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(-\frac{\pi }{2} \left(e + \frac{1}{e}\right)i\).

title: Power series and elementary functions
text:
WarningDraft



These notes are still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and places that have not been fully worked out locally. If you find something, please let the author know (contact info on the course page).


\(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty }c_n(z-z_0)^n\) — a power series. Properties:

There exists a unique \(R \in [0, +\infty ]\) such that the series converges for \(\left|z - z_0\right| < R\) and diverges for \(\left|z - z_0\right| > R\) (\(R\) is the radius of convergence, the disk \(\left|z - z_0\right| < R\) is the disk of convergence);
The series converges uniformly on every compact subset of the disk of convergence;
A power series may be differentiated term by term, and the radius of convergence does not change.

Corollary: the sum of the series is holomorphic in the disk of convergence.
Formula:
\[
  R = \left(\varlimsup _{n \to \infty }\left|c_n\right|^{1/n}\right)^{-1}
\]






ExampleExample 1





Find the radius of convergence of \[
  \sum _{m=0}^{\infty } \left(\frac{27 - 26i^m}{27 + 26i^m}\right)^{m^2} z^{m^2}
\]






SolutionSolution





We have a power series \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty }c_n z^n\), where \[
  c_n = \begin{cases}  \left(\frac{27 - 26i^m}{27 + 26i^m}\right)^{m^2}, &  n = m^2 \text{ for some }m \in \mathbb {Z}_+ \\ 0, &  n \text{ is not a perfect square} \end{cases}
\] Note that for \(n = m^2\) \[
  \left|c_n\right|^{1/n} = \left|\left(\frac{27 - 26i^m}{27 + 26i^m}\right)^{m^2}\right|^{1/n} = \left|\frac{27 - 26i^m}{27 + 26i^m}\right| = \begin{cases}  \frac{1}{53}, &  m \equiv _4 0 \\ 1, &  m \equiv _4 1 \\ 53, &  m \equiv _4 2 \\ 1 , &  m \equiv _4 3 \end{cases}
\] Consequently, \[
  \varlimsup _{n \to \infty }\left|c_n\right|^{1/n} = 53, \qquad \text{i.e. } R = \frac{1}{53}
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(R = 1/53\).






A function is called analytic in a domain \(D \subset \mathbb {C}\) if for every point \(z_0 \in D\) there exists a neighborhood \(U(z_0)\) in which the function can be represented as a power series (in powers of \((z - z_0)\)).







Theorem 1 A function \(f\) is holomorphic in \(D\) \(\iff\) \(f\) is analytic in \(D\).










ProblemProblem T.11





Find the radii of convergence of the power series:

\(\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty }\left(\frac{1-i n}{1+i n}\right)^{n^{2}} z^{n}\);
\(\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty }\left(1+i^{n}\right)^{n} z^{n}\);
\(\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty } 2^{n} z^{n!}\);
\(\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty }\left((1+i)^{n}+(1-i)^{n}\right) z^{n}\).





1 The complex exponential, trigonometric functions
\(e^{z} = \exp (z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{z^n}{n!}\).
\[
\begin{align}  \sin (z) & := \frac{e^{iz} - e^{-iz}}{2i}, \quad \cos (z) = \frac{e^{iz} + e^{-iz}}{2} \\ \operatorname {sh}(z) & := \frac{e^{z} - e^{-z}}{2}, \quad \operatorname {ch}(z) := \frac{e^{z} + e^{-z}}{2} \end{align}
\]






ExampleExample (Problem 3.17(6))





Find all solutions of the following equations:

\(\operatorname {ctg} z = -\frac{3 i}{5}\);







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Essentially we need to find \(\operatorname {Arcctg}\left(-\frac{3}{5}i\right)\).
\[
\begin{align}  -\frac{3}{5}i & = \operatorname {ctg}z = \frac{\cos z}{\sin z} = \frac{2i}{2} \frac{\operatorname {exp}\left(iz\right) + \operatorname {exp}\left(-iz\right)}{\operatorname {exp}\left(iz\right) - \operatorname {exp}\left(-iz\right)} \\ 3\operatorname {exp}\left(-iz\right) - 3\operatorname {exp}\left(iz\right) & = 5\operatorname {exp}\left(iz\right) + 5\operatorname {exp}\left(-iz\right) \\ 8\operatorname {exp}\left(2iz\right) & = -2 \\ \operatorname {exp}\left(-2y + 2ix\right) & = -\frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \operatorname {exp}\left(i\pi \right) \end{align}
\]
I.e. \(y = -\frac{1}{2}\ln \frac{1}{4} = \ln (2)\), \(2x = \pi + 2\pi k\),
\[
  z = \frac{\pi }{2} + \pi k + i\ln (2), \quad k \in \mathbb {Z}
\]











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(z = i \ln 2+\pi \left(k+\frac{1}{2}\right), k \in \mathbb {Z}\);








Formulas:
\[
\begin{align}  \cos (z_1 + z_2) & = \cos (z_1)\cos (z_2) - \sin (z_1)\sin (z_2) \\ \sin (z_1 + z_2) & = \sin (z_1)\cos (z_2) + \cos (z_1)\sin (z_2) \\ \operatorname {ch}(z_1 + z_2) & = \operatorname {ch}z_1 \operatorname {ch}z_2 + \operatorname {sh}z_1\operatorname {sh} z_2 \\ \operatorname {sh}(z_1 + z_2) & = \operatorname {sh}z_1 \operatorname {ch}z_2 + \operatorname {ch}z_1\operatorname {sh} z_2 \end{align}
\]
Easy to prove if one knows the multiplicativity of the exponential.
Also:
\[
\begin{align}  \operatorname {sh} z & = -i \sin (iz) &  \operatorname {ch}z & = \cos (iz) \\ \operatorname {th} z & = -i \operatorname {tg}(iz), &  \operatorname {cth}z & = i\operatorname {ctg}(iz) \end{align}
\]






ExampleExample (Problem 3.12(2))





Let \(x = \operatorname {Re} z, y = \operatorname {Im} z\). Find \(\operatorname {Re} \cos z\) and \(\operatorname {Im} \cos z\).






SolutionSolution





We have \[
  \cos z = \cos (x + iy) = \cos (x)\cos (iy) -\sin (x) \sin (iy) = \cos x \operatorname {ch}y - i \sin x \operatorname {sh}y
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(\operatorname {Re} \cos z = \cos x \cdot \operatorname {ch} y, \quad \operatorname {Im} \cos z = -\sin x \cdot \operatorname {sh} y\).












ExampleExample (Problem 3.13(2))





Let \(x = \operatorname {Re} z, y = \operatorname {Im} z\). Find \(\left|\cos z\right|\).






SolutionSolution





\[
\begin{align}  \left|\cos z\right|^2 & = \cos ^2(x) \operatorname {ch}^2(y) + \sin ^2(x) \operatorname {sh}^2(y) = \operatorname {ch}^2(y) - \sin ^2(x)\operatorname {ch}^2(y) + \sin ^2(x) \operatorname {sh}^2(y) = \\ & =\operatorname {ch}^2(y) - \sin ^2(x) \left(\operatorname {ch}^2(y) - \operatorname {sh}^2(y)\right) = \operatorname {ch}^2(y) - \sin ^2(x) \end{align}
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(\left|\cos z\right| = \sqrt{\operatorname {ch}^2 y - \sin^2 x}\).












ProblemProblem 3.10





Prove the formulas:

\(\operatorname {ch}^{2} z-\operatorname {sh}^{2} z = 1\);
\(\operatorname {ch}\left(z_{1}+z_{2}\right) = \operatorname {ch} z_{1} \operatorname {ch} z_{2}+\operatorname {sh} z_{1} \operatorname {sh} z_{2}\);










ProblemProblem 3.11





Prove the formulas:

\(\operatorname {sh} z = -i \sin (i z)\);
\(\cos (i z) = \operatorname {ch} z\);










ExampleExample (Problem 3.12)





Let \(x = \operatorname {Re} z, y = \operatorname {Im} z\). Prove that:

\(\operatorname {Re} \cos z = \cos x \cdot \operatorname {ch} y, \quad \operatorname {Im} \cos z = -\sin x \cdot \operatorname {sh} y\);
\(\operatorname {Re} \operatorname {sh} z = \operatorname {sh} x \cdot \cos y, \quad \operatorname {Im} \operatorname {sh} z = \operatorname {ch} x \cdot \sin y\);







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



We have
\[
  \cos z = \cos (x + iy) = \cos (x)\cos (iy) -\sin (x) \sin (iy) = \cos x \operatorname {ch}y - i \sin x \operatorname {sh}y
\]








Enum-item2.



We have
\[
  2\operatorname {sh}z = e^{z} - e^{-z} = \underbrace{\left(e^{x} - e^{-x}\right)}_{=2\operatorname {sh}x}\cos (y) + i\underbrace{\left(e^{x} + e^{-x}\right)}_{=2\operatorname {ch}x}\sin (y)
\]














ProblemProblem 3.12





Let \(x = \operatorname {Re} z, y = \operatorname {Im} z\). Prove that:

\(\operatorname {Re} \sin z = \sin x \cdot \operatorname {ch} y, \quad \operatorname {Im} \sin z = \cos x \cdot \operatorname {sh} y ;\)










ExampleExample (Problem 3.17)





Find all solutions of the following equations:

\(\cos z = \frac{3 i}{4}\);







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\(\frac{3}{2}i = e^{iz} + e^{-iz} = e^{-y + ix} + e^{y - ix} = e^{-y}\cdot \left(\cos (x) + i\sin (x)\right) + e^{y} \cdot \left(\cos (x) - i\sin (x)\right)\), i.e.
\[
\begin{aligned}
            \begin{cases}
                (e^{-y} + e^{y}) \cos(x) = 0 \\
                (e^{-y} - e^{y}) \sin(x) = \frac{3}{2}
            \end{cases} &\iff
            \begin{cases}
                \cos(x) = 0 \\
                (e^{-y} - e^{y}) \sin(x) = \frac{3}{2}
            \end{cases}
            \left[ \begin{array}{c}
                 \begin{cases}
                    x = \frac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k \\
                    e^{-y} - e^{y} = \frac{3}{2}
                \end{cases}
                 \\
                 \begin{cases}
                    x = -\frac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k \\
                    e^{-y} - e^{y} = -\frac{3}{2}
                \end{cases}
            \end{array}\right. \iff \\
            &\iff \left[ \begin{array}{c}
                 \begin{cases}
                    x = \frac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k \\
                    y = -\ln(2)
                \end{cases}
                 \\
                 \begin{cases}
                    x = -\frac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k \\
                    y = \ln(2)
                \end{cases}
            \end{array} \right.
\end{aligned}
\] (the first system used \(e^{-y} - e^{y} = -2\operatorname {sh}(y) = \frac{3}{2}\) \(\iff\) \(\operatorname {sh}(y) = -\frac{3}{4}\) \(\iff\) \(y = \ln \left(-\frac{3}{4} + \sqrt{\frac{9}{16}+1}\right) = -\ln 2\); the second is solved symmetrically). In total
\[
  z = \pm \left(\frac{\pi }{2} - i \ln 2\right) + 2\pi k, \quad k \in \mathbb {Z}
\]






Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: the solution set of cos z = 3i/4 — two series of points on the lines Im z = ∓ln2 with step 2pi. Interactive: input/slider for the right-hand side w (complex), regenerating the series of solutions of cos z = w; highlight the symmetry z -> -z and the periodicity z -> z + 2pi.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/120/010_cos_equation_solutions_fig.tex













AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(z = \pm \left(-i \ln 2+\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+2 k \pi , k \in \mathbb {Z}\);














ProblemProblem 3.17





Find all solutions of the following equations:

\(\sin z = \frac{4 i}{3}\);
\(\cos z = \frac{3+i}{4}\);
\(\operatorname {ctg} z = -\frac{3 i}{5}\);










ExampleExample 5.9





Let the function \(f(z) = u(x, y)+i v(x, y)\) be differentiable in a domain \(G \subset \mathbb {C}\), and suppose one of the functions

\(r(x, y) = |f(z)|\); keeps a constant value in the domain \(G\). Prove that \(f(z) \equiv \operatorname {const}\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



We have \(u^2 + v^2 \equiv \operatorname {const}\) in the domain \(G\). If this constant equals \(0\), then \(f \equiv 0\), and we are done. Otherwise we differentiate the identity with respect to \(x\) and \(y\), and also apply the Cauchy-Riemann conditions:
\[
  \begin{cases}  0 = 2uu_x + 2vv_x = 2uv_y + 2vv_x \\ 0 = 2uu_y + 2vv_y = -2uv_x + 2vv_y \end{cases}
\]
This is a linear system for the pair \((v_x, v_y)\) with determinant
\[
  \begin{vmatrix}  v &  u \\ -u &  v \end{vmatrix} = u^2 + v^2 \neq 0,
\]
i.e. \(v_x = v_y = 0\) throughout the domain \(G\). Taking into account the differentiability of \(v\), we obtain that \(v \equiv \operatorname {const}\) on \(G\). By the Cauchy-Riemann conditions also \(u_x = v_y = 0\) and \(u_y = -v_x = 0\), i.e. \(u \equiv \operatorname {const}\) as well.














ProblemProblem 5.9





Let the function \(f(z) = u(x, y)+i v(x, y)\) be differentiable in a domain \(G \subset \mathbb {C}\), and suppose one of the functions

\(u(x, y)\);
\(\varphi (x, y) = \arg f(z)\) keeps a constant value in the domain \(G\). Prove that \(f(z) \equiv \operatorname {const}\).










ExampleExample 5.17





Recover the regular function \(f(z)\) from the condition

\(\operatorname {Im} f(z) = x \sin y \operatorname {ch} x+y \operatorname {sh} x \cos y, f(0) = 0\);







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\(f(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y)\), and moreover
\[
\begin{align}  v(x,y) & = x \sin y \operatorname {ch} x+y \operatorname {sh} x \cos y = \\ & =x \cdot \operatorname {Im}\operatorname {sh}z + y \cdot \operatorname {Re}\operatorname {sh}z \end{align}
\]
The first Cauchy-Riemann condition:
\[
\begin{align}  \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & = x \operatorname {ch}x \cos y + \operatorname {sh}x \cos y - y \operatorname {sh}x \sin y = \\ & = \cos y \cdot x\operatorname {ch}x + \left(\cos y - y \sin y\right)\operatorname {sh}x \end{align}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{align}  u(x,y) & = \cos y \cdot \left(x \operatorname {sh}x - \operatorname {ch}x\right) + \left(\cos y - y \sin y\right)\operatorname {ch}x + \varphi (y) = \\ & = x \cos y \operatorname {sh}x - y \operatorname {sin} y \operatorname {ch}x + \varphi (y) = \\ & = x \operatorname {Re}\operatorname {sh}z - y \operatorname {Im}\operatorname {sh}z + \varphi (y) \end{align}
\]
The second Cauchy-Riemann condition:
\[
\begin{align}  -\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & = \sin y \operatorname {ch}x + x \sin y \operatorname {sh}x + y \cos y \operatorname {ch}x \end{align}
\]
At the same time
\[
\begin{align}  -\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & =\sin y \cdot x \operatorname {sh}x + \sin y \operatorname {ch}x + y \cos y \operatorname {ch}x - \varphi '(y) \end{align}
\]
I.e. \(\varphi '(y) = 0\), \(\varphi (y) = C\),
\[
  u(x,y) = \cos y \cdot \left(x \operatorname {sh}x - \operatorname {ch}x\right) + \left(\cos y - y \sin y\right)\operatorname {ch}x + C
\]
Further, \(f(0) = 0\), i.e. \(0 = u(0,0) = -1 + 1 + C\), \(C = 0\). In total,
\[
\begin{align}  f(z) & = u + iv = x \operatorname {Re}\operatorname {sh}z - y \operatorname {Im}\operatorname {sh}z + i \cdot \left(x \cdot \operatorname {Im}\operatorname {sh}z + y \cdot \operatorname {Re}\operatorname {sh}z\right) =\\ & =x \cdot \left(\operatorname {Re}\operatorname {sh}z + i \operatorname {Im}\operatorname {sh}z\right) + iy \cdot \left(\operatorname {Re}\operatorname {sh}z + i \operatorname {Im}\operatorname {sh}z\right) = x \cdot \operatorname {sh}z + iy \cdot \operatorname {sh}z = \\ & = z \cdot \operatorname {sh}z \end{align}
\]











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(z \operatorname {sh} z\);














ProblemProblem 5.17





Recover the regular function \(f(z)\) from the condition

\(\operatorname {Im} f(z) = y \operatorname {ch} x \cos y+x \sin y \operatorname {sh} x, f(0) = 1\);
\(\operatorname {Re} f(z) = x e^{x} \cos y-(y+1) e^{x} \sin y, \quad f(0) = i\);










ProblemProblem T.12





Find the values \(\sin i, \operatorname {tg}(1+i), \operatorname {ctg}(\pi / 4-i \ln 2)\).





2 The complex logarithm, complex powers
\(\operatorname {Ln}(z)\) denotes all possible solutions of the equation \(e^{w} = z\). We have
\[
  e^{w} = z \iff e^{\operatorname {Re}(w)} \cdot e^{i\operatorname {Im}(w)} = \left|z\right| \cdot e^{i\operatorname {arg}(z)}
\]
I.e.
\[
  \begin{cases}  \operatorname {Re}(w) = \ln (\left|z\right|) \\ \operatorname {Im}(w) = \operatorname {arg}(z) + 2 \pi k, \;  k \in \mathbb {Z} \end{cases}
\]
Thus,
\[
  \operatorname {Ln}(z) = \ln (\left|z\right|) + i \cdot \operatorname {Arg}z
\]
where
\[
  \operatorname {Arg}z := \underbrace{\operatorname {arg}(z)}_{\in (-\pi , \pi ]} + 2 \pi k
\]
is the generalized argument. Both \(\operatorname {Arg}z\) and \(\operatorname {Ln}z\) are multivalued functions.
Power: \(a^b := \operatorname {exp}\left(b \cdot \operatorname {Ln}a\right)\), \(a,b \in \mathbb {C}\), \(a \neq 0\). A multivalued function.






ExampleExample 9





Compute:

\(1^i\);
\(i^1\);
\(i^i\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\(1^i = \operatorname {exp}\left(i\operatorname {Ln}1\right) = \operatorname {exp}\left(i \cdot 2\pi k i\right) = \operatorname {exp}\left(-2\pi k\right)\), \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\);








Enum-item2.



\(i^1 = \operatorname {exp}\left(\operatorname {Ln} i\right) = \operatorname {exp}\left(i\left(\frac{\pi }{2} + 2\pi k\right)\right) = i\);








Enum-item3.



\(i^i = \operatorname {exp}\left(i \operatorname {Ln} i\right) = \operatorname {exp}\left(-\frac{\pi }{2} - 2\pi k\right)\), \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\).








\(e^z\) can be understood in two ways: either as the single-valued function \(\operatorname {exp}z = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty } \frac{z^n}{n!}\), or as exponentiation, that is, as the multivalued function
\[
  e^z = \operatorname {exp}\left(\operatorname {Ln}e \cdot z\right) = \operatorname {exp}\left(\left(1 + 2\pi k i\right) \cdot z\right) = \operatorname {exp}(z) \cdot \operatorname {exp}(2\pi k i z)
\]
For example, \(e^{i\pi } = - \operatorname {exp}\left(-2\pi^2 k\right)\), \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\), but \(\operatorname {exp}(i \pi ) = -1\).
As a rule, \(e^z\) is understood as \(\operatorname {exp}(z)\), i.e. the single-valued function, while \(a^{z}\), \(a \neq e\) is understood as the multivalued function, exponentiation.


3 Inverse trigonometric functions
\(\operatorname {Arctg}(z)\) denotes all possible solutions of the equation \(z = \operatorname {tg} w\). Let us solve it. We have
\[
  z = \operatorname {tg}w = \frac{\sin w}{\cos w} = \frac{e^{i w} - e^{-iw}}{i(e^{iw} + e^{-iw})} = \frac{e^{2iw} - 1}{i(e^{2iw} + 1)}
\]
Then \(e^{2iw} (zi - 1) = -(1 + zi)\), i.e.
\[
  w = \frac{1}{2i} \operatorname {Ln} \left(\frac{1 + zi}{1 - zi}\right) =: \operatorname {Arctg}(z)
\]






ProblemProblem T.13





Find all values of \(2^{i}, i^{i},(-1)^{2 i}, \operatorname {Arctg}(5 i / 3)\).









ProblemProblem T.14





Find the sum of the trigonometric series \[
  \sum _{n = 0}^{\infty } \frac{\cos n \varphi }{n!}, \quad \varphi \in \mathbb {R}
\]

title: About the project
text:
“FPMI Courses” is a collection of open course materials for the subjects taught at the Phystech School of Applied Mathematics and Informatics of MIPT. The website format makes it possible to combine lecture notes with interactive plots and visualizations, site-wide navigation and cross-references between topics.
The site is intended primarily for FPMI students and instructors, and also for anyone else who finds these materials useful. The catalog and the curriculum help show which courses are covered; the content of a published course is on that course’s own page.

text:

ExampleExample 1.1





Compute:

\((1+2 i)(2-i)+(1-2 i)(2+i)\);
\(\left(\frac{1-i}{1+i}\right)^{3}\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\((1+2 i)(2-i)+(1-2 i)(2+i) = 2 + 4i -i + 2 + 2 -4i + i + 2 = 8\);








Enum-item2.



We have
\[
  \frac{1 - i}{1 + i} = \frac{(1-i)^2}{(1+i) (1-i)} = \frac{-2i}{2} = -i
\]
I.e. \(\left(\frac{1 - i}{1 + i}\right)^{3} = (-i)^3 = -i^3 = i\).











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.














Enum-item2.



\(i\).














ProblemProblem 1.1(2)





Compute: \(\frac{5}{1+2 i}+\frac{5}{2-i}\).









ExampleExample 1.3





Find all roots of the equation:

\(z+|z+1|+i = 0\);







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Let \(z = x + iy\). \(-i - z = \left|z + 1\right| \in [0, +\infty )\), i.e. \(\operatorname {Im}(-i-z) = - 1 - y = 0\), \(y = -1\).
Further, \(\left|z + 1\right| = \left|x + 1 - i\right| = \sqrt{(x+1)^2 + 1}\); \(-i-z = -x\). We obtain
\[
  -x = \sqrt{(x+1)^2 + 1} \iff \begin{cases}  x \leq 0 \\ x^2 = (x+1)^2 + 1 \end{cases} \iff \begin{cases}  x \leq 0 \\ 0 = 2x + 2 \end{cases} \iff x = -1
\]











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(z = -1-i\);














ProblemProblem 1.3(4)





Find all roots of the equation: \(|z|^{2}-2 i z+2 i = 0\).









ExampleExample 1.4





Solve the system of equations:

\(\left\{ \begin{array}{l}|z-2 i| = \left|z\right|, \\ |z-i| = |z-1| ;\end{array}\right.\)







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



The point \(z = x + iy\) is equidistant from \(0\) and from \(2i\), i.e. it lies on the line \(\operatorname {Im}z = y = 1\). Further, the point \(z\) is equidistant from \(i\) and from \(1\), i.e. it lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, on the line \(x = y\).











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(z = 1+i\);














ProblemProblem 1.4(2)

ExampleExample 4





Solve the equation: \(z^{7} = -2 + i\);






SolutionSolution





We have \(-2 + i = r e^{i \varphi }\), where \(r = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{5}\), \(\varphi = \arctan \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) + \pi\). Then \[
  z^7 = \sqrt{5}\,  e^{i\varphi } \iff z = \left(\sqrt{5}\right)^{1/7} \cdot \exp \left(i\frac{\varphi + 2\pi k}{7}\right), \qquad k \in \left\{ 0, 1, \ldots , 6\right\}
\] — all \(7\) values of the root.









AnswerAnswer





7 roots: \(z = \left(\sqrt{5}\right)^{1/7} \cdot \exp \left(i\frac{1}{7}\left(\varphi + 2\pi k\right)\right)\), where \(\varphi = \arctan \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) + \pi\), \(k \in \left\{ 0,1\ldots ,6\right\}\).

ExampleExample 1.9





Determine what curve in the plane is defined by the equation:

\(\operatorname {Re} \frac{1}{z} = \frac{1}{a}(a > 0)\);
\(\operatorname {Im} \frac{z-1}{z+1} = 0\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Recall that \(z\cdot \overline{z} = \left|z\right|^2\), i.e. \(\frac{1}{z} = \frac{1}{\left|z\right|^2}\overline{z}\),
\[
  \operatorname {Re}\frac{1}{z} = \frac{1}{\left|z\right|^2} \operatorname {Re}\overline{z} = \frac{1}{\left|z\right|^2}\operatorname {Re}z = \frac{x}{x^2 + y^2}
\]
We have
\[
  \frac{1}{a} = \frac{x}{x^2 + y^2} \iff x^2 - ax + y^2 = 0 \iff \left(x - \frac{a}{2}\right)^2 + y^2 = \left(\frac{a}{2}\right)^2
\]
A circle centered at \(\left(\frac{a}{2}, 0\right)\) with radius \(\frac{a}{2}\) (excluding the point \(z = 0\), where \(\frac{1}{z}\) is undefined).








Enum-item2.



We have
\[
  \frac{z-1}{z+1} = (z-1) \cdot \frac{1}{\left|z+1\right|^2}\overline{(z + 1)} = \frac{(z-1)(\overline{z} + 1)}{\left|z+1\right|^2} = \frac{\left|z\right|^2 + z - \overline{z} - 1}{\left|z+1\right|^2}
\]
I.e.
\[
  \operatorname {Im}\frac{z-1}{z+1} = \frac{1}{\left|z+1\right|^2} \operatorname {Im}\left(\left|z\right|^2 + z - \overline{z} - 1\right) = \frac{1}{\left|z+1\right|^2} \operatorname {Im}\left(z - \overline{z}\right) = \frac{1}{\left|z+1\right|^2} 2\operatorname {Im}z
\]
Thus, \(\operatorname {Im} \frac{z-1}{z+1} = 0\) \(\iff\) \(\operatorname {Im}z = 0\) (and \(z \neq -1\), where the expression is undefined).











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



The circle constructed on the segment \([0, a]\) as diameter (excluding the point \(z = 0\))








Enum-item2.



The real axis (excluding the point \(z = -1\)).

ExampleExample 1.10





Determine what set of points \(z\) in the complex plane satisfies the inequality:

\(0 < \arg \frac{i-z}{z+i} < \frac{\pi }{2}\);
\(|z| > 1-\operatorname {Re} z\);







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Let us transform:
\[
  \frac{i-z}{z+i} = \frac{(i-z)\overline{(z+i)}}{\left|z+i\right|^2} = \frac{(i-z)(\overline{z}-i)}{\left|z+i\right|^2} = \frac{i\overline{z} + 1 - z\overline{z} + iz}{\left|z+i\right|^2} = \frac{1 - \left|z\right|^2 + 2ix}{\left|z+i\right|^2}
\]
The condition \(0 < \arg w < \frac{\pi }{2}\) means that \(w\) lies in the open first quadrant, i.e. \(\operatorname {Re}w > 0\) and \(\operatorname {Im}w > 0\):
\[
  \begin{cases}  1 - \left|z\right|^2 > 0 \\ 2x > 0 \end{cases} \iff \begin{cases}  \left|z\right| < 1 \\ \operatorname {Re}z > 0 \end{cases}
\]
— the right half of the unit disk, boundary excluded.






Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: the right half of the unit disk (the set 0 < arg((i-z)/(z+i)) < pi/2), boundaries dashed. Interactive: two sliders for the bounds of the argument sector (currently 0 and pi/2) that recompute the shaded region; on hovering over a point z, show w = (i-z)/(z+i) on a second panel along with its argument.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/110/010_arg_halfdisk_fig.tex










Enum-item2.



If \(\operatorname {Re}z = x > 1\), then the right-hand side \(1 - x\) is negative and the inequality holds. For \(x \leq 1\) both sides are nonnegative, so let us square:
\[
  \left|z\right| > 1 - x \iff x^2 + y^2 > 1 - 2x + x^2 \iff y^2 > 1 - 2x
\]
(for \(x > 1\) the inequality \(y^2 > 1 - 2x\) also holds, since the right-hand side is negative). In total: the set \(\left\{ y^2 > 1 - 2x\right\}\) is the part of the plane on the same side of the parabola \(y^2 = 1 - 2x\) as the point \(z = 1\); the parabola itself is excluded.






Note

Plan: TikZ: the region |z| > 1 - Re z (to the right of the parabola y^2 = 1-2x), parabola dashed, point z = 1. Interactive: a slider for the parameter c in the inequality |z| > c - Re z (the family of parabolas y^2 = c^2 - 2cx), with a check of whether a draggable point belongs to the region.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/110/020_parabola_region_fig.tex













AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



The right half of the disk of radius 1 centered at the point \(z = 0\).








Enum-item2.



The part of the plane lying on the same side of the parabola \(y^{2} = 1-2 x\) as the point \(z = 1\) (and bounded by this parabola).


In all cases the points of the boundary curves are excluded.

A function \(f: U(z_0) \to \mathbb {C}\) is called differentiable at the point \(z_0 \in \mathbb {C}\) if there exist a number \(A \in \mathbb {C}\) and a function \(\alpha (\Delta z) \xrightarrow [\Delta z \to 0]{} 0\) (\(\Delta z := z - z_0\)), such that
\[
  \Delta f = f(z) - f(z_0) = A \cdot \Delta z + \alpha (\Delta z) \cdot \Delta z, \qquad z \in U(z_0)
\]
\(A = \lim_{\Delta z \to 0} \frac{\Delta f}{\Delta z} =: f'(z_0)\).
\(f(z) = u(z) + iv(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y)\), where \(u,v: \mathbb {R}^{2} \to \mathbb {R}\).







Theorem 1 (The Cauchy-Riemann equations) Let \(f: U(z_0) \to \mathbb {C}\), \(z_0 = x_0 + iy_0 \in \mathbb {C}\). \(f\) is differentiable at \(z_0\) if and only if

\(u\), \(v\) are differentiable at \((x_0, y_0)\) (in the real sense);
\(u_x = v_y\), \(u_y = -v_x\).











ExampleExample (Problem 5.1(3,6))





Find all points \(z = x+i y\) at which the following functions are differentiable:

\(x^{2}-i y^{2}\);
\(z \operatorname {Re} z\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\(u(x,y) = x^2\), \(v(x,y) = -y^2\). \(u_x = 2x\), \(v_y = -2y\). \(u_y = 0\), \(v_x = 0\).

First Cauchy-Riemann condition: \(u_x = v_y\) only on the line \(x= -y\);
Second Cauchy-Riemann condition: \(u_y = -v_x = 0\) everywhere.









Enum-item2.



\(f(z) = (x + iy) \cdot x = x^2 + ixy\), \(u(x,y) = \operatorname {Re}f(z) = x^2\), \(v(x,y) = \operatorname {Im}f(z) = xy\). They are differentiable everywhere. The Cauchy-Riemann conditions:
\[
  \begin{cases}  \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 2x = x = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 0 = -y = -\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \end{cases}
\]
I.e. differentiable only when \(x = y=0\).











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



on the line \(\operatorname {Re} z = -\operatorname {Im} z\);








Enum-item2.



at the point \(z = 0\).








Geometric meaning of the Cauchy-Riemann conditions:
\[
\begin{align}  u_x + iv_x & = \lim _{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{f(x_0 + \Delta x + iy_0) - f(x_0 + iy_0)}{\Delta x} = \lim _{i\Delta y \to 0} \frac{f(x_0 + i(y_0 + \Delta y)) - f(x_0 + iy_0)}{i\Delta y} = \\ & = \lim _{\Delta y \to 0} \frac{\Delta u + i\Delta v}{i\Delta y} = \lim _{\Delta y \to 0} \frac{\Delta v - i\Delta u}{\Delta y} = v_y - iu_y \end{align}
\]
The partial derivatives are equal only along 2 directions. And this is sufficient for differentiability.
Another interpretation of the Cauchy-Riemann conditions: introduce new “coordinates”: \((x,y) \mapsto (z, \overline{z})\),
\[
  \begin{cases}  z = x + iy \\ \overline{z} = x - iy \end{cases}, \qquad \begin{cases}  x = \frac{z + \overline{z}}{2} \\ y = \frac{z - \overline{z}}{2i} \end{cases}
\]
We have
\[
  df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} dy = \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} dz + \frac{\partial f}{\partial \overline{z}} d\overline{z}
\]
What are \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\), \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial \overline{z}}\)? We have
\[
\begin{align}  \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} & = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \frac{\partial x}{\partial {z}} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \frac{\partial y}{\partial {z}} = \left(u_x + iv_x\right)\frac{1}{2} + (u_y + iv_y)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2i}\right) = \\ & = \frac{(u_x + v_y) + i(v_x - u_y)}{2} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial \overline{z}} & = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \frac{\partial x}{\partial \overline{z}} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \frac{\partial y}{\partial \overline{z}} = \left(u_x + iv_x\right) \frac{1}{2} + \left(u_y + iv_y\right)\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2i}\right) = \\ & = \frac{1}{2} \left[\left(u_x - v_y\right) + i \left(v_x + u_y\right)\right] \end{align}
\]
Thus, the Cauchy-Riemann conditions in short form: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial \overline{z}} = 0\). In this case \(df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} dz\), and moreover
\[
  \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} = f'(z) = u_x - iu_y = v_y + iv_x
\]
For example, \(f(z) = z^2 = (x + iy)^2\). It is differentiable everywhere (this can be verified from the definition), and \(f(z) = x^2 - y^2 + 2ixy\), \(u = x^2 - y^2\), \(v = 2xy\). \(u_x = 2x\), \(u_y = -2y\), \(v_x = 2y\), \(v_y = 2x\).
\[
  \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} = 2x + 2iy = 2z
\]






ExampleExample 8





Write the Cauchy-Riemann conditions in polar coordinates.






SolutionSolution





Let \(z = re^{i\varphi }\), i.e. \(x = r\cos \varphi\), \(y = r\sin \varphi\). By the chain rule \[
\begin{align}  u_r & = u_x \cos \varphi + u_y \sin \varphi , &  u_\varphi & = -u_x r\sin \varphi + u_y r \cos \varphi , \\ v_r & = v_x \cos \varphi + v_y \sin \varphi , &  v_\varphi & = -v_x r\sin \varphi + v_y r \cos \varphi . \end{align}
\] Substitute the Cauchy-Riemann conditions \(u_x = v_y\), \(u_y = -v_x\): \[
\begin{align}  v_\varphi & = -v_x r \sin \varphi + v_y r\cos \varphi = u_y r \sin \varphi + u_x r \cos \varphi = r \cdot u_r, \\ u_\varphi & = -u_x r\sin \varphi + u_y r\cos \varphi = -v_y r \sin \varphi - v_x r \cos \varphi = -r \cdot v_r. \end{align}
\] In total, the Cauchy-Riemann conditions in polar coordinates: \[
  u_r = \frac{1}{r} v_{\varphi }, \qquad v_r = -\frac{1}{r} u_{\varphi }
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(u_r = \frac{1}{r} v_{\varphi }\), \(v_r = -\frac{1}{r} u_{\varphi }\).






Let \(D\) be a domain (i.e. an open connected set). A function \(f: D \to \mathbb {C}\) is called holomorphic (also called regular, analytic) if \(f\) is differentiable at every point of \(D\).






ExampleExample 9





Let \(D \subset \mathbb {C}\) be a domain. Find all functions \(f\) holomorphic in \(D\) such that

\(v \equiv \operatorname {const}\) in \(D\);
\(\operatorname {arg}f(z) \equiv \operatorname {const}\) in \(D\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\(v \equiv \operatorname {const}\), i.e. \(v_x = v_y = 0\) in \(D\). By the Cauchy-Riemann conditions \(u_x = v_y = 0\) and \(u_y = -v_x = 0\), i.e. \(u \equiv \operatorname {const}\) (the domain \(D\) is connected). In total \(f \equiv \operatorname {const}\).








Enum-item2.



\(\frac{v}{u} = \operatorname {tg}\operatorname {arg}f(z) = \alpha\) in \(D\), i.e. \(v = \alpha u\) (the case \(\operatorname {arg}f \equiv \pm \frac{\pi }{2}\), i.e. \(u \equiv 0\), is handled as in part 1). The Cauchy-Riemann conditions:
\[
  \begin{cases}  u_x = \alpha u_y \\ u_y = -\alpha u_x \end{cases}
\]
If there is at least one point in \(D\) where \(u_y \neq 0\), then \(-\alpha^2 = 1\), i.e. \(\alpha \in \left\{ i,-i\right\}\). Contradiction (since \(\alpha \in \mathbb {R}\)). I.e. \(u_x = u_y = v_x = v_y \equiv 0\), and again \(f \equiv \operatorname {const}\).











AnswerAnswer





In both cases only \(f \equiv \operatorname {const}\).












ExampleExample (Problem 5.13(2))





Let \(v = x^{2}-y^{2}+2 x y\). Recover the holomorphic function \(f(z)\).






SolutionSolution





Let us check that \(v\) is harmonic (if this is not the case, the problem cannot be solved).
\[
  \Delta v = v_{xx} + v_{yy} = 2 - 2 =0
\]
Indeed harmonic.
Further,
\[
\begin{align}  u_y & = -v_x = -2x - 2y \;  \Rightarrow \;  u = -2xy - y^2 + \varphi (x) \\ -2y + \varphi '(x) = u_x & = v_y = -2y + 2x \;  \Rightarrow \;  \varphi (x) = x^2 + C \end{align}
\]
Let us obtain an expression for \(f\) in terms of \(z\). Note that \(z^2 = x^2 - y^2 + 2ixy\). We have
\[
  f(z) = u + iv = -2xy - y^2 + x^2 + C + i\left(x^{2}-y^{2}+2 x y\right) = z^2 + iz^2 + C, \qquad C \in \mathbb {R}
\]

Find all points \(z = x+i y\) at which the following functions are differentiable:

\]

title: Taylor series and the uniqueness theorem
text:
WarningDraft



These notes are still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and places that have not been fully worked out locally. If you find something, please let the author know (contact info on the course page).



1 Taylor series
As we recall, holomorphy in a domain implies analyticity at every point \(z_0\) of the domain: the function expands into a power series in a neighborhood of \(z_0\). It turns out that this series is necessarily the Taylor series.







Theorem 1 If \(f\) is holomorphic in \(U(z_0)\) and \(f = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty }c_n(z-z_0)^n\) in \(U(z_0)\), then the coefficients of this series are determined uniquely: \[
  c_n = \frac{f^{(n)}(z_0)}{n!}
\] I.e. this is necessarily the Taylor series.










ExampleExample 1





Expand \(\frac{1}{(2 - z)^3}\) into a power series about zero.






SolutionSolution





By the formula for the sum of a geometric series we have \[
  \frac{1}{2- z} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{1 - z/2} = \sum _{n=0}^{\infty } \frac{1}{2^{n+1}}z^n, \qquad \left|z\right| < 2
\] Power series may be differentiated term by term, and the radius of convergence does not change. We have \[
\begin{align}  \frac{1}{(2-z)^2} & = \left(\frac{1}{2- z}\right)' = \sum _{n=0}^{\infty } \frac{1}{2^{n+1}}\left(z^n\right)' = \sum _{n=1}^{\infty } \frac{n}{2^{n+1}}z^{n-1} \\ 2\frac{1}{(2-z)^3} & = \left(\frac{1}{2- z}\right)^{''} = \sum _{n=0}^{\infty } \frac{1}{2^{n+1}}\left(z^n\right)'' = \sum _{n=2}^{\infty } \frac{n(n-1)}{2^{n+1}}\left(z^{n-2}\right) = \sum _{n=0}^{\infty } \frac{(n+2)(n+1)}{2^{n+3}}\left(z^{n}\right) \end{align}
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(\frac{1}{(2 - z)^3} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2^{n+4}}z^n\), \(\left|z\right| < 2\).












ExampleExample 2





Expand \(e^{2z} \sin (4z)\) into a power series about zero.






SolutionSolution





We have \[
  e^{2z} \sin (4z) = e^{2z} \cdot \frac{e^{4iz} - e^{-4iz}}{2i} = \frac{e^{z(2 + 4i)} - e^{z(2 - 4i)}}{2i}
\] It remains to expand each of the exponentials into a power series. Their radii of convergence are \(+\infty\), so the radius of convergence of the resulting series will also be \(+\infty\).









AnswerAnswer





\(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty } \left(\frac{(4i + 2)^n - (2-4i)^n}{2in!}\right) z^{n}\), \(z \in \mathbb {C}\).












ProblemProblem 7.5





Expand the function \[
  f(z) = \frac{z^{2}+2 z}{(z+1)^{3}}
\] into a Taylor series about the point \(z = 1\).









ProblemProblem 7.6





Expand into a Taylor series about the point \(z = 0\) the functions:

\(\cos^{3} z\);










ProblemProblem 7.12





Find the Taylor expansion about the point \(z = 0\) of the function satisfying the conditions given below:

\(\left(1-z^{2}\right) f^{\prime \prime }(z)-5 z f^{\prime }(z)-4 f(z) = 0, \quad f(0) = 0, \quad f^{\prime }(0) = 1\).






2 Orders of zeros
Let \(f \in H(D)\), i.e. \(f\) is holomorphic in some domain \(D\). A point \(a\in D\) is called a zero of the function \(f\) if \(f(a) = 0\).
Let \(a\) be a zero of \(f\), and \(f \neq 0\). In some neighborhood \(U(a)\) the function \(f\) expands into a power series, and this is necessarily the Taylor series. Consider it:
\[
  f(z) = c_{N}(z-a)^N + c_{N+1}(z-a)^{N+1} + \ldots ,
\]
where \(c_N \neq 0\), \(N \in \mathbb {N}\). \(N\) is called the order of the zero of the point \(z = a\) for the function \(f\). We also say that \(a\) is a zero of order \(N\), or an order-\(N\) zero.






ExampleExample 3





Let \(z = a\) be a zero of order \(m\) for \(f\) and a zero of order \(k\) for \(g\). Prove that then the point \(a\) is a zero of order \((m+k)\) for \(fg\).






SolutionSolution





\(f(z) = (z-a)^m h(z)\), where \(h\) is holomorphic in a neighborhood of \(a\) and does not vanish at \(z = a\): \(h(z) = c_m + c_{m+1}(z - a) + \ldots\), \(h(a) = c_m \neq 0\). (This is in fact an equivalent definition of the order of a zero.) Similarly \(g(z) = (z-a)^{k}\tilde{h}(z)\), \(\tilde{h}(a) \neq 0\). Then \[
  f(z)g(z) = (z-a)^{m+k} \cdot h(z)\tilde{h}(z), \qquad h(a)\tilde{h}(a) \neq 0,
\] i.e. \(a\) is a zero of order \((m+k)\) for \(fg\).












ExampleExample 4





Let \(f(z) = (e^{i\pi z} + 1)^3\). Find the order of the zero at \(a = -1\).






SolutionSolution





Substitute \(w = z + 1\). We need to find the order of the zero at \(w = 0\) for the function \((e^{i\pi (w-1)} + 1)^3\). We have \[
  g(w) := e^{i\pi (w-1)} + 1 = e^{-i\pi }e^{i\pi w} + 1 = -e^{i\pi w} + 1 = -\sum _{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(i\pi )^n}{n!}w^n
\] I.e. \(w = 0\) is a zero of order \(1\) for \(g(w)\). Hence, by the previous example, \(w=0\) is a zero of order \(3\) for \(g^3(w)\).









AnswerAnswer





\(3\).












ExampleExample 5





Let \(f(z) = \left(\cos 3z - \cos 5z\right)^2\left(1 - \cos 2z\right)^3\). Find the order of the zero at \(a = 0\).






SolutionSolution





Let us expand the factors into Taylor series: \[
\begin{align}  \cos 3z - \cos 5z & = \left(1 - \frac{(3z)^2}{2} + \ldots \right) - \left(1 - \frac{(5z)^2}{2} + \ldots \right) = \frac{5^2 - 3^2}{2}z^2 + \ldots = 8z^2 + \ldots \\ 1 - \cos 2z & = \frac{(2z)^2}{2} + \ldots = 2z^2 + \ldots \end{align}
\] I.e. \(0\) is a zero of order 2 for both factors. The order of the zero of a product equals the sum of the orders (previous example), so the answer is \(2 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 = 10\).









AnswerAnswer





\(10\).






All zeros of \(\sin , \cos , \operatorname {ch}, \operatorname {sh}\) have order 1.






ProblemProblem 7.11





Determine the order \(m\) of the zero \(z = a\) of the function \(f(z)\), if:

\(f(z) = (\cos 3 z-\cos 5 z)^{2}(1-\cos 2 z)^{3}, \quad a = 0\);
\(f(z) = \left(z^{4}+2 z^{3}-2 z-1\right)^{2}\left(e^{i \pi z}+1\right)^{3}, a = -1\).






3 The uniqueness theorem and its corollaries







Theorem 2 (The uniqueness theorem) Let \(D\) be a domain, \(E \subset D\), and let \(E\) have a limit point \(a\) in \(D\). Let \(f, g \in H(D)\). Then if they coincide on \(E\), they coincide on \(D\) as well: \[
  f|_E \equiv g|_E \;  \Rightarrow \;  f \equiv g
\]




That is, for two functions holomorphic in the same domain to coincide, it suffices that they coincide on some sequence in the domain having a limit point.






ExampleExample 6





Does the uniqueness theorem remain valid if \(a \not\in D\)?






SolutionSolution





The key idea in the proof of the uniqueness theorem is expanding the function \(f - g\) into a power series in powers of \((z - a)\) in some neighborhood of \(a\). If \(a\) is not in the domain, this cannot be done, and the proof breaks down.
As a concrete example: let \(f(z) = \sin \left(\frac{1}{z}\right)\), \(g \equiv 0\). The functions \(f\), \(g\) are holomorphic in the domain \(D = \mathbb {C} \setminus \left\{ 0\right\}\), and coincide at least on the set
\[
  E = \left\{ z = \frac{1}{\pi k}, \;  k \in \mathbb {Z}\right\}
\]
Yet these functions are different.
The uniqueness theorem is not applicable in this case: the limit point of \(E\) is the point \(0\), but it does not belong to \(D\).
