ExampleExample 7





Does there exist \(f \in H(D)\) for some neighborhood of zero \(D = U(0)\) such that \[
  f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) = \frac{\sin ^2 \frac{\pi n}{2}}{n}, \quad \forall n \in \mathbb {N}
\]






SolutionSolution





We have \[
  f\left(\frac{1}{2k}\right) = 0, \qquad f\left(\frac{1}{2k + 1}\right) = \frac{1}{2k + 1}
\] Consider \(E_1 = \left\{ \frac{1}{2k}, \;  k \in \mathbb {N}\right\}\), \(E_2 = \left\{ \frac{1}{2k+1}, \;  k \in \mathbb {N}\right\}\). By the uniqueness theorem for \(g_1 \equiv 0\) and \(E_{1}\) we obtain that \(f \equiv 0\) on \(D\). By the uniqueness theorem for \(g_2(z) = z\) and \(E_{2}\) we obtain that \(f(z) = z\) on \(D\). Contradiction.









AnswerAnswer





No.












ExampleExample (Problem 9.2)





Does there exist a function \(f(z)\), regular in some neighborhood of the point \(z = 0\), satisfying one of the following conditions (for all \(n = 1,2, \ldots )\):

\(f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) = \frac{\cos^{2} \pi n}{2 n+1}\);
\(2^{-n} < \left|f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right| < 2^{1-n}\);
\(\left|f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)-\frac{\cos \pi n}{2 n+1}\right| < \frac{1}{n^{2}}\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\(\cos^2 \pi n = 1\) for all \(n \in \mathbb {N}\), i.e. \(f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) = \frac{1}{2n + 1} = \frac{1/n}{2 + 1/n}\). Consider the function
\[
  f(z) = \frac{z}{2 + z}
\]
Note that
\[
  f(z) = z \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + z/2} = z \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \sum _{n=0}^{\infty } \frac{(-1)^n}{2^n}z^n, \quad \left|z\right| < 2
\]
\(f(z)\) is represented as the sum of a power series in the open ball of radius \(2\) about zero. Hence it is regular there.








Enum-item2.



If \(f\) is regular in a neighborhood of \(z= 0\), then it is analytic there. I.e. there is some neighborhood \(U(0)\) in which \(f\) expands into the sum of a power series:
\[
  f(z) = \sum _{n=N}^{\infty } a_n z^n = z^{N} \cdot \underbrace{\left(\sum _{k=0}^{\infty } a_{k+N} z^k\right)}_{:= h(z)},
\]
where \(a_N \neq 0\) (\(N \in \mathbb {Z}_+\)) is the first nonzero coefficient in the series (\(f \equiv 0\) in any neighborhood of zero is impossible in view of \(2^{-n} < \left|f(1/n)\right|\)). Note that \(h(z)\) is a function holomorphic in the same domain \(U(0)\), with \(h(0) = a_{N} \neq 0\). Moreover, we have
\[
  2^{-n} < \left|\frac{1}{n^{N}} \cdot h\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right| < 2 \cdot 2^{-n}
\]
Further,
\[
  n^{N} \cdot 2^{-n} < \left| h\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right| < 2 \cdot n^{N} \cdot 2^{-n} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} 0,
\]
i.e. \(\left|h(1/n)\right| \to 0\). Holomorphy implies continuity. We arrive at a contradiction with \(h(0)\neq 0\).








Enum-item3.



We have \(\cos \pi n = (-1)^n\). The condition:
\[
  \left|f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)-\frac{\cos \pi n}{2 n+1}\right| < \frac{1}{n^{2}} \iff \left|f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)-\frac{(-1)^n \cdot \frac{1}{n}}{2+\frac{1}{n}}\right| < \left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^2
\]
Consider the functions
\[
  g_1(z) = f(z) + \frac{z}{2 + z}, \qquad g_2(z) = f(z) - \frac{z}{2+z}
\]
If \(f\) is regular in a neighborhood of \(z= 0\), then it is analytic there. I.e. there is some neighborhood \(U_{\varepsilon }(0)\) in which \(f\) expands into the sum of a power series in powers of \(z\). Without loss of generality, let \(\varepsilon < 2\). We know that in \(U_{2}(0)\) the function \(\frac{z}{2 + z}\) expands into a power series. By the properties of sums of power series we conclude that \(g_1\), \(g_2\) must also expand into power series in \(U_{\varepsilon }(0)\).
Let \(g_1(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty }a_nz^n\) for \(z \in U_{\varepsilon }(0)\). For odd \(n\) we have \(\cos \pi n = -1\), i.e. the condition becomes \(\left|g_1\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right| < \frac{1}{n^2}\). We have
\[
  \left|g_1(z)\right| < z^2 \qquad \text{for } z = \frac{1}{2n+1} \qquad \;  \Rightarrow \;  \qquad \left|\sum _{k=0}^{\infty }a_kz^{k-2}\right| < 1 \qquad \text{for } z = \frac{1}{2n+1}
\]
It follows that \(a_0 = a_1 = 0\) (otherwise the sum of the series would not be bounded).
Similarly for \(g_2(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty }b_nz^n\) (even \(n\), \(\cos \pi n = 1\)): we have
\[
  \left|g_2(z)\right| < z^2 \qquad \text{for } z = \frac{1}{2n}
\]
Consequently, \(b_0=b_1 = 0\).
Thus, in the expansion of \(g_1(z) - g_2(z)\) about zero, the coefficient of the first power is also absent. However
\[
  g_1(z) - g_2(z) = \frac{2z}{2+z} = z \cdot \sum _{n=0}^{\infty } \frac{(-1)^n}{2^n}z^n = z - \frac{1}{2}z^2 + \frac{1}{4}z^3 - \ldots , \quad z \in U_{\varepsilon }(0)
\]
We arrive at a contradiction, since the power-series expansion of a holomorphic function in a neighborhood of a point of the domain is determined uniquely.











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



yes.








Enum-item2.



no;








Enum-item3.



no.














ProblemProblem 9.2





Does there exist a function \(f(z)\), regular in some neighborhood of the point \(z = 0\), satisfying one of the following conditions (for all \(n = 1,2, \ldots )\):

\(f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) = \sin \frac{\pi n}{2}\);
\(f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) = \frac{1}{2 n+\cos \pi n}\);
\(\left|f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right| < e^{-n}\);
\(n^{-5 / 2} < \left|f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right| < 2 n^{-5 / 2}\);




A function of a complex argument \(f\) is called entire if it is holomorphic in the entire complex plane:
\[
  f \in H(\mathbb {C})
\]






ExampleExample 9





Prove that \(e^{z_1 + z_2} = e^{z_1} \cdot e^{z_2}\) for \(z_1, z_2 \in \mathbb {C}\).






SolutionSolution





What do we know? \(e^z = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{n!}z^n\). This power series converges everywhere, i.e. \(e^{z}\) is an entire function. We also know that \(e^{z_1 + z_2} = e^{z_1} \cdot e^{z_2}\) for \(z_1, z_2 \in \mathbb {R}\).

Fix \(z_1 \in \mathbb {R}\) and consider \(f(z) = e^{z_1 + z} - e^{z_1}e^{z}\). We know that \(f\) is an entire function, and that \(f \equiv 0\) on \(\mathbb {R}\). \(\mathbb {R} \subset D = \mathbb {C}\), and \(\mathbb {R}\) has a limit point in \(\mathbb {C}\). By the uniqueness theorem we obtain that \(f \equiv 0\) on \(\mathbb {C}\), i.e. \(e^{z_1 + z_2} = e^{z_1} \cdot e^{z_2}\) for \(z_1 \in \mathbb {R}, z_2 \in \mathbb {C}\).
Fix \(z_2 \in \mathbb {C}\) and consider \(f(z) = e^{z + z_2} - e^{z}e^{z_2}\). We know that \(f\) is an entire function, and that \(f \equiv 0\) on \(\mathbb {R}\) (by the previous point). By the uniqueness theorem we obtain that \(f \equiv 0\) on \(\mathbb {C}\), i.e. \(e^{z_1 + z_2} = e^{z_1} \cdot e^{z_2}\) for \(z_1 \in \mathbb {C}, z_2 \in \mathbb {C}\).













ProblemProblem 9.13





Relying on the validity of the formulas given below for real values of the variables, and on the uniqueness theorem, prove their validity for arbitrary complex values of these variables:

\(\operatorname {ch} 2 z = \operatorname {ch}^{2} z+\operatorname {sh}^{2} z\);
\(\sin \left(z_{1}+z_{2}\right) = \sin z_{1} \cos z_{2}+\cos z_{1} \sin z_{2}\);











Theorem 3 (Liouville’s theorem) \(f\) entire and bounded (i.e. \(\exists M > 0\): \(\left|f(z)\right| \leq M\) \(\forall z \in \mathbb {C}\)) \(\;  \Rightarrow \;\) \(f \equiv \operatorname {const}\) on all of \(\mathbb {C}\).










ExampleExample 10





Describe all entire doubly periodic \(f\), i.e. entire functions \(f\) such that \[
  f(z+i) = f(z+1) =f(z), \qquad z \in \mathbb {C}
\]






SolutionSolution






Note that \(f\) is uniquely determined by its values on the set
\[
  z = x + iy \;  : \;  x,y \in [0,1)
\]
Indeed, for all \(z \in \mathbb {C}\) we have
\[
  f(z) = f(x + iy) =f((x - \lfloor x \rfloor ) + i(y - \lfloor y \rfloor )),
\]
where \((x - \lfloor x \rfloor ), (y - \lfloor y \rfloor ) \in [0,1)\).
Consider \(f\) on the square \(z = x + iy\), \(x,y \in [0,1]\). This is a compact set, \(f\) is continuous, hence \(f\) is bounded on this set. By periodicity it is bounded on the entire complex plane as well. By Liouville’s theorem, it is identically constant.










AnswerAnswer





\(f \equiv \operatorname {const}\)

Suppose all values of the entire function \(f\) lie in the upper half-plane. Find the form of this function.

title: Isolated singular points
section: 1 Remark: the Laurent series in a neighborhood of infinity
text:
1 Remark: the Laurent series in a neighborhood of infinity
Consider the function \(f(z)\) in a punctured neighborhood of infinity
\[
\dot{U}_{\varepsilon }(\infty ) = \left\{ z \in \mathbb {C} \;  : \;  \left|z\right| > 1/\varepsilon \right\} .
\]
The Laurent series in this neighborhood: \(\zeta := \frac{1}{z}\),
\[
  f(z) = \sum _{-\infty }^{+\infty } c_n \zeta ^n = \underbrace{\sum _{n=0}^{+\infty } c_n \zeta ^n}_{\text{regular part}} + \underbrace{\sum _{n=1}^{+\infty } c_{-n}\frac{1}{\zeta ^n}}_{\text{principal part}} = \underbrace{\sum _{n=0}^{+\infty } c_n \frac{1}{z^n}}_{\text{regular part}} + \underbrace{\sum _{n=1}^{+\infty } c_{-n}z^n}_{\text{principal part}}
\]
That is, expanding a function into a Laurent series in a neighborhood of \(\infty\) is the same as expanding it in powers of \(z\), except the terminology changes: the part with positive powers is now the principal part, and the part with nonpositive powers is the regular part.






ExampleExample 1





Expand \(e^z\) into a Laurent series

in a neighborhood of zero;
in a neighborhood of \(\infty\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\[
  e^z = \underbrace{1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2!} + \frac{z^3}{3!} + \ldots }_{\text{regular part}}
\]
the principal part is zero here








Enum-item2.



\[
  e^z = \underbrace{1}_{\substack {\text{regular}\\ \text{part}}} + \underbrace{z + \frac{z^2}{2!} + \frac{z^3}{3!} + \ldots }_{\text{principal part}}
\]














ExampleExample 2





Determine the character of the singular point \(z_0\) for the function

\(\dfrac {\operatorname {tg}z}{z}\), \(z_0 = 0\);
\(\dfrac {1}{z^3 \operatorname {tg}z}\), \(z_0 = 0\);
\(\dfrac {1}{z^3 \operatorname {tg}z}\), \(z_0 = \infty\).







SolutionSolution





The Laurent series (in this case simply the Taylor series) in some neighborhood of zero \(U_{\varepsilon }(0)\) (it does not even matter which \(\varepsilon\)) is known for \(\operatorname {tg}z\): \[
  \operatorname {tg}(z) = z + \frac{1}{3}z^3 + \frac{2}{15}z^5 + \frac{17}{315}z^7 + \ldots
\]






Enum-item1.



In \(\dot{U}_{\varepsilon }(0)\) we have \(\frac{\operatorname {tg}z}{z} = 1 + \frac{1}{3}z^2 + \frac{2}{15}z^4 + \frac{17}{315}z^6 + \ldots\). There are no negative powers, the principal part is zero, i.e. for this function \(0\) is a removable singularity.








Enum-item2.



We have
\[
  \operatorname {tg}(z) = z + \frac{1}{3}z^3 + \frac{2}{15}z^5 + \frac{17}{315}z^7 + \ldots = z \cdot \left(1 + \underbrace{\frac{1}{3}z^2 + \frac{2}{15}z^4 + \frac{17}{315}z^6 + \ldots }_{=: h(z)}\right)
\]
Further,
\[
  \frac{1}{\operatorname {tg}(z)} = \frac{1}{z} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + h(z)}
\]
Note that \(h(z)\) is holomorphic in some neighborhood of zero, with \(h(0) = 0\). Holomorphy implies continuity, and continuity implies boundedness. Hence there is some neighborhood of zero in which \(\left|h(z)\right| < 1\). In this neighborhood, by the geometric series formula, we have
\[
\begin{align}  \frac{1}{1 + h(z)} & = \frac{1}{1 - (-h(z))} = 1 - h(z) + h^2(z) - h^3(z) + \ldots = \\ & = 1 - \left(\frac{1}{3}z^2 + \frac{2}{15}z^4 + \frac{17}{315}z^6 + \ldots \right) + \left(\frac{1}{3}z^2 + \frac{2}{15}z^4 + \ldots \right)^2 - \left(\frac{1}{3}z^2 + \ldots \right)^3 + \ldots = \\ & = 1 - \frac{1}{3}z^2 + \left(-\frac{2}{15} + \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\right)z^4 + \left(-\frac{17}{315} + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{2}{15} - \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^3\right)z^6 + \ldots = \\ & = 1 - \frac{1}{3}z^2 - \frac{1}{45}z^4 - \frac{2}{945}z^6 + \ldots \end{align}
\]
Then the Laurent series for \(\frac{1}{z^3 \operatorname {tg}z}\) in the same neighborhood, but now punctured:
\[
  \frac{1}{z^3 \operatorname {tg}(z)} = \frac{1}{z^4} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + h(z)} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{z^4}- \frac{1}{3}\frac{1}{z^2}}_{\text{principal part}} \underbrace{ - \frac{1}{45}- \frac{2}{945}z^2 + \ldots }_{\text{regular part}}
\]
\(0\) is a pole of order \(4\) for \(\frac{1}{z^{3}\operatorname {tg}z}\).








Enum-item3.



The function \(\frac{1}{z^3\operatorname {tg}z} = \frac{\operatorname {ctg}z}{z^3}\) has poles at all zeros of sine: \(z = \pi k\), \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\). These accumulate toward \(\infty\), so no punctured neighborhood \(\dot{U}(\infty )\) is free of singular points: \(\infty\) is not an isolated singular point, but a limit point of poles. (The expansion from part 2 is valid only for \(0 < \left|z\right| < \frac{\pi }{2}\) — it cannot be “continued” into a neighborhood of infinity; this function simply has no Laurent series in \(\dot{U}(\infty )\).)











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



removable singularity;








Enum-item2.



pole of order \(4\);








Enum-item3.



\(\infty\) is not an isolated singular point (a limit point of the poles \(\pi k\)).

Prove that the point \(z = a\) is a removable singularity for the following functions:

\(\frac{\sin z}{z} \quad (a = 0)\);
\(\frac{1}{e^{z}-1}-\frac{1}{\sin z} \quad (a = 0)\);

Prove that the point \(z = a\) is a pole of the following functions:

ProblemProblem 12.8





Find all isolated singular points of single-valued character for the following functions and determine their type:

\(\frac{1}{z^{2}-1} \cos \frac{\pi z}{z+1}\);
\(e^{\operatorname {ctg} \frac{\pi }{z}}\);





Let \(z = z_0\) be a zero of order \(n_1\) for \(f_1\), and a zero of order \(n_2\) for \(f_2\), i.e.
\[
  f_1(z) = (z-z_0)^{n_1} \cdot h_1(z), \quad f_2(z) = (z-z_0)^{n_2} \cdot h_2(z)
\]
where \(h_1, h_2\) are holomorphic in some neighborhood of \(z_0\), and nonzero at the point \(z_0\) itself. Then
\[
  \frac{f_1}{f_2} = (z-z_0)^{n_1-n_2} \cdot \frac{h_1(z)}{h_2(z)},
\]
where \(\frac{h_1}{h_2}\) is holomorphic in some neighborhood of \(z_0\), and nonzero at \(z_0\). Hence \(z = z_0\) for the function \(f_1/f_2\) is

a zero of order \((n_1-n_2)\), if \(n_1 > n_2\); also a removable singularity;
a removable singularity, if \(n_1 = n_2\);
a pole of order \((n_2-n_1)\), if \(n_1 < n_2\);

Let \(z = a\) be a removable singularity or a pole for \(f\) and for \(g\). Then for \(fg\) this is also a removable singularity or a pole. And for \(f/g\) as well (if \(g \not\equiv 0\)).
Let \(z = a\) be a removable singularity or a pole for \(f\), and an essential singularity for \(g\), with \(f \not\equiv 0\). Then for \(fg\) it is an essential singularity.








Theorem 1 (Sokhotski’s theorem) Let \(a\) be an essential singularity for \(f\). Then for every \(A \in \bar{\mathbb {C}}\) there is a sequence from the punctured neighborhood \(\left\{ z_n\right\}  \subset \dot{U}(a)\) such that \[
  z_n \to a, \qquad f(z_n) \to A
\]











Theorem 2 (Picard’s great theorem) Let \(a\) be an essential singularity for \(f\). Then for every \(A \in \mathbb {C}\) (with possibly one exception), and for every \(\dot{U}(a)\), the equation \(f(z) = A\) has infinitely many solutions in \(\dot{U}(a)\).




Example: \(e^z\), \(a = \infty\). \(e^z \neq 0\).






ExampleExample 3





Find the singular points of the function \(f(z) = e^{\sin z}\), and classify them.






SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\(a = \infty\). This is an essential singularity: along the 2 sequences \(z^{(1)}_n = 2\pi n\), \(z^{(2)}_n = \frac{\pi }{2} + 2\pi n\), the limit is different: \(e^{\sin z^{(1)}_n} = e^0 = 1\), \(e^{\sin z^{(2)}_n} = e^1 = e\).











AnswerAnswer





\(z = \infty\) is an essential singularity; there are no other singular points (\(f\) is entire).












ExampleExample 4





Find the singular points of the function \(f(z) = \frac{1 - \cos (z)}{z^3}\), and classify them.






SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\(a = \infty\). This is an essential singularity: an essential singularity for \(1 - \cos (z)\), a pole of order \(3\) for \(z^3\).








Enum-item2.



\(a = 0\). \(1 - \cos (z) = 1 - 1 + \frac{z^2}{2} - \ldots\). For the numerator, \(a\) is a zero of order \(2\). For the denominator, it is a zero of order \(3\). Hence this is a pole of order \(1\).











AnswerAnswer





\(0\) is a pole of order \(1\), \(\infty\) is an essential singularity.












ExampleExample 5





Find the singular points of the function \(f(z) = \frac{1}{z^2 - 1} \cos \frac{\pi z}{z + 1}\) and classify them.






SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\(a = \infty\). \(\frac{\pi z}{z+1} = \frac{\pi }{1 + \frac{1}{z}} \to \pi\), i.e. the cosine tends to \(\cos \pi = -1\), while \(\frac{1}{z^2-1} \to 0\).
\(f(z) \to 0\). \(\infty\) is a removable singularity.








Enum-item2.



\(a = 1\). For \(\frac{1}{z^2 - 1}\) this is a pole of order \(1\).
For \(g(z) = \cos \frac{\pi z}{z+1}\): \(g(1) = \cos \frac{\pi }{2} = 0\), and moreover
\[
  g'(z) = -\sin \left(\frac{\pi z}{z+1}\right) \cdot \frac{\pi }{(z+1)^2}, \qquad g'(1) = -\sin \left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \cdot \frac{\pi }{4} = -\frac{\pi }{4} \neq 0,
\]
i.e. \(a = 1\) is a zero of order \(1\) for \(g\). A first-order zero cancels a first-order pole:
removable singularity.








Enum-item3.



\(a = -1\). For \(\frac{1}{z^2 - 1}\) this is a pole of order \(1\).
For the cosine: consider \(z = -1 + \varepsilon\).
\(\cos \frac{\pi (\varepsilon - 1)}{\varepsilon } = \cos (\pi - \frac{\pi }{\varepsilon }) = -\cos (\pi /\varepsilon )\) — the principal part in powers of \(\frac{1}{\varepsilon } = \frac{1}{z+1}\) is infinite. I.e. this is an essential singularity.
Multiplying by \(\frac{1}{z^2 - 1} \not\equiv 0\) (a pole) preserves the essential singularity (rule 3 above). I.e. it is an essential singularity for \(f(z)\).











AnswerAnswer





\(z = 1\) and \(z = \infty\) are removable singularities, \(z = -1\) is an essential singularity.












ExampleExample 6





Find the singular points of the function \[
f(z) = \frac{1}{z\sin \frac{1}{z}}
\] and classify them.






SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



\(a = \infty\). In some punctured neighborhood of infinity we have
\[
\begin{align}  f(z) & = \frac{1}{z} \cdot \frac{1}{\frac{1}{z} - \frac{1}{3!}\frac{1}{z^3} + \frac{1}{5!}\frac{1}{z^5} - \ldots } = \frac{1}{1 - \left(\frac{1}{3!}\frac{1}{z^2} - \frac{1}{5!}\frac{1}{z^4} + \ldots \right)} = \\ & = \sum _{k=0}^{\infty }\left(\frac{1}{3!}\frac{1}{z^2} - \frac{1}{5!}\frac{1}{z^4} + \ldots \right)^k = 1 + \frac{1}{3!}\frac{1}{z^2} + \ldots \end{align}
\]
— only nonpositive powers, no principal part. Removable singularity.
Alternatively, one could simply note that as \(z \to \infty\), \(\sin \frac{1}{z} \sim \frac{1}{z}\), i.e.
\[
  f(z) = \frac{1}{z\sin \frac{1}{z}} \xrightarrow [z \to \infty ]{} 1
\]








Enum-item2.



The points where sine vanishes: \(\frac{1}{z} = \pi k\). I.e. \(a = a_k = \frac{1}{\pi k}\), \(k \in \mathbb {Z} \setminus \left\{ 0\right\}\). \(a_k\) is a zero of some order for \(\sin \frac{1}{z}\). Differentiating, we get \(-\frac{1}{z^2}\cos \frac{1}{z}\). At the point \(a_k\) this is not zero. I.e. \(a_k\) is a zero of order \(1\) for \(\sin \frac{1}{z}\). Hence it is a pole of order \(1\) for \(f\).








Enum-item3.



\(a = 0\). This is a non-isolated singular point: a limit point of the poles \(a_k\).











AnswerAnswer





\(\infty\) is a removable singularity; \(\frac{1}{\pi k}\), \(k \in \mathbb {Z} \setminus \left\{ 0\right\}\), are poles of order \(1\); \(0\) is a non-isolated singular point (a limit point of poles).












ProblemProblem 12.17





Find all singular points of the function \(f(z)\) and determine their type, if:

\(f(z) = \frac{8 z^{2}-6 z+1}{1-\cos \frac{\pi }{z}}\);










ProblemProblem 12.18





Let \(z = 0\) be a pole of the function \(f(z)\). Prove that for the function \(e^{f(z)}\) the point \(z = 0\) is essentially singular.









ProblemProblem 12.20





Find all singular points of the function \(f(z)\) and determine their type, if:

\(f(z) = \frac{\operatorname {sh} \pi z-\cos \frac{i \pi }{z}}{\left(i-e^{\pi / z}\right)^{2}}\);




A typical exam-style problem:






ExampleExample 7





Find the singular points of the function \[
f(z) = \frac{4z^2 + \pi ^2}{\operatorname {ch}3z}\left(\exp \left(\frac{z}{z-2}\right) - 1\right)\operatorname {ctg}^2z
\] and classify them.






SolutionSolution





Denote
\[
\begin{align}  f_1(z) & = 4z^2 + \pi ^2 &  f_3(z) & = \exp \left(\frac{z}{z-2}\right) - 1 = \exp \left(1 + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{z-2}\right) - 1 \\ f_2(z) & = \operatorname {ch}3z&  f_4(z) & = \operatorname {ctg}z \end{align}
\]
We have
\[
  f = \frac{f_1}{f_2} \cdot f_3 \cdot f_4^2
\]
Singular points of \(f\):

\(a = 2\). We have
\[
  f_3(z) = e \cdot \exp \left(2\frac{1}{z-2}\right) - 1= e \cdot \sum _{k=0}^{\infty }\frac{2^k}{k!}\left(\frac{1}{z-2}\right)^k - 1
\]
\(a = 2\) is an essential singularity for \(f_3\).
Alternatively, one can justify that \(a = 2\) is an essential singularity for \(f_3\) as follows:
\[
  f_3(z) \xrightarrow [z = x \to 2-]{} -1, \qquad f_3(z) \xrightarrow [z = x \to 2+]{} \infty
\]
i.e. \(f_3(z)\) has no limit as \(z \to 2\).
The remaining functions \(f_1,f_2,f_4\) have neither zeros nor singularities at \(a=2\). In total, \(a = 2\) is an essential singularity for \(f\)
The points where the denominator \(f_2(z) = \operatorname {ch}3z\) vanishes.
\[
  0 = \operatorname {ch}3z = \frac{e^{3z} + e^{-3z}}{2}
\]
We get
\[
  e^{6z} + 1 = 0 \iff e^{6z} = -1 \iff 6z = \operatorname {Log}(-1) = i\left(\pi + 2\pi k\right)
\]
\(a = a_k = i\left(\frac{1}{6}\pi + \frac{1}{3}\pi k\right)\). What order do these zeros have for \(f_2\)? Let us take the derivative: \(f_2'(z) = 3\operatorname {sh}3z\), which is nonzero at the points \(a\). Accordingly, \(a\) is a zero of order \(1\) for \(f_2\).
What will these points be for the remaining functions? For \(f_3\), \(f_4\) they are neither zeros nor singularities (see above). For \(f_1(z) = 4z^2 + \pi^2\) the zeros are \(\pm i \frac{\pi }{2}\), of order \(1\). Consider the cases:

\(a = a_k = i\left(\frac{1}{6}\pi + \frac{1}{3}\pi k\right)\), \(k \in \left\{ 1,-2\right\}\), i.e. \(a = \pm i \frac{\pi }{2}\). This is a removable singularity for \(f\).
\(a = a_k = i\left(\frac{1}{6}\pi + \frac{1}{3}\pi k\right)\), \(k \not\in \left\{ 1,-2\right\}\). This is a pole of order \(1\) for \(f\).

The points where \(f_4(z) = \operatorname {ctg}z\) is undefined. These are \(a_4 = \pi k\). For \(\operatorname {ctg}z = \frac{\cos z}{\sin z}\) this is a pole of order \(1\), since the numerator \(\cos\) is nonzero there, while for the denominator, \(\sin\), it is a zero of order \(1\).
For \(f_1\), \(f_2\) these are not zeros, and there are no singularities there. For \(f_3\) there are some subtleties:

for \(k \neq 0\), i.e. for \(a = \pi k \neq 0\), \(f_3\) has neither zeros nor singularities at \(a\). In total, in this case, for \(f\) the points of the form \(\pi k\), \(k \neq 0\), are poles of order \(2\).
for \(k = 0\), i.e. for \(a = 0\), \(f_3\) has a zero. Of what order? Let us differentiate:
\[
  f_3'(z) = -2\frac{1}{(z-2)^2} \exp \left(1 + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{z-2}\right)
\]
As we see, \(f'_3(z)|_{z = 0} \neq 0\), i.e. \(a = 0\) is a zero of order \(1\) for \(f_3\).
In total, for \(f\) the point \(a = 0\) is a pole of order \(1\).

\(a = \infty\). A non-isolated singular point, a limit of poles, in particular, of poles of the form \(i\left(\frac{1}{6}\pi + \frac{1}{3}\pi k\right)\)







Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: the singular points of the function, marked with colors.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/210/010_singular_points_colored_fig.tex











AnswerAnswer






\(\infty\): non-isolated singular point, a limit point of the poles below
\(2\) is an essential singularity
\(\pm i \frac{\pi }{2}\) are removable singularities
\(0\) is a pole of order \(1\);
\(\frac{i}{3}\left(\frac{\pi }{2} + \pi k\right)\), \(k \not\in \left\{ 1,-2\right\}\), are poles of order \(1\).
\(\pi k\), \(k \neq 0\), are poles of order \(2\).













ProblemProblem T.1





Find all singular points of the function \(f\) and determine their type, if \[
  f(z) = \frac{\cos ^{2}\left(z+\frac{1}{z}\right)-\sin ^{2}\left(z-\frac{1}{z}\right)}{\sin (2 z) \cos \frac{2}{z}} \operatorname {th} \frac{1}{z+i}
\]









ExampleExample 8





Find the principal part of the Laurent series of the function \[
  f(z) = \frac{1}{e^{z} - 1}
\] in the annulus centered at the origin that contains the point \(z_0 = 10\).






SolutionSolution





Singular points: \(\operatorname {Ln}1 = 2\pi k i\), \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\). We must expand in the annulus
\[
  D = \left\{ z \in \mathbb {C} \;  : \;  2\pi < \left|z\right| < 4 \pi \right\}
\]






Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: the singular points of the function (in red).
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/210/020_singular_points_fig.tex


How do we do this?






Enum-item1.



Consider \(f(z)\) in some \(\dot{U}(0)\):
\[
  f(z) = \frac{1}{z} \cdot \overbrace{\frac{1}{1 + \frac{z}{2!} + \frac{z^2}{3!} + \ldots }}^{=: h(z)} = \frac{1}{z} \cdot h(z)
\]
\(h\) is a function holomorphic at zero (unlike \(f\), it no longer has a singularity at zero), i.e. it expands in some neighborhood of zero simply into a Taylor series:
\[
  h(z) = h(0) + h'(0)z + \ldots = 1 + h'(0)z + \ldots
\]
Hence in \(\dot{U}(0)\) we have
\[
  f(z) = \frac{1}{z} + \frac{1}{z}\left(h(z) - 1 \right) = \frac{1}{z} + \underbrace{h'(0) + \frac{h''(0)}{2}z + \ldots }_{=: f_1(z)}
\]
where \(f_1(z)\) is holomorphic at zero.








Enum-item2.



In \(\dot{U}(2\pi i)\):
\[
  f(z) = \frac{1}{e^{z} - 1} = \frac{1}{e^{z - 2\pi i} - 1} = \frac{1}{e^{w} - 1} = \frac{1}{w} + f_1(w) = \frac{1}{z - 2\pi i} + f_2(z)
\]
where \(w = z - 2\pi i\), \(f_1\) is from the previous point, \(f_2(z) = f_1(z - 2\pi i)\), and \(f_2(z)\) is holomorphic in a neighborhood of \(2 \pi i\).








Enum-item3.



In \(\dot{U}(-2\pi i)\):
\[
  f(z) = \frac{1}{z + 2\pi i} + f_3(z),
\]
\(f_3\) is holomorphic in a neighborhood of \(-2\pi i\).


In total, the function
\[
  g(z) = \frac{1}{e^z - 1} - \frac{1}{z} - \frac{1}{z + 2\pi i} - \frac{1}{z - 2\pi i}
\]
is a function that, in the open disk \(\left\{ \left|z\right| < 4 \pi \right\}\), has only removable singular points. I.e. it is regular in this neighborhood (once redefined by continuity). It can be expanded in a Taylor series! Then in \(\left\{ \left|z\right| < 4 \pi \right\}\) (in particular, in the annulus \(\left\{ 2 \pi <\left|z\right| < 4 \pi \right\}\)), \(g(z)\) has no principal part (it is zero). Consequently, the principal part of the Laurent series for \(f(z)\) is the principal part of the Laurent series for
\[
  \frac{1}{z} + \frac{1}{z + 2\pi i} + \frac{1}{z - 2\pi i}
\]
Meaning: only the singular points contained within the annulus contribute to the principal part of the Laurent series.
Let us carry the problem through to the end:
\[
\begin{align}  \frac{1}{z} + \frac{1}{z + 2\pi i} + \frac{1}{z - 2\pi i} & = \frac{1}{z} + \frac{2z}{z^2 + 4\pi ^2} = \frac{1}{z} + \frac{2z}{z^2} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - (- 4\pi ^2/z^2)} = \\ & = \frac{1}{z} + \frac{2}{z} \cdot \sum _{n=0}^{\infty } (-1)^n \cdot \left(4\pi ^2\right)^{n} \cdot \frac{1}{z^{2n}} = \\ & = \frac{3}{z} + \sum _{n=1}^{\infty }(-1)^n \cdot 2^{2n+1} \cdot \pi ^{2n} \frac{1}{z^{2n + 1}} \end{align}
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(\frac{3}{z} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty }(-1)^n \cdot 2^{2n+1} \cdot \pi^{2n} \cdot \frac{1}{z^{2n + 1}}\).












ProblemProblem T.2





Find the principal part of the Laurent series of the function \[
  f(z) = \frac{1}{\sin z}
\] in the annulus centered at the origin that contains the point \(z = 4\).









ProblemProblem T.3





Let the function \(f\) be holomorphic in the punctured unit disk \(0 < \left|z\right| < 1\), and suppose that for some \(A > 0\) and \(\alpha \in [0,1]\) the inequality \(\left|f(z)\right| < \frac{A}{\left|z\right|^{\alpha }}\) holds. Determine the type of the isolated singular point \(z = 0\) for various values of \(\alpha\).

text:
2.1 Integrals over the interval \([0,2\pi ]\)






ExampleExample 6





Compute \[
  \int _{0}^{2\pi } \frac{1}{a + b\sin \varphi } d\varphi
\] \(0 < b < a\).






SolutionSolution





Note that \[
  \oint _{\left|z\right| = 1}f(z)dz = \int _{0}^{2\pi } f(e^{i\varphi }) ie^{i\varphi } \;  d\varphi
\] We have \(\sin \varphi = \frac{e^{i\varphi } - e^{-i\varphi }}{2i}\), \[
\begin{align}  \int _{0}^{2\pi } \frac{1}{a + b\sin \varphi } d\varphi & = \int _{0}^{2\pi } \frac{2i}{2ai + b\left(e^{i\varphi } - e^{-i\varphi }\right)} d\varphi = \\ & = \int _{0}^{2\pi } \frac{2}{2aie^{i\varphi } + b\left(e^{2i\varphi } - 1\right)} \cdot ie^{i\varphi } \cdot d\varphi = \\ & = 2\oint _{\left|z\right| = 1} \underbrace{\frac{1}{2aiz + b(z^2 - 1)}}_{= f(z)} dz \end{align}
\] Singular points of \(f\): \[
\begin{align}  0 & = z^2 + 2\frac{a}{b}iz - 1 = \left(z + \frac{a}{b}i\right)^2 -1 + \frac{a^2}{b^2} = \left(z + \frac{a}{b}i\right)^2 - \left(\frac{\sqrt{a^2 - b^2}}{b}i\right)^2 = \\ & = \left(z - \left(\frac{-a + \sqrt{a^2 - b^2}}{b}\right)i\right)\left(z - \left(\frac{-a - \sqrt{a^2 - b^2}}{b}\right)i\right) \end{align}
\] \(z_2\) lies outside the unit disk, \(z_1\) inside. Hence we need to find the residue there. This is a zero of order \(1\) for the denominator, so \[
  \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z_1}f = \frac{1}{\left(bz^2 + 2aiz - b\right)'}\bigg|_{z = z_1} = \frac{1}{2bz_1 + 2ai} = \frac{1}{2i} \cdot \frac{1}{-a + \sqrt{a^2 - b^2} + a} = \frac{1}{2i}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 - b^2}}
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(2 \cdot 2 \pi i \cdot \frac{1}{2i}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 - b^2}} = \frac{2\pi }{\sqrt{a^2 - b^2}}\).

Compute the integral \[
  \int _{0}^{2 \pi } \frac{\cos 2 \varphi d \varphi }{4+2 \cos \varphi }
\]

section: 2.2 Improper integrals over an infinite interval
text:
2.2 Improper integrals over an infinite interval

2.2.1 The integral of a rational function
We need to compute
\[
  \int _{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x) dx
\]






Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: the contour of integration.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/230/010_integration_contour_fig.tex








ExampleExample 7





Compute \[
  I = \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty }\frac{1}{x^2 - 2ix -2}dx
\]






SolutionSolution






Consider the function
\[
  f(z) = \frac{1}{z^2 - 2iz -2} = \frac{1}{\left(z - (i + 1)\right) \cdot \left(z - (i-1)\right)}
\]
Singularities of \(f\): \(z_1 = i + 1\), \(z_2 = i-1\). They lie at distance \(\sqrt{2}\) from the origin, in the upper half-plane. We can then write Cauchy’s theorem for the curve \([-R, R] \cup C_{R}\), \(R > \sqrt{2}\):
\[
  \underbrace{\int _{[-R,R]}f(z) dz}_{I_1(R)} + \underbrace{\int _{C_{R}}f(z)dz}_{I_2(R)} = 2\pi i \cdot \left(\mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z_1}f + \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z_2}f\right)
\]
Note that the right-hand side does not depend on \(R\). Meanwhile \(I_{1}(R) \to I\) as \(R \to +\infty\). What about \(I_2\)? We have
\[
  \left|I_2(R)\right| \leq \int _{C_{R}}\left|f(z)\right|\left|dz\right| \leq \max _{z \in C_{R}}\left|f(z)\right| \cdot \left|C_R\right| = \max _{z \in C_{R}}\left|f(z)\right| \cdot \pi R
\]
Hence if \(\max_{z \in C_{R}}\left|f(z)\right| = o(1/R)\) as \(R \to +\infty\), then \(I_2(R) \to 0\) and the integral \(I\) in question will simply equal the sum of the residues at \(z_1\), \(z_2\) (with coefficient \(2 \pi i\)).
Note that
\[
  \max _{z \in C_{R}}\left|f(z)\right| = \max _{\varphi \in [0, \pi ]}\left|f\left(Re^{i \varphi }\right)\right|
\]
We have as \(z \to \infty\), \(R \to +\infty\)
\[
  f(z) \sim \frac{1}{z^2}, \quad \left|f(z)\right| \sim \frac{1}{\left|z\right|^2}, \quad \left|f(Re^{i \varphi })\right| \sim \frac{1}{R^2} = o(1/R)
\]
Thus we have proved that \(I_2(R) \to 0\) as \(R \to +\infty\)
Computing the residues, we obtain
\[
  I = \lim _{R \to +\infty }I_{1}(R) = 2\pi i \cdot \left(\mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z_1}f + \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z_2}f\right) = 2\pi i \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2z_1 - 2i} + \frac{1}{2z_2 - 2i} \right) = 2\pi i \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\right) = 0
\]










AnswerAnswer





\(0\).






Note that in this example one could have used the lower half-plane instead, where there were no residues at all.
Note that this trick can be applied to any function of the form \(f(z) = \frac{P(z)}{Q(z)}\), where \(P\), \(Q\) are polynomials with \(\operatorname {deg}Q \geq \operatorname {deg}P + 2\).


2.2.2 The integral of a rational function times an exponential






Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: the contour of integration.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/230/020_integration_contour2_fig.tex









Lemma 1 (Jordan’s lemma) Let \(g(z)\) be continuous on \(G = \left\{ z \;  : \;  \operatorname {Im}z \geq 0, \,  \left|z\right| \geq R_0\right\}\) for some \(R_{0} > 0\). Suppose that \[
  \max _{z \in C_{R}}\left|g(z)\right| \xrightarrow [R \to +\infty ]{} 0
\] Then \[
  \int _{C_{R}}g(z)e^{i\alpha z}dz \xrightarrow [R \to +\infty ]{} 0
\] for every \(\alpha > 0\).










ExampleExample 8





Compute \[
  I = \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } \frac{\cos (\alpha x)}{1 + x^2} dx
\] for arbitrary \(\alpha > 0\).






SolutionSolution





Note that \(\cos (\alpha x) = \operatorname {Re} e^{i\alpha x}\). Hence,
\[
  I = \operatorname {Re } \underbrace{\int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } \frac{e^{i\alpha x}}{1 + x^2} dx}_{=: \tilde{I}}
\]

Consider the functions
\[
  g(z) = \frac{1}{1 + z^2}, \qquad f(z) = e^{i\alpha z}g(z)
\]
Singularities of \(f\): \(z_1 = i\), \(z_2 = -i\). They lie at distance \(1\) apart, the first in the upper half-plane, the second in the lower. We can then write Cauchy’s theorem for the curve \([-R, R] \cup C_{R}\), \(R > 1\):
\[
  \underbrace{\int _{[-R,R]}f(z) dz}_{I_1(R)} + \underbrace{\int _{C_{R}}f(z)dz}_{I_2(R)} = 2\pi i \cdot \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z_1}f
\]
\(I_{1}(R) \to \tilde{I}\) as \(R \to +\infty\). What about \(I_2(R)\)?
Note that \(g(z) \sim \frac{1}{z^2}\) as \(z \to \infty\), hence
\[
  \max _{z \in C_{R}}\left|g(z)\right| \xrightarrow [R \to +\infty ]{} 0
\]
By Jordan’s lemma we obtain
\[
  I_2(R) = \int _{C_R}e^{i\alpha z}g(z) dz \to 0
\]
as \(R \to +\infty\).
Computing the residues, we obtain
\[
  \tilde{I} = \lim _{R \to +\infty }I_{1}(R) = 2\pi i \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{i}f(z) = 2\pi i \cdot \frac{e^{i\alpha z_{1}}}{2z_1} = \pi e^{-\alpha }
\]
\(I = \operatorname {Re}\tilde{I} = \pi e^{-\alpha }\).










AnswerAnswer





\(\pi e^{-\alpha }\).












ExampleExample 9





Compute \[
  I = \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } \frac{x \sin (x)}{x^2 + 1} dx
\]






SolutionSolution





Write \(\sin x = \frac{e^{ix} - e^{-ix}}{2i}\), then
\[
  I = \frac{1}{2i} \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } \frac{x(e^{ix} - e^{-ix})}{x^2 + 1} dx.
\]
Consider two integrals:
\[
  I_1 = \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } \frac{x e^{ix}}{x^2 + 1} dx, \quad I_2 = \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } \frac{x e^{-ix}}{x^2 + 1} dx.
\]
For \(I_1\): consider the function \(f(z) = \frac{z e^{iz}}{z^2 + 1}\). Singular points: \(z = \pm i\). In the upper half-plane lies \(z = i\).
Residue at the point \(z = i\):
\[
  \operatorname {Res}_{z=i} f(z) = \frac{z e^{iz}}{2z} \Big|_{z=i} = \frac{i e^{-1}}{2i} = \frac{e^{-1}}{2}.
\]
By Jordan’s lemma for \(e^{iz}\) in the upper half-plane:
\[
  I_1 = 2\pi i \cdot \frac{e^{-1}}{2} = \pi i e^{-1}.
\]
For \(I_2\): consider the function \(g(z) = \frac{z e^{-iz}}{z^2 + 1}\). In the lower half-plane lies \(z = -i\).
Residue at the point \(z = -i\):
\[
  \operatorname {Res}_{z=-i} g(z) = \frac{z e^{-iz}}{2z} \Big|_{z=-i} = \frac{-i e^{-1}}{-2i} = \frac{e^{-1}}{2}.
\]
When traversing the lower half-plane the direction is negative:
\[
  I_2 = -2\pi i \cdot \frac{e^{-1}}{2} = -\pi i e^{-1}.
\]
Then
\[
  I = \frac{1}{2i}(I_1 - I_2) = \frac{1}{2i}(\pi i e^{-1} + \pi i e^{-1}) = \frac{1}{2i} \cdot 2\pi i e^{-1} = \pi e^{-1}.
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(\frac{\pi }{e}\).












ExampleExample 10





Compute \[
  I = \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty }\frac{x \cos (1 - 2x)}{x^2 + 4}dx
\]






SolutionSolution





Note that \(\cos (1 - 2x) = \cos (2x - 1)\),
\[
  I = \operatorname {Re } \underbrace{\int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } \frac{xe^{i(2x - 1)}}{x^2 + 4} dx}_{=: \tilde{I}}
\]
At the same time \(e^{i(2x - 1)} = e^{-i} \cdot e^{2ix}\)

Consider the functions
\[
  g(z) = \frac{ze^{-i}}{z^2 + 4}, \qquad f(z) = e^{2i z}g(z)
\]
Singularities of \(f\): \(z_1 = 2i\), \(z_2 = -2i\). They lie at distance \(2\) from the origin, the first in the upper half-plane, the second in the lower. We can then write Cauchy’s theorem for the curve \([-R, R] \cup C_{R}\), \(R > 2\):
\[
  \underbrace{\int _{[-R,R]}f(z)dz}_{I_1(R)} + \underbrace{\int _{C_{R}}f(z) dz}_{I_2(R)} = 2\pi i \cdot \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z_1}f
\]
\(I_{1}(R) \to \tilde{I}\) as \(R \to +\infty\). What about \(I_2(R)\)?
Note that \(g(z) \sim \frac{1}{z}\) as \(z \to \infty\), hence
\[
  \max _{z \in C_{R}}\left|g(z)\right| \xrightarrow [R \to +\infty ]{} 0
\]
By Jordan’s lemma we obtain
\[
  I_2(R) = \int _{C_R}e^{2i z}g(z) dz \to 0
\]
as \(R \to +\infty\).
Computing the residues, we obtain
\[
\begin{align}  \tilde{I} & = \lim _{R \to +\infty }I_{1}(R) = 2\pi i \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z_1}f(z) = 2\pi i \cdot \frac{z_1e^{-i} \cdot e^{2iz_1}}{2z_1} = \pi i \cdot e^{-i} \cdot e^{-4} = \pi e^{-4} \left(\cos (1) - i\sin (1)\right) \\ & = \pi e^{-4} \left(\sin (1) + i\cos (1)\right) \end{align}
\]
\(I = \operatorname {Re}\tilde{I} = \pi e^{-4}\sin (1)\).










AnswerAnswer





\(\pi e^{-4}\sin (1)\).












ExampleExample 11





Compute \[
  I = \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty }\frac{\sin (x)}{x^2 - 2x + 4 - 4i}dx
\]






SolutionSolution





We cannot simply replace \(\sin (x)\) with \(e^{ix}\) and put \(\operatorname {Im}\) in front of the integral, since the function is not real.
Note that
\[
\begin{align}  I & = \frac{1}{2i} \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty }\frac{e^{ix} - e^{-ix}}{\left(x - (2+2i)\right) \left(x-(-2i)\right)} dx = \\ & = \frac{1}{2i} \left(\underbrace{\int _{-\infty }^{+\infty }\frac{e^{ix}}{\left(x - (2+2i)\right) \left(x-(-2i)\right)} dx}_{=:I_{1}} - \underbrace{\int _{-\infty }^{+\infty }\frac{e^{-ix}}{\left(x - (2+2i)\right) \left(x-(-2i)\right)} dx}_{=:I_{2}}\right) \end{align}
\]
To compute the integral with \(e^{-ix}\), we need to use the lower contour (or, alternatively, the substitution \(w = -x\)).

Let
\[
  g(z) = \frac{1}{\left(z - (2+2i)\right) \left(z-(-2i)\right)}
\]
Note that \(g(z) \sim \frac{1}{z^2}\), \(g(-z) \sim \frac{1}{z^2}\) as \(z \to \infty\), hence
\[
  \max _{z \in C_{R}}\left|g(z)\right|, \max _{z \in C_{R}}\left|g(-z)\right| \xrightarrow [R \to +\infty ]{} 0
\]
By Jordan’s lemma we obtain
\[
  \int _{C_R}e^{i\alpha z}g(z) dz, \int _{C_R}e^{i\alpha z}g(-z) dz \to 0
\]
as \(R \to +\infty\).
Let \(f_1(z) = g(z)e^{iz}\). Singularities of \(f_1\): \(z_1 = 2+2i\), \(z_2 = -2i\). Only \(z_1\) lies in the upper half-plane. Then, by Cauchy’s theorem, for \(R > 2\sqrt{2}\)
\[
  \int _{[-R,R]}f_1(z) dz + \int _{C_{R}}f_1(z)dz = 2\pi i \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{z_1} f_1 = 2\pi i \cdot \frac{e^{iz_1}}{2z_1 - 2} = 2\pi i \cdot \frac{e^{-2} \cdot e^{2i}}{2 + 4i}
\]
Letting \(R \to +\infty\), we obtain
\[
  I_{1} =2\pi i \cdot \frac{e^{-2} \cdot e^{2i}}{2 + 4i}
\]
Let \(f_2(w) = g(-w)e^{iw}\). Singularities of \(f_2\) in the upper half-plane: \(w_1 = 2i\). Then, by Cauchy’s theorem, for \(R > 2\)
\[
  \int _{[-R,R]}f_2(w) dw + \int _{C_{R}}f_2(w)dw = 2\pi i \mathop{\mathrm{res}}_{w_1} f_2 = 2\pi i \cdot \frac{e^{iw_1}}{2w_1 + 2} = 2\pi i \cdot \frac{e^{-2}}{2 + 4i}
\]
In total,
\[
  I = \frac{1}{2i} \cdot \left(2\pi i \cdot \frac{e^{-2} \cdot e^{2i}}{2 + 4i} - 2\pi i \cdot \frac{e^{-2}}{2 + 4i}\right) = \frac{\pi e^{-2}}{2 + 4i}\left(e^{2i} - 1\right)
\]










AnswerAnswer





\(\frac{\pi e^{-2}}{2 + 4i}\left(e^{2i} - 1\right)\).












ProblemProblem T.5





Compute the integral \[
  \int _{-\infty }^{\infty } \frac{\sin x d x}{x^{2}-3 i x+4}
\]









ProblemProblem T.6





Let \(f\) be a holomorphic and bounded function on the unit disk \(\left|z\right| < 1\). Show that for every \(\zeta ,\left|\zeta \right| < 1\), the equality \[
  f(\zeta ) = \frac{1}{\pi } \iint _{\left|z\right| < 1} \frac{f(z)}{(1-\overline{z} \zeta )^{2}} d x d y, \quad z = x+i y
\] holds.

title: The maximum modulus principle and Schwarz’s lemma
text:
WarningDraft



These notes are still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and places that have not been fully worked out locally. If you find something, please let the author know (contact info on the course page).



1 The open mapping theorem







Theorem 1 (On the local structure of a regular map) Let \(f\) be regular in \(D\), \(z_0 \in D\), \(f(z_0) = w_0\). Let \[
  f'(z_0) = \ldots = f^{(n-1)}(z_0) = 0, \quad f^{(n)}(z_0) \neq 0
\] Then there exist neighborhoods \(U(z_0)\), \(V(w_0)\) such that for every \(w \in \dot{V}(w_0)\) the equation \(f(z) = w\) has exactly \(n\) distinct solutions.




Indeed, we have \(f(z) - f(z_0) = c_{n}(z - z_0)^n + o((z - z_0)^n) \sim c_{n}(z-z_0)^n\) as \(z \to z_0\). The meaning of the theorem: a holomorphic function behaves, in a neighborhood of each of its points, like raising to a power. Raising to the power \(n\) wraps the circle \(U(z_0)\) around \(n\) times.
Criterion for local univalence (injectivity): the first derivative is nonzero.







Corollary 1 Let \(D\) be a domain, \(f\) regular in \(D\), \(f\) not constant. Then \(f(D)\) is a domain.










Mn-proofProof






Connectedness of \(f(D)\) follows from continuity of \(f\). Let us prove openness. By contradiction: suppose \(z_0 \in D\) is such that \(f(z_0) \not\in \operatorname {int}f(D)\). By the theorem above there is a neighborhood \(V(f(z_0))\) such that every point in it has at least 1 preimage. Contradiction.










ExampleExample 1





An old problem: let \(D\) be a domain, let \(f\) be regular in \(D\), \(\left|f(z)\right| \equiv \operatorname {const}\). Prove that \(f \equiv \operatorname {const}\).






SolutionSolution





Suppose \(f\) is not constant. By the theorem above, \(f(D)\) is a domain. But \(f(D)\) is a subset of a circle (since \(\left|f\right| \equiv \operatorname {const}\)). No subset of a circle can be open. Contradiction.








2 The maximum modulus principle







Theorem 2 (The maximum principle, 1st formulation) A function regular in a domain cannot attain the supremum of its modulus. Namely, let \(f\) be regular in the domain \(D\), \(f \not\equiv \operatorname {const}\). Then for every point \(z_0 \in D\)
\[
  \left|f(z_0)\right| < \sup _{z \in D} \left|f(z)\right|
\]











Theorem 3 (The maximum principle, 2nd formulation) Let \(f\) be continuous on \(\overline{D}\) and regular in \(D\) (\(D\) a bounded domain). Then
\[
  \max _{z \in \overline{D}}\left|f(z)\right| = \max _{z\in \partial D}\left|f(z)\right|
\]










Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: the maximum modulus principle.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/310/010_max_modulus_principle_fig.tex


Similarly one can prove the maximum (minimum) principle for \(\operatorname {Re}f\) (\(\operatorname {Im}f\)):

\(f\) regular in a bounded domain \(D\), \(f\) not constant. Then for every \(z_0 \in D\) we have
\[
  \operatorname {Re}f(z_0) < \sup _{z \in D}\operatorname {Re}f(z)
\]
similarly for the infimum: \(\operatorname {Re}f(z_0) > \inf_{z \in D}\operatorname {Re}f(z)\) (unlike for the modulus, here no conditions such as \(f \neq 0\) are needed: it suffices to apply the maximum principle to \(-f\));
the same two statements for \(\operatorname {Im}f\) (this is \(\operatorname {Re}(-if)\));
in the 2nd formulation: if \(f\) is continuous on \(\overline{D}\), then \(\max_{\overline{D}}\operatorname {Re}f = \max_{\partial D}\operatorname {Re}f\), and similarly for the minimum and for \(\operatorname {Im}f\).

What about a minimum modulus principle? For example, \(f(z) = z\), \(\left|z\right| < 1\). The minimum is attained: at zero.







Theorem 4 (The minimum modulus principle) \(f\) regular in a bounded domain \(D\), \(f \not\equiv \operatorname {const}\), \(f(z) \neq 0\) on \(D\). Then for every \(z_0 \in D\) \[
  \inf _{z \in D}\left|f(z)\right| < \left|f(z_0)\right|
\]










Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: the minimum modulus principle.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/310/020_min_modulus_principle_fig.tex








ExampleExample 2





Let \[
  P(z) = z^{n} + c_{n-1}z^{n-1} + \ldots + c_1z + c_0, \quad P(z) \not\equiv z^n
\] Prove that there exists a point \(z_0 \in \mathbb {C}\) such that \(\left|z_0\right| = 1\), \(\left|P(z_0)\right| > 1\).






SolutionSolution





Let
\[
  f(\zeta ) := \zeta ^{n}P(1/\zeta ) = 1 + c_{n-1}\zeta + \ldots + c_{1}\zeta ^{n-1} + c_0\zeta ^{n}
\]
\(f(0) = 1\), \(f\) is holomorphic in \(\left|\zeta \right| < 1\), continuous in \(\left|\zeta \right| \leq 1\). The maximum is not attained in the interior, hence
\[
  1 < \max _{\left|\zeta \right| \leq 1}\left|f(\zeta )\right| = \max _{\left|\zeta \right| = 1}\left|f(\zeta )\right| = \left|f(\zeta _0)\right|
\]
for some point \(\zeta_0 \in \left\{ \left|\zeta \right| = 1\right\}\). Let \(z_0 = \frac{1}{\zeta_0}\). Then
\[
  \left|P(z_0)\right| = \left|z_0^n\right| \cdot \left|f\left(\frac{1}{z_0}\right)\right| > 1
\]
Where did we use \(P(z) \not\equiv z^n\)? To be able to say that \(f(\zeta ) \not\equiv \operatorname {const}\).












ExampleExample 3





Let \(D\) be a bounded domain, \(f\) regular in \(D\), continuous on \(\overline{D}\), \(\left|f(z)\right| \equiv \operatorname {const}\) on \(\partial D\), \(f(z) \not\equiv \operatorname {const}\) on \(D\). Prove that there exists \(z_0 \in D\) with \(f(z_0) = 0\).






SolutionSolution





By contradiction: if \(f(z) \neq 0\) in \(D\), then for every \(z_0 \in D\) we have, by the maximum principle and the minimum principle (since the function does not vanish), \[
  \min _{z \in \partial D}\left|f(z)\right| =\min _{z \in \overline{D}}\left|f(z)\right| \leq \left|f(z_0)\right| \leq \max _{z \in \overline{D}}\left|f(z)\right| = \max _{z \in \partial D}\left|f(z)\right|
\] The outer quantities are equal, so all the inequalities become equalities. Hence \(\left|f(z)\right| \equiv \operatorname {const}\) in \(D\), and hence also \(f \equiv \operatorname {const}\) on \(D\). Contradiction.












ExampleExample 4





Given a square \(ABCD\) with side \(l\). Find the point \(P\) (in the closed square) at which the product of the distances to the vertices of the square attains its maximum. Find the value of this maximum.






SolutionSolution





Let \(z_A = 0\), \(z_{B} = il\), \(z_{C} = l + il\), \(z_{D} = l\). Let \(D = \left\{ 0 < \operatorname {Re}z, \operatorname {Im}z < l\right\}\) (the interior of the square). Consider the function \(f(z) = (z-z_A) \cdot \ldots \cdot (z-z_D)\). This is a polynomial, so \(f\) is holomorphic in the domain \(D\) and continuous up to the boundary. By the maximum principle, \[
  \max _{z \in \overline{D}}\left|f(z)\right| = \max _{z \in \partial D}\left|f(z)\right|
\] \(\partial D\) consists of 4 segments. By the symmetry of the square, it does not matter which segment we consider. Let us consider the one from \(z_A\) to \(z_D\): \(z = z(t) = (1-t)z_A + tz_D = tl\), \(t \in [0,1]\). Then \[
\begin{align}  \left|f(z(t))\right| & = \left|tl - 0\right|\cdot \left|tl - il\right|\cdot \left|tl - l - il\right| \cdot \left|tl - l\right| = \left|l\right|^4 \cdot \left|t\right| \cdot \sqrt{t^2 + 1} \cdot \sqrt{(t-1)^2 + 1} \cdot \sqrt{(t-1)^2} = \\ & = \left|l\right|^4 \cdot \sqrt{t^2(1-t)^2(t^2 + 1)((t-1)^2 + 1)} \end{align}
\] It is not hard to compute (an exercise in real analysis) that the function under the square root attains its maximum on \([0,1]\) at \(t = \frac{1}{2}\), with value there equal to \(\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{5}{4} \cdot \frac{5}{4} = \frac{5^2}{4^4}\). In total the maximum of the product equals \[
  l^4\sqrt{\frac{5^2}{4^4}} = \frac{5}{16}\, l^4,
\] attained at the midpoint of the side (\(t = \frac{1}{2}\)).









AnswerAnswer





\(P\) is the midpoint of an arbitrary side, and the maximum equals \(\frac{5}{16}\,  l^4\).








3 Schwarz’s lemma







Lemma 1 Let \(f\) be regular in \(D = \left\{ \left|z\right| < 1\right\}\), \(f(0) = 0\), \(\left|f(z)\right| \leq 1\), \(z \in D\). Then \[
  \left|f(z)\right| \leq \left|z\right|, \;  \forall z \in D, \qquad \left|f'(0)\right| \leq 1
\] moreover, if \(\left|f(z_0)\right| = \left|z_0\right|\) at even one point \(z_0 \neq 0\), or \(\left|f'(0)\right| = 1\), then \(f(z) = e^{i\alpha }z\), \(\alpha \in \mathbb {R}\).










Mn-proofProof






Consider \(g(z) = \frac{1}{z}f(z)\) (at zero we set it, by continuity, to \(f'(0)\) — the singularity is removable since \(f(0) = 0\)). It will be regular in the unit disk. Fix \(r < 1\): on the circle \(\left|z\right| = r\) we have \(\left|g(z)\right| \leq \frac{1}{r}\), hence, by the maximum principle (2nd formulation, for the disk \(\left|z\right| \leq r\)), \(\left|g(z)\right| \leq \frac{1}{r}\) throughout the disk \(\left|z\right| \leq r\) as well. Letting \(r \to 1-\), we obtain \(\left|g(z)\right| \leq 1\) everywhere, i.e. \(\left|f(z)\right| \leq \left|z\right|\) and \(\left|f'(0)\right| = \left|g(0)\right| \leq 1\).
Either equality case means that \(\left|g\right|\) attains the value \(1\) (its maximum) at an interior point of the disk. By the maximum principle, \(g \equiv \operatorname {const}\), and the constant has modulus \(1\): \(g \equiv e^{i\alpha }\), i.e. \(f(z) = e^{i\alpha }z\).










ExampleExample 5





Does there exist a regular \(f: B_{1}(0) \to B_{1}(0)\) such that \(f(0) = \frac{1}{2}\), \(f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{7}{8}\)?






SolutionSolution





First attempt: consider \(g(z) = \frac{f(z) - 1/2}{3/2}\). \(g(0) = 0\), \(\left|g(z)\right| < 1\). We have
\[
  g\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{f(1/2) - 1/2}{3/2} = \frac{7/8 - 1/2}{3/2} = \frac{1}{4}
\]
No contradiction with Schwarz’s lemma: \(\frac{1}{4} \leq \frac{1}{2}\). Normalizing by a shift is “too crude” — let us try differently.
The general form of a fractional-linear (Möbius) automorphism \(\varphi : B_{1}(0) \to B_{1}(0)\):
\[
  \varphi (z) = \frac{z - z_0}{1 - \overline{z_0}z}e^{i \alpha }
\]
In our case let \(\varphi (z) = \frac{z - \frac{1}{2}}{1 - \frac{1}{2}z} = \frac{2z - 1}{2-z}\). Let \(g(z) = \varphi (f(z))\). Then \(g: B_{1}(0) \to B_{1}(0)\), \(g(0) = 0\),
\[
  g\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \varphi \left(\frac{7}{8}\right) = \frac{2 \cdot \frac{7}{8} - 1}{2 - \frac{7}{8}} = \frac{3/4}{9/8} = \frac{2}{3}
\]
The modulus is greater than \(\frac{1}{2}\) — but Schwarz’s lemma for \(g\) requires \(\left|g\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right| \leq \frac{1}{2}\). Contradiction: no such function \(f\) exists.









AnswerAnswer





No: composing with a fractional-linear automorphism of the disk violates Schwarz’s lemma.












ProblemProblem T.1





Let \(P(z)\) be a polynomial of degree \(n\) and \(M(r) = \max_{|z| = r}|P(z)|\). Prove that for \(0 < r_{1} < r_{2}\) the inequality \(\frac{M\left(r_{1}\right)}{r_{1}^{n}} \geq \frac{M\left(r_{2}\right)}{r_{2}^{n}}\) holds.









ProblemProblem T.2





Let the function \(f(z)\) be holomorphic in the unit disk \(\mathbb {D}\) with \(|f(z)| < 1\) for \(z \in \mathbb {D}, f(0) = a \neq 0\). Prove that \(f(z) \neq 0\) for \(|z| < |a|\).









ProblemProblem T.3





Let \(a_{1}, \ldots , a_{n}\) be the vertices of a regular \(n\)-gon inscribed in the unit disk \(\mathbb {D}\). Prove that \[
  \sup _{z \in \mathbb {D}} \prod _{k = 1}^{n}\left|z-a_{k}\right| = 2
\]









ProblemProblem T.4





Let \(P\) be a polynomial with leading coefficient \(1\). Prove that on the unit circle there is a point \(z_{0}\) at which \(\left|P\left(z_{0}\right)\right| \geq 1\).









ProblemProblem T.5





Let the functions \(f\) and \(g\) be holomorphic in the unit disk \(\mathbb {D}\) and continuous on the closure \(\overline{\mathbb {D}}\). Prove that \[
  \max _{z \in \overline{\mathbb {D}}}(|f(z)|+|g(z)|) = \max _{|z| = 1}(|f(z)|+|g(z)|)
\]

title: Conformal maps
text:
2.1 Definition
Let \(a, b \in \mathbb {C}\), \(a \neq 0\). Consider the map
\[
  z \mapsto w(z) = \begin{cases}  az + b, &  z \neq \infty \\ \infty , &  z = \infty \end{cases}
\]
This map \(\overline{\mathbb {C}} \to \overline{\mathbb {C}}\) is called linear. For brevity we write this map as \(w(z) = az + b\), with the understanding that \(z\) may also be \(\infty\) (in which case \(w(\infty )= \infty\)).
Fractional-linear maps are a generalization of linear maps. Let \(a,b,c,d \in \mathbb {C}\), with \(ad - bc \neq 0\). A fractional-linear map (or Möbius map) is a map \(\overline{\mathbb {C}} \to \overline{\mathbb {C}}\) which, in the case \(c = 0\), equals \(\frac{a}{d}z +\frac{b}{d}\) and is given as above, and in the case \(c \neq 0\) is given by
\[
  z \mapsto w(z) = \begin{cases}  \frac{a z+b}{c z+d}, &  z \neq \infty , z \neq -\frac{d}{c} \\ \infty , &  z = -\frac{d}{c} \\ \frac{a}{c}, &  z = \infty \end{cases}
\]
The condition \(a d-b c \neq 0\) means that \(w \not\equiv \operatorname {const}\). Again, for brevity it is customary to write \(w(z) = \frac{a z+b}{c z+d}\), where \(z\) may be substituted by any point of \(\overline{\mathbb {C}}\).

title: Conformal maps
text:
2.2 Properties

2.2.1 Conformality







Lemma 1 (A Möbius map is conformal) The map \(w(z)=\frac{a z+b}{c z+d}\), regarded as a map \(\overline{\mathbb {C}} \to \overline{\mathbb {C}}\), is conformal (on the whole of \(\overline{\mathbb {C}}\)).




In particular, a Möbius map preserves angles between curves.


2.2.2 Möbius maps form a group
It is easy to check that the composition of 2 Möbius maps is again a Möbius map.







Lemma 2 The collection of all fractional-linear maps forms a group under composition (superposition).




Let \(ad - bc \neq 0\). Then the matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}  a &  b \\ c &  d \end{smallmatrix}\right)\) is nonsingular. To each such matrix corresponds a Möbius map:
\[
  \left(\begin{smallmatrix}  a &  b \\ c &  d \end{smallmatrix}\right) \mathrel {\leadsto } w = w(z)
\]
where \(w(z) = \frac{a z+b}{c z+d}\). It turns out (easy to check) that matrix multiplication corresponds to the composition of 2 Möbius maps: if \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}  a_1 &  b_1 \\ c_1 &  d_{1} \end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}  a_2 &  b_2 \\ c_2 &  d_{2} \end{smallmatrix}\right)\) are two nonsingular matrices, then
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}  a_1 &  b_1 \\ c_1 &  d_1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  a_2 &  b_2 \\ c_2 &  d_2 \end{pmatrix} \mathrel {\leadsto } w_1 \circ w_2
\]
where \(w_{1,2}(z) = \frac{a_{1,2}z + b_{1,2}}{c_{1,2}z + d_{1,2}}\)







Lemma 3 (Homomorphism of \(\operatorname {GL}_2(\mathbb {C})\) onto the group of Möbius maps) The map described above is a homomorphism of the group of nonsingular \(2\times 2\) matrices over the complex numbers (usually denoted \(\operatorname {GL}_2(\mathbb {C})\)) onto the group of Möbius maps under composition.




What use is this? If we want to find the inverse map to the Möbius map \(w(z) = \frac{a z+b}{c z+d}\), we just need to see which map corresponds to the matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}  a &  b \\ c &  d \end{smallmatrix}\right)^{-1}\). Namely,
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}  a &  b \\ c &  d \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc} \begin{pmatrix}  d &  -b \\ -c &  a \end{pmatrix} \quad \mathrel {\leadsto } \quad w^{-1}(z) = \frac{\frac{1}{ad - bc}dz - \frac{1}{ad - bc} b }{-\frac{1}{ad - bc} cz + \frac{1}{ad - bc} a} = \frac{dz - b}{-cz + a}
\]
This map is not an isomorphism for \(\operatorname {GL}_2(\mathbb {C})\), since the kernel is nontrivial. For example, the identity matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}  1 &  0 \\ 0 &  1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) maps to the identity map \(w(z) = \frac{1z + 0}{0z + 1} = z\). But so does, for example, \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}  2 &  0 \\ 0 &  2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\): in this case \(w(z) = \frac{2z + 0}{0z+ 2} =z\); the kernel consists of all scalar matrices \(\lambda E\), \(\lambda \neq 0\). If we restrict to matrices with unit determinant, the kernel shrinks but remains nontrivial: \(\operatorname {det}(-E) = 1\), and the corresponding Möbius map is the identity. That is, the kernel narrows to \(\left\{ \pm E\right\}\).







Lemma 4 (The group of Möbius maps is isomorphic to \(\operatorname {PSL}_2(\mathbb {C})\)) The map described above induces an isomorphism between the quotient group \(\operatorname {PSL}_2(\mathbb {C}) = \operatorname {SL}_2(\mathbb {C})/\left\{ \pm E\right\}\) (matrices with unit determinant, taken up to sign) and the group of Möbius maps under composition.






2.2.3 The circle-preserving property







Lemma 5 Under a fractional-linear map, the image of any circle on the Riemann sphere \(\overline{\mathbb {C}}\) is again a circle on the Riemann sphere.




Recall that a circle on the Riemann sphere (under stereographic projection) corresponds to a circle in the plane \(\mathbb {C}\) if, on the sphere, the circle did not pass through the top point, i.e. through \(\infty\). If it does pass through \(\infty\), then on the plane it corresponds to a line.


2.2.4 A Möbius map preserves symmetry of points
Let \(z_1, z_2 \in \overline{\mathbb {C}}\), and let \(\gamma\) be a line or a circle. We need to define symmetry of points with respect to \(\gamma\).

Let \(\gamma\) be a line. Finite points \(z_1, z_2 \in \mathbb {C}\) are called symmetric with respect to \(\gamma\) if they are symmetric in the ordinary geometric sense. That is, the segment \([z_1, z_2]\) crosses the line \(\gamma\) perpendicularly, with the distance from \(\gamma\) to \(z_1\) and to \(z_2\) equal.
Further, \(\infty\) is symmetric only to \(\infty\). It is convenient to adopt this convention, since every point on a line is symmetric to itself (with respect to that line), and \(\infty\) lies on the line (once we pass to the Riemann sphere).
Let \(\gamma\) be a circle. Points \(z_1\), \(z_2\) are symmetric with respect to \(\gamma\) if they are related by inversion. Namely, they lie on the same ray from the center \(z_0\) of the circle \(\gamma\), with \(\left|z_1 - z_0\right| \cdot \left|z_2 - z_0\right| = R^2\), where \(R\) is the radius of \(\gamma\).
In particular, the center \(z_0\) itself is symmetric to \(\infty\) with respect to \(\gamma\).








Lemma 6 (The symmetry-preservation property) Under a fractional-linear map, a pair of points symmetric with respect to a circle or a line maps to a pair of points symmetric with respect to the image of that circle or line.










ExampleExample 2





Given the fractional-linear function \[
w = f(z) = \frac{1 + iz}{1 - iz}.
\] Find the image of the upper half-plane \(D = \left\{ z \;  : \;  \operatorname {Im}z > 0\right\}\).






SolutionSolution





Let \(\gamma = \partial D = \left\{ z \;  : \;  \operatorname {Im} z = 0\right\}\). \(\gamma\) is the real axis. By the properties of conformal maps, the boundary of \(f(D)\) is the set \(f(\gamma )\). Elementary observations:
\[
  0 \mapsto f(0) = 1, \qquad 1 \mapsto \frac{1 + i}{1-i} = \frac{2i}{2} = i, \qquad \infty \mapsto \lim _{z \to \infty }f(z) = \lim _{z \to \infty }\frac{\frac{1}{z} + i}{\frac{1}{z} - i} = \frac{i}{-i} = -1
\]
Further, the point that sends the denominator to zero maps to \(\infty\), i.e. the point \(-i\). In total, \(-i \mapsto \infty\).
Let us find \(f(\gamma )\), i.e. the image of the line \(\operatorname {Im} z = 0\). The image of any line under a Möbius map is a line (if a point on the line maps to infinity) or a circle (otherwise). In our case \(-i \mapsto \infty\), and \(-i \not\in \gamma\) does not lie on the line in question. Hence, \(\infty \not\in f(\gamma )\), so \(f(\gamma )\) is indeed a circle. How do we find this circle?

Method 1, using 3 points. \(0,1,\infty\) lay on \(\gamma\) (in \(\overline{\mathbb {C}}\)), so \(f(\gamma )\) will pass through \(1, i, -1\). The unique line or circle passing through these points is the circle \(\left\{ \left|z\right| = 1\right\}\). Hence, that is \(f(\gamma )\).
Method 2, via intersection angles and 2 points. We need to understand where the real axis goes. One can note that substituting into \(f(z) = \frac{1 + iz}{1 - iz}\) points from the line \(\operatorname {Re}z = 0\), i.e. points of the form \(z = iy\), yields real numbers. Hence, the imaginary axis maps to the real axis. The imaginary and real axes intersect at a right angle, so their images must intersect at a right angle too. Moreover, we know that \(-1, 1 \in f(\gamma )\). Hence \(f(\gamma )\) is a line or circle passing through \(-1,1\) that intersects the real axis at right angles. The only option is the circle \(\left|z\right| = 1\).
Method 3, using the center and a point on the circle. We have found that \(f(\gamma )\) is a circle. How do we find the point \(w_0\), the center of this circle? \(w_0\) is symmetric to \(\infty\) with respect to \(f(\gamma )\), so \(z_0 := f^{-1}(w_0)\) is symmetric to \(f^{-1}(\infty ) = -i\) with respect to \(\gamma\). I.e. \(z_0 = i\), \(w_0 = f(z_0) = 0\). Further, we know that \(1 \in f(\gamma )\). \(f(\gamma )\) is a circle centered at \(0\) and passing through \(1\). The only option: \(f(\gamma ) = \left\{ \left|z\right| = 1\right\}\).







Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: the conformal map D -> f(D).
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/330/010_conformal_map_D_fig.tex


We have found the boundary of the image. It remains to determine on which side of this boundary the image lies. We have already said that \(-i \mapsto \infty\). Moreover \(-i \not\in D\), so \(\infty \not\in f(D)\), so \(f(D) = \left\{ \left|z\right| < 1\right\}\).









AnswerAnswer





\(f(D) = \left\{ \left|z\right| < 1\right\}\).












ExampleExample 3





Given the Möbius map \[
w = f(z) = \frac{2iz}{z + 3}
\] Find the image of \(D = \left\{ \left|z - 1\right| < 2\right\}\).






SolutionSolution











Note



Figure in development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: TikZ: D -> f(D), the image is the unit disk.
Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/CA/contents/specials/330/020_conformal_map_unit_disk_fig.tex


\(-3 \mapsto \infty\). \(-3 \not\in \gamma = \partial D = \left\{ \left|z-1\right| = 2\right\}\). Hence, the image of the boundary \(f(\gamma )\) is a circle.
\(-1 \mapsto \frac{-2i}{2} = -i\), \(3 \mapsto \frac{6i}{6} = i\). Further, the points \(-3\) and \(0\) are symmetric with respect to \(\gamma\) (they lie on the same ray from the center \(1\), and \(\left|-3-1\right|\cdot \left|0-1\right| = 4 = R^2\)), so their images \(\infty\) and \(f(0) = 0\) are symmetric with respect to \(f(\gamma )\), i.e. \(0\) is the center of the circle \(f(\gamma )\). It passes through \(\pm i\), i.e. \(f(\gamma ) = \left\{ \left|w\right| = 1\right\}\).
Finally, \(-3 \not\in D\), so \(\infty = f(-3) \not\in f(D)\): the image is the interior of the disk, \(f(D) = \left\{ \left|w\right| < 1\right\}\).









AnswerAnswer





\(f(D) = \left\{ \left|z\right| < 1\right\}\).












ProblemProblem 27.4





Find the image of the half-plane \(\left\{ z: \operatorname {Re} z < 1\right\}\) under the following maps:

\(w = \frac{z-3+i}{z+1+i}\).






2.2.5 A Möbius map preserves the cross-ratio of 4 points
Let \(z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4 \in \overline{\mathbb {C}}\). The cross-ratio of these four numbers is defined as
\[
  (z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4 ) \quad := \quad \frac{z_3 - z_1}{z_3 - z_2} \;  \colon \;  \frac{z_4 - z_1}{z_4 - z_2} = \frac{(z_3 - z_1) (z_4 - z_2)}{(z_3 - z_2) (z_4 - z_1)}
\]
In particular, if \(z_1 = \infty\), then
\[
  (\infty , z_2, z_3, z_4 ) = \frac{(z_3 - \infty ) (z_4 - z_2)}{(z_3 - z_2) (z_4 - \infty )} = \lim _{z_1 \to \infty } \frac{(z_3 - z_1) (z_4 - z_2)}{(z_3 - z_2) (z_4 - z_1)} = \frac{z_4 - z_2}{z_3 - z_2}
\]







Lemma 7 Let \(w = w(z)\) be a Möbius map, \(w_i := w(z_i)\). Then \[
  (z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4 ) = (w_1, w_2, w_3, w_4 )
\]

title: Conformal maps
text:
2.3 Examples of fractional-linear maps

2.3.1 3 points to 3 points
There exists a unique fractional-linear map under which three distinct points \(z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}\) of \(\overline{\mathbb {C}}\) map respectively to three distinct points \(w_{1}, w_{2}, w_{3}\) of \(\overline{\mathbb {C}}\). This map can be found from the equality of cross-ratios: \((z_1, z_2, z_3, z) = (w_1, w_2, w_3, w)\). Namely,
\[
  \frac{w_3-w_{1}}{w_3-w_{2}} \colon \frac{w-w_{1}}{w-w_{2}}=\frac{z_3-z_{1}}{z_3-z_{2}} \colon \frac{z-z_{1}}{z-z_{2}} .
\]


2.3.2 Upper half-plane to the unit disk
Every conformal map from the upper half-plane \(\{ z: \operatorname {Im} z>0\}\) onto the disk \(\{ w:|w|<1\}\) has the form
\[
  w(z)=\frac{z-z_{0}}{z-\bar{z}_{0}} \cdot e^{i \alpha }
\]
where \(\operatorname {Im} z_{0}>0, \quad \alpha \in \mathbb {R}\).


2.3.3 Unit disk to the upper half-plane
We seek the inverse of the previous map:
\[
  we^{-i\alpha } (z - \overline{z_0}) = z - z_0 \iff z = \frac{we^{-i\alpha }\overline{z_0} - z_0}{we^{-i\alpha } - 1} = \frac{we^{-2i\operatorname {arg}z_0} - e^{i\alpha }}{w - e^{i\alpha }}z_0 = \frac{we^{-2i\beta } - e^{i\alpha }}{w - e^{i\alpha }}r \cdot e^{i\beta }
\]
So, every conformal map from the unit disk \(\{ w:|w|<1\}\) to the upper half-plane \(\{ z: \operatorname {Im} z>0\}\) has the form
\[
  w(z)=\frac{z e^{-2i\beta } - e^{i\alpha }}{z - e^{i\alpha }}r \cdot e^{i\beta }
\]
where \(r > 0, \beta \in (0,\pi ), \quad \alpha \in \mathbb {R}\).
The simplest example: \(\alpha = 0\), \(\beta = \pi /2\), \(r= 1\),
\[
  w(z) = \frac{-z - 1}{z-1}i = \frac{1 + z}{1 - z}i
\]


2.3.4 Unit disk to the unit disk
Every conformal map from the disk \(\{ z:|z|<1\}\) onto the disk \(\{ w:|w|<1\}\) has the form
\[
  w(z)=\frac{z-z_{0}}{1-\bar{z}_{0}z} \cdot e^{i \alpha }
\]
where \(\left|z_{0}\right|<1, \quad \alpha \in \mathbb {R}\).


2.3.5 Upper half-plane to the upper half-plane
Every conformal map from the upper half-plane \(\{ z: \operatorname {Im} z>0\}\) onto the upper half-plane \(\{ w: \operatorname {Im} w>0\}\) has the form
\[
  w(z)=\frac{a z+b}{c z+d}
\]
where \(a, b, c, d \in \mathbb {R}\) and \(a d-b c>0\).






ExampleExample 27.7





Find the fractional-linear functions \(w(z)\) satisfying the conditions:

\(w(i) = 0, w(\infty ) = 1, w(-i) = \infty\); Find the image of the half-plane \(\left\{ z: \operatorname {Re} z > 0\right\}\) under the maps given by these functions.







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Equality of cross-ratios: \((i, \infty , -i, z) = (0,1,\infty , w)\). Let us simplify:
\[
\begin{align}  (i, \infty , -i, z) & = \frac{-i - i}{-i -\infty } \colon \frac{z - i}{ z - \infty } = \frac{-2i}{-i -\infty } \cdot \frac{z - \infty }{z - i} = \frac{-2i}{z - i} \\ (0,1,\infty , w) & = \frac{\infty - 0}{\infty - 1} \colon \frac{w - 0}{w - 1} = \frac{w-1}{w} = 1 - \frac{1}{w} \end{align}
\]
We get \(1 - \frac{1}{w} = \frac{-2i}{z - i}\) and
\[
  w = \left(1 - \frac{-2i}{z - i}\right)^{-1} = \left(\frac{z - i - (-2i)}{z - i}\right)^{-1} = \frac{z-i}{z + i}
\]
Further, let \(D = \left\{ \operatorname {Re}z > 0\right\}\), then \(\gamma = \partial D = \left\{ \operatorname {Re}z = 0\right\}  = \left\{ z = iy, \;  y \in \mathbb {R}\right\}\). Substituting:
\[
  w(iy) = \frac{iy-i}{iy + i} = \frac{y-1}{y+1}
\]
This is always a real number. Hence the imaginary line \(\gamma = \left\{ \operatorname {Re}z = 0\right\}\) maps to the real line \(\left\{ \operatorname {Im}z = 0\right\}\).
Further, \(1 \mapsto \frac{1-i}{1+i} = \frac{(1-i)^2}{2} = -i\). Hence, \(-i \in f(D)\). Hence, \(f(D) = \left\{ \operatorname {Im}z < 0\right\}\).











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(w = \frac{z-i}{z+i}, \operatorname {Im} w < 0\);














ProblemProblem 27.7





Find the fractional-linear functions \(w(z)\) satisfying the conditions:

\(w(i) = 2, w(\infty ) = 1+i, w(-i) = 0\); Find the image of the half-plane \(\left\{ z: \operatorname {Re} z > 0\right\}\) under the maps given by these functions.










ExampleExample 27.8





Find a function \(w(z)\) that conformally maps the domain \(D\) onto the domain \(D_{1}\) and satisfies the given conditions:

\(D = \left\{ z: \operatorname {Re} z > -1\right\} , D_{1} = \left\{ w:|w| < 1\right\} , w(0) = 0, \arg w^{\prime }(0) = \pi\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



We know how to map the upper half-plane to the unit disk. So the first step is to turn the domain \(\left\{ \operatorname {Re}z > -1\right\}\) into the upper half-plane.
\[
  \left\{ \operatorname {Re}z > -1\right\}  \quad \xmapsto {\, w_1(z)=z + 1\, } \quad \left\{ \operatorname {Re}w_1 > 0\right\}  \quad \xmapsto {\, w_2(w_1)= w_1 \cdot e^{i \pi /2} = iw_1\, } \quad \left\{ \operatorname {Im}w_2 > 0\right\}
\]
Further, the general form of a conformal map from \(\left\{ \operatorname {Im}w_2 > 0\right\}\) to \(\left\{ \left|w\right| < 1\right\}\):
\[
  w(w_2) = \frac{w_2 - z_0}{w_2 - \overline{z_0}}e^{i\alpha }
\]
where \(\operatorname {Im}z_0 > 0\).
The resulting map:
\[
  w(z) = \left(w \circ w_2 \circ w_1 \right)(z) =\frac{i(z+1) - z_0}{i(z+1) - \overline{z_0}}e^{i\alpha }
\]
Substituting the conditions:
\[
  0 = w(0) = \frac{i - z_0}{i - \overline{z_0}}e^{i\alpha }
\]
Hence \(z_0 = i\) and \(w(z) = \frac{iz}{iz + 2i}e^{i\alpha } = \frac{z}{z + 2}e^{i\alpha }\). Further,
\[
  \pi = \operatorname {arg}w'(0) = \operatorname {arg}\left(\frac{d}{dz}\left(\frac{z}{z + 2}e^{i\alpha }\right)\right)\bigg\rvert _{z = 0} = \operatorname {arg}\left(\frac{2}{(0 + 2)^2}e^{i\alpha }\right) = \alpha
\]
In total \(\alpha = \pi\) and
\[
  w(z) = \frac{z}{z+2}e^{i\pi } = -\frac{z}{z+2}
\]











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(w = -\frac{z}{z+2}\).














ProblemProblem 27.8





Find a function \(w(z)\) that conformally maps the domain \(D\) onto the domain \(D_{1}\) and satisfies the given conditions:

\(D = \left\{ z:|z| < 1\right\} , D_{1} = \left\{ w:|w| < 1\right\} , w\left(z_{0}\right) = w_{0}\), \(\arg w^{\prime }\left(z_{0}\right) = \alpha\), \(\left(\left|z_{0}\right| < 1,\left|w_{0}\right| < 1\right)\);
\(D = \left\{ z: \operatorname {Im} z > 0\right\} , D_{1} = \left\{ w:|w| < 1\right\} , w(0) = i, w(-1) = 1\), \(w(\infty ) = -1\);










ExampleExample 6





Find the Möbius map \(0 \mapsto 4\), \(1 + i \mapsto 2 + 2i\), \(2i \mapsto 0\).






SolutionSolution





One can solve this directly using the equality of cross-ratios.
Or as follows: from \(2i \mapsto 0\) we seek \(f\) in the form \(f(z) = \frac{a(z-2i)}{cz + d}\). The condition \(0 \mapsto 4\): \(\frac{-2ia}{d} = 4\), i.e. \(d = -\frac{ia}{2}\). The condition \(1+i \mapsto 2+2i\):
\[
  \frac{a(1+i-2i)}{c(1+i) + d} = 2 + 2i \iff a(1-i) = \underbrace{(2+2i)(1+i)}_{=4i}c + \underbrace{(2+2i)\left(-\tfrac {ia}{2}\right)}_{= a(1-i)} \iff 4ic = 0
\]
I.e. \(c = 0\): the map is linear, \(f(z) = \frac{a}{d}(z - 2i)\), where \(\frac{a}{d} = \frac{a}{-ia/2} = 2i\). In total
\[
  f(z) = 2i(z - 2i) = 2iz + 4
\]
Check: \(f(1+i) = 2i + 2i^2 + 4 = 2 + 2i\) \(\checkmark\).









AnswerAnswer





\(f(z) = 2iz + 4\).

title: Complex Analysis
text:
Seminars on the theory of functions of a complex variable: from complex differentiability and holomorphic functions to conformal maps. The course successively introduces power series and elementary functions of a complex variable, Laurent series and isolated singular points, residues and their application to computing integrals, the argument principle and Rouché’s theorem, the maximum modulus principle and Schwarz’s lemma, concluding with the geometry of conformal maps.
Information about the course from open MIPT sources (semester, workload, department, exam syllabi, point-based grading scheme) is collected on the “Course passport” page.

title: Metric spaces: an introduction
text:
4.1 Cauchy sequences
A Cauchy sequence (also a fundamental sequence) is …






ExampleExample 8





In a metric space \(X\), show

that a convergent sequence is a Cauchy sequence,
that a Cauchy sequence is bounded.







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)



Let \(x_n \to x\). For every \(\varepsilon >0\) there exists \(N\) such that \(n\ge N \Rightarrow \rho (x_n,x)<\varepsilon /2\). Then for \(m,n\ge N\): \(\rho (x_n,x_m) \le \rho (x_n,x)+\rho (x_m,x)<\varepsilon\). Hence \(x_n\) is a Cauchy sequence.








Enum-item(2)



For a Cauchy sequence \(\{ x_n\}\) there exists \(N\) such that \(m,n\ge N \Rightarrow \rho (x_n,x_m)<1\). Then all \(x_n\) for \(n\ge N\) lie in the ball of radius \(1\) around \(x_N\), and the finite set of the first \(N-1\) terms is also bounded. Hence the whole sequence is bounded.








An MS is called complete if every Cauchy sequence in it converges to some element of the MS.
Examples of complete MSs:

\(\mathbb {R}^{n}\);
\(C[a,b]\) with the sup-metric (unless stated otherwise, we always assume that \(C[0,1]\) is equipped with the sup-metric);
\(L^p(X, \mathcal{F}, \mu )\), \(1 \leq p \leq \infty\), for any measure space \((X, \mathcal{F}, \mu )\). This statement is called the Riesz-Fischer theorem.







ProblemProblem 8





For each index \(n\), define \(f_{n}(x) = \alpha x^{n}+\beta \cos (x / n)\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 1\). For which values of the parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is the sequence \(\left\{ f_{n}\right\}\) a Cauchy sequence in the metric space \(C[0,1]\)?

title: Metric spaces: an introduction
text:
4.2 Subspaces of complete MSs
In general, a subspace of a complete MS need not be complete. However,







Proposition 6 Let \(X\) be a complete MS and \(E \subset X\) a subspace of it. \(E\) is complete \(\iff\) \(E\) is closed.










ExampleExample 9





Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be the subspace of \(C[-1,1]\) consisting of continuous functions \(f:[-1,1] \rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) that are differentiable on \((-1,1)\). Is \(\mathcal{D}\) complete?
Unless stated otherwise, \(C[-1,1]\) is equipped with the sup-metric (the metric of uniform convergence).






SolutionSolution





\(C[-1,1]\) is complete, so to check whether a subset of it is complete, it suffices to check whether it is closed.
The functions \(f_n(x)=\sqrt{x^2+1/n}\) are differentiable and converge uniformly to \(f(x)=|x|\), which is continuous but not differentiable at \(0\). That is, \(\mathcal{D}\) is not closed.









AnswerAnswer





No












ExampleExample 10





Define \(\mathcal{L}\) as the subspace of \(C[0,1]\) consisting of functions \(f:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) that are Lipschitz. Is \(\mathcal{L}\) complete?






SolutionSolution





We need to check whether \(\mathcal{L}\) is closed in \(C[0,1]\).

Consider the function \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\), and consider the sequence of functions
\[
  f_n(x) = \begin{cases}  \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}nx, &  x < \frac{1}{n}\\ \sqrt{x}, &  x \geq \frac{1}{n} \end{cases}
\]
That is, the graph of \(f_n\) is a line segment from \((0,0)\) to \(\left(\frac{1}{n}, \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}\right)\), followed by the graph of the square root \(\sqrt{x}\).
It is clear that \(f_n\) converges to \(f\) pointwise. One can prove by hand, or use Dini’s theorem, that \(f_n\) converges uniformly to \(f\), i.e., in the norm of the space \(C[0,1]\).
\(f_n\) is Lipschitz for every \(n\) (this is a straightforward exercise), while \(f\) is not.
We conclude that \(\mathcal{L}\) is not closed.










AnswerAnswer





No.












ExampleExample 11





Define \(\mathcal{L}_3\) as the subspace of \(C[0,1]\) consisting of functions \(f:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) that are Lipschitz with one and the same constant (in this case, \(3\)): \[
  \mathcal{L}_3 = \left\{ f \in C[0,1] \;  : \;  \left|f(x) - f(y)\right| \leq 3 \cdot \left|x-y\right|, \;  \forall x,y \in [0,1]\right\}
\] Is \(\mathcal{L}_3\) complete?






SolutionSolution





A uniform (or even pointwise) limit of Lipschitz functions with one and the same constant will be Lipschitz with the same constant. Indeed, let \(f_n \in \mathcal{L}_3\), \(f_n \xrightarrow []{\rho }f\). Then \[
\begin{align}  \left|f(x) - f(y)\right| & \leq \left|f(x) - f_n(x)\right| + \left|f_n(x) - f_n(y)\right| + \left|f_n(y) - f(y)\right| \\ & \leq \left|f(x) - f_n(x)\right| + 3 \cdot \left|x-y\right| + \left|f_n(y) - f(y)\right| \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} 3 \cdot \left|x-y\right| \end{align}
\] That is, \(\mathcal{L}_3\) is closed in \(C[0,1]\).









AnswerAnswer





Yes.












ProblemProblem 9





Let \(X = C[0,1]\) with the sup-metric. Determine, for the following subsets (subspaces), whether they are complete.

Continuous functions having a root. That is,
\[
  \mathcal{R} = \left\{ f \in C[0,1] \;  : \;  \exists x \in [0,1] \;  \;  f(x) = 0\right\}
\]
Continuous functions having a fixed point. That is,
\[
  \mathcal{FP} = \left\{ f \in C[0,1] \;  : \;  \exists x \in [0,1] \;  \;  f(x) = x\right\}
\]
Continuous functions having at least 2 distinct fixed points. That is,
\[
  \mathcal{FPP} = \left\{ f \in C[0,1] \;  : \;  \exists x_1, x_2 \in [0,1]\;  : \;  x_1 \neq x_2, \,  f(x_i) = x_i\right\}
\]










Note



Figure under development. Will be recreated as an interactive figure (Plotly/Three.js).
Plan: : \(g_n(x) = x^2 - x/n = f_n(x) - x\) for \(n=1,2,5\) and the limit \(g(x)=x^2\); the roots of \(g_n\) are the fixed points of \(f_n(x)=x+x^2-x/n\). Curve points computed in Python (numpy, \(x=-0.05..1.06\) step \(0.05\)), deterministic, no seed needed. Interactive: slider over \(n\) (continuous, not just \(1/2/5\)), redrawing the curve \(g_n\) and marking its two roots \(0\) and \(1/n\); as \(n \to \infty\) the roots visually merge into one – the slider-to-limit animation clearly shows why the set FPP (\(\ge 2\) fixed points) is not closed.
