title: Metric spaces: an introduction
text:
4.3 Completion of an incomplete MS







Theorem 1 (on completion) Let \((X,\rho )\) be an MS. Then there exists a complete MS \((\hat{X}, \sigma )\) such that \(X\) is dense in \(\hat{X}\) (more precisely, \(X\) can be isometrically mapped into some subset \(\tilde{X} \subset \hat{X}\) that is dense in \(\hat{X}\)) and \[
  \rho (u,v) = \sigma (u,v), \qquad \forall u,v \in X
\]




The complete MS \((Y, \sigma )\) described above is called the completion of \((X,\rho )\). The completion is unique in the sense that any two completions are isometric via an isometry that is the identity map on \(X\).






Mn-proofProof






4.4 Proof sketch

If \(\left\{ x_{n}\right\}\) and \(\left\{ y_{n}\right\}\) are Cauchy sequences in \(X\), one needs to show that \(\left\{ \rho (x_{n}, y_{n})\right\}\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(\mathbb {R}\) and hence converges.
Define \(X^{\prime }\) as the set of Cauchy sequences in \(X\). For two Cauchy sequences \(\left\{ x_{n}\right\}\) and \(\left\{ y_{n}\right\}\), define \(\rho^{\prime }(\left\{ x_{n}\right\} ,\left\{ y_{n}\right\} ) = \lim \rho (x_{n}, y_{n})\).
Define two sequences \(\left\{ x_{n}\right\}\) and \(\left\{ y_{n}\right\}\) in \(X^{\prime }\) to be equivalent if \(\rho^{\prime }(\left\{ x_{n}\right\} ,\left\{ y_{n}\right\} ) = 0\). One needs to show that this is an equivalence relation. Denote by \(\widehat{X}\) the set of equivalence classes. Define the distance \(\widehat{\rho }\) between classes as \(\rho^{\prime }\) between representatives of the classes. One needs to show that \(\widehat{\rho }\) is well defined and is a metric on \(\widehat{X}\).
One needs to show that the metric space \((\widehat{X}, \widehat{\rho })\) is complete.
Hint: If \(\left\{ x_{n}\right\}\) is a Cauchy sequence from \(X\), one may assume [by passing to a subsequence] that \(\rho (x_{n}, x_{n+1}) < 2^{-n}\) for all \(n\). If \(\left\{ \{ x_{n, m}\}_{n = 1}^{\infty }\right\}_{m = 1}^{\infty }\) is a sequence of such Cauchy sequences representing a Cauchy sequence in \(\widehat{X}\), then the diagonal sequence \(\left\{ x_{n, n}\right\}_{n = 1}^{\infty }\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(X\) representing the limit of the Cauchy sequences from \(\widehat{X}\).
Define a map \(h\) from \(X\) to \(\widehat{X}\) by assigning to each \(x \in X\) the equivalence class of the constant sequence all of whose terms equal \(x\). One needs to show that \(h(X)\) is dense in \(\widehat{X}\) and that \(\widehat{\rho }(h(u), h(v)) = \rho (u, v)\) for all \(u, v \in X\).
Define the set \(\widetilde{X}\) as the disjoint union of \(X\) and \(\widehat{X} \setminus h(X)\). For \(u, v \in \widetilde{X}\), define \(\widetilde{\rho }(u, v)\) as follows: \(\widetilde{\rho }(u, v) = \rho (u, v)\) if \(u, v \in X\); \(\widetilde{\rho }(u, v) = \widehat{\rho }(u, v)\) if \(u, v \in \widehat{X} \setminus h(X)\); and \(\widetilde{\rho }(u, v) = \widehat{\rho }(h(u), v)\) for \(u \in X, v \in \widehat{X} \setminus h(X)\). From the previous parts it follows that the metric space (\(\widetilde{X}, \widetilde{\rho }\)) is complete and contains (\(X, \rho\)) as a dense subspace.











ProblemProblem 10





Recall that the support of a function \(f: X \to \mathbb {R}\) on an MS \(X\) is the set \[
  \operatorname {supp}f = \overline{\left\{ x \in X \;  : \;  f(x) \neq 0\right\} }
\] Consider the set \(C(\mathbb {R})\) of all continuous functions on \(\mathbb {R}\). Consider its subset \(C_{C}(\mathbb {R})\) of continuous functions on \(\mathbb {R}\) with compact support (such functions are also called compactly supported). Equip it with the sup-metric \[
  \rho (x, y) = \sup _{t\in \mathbb {R}}|x(t)-y(t)|, \qquad x,y \in C_{C}(\mathbb {R})
\] (you may check for yourself that this is indeed a metric on \(C_C(\mathbb {R})\)).
Characterize the completion of \(C_C(\mathbb {R})\) as a subset of \(C(\mathbb {R})\).
[@VKK, Problem  2.6]

title: Metric spaces: an introduction
section: 5.1 A generalization of the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem: a compactness criterion for an arbitrary metric space
text:
5.1 A generalization of the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem: a compactness criterion for an arbitrary metric space
Let us recall the compactness criterion in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) (and, in essence, in any finite-dimensional normed space over \(\mathbb {R}\), since it is always isomorphic to \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\)).







Theorem 2 (Bolzano-Weierstrass) Let \(X = \mathbb {R}^{n}\) with the standard Euclidean metric. Let \(A \subset \mathbb {R}^{n}\). \(A\) can be regarded as a subspace of the metric space \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\). Then \[
  A \text{ is compact} \iff A \text{ is closed (in $\mathbb {R}^{n}$) and bounded}
\]




Let us try to obtain a compactness criterion for an arbitrary MS. The closedness condition loses its meaning in this case, since every space is closed (in itself). It should be replaced by completeness. In fact, since \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) is complete, a subspace of it is closed if and only if it is complete. Hence, in the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, closedness in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) can be replaced by completeness.
Let us now discuss boundedness. An arbitrary metric space \(X\) is bounded if it lies entirely within some ball of finite radius. Equivalently: an MS is bounded if its diameter is finite:
\[
  \operatorname {diam}X = \sup _{x_1,x_2 \in X} \rho (x_1,x_2) < \infty
\]
It turns out that compactness implies boundedness. However, boundedness (together with completeness) is in general not sufficient for compactness.






ExampleExample 12





Show that the closed unit ball centered at the zero vector (the zero sequence) in \(\ell^2\) is a complete and bounded subspace, but is not compact.
Recall that \(\ell^2\) is the linear space of square-summable sequences \[
  \ell ^2 = \left\{ x = (x_n)_{n \in \mathbb {N}} \;  : \;  x_n \in \mathbb {R}, \;  \sum _{n=1}^{\infty }\left|x_n\right|^2 < \infty \right\}
\] The norm on this space: \(\left\| x\right\|_{2} := \sqrt{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }\left|x_n\right|^2 }\).






SolutionSolution





Denote for brevity \(\bar{B} := \bar{B}_1(0)\).

Note that \(\ell^2 = L^{2}(\mathbb {N}, 2^{\mathbb {N}}, \# )\), where \(\#\) is counting measure. That is, \(\ell^2\) is a special case of a Lebesgue space. For \(L^p\) spaces, it is known that they are complete. Hence \(\ell^2\) is complete.
A closed ball is always a closed set. \(\ell^2\) itself is complete, and, as we know, in a complete space closedness of a subset is equivalent to its completeness. Hence \(\bar{B}\) is a complete subspace.
\(\bar{B}\) is clearly bounded.
Consider the vectors \(e^{(i)} \in \ell^2\), \(i \in \mathbb {N}\): \(e^{(i)}\) has \(1\) in the \(i\)-th position and \(0\) elsewhere. This is a sequence of points from \(\bar{B}\), and the distance between any two of them equals \(\sqrt{2}\). That is, it is impossible to find a convergent subsequence among them. Hence \(\bar{B}\) is not sequentially compact, and therefore not compact.







As the example shows, compactness requires a stronger condition than ordinary boundedness.
By an \(\varepsilon\)-net for a metric space \(X\) we mean a finite collection of open balls \(\left\{ B_{\varepsilon }\left(x_k\right)\right\}_{k=1}^n\) centered at \(x_k \in X\) that covers \(X\). A metric space \(X\) is said to be totally bounded if for every \(\epsilon >0\) there exists an \(\epsilon\)-net for \(X\).
If a metric space \(X\) is totally bounded, then it is bounded in the sense that its diameter is finite. Indeed, if \(X\) is covered by finitely many balls of radius \(r\), then by the triangle inequality \(\operatorname {diam} X \leq c\), where \(c = 2 \cdot r + d\), and \(d\) is the maximum distance between the centers of the covering balls. However, as the following example shows, a bounded metric space need not be totally bounded.






ExampleExample 13





Show that \(\bar{B}_1(0)\) in \(\ell^2\) is not totally bounded.






SolutionSolution





See the example below.













Theorem 3 (Compactness criterion for an MS) Let \(X\) be a metric space. \[
  X \text{ is compact} \iff X \text{ is complete and totally bounded}
\]




In finite-dimensional normed spaces, a bounded set is always totally bounded.







Proposition 8 A subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) is bounded \(\iff\) it is totally bounded.




The difference between the notions shows up in infinite-dimensional normed spaces. As we will prove later, the following theorem holds.







Theorem 4 (Riesz) Let \(X\) be a normed space. Then \[
  \text{The closed unit ball $\bar{B}_1(0)$ is compact} \iff X \text{ is finite-dimensional}
\]

title: Metric spaces: an introduction
text:
5.2 Properties of a compact MS







Proposition 9 (A continuous image of a compact set is compact) Let \(X\) be a compact MS, \(Y\) an arbitrary MS, \(f : X \to Y\) continuous. Then \(f(X)\) is also compact.











Proposition 10 (The Weierstrass theorem on functions on a compact set) Let \(X\) be a compact MS, \(f : X \to \mathbb {R}\). Then \(f\) attains its maximum and minimum.











Proposition 11 (A continuous map on a compact set is uniformly continuous) Let \(X\) be a compact MS, \(Y\) an arbitrary MS, \(f: X \to Y\) continuous. Then \(f\) is uniformly continuous.










ProblemProblem 11





Prove that a compact set cannot be mapped isometrically onto a proper subset of itself.
[@VKK, Problem  3.10]









ExampleExample 14





Let \[
  \bar{B} := \left\{ x = (x_1, x_2, \ldots ) \in \ell ^{2} \quad : \quad \sqrt{\sum _{n = 1}^{\infty } x_{n}^{2}} \leq 1\right\}
\] be the closed unit ball in \(\ell^{2}\). Show that \(\bar{B}\) is not compact,

by showing that \(\bar{B}\) is not sequentially compact,
by showing that \(\bar{B}\) is not compact,
by showing that \(\bar{B}\) is not totally bounded.







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)



Consider the vectors (sequences) \(e^{(n)}\), which have \(1\) in position \(n\) and \(0\) elsewhere. Each \(e^{(n)} \in \bar{B}\), but no subsequence converges in \(\ell^{2}\). Indeed, if one did, it would be a Cauchy sequence. But the distance between any two vectors of the sequence equals \(\sqrt{2}\). That is, no Cauchy subsequence can be found among them. Thus \(\bar{B}\) is not sequentially compact.








Enum-item(2)



We need to find an open cover of \(\bar{B}\) with no finite subcover. Consider the open sets \(U_0 = \ell^2 \setminus \left\{ e^{(n)}\right\}_{n \in \mathbb {N}}\) and \(U_n = B_1\left(e^{(n)}\right)\), \(n \in \mathbb {N}\).

\(U_0\) is open: the set \(\left\{ e^{(n)}\right\}_{n \in \mathbb {N}}\) is closed (even discrete) in \(\ell^2\), since any two of its points are at distance \(\sqrt2\) apart (see part (1)), and hence it has no limit points.
\(\left\{ U_n\right\}_{n \geq 0}\) covers \(\bar B\): the points of \(\bar B \setminus \left\{ e^{(n)}\right\}_n\) lie in \(U_0\), and the point \(e^{(n)}\) itself lies in its own \(U_n\).
It is impossible to choose a finite subcover from this cover. Indeed, \(U_0\) contains none of the points \(e^{(n)}\), and each \(U_n\) contains, among the points \(\left\{ e^{(m)}\right\}_m\), only \(e^{(n)}\) itself (the distance to any other \(e^{(m)}\) equals \(\sqrt2 > 1\)). Hence a finite union \(U_0, U_{n_1}, \ldots , U_{n_k}\) contains, among \(\left\{ e^{(n)}\right\}_n\), only the finite set \(e^{(n_1)}, \ldots , e^{(n_k)}\) and misses infinitely many of the remaining points of this (infinite) set lying in \(\bar B\).









Enum-item(3)



Let \(\varepsilon < \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) be arbitrary. As already shown above, \(\bar{B}\) contains an infinite collection of vectors whose pairwise distances all exceed \(2 \varepsilon\). By the triangle inequality, it is impossible to find a (finite) \(\varepsilon\)-net for \(\bar{B}\).














ProblemProblem 12





Let \(\bar{B} = \{ f \in L^{2}[0, 1] \mid \| f\|_{2} \leq 1\}\) be the closed unit ball in \(L^{2}[0, 1]\). Show that \(B\) is not compact,

by showing that \(\bar{B}\) is not sequentially compact,
by showing that \(\bar{B}\) is not compact,
by showing that \(\bar{B}\) is not totally bounded.

text:
8.1 Corollaries and remarks

It follows from the theorem that if a sequence of functions \((f_n)\) is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous, then a subsequence of it can be extracted that converges uniformly on \([0,1]\).
The statement and proof carry over to the space of continuous functions with the metric topology of a compact metric space in place of \([0,1]\).







ProblemProblem 20





Let \(X = \ell^2\), and let \(M \subset \ell^2\) be a subspace. Prove that \[
  M \text{ is compact} \iff \begin{cases}  M \text{ is closed} \\ M \text{ is bounded} \\ \forall \varepsilon > 0 \quad \exists n \quad \forall x \in M \quad \sum _{k = n}^{\infty }\left|x_{k}\right|^{2} < \varepsilon \end{cases}
\]
[@VKK, Problem  3.11]

title: Banach spaces
text:
1.1 Vector spaces and subspaces
\(\mathbb {F}\) denotes either \(\mathbb {R}\) or \(\mathbb {C}\).
A vector space \(V\) over a field \(\mathbb {F}\) is …
Recall that a subset \(U\) of a vector space \(V\) is a subspace of \(V\) if and only if \(U\) satisfies the following three conditions:

zero element: \(0 \in U\);
closure under addition: \(f, g \in U \implies f+g \in U\);
closure under scalar multiplication: \(\alpha \in \mathbb {F}, f \in U \implies \alpha f \in U\).

These three conditions usually allow one to quickly determine whether a given subset of \(V\) is a subspace of \(V\), as illustrated below. All the examples below except the first item are related to the notion of measure.

title: Banach spaces
text:
2.1 Norms and complete norms
Let \(V\) be a vector space over a field \(\mathbb {F}\) (\(\mathbb {F} = \mathbb {R}\) or \(\mathbb {C}\)). A function \(\left\| \cdot \right\| : V \to [0, +\infty )\) is called a norm if it is positive definite, absolutely homogeneous, and subadditive (i.e., it satisfies the triangle inequality; see the detailed definition above). A vector space \(V\) equipped with a norm is called a normed space (NS).






ExampleExample 1





Determine whether the following functions are norms on the corresponding vector spaces.

\(\left\| \cdot \right\|_1\) and \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{\infty }\) on \(\mathbb {F}^n\);
\(\left\| \cdot \right\|_1\) on \(\ell^1\);
Let \(X \neq \varnothing\). Let \(b(X)\) be the set of bounded functions on \(X\). For \(f \in b(X)\) define

\[
  \left\| f\right\|  := \sup _{x \in X}\left|f(x)\right|
\]

On \(C[0,1]\) define

\[
  \left\| f\right\|  = \int _0^1 \left|f\right|
\]

\(\left\| \cdot \right\|_1\) on \(\mathcal{L}^1(\mathbb {R})\): homogeneity and the triangle inequality hold, but positive definiteness fails;
\(\sqrt{\left|x_1\right|} + \ldots + \sqrt{\left|x_n\right|}\) on \(\mathbb {F}^n\): positive definiteness and the triangle inequality hold, but homogeneity fails;
\(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{1/2}\) on \(\mathbb {F}^n\): homogeneity and positive definiteness hold, but the triangle inequality fails.







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)



Both are norms: positive definiteness and homogeneity are obvious from the corresponding properties of \(\left|\cdot \right|\) on \(\mathbb F\); the triangle inequality for \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_1\) and \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_\infty\) follows coordinatewise from \(\left|x_i+y_i\right| \leq \left|x_i\right|+\left|y_i\right|\) (by summing or taking the maximum over \(i\)).








Enum-item(2)



A norm: the same three axioms as in (1), only with an infinite sum instead of a finite one; the series \(\sum \left|x_i+y_i\right|\) converges and is dominated termwise by \(\sum \left|x_i\right|+\sum \left|y_i\right|\).








Enum-item(3)



A norm: \(\left\| f\right\| =0 \iff \sup_X\left|f\right| = 0 \iff f\equiv 0\); homogeneity and the triangle inequality are as for \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_\infty\), except that the \(\sup\) is taken over all of \(X\) rather than over a finite set of indices.








Enum-item(4)



A norm (it is important that we consider exactly \(C[0,1]\), not arbitrary measurable functions): homogeneity and the triangle inequality follow from monotonicity and linearity of the integral: \(\int_0^1\left|f+g\right| \leq \int_0^1(\left|f\right|+\left|g\right|)\). Positive definiteness: if \(\int_0^1\left|f\right| = 0\) for a continuous \(f\geq 0\), then \(f\equiv 0\) (otherwise \(f(x_0)>0\) at some point, and by continuity \(f>c>0\) on an entire interval around \(x_0\), whence \(\int_0^1\left|f\right| \geq c\cdot (\text{length of the interval})>0\) — a contradiction).


As parts (5)–(7) below show (stated directly in the problem): without continuity (5) or when \(p<1\) (7), positive definiteness and the triangle inequality are no longer automatic, and with an exponent \(<1\) in the definition of homogeneity (6), homogeneity itself breaks down.






Every normed space is a metric space: a norm naturally induces a metric. A Banach space is a normed space that is complete with respect to the metric induced by the norm.






ExampleExample 2





Determine whether the following normed spaces are Banach spaces.

\(C[0,1]\) with \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{\infty }\);
\(\ell^1\) with \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{1}\);
\(C[0,1]\) with \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_1\);
\(\ell^1\) with \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{\infty }\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)



Yes, it is Banach. Let \((f_n)\) be a Cauchy sequence in \((C[0,1],\left\| \cdot \right\|_{\infty })\). For each \(x\in [0,1]\) the numerical sequence \((f_n(x))\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(\mathbb F\) (since \(\left|f_n(x)-f_m(x)\right|\leq \left\| f_n-f_m\right\|_{\infty }\)), hence it converges; denote the limit by \(f(x)\). From the Cauchy condition, for every \(\varepsilon >0\) there is \(N\) such that for \(n,m\geq N\) and all \(x\) we have \(\left|f_n(x)-f_m(x)\right|<\varepsilon\); letting \(m\to \infty\), we get \(\left|f_n(x)-f(x)\right|\leq \varepsilon\) for all \(n\geq N\) and all \(x\), i.e., \(f_n\to f\) uniformly. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, so \(f\in C[0,1]\), and \(\left\| f_n-f\right\|_{\infty }\to 0\).








Enum-item(2)



Let \((a^{n})_{n\in \mathbb {N}}\) be a Cauchy sequence in \((\ell^1,\left\| \cdot \right\|_{1})\). Then for every \(\varepsilon >0\) there is \(N\) such that for all \(m,n\ge N\)
\[
  \sum _{i=1}^{\infty }\left|a^n_i - a^m_i\right| < \varepsilon .
\]
In particular, for each fixed \(j\) we have \(\left|a^n_j - a^m_j\right| \le \sum_{i=1}^{\infty }\left|a^n_i - a^m_i\right| < \varepsilon\), so for each \(j\) the sequence \((a^n_j)_{n}\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(\mathbb {F}\) and therefore converges; denote \(a_j = \lim_{n\to \infty } a^n_j\). This gives a limiting sequence \(a=(a_1,a_2,\dots )\). It remains to show that \(a\in \ell^1\) and \(a^n\to a\) in the norm \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{1}\) — this is done by the standard trick of estimating the tail of the sums and passing to the limit inside the sum (using the triangle inequality and the fact that the sums \(\sum_{i=1}^N |a^n_i-a_i|\) are small for large \(n\), while the tail \(\sum_{i>N}|a_i|\) is small for large \(N\)).








Enum-item(3)



No, it is not Banach. Let us exhibit a sequence of continuous functions that is Cauchy in the norm \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_1\) but does not converge (in this norm) to any continuous function. Let
\[
  f_n(x) = \begin{cases}  0, &  x \in [0, \tfrac 12-\tfrac 1n], \\ n\left(x - \tfrac 12 + \tfrac 1n\right), &  x \in \left(\tfrac 12-\tfrac 1n, \tfrac 12\right), \\ 1, &  x \in [\tfrac 12, 1]. \end{cases}
\]
Then \(f_n \in C[0,1]\), and with \(g := \; \mathbb {1}_{[1/2,1]}\) (discontinuous at \(\tfrac 12\)) we have \(f_n = g\) outside the interval \(\left(\tfrac 12-\tfrac 1n,\tfrac 12\right)\) of length \(\tfrac 1n\), while on it \(\left|f_n - g\right|\leq 1\), so that
\[
  \left\| f_n - g\right\| _1 = \int _0^1 \left|f_n - g\right| \leq \frac1n \xrightarrow [n\to \infty ]{} 0.
\]
In particular, \((f_n)\) is Cauchy in \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_1\) (since it converges to \(g\) in this seminorm). If \(f_n \to h\) in \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_1\) for some \(h \in C[0,1]\), then \(h=g\) almost everywhere (the limit in \(L^1\) is unique up to a.e.-equivalence); but no continuous function can agree a.e. with \(g\), which has a jump at \(\tfrac 12\) (a continuous \(h\) agreeing with \(g\) on a dense set on both sides of \(\tfrac 12\) would have to satisfy \(h(\tfrac 12^-)=0\) and \(h(\tfrac 12^+)=1\) — a contradiction with continuity at \(\tfrac 12\)). Hence there is no limit in \(C[0,1]\), and the space \((C[0,1],\left\| \cdot \right\|_1)\) is not complete.








Enum-item(4)



Consider the sequence
\[
  a^n = \bigl(1,\tfrac {1}{2},\ldots ,\tfrac {1}{n}, 0, 0, \ldots \bigr), \qquad n \in \mathbb {N}.
\]
In the norm \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{\infty }\) this sequence is Cauchy (the truncations of the sequence become close in the supremum norm), but its limit in \(\ell^1\) with this norm would have to be the sequence \((1,\tfrac 12,\tfrac 13,\ldots )\), whose supremum is \(1\) and which does not belong to \(\ell^1\) in the sense of the sum of absolute values — however, what matters here is that there is no limit lying in \(\ell^1\) (the sequence does not converge in \((\ell^1,\left\| \cdot \right\|_{\infty })\)). Hence the space is not complete.














ExampleExample 3





Let \(X\) be a nonempty set, and let \(b(X)\) be the vector space of bounded functions \(X \to \mathbb {F}\). Prove that if \(b(X)\) is equipped with the norm \(\left\| f\right\|  = \sup_X \left|f\right|\), then \(b(X)\) is a Banach space.






SolutionSolution





Let \((f_n)\) be a Cauchy sequence in \((b(X),\left\| \cdot \right\| )\). Then for each \(x\in X\) the sequence of numbers \((f_n(x))\) is Cauchy in \(\mathbb {F}\), hence converges to some \(f(x)\in \mathbb {F}\). This defines a function \(f:X\to \mathbb {F}\). We need to show that \(f\) is bounded and \(f_n \to f\) in the supremum norm. From the Cauchy condition there is \(N\) such that for all \(m,n\ge N\) we have \(\sup_X|f_n - f_m|<\varepsilon\), whence for \(n\ge N\) letting \(m\to\infty\) gives \(\sup_X|f_n - f| \le \varepsilon\). Hence \(f\) is bounded and \(f_n \to f\) in norm, and the space is complete.







2.1.1 Banachness \(\iff\) every absolutely convergent series of vectors converges (in the norm of the space)
An infinite sum of vectors in a normed space:
\[
  \sum _{k=1}^{\infty }v_k := \lim _{n \to \infty }\sum _{k=1}^{n}v_k
\]
We will call a sequence \(v_1, v_2, \ldots \in V\) a rapid Cauchy sequence if
\[
  \sum _{n=1}^{\infty }\left\| v_{n+1} - v_{n}\right\|  < \infty .
\]
Every rapid Cauchy sequence is a Cauchy sequence in the usual sense. Indeed, if
\[
  \sum _{n=1}^{\infty }\left\| v_{n+1} - v_{n}\right\|  < \infty ,
\]
then for any \(m > n\) we have
\[
  \left\| v_m - v_n\right\|  \leq \sum _{k=n}^{m-1}\left\| v_{k+1} - v_k\right\|  \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} 0,
\]
which is exactly the definition of a Cauchy sequence.







Proposition 1 (Equivalent conditions for completeness of a normed space, i.e., for being Banach) Let \(V\) be a normed space. The following conditions are equivalent:

Every Cauchy sequence in \(V\) converges to an element of \(V\) (i.e., \(V\) is a Banach space);
Every rapid Cauchy sequence in \(V\) converges to an element of \(V\);
Absolute convergence of an arbitrary series implies its convergence in norm:
\[
  \sum _{k=1}^{\infty } \left\| v_k\right\|  < \infty \; \;  \Rightarrow \; \;  \sum _{k=1}^{\infty }v_k \text{ converges in } V.
\]











ProblemProblem 1





Prove that a normed space is complete \(\Longleftrightarrow\) every absolutely convergent series in it converges.
[@VKK, Problem  4.1]

title: Banach spaces

2.2 Bounded linear maps
Let \(V\), \(W\) be vector spaces over the same field \(\mathbb {F}\). A map \(T: V \to W\) is called linear if …
The set \(\mathcal{L}(V,W)\) is also a vector space. Now suppose \(V\) and \(W\) are equipped with norms (which may differ, but we will denote them the same way). We will focus on the subset \(\mathcal{B}(V,W)\) of bounded linear maps. Namely, for a linear map \(T: V \to W\) define
\[
  \left\| T\right\|  := \sup _{f \in V, \left\| f\right\|  \leq 1}\left\| Tf\right\|
\]







Lemma 1 (Equivalent definitions of the norm of a linear map) Let \(V\) and \(W\) be normed vector spaces, with \(V\neq \{ 0\}\), and let \(T:V\to W\) be a linear operator. Then \[
\begin{align}  \left\| T\right\|  & = \sup _{f \in V, \left\| f\right\|  \leq 1}\left\| Tf\right\|  =\sup _{f \in V, \left\| f\right\|  < 1}\left\| Tf\right\|  = \sup _{f \in V, \left\| f\right\|  = 1}\left\| Tf\right\|  = \sup _{f \in V\setminus \left\{ 0_V\right\} }\frac{\left\| Tf\right\| }{\left\| f\right\| } = \\ & = \inf \left\{ c\in [0,\infty ): \left\| Tf\right\| \le c\left\| f\right\| \  \forall f\in V\right\}  \end{align}
\]




A map is called bounded if \(\left\| T\right\|  < \infty\).
\[
  \mathcal{B}(V,W) = \left\{ T \in \mathcal{L}(V,W) \;  : \;  \left\| T\right\|  < \infty \right\}
\]
One can check that \(\mathcal{B}(V,W)\) is also a normed space.






ExampleExample 4






Let \(V = W = C[0,3]\), and let \((Tf)(x) := x^2f(x)\). Verify that \(T\) is linear. Find \(\left\| T\right\|\). Is \(T\) bounded?
Let \(V = W = c_{00}\) with the norm from \(\ell^{\infty }\), and let
\[
  T(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots ) := (a_1, 2a_2, 3a_3, \ldots )
\]
Verify that \(T\) is linear. Find \(\left\| T\right\|\). Is \(T\) bounded?







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Let \(V = W = C[0,3]\) with the standard supremum norm \(\left\| f\right\| =\sup_{x\in [0,3]}|f(x)|\), and let
\[
  Tf(x):=x^2 f(x).
\]
Let us check linearity. For any \(f,g\in C[0,3]\) and scalars \(\alpha ,\beta\) we have
\[
  T(\alpha f+\beta g)(x)=x^2(\alpha f(x)+\beta g(x))=\alpha x^2 f(x)+\beta x^2 g(x)=\alpha Tf(x)+\beta Tg(x),
\]
so the operator \(T\) is linear.
Let us find the norm of the operator. For any \(f\) with \(\left\| f\right\| =1\) we have
\[
  \left\| Tf\right\| =\sup _{x\in [0,3]}|x^2 f(x)|\leq \sup _{x\in [0,3]}x^2\cdot \sup _{x\in [0,3]}|f(x)|=9\cdot 1=9.
\]
On the other hand, taking a function \(f_0\) such that \(f_0(3)=1\) and \(\left\| f_0\right\| =1\) (for example, the constant function \(f_0\equiv 1\)), we get
\[
  \left\| T f_0\right\| =\sup _{x\in [0,3]} x^2 |f_0(x)| \ge 3^2\cdot |f_0(3)|=9.
\]
Hence \(\left\| T\right\| =9\). So \(T\) is bounded (and boundedness is expressed by the inequality \(\left\| Tf\right\| \le 9\left\| f\right\|\)).








Enum-item2.



Let \(V = W = c_{00}\), with the norm induced by the \(\ell^\infty\)-norm, and let
\[
  T(a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots ):=(1\cdot a_1,\, 2\cdot a_2,\, 3\cdot a_3,\ldots ).
\]
Linearity is obvious, since \(T\) acts coordinatewise via the formula \(T(a)_n = n a_n\).
Let us consider boundedness. If \(T\) were bounded, there would exist \(C>0\) such that for all \(a\in c_{00}\)
\[
  \left\| T a\right\| _{\infty }=\sup _{n\ge 1} n|a_n| \le C\sup _{n\ge 1}|a_n|=\; C\left\| a\right\| _{\infty }.
\]
Take the standard vectors \(e^{(N)}=(0,\dots ,0,1,0,\dots )\), where the \(1\) stands in the \(N\)-th position. Then \(\left\| e^{(N)}\right\|_{\infty }=1\), but
\[
  \left\| T e^{(N)}\right\| _{\infty }=\sup _{n} n|e^{(N)}_n| = N.
\]
If the inequality held with some constant \(C\), then \(N\le C\) for all \(N\), which is impossible. Hence no finite \(C\) exists, and \(T\) is not bounded (the operator norm would be \(\sup_{n} n = +\infty\)).
Thus, in the first part \(T\) is linear and bounded, \(\left\| T\right\| =9\); in the second part \(T\) is linear but not bounded.











AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



Yes. \(\left\| T\right\|  = 9\);








Enum-item2.



No.















Proposition 2 (\(W\) Banach \(\;  \Rightarrow \;\) \(\mathcal{B}(V, W)\) Banach) Let \(V\) be a normed space, \(W\) a Banach space. Then \(\mathcal{B}(V, W)\) is a Banach space with the norm defined above.




Note that \(V\) itself need not be Banach.







Proposition 3 Let \(V\) and \(W\) be normed vector spaces and \(T:V\to W\) a linear map. The following statements are equivalent:

\(T\) is bounded.
\(T\) is continuous.
\(T\) is continuous at some single point: there exists \(f_0\in V\) such that \(T\) is continuous at \(f_0\).
\(T\) is uniformly continuous (i.e., for every \(\varepsilon >0\) there exists \(\delta >0\) such that \(\left\| Tf - Tg\right\|  < \varepsilon\) for all \(f,g\in V\) with \(\left\| f-g\right\| <\delta\)).
The preimage of some open ball around the zero vector is open: there exists \(r > 0\) such that \(T^{-1}\left(B_{r}(0_W)\right)\) is an open subset of \(V\).





If \(W = V\), then a linear map \(T: V\to V\) is called an operator. The set of all operators is denoted \(\mathcal{L}(V)\). The set of all bounded operators on \(V\) is denoted \(\mathcal{B}(V)\).

title: Banach spaces
text:
4.1 Bounded linear functionals
Linear maps into the scalar field \(\mathbb {F}\) (\(\mathbb {F}=\mathbb {R}\) or \(\mathbb {F} = \mathbb {C}\)) are so important that they receive a special name. A linear functional on a vector space \(V\) is a linear map from \(V\) into \(\mathbb {F}\).
When we regard the scalar field \(\mathbb {F}\) as a normed vector space, the norm \(\| z\|\) of a number \(z \in F\) is understood as the ordinary absolute value \(|z|\). This norm makes \(\mathbb {F}\) a Banach space.






ExampleExample 5





Let \(V = c_{00}\) be the space of sequences \((a_1, a_2, \ldots )\) of elements of \(\mathbb {F}\) such that \(a_k = 0\) for all but finitely many \(k \in \mathbb {Z}^+\). Define \(\varphi : c_{00} \to \mathbb {F}\) by \[
  \varphi (a_1, a_2, \ldots ) = \sum _{k=1}^{\infty } a_k.
\] Then \(\varphi\) is clearly a linear functional on \(V\). Prove that

if \(c_{00}\) is equipped with the norm \(\| (a_1, a_2, \ldots )\|_1 = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty }|a_k|\), then \(\varphi\) is a bounded linear functional.
if \(c_{00}\) is equipped with the norm \(\| (a_1, a_2, \ldots )\|_{\infty } = \max_{k \in \mathbb {Z}^+}|a_k|\), then \(\varphi\) is not a bounded linear functional.







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



We have
\[
  \left\| \varphi (a)\right\|  = \left|\sum _{k=1}^{\infty }a_k\right| \leq \sum _{k=1}^{\infty }\left|a_k\right| = \left\| a\right\| _{1}
\]








Enum-item2.



Consider \(a^{(n)} = (1,1,1,\ldots , 1, 0, 0, \ldots )\) (the first \(n\) places are \(1\), the rest are \(0\)). \(\left\| a^{(n)}\right\|_{\infty } = 1\), while
\[
  \left\| \varphi \left(a^{(n)}\right)\right\|  = \left|\sum _{k=1}^{\infty } a^{(n)}_k\right| = \left|n\right| \to \infty
\]








Let \(V\) and \(W\) be vector spaces and \(T: V \to W\) a linear map. The kernel (null space) of \(T\) is the set
\[
  \text{null } T = \{  f \in V : Tf = 0 \} .
\]
The kernel of a linear map is a subspace. If \(T\) is a continuous linear map between normed spaces, then \(\text{null } T\) is closed, being the preimage of the closed set \(\{ 0\}\).
The converse is false for general linear maps: a linear map can have closed kernel without being continuous. For linear functionals, however, this is equivalent.







Theorem 1 (Equivalence of boundedness, continuity, and a closed kernel) Let \(V\) be a normed vector space and \(\varphi : V \to \mathbb {F}\) a linear functional not identically zero. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

\(\varphi\) is a bounded linear functional.
\(\varphi\) is a continuous linear functional.
\(\operatorname {null}\varphi\) is a closed subspace of \(V\).
\(\overline{\operatorname {null}\varphi } \neq V\).

title: Banach spaces
text:
4.2 Discontinuous linear functionals
We have already seen discontinuous linear functionals. The main goal of this section is to show that every infinite-dimensional normed vector space has a discontinuous linear functional.
Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a collection of subsets of a set \(V\). A set \(\Gamma \in \mathcal{A}\) is called a maximal element of \(\mathcal{A}\) if there is no \(\Gamma ' \in \mathcal{A}\) such that \(\Gamma \subsetneq \Gamma '\).







Theorem 2 A subset of a vector space \(V\) is a Hamel basis of \(V\) if and only if it is a maximal element in the collection of all linearly independent subsets of \(V\).




A collection \(C\) of subsets of a set \(V\) is called a chain if \(\Omega , \Gamma \in C\) implies \(\Omega \subseteq \Gamma\) or \(\Gamma \subseteq \Omega\).







Lemma 2 (Zorn’s lemma, simplified version) Let \(V\) be a set and \(\mathcal{A}\) a collection of subsets of \(V\) with the property that the union of all sets in \(C\) belongs to \(\mathcal{A}\) for every chain \(C \subseteq \mathcal{A}\). Then \(\mathcal{A}\) contains a maximal element.











Theorem 3 Every vector space has a Hamel basis.




This theorem only asserts existence of a basis. No one has ever managed to construct an explicit example of a Hamel basis in an infinite-dimensional Banach space.







Theorem 4 Every infinite-dimensional normed vector space has a discontinuous linear functional.










Mn-proofProof






Take a Hamel basis \(\left\{ e_k\right\}_{k \in \Gamma }\) for \(V\). It is infinite, so we may assume \(\mathbb {N} \subset \Gamma\). Define \(\varphi\) as follows: \(\varphi (e_k) := k \left\| e_k\right\|\), where \(k \in \mathbb {N}\). On the remaining basis vectors, let the functional be zero. In other words, if \(f \in V\) is arbitrary, it can be uniquely decomposed as \(f = \sum_{k \in \Gamma '}\alpha_{k}e_k\), where \(\Gamma '\) is a finite subset of \(\Gamma\). Then
\[
  \varphi (f) := \sum _{k \in \Gamma ' \cap \mathbb {N}} k\cdot \left\| e_k\right\|
\]
\(\varphi\) is linear and discontinuous.

ExampleExample 6





Let \(n \in \mathbb {N}\), \(V\) a normed vector space. Prove that any linear operator from \(\mathbb {F}^{n}\) with the maximum norm \(\left\| x\right\|_{\infty } := \max_{i}\left|x_i\right|\) into \(V\) is continuous.






SolutionSolution





Let \(T: \mathbb {F}^n \to V\) be a linear map. Let us show it is bounded. Let \(\overrightarrow {e}_1, \ldots , \overrightarrow {e}_n\) be the standard basis in \(\mathbb {F}^n\). For any \(\overrightarrow {x} = (x_1, \ldots , x_n) \in \mathbb {F}^n\) we have: \[
\begin{align}  T\overrightarrow {x} & = x_1T\overrightarrow {e}_1 + \ldots + x_nT\overrightarrow {e}_n, \\ \left\| T\overrightarrow {x}\right\|  & \leq \left|x_1\right| \cdot \left\| T\overrightarrow {e}_1\right\|  + \ldots + \left|x_n\right| \cdot \left\| T\overrightarrow {e}_n\right\|  \leq n \cdot \max _i\left\| T\overrightarrow {e}_i\right\|  \cdot \left\| \overrightarrow {x}\right\| _{\infty }. \end{align}
\] Hence, \[
  \left\| T\right\|  \leq n \cdot \max _{i \in \left\{ 1, \ldots , n\right\} }\left\| T\overrightarrow {e}_i\right\|  < \infty
\]

title: Banach spaces
text:
4.3 The Hahn-Banach theorem
In the previous section we proved that every infinite-dimensional normed space has a discontinuous linear functional. But what about continuous ones? The existence of nonzero continuous linear functionals on an arbitrary normed space is nontrivial. The Hahn-Banach theorem guarantees that a bounded linear functional defined on a subspace of a normed space (a finite-dimensional one, say) can be extended to the whole space without increasing its norm.
For example, the quotient space \(\ell^{\infty } / c_{0}\) is an infinite-dimensional Banach space. Yet no one has managed to exhibit an explicit example of a continuous linear functional on it.
In this section we will not need Banachness.







Lemma 3 (Extension lemma (real case)) Let \(V\) be a real normed space, \(U\) a subspace, \(\psi : U \to \mathbb {R}\) a bounded linear functional, and \(h \in V \setminus U\). Then \(\psi\) can be extended to a bounded linear functional \(\varphi : U + \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {R}\) such that \(\| \varphi \|  = \| \psi \|\).











Theorem 5 (Hahn-Banach) Let \(V\) be a normed vector space, \(U\) a subspace, \(\psi : U \to \mathbb {F}\) a bounded linear functional. Then \(\psi\) can be extended to a bounded linear functional \(\varphi\) on all of \(V\) such that \(\| \varphi \|  = \| \psi \|\).




Idea of proof for the real case: using Zorn’s lemma we extend the functional step by step, preserving the norm. For the complex case, one passes to the real part of the functional.

4.3.1 Consequences of the Hahn-Banach theorem
The Hahn–Banach theorem points to an important principle in functional analysis: to understand a space, one needs to understand its continuous functionals.
The dual space of a normed space \(V\) is the space \(V' = \mathcal{B}(V, \mathbb {F})\) of all bounded linear functionals on \(V\). This is a Banach space, since the target \(\mathbb {F}\) is Banach (recall that Banachness of \(W\) suffices for Banachness of \(\mathcal{B}(V,W)\)).






ExampleExample 7





Prove that

for any nonzero fixed vector \(f\) of a normed space \(V\) there exists a functional \(\varphi = \varphi_{f} \in V'\) such that \(\| \varphi_{f}\|  = 1\) and \(\varphi_{f}(f) = \| f\|\);
the norm of a vector can be found as the maximum over the values of all bounded linear functionals at it:
\[
  \left\| f\right\|  = \max _{\substack {\varphi \in V’ \\ \left\| \varphi \right\|  = 1}}\left|\varphi (f)\right|
\]







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Note that the functional \(\psi (g) := \left\| g\right\|\) does not work, since it is not linear: \(\psi (\alpha f) = \left|\alpha \right| \cdot f \neq \alpha \cdot f\).
Consider the one-dimensional subspace \(U = \operatorname {span}(f) = \left\{ \alpha f \;  : \;  \alpha \in \mathbb {F}\right\}\). Define on it the functional \(\psi (\alpha f) := \alpha \cdot \left\| f\right\|\). It is linear on \(U\), and
\[
  \left\| \psi \right\|  = \sup _{\left\| \alpha f\right\|  = 1}\left|\psi (\alpha f)\right| = \sup _{\left\| \alpha f\right\|  = 1}\left|\alpha \cdot \left\| f\right\| \right| = \sup _{\left\| \alpha f\right\|  = 1}\left|\alpha \right| \cdot \left\| f\right\|  = \sup _{\left\| \alpha f\right\|  = 1}\left\| \alpha f\right\|  = 1
\]
Hence \(\psi\) is bounded on \(U\). By the Hahn-Banach theorem, there is a linear functional \(\varphi\) on \(V\) with the same norm, extending \(\psi\), i.e., agreeing with it on \(\operatorname {span}(f)\).








Enum-item2.



Using the previous part, we immediately get one inequality:
\[
  \left\| f\right\|  = \varphi _f(f) = \left|\varphi _f(f)\right| \leq \max _{\substack {\varphi \in V’ \\ \left\| \varphi \right\|  = 1}}\left|\varphi (f)\right|
\]
The reverse inequality: if \(\varphi \in V'\), \(\left\| \varphi \right\|  = 1\), then by definition \(\left|\varphi (f)\right| \leq \left\| \varphi \right\|  \cdot \left\| f\right\|  = \left\| f\right\|\). Hence,
\[
  \left\| f\right\|  \geq \max _{\substack {\varphi \in V’ \\ \left\| \varphi \right\|  = 1}}\left|\varphi (f)\right|
\]














ExampleExample 8 - Criterion for membership in the closure of a subspace





Let \(U\) be a subspace of a normed space \(V\), \(h \in V\). Then \(f\) belongs to the closure of the subspace \(U\) if and only if every bounded linear functional vanishing on \(U\) also vanishes at \(f\). In other words, \[
  f \in \overline{U} \quad \iff \quad \varphi (f) = 0 \text{ for every } \varphi \in V' \text{ such that } \varphi |_{U} \equiv 0
\]






SolutionSolution






\(\stackrel{?}{\;  \Rightarrow \; }\). Consider an arbitrary \(\varphi \in V'\) such that \(\varphi |_{U} \equiv 0\). Let us prove that \(\varphi (f) = 0\). It is known that \(f \in \overline{U}\). Hence there is a sequence of vectors \(f_1, f_2, \ldots\) in \(U\) converging to \(f\). But \(\varphi (f_n) =0\) for all \(n\) and \(\varphi\) is continuous. Hence \(\varphi (f) = 0\).
\(\stackrel{?}{\Leftarrow }\). We need to prove that \(f \in \overline{U}\). Suppose this is not the case. Define \(\psi\) on the subspace \(\operatorname {span}(U, f) = U + \mathbb {F} f\) by
\[
  \psi (g+\alpha f) = \alpha
\]
for \(g \in U\) and \(\alpha \in \mathbb {F}\). Then \(\psi\) is a linear functional on \(U+\mathbb {F} h\), which vanishes on \(U\) and \(\psi (f) = 1\).
Since \(h \notin \overline{U}\), the closure of the kernel of \(\psi\) is not \(U+\mathbb {F} h\). Thus, by the theorem above, \(\psi\) is a bounded linear functional on \(U+\mathbb {F} h\).
By the Hahn-Banach theorem, \(\psi\) can be extended to a bounded linear functional \(\varphi\) on \(V\). Thus, we have found \(\varphi \in V^{\prime }\) such that \(\left.\varphi \right|_U=0\), but \(\varphi (f) \neq 0\). Contradiction.







Let \(1 \leq p \leq +\infty\). The conjugate index to \(p\) is the index \(q\) such that
\[
  \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q} = 1
\]
It is easy to show that \(1 \leq q \leq +\infty\).
Consider the space \(\left(\mathbb {R}^{n}, \left\| \cdot \right\|_{p}\right)\), \(1 \leq p \leq +\infty\). We have already proved that it is necessarily Banach. What does its dual space look like? The following statement will be proved in greater generality a bit later.







Lemma 4 If \(V = \left(\mathbb {R}^{n}, \left\| \cdot \right\|_{p}\right)\), then \(V' \cong \left(\mathbb {R}^{n}, \left\| \cdot \right\|_{q}\right)\) in the sense that any bounded functional \(\varphi\) on \(\left(\mathbb {R}^{n}, \left\| \cdot \right\|_{p}\right)\) has the form \[
  \varphi (x) = \left\langle x, a \right\rangle = x_1a_1 + \ldots + x_na_n, \quad x \in \mathbb {R}^{n}
\] for some \(a = (a_1, \ldots , a_{n}) \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\), with \(\left\| \varphi \right\|  = \left\| a\right\|_{q}\).










ExampleExample 9





The functional \(\psi\) on the subspace \(U = \left\{ \left(x_{1}, 0\right) \mid x_{1} \in \mathbb {R}\right\}\) of the space \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\) is defined by \(\psi (x) = \alpha x_{1}, x = \left(x_{1}, 0\right) \in U\), where \(\alpha \in \mathbb {R}\) is fixed.

Describe all linear extensions \(\varphi\) of the functional \(\psi\) to \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\).
For which of these extensions is \(\| \varphi \|  = \| \psi \|\), if \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\) is equipped with the norm \(\| \cdot \|_{p}, 1 \leq p \leq +\infty\)? In which cases is the norm-preserving extension unique?







SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Every linear functional on \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\) has the form
\[
  \varphi (x) = a_{1} x_{1}+a_{2} x_{2}, x = \left(x_{1}, x_{2}\right) \in \mathbb {R}^{2},
\]
where \(a_{1}, a_{2} \in \mathbb {R}\) are fixed numbers (different for different functionals \(\varphi\)). If \(\varphi\) is an extension of \(\psi\), then \(\varphi \left(\left(x_{1}, 0\right)\right) = \psi \left(\left(x_{1}, 0\right)\right), \quad \left(x_{1}, 0\right) \in U\), i.e., \(a_{1} x_{1} = \alpha x_{1}, x_{1} \in \mathbb {R}\). Hence any extension \(\varphi\) to \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\) has the form \(\varphi (x) = \alpha x_{1}+ a_{2} x_{2}, x = \left(x_{1}, x_{2}\right) \in \mathbb {R}^{2}\), where \(a_{2} \in \mathbb {R}\) is an arbitrary number.








Enum-item2.



Let us find the norm of \(\varphi\). By the lemma above,
\[
  \left\| \varphi \right\|  = \left\| (\alpha , a_{2})\right\| _{q} = \begin{cases}  \left|\alpha \right| + \left|a_{2}\right|, &  q = 1 \text{ (equivalently: $p = +\infty $),} \\[6pt] \left( \left|\alpha \right|^{q} + \left|a_{2}\right|^{q} \right)^{1/q}, &  1 < q < +\infty \text{ (equivalently: $1 < p < +\infty $),} \\[6pt] \max \left\{ \left|\alpha \right|, \left|a_{2}\right|\right\} , &  q = +\infty \text{ (equivalently: $p = 1$)} \end{cases}
\]
Let us find \(\| \psi \|\). We have
\[
  \| \psi \|  = \sup _{\left(x_{1}, 0\right) \in U \backslash \left\{ 0\right\} } \frac{\left|\psi \left(\left(x_{1}, 0\right)\right)\right|}{\left\| \left(x_{1}, 0\right)\right\| _{p}} = \sup _{x_{1} \neq 0} \frac{\left|\alpha x_{1}\right|}{\left|x_{1}\right|} = |\alpha | .
\]
Now for each \(1 \leq p \leq +\infty\) let us determine when \(\| \varphi \|  = \| \psi \|\) and when such an extension is unique.
If \(p = 1\), then \(\| \varphi \|  = \| \psi \|\) if and only if \(\max \left\{ |\alpha |,\left|a_{2}\right|\right\}  = |\alpha |\). Hence the norm-preserving extension \(\varphi\) of \(\psi\) has the form
\[
  \varphi (x) = \alpha x_{1}+a_{2} x_{2}, x = \left(x_{1}, x_{2}\right) \in \mathbb {R}^{2}
\]
where \(a_{2} \in [-|\alpha |,|\alpha |]\) is an arbitrary number. Such an extension is unique if and only if \(\alpha = 0\).
If \(1 < p \leq +\infty\), then \(1 \leq q < +\infty\), and \(\| \varphi \|  = \| \psi \|\) if and only if \(|\alpha |^{q}+\left|a_{2}\right|^{q} = |\alpha |^{q}\), hence \(a_{2} = 0\). Hence the norm-preserving extension of \(\psi\) is unique and has the form \(\varphi (x) = \alpha x_{1}, x = \left(x_{1}, x_{2}\right) \in \mathbb {R}^{2}\).














ProblemProblem 14





Let \(\alpha > 0\) be given, \(U = \left\{ \left(x_{1}, x_{1}\right) \mid x_{1} \in \mathbb {R}\right\}  \subset \mathbb {R}^{2}\), \(\psi (x) = \alpha x_{1}, x \in U\).

Describe all linear extensions \(\varphi\) of the functional \(\psi\) to \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\).
For which of these extensions is \(\| \varphi \|  = \| \psi \|\), if \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\) is equipped with the norm \(\| \cdot \|_{p}, \quad 1 \leq p \leq +\infty\)?
In which cases is the norm-preserving extension unique? Investigate the question for all norms \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{p}\), \(1 \leq p \leq +\infty\).










ProblemProblem 15





Let \(V = \ell^{1}\), let \[
  M = \left\{ x \in \ell ^{1}: \sum _{n = 1}^{\infty } x_{2 n} = 0\right\} ,
\] and let the functional \(\psi\) on the subspace \(M\) be given by \(\psi (x) = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty } x_{2 n-1}\). Give examples of different norm-preserving extensions of \(\psi\) to a functional \(\varphi \in V'\).
[@VKK, Problem  9.8]









ProblemProblem 16





Show that there exists a linear functional \(\varphi : \ell^{\infty } \to \mathbb {F}\) such that \[
  \left|\varphi \left(a_1,a_2,\ldots \right)\right| \le \left\| (a_1,a_2,\ldots )\right\| _{\infty }
\] for all \(\left(a_1,a_2,\ldots \right) \in \ell^{\infty }\), and \[
  \varphi \left(a_1,a_2,\ldots \right) = \lim _{k \to \infty } a_k
\] for all \(\left(a_1,a_2,\ldots \right) \in \ell^{\infty }\) for which the limit on the right-hand side exists.









ProblemProblem 17





Prove that the dual space of any infinite-dimensional normed vector space is infinite-dimensional.






The dual of the dual space \(V''\) is defined as the dual space of \(V'\). If \(V\) is a normed space, then \(V'' = (V')'\). The norm on \(V''\) is defined as the norm it acquires as the dual space of \(V'\).









ProblemProblem 18





Define a map \(\Phi : V \to V''\) by \[
  (\Phi f)(\varphi ) = \varphi (f)
\] for all \(f \in V\) and \(\varphi \in V'\). Show that \(\left\| \Phi f\right\|  = \left\| f\right\|\) for every \(f \in V\).
The map \(\Phi\) defined above is called the canonical isometric embedding* of \(V\) into \(V''\). Recall that in linear algebra, i.e., in the finite-dimensional case, \(V''\) simply turned out to be isomorphic to \(V\). That is, the map constructed above was bijective. In the general (infinite-dimensional) case this need not hold. The map above is not always surjective.*

title: Banach spaces
text:
5.1 The Baire category theorem
The Baire category theorem (sometimes called the Baire theorem on categories) is a fundamental result on complete metric spaces. It has important consequences for Banach spaces.







Theorem 6 (Baire) Let \((V, d)\) be a complete metric space.

\(V\) cannot be represented as a countable union of closed sets with empty interior (closed nowhere dense sets).
The intersection of any countable sequence of dense open subsets of \(V\) is nonempty.





The proof of (b) uses a construction of a sequence of nested closed balls whose radii tend to zero. Their centers form a fundamental sequence that converges to a point belonging to all the open sets in the sequence. Statement (a) follows from (b) by passing to complements.






ExampleExample 10





Using the Baire category theorem, prove that

\(\mathbb {R}\) is uncountable;
the irrational numbers cannot be represented as a countable union of sets closed in \(\mathbb {R}\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)



Suppose \(\mathbb {R}\) is countable. Then it can be represented as
\[
  \mathbb {R} = \{ x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots \}
\]
Each singleton \(\{ x_n\}\) is closed in \(\mathbb {R}\) and nowhere dense (since a singleton contains no intervals). Then \(\mathbb {R}\) is represented as a countable union of nowhere dense closed sets:
\[
  \mathbb {R} = \bigcup _{n=1}^\infty \{ x_n\}
\]
But by the Baire category theorem a complete metric space (as \(\mathbb {R}\) with the usual metric) cannot be represented as a countable union of nowhere dense sets. Contradiction.
The resulting contradiction shows that \(\mathbb {R}\) is uncountable.








Enum-item(2)



Suppose the contrary: the irrational numbers can be represented as a countable union of sets closed in \(\mathbb {R}\):
\[
  \mathbb {R} \setminus \mathbb {Q} = \bigcup _{n=1}^\infty F_n, \quad \text{where } F_n \text{ are closed in } \mathbb {R}
\]
Since \(\mathbb {Q}\) is countable, it can be represented as
\[
  \mathbb {Q} = \bigcup _{m=1}^\infty \{ q_m\}
\]
where each \(\{ q_m\}\) is closed and nowhere dense. Then all of \(\mathbb {R}\) is represented as:
\[
  \mathbb {R} = (\mathbb {R} \setminus \mathbb {Q}) \cup \mathbb {Q} = \left(\bigcup _{n=1}^\infty F_n\right) \cup \left(\bigcup _{m=1}^\infty \{ q_m\} \right) = \bigcup _{k=1}^\infty A_k
\]
where \(\{ A_k\}\) is an at most countable family of closed sets. Let us show that each \(A_k\) is nowhere dense. Indeed:

\(\{ q_m\}\) is nowhere dense, since singletons contain no intervals.
\(F_n\) is also nowhere dense. If some \(F_n\) contained an interval \((a,b)\), then this interval would consist entirely of irrational numbers (since \(F_n \subset \mathbb {R} \setminus \mathbb {Q}\)), which is impossible, since every interval contains rational numbers.

Thus, \(\mathbb {R}\) is represented as a countable union of nowhere dense closed sets, contradicting the Baire category theorem.
Hence the irrational numbers cannot be represented as a countable union of closed sets, i.e., neither can \(\mathbb {R} \setminus \mathbb {Q}\).














ProblemProblem 19





Let \(U\) be a subset of a metric space \(V\). Prove that \(U\) has empty interior if and only if \(V \setminus U\) is dense in \(V\).









ProblemProblem 20





Let \[
  X = \left\{ 0\right\}  \cup \bigcup _{k = 1}^{\infty }\left\{ \frac{1}{k}\right\} ,
\] and \(d(x, y) = \left|x - y\right|\) for \(x, y \in X\).

Prove that \((X, d)\) is a complete metric space.
Every set of the form \(\left\{ x\right\}\) for \(x \in X\) is a closed subset of \(\mathbb {R}\) and has empty interior in \(\mathbb {R}\). Clearly, \(X\) is a countable union of such sets. Explain why this does not contradict the Baire category theorem, which states that a complete metric space cannot be a countable union of closed sets with empty interior.










ProblemProblem 21





Prove that there is no infinite-dimensional Banach space with a countable Hamel basis.
This exercise shows, for example, that there is no norm turning the space of polynomials over \(\mathbb {F}\) into a Banach space.






HintHint





Let \(V\) be an infinite-dimensional Banach space. By contradiction: suppose \(\left\{ e_k\right\}_{k \in \mathbb {N}}\) is a Hamel basis in \(V\). Every vector in \(V\) can be represented as a finite linear combination of vectors from the system: \[
  V = \operatorname {span}\left\{ e_k\right\} _{k \in \mathbb {N}} = \bigcup _{n=1}^{\infty }U_{n}
\] where \(U_{n} = \operatorname {span}\left\{ e_k\right\}_{k=1}^{n}\). What can be said about \(U_n\)? Are they closed? What is their interior? Justify your answer.

section: 5.2 The open mapping theorem (the Banach-Schauder theorem) and the bounded inverse theorem
text:
5.2 The open mapping theorem (the Banach-Schauder theorem) and the bounded inverse theorem
A map between two topological spaces is called open if the image of every open set (in the domain) is open (in the codomain).







Theorem 7 (Open mapping theorem, Banach-Schauder) Let \(V\) and \(W\) be Banach spaces and \(T: V \to W\) a surjective bounded linear map. Then \(T\) maps open sets to open sets, i.e., for every open \(G \subseteq V\) the set \(T(G)\) is open in \(W\).










ProblemProblem 22





Give an example of a Banach space \(V\), a normed space \(W\), a surjective bounded linear map \(T\) from \(V\) onto \(W\), and an open set \(G \subset V\) such that \(T(G)\) is not an open set in \(W\).
This exercise shows that in the open mapping theorem the requirement that \(W\) be Banach cannot be replaced by the weaker condition that \(W\) is merely normed.






HintHint





Let \(V = \left(\ell^1, \left\| \cdot \right\|_{1}\right)\), \(W = \left(\ell^1, \left\| \cdot \right\|_{\infty }\right)\), \(T = I\) (the identity map), \(G = B_1(0) = \left\{ \left\| a\right\|_{1} < 1\right\}\).













Theorem 8 (Bounded inverse theorem) Let \(V\) and \(W\) be Banach spaces and \(T: V \to W\) a bijective bounded linear map. Then the inverse map \(T^{-1}: W \to V\) is also linear and bounded.




A linear map \(T: V \to W\) between normed spaces is called bounded below if there exists \(c > 0\) such that \(\left\| f\right\|  \le c\left\| Tf\right\|\) for all \(f \in V\).






ProblemProblem 23





Let \(T: V \to W\) be a bounded linear map between Banach spaces \(V\) and \(W\). Prove that \(T\) is bounded below if and only if \(T\) is injective and its image is a closed subspace of \(W\).

title: Banach spaces
text:
5.3 The closed graph theorem
Let \(V\), \(W\) be vector spaces over the same field \(\mathbb {F}\). The Cartesian product \(V \times W\) can readily be given a linear structure: \((v_1, w_1) + (v_2,w_2) := (v_1+v_2, w_1 + w_2)\), etc. It is easy to show that \(V \times W\) is also a vector space over \(\mathbb {F}\).







Theorem 9 Let \(V\), \(W\) be Banach spaces (over the same field \(\mathbb {F}\)). Then the function \[
  \left\| (f,g)\right\|  := \max \left\{ \left\| f\right\| _{V}, \left\| g\right\| _{W}\right\}
\] is a norm on \(V \times W\), and with respect to this norm \(V \times W\) is Banach. Convergence in this norm of \((f_1, g_1), (f_2,g_2), \ldots\) to \((f,g)\) is equivalent to coordinatewise convergence: \(\lim_{n\to \infty }f_n = f\) and \(\lim_{n\to \infty }g_n = g\).




The following result gives a splendid way to show that a linear map between Banach spaces is bounded. The proof is remarkably simple, since most of the work was done in proving the open mapping theorem (which was in turn used to prove the bounded inverse theorem).







Theorem 10 (Closed graph theorem) Let \(V\) and \(W\) be Banach spaces and \(T: V \to W\) a linear map. Then \(T\) is bounded if and only if its graph \(\operatorname {graph}(T) = \{  (f, Tf) : f \in V \}\) is a closed subspace of \(V \times W\): \[
  T \in \mathcal{B}(V,W) \quad \iff \quad \operatorname {graph}(T) \text{ is closed in } V \times W
\]




Explanation. Let \(T: X \rightarrow Y\) be a linear operator between Banach spaces. Then continuity of \(T\) means that \(T x_i \rightarrow T x\) for every convergent sequence \(x_i \rightarrow x\). On the other hand, closedness of the graph of \(T\) means that for every convergent sequence \(x_i \rightarrow x\) such that \(T x_i \rightarrow y\), we have \(y=T x\). Hence the closed graph theorem states that to verify continuity of \(T\) it suffices to show that \(T x_i \rightarrow T x\) under the additional assumption that \(T x_i\) converges.
In fact, for closedness of the graph of \(T\) it suffices that if \(x_i \rightarrow 0, T x_i \rightarrow y\), then \(y=0\). Indeed, if this condition holds, and if \(\left(x_i, T x_i\right) \rightarrow (x, y)\), then \(x_i-x \rightarrow 0\) and \(T\left(x_i-x\right) \rightarrow y-T x\). Thus \(y=T x\), that is, \((x, y)\) belongs to the graph of \(T\).






ProblemProblem 24





Consider the spaces \(C^{1}[0,1]\), \(C[0,1]\) with the supremum norm \(\left\| f\right\|  = \sup_{x \in [0,1]}\left|f(x)\right|\). Let \(T: C^{1}[0,1] \rightarrow C[0,1]\) be defined by \[
  Tf = f'
\] Show that the graph of \(T\) is closed, but \(T\) is not bounded. Does this contradict the closed graph theorem?

title: Banach spaces
section: 5.4 The uniform boundedness principle (the Banach-Steinhaus theorem)
text:
5.4 The uniform boundedness principle (the Banach-Steinhaus theorem)







Theorem 11 (Uniform boundedness principle, Banach-Steinhaus theorem) Let \(V\) be a Banach space, \(W\) a normed space, and \(\mathcal{A}\) a family of bounded linear operators from \(V\) into \(W\). If for every \(f \in V\) \[
  \sup \{  \| Tf\|  : T \in \mathcal{A} \}  < \infty \quad \text{(pointwise boundedness)},
\] then \[
  \sup \{  \| T\|  : T \in \mathcal{A} \}  < \infty \quad \text{(uniform boundedness in norm)}.
\]




The proof uses the Baire category theorem. The sets \(V_n = \{  f \in V : \| Tf\|  \leq n \  \forall T \in \mathcal{A} \}\) are closed. Their union is all of \(V\). By the Baire category theorem, some \(V_n\) has nonempty interior, which allows the operator norms to be estimated uniformly.






ProblemProblem 25





Let \(V\) be a Banach space, \(W\) a normed space, and \(T_1, T_2, \ldots\) a sequence of bounded linear maps from \(V\) into \(W\) such that the limit \(\lim_{k \to \infty } T_k f\) exists for every \(f \in V\). Define \(T: V \to W\) as the pointwise limit of the \(T_n\): \[
  T f := \lim _{k \to \infty } T_k f.
\]

Prove that \(T \in \mathcal{B}(V,W)\), i.e., that \(T\) is a bounded linear map from \(V\) into \(W\).
Is it true that \(T_{n} \to T\) in \(\mathcal{B}(V,W)\), i.e., is it true that \(T_{n}\) converges to \(T\) in the operator norm?

This statement says that the pointwise limit of a sequence of bounded linear operators on a Banach space is also a bounded linear operator.






HintHint





For part (2): see problem Problem 8.

title: Hilbert spaces
text:
1.1 Norm and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
The norm induced by an inner product is the function:
\[
  \| f\|  = \sqrt{\langle f, f \rangle }.
\]
Vectors \(f\) and \(g\) are called orthogonal if \(\langle f, g \rangle = 0\).







Theorem 1 (Pythagorean theorem) If \(f \perp g\), then \(\| f + g\|^2 = \| f\|^2 + \| g\|^2\).











Lemma 2 (Orthogonal decomposition) If \(g \neq 0\), then any vector \(f\) can be uniquely represented as: \[
  f = \frac{\langle f, g \rangle }{\| g\| ^2}g + h,
\] where \(h \perp g\).











Theorem 2 (Cauchy-Schwarz inequality) For all \(f, g \in V\): \[
  |\langle f, g \rangle | \leq \| f\|  \cdot \| g\| .
\] Equality holds if and only if \(f\) and \(g\) are linearly dependent.











Lemma 3 (Triangle inequality) For all \(f, g \in V\): \[
  \| f + g\|  \leq \| f\|  + \| g\| .
\] Equality holds if and only if one of the vectors is a nonnegative multiple of the other.











Theorem 3 The function \(\| f\|  = \sqrt{\langle f, f \rangle }\) is a norm on \(V\).











Lemma 4 (Parallelogram identity) For all \(f, g \in V\): \[
  \| f + g\| ^2 + \| f - g\| ^2 = 2\| f\| ^2 + 2\| g\| ^2.
\]




Geometric interpretation: the sum of the squares of the lengths of the diagonals of a parallelogram equals the sum of the squares of the lengths of all its sides.






ExampleExample 2





Suppose \(f\) and \(g\) are elements of an inner product space and \[
  \left\| f+g\right\| ^{2} = \left\| f\right\| ^{2}+\left\| g\right\| ^{2}
\]

Prove that if \(\mathbf{F} = \mathbb {R}\), then \(f\) and \(g\) are orthogonal.
Give an example showing that if \(\mathbf{F} = \mathbb {C}\), then \(f\) and \(g\) may satisfy the equation above without being orthogonal.







SolutionSolution





\[
  \left\| f+g\right\| ^{2} = \left\langle f+g, f+g \right\rangle = \left\| f\right\| ^2 + \left\langle f, g \right\rangle + \left\langle g, f \right\rangle + \left\| g\right\| ^2 = \left\| f\right\| ^2 + \left\langle f, g \right\rangle + \overline{ \left\langle f, g \right\rangle } + \left\| g\right\| ^2  
\]






Enum-item1.



From the computation above, \(\left\langle f, g \right\rangle + \overline{ \left\langle f, g \right\rangle } = 0\), i.e., \(2\operatorname {Re} \left\langle f, g \right\rangle = 0\). If \(\mathbb {F} = \mathbb {R}\), then \(\left\langle f, g \right\rangle \in \mathbb {R}\), so \(\left\langle f, g \right\rangle = \operatorname {Re} \left\langle f, g \right\rangle = 0\), i.e., \(f \perp g\).








Enum-item2.



\(V = \mathbb {C}^2\), \(f = (0,i)\), \(g = (0,1)\).

title: Hilbert spaces
text:
2.1 Orthogonal projections
The previous section developed the theory of inner product spaces following the standard approach of linear algebra. Linear algebra is mostly concerned with finite-dimensional vector spaces. Many interesting results about infinite-dimensional inner product spaces require an additional condition, which we now introduce.
A Hilbert space is an inner product space that is a Banach space with respect to the norm induced by that inner product.






ExampleExample 3











SolutionSolution





Hilbert spaces

Let \(\mu\) be a measure. Then \(L^2(\mu )\) with its usual inner product is a Hilbert space.
As a special case of the first item, if \(n \in \mathbb {Z}^+\) and \(\mu\) is taken to be counting measure on \(\{ 1, \ldots , n\}\), then \(F^n\) with its usual inner product is a Hilbert space.
As another special case of the first item, taking \(\mu\) to be counting measure on \(\mathbb {Z}^+\), we get that \(\ell^2\) with its usual inner product is a Hilbert space.
Every closed subspace of a Hilbert space is a Hilbert space.

Non-Hilbert spaces

The inner product space \(\ell^1\), where \(\langle (a_1, a_2, \ldots ), (b_1, b_2, \ldots ) \rangle = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty } a_k \overline{b_k}\), is not a Hilbert space, because the corresponding norm is not complete on \(\ell^1\).
The inner product space \(C([0, 1])\) of continuous \(\mathbb {F}\)-valued functions on the interval \([0, 1]\), where \(\langle f, g \rangle = \int_0^1 f \,  \overline{g}\), is not a Hilbert space, because the corresponding norm is not complete on \(C([0, 1])\).













ExampleExample 4





Let \(V = C[0,1]\) with the supremum norm \(\left\| f\right\|  = \sup_{t \in [0,1]}\left|f(t)\right|\). Consider the subset \[
  U = \left\{ g \in C[0,1] \;  :\;  g(0) = 0, \;  \int _0^1 g(t) dt = 0\right\}
\]

Prove that \(U\) is a closed subspace of \(V\);
Let \(f(t) = t\). Find \(\operatorname {dist}_U(t)\).
Prove that \(\operatorname {dist}_U(t)\) is not attained, i.e., there is no \(g \in U\) such that \(\left\| f-g\right\|  = \operatorname {dist}_U(f)\).

This example shows that in a general Banach space the distance to a closed convex set need not be attained.






SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)



\(U\) is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, so it is a subspace. Next, we need to prove that \(U\) is closed. Let \(g_1, g_2, \ldots \in U\), \(g_n \to h\) in \(V\). The \(g_n\) converge uniformly to \(h\). Hence the integral of the limit \(\int_0^1 h\) equals the limit of the integrals \(\lim_{n \to \infty }\int_0^1 g_n = \lim_{n \to \infty } = 0\). Furthermore, uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence, i.e., \(h(0) = \lim_{n \to \infty }g_n(0) = 0\). Altogether, \(g \in U\). We have proved that \(U\) is closed.








Enum-item(2)




Let \(g \in U\) be arbitrary. We know that \(\int_0^1 f - g = \int_{0}^{1}f(t)dt= \frac{1}{2}\). Then
\[
  \frac{1}{2} = \left|\int _0^1 f - g\right| \leq \int _{0}^{1}\left|f-g\right| \stackrel{*}{\leq } 1 \cdot \sup _{t \in [0,1]}\left|f(t) - g(t)\right| = \left\| f-g\right\|
\]
Therefore \(\operatorname {dist}_U(f) \geq \frac{1}{2}\).
Let us show that \(\operatorname {dist}_U(f) \geq \frac{1}{2}\). Consider the sequence of functions \(g_n\) (\(n \geq 3\)): \(g_n\) goes linearly from \((0,0)\) to \((\frac{1}{n}, -\frac{1}{2})\), then linearly to the point \((\frac{1}{2}, 0)\), then linearly to the point \((1, \frac{1}{2})\). The area of the lower triangle (from \(0\) to \(\frac{1}{2}\)) equals \(\frac{1}{2}\), and equals the area of the triangle from \(\frac{1}{2}\) to \(1\). Hence \(\int_0^1 g_n(t) dt = 0\). Altogether, \(g_n \in U\) for all \(n \geq 3\). Moreover, \(\left\| f - g_n\right\|  \to \frac{1}{2}\) as \(n \to +\infty\) (this should be clear from the figure).
