title: Bounded operators on Hilbert spaces
text:
5.1 Self-adjoint operators
A bounded operator \(T\) on a Hilbert space is called self-adjoint if \(T^{*}=T\). \(T \in \mathcal{B}(V)\) is self-adjoint if and only if
\[
  \left\langle T f, g \right\rangle = \left\langle f, T g \right\rangle
\]
for all \(f, g \in V\).






ExampleExample 11











SolutionSolution






Suppose \(b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots\) is a bounded sequence in \(\mathbb {F}\). Define the bounded operator \(T: \ell^{2} \rightarrow \ell^{2}\) as follows:
\[
  T\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots \right)=\left(a_{1} b_{1}, a_{2} b_{2}, \ldots \right) .
\]
Then \(T^{*}: \ell^{2} \rightarrow \ell^{2}\) is the operator defined as follows:
\[
  T^{*}\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots \right)=\left(a_{1} \overline{b_{1}}, a_{2} \overline{b_{2}}, \ldots \right) .
\]
Hence, \(T\) is self-adjoint if and only if \(b_{k} \in \mathbb {R}\) for all \(k \in \mathbb {N}\).
More generally, suppose ( \(X, \mathcal{S}, \mu\)) is a finite-dimensional measure space and \(h \in \mathcal{L}^{\infty }(\mu )\). Define the bounded operator \(M_{h} \in \mathcal{B}\left(L^{2}(\mu )\right)\) as \(M_{h} f=f h\). Then \(M_{h}{ }^{*}=M_{\overline{h}}\). Thus, \(M_{h}\) is self-adjoint if and only if \(\mu (\left\{ x \in X: h(x) \notin \mathbb {R}\right\} )=0\).
More generally, suppose ( \(X, \mathcal{S}, \mu\)) is a finite-dimensional measure space and \(h \in \mathcal{L}^{\infty }(\mu )\). — Suppose \(n \in \mathbb {N}, K\) is an \(n\) by \(n\) matrix, and \(T_K: \mathbb {F}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb {F}^{n}\) is the operator of multiplication of a vector by the matrix \(K\) (regarding elements of \(\mathbb {F}^{n}\) as column vectors). Then \(\left(T_K\right)^{*}\) is the operator of multiplication by the conjugate transpose matrix of \(K\), as shown in example 10.10. Thus, \(T_K\) is a self-adjoint operator if and only if the matrix \(K\) equals its conjugate transpose matrix.
More generally, suppose \((X, \mathcal{S}, \mu )\) is a finite-dimensional measure space, \(K \in \mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu \times \mu )\), and \(T_K\) is the integral operator on \(L^{2}(\mu )\) defined in example 10.5. Define \(K^{*}: X \times X \rightarrow \mathbb {F}\) as \(K^{*}(y, x)=\overline{K(x, y)}\). Then \(\left(T_K\right)^{*}\) is the integral operator induced by \(K^{*}\), as shown in example 10.5. Thus, if \(K^{*}=K\), or, in other words, if \(K(x, y)=\overline{K(y, x)}\) for all \((x, y) \in X \times X\), then \(T_K\) is self-adjoint.
Suppose \(U\) is a closed subspace of a Hilbert space \(V\). Recall that \(P_{U}\) denotes the orthogonal projection of \(V\) onto \(U\) (see section 8B). We have
\[
  \begin{aligned}  \left\langle P_{U} f, g \right\rangle &  = \left\langle P_{U} f, P_{U} g+\left(I-P_{U}\right) g \right\rangle \\ &  = \left\langle P_{U} f, P_{U} g \right\rangle \\ &  = \left\langle f-\left(I-P_{U}\right) f, P_{U} g \right\rangle \\ &  = \left\langle f, P_{U} g \right\rangle , \end{aligned}
\]
where the second and fourth equalities above hold by virtue of 8.37(a). The equation above shows that \(P_{U}\) is a self-adjoint operator.














Lemma 14 (\(\left\langle T f, f \right\rangle =0\) for all \(f\) \(\;  \Rightarrow \;\) \(T=0\)) Suppose \(V\) is a Hilbert space, \(T \in \mathcal{B}(V)\), and \(\left\langle T f, f \right\rangle =0\) for all \(f \in V\).

If \(\mathbb {F}=\mathbb {C}\), then \(T=0\).
If \(\mathbb {F}=\mathbb {R}\) and \(T\) is self-adjoint, then \(T=0\).





Some insight into the adjoint operator can be gained by regarding the operation \(T \mapsto T^{*}\) on \(\mathcal{B}(V)\) as an analogue of the operation \(z \mapsto \overline{z}\) on \(\mathbb {C}\). Under this analogy, self-adjoint operators (characterized by \(T^{*}=T\)) correspond to real numbers (characterized by \(\overline{z}=z\)).
The following two results deepen the analogy between self-adjoint operators and real numbers. First we see this analogy reflected in the behavior of \(\left\langle T f, f \right\rangle\), and then in the spectrum of \(T\).







Lemma 15 Suppose \(T\) is a bounded operator on a complex Hilbert space \(V\). Then \(T\) is self-adjoint if and only if \[
  \left\langle T f, f \right\rangle \in \mathbb {R}
\] for all \(f \in V\).











Lemma 16 (Self-adjoint operators have real spectrum) Let \(T\) be a bounded self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space. Then \(\sigma (T) \subseteq \mathbb {R}\).




This lemma is vacuous in the case \(\mathbb {F} = \mathbb {R}\) (in this case the spectrum cannot fall outside the eigenvalues anyway), but in the case \(\mathbb {F} = \mathbb {C}\) it acquires content.
We have shown that a bounded operator on a nonzero complex Hilbert space has nonempty spectrum. This result can fail on real Hilbert spaces (where by definition the spectrum is contained in \(\mathbb {R}\)). For example, the operator \(T\) on \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\) defined by \(T(x, y)=(-y, x)\) has empty spectrum.
Although the spectrum of every self-adjoint operator is nonempty, it is not true that every self-adjoint operator has an eigenvalue. For example, the self-adjoint operator \(M_{x} \in \mathcal{B}\left(L^{2}[0,1]\right)\), defined by \(\left(M_{x} f\right)(x)=x f(x)\), has no eigenvalues.

title: Bounded operators on Hilbert spaces
text:
5.2 Normal operators
Now let us consider another good special class of operators. A bounded operator \(T\) on a Hilbert space is called normal if it commutes with its adjoint:
\[
  T^{*} T=T T^{*} .
\]
Clearly every self-adjoint operator is normal, but there exist normal operators that are not self-adjoint, as shown in the following example.






ExampleExample 12











SolutionSolution







Suppose \(\mu\) is a positive measure, \(h \in \mathcal{L}^{\infty }(\mu )\), and \(M_{h} \in \mathcal{B}\left(L^{2}(\mu )\right)\) is the multiplication operator defined as \(M_{h} f=f h\). Then \(M_{h}{ }^{*}=M_{\overline{h}}\), which means that \(M_{h}\) is self-adjoint if \(h\) is real-valued. If \(\mathbb {F}=\mathbb {C}\), then \(h\) may be complex-valued, and \(M_{h}\) need not be self-adjoint. However,

\[
  M_{h}^{*} M_{h}=M_{|h|^{2}}=M_{h} M_{h}^{*}
\]
and, hence, \(M_{h}\) is a normal operator, even when \(h\) is complex-valued.
Suppose \(T\) is the operator on \(\mathbb {F}^{2}\) whose matrix with respect to the standard basis equals
\[
  \left(\begin{array}{cc} 2 &  -3 \\ 3 &  2 \end{array}\right) .
\]
Then \(T\) is not self-adjoint, since the matrix above is not equal to its conjugate transpose. However \(T^{*} T=13 I\) and \(T T^{*}=13 I\), as you should check. Since \(T^{*} T=T T^{*}\), we conclude that \(T\) is a normal operator.
Example of a non-normal operator: Suppose \(T\) is the right shift on \(\ell^{2}\); thus, \(T\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots \right)=\left(0, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots \right)\). Then \(T^{*}\) is the left shift: \(T^{*}\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots \right)=\left(a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots \right)\). Hence, \(T^{*} T\) is the identity operator on \(\ell^{2}\), while \(T T^{*}\) is the operator \(\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots \right) \mapsto \left(0, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots \right)\). Thus, \(T^{*} T \neq T T^{*}\), which means that \(T\) is not a normal operator.














Lemma 17 (Criterion for a normal operator) Let \(T\) be a bounded operator on a Hilbert space \(V\). Then \(T\) is normal if and only if \[
  \left\| T f\right\| =\left\| T^{*} f\right\|
\] for all \(f \in V\).




Every complex number \(z\) can be written as \(a+b i\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are real numbers, with \(a = \frac{z + \overline{z}}{2}\) and \(b = \frac{z - \overline{z}}{2i}\). Let us try to apply the same idea to a bounded operator \(T\) on a Hilbert space \(V\): let
\[
  \operatorname {Re}T := A = \frac{T + T^*}{2}, \qquad \operatorname {Im}T := B = \frac{T - T^*}{2i}
\]
The first part of the following result gives an analogous result for bounded operators on a complex Hilbert space, where self-adjoint operators play the role of real numbers. The operators \(A\) and \(B\) can be called the real and imaginary parts of the operator \(T\). The second part below shows that normality depends on whether these real and imaginary parts commute.







Lemma 18 (An operator is normal if and only if its real and imaginary parts commute) Let \(T\) be a bounded operator on a complex Hilbert space \(V\).

There exist unique self-adjoint operators \(A, B\) on \(V\) such that \(T=A+i B\).
\(T\) is normal if and only if \(A B=B A\), where \(A, B\) are as in part (a).











ExampleExample 13





Prove the preceding lemma.






SolutionSolution





Proof. Suppose \(T=A+i B\), where \(A\) and \(B\) are self-adjoint. Then \(T^{*}=A-i B\). Adding these equations for \(T\) and \(T^{*}\) and then dividing by 2, we get the formula for \(A\); subtracting the equation for \(T^{*}\) from the equation for \(T\) and then dividing by \(2 i\), we get the formula for \(B\). In particular, we have:
\[
  A=\frac{T+T^{*}}{2} \quad \text{ and } \quad B=\frac{T-T^{*}}{2 i},
\]
which proves the uniqueness in part (a). Existence in part (a) is proved by defining \(A\) and \(B\) via the equations above and observing that \(A\) and \(B\), as defined above, are self-adjoint and \(T=A+i B\).
To prove (b), let us check that if \(A\) and \(B\) are defined as in the equations above, then
\[
  A B-B A=\frac{T^{*} T-T T^{*}}{2 i} .
\]
Thus, \(A B=B A\) if and only if \(T\) is normal.






An operator on a finite-dimensional vector space is left-invertible if and only if it is right-invertible. We have seen that this result fails for bounded operators on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. However, the following result shows that we recover this equivalence for normal operators.







Lemma 19 (Invertibility for normal operators) Suppose \(V\) is a Hilbert space, and \(T \in \mathcal{B}(V)\) is a normal operator. Then the following statements are equivalent:

\(T\) is invertible.
\(T\) is left-invertible.
\(T\) is right-invertible.
\(T\) is surjective.
\(T\) is injective and bounded below;
\(T\) is injective and has closed range.
\(T^{*} T\) is invertible.
\(T T^{*}\) is invertible.





The following result shows that a normal operator and its adjoint have the same eigenvectors, with their eigenvalues being complex conjugates of each other. This result can fail for operators that are not normal. For example, 0 is an eigenvalue of the left shift on \(\ell^{2}\), but its adjoint, the right shift, has no eigenvectors or eigenvalues.







Lemma 20 (For a normal operator, \(\sigma_p(T^*) = \overline{\sigma_p(T)}\)) Let \(T\) be a normal operator on a Hilbert space \(V, \alpha \in \mathbb {F}\), and \(f \in V\). Then \(\alpha\) is an eigenvalue of \(T\) with eigenvector \(f\) if and only if \(\overline{\alpha }\) is an eigenvalue of \(T^{*}\) with eigenvector \(f\).




Since every self-adjoint operator is normal, the following result also holds for self-adjoint operators.







Lemma 21 (Eigenvectors of normal operators are orthogonal) Eigenvectors of a normal operator corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.

title: Bounded operators on Hilbert spaces
text:
5.3 Isometries and unitary operators
Let \(T\) be a bounded operator on a Hilbert space \(V\).

\(T\) is called an isometry if \(\left\| T f\right\| =\left\| f\right\|\) for every \(f \in V\).
\(T\) is called unitary if \(T^{*} T=T T^{*}=I\). In other words, \(T^{-1} = T^*\).







ExampleExample 14











SolutionSolution







Let \(T \in \mathcal{B}\left(\ell^{2}\right)\) be the right shift, defined as follows:

\[
  T\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots \right)=\left(0, a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots \right) .
\]
Then \(T\) is an isometry, but is not a unitary operator, since \(T T^{*} \neq I\) (which is clear even without computing \(T^{*}\), since \(T\) is not surjective).
Suppose \(T \in \mathcal{B}\left(\ell^{2}(\mathbb {Z})\right)\) is the right shift, defined as follows:
\[
  (T f)(n)=f(n-1)
\]
for \(f: \mathbb {Z} \rightarrow \mathbb {F}\) with \(\sum_{k=-\infty }^{\infty }|f(k)|^{2}<\infty\). Then \(T\) is an isometry and is unitary.
Suppose \(b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots\) is a bounded sequence in \(\mathbb {F}\). Define \(T \in \mathcal{B}\left(\ell^{2}\right)\) as follows:
\[
  T\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots \right)=\left(a_{1} b_{1}, a_{2} b_{2}, \ldots \right) .
\]
Then \(T\) is an isometry if and only if \(T\) is unitary if and only if \(\left|b_{k}\right|=1\) for all \(k \in \mathbb {N}\).
More generally, suppose ( \(X, \mathcal{S}, \mu\)) is a \(\sigma\)-finite space and \(h \in \mathcal{L}^{\infty }(\mu )\). Define \(M_{h} \in \mathcal{B}\left(L^{2}(\mu )\right)\) as \(M_{h} f=f h\). Then \(T\) is an isometry if and only if \(T\) is unitary if and only if \(\mu (\left\{ x \in X:|h(x)| \neq 1\right\} )=0\).














Lemma 22 (Equivalent conditions for an isometry) Let \(T\) be a bounded operator on a Hilbert space \(V\). Then the following statements are equivalent:

\(T\) is an isometry.
\(T\) preserves the inner product: \(\left\langle Tf, Tg \right\rangle = \left\langle f, g \right\rangle\) for any \(f,g \in V\).
\(T^*T = I\).
\(T\) maps any orthonormal family of vectors to another orthonormal family;
\(T\) maps some orthonormal family of vectors to another orthonormal family.












Lemma 23 (Equivalent conditions for a unitary operator) Let \(T\) be a bounded operator on a Hilbert space \(V\). Then the following statements are equivalent:

\(T\) is a unitary operator.
\(T\) is a surjective isometry.
\(T\) and \(T^{*}\) are isometries.
\(T^{*}\) is a unitary operator.
\(T\) is an invertible operator, and \(T^{-1}=T^{*}\).
\(T\) maps any orthonormal basis to another orthonormal basis;
\(T\) maps some orthonormal basis to another orthonormal basis.





The equations \(T^{*} T=T T^{*}=I\) are analogous to the equation \(|z|^{2}=1\) for \(z \in \mathbb {C}\). Let us now extend this analogy to the behavior of the spectrum of a unitary operator.







Lemma 24 (Spectrum of a unitary operator) Let \(T\) be a unitary operator on a Hilbert space. Then \[
  \sigma (T) \subseteq \left\{ \alpha \in \mathbb {F}:|\alpha |=1\right\}  .
\]




As a special case of the following result we can conclude (without any computation!) that the spectrum of the right shift on \(\ell^{2}\) equals \(\left\{ \alpha \in \mathbb {F}:|\alpha | \leq 1\right\}\).







Lemma 25 (Spectrum of an isometry) Let \(T\) be an isometry on a Hilbert space, and \(T\) is not unitary. Then \[
  \sigma (T)=\left\{ \alpha \in \mathbb {F}:|\alpha | \leq 1\right\}  .
\]










ProblemProblem 14





Let \(V\) be a Hilbert space, the operator \(T: V \to V\) be linear and \(\left\langle Tf, g \right\rangle = \left\langle f, Tg \right\rangle\) for all \(f, g \in V\). Prove that \(T\) is bounded, i.e., \(T \in \mathcal{B}(V)\).
[@VKK, Problem 11.11]

title: Bounded operators on Hilbert spaces
text:
7.1 Orthonormal bases consisting of eigenvectors
Let us begin this section with the following useful lemma.







Lemma 27 (\(T^{*} T-\left\| T\right\|^{2} I\) is not invertible) If \(T\) is a bounded operator on a nonzero Hilbert space, then \(\left\| T\right\|^{2} \in \sigma \left(T^{*} T\right)\).




The following result points to one of the ways in which self-adjoint compact operators behave like self-adjoint operators on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.







Lemma 28 (Every self-adjoint compact operator has an eigenvalue) Let \(T\) be a self-adjoint compact operator on a nonzero Hilbert space. Then either \(\left\| T\right\|\) or \(-\left\| T\right\|\) is an eigenvalue of \(T\).




If \(T\) is an operator on a vector space \(V\), and \(U\) is a subspace of \(V\), then \(\left.T\right|_{U}\) is a linear map from \(U\) to \(V\). For \(\left.T\right|_{U}\) to be an operator (that is, a linear map from a vector space into itself), we need \(T(U) \subseteq U\). Thus, we arrive at the following definition.
Let \(T\) be an operator on a vector space \(V\). A subspace \(U\) of \(V\) is called an invariant subspace for \(T\) if \(T f \in U\) for every \(f \in U\).






ExampleExample 16





Examples of invariant subspaces






SolutionSolution





You should check each of the statements below.

For \(b \in [0,1]\) the subspace

\[
  \left\{ f \in L^{2}([0,1]): f(t)=0 \text{ for almost every } t \in [0, b]\right\}
\]
is an invariant subspace for the Volterra operator \(\mathcal{V}: L^{2}([0,1]) \rightarrow L^{2}([0,1])\), defined as \((\mathcal{V} f)(x)=\int_{0}^{x} f\).

Suppose \(T\) is an operator on a Hilbert space \(V\) and \(f \in V\) with \(f \neq 0\). Then \(\operatorname {span}\left\{ f\right\}\) is an invariant subspace for \(T\) if and only if \(f\) is an eigenvector of \(T\).

— Suppose \(T\) is an operator on a Hilbert space \(V\). Then \(\left\{ 0\right\} , V\), \(\operatorname {Ker}T\), and \(\operatorname {Im}T\) are invariant subspaces for \(T\).
— If \(T\) is a bounded operator on a Hilbert space and \(U\) is an invariant subspace for \(T\), then \(\overline{U}\) is an invariant subspace for \(T\).






If \(T\) is a compact operator on a Hilbert space and \(U\) is a closed invariant subspace for \(T\), then \(\left.T\right|_{U}\) is a compact operator on \(U\), as follows from the definitions.
If \(U\) is a closed invariant subspace for a self-adjoint operator \(T\), then \(\left.T\right|_{U}\) is self-adjoint, because
\[
  \left\langle \left(\left.T\right|_{U}\right) f, g \right\rangle = \left\langle T f, g \right\rangle = \left\langle f, T g \right\rangle = \left\langle f, \left(\left.T\right|_{U}\right) g \right\rangle
\]
for all \(f, g \in U\). The following result shows that a bit more is true.
The most important open problem in operator theory is the invariant subspace problem, which asks whether every bounded operator on a Hilbert space of dimension greater than 1 has a closed invariant subspace other than \(\left\{ 0\right\}\) and \(V\).







Lemma 29 (Invariance of U for a self-adjoint operator T implies invariance of \(U^{\perp }\) for \(T\)) Let \(U\) be an invariant subspace for a self-adjoint operator \(T\). Then (a) \(U^{\perp }\) is also an invariant subspace for \(T\); (b) \(\left.T\right|_{U^{\perp }}\) is a self-adjoint operator on \(U^{\perp }\).




Operators for which there exists an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors may be the simplest operators to understand. The following result states that any such operator must be self-adjoint in the case of a real Hilbert space and normal in the case of a complex Hilbert space.







Lemma 30 (An orthonormal basis of eigenvectors implies self-adjointness or normality) Let \(T\) be a bounded operator on a Hilbert space \(V\), and suppose there exists an orthonormal basis of \(V\) consisting of eigenvectors of the operator \(T\).

If \(\mathbb {F}=\mathbb {R}\), then \(T\) is self-adjoint.
If \(\mathbb {F}=\mathbb {C}\), then \(T\) is normal.





The following result is one of the main achievements of the theory of compact operators on Hilbert spaces. The result below applies to both real and complex Hilbert spaces. In the case of a real Hilbert space, the result below can be combined with 10.103(a) to obtain the following result: A compact operator on a real Hilbert space is self-adjoint if and only if there exists an orthonormal basis of the Hilbert space consisting of eigenvectors of the operator.







Theorem 7 (Spectral theorem for self-adjoint compact operators) Let \(T\) be a self-adjoint compact operator on a Hilbert space \(V\). Then (a) there exists an orthonormal basis of \(V\) consisting of eigenvectors of \(T\); (b) there exists a countable set \(\Omega\), an orthonormal family \(\left\{ e_{k}\right\}_{k \in \Omega }\) in \(V\), and a family \(\left\{ \alpha_{k}\right\}_{k \in \Omega }\) in \(\mathbb {R} \backslash \left\{ 0\right\}\) such that
\[
  T f=\sum _{k \in \Omega } \alpha _{k} \left\langle f, e_{k} \right\rangle e_{k}
\]
for every \(f \in V\).




A normal compact operator on a nonzero real Hilbert space may have no eigenvalues [consider, for example, the normal operator \(T\) of counterclockwise rotation by a right angle on \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\), defined by \(\left.T(x, y)=(-y, x)\right]\). However, the following result shows that normal compact operators on complex Hilbert spaces behave better. The key idea in the proof of this result is that on a complex Hilbert space the real and imaginary parts of a normal compact operator are commuting self-adjoint compact operators, which allows us to apply the spectral theorem for self-adjoint compact operators.







Theorem 8 (Spectral theorem for normal compact operators) Let \(T\) be a compact operator on a complex Hilbert space \(V\). Then there exists an orthonormal basis of \(V\) consisting of eigenvectors of \(T\) if and only if \(T\) is normal.




The following example demonstrates the power of the spectral theorem for normal compact operators. Finding the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the normal compact operator \(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\) in the following example leads us to an orthonormal basis of \(L^{2}([0,1])\). A simple computation shows that the family \(\left\{ e_{k}\right\}_{k \in \mathbb {Z}}\), where \(e_{k}\) is defined as in 10.112, is an orthonormal family in \(L^{2}([0,1])\). The hard part of proving that \(\left\{ e_{k}\right\}_{k \in \mathbb {Z}}\) is an orthonormal basis of \(L^{2}([0,1])\) is to show that the closed linear span of this family equals \(L^{2}([0,1])\). However, the spectral theorem for normal compact operators (10.107) provides this information without any further work.






ExampleExample 17





An example of an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors






SolutionSolution





Let \(\mathcal{V}: L^{2}([0,1]) \rightarrow L^{2}([0,1])\) be the Volterra operator, defined as follows:
\[
  (\mathcal{V} f)(x)=\int _{0}^{x} f
\]
The operator \(\mathcal{V}\) is compact (see the paragraph after the proof of 10.70), but it is not normal. Since \(\mathcal{V}\) is compact, \(\mathcal{V}^{*}\) is also compact (by 10.73). Hence \(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\) is compact. Also, \(\left(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\right)^{*}=\mathcal{V}^{*}-\mathcal{V}=-\left(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\right)\). Since every operator commutes with its negative, we conclude that \(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\) is a compact normal operator. Since we want to apply the spectral theorem, for the rest of this example we take \(\mathbb {F}=\mathbb {C}\).
If \(f \in L^{2}([0,1])\) and \(x \in [0,1]\), then the formula for \(\mathcal{V}^{*}\) given by formula 10.16 shows that
\[
  \left(\left(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\right) f\right)(x)=2 \int _{0}^{x} f-\int _{0}^{1} f
\]
The right-hand side of the equation above is a continuous function of \(x\) whose value at \(x=0\) is the negative of its value at \(x=1\).
Differentiating both sides of the equation above and using the Lebesgue differentiation theorem (4.19), we see that
\[
  \left(\left(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\right) f\right)^{\prime }(x)=2 f(x)
\]
for almost every \(x \in [0,1]\). If \(f \in \operatorname {null}\left(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\right)\), then differentiating both sides of the equation \(\left(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\right) f=0\) shows that \(2 f(x)=0\) for almost every \(x \in [0,1]\); hence \(f=0\), and we conclude that \(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\) is injective (hence 0 is not an eigenvalue).
Suppose \(f\) is an eigenvector of \(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\) with eigenvalue \(\alpha\). Thus, \(f\) is in the range of \(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\), which, by 10.109, implies that \(f\) is continuous on [ 0,1 ], and, again by 10.109, implies that \(f\) is continuously differentiable on \((0,1)\). Differentiating both sides of the equation \(\left(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\right) f=\alpha f\), we obtain:
\[
  2 f(x)=\alpha f^{\prime }(x)
\]
for all \(x \in (0,1)\). Hence, the function whose value at \(x\) equals \(e^{-(2 / \alpha ) x} f(x)\) has derivative 0 everywhere on \((0,1)\) and, thus, is a constant function. In other words,
\[
  f(x)=c e^{(2 / \alpha ) x} \tag {10.110}
\]
for some constant \(c \neq 0\). Since \(f \in \operatorname {range}\left(V-\mathcal{V}^{*}\right)\), we have \(f(0)=-f(1)\), which together with the equation above implies the existence of \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\) such that
\[
  2 / \alpha =i(2 k+1) \pi . \tag {10.111}
\]
Substituting into 10.110 the value of \(2 / \alpha\) obtained in 10.111, we see that for \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\) one should define \(e_{k} \in L^{2}([0,1])\) as follows:
\[
  e_{k}(x)=e^{i(2 k+1) \pi x} \tag {10.112}
\]
Clearly \(\left\{ e_{k}\right\}_{k \in \mathbb {Z}}\) is an orthonormal family in \(L^{2}([0,1])\) [orthogonality can be checked by direct computation or via 10.57]. The preceding paragraph together with the spectral theorem for normal compact operators (10.107) implies that this orthonormal family is an orthonormal basis of \(L^{2}([0,1])\).

title: Bounded operators on Hilbert spaces
text:
7.2 Singular value decomposition
The following result gives an important generalization of the spectral theorem to arbitrary compact operators, which need not be self-adjoint or normal. This generalization requires two orthonormal families, in contrast to the single orthonormal family in the usual spectral theorem.







Theorem 9 (Singular value decomposition) Let \(T\) be a compact operator on a Hilbert space \(V\). Then there exists a countable set \(\Omega\), orthonormal families \[
  \left\{ e^{(1)}_k\right\} _{k \in \Omega } \qquad \text{ and } \qquad \left\{ e^{(2)}_k\right\} _{k \in \Omega }
\] in \(V\), and a family \(\left\{ \alpha_{k}\right\}_{k \in \Omega }\) of positive numbers such that \[
  Tf = \sum _{k \in \Omega } \alpha _{k} \cdot \left\langle f, e^{(1)}_{k} \right\rangle \cdot e^{(2)}_{k}
\] for every \(f \in V\).




The orthonormal families \(\left\{ e^{(1)}_{k}\right\}_{k \in \Omega }\) and \(\left\{ e^{(2)}_{k}\right\}_{k \in \Omega }\) in the singular value decomposition are not uniquely determined by the operator \(T\). However, the positive numbers \(\left\{ \alpha_{k}\right\}_{k \in \Omega }\) are uniquely determined as the positive square roots of the positive eigenvalues of \(T^{*}T\). These positive numbers can be arranged in decreasing order (since, if there are infinitely many of them, they form a sequence with limit \(0\)). This procedure leads to the definition of singular values below.
Suppose \(T\) is a compact operator. Recall that the geometric multiplicity of a positive eigenvalue \(\alpha\) of the operator \(T^{*} T\) is defined as \(\operatorname {dim} \operatorname {null}\left(T^{*} T-\alpha I\right)\) [see 10.81]. This geometric multiplicity is the number of times \(\sqrt{\alpha }\) appears in the family \(\left\{ s_{k}\right\}_{k \in \Omega }\) corresponding to the singular value decomposition of the operator \(T\). By 10.82, this geometric multiplicity is finite.
We can now define the singular values of a compact operator \(T\), where we carefully list the square root of each positive eigenvalue of the operator \(T^{*} T\) as many times as its geometric multiplicity.

Suppose \(T\) is a compact operator on a Hilbert space. The singular values of \(T\), denoted \(s_{1}(T) \geq s_{2}(T) \geq s_{3}(T) \geq \cdots\), are the positive square roots of the positive eigenvalues of \(T^{*} T\), arranged in decreasing order, with each singular value \(s\) listed as many times as the geometric multiplicity of \(s^{2}\) as an eigenvalue of \(T^{*} T\).
If \(T^{*} T\) has only finitely many positive eigenvalues, then define \(s_{n}(T)=0\) for all \(n \in \mathbb {N}\) for which \(s_{n}(T)\) is not defined by the first item.







ExampleExample 18





An example of singular values on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space






SolutionSolution





Define \(T: \mathbb {F}^{4} \rightarrow \mathbb {F}^{4}\) as follows:
\[
  T\left(z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}, z_{4}\right)=\left(0,3 z_{1}, 2 z_{2},-3 z_{4}\right) .
\]
A computation shows that
\[
  \left(T^{*} T\right)\left(z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}, z_{4}\right)=\left(9 z_{1}, 4 z_{2}, 0,9 z_{4}\right) .
\]
Thus, the eigenvalues of \(T^{*} T\) equal \(9, 4, 0\) and
\[
  \operatorname {dim}\left(T^{*} T-9 I\right)=2 \quad \text{ and } \quad \operatorname {dim}\left(T^{*} T-4 I\right)=1 .
\]
Taking the square roots of the positive eigenvalues of \(T^{*} T\) and then appending an infinite sequence of zeros, we see that the singular values of \(T\) equal \(3 \geq 3 \geq 2 \geq 0 \geq 0 \geq \cdots\).
Note that -3 and 0 are the only eigenvalues of \(T\). Thus, in this case the list of eigenvalues of \(T\) does not contain the number 2, which appears in the definition (and hence in the behavior) of \(T\), but the list of singular values of \(T\) does include 2.






The following result establishes an important relationship between \(K \in L^{2}(\mu \times \mu )\) and the singular values of the integral operator associated with \(K\).







Lemma 31 (Sum of the squares of the singular values of an integral operator) Let \(\mu\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite measure and \(K \in L^{2}(\mu \times \mu )\). Let \(T_K\) be the integral operator with kernel \(K\). Then \[
  \left\| K\right\| _{L^{2}(\mu \times \mu )}^{2}=\sum _{n=1}^{\infty }\left(s_{n}\left(T_K\right)\right)^{2} .
\]




We can now give an impressive application of the preceding result.






ExampleExample 19





Let \(\mathcal{V} \in \mathcal{B}(L^2[0,1])\) be the Volterra operator.

Find the singular values for the (normal) operator \(T = \mathcal{V} - \mathcal{V}^*\);
Find \(\frac{1}{1^{2}}+\frac{1}{3^{2}}+\frac{1}{5^{2}}+\cdots\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(i)



In example 10.108 we saw that if \(e_{k}\) is defined by formula 10.112, then \(\left\{ e_{k}\right\}_{k \in \mathbb {Z}}\) is an orthonormal basis of \(L^{2}([0,1])\) and
\[
  T e_{k}=\frac{2}{i(2 k+1) \pi } e_{k}
\]
for each \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\), where the eigenvalue shown above corresponding to \(e_{k}\) is taken from formula 10.111. Now formula 10.56 implies that
\[
  T^{*} e_{k}=\frac{-2}{i(2 k+1) \pi } e_{k}
\]
for each \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\). Hence,
\[
  T^{*} T e_{k}=\frac{4}{(2 k+1)^{2} \pi ^{2}} e_{k}
\]
for each \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\). After taking positive square roots of the eigenvalues, we see that the equation above shows that the singular values of \(T\) equal:
\[
  \frac{2}{\pi } \geq \frac{2}{\pi } \geq \frac{2}{3 \pi } \geq \frac{2}{3 \pi } \geq \frac{2}{5 \pi } \geq \frac{2}{5 \pi } \geq \cdots ,
\]
where the first two singular values above come from taking \(k=-1\) and \(k=0\) in 10.119, the next two singular values above come from taking \(k=-2\) and \(k=1\), the next two singular values above come from taking \(k=-3\) and \(k=2\), and so on. Each singular value of \(T\) appears twice in the list of singular values above, since each eigenvalue of \(T^{*} T\) has geometric multiplicity 2.








Enum-item(ii)



Define \(K:[0,1] \times [0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb {R}\) as follows:
\[
  K(x, y)= \begin{cases}  1 &  \text{ if } x>y \\ 0 &  \text{ if } x=y \\ -1 &  \text{ if } x<y \end{cases}
\]
Let \(\lambda\) be Lebesgue measure on \([0,1]\), and note that the integral operator \(T_{K}\) is the normal compact operator \(\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{V}^{*}\) on \(L^2[0,1]\), where \(\mathcal{V}\) is the Volterra operator.
It is easy to compute \(\left\| K\right\|_{L^{2}(\lambda \times \lambda )}=1\). We have
\[
  1=2 \sum _{k=0}^{\infty } \frac{4}{(2 k+1)^{2} \pi ^{2}}
\]
Thus,
\[
  \frac{1}{1^{2}}+\frac{1}{3^{2}}+\frac{1}{5^{2}}+\cdots =\frac{\pi ^{2}}{8} .
\]














ProblemProblem 16





Find the norm of the Volterra operator \(\mathcal{V}: L^2[0,1] \to L^2[0,1]\), \[
  (\mathcal{V} f)(x) = \int _{0}^{x} f(y) dy
\]
[@VKK, Problem 12.18]

1 The Fourier transform on \(L^{1}(\mathbb {R})\)
In this section \(\mathbb {F} = \mathbb {C}\).
Let \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\). The Fourier transform of \(f\) is a new function from \(\mathbb {R}\) to \(\mathbb {C}\), defined by two similar methods:



\[
  (\mathcal{F}_1f)(\omega ) = \widehat{f}^{1}(\omega ) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }} \int _{\mathbb {R}} f(x) \cdot e^{-i\omega x} \;  dx
\]
This convention is more common in the Russian-language literature.


\[
  (\mathcal{F}_2f)(t) = \widehat{f}^{2}(t) := \int _{\mathbb {R}} f(x) \cdot e^{-2\pi i tx} \;  dx
\]
This convention is more common in the English-language literature.



The inverse Fourier transform of a function \(h \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\) is defined as:



\[
  (\mathcal{F}^{-1}_1 h)(x) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }} \int _{\mathbb {R}} h(\omega ) \cdot e^{i\omega x} \;  d\omega
\]


\[
  (\mathcal{F}^{-1}_2 h)(x) := \int _{\mathbb {R}} h(t) \cdot e^{2 \pi i t x} \;  dt
\]



For now we only define the inverse Fourier transform formally. We do not claim that the Fourier transform is invertible on \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\). In general this is false: as we will see below, the image of the Fourier transform on \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\) falls outside \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\). That is, there exists a function in \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\) whose Fourier transform turns out not to be integrable. However, on certain subspaces of \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\) — for example, on the space of Schwartz test functions \(\mathcal{S}\) — the Fourier transform \(\mathcal{F}_{1,2}\) will be invertible (in particular, the image will not fall outside the space itself), and the inverse will be given by \(\mathcal{F}^{-1}_{1,2}\) defined above.
Let us immediately discuss the relationship between these two ways of defining the Fourier transform:
\[
  \widehat{f}^{1}(\omega ) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }} \cdot \widehat{f}^{2}\left(\frac{\omega }{2\pi }\right), \qquad \widehat{f}^{2}(t) = \sqrt{2\pi } \cdot \widehat{f}^{1}(2\pi t)
\]
In terms of operators: if we define the operator \(\operatorname {DIL}_{b}\) by \((\operatorname {DIL}_b f)(x) = f(bx)\), then
\[
\begin{align}  \mathcal{F}_1 & = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }} \cdot \mathcal{F}_2 \cdot \operatorname {DIL}_{1/2\pi } \\ \mathcal{F}_2 & = \sqrt{2\pi } \cdot \mathcal{F}_1 \cdot \operatorname {DIL}_{2\pi } \end{align}
\]
In what follows, when the notation carries no index, the computation applies to both ways of defining the FT.






ExampleExample 1





Find the Fourier transform of the function

\(f = \; \mathbb {1}_{[b,c]}\), \(b \leq c\);
\(f(x) = e^{-\left|x\right|}\)







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)






\[
  \widehat{f}^{1}(\omega ) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\int _b^c e^{-ix\omega } dx = \begin{cases}  i\frac{e^{-ict} - e^{-ibt}}{t\sqrt{2\pi }}, & \omega \neq 0 \\ \frac{c-b}{\sqrt{2 \pi }}, &  \omega = 0 \end{cases}
\]


\[
  \widehat{f}^{2}(t) = \ldots = \begin{cases}  i\frac{e^{-2\pi i ct} - e^{-2\pi i b t}}{2 \pi t}, &  t \neq 0 \\ c - b, &  t = 0 \end{cases}
\]



In particular, if the interval is symmetric (\(f = \; \mathbb {1}_{[-r,r]}\), \(r > 0\)), then



\[
\begin{align}  \widehat{\; \mathbb {1}_{[-r, r]}}^{1}(\omega ) & = \frac{i}{\omega \sqrt{2\pi }} \left(e^{-ri\omega } - e^{ri\omega }\right) = \\ & = \frac{2i^2}{\omega \sqrt{2\pi }} \cdot \frac{-\left(e^{-ri\omega } - e^{ri\omega }\right)}{2i} = \\ & = \frac{2}{\omega \sqrt{2\pi }} \cdot \sin (r\omega ) = \\ & = \frac{r}{\sqrt{\pi /2}} \cdot \frac{\sin (r \omega )}{r \omega } \end{align}
\] for \(\omega \neq 0\), and for \(\omega = 0\) we have \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi /2}}\). In other words, \[
  \widehat{\; \mathbb {1}_{[-r, r]}}^{1}(\omega ) = \frac{r}{\sqrt{\pi /2}} \cdot \operatorname {sinc}(r\omega )
\]


\[
\begin{align}  \widehat{\; \mathbb {1}_{[-r, r]}}^{2}(t) & = \sqrt{2\pi }\frac{r}{\sqrt{\pi /2}} \cdot \frac{\sin (2\pi r t)}{2\pi rt} = \\ & = 2r \cdot \frac{\sin (2 \pi r t)}{2\pi r t} \end{align}
\] for \(t \neq 0\), and for \(t = 0\) we have \(2r\). In other words, \[
  \widehat{\; \mathbb {1}_{[-r, r]}}^{2}(\omega ) = 2r \cdot \operatorname {sinc}(2\pi rt)
\]









Note

Illustrates the classical “rectangle \(\leftrightarrow\) sinc” pair. Source: courses/nedosh_courses/courses/01-analysis/FA/contents/specials/090/010_rect_sinc_fig.tex










Enum-item(2)






\[
\begin{align}  \widehat{f}^{1}(\omega ) & = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\int _{0}^{+\infty }e^{-x - i\omega x}dx + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }} \int _{-\infty }^{0}e^{x - i\omega x}dx =\\ & = +\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\frac{1}{1 + i\omega } + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\frac{1}{1 - i\omega } = \frac{\sqrt{2/\pi }}{1 + \omega ^2} \end{align}
\]


For the right-hand column it is natural to take \(f(x) = e^{-2\pi \left|x\right|}\) (the analogue of \(e^{-\left|x\right|}\), consistent with the factor \(2\pi\) in \(\mathcal F_2\)): \[
\begin{align}  \widehat{f}^{2}(t) & = \int _{0}^{+\infty }e^{-2\pi x - 2\pi i tx}dx + \int _{-\infty }^{0}e^{2\pi x - 2\pi i tx}dx = \\ & = \frac{1}{2\pi }\frac{1}{1 + it} + \frac{1}{2\pi }\frac{1}{1 - it} = \frac{1}{\pi (1+t^2)} \end{align}
\] (used in example Example 3 below; also verified numerically.)


















Lemma 1 The Fourier transform is a linear map on \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\).







\[
  f(x) = x
\]


\[
  f(x) = x^2
\]










Lemma 2 (Riemann–Lebesgue) Let \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\). Then \(\mathcal{F}_{1,2}f \in C_0(\mathbb {R})\), and moreover



\[
  \left\| \widehat{f}^{1}\right\| _{\infty } \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }} \left\| f\right\| _{1}
\]


\[
  \left\| \widehat{f}^{2}\right\| _{\infty } \leq \left\| f\right\| _{1}
\]



In short: \(\mathcal{F}: L^1(\mathbb {R}) \to C_0(\mathbb {R})\) is a bounded linear map, with



\[
  \left\| \mathcal{F}_1\right\|  \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}
\]


\[
  \left\| \mathcal{F}_2\right\|  \leq 1
\]







Recall that \(C_0(\mathbb {R})\) is the space of continuous functions on \(\mathbb {R}\) that tend to zero at infinity: \(f(x) \xrightarrow [x \to \infty ]{} 0\). Together with the norm \(\left\| f\right\|_{\infty } = \sup_{x \in \mathbb {R}} \left|f\right|\) it forms a Banach space, more precisely a Banach subspace of \(L^\infty (\mathbb {R})\). Moreover, if \(f\in C_0(\mathbb {R})\), then \(f\) is uniformly continuous. That is, the Fourier transform of a function in \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\) is necessarily a uniformly continuous function.






ProblemProblem 1





Prove the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma: \(\mathcal{F}\) is a continuous linear map from \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\) to \(C_0(\mathbb {R})\), with \(\left\| \mathcal{F}\right\|  = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\).
[@BSSH, Problem  17.3]









ProblemProblem 2





Give an example of a function \(f \in L^{1}(\mathbb {R})\) for which \(\widehat{f} \notin L^{1}(\mathbb {R})\).
[@BSSH, Problem  17.4]










Lemma 3 (Derivative of the Fourier transform) Let \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\). Suppose that \(xf(x) =: g(x)\) is also an integrable function: \(g \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\). Then the Fourier transform is continuously differentiable on all of \(\mathbb {R}\), with



\[
  \left(\widehat{f}^{1}\right)' = -i \cdot \widehat{g}^{1}
\]


\[
  \left(\widehat{f}^{2}\right)' = - 2\pi i \cdot \widehat{g}^{2}
\]



In terms of maps: denote by \(M\) multiplication by the identity function, \((Mf)(x) = x\cdot f(x)\). Then if \(f, Mf \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\), we have \(\mathcal{F}_{1,2}f \in C^1(\mathbb {R})\), and for the function \(f\) we have



\[
  D\mathcal{F}_1 = -i \cdot \mathcal{F}_1M
\]


\[
  D\mathcal{F}_2 = -2\pi i \cdot \mathcal{F}_2M
\]



where \(Df := f'\) is the differentiation operator.











Lemma 4 (Fourier transform of a derivative) Let \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\) be a continuously differentiable function whose derivative is also integrable: \(f' \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\). Then



\[
  \widehat{f'}^{1} = i t \cdot \widehat{f}^{1}
\]


\[
  \widehat{f'}^{2} = 2\pi i t \cdot \widehat{f}^{2}
\]



Among other things, this means that \(\widehat{f}^{1,2}(y) = o(1/y)\) as \(y \to \infty\).
In terms of maps: if \(f \in C^1(\mathbb {R})\), \(Df \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\), then for the function \(f\) we have



\[
  \mathcal{F}_1D =i \cdot M\mathcal{F}_1
\]


\[
  \mathcal{F}_2D = 2\pi i \cdot M\mathcal{F}_2
\]













ExampleExample 2





Let



\[
  f(x) = e^{-x^2/2}
\]


\[
  f(x) = e^{-\pi x^2}
\]



Find the Fourier transform of \(f\).






SolutionSolution






Method 1: direct computation. We know the Gaussian integral: \(\int_{-\infty }^{+\infty }e^{-x^2}dx = \sqrt{\pi }\). Then



\[
\begin{align}  \widehat{f}^{1}(\omega ) & = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }} \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } e^{- x^2/2} \cdot e^{-i \omega x} \;  dx = \\ & = \frac{e^{-\frac{1}{2}\omega ^2}}{\sqrt{2\pi }} \;  \cdot \;  \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(x + i\omega \right)^2} \;  dx = \\ & = \frac{e^{-\frac{1}{2}\omega ^2}\cdot \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi }} \cdot \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left(x + it\right)^2} \;  d\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(x + it\right)\right) = \\ & = e^{-\frac{1}{2}\omega ^2} \end{align}
\]


\[
\begin{align}  \widehat{f}^{2}(t) & = \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } e^{-\pi x^2} \cdot e^{-2\pi i t x} \;  dx = \\ & = e^{-\pi t^2} \;  \cdot \;  \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } e^{-\pi \left(x + it\right)^2} \;  dx = \\ & = e^{-\pi t^2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi }} \cdot \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } e^{-\pi \left(x + it\right)^2} \;  d\left(\sqrt{\pi }\left(x + it\right)\right) = \\ & = e^{-\pi t^2} \end{align}
\]



Method 2: via derivatives. We know that \(g(x) = xe^{-\pi x^2}\) is integrable on all of \(\mathbb {R}\). Hence
\[
\begin{align}  \left(\widehat{f}^{2}\right)'(t) & = - 2\pi i \widehat{g}^{2}(t) = -2\pi i \cdot \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty }xe^{-\pi x^2} \cdot e^{-2\pi i t x} \;  dx = \\ & = \underbrace{\left(ie^{-\pi x^2} \cdot e^{-2\pi i t x}\right)\bigg\rvert _{x=-\infty }^{x=+\infty }}_{=0} \quad - \quad 2\pi t \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } e^{-\pi x^2} \cdot e^{-2\pi i t x} \;  dx = \\ & = -2\pi t \widehat{f}^{2}(t) \end{align}
\]
for every \(t \in \mathbb {R}\). Moreover, \(f'(t) = -2\pi i e^{\pi t^2} = -2\pi t f(t)\). Hence,
\[
  \left(\frac{\widehat{f}^{2}}{f}\right)'(t) = \frac{f(t) \cdot \left(\widehat{f}^{2}\right)'(t) - f'(t) \cdot \widehat{f}^{2}(t)}{f^2(t)} = -2\pi t \frac{f(t) \widehat{f}^{2}(t) - f(t) \widehat{f}^{2}(t)}{f^2(t)} = 0
\]
for all \(t \in \mathbb {R}\). Hence \(\frac{\widehat{f}^{2}}{f}\) is a constant: there exists \(c\in \mathbb {C}\) such that \(\frac{\widehat{f}^{2}(t)}{f(t)} = c\) for all \(t \in \mathbb {R}\). That is, \(\widehat{f}^{2}(t) = cf(t)\).
Let us find \(c\):
\[
  \widehat{f}^{2}(0) = \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } e^{-\pi x^2} \;  dx = f(0)
\]
Hence \(c = 1\).










AnswerAnswer





\(\widehat{f} = f\).













Lemma 5 (The Fourier transform versus translation, modulation, and dilation) Let \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\), \(b \in \mathbb {R}\), \(t \in \mathbb {R}\). Then

If \(g(x) := f(x - b)\), then



\[
  \widehat{g}^{1}(t) = e^{-i b t} \cdot \widehat{f}^{1}(t)
\]


\[
  \widehat{g}^{2}(t) = e^{-2\pi i b t} \cdot \widehat{f}^{2}(t)
\]






If \(g(x) := e^{i b x} \cdot f(x)\), then \[
  \widehat{g}^{1}(t) =\widehat{f}^{1}(t - b)
\]


If \(g(x) := e^{2\pi i b x} \cdot f(x)\), then \[
  \widehat{g}^{2}(t) =\widehat{f}^{2}(t - b)
\]



If \(b \neq 0\) and \(g(x) := f(bx)\), then



\[
  \widehat{g}^{1}(\omega ) =\frac{1}{\left|b\right|}\widehat{f}^{1}\left(\frac{\omega }{b}\right)
\]


\[
  \widehat{g}^{2}(t) =\frac{1}{\left|b\right|}\widehat{f}^{2}\left(\frac{t}{b}\right)
\]














ExampleExample 3





Let \(y > 0\) be an arbitrary fixed number, and let



\[
  h(t) = e^{-y \left|t\right|} \cdot e^{i x t}
\]


\[
  h(t) = e^{-2\pi y \left|t\right|} \cdot e^{2\pi i x t}
\tag{1}\]



i.e., this is a modulation of the exponential function. Find the Fourier transform of \(h\).






SolutionSolution








Let \(g(t) = e^{-y \left|t\right|}\), and let \(f(t) = e^{-\left|t\right|}\). Then \[
  g(t) = f(yt), \qquad h(t) = e^{i x t} \cdot g(t)
\]

From the example above we know that \(\widehat{f}^{1}(\omega ) = \frac{\sqrt{2/\pi }}{\omega^2 + 1}\);
\(g(t) = f(yt)\), so \(\widehat{g}^{1}(t) = \frac{1}{y}\widehat{f}^{1}\left(\frac{\omega }{y}\right) = \frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2/\pi }y}{\omega^2 + y^2}\);
\(h(t) = e^{i x t} \cdot g(t)\), so \(\widehat{h}^{1}(t) = \widehat{g}^{1}(t - x)\).



Let \(g(t) = e^{-2\pi y \left|t\right|}\), and let \(f(t) = e^{-2\pi \left|t\right|}\). Then \[
  g(t) = f(yt), \qquad h(t) = e^{2\pi i x t} \cdot g(t)
\]

From the example above we know that \(\widehat{f}^{2}(t) = \frac{1}{\pi (t^2 + 1)}\);
\(g(t) = f(yt)\), so \(\widehat{g}^{2}(t) = \frac{1}{y}\widehat{f}^{2}\left(\frac{t}{y}\right) = \frac{1}{\pi } \frac{y^2}{t^2 + y^2}\);
\(h(t) = e^{2\pi i x t} \cdot g(t)\), so \(\widehat{h}^{2}(t) = \widehat{g}^{2}(t - x)\).













AnswerAnswer








\[
  \widehat{h}^{1}(t) = \frac{\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi }} y}{(t - x)^2 + y^2}
\]


\[
  \widehat{h}^{2}(t) = \frac{1}{\pi } \frac{y}{(t - x)^2 + y^2}
\]
















Lemma 6 (Integral of a function multiplied by the Fourier transform) Let \(f, g \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\). Then \[
  \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } \widehat{f}(t) \cdot g(t) \;  dt = \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } f(t) \cdot \widehat{g}(t) \;  dt =
\tag{2}\] (this formula holds for both ways of defining the Fourier transform).






2 Convolution on \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\)
Our goal is to prove the Fourier inversion formula: if \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\) and \(\mathcal{F}_{1,2}{f} \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\), then



\[
  f = \mathcal{F}_{1}^{-1} \mathcal{F}_{1} f
\]


\[
  f = \mathcal{F}_{2}^{-1} \mathcal{F}_{2} f
\tag{3}\]



for almost every \(x \in \mathbb {R}\). In other words,



\[
  f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } \widehat{f}^{1}(\omega ) \cdot e^{i x \omega } d\omega
\]


\[
  f(x) = \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } \widehat{f}^{2}(t) \cdot e^{2\pi i x t} dt
\]



To understand this equality, fix \(x\) and try to express the right-hand side in terms of \(f\). Direct application of formula Equation 2 is impossible, since the function



\[
\omega \mapsto e^{ix\omega }
\]


\[
t \mapsto e^{2\pi ixt}
\]



does not lie in \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\). We therefore introduce a smoothing factor: for fixed \(y>0\), consider



\[
  \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }\widehat{f}^{1}(\omega ) \cdot \underbrace{e^{-y|\omega |} \cdot e^{ix\omega }}_{=: h(t)}\; d\omega \enclose {circle}{=}
\]


\[
  \int _{-\infty }^{\infty }\widehat{f}^{2}(t) \cdot \underbrace{e^{-2\pi y|t|} \cdot e^{2\pi ixt}}_{=: h(t)}\; dt \enclose {circle}{=}
\tag{4}\]



Here \(t \mapsto e^{-y|t|}\) (resp. \(t \mapsto e^{-2\pi y|t|}\)) and \(h\) itself lie in \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\), and as \(y \downarrow 0\) we have



\[
  e^{-y|\omega |} \xrightarrow []{} 1 \quad \text{ and } \quad h(\omega ) \xrightarrow []{} e^{i x \omega }
\]


\[
  e^{-2\pi y|t|} \xrightarrow []{} 1 \quad \text{ and } \quad h(t) \xrightarrow []{} e^{2\pi i x t}
\]



That is, formula Equation 4 is a good approximation of the right-hand side in Equation 3. Let us expand:



\[
\begin{align}  & \enclose {circle}{=} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\int _{-\infty }^{\infty } \widehat{f}^{1}(\omega ) \cdot h(\omega ) \;  d\omega = \\ & \text{ (using formula \ref{FourierTransform:DualityFormula})}\\ & = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }f(\omega ) \cdot \widehat{h}^{1}(\omega ) = \\ & \text{ (using example \ref{FourierTransform:ExpRotatedFourierTr})}\\ & = \int _{-\infty }^{\infty }f(\omega ) \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\pi }\frac{y}{(x-\omega )^2 + y^2}}_{=:P_y(x-\omega )} \;  d\omega \\ & = \int _{-\infty }^{\infty }f(\omega ) \cdot P_y(x-\omega ) \;  d\omega \end{align}
\]


\[
\begin{align}  & \enclose {circle}{=} \int _{-\infty }^{\infty } \widehat{f}^{2}(t) \cdot h(t) \;  dt = \\ & \text{ (using formula \ref{FourierTransform:DualityFormula})}\\ & = \int _{-\infty }^{\infty }f(t) \cdot \widehat{h}^{2}(t) = \\ & \text{ (using example \ref{FourierTransform:ExpRotatedFourierTr})}\\ & = \int _{-\infty }^{\infty }f(t) \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\pi }\frac{y}{(x-t)^2 + y^2}}_{=:P_y(x-t)} \;  dt \\ & = \int _{-\infty }^{\infty }f(t) \cdot P_y(x-t) \;  dt \end{align}
\]



The function \(P_y: \mathbb {R} \to (0,+\infty )\), defined by \(P_y(x) = \frac{1}{\pi }\frac{y}{x^2 + y^2}\), is called the Poisson kernel. The formula obtained leads us to study integrals of the form
\[
  \int _{-\infty }^{\infty } f(t) \cdot g(x-t)\; dt,
\]
that is, convolutions.







Definition 1 Let \(f,g : \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {C}\) be measurable functions. The convolution of \(f\) and \(g\) is the function \[
  \left(f \ast g\right)(x) := \int _{-\infty }^{+\infty } f(t) \cdot g(x-t) \;  dt
\]











Lemma 7 If \(f, g \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\), then \(f \ast g\) is defined for almost every \(x \in \mathbb {R}\), \(f \ast g \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\), and \[
  \left\| f \ast g\right\| _{1} \leq \left\| f\right\| _{1} \cdot \left\| g\right\| _{1}
\]




If \(p \in (1, \infty ]\), then neither \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\) nor \(L^p(\mathbb {R})\) is a subset of the other. Thus we do not yet know whether the expression \(f * g\) makes sense for \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\) and \(g \in L^p(\mathbb {R})\). However, the following result, a strengthening of the previous lemma, shows that everything works out.







Lemma 8 (The \(L^p\)-norm of a convolution) Let \(1\leq p \leq \infty\), \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\), \(g \in L^p(\mathbb {R})\). Then \((f \ast g)(x)\) is defined for almost every \(x \in \mathbb {R}\) (with respect to Lebesgue measure), and
\[
  \left\| f \ast g\right\| _{p} \leq \left\| f\right\| _{1} \cdot \left\| g\right\| _{p}
\]











Lemma 9 (Convolution is commutative) Let \(f,g : \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {C}\) be measurable functions, \(x \in \mathbb {R}\), and suppose \((f \ast g)(x)\) is defined. Then \[
  (f \ast g)(x) = (g \ast f)(x)
\]











Lemma 10 (Convolution versus the Fourier transform) Let \(f,g \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\). Then



\[
  \widehat{f \ast g}^{1} = \sqrt{2\pi } \cdot \widehat{f}^{1} \cdot \widehat{g}^{1}
\]


\[
  \widehat{f \ast g}^{2} = \widehat{f}^{2} \cdot \widehat{g}^{2}
\]













ProblemProblem 3





Let \(f, g \in L^{1}(\mathbb {R})\).

Prove Lemma Lemma 7: \(f * g \in L^{1}(\mathbb {R})\) and \(\left\| f \ast g\right\|_{1} \leq \left\| f\right\|_{1} \cdot \left\| g\right\|_{1}\);
Prove Lemma Lemma 9: \(f * g = g * f\).

[@BSSH, Problem  18.2]









ProblemProblem 4





Prove Lemma Lemma 10: if \(f, g \in L^{1}(\mathbb {R})\), then \[
\widehat{f * g}^{1} = \sqrt{2 \pi } \cdot \widehat{f}^{1} \cdot \widehat{g}^{1}
\]
[@BSSH, Problem  18.8]





3 The inverse Fourier transform







Theorem 1 If \(f, \widehat{f} \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\), then \[
  f = \mathcal{F}^{-1}f
\] Equivalently: \[
  f(x) = \widehat{\widehat{f}}(-x)
\]










ExampleExample 4 - The Fourier transform of the Poisson kernel





Find \(\widehat{P_y}^{2}\), where \(P_y(t) = \frac{1}{\pi } \frac{y}{t^2 + y^2}\), \(y > 0\) an arbitrary fixed number.






SolutionSolution





From example Example 3 we know that the Poisson kernel is the Fourier transform of the function \(h_y(t) = e^{-2\pi y \left|t\right|}\). Moreover \(h_y, P_y \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\). Hence \[
  \widehat{P_y}(t) = \widehat{\widehat{h}}(t) = h(-t) = e^{-2 \pi y \left|t\right|}
\]













Lemma 11 A function in \(L^1\) can be uniquely recovered from its Fourier transform. In other words, \(\mathcal{F}: L^1(\mathbb {R}) \to C_{0}(\mathbb {R})\) is an injective map.










ExampleExample 5





Prove the injectivity of \(\mathcal{F}\).






SolutionSolution





Since \(\mathcal{F}\) is a linear map, it suffices to prove that no function other than zero maps to zero. Suppose \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\) and \(\widehat{f} \equiv 0\). But then \(\widehat{f} \in L^1\) and the inverse transform applies: \(f = \mathcal{F}^{-1}f = 0\).












ExampleExample 6





Prove that convolution is associative: \[
  \left(f \ast g\right) \ast h = f \ast \left(g \ast h\right)
\] for all \(f,g,h \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\).






SolutionSolution





This result could be proved directly, using the definition of convolution together with the Tonelli/Fubini theorems. However, the following elegant proof deserves attention.
The Fourier transform turns the left-hand and right-hand sides into



\[
  2\pi \cdot \widehat{f}^{1} \cdot \widehat{g}^{1} \cdot \widehat{h}^{1}
\]


\[
  \widehat{f}^{2} \cdot \widehat{g}^{2} \cdot \widehat{h}^{2}
\]



(we no longer include parentheses, since ordinary multiplication is associative). Moreover, the Fourier transform is an injective map. Hence the original elements are equal as well.








4 The Fourier transform on \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\)
Recall that neither \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\) embeds into \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\), nor conversely.







Theorem 2 (Plancherel; the FT preserves the 2-norm) Let \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R}) \cap L^2(\mathbb {R})\). Then \[
  \left\| f\right\| _{2} = \left\| \mathcal{F}f\right\| _{2}
\]




Note that \(L^1(\mathbb {R}) \cap L^2(\mathbb {R})\) is everywhere dense in \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\). Indeed, let \(f \in L^2(\mathbb {R})\) be an arbitrary element of \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\), and let \(f_n := f \cdot \; \mathbb {1}_{[-n,n]}\). Then the restriction of \(f_n\) to \([-n,n]\) lies in \(L^2[-n,n]\), and hence also in \(L^1[-n,n]\), so \(f_n \in L^1(\mathbb {R}) \cap L^2(\mathbb {R})\). Moreover,
\[
  f_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{L^2(\mathbb {R})} f
\]
Indeed, let \(g_n = \left|f - f_n\right|^2 = \left|f\right|^2 \cdot \; \mathbb {1}_{[-n,n]^{\complement }}\). Then \(g_n \geq 0\) for all \(n\), \(g_n\) decreases monotonically pointwise to zero, and \(\left|g_n\right| \leq \left|f\right|^2\) for all \(n\), where \(\left|f\right|^2\) is integrable. Then, by the dominated convergence theorem, \(g_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{L^1(\mathbb {R})} 0\).







Definition 2 The Fourier transform \(\mathcal{F}\) on \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\) is the continuous extension of the FT from \(L^1(\mathbb {R}) \cap L^2(\mathbb {R})\) to \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\).
The inverse Fourier transform \(\mathcal{F}^{-1}\) is defined analogously.




Suppose \(f \in L^2(\mathbb {R})\) and \(f \not\in L^1(\mathbb {R})\). One should not mistakenly assume that



\[
  \widehat{f}^{1}(\omega ) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\int _{-\infty }^{\infty } f(x) e^{-i\omega x} d x
\]


\[
  \widehat{f}^{2}(t) = \int _{-\infty }^{\infty } f(x) e^{-2 \pi i t x} d x
\]



Indeed, the integral above is meaningless, since the modulus of the function under the integral coincides with \(\left|f\right|\) and \(f \notin L^1(\mathbb {R})\). Instead of defining \(\mathcal{F} f\) via the equation above, \(\mathcal{F} f\) must be defined as the limit in \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\) of the sequence \(\mathcal{F}f_1, \mathcal{F}f_2, \ldots\), where \(f_1, f_2, \ldots\) is a sequence in \(L^1(\mathbb {R}) \cap L^2(\mathbb {R})\) such that
\[
  \left\| f - f_n\right\| _{2} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} 0
\]
For example, one can take \(f_n=f \cdot \; \mathbb {1}_{[-n,n]}\). That is, the FT for \(f \in L^2(\mathbb {R})\) can be defined as



\[
  \widehat{f}^{1}(\omega ) = \lim _{n \to +\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }} \int _{-n}^{n} f(x) \cdot e^{-i\omega x} \;  dx
\]


\[
  \widehat{f}^{2}(t) = \lim _{n \to +\infty } \int _{-n}^{n} f(x) \cdot e^{-2\pi it x} \;  dx
\]



Since \(\mathcal{F}\) is obtained by continuously extending [in the norm of \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\)] the Fourier transform from \(L^1(\mathbb {R}) \cap L^2(\mathbb {R})\) to \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\), we know that \(\| \mathcal{F} f\|_2=\| f\|_2\) for all \(f \in L^2(\mathbb {R})\). In other words, \(\mathcal{F}\) is an isometry on \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\). The following result shows that a much stronger statement holds: \(\mathcal{F}\) is a unitary operator.







Theorem 3 (Properties of the FT on \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\)) Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be the FT on \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\).

\(\mathcal{F}\) is a unitary operator on \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\). In more detail:

The image of \(\mathcal{F}\) on \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\) lies entirely in \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\), i.e., \(\mathcal{F}: L^2(\mathbb {R}) \to L^2(\mathbb {R})\);
\(\mathcal{F}\) is a bounded linear operator on \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\);
\(\mathcal{F}\) is invertible, and its inverse is the inverse Fourier transform \(\mathcal{F}^{-1}\);
\(\mathcal{F}^{-1} = \mathcal{F}^{*}\), i.e., \(\mathcal{F}^{*}\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{F}\mathcal{F}^{*} = I\).

\(\mathcal{F}^2 = \mathcal{R}\), where \((\mathcal{R}f)(x) := f(-x)\) is the operator reflecting a function about the vertical axis. As a consequence we obtain \(\mathcal{F}^{4} = I\).
\(\sigma (\mathcal{F}) = \left\{ 1,i, -1, -i\right\}\).











ProblemProblem 5





Is the Fourier transform \(\mathcal{F}\) a compact operator in the case

\(\mathcal{F}: L^{2}(\mathbb {R}) \rightarrow L^{2}(\mathbb {R})\),
\(\mathcal{F}: L^{1}(\mathbb {R}) \rightarrow C_b(\mathbb {R})\).

[@VKK, Problem  12.10]





5 The Fourier transform on \(\mathcal{S}\) and on \(\mathcal{S}'\)
By definition \(f \in \mathcal{S}\) if \(f\) is infinitely continuously differentiable, and \(f\) together with every derivative of it decays at infinity to zero faster than any polynomial. This is equivalent to saying that \(f\) is infinitely differentiable and all of its seminorms are finite:
\[
  p_{n,k}(f) := \sup _{t \in \mathbb {R}} \left|t^n \cdot f^{(k)}(t)\right|, \qquad n,k \in \mathbb {Z}_+ = \left\{ 0,1,2,\ldots \right\}
\]
In terms of operators:
\[
  p_{n,k}(f) = \left\| M^n D^k f\right\| _{\infty }
\]
where \((Mf)(t) = t \cdot f(t)\), \(Df = f'\).
It is easy to show that \(\mathcal{S}\) is contained in both \(L^1(\mathbb {R})\) and \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\).






ProblemProblem 6





Prove that \(\mathcal{F}\) is an isomorphism of the space \(\mathcal{S}\) onto itself, with \(\mathcal{F}^{-1} \mathcal{F}= I\).
[@BSSH, Problem  17.12*]









ProblemProblem 7





Prove that for any functions \(f, g \in \mathcal{S}\) Parseval’s identity holds: \[
  \left\langle f, g \right\rangle = \left\langle \widehat{f}, \widehat{g} \right\rangle
\] (the inner product is taken in \(L^2(\mathbb {R})\))
[@BSSH, Problem  17.20]









ProblemProblem 8





Prove that in the spaces \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(L^{2}(\mathbb {R})\) the following identities hold:

\(\left(\mathcal{F}^{2} f\right)(x) = f(-x)\);
\(\mathcal{F}^{4} = I\).

[@BSSH, Problem  17.23]

title: Functional Analysis
text:
A course in functional analysis: from metric and topological spaces to operators on Hilbert spaces and nonlinear analysis. The course builds up a hierarchy of abstract spaces (metric → Banach → Hilbert), introduces Lebesgue spaces \(L^p\) and generalized functions, studies bounded operators and weak convergence, the Fourier transform, and concludes with elements of nonlinear analysis.
Information about the course from open MIPT sources (semester, workload, department, exam syllabi, point-based grading scheme) is collected on the “Course passport” page.

title: Differential Equations
text:
Contents of the published program
The department published a link to the program of the “all except LFI” version, which covers FPMI, but when checked the page returns 404. Therefore its contents are not reconstructed and are not presented as current. The complete available official version is A. O. Remizov’s program for LFI, 2024/25; this is an adjacent stream, not the FPMI program. Its full list is given here so that the information does not remain only in a PDF:

Basic notions of the theory of differential equations: phase spaces, solutions, phase and integral curves, vector fields, singular points, first integrals, Pfaffian systems, autonomous systems and the phase flow.
Exact and closed 1-forms, the Poincaré lemma, exact differential equations and the integrating factor.
The main types of first-order differential equations and methods of reducing the order.
Linear equations with constant coefficients, quasi-polynomials, the Euler–Cauchy equation.
Newton’s equations, the first integral, the Hamiltonian form and the phase portrait.
Linear systems with continuous coefficients, extendability and the general solution.
The fundamental matrix, the Wronskian and the Liouville–Ostrogradsky formula.
Inhomogeneous systems and the method of variation of constants.
Boundary value problems for linear equations and the alternative theorem.
Sturm’s zero and comparison theorem.
Linear systems with constant coefficients, the matrix exponential.
The Cauchy problem, the Lipschitz condition, existence and uniqueness, examples of non-existence and non-uniqueness.
The existence and uniqueness theorem in the analytic case and the method of majorants.
Extendable and non-extendable solutions, leaving a compact set, extendability of linear systems.
Continuous dependence of solutions on parameters and initial conditions.
Hadamard’s lemma.
Smooth dependence, the first variation and expansion in a parameter.
Straightening theorems.
First integrals of an autonomous system and local existence of a complete set of independent integrals.
Linear homogeneous first-order partial differential equations: general solution and the Cauchy problem.
Linear inhomogeneous first-order partial differential equations.
Quasilinear first-order equations, the Cauchy problem and multivalued solutions.
Lyapunov stability, asymptotic stability, Lyapunov and Chetaev functions.
Limit points and limit sets, the Barbashin–Krasovskii theorem, the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem.
Monodromy and limit cycles, structurally stable and structurally unstable cycles.
Necessary conditions for the existence of cycles: the Bendixson–Dulac theorem and indices of singular points.
Sufficient conditions for the existence of cycles and Poincaré’s topographic system.
Implicit first-order differential equations, the method of introducing a parameter, cusps and envelopes.
The Legendre transform and Clairaut’s equation.
The simplest problem of the calculus of variations and problems with one or two constraints.

title: Multiple Integrals and Field Theory
text:
Contents of the published program
Below is the complete list of sections from V. V. Redkozubov’s published exam program for 2025. The wording is condensed but keeps all 27 items of the document.

Cavalieri’s principle and the measure of the subgraph of a function.
The Tonelli and Fubini theorems; volume of the \(n\)-dimensional ball.
An estimate of the measure of the image of a measurable set, and change of variables in the Lebesgue integral.
The Banach fixed-point theorem.
The inverse function theorem for a nonzero Jacobian, openness of the map, and curvilinear coordinates.
The implicit function theorem and differentiation of the implicit function.
Smooth manifolds in \(\mathbb R^n\): graph, local straightening, and definition by a system of equations.
Smooth maps of manifolds, smoothness of the inverse parametrization and of transition maps; checking smoothness in coordinates.
Tangent space and tangent plane: equivalent definitions.
Differential of a smooth map and regular value.
Local extrema.
Constrained extrema and the method of Lagrange multipliers.
Measurable sets on a manifold and surface measure.
Integral of a measurable function over a manifold; line and surface integrals of the first kind.
The area formula and the total surface measure of the sphere.
Differential 1-forms, integration along a curve, exactness, local exactness, path independence, homotopy and simple connectedness.
Alternating \(k\)-forms, basis, exterior product and linear pullback of forms.
Forms on an open subset of \(\mathbb R^m\), smoothness, pullback of a form, and transformation of higher-degree forms under a diffeomorphism.
The exterior differential and its commutation with the pullback of a form.
Differential forms on manifolds, two definitions of smoothness, and the exterior differential.
Smooth partition of unity.
Regular domains, their boundary, and definition by inequalities.
Orientable manifolds, orientation of the boundary, and orientation when defined by an equation.
Integration of differential forms, change of variables, integration over a measurable set; line and surface integrals of the second kind.
Stokes’ theorem and its special cases in \(\mathbb R^3\).
Closed and exact forms, the Poincaré lemma.
Applications of the methods of vector analysis.

title: Optimization Methods
text:
Contents
No separate published syllabus specifically for FPMI has been found. As adjacent material, not identical to FPMI, V. F. Demyanov’s program for PISh FALT, spring 2026, has been published. Its full list of topics:

The Lagrange function and the Lagrange principle. Necessary condition for an extremum, degenerate problems and a Jacobian of incomplete rank, the meaning of the multipliers; inequalities, complementary slackness, nonnegativity and the Karush–John theorem.
Calculus of variations. The Lagrange principle, the Euler–Lagrange equation, the Bolza conditions, variable endpoints, multipliers and the generalized Karush–John theorem.
Minimal surfaces. The Euler–Lagrange equation for functions of several variables, the problem of minimizing a functional, quadratic forms, normal and Gaussian curvatures, linearization and examples.
Optimal control. Problem formulation, the Lagrange principle and Pontryagin’s maximum principle.
Convex optimization. Convex sets and hulls, simplices, convex and strongly convex functionals, Jensen’s inequality, the Minkowski functional, the Hahn–Banach theorem, separation, Kuhn–Tucker and Slater’s condition.
Duality. The Legendre transform, the Fenchel–Moreau and Moreau–Rockafellar theorems, the subdifferential, the dual problem, the saddle point and a criterion for the solutions of the primal and dual problems to coincide.
Numerical methods. Gradient and steepest descent, Newton’s method, local minima and simulated annealing, Tikhonov regularization and the pseudoinverse matrix, the genetic algorithm.
