title: Algebra and Geometry
text:
Contents of the published program
Below are all items of the two published programs of I. I. Bogdanov’s stream: winter 2025 and summer 2026. The wording is condensed, but the list is not a selection.

Semester I: analytic geometry

Collinear and coplanar vectors, linear operations, dependence and independence, bases and coordinates, change of basis.
Cartesian and orthonormal coordinate systems, coordinates of a directed segment, ways of specifying a line and a segment, transition between coordinate systems.
The scalar product in an orthonormal and in an arbitrary basis, orthogonal projection, distances and angles.
Orientation in the plane and in space, oriented area and volume (the scalar triple product).
The vector product and the vector triple product, criteria of collinearity and coplanarity.
Equations of sets, polynomials in several variables, algebraic curves and surfaces, preservation of the degree under a change of coordinates.
A line in the plane: ways of specifying it, distance to a point, intersection, parallelism and pencils of lines.
A plane in space: ways of specifying it, parallelism, intersection and pencils of planes.
A line in space, relative position of lines, distances to a plane and between skew lines.
Ellipse, hyperbola and parabola: canonical equations, foci, directrices, asymptotes, conjugate diameters and tangents.
Second-order curves: classification, reduction to canonical form, the center of a curve.
The main types of second-order surfaces.



Semester I: linear spaces, matrices and determinants

Matrices, operations on them and their properties.
Groups, rings and fields; complex numbers, characteristic and the prime subfield; permutations and their sign; isomorphisms, Cayley’s theorem, cyclic groups and Lagrange’s theorem.
Linear spaces, dependent and independent systems, subspaces and linear span.
Systems of linear equations: elementary transformations, row echelon form, the fundamental system and the general solution.
Basis, dimension, isomorphism, coordinates and the change-of-basis matrix; cardinalities of a finite vector space and of a finite field.
Rank of a system and of a matrix, basis minor, the Kronecker–Capelli theorem, invertible matrices and how to find the inverse.
Sum, intersection and direct sum of subspaces; the relation between dimensions.
Linear functionals, the dual space, the dual basis, the canonical embedding into the double dual space, and annihilators.
Linear maps: matrix, kernel, image, injectivity, operations and change of bases.
Multilinear and skew-symmetric functions, the determinant, its properties, expansions and Cramer’s rule.



Semester II

Polynomials over a field: division with remainder, GCD and the Euclidean algorithm, irreducibility and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.
Roots of polynomials, Bézout’s theorem, the formal derivative and multiple roots.
Invariant subspaces, eigenvectors and eigenvalues, the characteristic polynomial, determinant and trace of an operator.
Linear independence of eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues, multiplicities and diagonalizability.
Cyclic subspaces and the Cayley–Hamilton theorem.
Annihilating polynomials, root subspaces and their direct sum.
The Jordan normal form, its uniqueness, how to find it, and its relation to the minimal polynomial.
Linear recurrences over a field.
Bilinear forms, their matrices and change of basis.
Symmetric and skew-symmetric forms, kernel and orthogonal complement.
Quadratic forms and Lagrange’s method of reduction to diagonal form.
Positive definite forms, indices of inertia, the law of inertia, Jacobi’s method and Sylvester’s criterion.
The canonical form of a skew-symmetric bilinear form.
Sesquilinear, Hermitian and Hermitian quadratic forms; canonical form, the law of inertia and Sylvester’s criterion.
Euclidean and Hermitian spaces, the Gram matrix, the Cauchy–Bunyakovsky and triangle inequalities.
Orthonormal bases, orthogonal and unitary matrices, isomorphisms; the canonical isomorphism with the dual space.
Orthogonal complement and projection, the Gram–Schmidt process, volume of a parallelepiped.
The relation between forms and linear transformations, the adjoint operator and the Fredholm theorem.
Self-adjoint operators and an orthonormal basis of their eigenvectors.
Orthogonal and unitary operators, their canonical form and the polar decomposition.
Principal axes of a quadratic form and simultaneous diagonalization of a pair of quadratic forms.
Tensors as multilinear maps, the tensor product and coordinate notation.
Operations on tensors: contraction, permutation of indices, symmetrization and alternation.

title: Preface. Complexity classes. NP-hard problems
text:
ExampleExample 1





Consider the languages \[
\begin{align}  \mathrm{HAMPATH} & = \left\{ \langle G\rangle \;  : \;  G = (V,E) \text{ is a digraph with a Hamiltonian path}\right\}  \\ \mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st} & = \left\{ \langle G, s, t\rangle \;  : \;  G = (V,E), \;  s,t \in V, \text{the digraph $G$ has a Hamiltonian path from $s$ to $t$}\right\}  \\ \mathrm{HAMCYCLE} & = \left\{ \langle G\rangle \;  : \;  G = (V,E) \text{ is a digraph with a Hamiltonian cycle}\right\}  \\ \mathrm{UHAMPATH} & = \left\{ \langle G\rangle \;  : \;  G = (V,E) \text{ is an undirected graph with a Hamiltonian path}\right\}  \\ \mathrm{UHAMPATH}_{st} & = \left\{ \langle G, s, t\rangle \;  : \;  G = (V,E), \;  s,t \in V, \text{the undirected graph $G$ has a Hamiltonian path from $s$ to $t$}\right\}  \\ \mathrm{UHAMCYCLE} & = \left\{ \langle G\rangle \;  : \;  G = (V,E), \text{the undirected graph $G$ has a Hamiltonian cycle}\right\}  \\ \end{align}
\] Reduce these languages to one another in polynomial time.






SolutionSolution






\(\mathrm{HAMPATH} \stackrel{?}{\leq }_p \mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st}\).


  Reduction of \(\mathrm{HAMPATH}\) to \(\mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st}\)
  We add vertices \(s'\) and \(t'\), connected to all vertices of the graph (red arcs from \(s'\), green ones into \(t'\)), plus the endpoints \(s\to s'\), \(t'\to t\). The steps show the construction; hover over a vertex to highlight its arcs.
  
  
    
    ⟶
    
  
  



\(\mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st} \stackrel{?}{\leq }_p \mathrm{HAMPATH}\).


  Reduction of \(\mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st}\) to \(\mathrm{HAMPATH}\)
  We add a vertex \(s'\) with the single arc \(s'\to s\) and a vertex \(t'\) with the single arc \(t\to t'\). Hover over a vertex to see its degrees and highlight its arcs.
  
  
    
    ⟶
    
  
  



\(\mathrm{HAMPATH} \stackrel{?}{\leq }_p \mathrm{HAMCYCLE}\) (and similarly \(\mathrm{UHAMPATH} \leq_p \mathrm{UHAMCYCLE}\)).


  Reduction of \(\mathrm{HAMPATH}\) to \(\mathrm{HAMCYCLE}\)
  We add a new vertex \(s\), connected by arcs in both directions to every vertex of the graph: \(s\to v\) (red) and \(v\to s\) (green). Hover over \(s\) to highlight all of its arcs.
  
  
    
    ⟶
    
  
  



\(\mathrm{HAMCYCLE} \stackrel{?}{\leq }_p \mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st}\) (the same construction also gives \(\mathrm{HAMCYCLE} \leq_p \mathrm{HAMPATH}\)).


  Reduction of \(\mathrm{HAMCYCLE}\) to \(\mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st}\)
  Take an arbitrary vertex \(v_1\) and duplicate it: the new vertex \(v_1'\) receives the same arcs (red). Then add \(s\) and \(t\) with arcs \(s\to v_1'\) and \(v_1\to t\) (green). Hover over \(v_1\) and \(v_1'\) to compare their arcs.
  
  
    
    ⟶
    
  
  



\(\mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st} \stackrel{?}{\leq }_p \mathrm{UHAMPATH}_{st}\).


  Reduction of \(\mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st}\) (digraph) to \(\mathrm{UHAMPATH}_{st}\) (undirected graph)
  We split every vertex \(v\) other than \(s\) and \(t\) into a triple \(v^{\mathrm{in}}-v^{\mathrm{mid}}-v^{\mathrm{out}}\); for \(s\) we keep only \(s^{\mathrm{out}}\), and for \(t\) only \(t^{\mathrm{in}}\). An arc \(u\to v\) becomes an edge \(\{u^{\mathrm{out}},v^{\mathrm{in}}\}\). Hover over a vertex of the lower graph to see which vertex of the original digraph it corresponds to.
  
  
  
  
  



\(\mathrm{UHAMPATH}_{st} \stackrel{?}{\leq }_p \mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st}\).


  Reduction of \(\mathrm{UHAMPATH}_{st}\) to \(\mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st}\)
  We replace every edge \(\{u,v\}\) by a pair of opposing arcs \(u\to v\) and \(v\to u\); the vertices, including \(s\) and \(t\), stay the same. The button below traces the same Hamiltonian \(s\)–\(t\) path in both graphs: on the left along edges, on the right along the arcs pointing the right way.
  Show the Hamiltonian pathHide
  
    
    ⟶
    
  
  














ExampleExample 2





Show that deciding whether a graph contains a clique of a given size is an NP-hard problem.






SolutionSolution





We prove
\[
  \mathrm{3SAT} \leq _p \mathrm{CLIQUE}
\]
where
\[
  \mathrm{CLIQUE} = \left\{ \langle G,k\rangle \;  : \;  \text{$G$ is an undirected graph, $k \in \mathbb {N}$, and $G$ has a clique of size $k$}\right\}
\]
Let \(\phi\) be a 3-CNF formula with \(k\) clauses \(c_1, \ldots , c_k\). From it we build a graph \(G\): for each clause \(c_i = (a_i \lor b_i \lor d_i)\) we introduce a triple of vertices labeled with the literals \(a_i\), \(b_i\), \(d_i\). We connect by an edge every pair of vertices from different triples, except pairs of contradictory literals of the form \(x\) and \(\bar{x}\); there are no edges within a triple. Set \(f(\phi ) = \langle G, k \rangle\); this construction takes polynomial time.
Suppose \(\phi\) is satisfiable. Fix a satisfying assignment and choose in each clause one vertex whose literal is true. The \(k\) chosen vertices lie in different triples and are pairwise non-contradictory (all their literals are true simultaneously), so they are pairwise connected by edges — we obtain a clique of size \(k\).
Conversely, suppose \(G\) has a clique of size \(k\). There are no edges within a triple, so the clique contains exactly one vertex from each triple. The literals of these vertices are pairwise non-contradictory, so there exists an assignment of values to the variables that makes all of them true (variables not occurring among the clique’s literals are given arbitrary values). Such an assignment makes at least one literal true in every clause, i.e., it satisfies \(\phi\).

  Reduction of \(\mathrm{3SAT}\) to \(\mathrm{CLIQUE}\)
  The graph for the formula \(\phi=(x_1\lor x_1\lor x_2)\land(\bar x_1\lor\bar x_2\lor\bar x_2)\land(\bar x_1\lor x_2\lor x_2)\), \(k=3\): a triple of vertices per clause, with edges between non-contradictory literals from different triples (no edges within a clause). Choose an assignment: true literals are highlighted, and if every clause is satisfied, they form a clique of size \(3\).
  
    \(x_1=\)01
    \(x_2=\)01
    No assignment
  
  
  














ExampleExample 3





Show that deciding whether a digraph has a Hamiltonian path is an NP-hard problem.






SolutionSolution





We prove
\[
  \mathrm{3SAT} \leq _p \mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st}
\]
Suppose we have the formula
\[
  \phi = \underbrace{\left(x_1 \lor \bar{x}_2 \lor x_3 \right)}_{c_1} \land \underbrace{\left(\bar{x}_1 \lor x_2 \lor x_4\right)}_{c_2} \land \underbrace{\left(\bar{x}_1 \lor x_3 \lor x_5\right)}_{c_3} \land \underbrace{\left(x_1 \lor \bar{x}_4 \lor \bar{x}_5\right)}_{c_4}
\]
We need to construct \(f(\phi ) = (G,s,t)\). For each variable \(x_i\) we introduce a “diamond” with a horizontal chain of vertices inside it, and for each clause \(c_j\) a separate vertex. A Hamiltonian path from \(s\) to \(t\) is forced to pass through the diamonds from top to bottom, and within each diamond it must traverse the chain either left to right (corresponding to \(x_i = 1\)) or right to left (\(x_i = 0\)). If the literal \(x_i\) occurs in clause \(c_j\), then from the chain of the \(i\)-th diamond one can make a “hook” to vertex \(c_j\) and back while moving left to right; for the literal \(\bar{x}_i\), while moving right to left. Then a Hamiltonian path visiting all clause-vertices exists precisely when there is an assignment of values to the variables under which every clause has a true literal.

  Reduction of \(\mathrm{3SAT}\) to \(\mathrm{HAMPATH}_{st}\)
  Five variable "diamonds" \(x_1,\ldots,x_5\) (\(s\) is the top vertex, \(t\) the bottom one) and clause vertices \(c_1,\ldots,c_4\) on the right. The diagram is simplified: only the "hooks" out of the \(x_1\) diamond are shown (red — for occurrences of \(x_1\) in \(c_1\) and \(c_4\), traversed left to right; green — for \(\bar x_1\) in \(c_2\) and \(c_3\), right to left), and the chain inside the diamond is shortened to three vertices (in the full construction there are \(3k+1\) of them). Choose a value for \(x_1\) to trace a path: the direction in which the diamond is traversed encodes the variable's value, and a detour into a clause is possible only "along the way".

title: The set cover problem
text:
Let a finite set \(U\) of \(n\) elements be given, together with a collection of its subsets \(\mathcal{S}=\left\{ S_{1}, \ldots , S_{k}\right\}  \subset 2^U\). In particular, if \(\left|S_i\right| = 2, \;  \forall i\), then \((U, \mathcal{S})\) is an undirected graph. A sub-collection \(\mathcal{S}^{\prime } \subseteq \mathcal{S}\) is called a cover if every element of \(U\) belongs to at least one member of \(\mathcal{S}^{\prime }\), i.e.,
\[
  \bigcup _{S \in \mathcal{S}'}S = U
\]
A generalization of this problem is the minimum-weight set cover problem. This is the version we will study.

title: The set cover problem
text:
2.1 Using a set-cover algorithm
Note that the minimum-weight vertex cover problem (in particular, the minimum-cardinality version) is a special case of the set cover problem. Indeed, let a graph \(G=(V, E)\) be given, and suppose we must find a vertex cover of minimum weight. We can build the following instance of the set cover problem:

Identify the universe \(U\) with the edge set \(E\), i.e., \(U = E\).
Each vertex \(v \in V\) corresponds to a set \(S_v \subseteq U\) consisting of all edges incident to \(v\).
The cost function is \(c: S_v \mapsto \text{the weight of vertex } v\).

Then any set cover \(S' \subseteq \{ S_v : v \in V\}\) covering \(U\) corresponds to a choice of vertices \(V' \subseteq V\) forming a vertex cover of the graph. Minimizing the total weight of the chosen sets \(S'\) is equivalent to minimizing the weight of the vertex cover.
Note that the greedy algorithm for the minimum-cardinality vertex cover problem is a special case of Chvátal’s algorithm. We thus obtain its accuracy bound: \(H_{\tilde{n}}\), where \(\tilde{n}\) is the maximum vertex degree in \(G\).

title: The set cover problem
text:
2.2 Constant-factor algorithms via weight splitting
In the introduction we obtained an algorithm for the minimum-cardinality vertex cover problem with a fixed accuracy bound of \(2\). Will it achieve the same accuracy for the more general problem, i.e., the minimum-weight cover problem? No!

  A minimum-weight cover does not reduce to a minimum-cardinality cover
  The same graph on 7 vertices: first without weights, with its minimum-cardinality cover, then with vertex weights — and a cover of smaller weight but larger cardinality. Hover over a vertex to see its weight.
  
    Unweighted graph
    Min.-cardinality cover
    Weighted problem
    Min.-weight cover
  
  
  



2.2.1 The local ratio algorithm

  The idea of the local ratio algorithm: splitting \(w=w_1+w_2\)
  We choose an edge \(\{v,v'\}\) incident to the cheapest vertex and subtract \(c=\min(w(v),w(v'))\) from both of its endpoints: \(w_1\) is concentrated on these two vertices (\(c\) at each, zero elsewhere), and \(w_2=w-w_1\) is the same graph with reduced weights. Any cover of the graph \((V,E,w_1)\) is a 2-approximation: at least one of the edge's two endpoints must be covered. Hover over a vertex to track its weight across all three panels.

  At each step \(i\) the algorithm takes an edge incident to the cheapest of the still-nonzero vertices and subtracts \(c\) from both of its endpoints — the weight \(t_i\) is concentrated on these two vertices. After 5 steps, the residual \(t_6\) marks the outlined vertices — this is the algorithm's solution. Hover over a vertex to see its residual weight.

Theorem 2 (On splitting a graph) Let a graph \((V,E)\) and a vertex weight function \(w: V \to \mathbb {R}_+\) be given, and suppose the weight function splits as a sum of functions: \(w = w_1 + w_2\). If \(V' \subset V\) is a vertex cover that is a \(\rho\)-approximation of the optimal cover both for \((V,E,w_1)\) and for \((V,E,w_2)\), then \(V'\) is also a \(\rho\)-approximation for the original vertex-weighted graph \((V,E,w)\).










Mn-proofProof






Let \(V^*\), \(V^*_1\), \(V^*_2\) be optimal covers for the graph \((V,E)\) with weight functions \(w\), \(w_1\), \(w_2\) respectively. We are given: \[
\begin{align}  w_1(V') & \leq \rho w_1(V^*_1) \leq \rho w_1(V^*) \\ w_2(V') & \leq \rho w_2(V^*_2) \leq \rho w_2(V^*) \\ \end{align}
\] We obtain \[
  w(V') = w_1(V') + w_2(V') \leq \rho \left(w_1(V^*) + w_2(V^*)\right) = \rho w(V^*)
\]






2.2.2 The level algorithm
A second way to split the weights: do it globally rather than edge by edge.
Call a function \(w: V \to \mathbb {Q}_+\) of vertex weights degree-proportional if there exists a constant \(c>0\) such that the weight of every vertex \(v \in V\) equals \(w(v) = c \cdot \operatorname {deg}(v)\).

  The level algorithm: another way to split the weights
  A global subtraction proportional to vertex degree: \(c=\min_v w(v)/\deg(v)=3.5\) (attained at vertex \(ML\), \(\deg=4\)), so \(w_1(v)=c\cdot\deg(v)\) for every vertex, and \(w_2=w-w_1\) is the residual function (the residual at \(ML\) equals \(0\)). Hover over a vertex to see its degree and all three weights.
  
    
    =
    
    +
    
  
  w₁ = 3.5·deg — the minimum of w/degresidual 0









Lemma 2 Let \(w: V \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}^{+}\) be a degree-proportional function. Then \[
  w(V) \leq 2 \operatorname {OPT}
\]










Mn-proofProof






Let \(c>0\) be the constant such that \(w(v)=c \cdot \operatorname {deg}(v)\). Let \(U\) be an optimal vertex cover of the graph \(G\). Since \(U\) covers all edges, \[
  \sum _{v \in U} \operatorname {deg}(v) \geq |E|
\] It follows that \(w(U) \geq c|E|\). Recalling that \(\sum_{v \in V} \operatorname {deg}(v)=\) \(2|E|\), we get \(w(V)=2 c|E|\). Altogether \(w(V) = 2c\left|E\right| \leq 2 w(U) = 2\operatorname {OPT}\).




Let \(w: V \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}^{+}\) be an arbitrary function. Define the largest degree-proportional function relative to \(w\) in the graph \(G\) as follows:

Remove from the graph all vertices of degree 0;
Among the remaining vertices, compute the value \(c=\min \left\{ \frac{w(v)}{\operatorname {deg}(v)}\right\}\).

Then the function \(t(v)=c \cdot \operatorname {deg}(v)\) is the one sought.
Define \(w^{\prime }(v)=w(v)-t(v)\) as the residual weight function.
We now present an algorithm that splits the original weight function into degree-proportional functions and builds a vertex cover.







Algorithm 2 Level algorithm for the weighted vertex cover problem (\(G=(V, E), w: V \rightarrow \mathbb {Q}^{+}\))

\(\operatorname{Sol} \gets \varnothing\), \(i \gets 0\)
\(w'(v) \gets w(v)\) for all \(v \in V\) (initialize residual weights)
\(D_0 \gets \{v \in V \mid \deg(v) = 0\}\) (vertices of degree \(0\) never join the cover)
\(V_0 \gets V \setminus D_0\) (remove vertices of degree \(0\))
while \(V_i \neq \varnothing\) do

\(c \gets \min_{v \in V_i} \frac{w'(v)}{\deg_i(v)}\) (\(\deg_i\) is the degree in the current subgraph \(G_i = G[V_i]\))
for each \(v \in V_i\) do

\(t_i(v) \gets c \cdot \deg_i(v)\) (amount subtracted for the vertex)
\(w'(v) \gets w'(v) - t_i(v)\) (update the residual weight)

\(W_i \gets \{v \in V_i \mid w'(v) = 0\}\) (vertices that reached zero residual weight)
\(\operatorname{Sol} \gets \operatorname{Sol} \cup W_i\) (add these vertices to the solution)
\(V_{i+1} \gets V_i \setminus W_i\)
\(D_{i+1} \gets \{v \in V_{i+1} \mid \deg_{G[V_{i+1}]}(v) = 0\}\) (vertices of degree \(0\) after removing \(W_i\))
\(V_{i+1} \gets V_{i+1} \setminus D_{i+1}\) (remove vertices of degree \(0\))
\(i \gets i + 1\)

return \(\operatorname{Sol}\)







2.2.3 Accuracy bounds







Theorem 3 The local ratio algorithm and the level algorithm are \(2\)-approximation algorithms for the vertex cover problem.










Mn-proofProof






We prove the statement for the level algorithm. Let \(t_{0}, \ldots , t_{k-1}\) be the degree-proportional functions on the graphs \(G_{0}, \ldots , G_{k-1}\) constructed by the algorithm. Then \(\operatorname {Sol}=W_{0} \cup \ldots \cup W_{k-1}\) is the solution obtained by the algorithm, and \(V \backslash \operatorname {Sol}=D_{0} \cup \ldots \cup D_{k}\).
First we show that the set \(\operatorname {Sol}\) is a vertex cover of the graph \(G\). Suppose not. Then there is an edge \((u, v)\) such that \(u \in D_{i}, v \in D_{j}\) for some \(i, j\). Say \(i \leq j\); the vertex \(v\) is removed later, so at time \(i\) both vertices are still present, and the edge \((u, v)\) lies in \(G_{i}\). This contradicts the fact that the degree of \(u\) in \(G_i\) is zero.
Let \(C^{*}\) be an optimal vertex cover. We prove that \(w(\operatorname {Sol}) \leq 2 \cdot \operatorname {OPT}\). Consider a vertex \(v \in \operatorname {Sol}\). Let \(v \in W_{j}\) for some \(j\); its residual weight became zero, so
\[
  w(v)=\sum _{i \leq j} t_{i}(v)
\]
Now consider a vertex \(v \in V \backslash \mathrm{Sol}\). Let \(v \in D_{j}\) for some \(j\); the residual weight is nonnegative, so
\[
  w(v) \geq \sum _{i<j} t_{i}(v)
\]
Note that in each layer \(i\) the set of vertices \(C^{*} \cap V_{i}\) is a cover of \(G_{i}\), since \(G_{i}\) is an induced subgraph (\(C^*\) covers every edge of \(G_i\), and the covering endpoint itself lies in \(V_i\)). Applying the lemma above to the degree-proportional function \(t_i\) on the graph \(G_i\), we get \(t_{i}\left(\operatorname {Sol} \cap V_{i}\right) \leq t_i(V_i) \leq 2 \cdot t_{i}\left(C^{*} \cap V_{i}\right)\). Finally:
\[
  w(\operatorname {Sol}) = \sum _{i=0}^{k-1} t_{i}\left(\mathrm{Sol} \cap V_{i}\right) \leq 2 \sum _{i=0}^{k-1} t_{i}\left(C^{*} \cap V_{i}\right) \leq 2 \cdot w\left(C^{*}\right)
\]
(in the first equality the weight of each vertex \(v \in W_j\) is decomposed over layers \(i \leq j\), and the last inequality uses the fact that for every vertex \(\sum_{i \colon v \in V_i} t_i(v) \leq w(v)\)).
For the local ratio algorithm the bound follows from the graph-splitting theorem: at each step the subtracted weight function \(w_1\) is concentrated on the two endpoints of a single edge \((u,v)\) (\(\varepsilon\) on each), and any vertex cover has \(w_1\)-weight at least \(\varepsilon\), whereas the \(w_1\)-weight of any set of vertices is at most \(2\varepsilon\) — that is, with respect to each subtracted function an arbitrary cover is a \(2\)-approximation. The algorithm’s solution consists of vertices with zero residual weight, so its weight equals the sum of the weights over the subtracted functions, and by the splitting theorem it is a \(2\)-approximation for the original weights.




Let us give an example on which this bound is achieved. Let \(K_{n, n}\) be a complete bipartite graph in which all vertices have unit weight. The level algorithm will place all \(2n\) vertices of \(K_{n, n}\) into the cover, whereas the optimal solution consists of the vertices of a single side.

title: The \(k\)-center problem
text:
Consider the following problem. A rural district contains several small towns connected by roads. We must build \(k\) hospitals so as to minimize the maximum distance from any town to its nearest hospital. We call this the \(k\)-center problem. This chapter treats the \(k\)-center problem and its weighted version, under the assumption that distances between towns satisfy the triangle inequality. Without this restriction, no \(\alpha (n)\)-approximation algorithm exists for the \(k\)-center problem, for any polynomially computable function \(\alpha (n)\), assuming \(P \neq N P\).
Given an arbitrary subset of vertices \(S \subseteq V\) and an arbitrary vertex \(v \in V\), define the distance from \(v\) to \(S\) as
\[
  \operatorname {connect}(v, S) := \min \{ \operatorname {cost}(u, v) \mid u \in S\}
\]


The metric \(k\)-center problem


\(I = \left(G, \operatorname {cost}, k\right)\), where

\(G=(V, E)\) is a complete graph;
edge costs \(\operatorname {cost}: E \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}^{+}\) such that for any three vertices \(u, v\) and \(w\)
\[
  \operatorname {cost}(u, v) \leq \operatorname {cost}(u, w)+\operatorname {cost}(w, v)
\]
a natural number \(k \in \mathbb {N}\) (\(k \leq \left|V\right|\)), fixing the size of \(S\).



A subset of vertices \(S \subseteq V\), with \(|S|=k\), minimizing the quantity \[
  \max _{v \in V} \left\{ \operatorname {connect}(v,S)\right\}
\]



  The metric \(k\)-center problem: an example
  A complete graph on \(17\) vertices, \(k=3\) (only some edges are shown for clarity). Hover over a vertex to see which center it is assigned to.
  
  
  



1 Parametric pruning for the metric \(k\)-center problem
Knowing the cost of an optimal solution often makes it easier to find a good approximate solution. In particular, it lets us discard clearly unsuitable inputs and narrow the search space. Unfortunately, computing the cost of an optimal solution is just as hard as finding the solution itself for an NP-hard optimization problem. The technique of parametric pruning allows us to work around this difficulty for some problems. We choose a parameter \(t\), which is a guess for the cost of the optimal solution. For the chosen value of \(t\), from the given instance \(I\) we remove any data that cannot be used in any solution of cost at most \(t\). We denote such a pruned instance by \(I(t)\).
The algorithm rests on several ideas. Let an individual problem \(I\) be given.

Parametrization. Obtain a parametrized decision problem (i.e., a problem with a “YES”/“NO” answer) \(\operatorname {decision}(I, t)\) for the original optimization problem:

\(\operatorname {optimization}(I)\): minimize (maximize) the cost of the solution;
\(\operatorname {decision}(I, t)\): determine whether there is a feasible solution of cost \(\operatorname {cost} \leq t\) (\(\operatorname {cost} \geq t\)).

Reduce the optimization problem to the decision problem \(\operatorname {decision}(t)\): solve \(\operatorname {decision}(t)\) for increasing \(t\) until we get the answer “YES”.
Parameter pruning. When considering \(\operatorname {decision}(I, t)\) for fixed \(I, t\), pass from \(I\) to an individual problem \(I' = I'(t)\) by removing those parts of \(I\) that clearly cannot be used in a feasible solution \(\sigma\) with \(\operatorname {cost}(\sigma ) \leq t\).
Lower bound. An \(\alpha\)-approximation algorithm consists of 2 steps:

the family of instances \(I(t)\) is used to compute a lower bound on \(\operatorname {OPT}\), call it \(t^{*}\);
a feasible solution is found on the instance \(I\left(\alpha \cdot t^{*}\right)\).


Let us show how to apply the parametric pruning technique to the \(k\)-center problem. Number the edges of the graph \(G\) in nondecreasing order of cost, i.e.,
\[
  \operatorname {cost}\left(e_{1}\right) \leq \operatorname {cost}\left(e_{2}\right) \leq \ldots \leq \operatorname {cost}\left(e_{m}\right),
\]
and let \(G_{i}=\left(V, E_{i}\right)\), where \(E_{i}=\left\{ e_{1}, e_{2}, \ldots , e_{i}\right\}\).

Parametrization. Instead of the original problem we consider the following decision problem \(\operatorname {decision}(I,t)\): given \(I = (G, \operatorname {cost}, k)\) and given \(t \in \mathbb {Q}_+\), determine whether \(G\) has a subset of vertices \(S \subset V\) such that
\[
  \max _{v \in V} \left\{ \operatorname {connect}(v,S)\right\}  \leq t
\]
Note that it suffices to solve \(\operatorname {decision}(I, t)\) for \(t \in \left\{ \operatorname {cost}(e) \mid e \in E\right\}\). Let \(t = \operatorname {cost}(e_j)\) for some \(j = 1, \ldots , m\).
Parameter pruning. When considering the decision problem \(\operatorname {decision}(I,t)\) above, edges whose cost exceeds \(t = \operatorname {cost}(e_j)\) do not affect the answer. They can be removed from the individual problem \(I\): we pass to \(I' = I_j = (G_j, \operatorname {cost}_j, k)\), where

\(G_j = (V, E_j)\);
\(\operatorname {cost}_j = \operatorname {cost}|_{E_j}\).

We pass from \(\operatorname {decision}(I,t)\) to \(\operatorname {decision}(I_j,t)\).


  Parametric pruning for the \(k\)-center problem
  The solution \(\{s_1,s_2,s_3\}\) (green); blue edges are stars centered at \(S\); the red edge \(e_j\) is the most expensive of them. On the right, the pruned graph \(G_j=(V,\{e_1,\ldots,e_j\})\): every edge more expensive than \(\mathrm{cost}(e_j)\) has been removed. Hover over an edge to see whether it survives the pruning.
  
    
    ⇒
    
  
  \(G\)\(G_j:=(V,\{e_1,\ldots,e_j\})\)


A dominating set in an undirected graph \(H=(U, F)\) is a subset \(S \subset U\) such that every vertex in \(U \setminus S\) is adjacent to some vertex in \(S\). Denote by \(\operatorname {dom}(H)\) the size of a minimum (by cardinality) dominating set in \(H\). Note that the problem \(\operatorname {decision}(I_j, \operatorname {cost}(e_j))\) is, in essence, the problem of checking the inequality \(\operatorname {dom}(G_j) \leq k\).
The \(k\)-center problem is equivalent to finding the minimum index \(j\) such that \(G_{j}\) contains a dominating set of size at most \(k\), i.e., \(G_{j}\) contains \(k\) stars covering all vertices, where a star is a graph \(K_{1, p}, p \geq 1\). If \(j^{*}\) is the minimum such index, then the quantity \(\operatorname {cost}\left(e_{j^{*}}\right)\) is the optimal value of the \(k\)-center problem. Denote this quantity by \(\operatorname {OPT}\).
Reducing the original problem to computing \(\operatorname {dom}(G_j)\) does not directly help us: computing the size of a dominating set for an arbitrary graph is an NP-hard problem.
An independent set in a graph \(H=(U, F)\) is a subset of vertices \(I \subset U\) containing no adjacent vertices.
Call the square of a graph \(H=(V, F)\) the graph \(H^{2}=(V, E)\) such that the edge \((u, v) \in E\) if and only if \(H\) contains a path between vertices \(u\) and \(v, u \neq v\), of length at most 2.

  The square of a graph
  In \(G_j^2\), vertex \(u\) is joined not only to its neighbors (bold edges) but also to their neighbors — to everyone reachable by a path of length \(\le2\) (light arcs). For example, \(u\) and \(u'\) are not adjacent in \(G_j\), but are joined in \(G_j^2\). Hover over a vertex in the right-hand panel.
  
    
    
  
  \(G_j\)\(G_j^2\): the star at \(u\) and the new edges through \(u\)









Lemma 1 Let a graph \(H\) be given, and let \(I\) be an independent set in \(H^{2}\). Then \(|I| \leq \operatorname {dom}(H)\).










Mn-proofProof






Let \(D\) be a minimum dominating set in \(H\), \(\left|D\right| = \operatorname {dom}(H)\). Then \(H\) contains \(|D|\) stars covering all vertices. Since each star becomes a clique in \(H^{2}\), \(H^{2}\) contains \(|D|\) cliques covering all vertices. Since \(I\) can contain at most one vertex from each clique of \(H^{2}\), \(|I| \leq \operatorname {dom}(H)\).

  A dominating set in \(H\) and an independent set in \(H^2\)
  The green crosses are a dominating set of 2 vertices. The steps show why any independent set in \(H^2\) is no larger than the dominating set in \(H\).
  
  
  













Algorithm 1 Hochbaum–Shmoys algorithm (\(G = (V,E), \;  \operatorname {cost}, \;  k\))

Build the family of graphs \(G_{1}^{2}, G_{2}^{2}, \ldots, G_{m}^{2}\).
Find a maximal (by inclusion) independent set \(I_{r}\) in each graph \(G_{r}^{2}\).
Compute the smallest index \(r\) such that \(\left|I_{r}\right| \leq k\). Call it \(j\).
return \(I_{j}\).












Lemma 2 For the \(j\) obtained by the Hochbaum–Shmoys algorithm, we have \(\operatorname {cost}\left(e_{j}\right) \leq \operatorname {OPT}\).










Mn-proofProof






For every \(i<j\) we have \(\left|I_{i}\right|>k\). By the lemma above, \(\operatorname {dom}\left(G_{i}\right) \geq \left|I_{i}\right|>k\), so \(j^{*}>i\). This holds for all \(i < j\), hence \(j \leq j^{*}\) and \(\operatorname {cost}\left(e_{j}\right) \leq \operatorname {cost}(e_{j^*}) = \operatorname {OPT}\).











Theorem 1 The Hochbaum–Shmoys algorithm is a 2-approximation algorithm for the metric \(k\)-center problem.










Mn-proofProof






First note that a maximal (by inclusion) independent set \(I\) in an arbitrary graph is also a dominating set (since if some vertex \(v\) is not dominated by any vertex of \(I\), then \(I \cup \{ v\}\) is an independent set, contradicting the maximality of \(I\)). Hence in the graph \(G_{j}^{2}\) there are stars centered at the vertices of \(I_{j}\) that cover all vertices of \(G\). By the triangle inequality, the cost of edges in \(G_{j}^{2}\) does not exceed \(2 \cdot \operatorname {cost}\left(e_{j}\right)\), so the cost of the solution \(I_j\) does not exceed \(2 \cdot \operatorname {cost}(e_j)\). By the lemma above, \(\operatorname {cost}(e_j) \leq \operatorname {OPT}\), whence the cost of the solution does not exceed \(2 \cdot \operatorname {OPT}\).




Let us give an example showing that this bound is tight. Consider a graph on \(n+1\) vertices with a single central vertex. Edges incident to the central vertex have cost 1, and all other edges have cost 2. An example of such a graph is shown in the figure below.

  Tightness of the factor-2 bound for the Hochbaum-Shmoys algorithm
  A star \(K_{1,n}\): edges at the center \(c\) cost \(1\), all others cost \(2\) (dotted, only some shown). For \(k=1\), the optimum is the center, \(\mathrm{OPT}=1\). The algorithm stops at some \(j\) where \(G_j\) is a star of unit edges and \(G_j^2\) is a complete graph: any vertex is a maximal independent set. Click a vertex to choose it as the center.
  
    \(n=\)8
    Center (optimum)Leaf (a bad choice)
  
  
  


For \(k=1\) the optimal solution is the central vertex, and \(\operatorname {OPT}=1\). The Hochbaum–Shmoys algorithm will obtain index \(j=n\). The graph \(G_{n}^{2}\) is a complete graph, and if a non-central vertex is chosen as the maximal independent set, the cost of the solution obtained by the algorithm will be 2.







Theorem 2 For any \(\varepsilon >0\) there is no \((2-\varepsilon )\)-approximation algorithm for the metric \(k\)-center problem, assuming \(P \neq N P\).










Mn-proofProof






We show that if such an algorithm existed, it could solve the dominating set problem in polynomial time. Let a graph \(G=(V, E)\) and a number \(k\) be the input of the dominating set problem. Construct a complete graph \(G^{\prime }=\left(V, E^{\prime }\right)\) with cost function
\[
  \operatorname {cost}(u, v)= \begin{cases} 1, &  \text{ if }(u, v) \in E \\ 2, &  \text{ if }(u, v) \notin E\end{cases}
\]
Note that the graph \(G^{\prime }\) satisfies the triangle inequality and the following conditions:

if \(\operatorname {dom}(G) \leq k\), then \(G^{\prime }\) has a solution of the \(k\)-center problem of cost 1;
if \(\operatorname {dom}(G)>k\), then the cost of an optimal solution of the \(k\)-center problem on the graph \(G^{\prime }\) equals 2.

In the first case, a \((2-\varepsilon )\)-approximation algorithm must find a solution of cost \(1\), since a \((2-\varepsilon )\)-approximate solution cannot use edges of cost 2. Hence such an algorithm would solve the NP-complete dominating set problem in polynomial time.






2 The weighted \(k\)-center problem
The parametric pruning technique can also be used to solve the metric weighted-center problem.


The metric weighted-center problem



a complete graph \(G=(V, E)\);
edge costs \(\operatorname {cost}: E \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}^{+}\) such that for any three vertices \(u, v\) and \(w\), \(\operatorname {cost}(u, v) \leq\) \(\operatorname {cost}(u, w)+\operatorname {cost}(w, v)\);
vertex weights \(w: V \rightarrow \mathbf{R}^{+}\) and an upper bound \(W \in \mathbf{R}^{+}\).



A set \(S \subseteq V\) of total weight \(w(S) \leq W\) that minimizes the quantity \(\max_{v}\{ \operatorname {connect}(v, S)\}\).



  The weighted centers problem
  Vertex weights \(1\), \(2\), \(3\) are labeled on the vertices; the upper bound on the total weight of the centers is \(W=4\). Green vertices are the chosen centers, yellow edges are their stars. Hover over a vertex to see its weight and its center.
  
    Infeasible solutionFeasible and optimal
  
  
  


Denote by \(w \operatorname {dom}(G)\) the weight of a minimum-weight dominating set in the graph \(G\). To solve the metric weighted-center problem, we must find the smallest index \(i\) such that \(w \operatorname {dom}\left(G_{i}\right) \leq\) \(W\). Let this be the index \(i^{*}\); then the cost of the optimal solution is \(\operatorname {OPT}=\operatorname {cost}\left(e_{i^{*}}\right)\).
Consider a vertex-weighted graph \(H\), and let \(I\) be an independent set in the graph \(H^{2}\). For each \(u \in I\) denote by \(s(u)\) the lightest neighbor of the vertex \(u\) in the graph \(H\) (a vertex \(u\) is also considered its own neighbor). Let \(S=\{ s(u) \mid u \in I\}\).







Lemma 3 For any vertex-weighted graph \(H\) the inequality \(w(S) \leq w \operatorname {dom}(H)\) holds.










Mn-proofProof






Let \(D\) be a minimum-weight dominating set in the graph \(H\). Then \(H\) contains a set of disjoint stars centered at the vertices of \(D\) covering all vertices. Since each star becomes a clique in the graph \(H^{2}\), \(I\) contains at most one vertex from each star. Moreover, every vertex of \(I\) has the center of the corresponding star as a neighbor in the graph \(H\). For each vertex of \(I\), the set \(S\) contains its lightest neighbor. Hence \(w(S) \leq w(D)\).




In the Hochbaum–Shmoys-2 algorithm, \(s_{i}(u)\) denotes the lightest neighbor of the vertex \(u\) in the graph \(G_{i}\).







Algorithm 2 Hochbaum–Shmoys-2 algorithm (\(G=(V, E), \operatorname {cost} : E \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}^{+}\))

Build the family of graphs \(G_{1}^{2}, G_{2}^{2}, \ldots, G_{m}^{2}\).
Find a maximal independent set \(I_{r}\) in each graph \(G_{r}^{2}\).
Build \(S_{r}=\left\{s_{r}(u) \mid u \in I_{r}\right\}\).
Compute the smallest index \(r\) such that \(w\left(S_{r}\right) \leq W\). Call it \(j\).
return \(S_j\).












Theorem 3 The Hochbaum–Shmoys-2 algorithm is a 3-approximation algorithm for the metric weighted-center problem.










Mn-proofProof






We show that \(\operatorname {cost}\left(e_{j}\right)\) is a lower bound on the cost \(\operatorname {OPT}\). Indeed, for every \(i<j\), by step 4 of the algorithm, \(w\left(S_{i}\right)>W\). By the lemma above, \(w \operatorname {dom}\left(G_{i}\right) \geq w\left(S_{i}\right)>W\). Hence \(i^{*}>i\) and \(j \leq i^{*}\).
Since \(I_{j}\) is a dominating set in \(G_{j}^{2}\), all vertices of \(V\) can be covered by stars in \(G_{j}^{2}\) centered at the vertices of \(I_{j}\). By the triangle inequality, the weight of the edges in these stars does not exceed \(2 \cdot \operatorname {cost}\left(e_{j}\right)\).
Each star’s center is connected to a vertex of \(S_{j}\) by an edge of cost at most \(\operatorname {cost}\left(e_{j}\right)\) (figure below). Shift each center to the vertex of the set \(S_{j}\) adjacent to it. By the triangle inequality we obtain \(\max_{v}\left\{ \operatorname {connect}\left(v, S_{j}\right)\right\}  \leq 3 \cdot \operatorname {cost}\left(e_{j}\right)\).

  Redistributing the stars
  The star center \(u\) is joined to its leaves by edges of cost \(\le\mathrm{cost}(e_i)\) (except the farthest leaf, for which it is \(\le2\,\mathrm{cost}(e_i)\)); \(s_i(u)\) is the lightest neighbor of \(u\), with an edge \(\le\mathrm{cost}(e_i)\) to \(u\), and hence, by the triangle inequality, \(\le3\,\mathrm{cost}(e_i)\) to any leaf (dashed). Hover over an edge to see the bound on its cost.
  







  A tight example for the 3-approximation of Hochbaum-Shmoys-2
  A path \(a\text{-}b\text{-}c\text{-}d\) with unit edges, vertex weights \(a{:}1,\ b{:}2,\ c{:}2,\ d{:}2\), and \(n\) infinite-weight vertices, each joined to \(a\) by an edge of cost \(1+\varepsilon\) (all other distances are shortest paths). For \(W=3\), compare the optimum with what the algorithm can output.
  
    \(n=\)3
    Optimum: centers \(\{a,c\}\)Algorithm: center \(\{a\}\)
  
  
  




3 Exercises






ProblemProblem 1





Consider the following problem. Place two kings on a chessboard so as to minimize the number of moves from one of the kings to any square of the board. Formulate this problem as a \(k\)-center problem and solve it using the Hochbaum–Shmoys algorithm.









ProblemProblem 2





Show that if the edge costs in a graph do not satisfy the triangle inequality, then no \(\alpha (n)\)-approximation algorithm exists for the \(k\)-center problem, for any polynomially computable function \(\alpha (n)\).









ProblemProblem 3





Consider step 2 of the Hochbaum–Shmoys algorithm, which requires finding a maximal independent set in the graph \(G_{i}^{2}\). Various methods are known for choosing a minimum dominating set. Modify the algorithm so that \(I_{r}\) is a minimum dominating set in the graph \(G_{i}^{2}\). Show that the new algorithm does not guarantee a bound of \(2\) for the \(k\)-center problem. What guaranteed accuracy bound does it have?









ProblemProblem 4





Consider the following greedy algorithm for the \(k\)-center problem.







Algorithm 3 Gonzalez algorithm (\(G=(V, E), \operatorname {cost} : E \rightarrow \mathbf{Q}^{+}\))

Choose an arbitrary vertex \(v\) and set \(S=\{v\}\).
while \(\left|S\right| < k\) do

find the vertex \(v\) farthest from the set \(S\), i.e., \(\operatorname{connect}(v, S)=\max _{u \in V} \operatorname{connect}(u, S)\).
Add \(v\) to \(S\).

return \(S\).





Prove that the Gonzalez algorithm is also a \(2\)-approximation algorithm for the \(k\)-center problem.

title: Fundamentals of Cryptography
text:
Contents
No separate program for “Fundamentals of Cryptography” as such was found. The department publishes a detailed but later program, “Cryptography on Elliptic Curves and Lattices”; it does not stand in for the core semester VII course, so below it is explicitly marked as related material.
The lecturer of the related program is A. A. Illarionov, D.Sc. (Phys.-Math.). The abstract says that the course covers public-key cryptosystems on elliptic curves and lattices, including post-quantum motivations. The document lists the following 24 topics:

Complexity of algorithms, polynomial and exponential algorithms, the \(P=NP\) problem.
Elliptic curves over \(\mathbb R\) and two descriptions of point addition.
Elliptic curves over an arbitrary field.
The order of the group of points over a finite prime field and Hasse’s theorem.
Elliptic-curve analogues of Diffie–Hellman and ElGamal.
Current digital signature standards of Russia and the USA.
Cryptographic strength of elliptic-curve schemes.
Constructing elliptic curves suitable for cryptography.
Projective coordinates and optimization of computations.
Directions for further development of elliptic-curve cryptography.
Lattices, basis and determinant.
Minkowski’s convex body theorem.
Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization.
\(\mu\)-reduced bases and their construction.
Successive minima of lattices and the Hermite constant.
Lagrange’s algorithm for an \(L\)-reduced basis.
Hermite’s algorithm for finding a short vector.
Algorithmic lattice problems used in cryptography.
The \(LLL\)-reduced basis and its properties.
The \(LLL\) algorithm.
The GGH cryptosystem.
The GGH digital signature.
The NTRU cipher.
The NTRUSign digital signature.

The document also gives the expected learning outcomes: to know the properties of elliptic curves, lattices and reduced bases, the Hermite and \(LLL\) algorithms, lattice problems and the GGH/NTRU systems; to be able to prove properties of these objects and to estimate the complexity and correctness of the algorithms; to have command of the basics of the geometry of numbers and the cryptographic applications of these objects. Ongoing assessment in the related program consists of homework assignments, a possible programming assignment and a mid-semester colloquium; no numerical weights or thresholds are given.

title: Probability Space. Classical Models. Independence
text:
WarningDraft



This lecture note is still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished spots. If you find something, please let the author know (contact information on the course page).


This entire first week relies on what you already know from school: classical probability (coins, dice, cards – probability equals the ratio of the number of favorable outcomes to the total number of outcomes) and geometric probability (for example, the meeting problem – probability equals the ratio of areas or lengths). Our goal here is not to tell you something fundamentally new, but to carefully formalize what you can already compute intuitively. We will start with the classical model (everything is simple there), then move on to the geometric one – and there we will run into a crack in this intuition: it will turn out that, unlike in the classical case, we cannot declare every subset of the sample space to be an event. This very crack is the main motivation for the whole course: to patch it up, in the second half of the semester we will build measure theory from scratch.

1 Classical Probability
The subject of study of probability theory is random events and their probabilities. By a random event we mean a collection of outcomes of some experiment.
Suppose some random experiment admits \(N\) distinct outcomes (for example, when tossing a coin there are only two outcomes: heads and tails). Denote these outcomes by \(\omega_{1}, \ldots , \omega_{N}\). The outcomes \(\omega_{1}, \ldots , \omega_{N}\) are called elementary events, and the set \(\Omega =\left\{ \omega_{1}, \ldots , \omega_{N}\right\}\) is the sample space (space of elementary events). In general, the sample space need not be finite, or even countable.







Definition 1 The elements \(\omega \in \Omega\) are called elementary events or elementary outcomes, and their collection \(\Omega\) is the sample space (space of elementary outcomes).




An event is an arbitrary subset \(A \subset \Omega\). We say that the event \(A\) has occurred if the experiment ended in one of the elementary outcomes belonging to \(A\).
As long as \(\Omega\) is finite (as in all the examples above), no difficulties arise regarding which subsets should count as events: any subset of \(\Omega\) can be taken as an event, i.e., as the collection of all events we take \(\mathcal{F} = 2^{\Omega }\) – the set of all subsets of \(\Omega\). Subtleties will appear later, in the section on geometric probability, once \(\Omega\) becomes infinite.
Let, as before, \(\left|\Omega \right| = N \in \mathbb {N}\), \(\mathcal{F} = 2^{\Omega }\). Assume in addition that all elementary outcomes are equally likely, i.e.,
\[
  \forall i \in \{ 1, \ldots , N\}  \quad \mathbb {P}\left(\omega \right) := \mathbb {P}\left(\left\{ \omega \right\} \right) =\frac{1}{N}
\]
This can also be written as \(\mathbb {P} = \frac{1}{N}\#\), where \(\#\) is the counting measure, which in general is defined by
\[
  \# (A) = \begin{cases}  n, &  \text{ if $A$ is finite and has $n$ elements} \\ + \infty , &  \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\]
An experiment described by such a probability space is called a classical probability model. Rolling a die can serve as an example of such an experiment. Here \(\Omega =\{ 1,2,3,4,5,6\} , \mathcal{F}=2^{\Omega }\) and \(\mathbb {P}\left(i\right)=\frac{1}{6}\).
As examples of the classical probability model, let us consider the standard urn schemes: from a basket of \(n\) items, \(k\) items are chosen at random. We assume that the appearance of any item is equally likely.






ExampleExample 1





Describe the probability space for the scheme of ordered sampling without replacement.






SolutionSolution





Suppose the choice of the \(i\)-th element corresponds to the elementary outcome \(\omega_{i}\). This is the scheme of ordered sampling without replacement. For this scheme, the sample space is as follows:
\[
  \Omega =\left\{  \omega = \left(\omega _{i_{1}}, \omega _{i_{2}}, \ldots , \omega _{i_{k}}\right) \;  , \;  i_{1}, i_{2}, \ldots , i_{k} \text{ -- distinct numbers from }\{ 1, \ldots , n\} \right\}
\]
That is, \(\omega\) is a tuple (an order-sensitive structure) of \(\omega_i\)’s, each denoting the drawing of one item or another; since sampling is without replacement, all the indices are distinct.
The number of elements in \(\Omega\) equals \(A_{n}^k = n(n-1)\cdots (n-k+1)\): at the first step we can equally likely choose any of the \(n\) items, at the second step – any of the remaining \(n-1\), and so on. Owing to this symmetry, any tuple occurs with equal probability. That is, \(\mathbb {P} = \frac{1}{A_{n}^k}\#\). Hence the probability space for this model is classical.












ProblemProblem 1





From a basket of \(n\) items, \(k\) items are chosen at random. Describe the probability space for the scheme of unordered sampling with replacement.









ProblemProblem 2





Two \(M\)-sided dice, with the numbers from 1 to \(M\) written on their faces, are thrown at random. Describe the probability space whose events correspond to all possible outcomes of this experiment. Find the probability of the event \(A_{i}\) defined by \(A_{i}=\{\) the sum of the numbers shown on the dice equals \(i\} , i=2,3, \ldots , 2 M\).









ProblemProblem 3





A random subset is chosen from a set of \(N\) objects. Describe the corresponding probability space and find the probability that this random subset has even cardinality.









ExampleExample 2





A set of \(n\) balls is randomly distributed among \(m\) boxes. Find the probability that all boxes are nonempty, given that the balls are distinguishable.






SolutionSolution





We are interested in the event
\[
  B = \{ \text{all boxes are nonempty}\} .
\]
We have
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(B\right) = 1 - \mathbb {P}\! \left(\bigcup _{i=1}^m A_i\right), \quad A_i = \{ \text{the $i$-th box is empty}\} .
\]
By the inclusion–exclusion formula:
\[
  \mathbb {P}\! \left(\bigcup _{i=1}^m A_i\right) = \sum _{j=1}^m (-1)^{j+1} \sum _{1\le i_1<\cdots <i_j\le m} \mathbb {P}\left(A_{i_1}\cap \cdots \cap A_{i_j}\right).
\]
But
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(A_{i_1}\cap \cdots \cap A_{i_j}\right) = \frac{(m-j)^n}{m^n},
\]
since all \(n\) balls must land in the remaining \(m-j\) boxes. Consequently,
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(B\right) = \frac{1}{m^n} \sum _{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom {m}{j} (m-j)^n.
\]
Thus,
\[
  \boxed {\; \mathbb {P}\left(\{ \text{all boxes are nonempty}\} \right) = \frac{\sum _{j=0}^{m} (-1)^j \binom {m}{j} (m-j)^n}{m^n}\; }
\]
is the desired probability.








2 Geometric Probability
Another construction familiar from school is geometric probability: a point is thrown at random into a region \(\Omega\) (a segment, a planar figure, a solid in space), and the probability of landing in a subregion \(A \subset \Omega\) is computed as the ratio of “sizes” (lengths, areas, volumes).






Figure 1: Geometric probability: \(\mathbb {P}(A) = \dfrac {\lambda (A)}{\lambda (\Omega )}\)



By analogy with the classical model, one would like to declare all subsets of \(\Omega\) to be events – just as we did for finite \(\Omega\). But here, for the first time in this course, this simple idea breaks down.
It turns out that there is no way to assign an “area” to all subsets of a square (a segment, a cube) such that the following reasonable requirements simultaneously hold: it should be countably additive (the area of a countable union of disjoint pieces equals the sum of their areas), it should not change under translations, and it should agree with the usual area at least for rectangles. The proof of this fact essentially uses the axiom of choice and is not given here (an explicit example of such a “non-measurable” set – the Vitali set – will be constructed in the second part of the course). But the fact itself already tells us: in geometric probability we cannot declare all subsets of \(\Omega\) to be events – we need to restrict in advance the collection of sets that we allow to have an “area” at all.
What properties, then, should this restricted collection \(\mathcal{F} \subset 2^{\Omega }\) of “good” (measurable) sets have? It is reasonable to require that:

the whole space \(\Omega\) itself is an event;
the complement of an event is an event (if we can measure \(A\), we should also be able to measure “everything else”);
the union of events is an event – and not just for finite unions, but also for countable ones: among other things we will need to find probabilities of limits of events, and this is impossible without countable unions.

(If we restrict ourselves to only finite unions, we get a weaker notion – an algebra of sets; we will study it, together with finer systems of sets – semirings and rings – in detail in the second part of the course.) A collection of sets closed under all three requirements above is called a sigma-algebra.







Definition 2 A system of sets \(\mathcal{F}\) is called a sigma-algebra if the following 3 properties hold:

\(\Omega \in \mathcal{F}\);
if a set \(A \in \mathcal{F}\), then its complement \(\bar{A} \in \mathcal{F}\) as well;
if the sets \(A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots \in \mathcal{F}\), then their infinite union \(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty } A_{i} \in \mathcal{F}\) as well.





By De Morgan’s rule it follows immediately that a sigma-algebra is also closed under countable intersections: \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty } A_i = \overline{\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty } \bar{A}_i} \in \mathcal{F}\). Also \(\varnothing = \bar{\Omega } \in \mathcal{F}\).
Suppose we are given a sample space \(\Omega\) and a sigma-algebra \(\mathcal{F}\) on it. A set \(A \in \mathcal{F}\) is called an event. (In the classical model we implicitly took \(\mathcal{F} = 2^{\Omega }\) – this is also a sigma-algebra, and in fact the largest possible one: all three properties hold for it automatically, which is why there was no need to think about any of this there.)
It remains to formalize probability itself.







Definition 3 A function \(\mathbb {P}: \mathcal{F} \to [0,1]\) is called a probability measure (or simply a probability) if \(\mathbb {P}\left(\varnothing \right) = 0\), \(\mathbb {P}\left(\Omega \right)= 1\), and \(\mathbb {P}\) is countably additive: \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\bigsqcup _{n=1}^{\infty } A_i\right) = \sum _{i=1}^{\infty } \mathbb {P}\left(A_i\right)
\] for any collection of pairwise disjoint sets \(\left\{ A_n\right\}_{n=1}^{\infty } \subset \mathcal{F}\). That is, \(A_n \in \mathcal{F}\) for all \(n\) and \(A_{n_1} \cap A_{n_2} = \varnothing\) for any distinct \(n_1 \neq n_2\).




Pairwise disjoint sets from \(\mathcal{F}\) are also called mutually exclusive events. Countable additivity means that the probability of the occurrence of a countable family of mutually exclusive events (at least one of them) can be computed as the sum of the series of their probabilities.
In the classical model this additivity is trivial: there are only finitely many (nonempty) events there, and countable additivity degenerates into ordinary finite additivity.







Definition 4 A triple \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mathbb {P})\), consisting of a set of elementary events, a sigma-algebra of events, and a probability measure, is called a probability space or a Kolmogorov triple.




We now have a common language in which we can complete the formalization of geometric probability.
The classical geometric probability model is the class of probability models where:

Sample space: \(\Omega \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^n\right)\) – a Borel subset of \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) with finite \(n\)-dimensional volume (\(n = 1, 2, 3\));
Events: \(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{B}(\Omega )\) – the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\);
Probability: uniform, namely \(\mathbb {P}(A) = \frac{\lambda (A)}{\lambda (\Omega )}\), where \(\lambda\) is \(n\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

Thus, the probability space has the form:
\[
  (\Omega , \mathcal{B}(\Omega ), \mathbb {P})
\]
where \(\mathbb {P}(A) = \dfrac {\lambda (A)}{\lambda (\Omega )}\) for any \(A \in \mathcal{B}(\Omega )\).
This model describes experiments in which a particle is uniformly distributed over the region \(\Omega\), and the probability of landing in a subregion \(A\) is proportional to its volume.
Borel sets and Lebesgue measureborel-lebesgue We have just referred to two specific objects that we have not defined: the Borel sigma-algebra \(\mathscr {B}\left(\Omega \right)\) (the chapter on systems of sets and the Borel sigma-algebra) and Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\) (the chapters on outer measure and Carathéodory’s theorem–on Lebesgue measure). We have already defined the abstract notion of a sigma-algebra above – it remains to understand why one takes specifically the Borel sigma-algebra (rather than some other one), and how to construct \(\lambda\) so that it is a genuine countably additive measure (rather than just an intuitive “size”). For now, let us agree to understand them naively: Borel sets are all the “reasonable” subsets of \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) (in particular, any polygons, disks, as well as their countable unions and intersections), and \(\lambda (A)\) is the familiar length/area/volume of the set \(A\).






ExampleExample 3





A point \(A\) is chosen uniformly at random inside a rectangle with sides \(1\) and \(2\). Find the probability that the distance from the point \(A\) to the nearest side of the rectangle does not exceed \(x\).






SolutionSolution





In this case \(\Omega = [0,2] \times [0,1]\), \(\mathcal{F} = \mathscr {B}\left(\Omega \right)\), \(\mathbb {P} = \frac{1}{\lambda (\Omega )}\lambda = \frac{1}{2} \lambda\), where \(\lambda\) is Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\).
Let us consider when the distance from the point \(A\) to the nearest side is greater than \(x\). This is possible only if the point \(A\) lies inside the “inner” rectangle with sides \(1-2x\) and \(2-2x\), obtained by moving in from each side of the original rectangle by \(x\).
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\rho (A,\partial R) > x\right) = \frac{(1-2x)(2-2x)}{\lambda (\Omega )} = (1-2x)(1-x)
\]
since the area of the original rectangle equals \(2\). Consequently,
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\rho (A,\partial R) \leq x\right) = 1 - \mathbb {P}\left(\rho (A,\partial R) > x\right) = 1 - (1-2x)(1-x) = 3x - 2x^2
\]
Note that when \(x \geq 0.5\) the inner rectangle disappears, and the probability equals \(1\).






Figure 2












AnswerAnswer





\(\begin{cases}  3x - 2x^2, &  x < 0.5, \\ 1, &  x \geq 0.5. \end{cases}\).

3 Discrete Model: The General Case
In the classical discrete model, all elementary outcomes are assumed to be equally likely. Let us consider a situation where this is not the case. Let \(\Omega = \{ \omega_1, \ldots , \omega_N\}\), \(\mathcal{F} = 2^{\Omega }\), and let the probability of each outcome be \(p_i = \mathbb {P}\left(\{ \omega_i\} \right)\). Then, clearly, \(\sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i = 1\) holds, and the probability of an arbitrary event is computed as follows: \(\mathbb {P}\left(A\right) = \sum_{i: \omega_i \in A} p_i\). This fully determines the probability space with a finite number of outcomes \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mathbb {P})\).
Everything said carries over verbatim to a countable \(\Omega = \{ \omega_1, \omega_2, \ldots \}\): one need only replace the finite sum \(\sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i = 1\) by the sum of the series \(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty } p_i = 1\), while \(\mathcal{F} = 2^{\Omega }\) remains a sigma-algebra as before (a countable union of subsets of a countable set is again at most countable). Then for any \(A \subset \Omega\) the probability \(\mathbb {P}\left(A\right) = \sum_{i \,  : \,  \omega_i \in A} p_i\) is well defined – this is a series with nonnegative terms, so its sum does not depend on the order of summation.






ExampleExample 5





A fair coin is tossed until the first heads appears. Describe the probability space and find the probability that an odd number of tosses is required.






SolutionSolution





The elementary outcome is the number of tosses until the first heads: \(\Omega = \mathbb {N} = \{ 1, 2, 3, \ldots \}\). The sample space is countable, but, unlike in the classical model, the outcomes are not equally likely. The event \(\{ \omega = k\}\) means: the first \(k-1\) tosses are tails, the \(k\)-th is heads; hence \[
  p_k := \mathbb {P}\left(\omega = k\right) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k-1}\cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2^k}, \qquad k \in \mathbb {N}
\] Let us check that this is a valid distribution: \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty }p_k = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2^k} = 1\). The desired probability: \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\text{the number of tosses is odd}\right) = \sum _{j=0}^{\infty }p_{2j+1} = \sum _{j=0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2^{2j+1}} = \frac{1}{2}\sum _{j=0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{4^j} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{1-1/4} = \frac{2}{3}
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(\frac{2}{3}\).

4 Conditional Probability
Let \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mathbb {P})\) be a probability space (typically finite, for the definitions considered in this section) and let \(A \in \mathcal{F}\) be some event. One often needs to compute the probability of an event given that another event has occurred.







Definition 5 The conditional probability of \(A\) given \(B\) is defined as \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(A \mid B\right) = \begin{cases}  \frac{\mathbb {P}\left(A \cap B\right)}{\mathbb {P}\left(B\right)}, &  \mathbb {P}\left(B\right) > 0 \\ \text{undefined}, &  \mathbb {P}\left(B\right) = 0 \\ \end{cases}
\]










ExampleExample 6





Three dice are thrown. Find the probability that all three dice show a “six,” given that the first die shows a “six.”






SolutionSolution





Denote \[
\begin{align}  A & = \left\{ \text{the first die shows a "six"}\right\}  \\ B & = \left\{ \text{all dice show a "six"}\right\}  \end{align}
\] Then, clearly, \(\mathbb {P}\left(A\right) = \frac{1}{6}\), since showing a “six” is one of six equally likely outcomes in the experiment of throwing a single die. The event \(B \subset A\), so \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(A \cap B\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(B\right) = \frac{1}{6^3},
\] since three “sixes” showing up is one of \(6^{3}\) equally likely outcomes in the experiment of throwing three dice. Hence \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A\right) = \frac{1/6^3}{1/6} = \frac{1}{6^2}
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(\frac{1}{36}\).






A partition of a probability space is a finite or countable system of events \(\left\{ A_1, A_2, \ldots \right\}  = \left\{ A_n \;  : \;  n \in \mathcal{N}\right\}\) (\(\mathcal{N} = \left\{ 1, \ldots , N\right\}\) if the system is finite, and \(\mathcal{N} = \mathbb {N}\) if the system is countable) such that distinct events are disjoint (if \(i \neq j\), then \(A_i \cap A_j = \varnothing\); such a system is also called disjoint) and, taken together, these events cover the whole sample space:
\[
  \bigsqcup _{n \in \mathcal{N}}A_n = \Omega
\]
Let there be some other event \(B\). Note that since \(B \subset \Omega\), we then have
\[
  B = \left(B \cap A_1\right) \sqcup \left(B \cap A_2\right) \sqcup \ldots = \bigsqcup _{n \in \mathcal{N}} B \cap A_n
\]
Using the property of finite or countable additivity of the probability measure, we obtain
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(B\right) = \sum _{n \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbb {P}\left(B \cap A_n\right)
\]
Suppose additionally that \(\mathbb {P}\left(A_n\right) > 0\), \(\forall n\). Then by the formula for conditional probability we have \(\mathbb {P}\left(B \cap A_n\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_n\right) \mathbb {P}\left(A_n\right)\), \(\forall n\). This brings us to the following theorem.







Theorem 1 (Law of Total Probability) Suppose we have a partition \(\left\{ A_n\right\}_{n \in \mathcal{N}}\) (finite or countable) with \(\mathbb {P}\left(A_n\right) > 0\), \(\forall n\). Then for any event \(B\) the following formula holds: \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(B\right) = \sum _{n \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_n\right) \mathbb {P}\left(A_n\right)
\]




Suppose in addition that \(\mathbb {P}\left(B\right) > 0\). Then for an arbitrary \(i \in \mathcal{N}\) we have
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(A_i \mid B\right) = \frac{\mathbb {P}\left(A_i \cap B\right)}{\mathbb {P}\left(B\right)} = \frac{\mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_i\right) \mathbb {P}\left(A_i\right)}{\mathbb {P}\left(B\right)}
\]
If, in addition, we replace \(\mathbb {P}\left(B\right)\) in the denominator using the law of total probability, we obtain the famous Bayes’ formula.







Theorem 2 (Bayes’ Formula) Suppose we have a partition \(\left\{ A_n\right\}_{n \in \mathcal{N}}\) (finite or countable) with \(\mathbb {P}\left(A_n\right) > 0\), \(\forall n\). Then for any event \(B\) with \(\mathbb {P}\left(B\right) > 0\) and for any \(i \in \mathcal{N}\) the following formula holds: \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(A_{i} \mid B \right)=\frac{\mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_i\right) \mathbb {P}\left(A_i\right)}{\sum _{n \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_n\right) \mathbb {P}\left(A_n\right)}
\]










ExampleExample 7





Young men pass by a donut shop with frequency \(0.6\), young women with frequency \(0.3\), and instructors with frequency \(0.1\). Young men buy a donut with probability \(0.4\), young women with probability \(0.9\), and instructors with probability \(0.2\). It is known that the last person bought a donut. Find the conditional probability that the donut was bought by an instructor.






SolutionSolution





Denote the events:

\(B = \{ \text{the last person bought a donut}\}\)
\(A_1 = \{ \text{this person is a young man}\}\)
\(A_2 = \{ \text{this person is a young woman}\}\)
\(A_3 = \{ \text{this person is an instructor}\}\)

By the conditions of the problem:
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(A_1\right) = 0.6,\quad \mathbb {P}\left(A_2\right) = 0.3,\quad \mathbb {P}\left(A_3\right) = 0.1
\] \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_1\right) = 0.4,\quad \mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_2\right) = 0.9,\quad \mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_3\right) = 0.2
\]
By Bayes’ formula:
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}\left(A_3 \mid B\right) & = \frac{\mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_3\right) \mathbb {P}\left(A_3\right)}{\mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_1\right) \mathbb {P}\left(A_1\right) + \mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_2\right) \mathbb {P}\left(A_2\right) + \mathbb {P}\left(B \mid A_3\right) \mathbb {P}\left(A_3\right)} = \\ & = \frac{0.2 \cdot 0.1}{0.4 \cdot 0.6 + 0.9 \cdot 0.3 + 0.2 \cdot 0.1} = \frac{0.02}{0.24 + 0.27 + 0.02} = \frac{0.02}{0.53} \approx 0.038 \end{align}
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(\frac{2}{53}\).

5 Independence
We say that an event \(B\) does not depend on an event \(A\) if the probability of their joint occurrence factors as the product of the individual probabilities:
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(A \cap B\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(A\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(B\right)
\]
Let there be a collection of events \(A_{1}, \ldots , A_{n}\).







Definition 6 Arbitrary events \(A, B \in \mathcal{F}\) are called independent if \(\mathbb {P}\left(A \cap B\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(A\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(B\right)\).
The events \(A_{1}, \ldots , A_{n}\) are called pairwise independent if for any distinct \(i, j \in \{ 1, \ldots , n\}\) the events \(A_i\) and \(A_j\) are independent.
The events \(A_{1}, \ldots , A_{n}\) are called mutually independent if for any collection of indices \(i_{1}, i_{2}, \ldots , i_{k}, 1 \leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\ldots <i_{k} \leq n\), we have
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(A_{i_1} \cap A_{i_2} \cap \ldots \cap A_{i_k}\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(A_{i_1}\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(A_{i_2}\right) \cdot \cdots \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(A_{i_k}\right)
\]




It is easy to see that mutual independence implies pairwise independence. The converse, as the following example shows, is false.






ExampleExample 8 - Bernstein’s Example





Give an example of events that are pairwise independent but not mutually independent.






SolutionSolution





Consider a tetrahedron \(A C D E\). Let us color vertex \(A\) red, vertex \(C\) green, \(D\) blue, and \(E\) in all three colors at once. Consider the experiment of choosing a vertex of the tetrahedron uniformly at random. Introduce the events \[
\begin{align}  R & = \left\{ \text{the chosen vertex is colored red}\right\} \\ G & = \left\{ \text{the chosen vertex is colored green}\right\}  \\ B & = \left\{ \text{the chosen vertex is colored blue}\right\}  \end{align}
\] Then \(\mathbb {P}\left(B\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(G\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(R\right) = \frac{1}{2}\), and the probabilities of the pairwise intersections are \(\mathbb {P}\left(B \cap G\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(G \cap R\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(B \cap R\right) = \frac{1}{4}\), i.e., the events \(B, G\), and \(R\) are pairwise independent. But \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(B \cap G \cap R\right) = \frac{1}{4} \neq \frac{1}{8} = \mathbb {P}\left(B\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(G\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(R\right)
\] i.e., the events are not mutually independent.

6 Bernoulli Scheme
Let us now introduce the so-called Bernoulli scheme. Consider a series of identical, mutually independent experiments, each having 2 outcomes (for example, repeatedly tossing a coin). Call one of these outcomes success (denote it \(\{ 1\}\)), and the other failure (denote it \(\{ 0\}\)). It is known that the probability of success in one experiment equals \(\mathbb {P}\left(\left\{ 1\right\} \right) =: p\), and the probability of failure is \(\mathbb {P}\left(\left\{ 0\right\} \right) = 1 - p =: q\). Then the sample space consists of all binary sequences of length \(n\):
\[
  \Omega = \left\{ \omega = (\varepsilon _1, \ldots , \varepsilon _n) \;  : \;  \varepsilon _1, \ldots , \varepsilon _n \in \left\{ 0,1\right\} \right\}
\]
and the probability of each elementary outcome equals
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\omega \right) = p^{\sum _{i=1}^{n} \varepsilon _{i}} q^{n-\sum _{i=1}^{n} \varepsilon _{i}}
\]
It is easy to check that the sum of the probabilities of all outcomes in this case equals 1. One is often required to find the probability that, in a scheme of \(n\) Bernoulli trials, \(k\) successes occurred: this probability equals \(C_{n}^{k} p^{k} q^{n-k}\).






ExampleExample 9





Two players carry out an infinite series of independent trials. In each trial, player \(A\) throws 3 dice, while player \(B\) throws 2 dice at the same time as player \(A\) and independently of him. They carry out these trials in sequence until a “six” first comes up on at least one of the dice. Find the probability that a “six” first came up for player \(A\), and not for \(B\).






SolutionSolution





Denote \[
  A_k = \left\{ \text{a "six" came up on the $k$-th trial for at least one of the players}\right\}
\] Let \[
\begin{align}  D_{k}& =\bigcap _{i=1}^{k-1} \overline{A_{i}} \\ B_k & = \left\{ \text{player $A$'s dice showed a "six" on the $k$-th trial}\right\}  \\ C_k & = \left\{ \text{player $B$'s dice showed a "six" on the $k$-th trial}\right\}  \end{align}
\] Call it a success on the \(k\)-th trial if, on the \(k\)-th trial, player \(A\)’s dice showed a “six” while \(B\)’s did not. This probability equals \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(B_k \cap \overline{C_k}\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(B_k\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(\overline{C_k}\right) = \left(1-\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{3}\right)\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{2}=\frac{91 \cdot 25}{6^{5}}
\] Since \(B_{k}\) and \(C_{k}\) are independent of each other and of \(D_{k}\) by assumption, the desired probability equals \[
\begin{align}  \sum _{k=1}^{n} \mathbb {P}\left(B_{k} \cap \overline{C_{k}} \mid D_{k}\right) \mathbb {P}\left(D_k\right) = \sum _{k=1}^{n} \mathbb {P}\left(B_{k} \cap \overline{C_{k}}\right) \mathbb {P}\left(D_{k}\right) = \frac{25 \cdot 91}{6^{5}} \sum _{k=1}^{\infty } \mathbb {P}\left(D_k\right) = \\ =\frac{25 \cdot 91}{6^{5}}\left(1+\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{5}+\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{10}+\ldots \right)=\frac{25 \cdot 91}{6^{5}-5^{5}} \end{align}
\] where \(D_{1}=\Omega\).












ExampleExample 10





Find the probability that, in \(2 n\) trials of a Bernoulli scheme with probability of success \(p\) and probability of failure \(q=1-p\), there are \(m+n\) successes and all trials with even indices end in success.






SolutionSolution





For the event whose probability we need to find to occur, given that the \(n\) trials with even indices ended in success (the probability of this event is clearly \(p^{n}\)), it is necessary and sufficient that \(m\) of the trials with odd indices end in success. Since the trials with even and odd indices are independent, the desired probability equals \(p^{n} C_{n}^{m} p^{m} q^{n-m}=C_{n}^{m} p^{n+m} q^{n-m}\).

text:
3.1 Convergence in probability







Definition 2 Let \(\xi , \xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) be random variables defined on the same probability space. The sequence \(\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) is said to converge in probability to \(\xi\) if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\left|\xi _n - \xi \right| \geq \varepsilon \right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} 0  
\] Notation: \[
  \xi _n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} \xi  
\]




Intuition: as \(n\) grows, the random variable \(\xi_n\) deviates from \(\xi\) by more than any fixed error \(\varepsilon\) less and less often. This is exactly the convergence that appears in the LLN: the sample mean \(\frac{S_n}{n}\) converges in probability to the expectation.
Note: for the expression \(\left|\xi_n - \xi \right|\) to make sense, the random variables \(\xi_n\) and \(\xi\) must be defined on the same \(\Omega\).






ProblemProblem 2





Is it true that convergence in probability implies convergence of expectations?









ProblemProblem 3





Let \(\left(\xi_{n}-\xi \right)^{2} \xrightarrow {\mathbb {P}} 0\). Show that \(\xi_{n}^{2} \xrightarrow {\mathbb {P}} \xi^{2}\).

title: Covariance, convergence of random variables, limit theorems
text:
3.2 Convergence in distribution
The second type of convergence answers a different question: not “are the values of \(\xi_n\) and \(\xi\) close as functions on \(\Omega\)”, but “does the distribution of \(\xi_n\) resemble the distribution of \(\xi\)”. Thus the CLT asserts that the distribution of a normalized sum approaches the normal distribution; the random variables themselves do not “approach” any particular random variable — it is their distributions that converge.
A distribution on \(\mathbb {R}\) is completely described by its distribution function (see the chapter on random variables and distribution functions), so it is natural to define convergence of distributions via convergence of distribution functions. The only subtlety is at which points to require convergence. Consider an example: let \(\xi_n \equiv \frac{1}{n}\) be constant random variables. It is reasonable to expect that \(\xi_n\) converges (in any sensible sense) to \(\xi \equiv 0\). Let us look at the distribution functions:
\[
  F_{\xi _n}(x) = \; \mathbb {1}_{x \geq \tfrac {1}{n}} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \begin{cases}  1, &  x > 0 \\ 0, &  x \leq 0\end{cases}, \qquad \text{while} \qquad F_{\xi }(x) = \; \mathbb {1}_{x \geq 0}
\]
The limits agree everywhere except at the single point \(x = 0\): \(F_{\xi_n}(0) = 0 \not\to 1 = F_{\xi }(0)\). Note that \(x=0\) is precisely the discontinuity (jump) point of the limiting distribution function. To prevent such natural examples from breaking the definition, convergence is not required at discontinuity points of the limiting \(F\).







Definition 3 A sequence of random variables \(\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) is said to converge in distribution to a random variable \(\xi\) if \[
  F_{\xi _n}(x) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} F_{\xi }(x) \qquad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb {R} \text{ at which } F_{\xi } \text{ is continuous}
\] Notation: \[
  \xi _{n} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \xi ,  
\] from the English distribution.




Since only distribution functions appear in the definition, the random variables \(\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) and \(\xi\) may be defined on entirely different probability spaces — unlike convergence in probability. For the same reason, instead of naming a limiting random variable one may specify the limiting distribution directly and write, for example, \(\xi_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\) (which is exactly what we will do in the CLT).






ProblemProblem 4





Is it true that convergence in distribution implies convergence of expectations? That is, \[
  \xi _n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \xi \quad \stackrel{?}{\;  \Rightarrow \; } \quad \mathbb {E}\left[\xi _n\right] \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right]  
\] Prove it if it is true. If it is false, give a counterexample.






HintHint





Take \(\xi\) to be the constant zero: \(\xi \equiv 0\). Check whether convergence \(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi_n\right] \to 0\) is guaranteed in this case.












ProblemProblem 5





Let \(\xi_n\) be uniformly distributed on \(\{ 1,2,\dots ,n\}\): \(\xi_n \sim \operatorname {Unif}\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\}\). Let \(\eta_n = \frac{\xi_n}{n}\). Does the sequence \(\eta_1, \eta_2, \ldots\) converge in distribution?

text:
3.3 The relationship between the two convergences







Lemma 1 Let \(\xi , \xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) be random variables on the same probability space. Then \[
  \xi _n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} \xi \quad \;  \Rightarrow \;  \quad \xi _n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \xi  
\] The converse is false in general (see the problems below). However, if the limit is a constant \(c \in \mathbb {R}\) (more precisely, a random variable identically equal to \(c\)), then the two convergences are equivalent: \[
  \xi _n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} c \quad \iff \quad \xi _n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} c  
\]










ExampleExample 3





Prove the \(\Leftarrow\) direction of the second part of the lemma: if \(\xi_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} c\), then \(\xi_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} c\).






SolutionSolution





The distribution function of the constant: \(F_c(x) = \; \mathbb {1}_{x \geq c}\). It is continuous at every point except \(x = c\). Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be arbitrary. The points \(c - \varepsilon\) and \(c + \frac{\varepsilon }{2}\) are different from \(c\), i.e., they are points of continuity of \(F_c\), so convergence of distribution functions holds at them. We have \[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}\left(\left|\xi _n - c\right| \geq \varepsilon \right) & = \mathbb {P}\left(\xi _n \leq c - \varepsilon \right) + \mathbb {P}\left(\xi _n \geq c + \varepsilon \right) \leq F_{\xi _n}(c-\varepsilon ) + 1 - F_{\xi _n}\left(c + \tfrac {\varepsilon }{2}\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \\ & \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} F_c(c - \varepsilon ) + 1 - F_c\left(c + \tfrac {\varepsilon }{2}\right) = 0 + 1 - 1 = 0 \end{align}
\] Explanation of the inequality: \(\mathbb {P}\left(\xi_n \geq c + \varepsilon \right) \leq \mathbb {P}\left(\xi_n > c + \frac{\varepsilon }{2}\right) = 1 - F_{\xi_n}\left(c + \frac{\varepsilon }{2}\right)\). This completes the proof.

Let \(\xi_n \sim \mathrm{Ber}\! \left(\tfrac {1}{n}\right)\). Does the sequence \(\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) converge in distribution (to some random variable)? What about in probability?

Let \(\Omega = \left\{ \omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\right\}\) with the classical (uniform) probability (\(\mathbb {P}\left(\omega_i\right) = \frac{1}{3}\)). Define random variables \(X\), \(Y\):
