text:
2.4 Linear functionals. The Hahn–Banach theorem







Definition 9 Let \(V, W\) be normed spaces. A linear map \(T: V \to W\) is called bounded if \[
  \left\| T\right\|  := \sup \left\{ \left\| Tf\right\| : f \in V, \;  \left\| f\right\| \leq 1\right\}  < \infty .  
\] A linear functional on \(V\) is a linear map \(\varphi : V \to \mathbb F\) (into the field of scalars).











Theorem 7 A linear map \(T: V \to W\) between normed spaces is continuous if and only if it is bounded.




The set of bounded linear functionals on \(V\) is called the dual space and is denoted \(V'\); this is itself a normed (and even Banach) space with the norm \(\left\| \varphi \right\|  = \sup \left\{ \left|\varphi (f)\right|: \left\| f\right\|  \leq 1\right\}\).






ExampleExample 6





Find the norm of the linear functional \(\varphi (f) = \int_0^1 f(x)\, dx\) on \((C[0,1], \left\| \cdot \right\|_{\infty })\).






SolutionSolution





On the one hand, for any \(f\) with \(\left\| f\right\|_{\infty }\leq 1\) we have \(\left|\varphi (f)\right| \leq \int_0^1 \left|f(x)\right|\, dx \leq \int_0^1 \left\| f\right\|_{\infty }\, dx \leq 1\), so \(\left\| \varphi \right\|  \leq 1\). On the other hand, for \(f \equiv 1\) (constant) we have \(\left\| f\right\|_{\infty }=1\) and \(\varphi (f) = 1\). Hence the supremum is attained and \(\left\| \varphi \right\|  = 1\).






The existence of discontinuous linear functionals on infinite-dimensional spaces is, oddly enough, a rather delicate fact, requiring a Hamel basis and Zorn’s lemma (we will not dwell on this). Far more useful for analysis is the following result — on the existence of continuous (= bounded) functionals “in sufficient quantity.”







Theorem 8 (Hahn–Banach, without proof) Let \(V\) be a normed space, \(U \subset V\) a subspace, \(\psi : U \to \mathbb F\) a bounded linear functional. Then \(\psi\) can be extended to a bounded linear functional \(\varphi : V \to \mathbb F\) with the same norm: \(\left\| \varphi \right\|  = \left\| \psi \right\|\).




One of the most useful consequences of the Hahn–Banach theorem is that on any nontrivial normed space there are enough functionals to “sense” the norm of any vector.







Corollary 2 Let \(V\) be a normed space, \(f \in V\), \(f \neq 0\). Then there exists \(\varphi \in V'\) such that \(\left\| \varphi \right\|  = 1\) and \(\varphi (f) = \left\| f\right\|\).




Indeed, it suffices to define \(\psi\) on the one-dimensional subspace \(U = \left\{ \alpha f: \alpha \in \mathbb F\right\}\) by the formula \(\psi (\alpha f) = \alpha \left\| f\right\|\) (then \(\left\| \psi \right\| =1\), \(\psi (f)=\left\| f\right\|\)) and extend it using the Hahn–Banach theorem.






ProblemProblem 7





Let \(V\) be a normed space such that \(V' = \left\{ 0\right\}\) (the only bounded linear functional on \(V\) is zero). Prove, using Corollary Corollary 2, that \(V = \left\{ 0\right\}\).



The topic of linear functionals and Banach spaces is much broader than what is described here: there is also the Baire category theorem and its consequences — the open mapping theorem, the closed graph theorem, the uniform boundedness principle (the Banach–Steinhaus principle). These results form the core of classical functional analysis, but lie beyond the scope of our course; those interested can consult, for example, (Axler 2020, sec. 6E) or any textbook on functional analysis.

title: Lebesgue spaces \(L^p(\mu )\)
text:
2.5 Completeness: the Riesz–Fischer theorem
Now we can use the completeness criterion via series (Theorem Theorem 6) to obtain one of the most important properties of \(L^p\)-spaces.







Theorem 9 (Riesz–Fischer) Let \(\mu\) be a measure, \(1\leq p \leq \infty\). Then \(L^p(\mu )\) is a Banach space.




(Idea, for \(1\leq p<\infty\): by criterion Theorem 6 it suffices to take an arbitrary series \(\sum_k g_k\) with \(\sum_k\left\| g_k\right\|_{p}<\infty\) and exhibit its sum. The majorant \(G:=\sum_k\left|g_k\right|\) lies in \(\mathcal L^p(\mu )\) by Minkowski’s inequality and the monotone convergence theorem, hence is finite a.e.; where it is finite, the series \(\sum_k g_k(x)\) converges absolutely to some \(f(x)\), and \(\left|f-F_N\right|^p\leq G^p\) gives, by the dominated convergence theorem, \(\left\| f-F_N\right\|_{p}\to 0\).)

title: Lebesgue spaces \(L^p(\mu )\)
text:
2.6 Density of simple functions







Theorem 10 Let \(1\leq p<\infty\), \(f \in \mathcal L^p(\mu )\). Then for every \(\varepsilon >0\) there exists a simple function \(s \in \mathcal L^p(\mu )\) such that \(\left\| f-s\right\|_{p}<\varepsilon\).

title: Lebesgue spaces \(L^p(\mu )\)
section: 2.7 Convergence in \(L^p\) and other types of convergence
text:
2.7 Convergence in \(L^p\) and other types of convergence
Convergence \(f_n \to f\) in \(L^p(\mu )\) (i.e., \(\left\| f_n-f\right\|_{p}\to 0\)) is the third type of convergence of measurable functions that we encounter in this course (after a.e. convergence and convergence in measure from the chapter on convergence of measurable functions). How are these convergences related?






ProblemProblem 8





Let \(1\leq p<\infty\), \(f_n \to f\) in \(L^p(\mu )\). Prove that \(f_n \to f\) in measure \(\mu\).






HintHint





Apply Markov’s inequality (theorem Markov’s inequality) to \(\left|f_n-f\right|^p\).






In particular, by F. Riesz’s theorem on convergence in measure (chapter on convergence of measurable functions), \(L^p\)-convergence implies the existence of a subsequence converging to \(f\) a.e. — entirely analogous to what happened with convergence in measure. The converse, of course, is false: a.e. convergence (and even uniform convergence) need not imply \(L^p\)-convergence without additional conditions (domination, etc.) — recall the counterexamples to Fatou’s lemma and the dominated convergence theorem from the chapter on the properties of the Lebesgue integral.

title: Lebesgue spaces \(L^p(\mu )\)
text:
3.1 Inner products







Definition 10 Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(\mathbb F\), where \(\mathbb F = \mathbb {R}\) or \(\mathbb F = \mathbb {C}\). An inner product on the vector space \(V\) over the field \(\mathbb {F}\) (\(\mathbb {R}\) or \(\mathbb {C}\)) is a function \(\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle : V \times V \to \mathbb {F}\) satisfying the properties:

Positive definiteness: \(\langle f, f \rangle \geq 0\) for all \(f \in V\), with \(\langle f, f \rangle = 0\) if and only if \(f = 0\).
Linearity in the first argument: \(\langle f + g, h \rangle = \langle f, h \rangle + \langle g, h \rangle\) and \(\langle \alpha f, g \rangle = \alpha \langle f, g \rangle\) for all \(f, g, h \in V\) and \(\alpha \in \mathbb {F}\).
Hermitian symmetry (conjugate symmetry): \(\langle f, g \rangle = \overline{\langle g, f \rangle }\) for all \(f, g \in V\). The pair \((V, \left\langle \cdot , \cdot \right\rangle )\) is called an inner product space (or a pre-Hilbert space).





From axioms 2-3 it is easy to derive linearity in the second argument with conjugation: \(\left\langle f, g+h \right\rangle = \left\langle f, g \right\rangle + \left\langle f, h \right\rangle\), \(\left\langle f, \alpha g \right\rangle = \bar\alpha \left\langle f, g \right\rangle\).
All the examples in this course coming from probability theory are real, so everywhere further in this section we take \(\mathbb F=\mathbb {R}\), unless explicitly stated otherwise. In this case axiom 3 turns into ordinary symmetry \(\left\langle f, g \right\rangle = \left\langle g, f \right\rangle\), and all the conjugations in the formulas below can simply be dropped. All definitions and theorems in this section carry over verbatim to the complex case (with a complex-conjugate bar appearing where appropriate); we will occasionally note this in remarks.
Examples.

Let \((X,\mathcal F,\mu )\) be a measure space. On \(L^2(\mu )\) define
\[
  \left\langle f, g \right\rangle := \int fg \;  d\mu .  
\]
This is well defined: by Hölder’s inequality with \(p=q=2\) (proved in §1), for \(f,g\in L^2(\mu )\) we have \(\int \left|fg\right|\; d\mu \leq \left\| [\right\| 2]f\cdot \left\| [\right\| 2]g <\infty\), so the integral \(\int fg\; d\mu\) converges absolutely and is finite. The inner product \(\left\langle f, g \right\rangle = \int fg\, d\mu\) is exactly the form that generates the norm \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{2}\) from §1 (see below for the definition of the norm generated by an inner product). This is the main example for us: almost everything we will need from probability theory later on is a special case of precisely this space.
Taking \(\mu = \#\) — the counting measure on \(\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\}\) — we get \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) with the standard inner product \(\left\langle (a_1,\ldots ,a_n), (b_1,\ldots ,b_n) \right\rangle = \sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_i\).
Taking \(\mu =\#\) — the counting measure on \(\mathbb {N}\) — we get \(\ell^2 := \left\{ (a_k)_{k=1}^\infty \;  : \;  \sum_k a_k^2 <\infty \right\}\) with the inner product \(\left\langle (a_k), (b_k) \right\rangle = \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_kb_k\).







Mn-remarkRemark




In the complex case (\(\mathbb F=\mathbb {C}\)) the same three examples give \(\mathbb {C}^{n}\), \(\ell^2\), and \(L^2(\mu )\) over \(\mathbb {C}\) with inner products \(\left\langle f, g \right\rangle = \int f\overline g\; d\mu\), etc. (the bar denotes complex conjugation).










Definition 11 Let \((V, \left\langle \cdot , \cdot \right\rangle )\) be an inner product space. The norm generated by the inner product is \[
  \left\| f\right\|  := \sqrt{ \left\langle f, f \right\rangle }, \qquad f \in V.  
\]




From axiom 1 it immediately follows that \(\left\| f\right\|  \geq 0\) and \(\left\| f\right\|  = 0 \iff f=0\); from linearity and Hermitian symmetry — homogeneity \(\left\| \alpha f\right\|  = \left|\alpha \right|\left\| f\right\|\) (check: \(\left\| \alpha f\right\|^2 = \left\langle \alpha f, \alpha f \right\rangle = \alpha \bar\alpha \left\langle f, f \right\rangle = \left|\alpha \right|^2\left\| f\right\|^2\)). What remains is the triangle inequality — it will follow from the following fundamental inequality.







Theorem 11 (Cauchy–Bunyakovsky–Schwarz inequality) Let \((V, \left\langle \cdot , \cdot \right\rangle )\) be a (real) inner product space, \(f,g\in V\). Then \[
  \left| \left\langle f, g \right\rangle \right| \leq \left\| f\right\|  \cdot \left\| g\right\| ,  
\] with equality holding if and only if \(f,g\) are linearly dependent.










Mn-remarkRemark




In the complex case, the proof repeats almost verbatim: one takes \(t=\overline{ \left\langle f, g \right\rangle }/\left\| g\right\|^2 \in \mathbb {C}\) instead of a real parameter (equivalently — apply the just-proved real case to the pair \(f, e^{i\theta }g\) for such \(\theta\) that \(\left\langle f, e^{i\theta }g \right\rangle \in \mathbb {R}\)).










Corollary 3 (\(\left\| \cdot \right\|\) is indeed a norm) \(\left\| \cdot \right\|\) is a norm on \(V\): nonnegativity, nondegeneracy, and homogeneity were treated above, and the triangle inequality follows from Theorem Theorem 11: \[
  \left\| f+g\right\| ^2 = \left\| f\right\| ^2+2 \left\langle f, g \right\rangle +\left\| g\right\| ^2 \leq \left\| f\right\| ^2 + 2\left\| f\right\| \left\| g\right\|  + \left\| g\right\| ^2 = \left(\left\| f\right\| +\left\| g\right\| \right)^2.  
\]











Theorem 12 (parallelogram identity) For all \(f,g\in V\) \[
  \left\| f+g\right\| ^2+\left\| f-g\right\| ^2 = 2\left\| f\right\| ^2+2\left\| g\right\| ^2.  
\]




Geometrically: the sum of the squares of the diagonals of a parallelogram equals the sum of the squares of all its sides. The parallelogram identity is exactly the property of a norm that distinguishes norms generated by an inner product from arbitrary norms: one can show (we will not prove this — see Axler, exercise 8A.16) that a norm on a vector space is generated by some inner product if and only if it satisfies the parallelogram identity.







Definition 12 (Hilbert space) A Hilbert space is an inner product space that is complete with respect to the norm generated by this inner product (i.e., a Banach space whose norm is generated by some inner product).




Examples. \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) and \(\ell^2\) with the standard inner products are Hilbert spaces (completeness is a standard fact of linear algebra / analysis). The main example for us: \(L^2(\mu )\) is a Hilbert space for any measure space \((X,\mathcal F,\mu )\), since it is already known to us to be complete (the Riesz–Fischer theorem from §2), and its norm \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{2}\) is generated by the inner product \(\left\langle f, g \right\rangle =\int fg\; d\mu\) introduced above.






ProblemProblem 9





Show that the norm \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{1}\) on \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\) (i.e., \(\left\| (a,b)\right\|_{1} = \left|a\right| + \left|b\right|\)) does not satisfy the parallelogram identity. Deduce from this that this norm is not generated by any inner product on \(\mathbb {R}^{2}\) (in particular, \(\ell^1\) and \(L^1(\mu )\) are, in general, not Hilbert spaces).









ProblemProblem 10





Let \(\mu\) be a measure, \(f,g\in L^2(\mu )\). Show directly (without using Hölder’s inequality) that \(\int \left|fg\right|\; d\mu <\infty\), using the elementary inequality \(\left|ab\right|\leq \frac12(a^2+b^2)\) for \(a,b\in \mathbb {R}\).






HintHint





Apply the inequality to \(a=\left|f(x)\right|\), \(b=\left|g(x)\right|\) and integrate.

title: Lebesgue spaces \(L^p(\mu )\)
text:
3.2 Orthogonality. The projection theorem







Definition 13 Elements \(f,g\) of an inner product space are called orthogonal (\(f\perp g\)) if \(\left\langle f, g \right\rangle =0\).











Theorem 13 (Pythagorean theorem) If \(f\perp g\), then \(\left\| f+g\right\|^2 = \left\| f\right\|^2+\left\| g\right\|^2\).











Definition 14 Let \(U\subseteq V\) be an arbitrary subset of an inner product space \(V\). The orthogonal complement of \(U\) is \[
  U^\perp := \left\{ h\in V \;  : \;  \left\langle g, h \right\rangle =0 \;  \;  \forall g\in U\right\} .  
\]











Lemma 4 (properties of the orthogonal complement) Let \(U,W\) be subsets of an inner product space \(V\). Then

\(U^\perp\) is a closed linear subspace of \(V\);
\(U\cap U^\perp \subseteq \left\{ 0\right\}\);
if \(W\subseteq U\), then \(U^\perp \subseteq W^\perp\);
\(U \subseteq U^{\perp \perp } := \left(U^\perp \right)^\perp\).





(Items (b)–(d) are direct consequences of the definition; in (a), linearity is also clear, and closedness follows from continuity of the inner product: if \(h_n\in U^\perp\), \(h_n\to h\), then \(\left| \left\langle g, h \right\rangle \right|=\left| \left\langle g, h-h_n \right\rangle \right|\leq \left\| g\right\| \left\| h-h_n\right\| \to 0\) by the Cauchy–Bunyakovsky–Schwarz inequality, for any \(g\in U\).)







Definition 15 A subset \(U\) of a vector space is called convex if \((1-t)f+tg \in U\) for all \(f,g\in U\), \(t\in [0,1]\).




Every linear subspace is convex (check!), but not conversely (for example, a ball).
The following theorem is the technical centerpiece of this section. It is here that completeness is first genuinely used: without it (i.e., in an arbitrary inner product space that is not Hilbert), the statement is, in general, false — a closest point may fail to exist.







Theorem 14 (on projection onto a closed convex set) Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, \(U\subseteq H\) a nonempty closed convex subset, \(f\in H\). Then there exists a unique element \(g\in U\) realizing the distance from \(f\) to \(U\): \[
  \left\| f-g\right\|  = \operatorname {dist}(f,U) := \inf _{u\in U}\left\| f-u\right\| .  
\]











Definition 16 (orthogonal projection) Let \(U\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(H\). The orthogonal projection of \(H\) onto \(U\) is the map \(P_U : H\to U\) that assigns to \(f\in H\) the unique (by Theorem Theorem 14) element of \(U\) closest to it.










ExampleExample 7





Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, \(U=\left\{ g\in H \;  : \;  \left\| g\right\| \leq 1\right\}\) the closed unit ball (it is convex and closed, so Theorem Theorem 14 applies). Find \(P_Uf\) for \(f\in H\).






SolutionSolution





If \(\left\| f\right\| \leq 1\), then \(f\in U\) and clearly the closest point is \(f\) itself: \(P_Uf=f\). If \(\left\| f\right\| >1\), then the claim is \(P_Uf = f/\left\| f\right\|\). Indeed, \(\left\| f/\left\| f\right\| \right\| =1\), so \(f/\left\| f\right\|  \in U\); for any \(g\in U\) (i.e., \(\left\| g\right\| \leq 1\)) one can check (by expanding the inner products) that \(\left\| f-g\right\| \geq \left\| f\right\|  - 1 = \left\| f-f/\left\| f\right\| \right\|\), i.e., \(f/\left\| f\right\|\) is indeed the closest point. This shows that \(P_U\) is defined not only on closed subspaces, but on arbitrary closed convex sets — however, from now on we will only be interested in the case of a subspace.






Let us specialize the projection theorem to the case where \(U\) is a closed linear subspace (rather than just a convex set). It is exactly this case that we will need for the Riesz theorem and (later in the probability theory course) for conditional expectation.







Theorem 15 (properties of orthogonal projection onto a subspace) Let \(U\) be a closed linear subspace of a Hilbert space \(H\), \(f\in H\). Then

\(f-P_Uf \perp g\) for every \(g\in U\);
if \(h\in U\) and \(f-h\perp g\) for every \(g\in U\), then \(h=P_Uf\);
\(P_U : H\to H\) is a linear map;
\(\left\| P_Uf\right\| \leq \left\| f\right\|\).





(Idea: (a) follows from the fact that \(P_Uf\) minimizes \(\left\| f-\cdot \right\|\) along the entire line \(P_Uf+\alpha g\subset U\), \(\alpha \in \mathbb {R}\) — a quadratic function of \(\alpha\) with a minimum at \(0\) must have zero derivative there, which gives orthogonality. (b) is a reformulation of (a): the characteristic property “\(f-h\perp U\)” uniquely determines \(h=P_Uf\). (c) linearity of \(P_U\) follows from (b), applied to \(h=P_Uf_1+\alpha P_Uf_2\). (d) the Pythagorean theorem for \(f=(f-P_Uf)+P_Uf\), with orthogonal summands by (a).)






ProblemProblem 11





Let \(U\) be a closed linear subspace of a Hilbert space \(H\). Prove that \(P_U\circ P_U = P_U\) (i.e., \(P_U\) is idempotent), and that \(P_Uf = f \iff f\in U\).



Now — a key geometric fact: a closed subspace and its orthogonal complement “split” the entire space.







Theorem 16 (orthogonal decomposition) Let \(U\) be a closed linear subspace of a Hilbert space \(H\). Then every element \(f\in H\) can be represented uniquely in the form \[
  f = g+h, \qquad g\in U, \; \;  h\in U^\perp ,  
\] namely \(g=P_Uf\), \(h=f-P_Uf\). This is written briefly as \(H = U\oplus U^\perp\).




(Existence: \(f=P_Uf+(f-P_Uf)\), where the first summand is in \(U\) and the second in \(U^\perp\) by Theorem Theorem 15(a). Uniqueness: if \(f=g_1+h_1=g_2+h_2\) are two such decompositions, then \(g_1-g_2=h_2-h_1\in U\cap U^\perp =\left\{ 0\right\}\) by Lemma Lemma 4(b).)







Corollary 4 If \(U\) is a closed linear subspace of a Hilbert space \(H\), then \(U^{\perp \perp }=U\).










Mn-remarkRemark




3.3 why all this is needed in probability theory
Let \((\Omega ,\mathcal F,\mathbb {P})\) be a probability space, \(\mathcal G\subseteq \mathcal F\) a sub-\(\sigma\)-algebra. The space \(L^2(\Omega ,\mathcal G,\mathbb {P})\) naturally embeds into \(L^2(\Omega ,\mathcal F,\mathbb {P})\) as a closed linear subspace, so that for any \(X\in L^2(\Omega ,\mathcal F,\mathbb {P})\), by Theorem Theorem 16, its orthogonal projection onto this subspace is well defined — and this is precisely the best way to understand conditional expectation: \(\mathbb {E}\left[X\mid \mathcal G\right] := P_{L^2(\Omega ,\mathcal G,\mathbb {P})}X\) (this construction is then extended from \(L^2\) to all integrable random variables by other means; we do not develop this theory here — it is a topic for a separate course in probability theory). Let us just note the fact itself: one of the central constructions of probability theory is literally a special case of orthogonal projection in a Hilbert space.









Mn-remarkRemark




3.4 regression, prediction, and the Karhunen–Loève expansion
The same geometric picture underlies several other central constructions in statistics and the theory of random processes.

The best mean-square predictor. Let \(X, Y \in L^2(\Omega ,\mathcal F,\mathbb {P})\). The quantity \(g(X)\) minimizing the mean-square prediction error \(\mathbb {E}\left[(Y-g(X))^2\right]\) over all measurable \(g\) (with \(g(X) \in L^2\)) is exactly the projection of \(Y\) onto the subspace \(L^2(\Omega ,\sigma (X),\mathbb {P}) \subset L^2(\Omega ,\mathcal F,\mathbb {P})\), i.e., \(\mathbb {E}\left[Y\mid X\right]\) from the previous remark. Linear regression is the same extremal problem, except that the projection is taken not onto the whole of \(L^2(\Omega ,\sigma (X),\mathbb {P})\), but onto its (finite-dimensional, hence automatically closed) subspace \(\left\langle 1,X\right\rangle\) of linear functions of \(X\); the explicit formula for the linear regression coefficients is exactly equations (a) of Theorem Theorem 15, written out for this subspace.
The Karhunen–Loève expansion. Let \((X_t)_{t\in [0,T]}\) be a random process with \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_t^2\right]<\infty\) for all \(t\) and a continuous covariance function. It turns out that the sample path of such a process can be represented as a series
\[
  X_t \;  = \;  \sum _{k=1}^\infty \xi _k \,  e_k(t), \qquad t \in [0,T],  
\]
where \((e_k)\) is a certain orthonormal basis (in a suitable \(L^2\)-space of functions on \([0,T]\), constructed from the eigenfunctions of the covariance operator), and the random variables \(\xi_k := \left\langle X, e_k \right\rangle\) are pairwise uncorrelated. Formally, this is exactly the formula for the expansion of an element of a Hilbert space with respect to an orthonormal basis (see Parseval’s identity, Theorem Theorem 20, and the remark after it), applied to the sample path \(X\) as a single element of a suitable \(L^2\)-space. We do not develop this theory here — constructing the basis \((e_k)\) itself requires separate techniques (the theory of integral operators) — but let us stress: without Hilbert space geometry, this construction would have to be reinvented from scratch every time.










ProblemProblem 12





Let \(U\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(g\in U\) be the element of \(U\) closest to \(0\) (i.e., \(g = P_U0\)). Prove that \(\left\langle g, h \right\rangle \geq \left\| g\right\|^2\) for all \(h\in U\).






HintHint





Apply the computation from the proof of Theorem Theorem 14(a) (see also the proof of Theorem Theorem 15(a)) to \(f=0\).







3.4.1 The Riesz representation theorem
The following result is a beautiful and practically important theorem, fully describing what bounded linear functionals on a Hilbert space look like.







Theorem 17 (F. Riesz, representation theorem) Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, \(\varphi : H\to \mathbb {R}\) a bounded linear functional (i.e., \(\varphi\) is linear and \(\left\| \varphi \right\|  := \sup \left\{ \left|\varphi (f)\right| \;  : \;  \left\| f\right\| \leq 1\right\}  <\infty\)). Then there exists a unique \(u\in H\) such that \[
  \varphi (f) = \left\langle f, u \right\rangle \qquad \forall f\in H.  
\] Moreover, \(\left\| \varphi \right\|  = \left\| u\right\|\).










Mn-remarkRemark




In particular, for \(H=L^2(\mu )\) the Riesz theorem means: every bounded linear functional on \(L^2(\mu )\) has the form \(\varphi (f) = \int fu\; d\mu\) for a unique \(u\in L^2(\mu )\). In other words, \(L^2(\mu )\) is (in a certain precise sense) “its own dual space”; this is a peculiarity specific to \(p=2\) — for other \(p\), the dual of \(L^p(\mu )\) is \(L^{p'}(\mu )\) (\(p'\) the conjugate exponent), for a different function \(u\) in general.

title: Lebesgue spaces \(L^p(\mu )\)
text:
3.5 Orthonormal systems and bases
Throughout this section we deal only with countable (finite or infinite) families — this suffices for all probabilistic applications (see the remark after the definition of an orthonormal basis).







Definition 17 A finite or countable system \((e_k)_k\) of elements of an inner product space \(V\) is called orthonormal if \[
  \left\langle e_j, e_k \right\rangle = \begin{cases}  1, &  j=k,\\ 0, &  j\neq k. \end{cases}  
\]




Examples. The standard basis vectors \(e_k=(0,\ldots ,0,1,0,\ldots )\) (a one in the \(k\)-th position) form an orthonormal system in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) and in \(\ell^2\).

3.5.1 The Gram–Schmidt process. Bessel’s inequality







Theorem 18 (Gram–Schmidt) Let \(f_1,f_2,\ldots\) be a finite or countable linearly independent system in an inner product space \(V\). Then there exists an orthonormal system \(e_1,e_2,\ldots\) (of the same length) such that for every \(n\) \[
  \left\langle f_1,\ldots ,f_n\right\rangle = \left\langle e_1,\ldots ,e_n\right\rangle .  
\]










ExampleExample 8





Orthonormalize the system \(f_0(x)=1\), \(f_1(x)=x\) in \(L^2([-1,1])\) (with respect to Lebesgue measure) using the Gram–Schmidt process.






SolutionSolution





\(\left\| f_0\right\|^2 = \int_{-1}^1 1\; dx = 2\), so \(e_0 = f_0/\left\| f_0\right\|  = 1/\sqrt2\).
Next, \(\left\langle f_1, e_0 \right\rangle = \int_{-1}^1 \frac{x}{\sqrt2}\; dx = 0\) (an odd function on a symmetric interval), so \(f_1\) is already orthogonal to \(e_0\), and it suffices to normalize it: \(\left\| f_1\right\|^2 = \int_{-1}^1x^2\; dx = \frac23\), so
\[
  e_1(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{2/3}} = x\sqrt{\frac32}.  
\]
(Continuing this process for \(f_2(x)=x^2\), \(f_3(x)=x^3,\ldots\), one obtains — up to normalization — the Legendre polynomials.)













Theorem 19 (Bessel’s inequality) Let \((e_k)_k\) be a finite or countable orthonormal system in an inner product space \(V\), \(f\in V\). Then \[
  \sum _k \left| \left\langle f, e_k \right\rangle \right|^2 \leq \left\| f\right\| ^2.  
\]




(Idea, for a finite index set \(1,\ldots ,n\) — the countable case follows by a limit passage: let \(g:=\sum_{k=1}^n \left\langle f, e_k \right\rangle e_k\); a direct check shows \(f-g\perp e_j\) for every \(j\), hence \(f-g\perp g\), and the Pythagorean theorem for \(f=(f-g)+g\) gives \(\left\| f\right\|^2 = \left\| f-g\right\|^2+\left\| g\right\|^2 \geq \left\| g\right\|^2 = \sum_{k=1}^n\left| \left\langle f, e_k \right\rangle \right|^2\).)


3.5.2 Orthonormal basis. Parseval’s identity






Mn-remarkRemark




In an arbitrary (not necessarily separable) Hilbert space, an orthonormal basis (in the sense of the definition below) always exists, but the proof in the general case relies essentially on Zorn’s lemma (see Axler, Theorem 8.75). We will not need this: in all probabilistic applications it suffices to consider separable Hilbert spaces (i.e., ones containing a countable dense subset) — for example, \(L^2(\Omega ,\mathcal F,\mathbb {P})\) for a countably generated \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal F\). For such spaces, an orthonormal basis can be constructed explicitly by the Gram–Schmidt process (Theorem Theorem 18), applied to a countable dense set. Therefore, from now on we speak only of countable orthonormal bases.










Definition 18 (orthonormal basis) A countable (finite or infinite) orthonormal system \((e_k)_{k=1}^\infty\) in a Hilbert space \(H\) is called an orthonormal basis of \(H\) if \[
  \overline{ \left\langle e_k \;  : \;  k\right\rangle } = H,  
\] i.e., finite linear combinations of the elements \(e_k\) are dense in \(H\).










Mn-remarkRemark




Despite the name, an orthonormal basis (when \(H\) is infinite-dimensional) is not a basis in the sense of linear algebra: an element \(f\in H\) is represented not by a finite linear combination of the \(e_k\), but — as the following theorem shows — by a convergent series.










Theorem 20 (Parseval’s identity) Let \((e_k)_{k=1}^\infty\) be an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space \(H\), \(f,g\in H\). Then

\(f = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \left\langle f, e_k \right\rangle e_k\) (the series converges in the norm of \(H\));
\(\left\langle f, g \right\rangle = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \left\langle f, e_k \right\rangle \left\langle g, e_k \right\rangle\);
\(\left\| f\right\|^2 = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \left| \left\langle f, e_k \right\rangle \right|^2\).





(Idea: set \(S_n:=\sum_{k=1}^n \left\langle f, e_k \right\rangle e_k\). By Bessel’s inequality the series \(\sum_k\left| \left\langle f, e_k \right\rangle \right|^2\) converges, whence (by the Pythagorean theorem for tails) \((S_n)\) is a Cauchy sequence, and hence converges to some \(s\in H\) (\(H\) is complete); from the orthogonality \(f-S_n\perp e_j\) for \(n\geq j\) and continuity of the inner product we obtain \(f-s\perp e_j\) for all \(j\), i.e., \(f-s\in \left(\overline{ \left\langle e_k:k\right\rangle }\right)^\perp = H^\perp =\left\{ 0\right\}\) — this gives (a); (b),(c) follow immediately from (a) by a limit passage.)






Mn-remarkRemark




3.6 projection via an orthonormal basis
If \((e_k)\) is an orthonormal basis of a closed subspace \(U\subseteq H\) (not necessarily all of \(H\)), then by the same argument as in the proof of Parseval’s identity (applied within the Hilbert space \(U\)), we obtain a formula for the orthogonal projection: \[
  P_Uf = \sum _k \left\langle f, e_k \right\rangle e_k, \qquad f\in H.  
\] In particular, this gives a practical way to compute conditional expectation: if an orthonormal basis \((e_k)\) of the space \(L^2(\Omega ,\mathcal G,\mathbb {P})\) is known, then \(\mathbb {E}\left[X\mid \mathcal G\right] = \sum_k \left\langle X, e_k \right\rangle e_k\).









ExampleExample 9





Let \(H=\ell^2\), and let \(\varphi : \ell^2 \to \mathbb {R}\) be defined by the formula \(\varphi \left((a_1,a_2,\ldots )\right) = a_1\) (projection onto the first coordinate). Check that \(\varphi\) is a bounded linear functional, and find its representative \(u\in \ell^2\) from the Riesz theorem (Theorem Theorem 17).






SolutionSolution





Linearity is clear. Boundedness: \(\left|\varphi (a)\right| = \left|a_1\right| \leq \left\| a\right\|\) (since \(a_1^2 \leq \sum_k a_k^2 = \left\| a\right\|^2\)), so \(\left\| \varphi \right\| \leq 1\); moreover, at \(a=e_1=(1,0,0,\ldots )\) (norm \(1\)) the value is \(\varphi (e_1)=1\), hence \(\left\| \varphi \right\| =1\).
Note that \(\varphi (a) = a_1 = \left\langle a, e_1 \right\rangle\) for the standard basis vector \(e_1=(1,0,0,\ldots )\). Hence \(u=e_1\) is the desired representative (and by the theorem, the unique one), \(\left\| u\right\|  = 1 = \left\| \varphi \right\|\), which agrees with the formula \(\left\| \varphi \right\| =\left\| u\right\|\).












ProblemProblem 13





Show that the standard basis vectors \(e_k=(0,\ldots ,0,1,0,\ldots )\) (\(k\in \mathbb {N}\)) form an orthonormal basis of \(\ell^2\) (i.e., that \(\overline{ \left\langle e_k\; :\; k\in \mathbb {N}\right\rangle }=\ell^2\)).






HintHint





For \(a=(a_1,a_2,\ldots )\in \ell^2\) consider \(S_n=\sum_{k=1}^n a_ke_k\) and show that \(\left\| a-S_n\right\| \to 0\), using convergence of the series \(\sum_ka_k^2\).

title: Lebesgue spaces \(L^p(\mu )\)
text:
4.1 Riesz representation theorem, without proof
Let \(\mu\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite measure, \(1<p<\infty\), \(p'\) the conjugate exponent. Then the map \(h \mapsto \varphi_h\), where \(\varphi_h(f) := \int fh\, d\mu\), establishes an isometric isomorphism between \(L^{p'}(\mu )\) and the dual space \(\left(L^p(\mu )\right)'\). In short, “\(\left(L^p\right)' = L^{p'}\)”. (For \(p=1\) this is also true, provided \(\mu\) is \(\sigma\)-finite; for \(p=\infty\) it is no longer true — the dual of \(L^\infty\) is structured substantially more complicated than \(L^1\).)

title: Differentiation of the Lebesgue integral. Absolutely continuous functions
text:
Unlike the previous chapters, here throughout \(X = \mathbb {R}\), and the measure is Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\) (or a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure generated by it), unless explicitly stated otherwise. We apply the abstract theory of measure (in particular, the Radon-Nikodym theorem from the chapter on signed measures) to this concrete case and obtain classical facts of mathematical analysis — differentiation of the integral, the Newton-Leibniz formula, and the relationship between a distribution’s density and the derivative of its distribution function.
Throughout the first three sections, the measure is Lebesgue measure \(\lambda\) on \(\mathbb {R}\). The notation \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\) means that \(f: \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {R}\) is Lebesgue measurable and \(\left\| f\right\|_{1} = \int_{\mathbb {R}} \left|f\right| \,  d\lambda < \infty\). For integrals over segments we use the abbreviation
\[
  \int _{a}^{b} f := \int _{[a,b]} f \,  d\lambda
\]

title: Differentiation of the Lebesgue integral. Absolutely continuous functions
section: 3.1 A Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure is a locally finite measure
text:
3.1 A Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure is a locally finite measure
Recall that a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure is defined for an arbitrary nondecreasing right-continuous function \(F: \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {R}\) via \(\mu_{F}((a,b]) = F(b) - F(a)\), \(-\infty < a < b < +\infty\). Note that a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure is sigma-finite:
\[
  \mathbb {R} = \bigcup _{n=1}^{+\infty }(-n,n], \quad \text{ with } \quad \mu _{F}((-n,n]) = F(n) - F(-n) < +\infty
\]
Moreover, a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure is finite on every bounded interval \((a,b)\). This property is actually stronger than sigma-finiteness on \(\mathbb {R}\) and is equivalent to every point \(x \in \mathbb {R}\) having a neighborhood of finite measure (this is the so-called local finiteness).






ProblemProblem 11





Let \(\mu\) be a (nonnegative) measure on \((\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\).

Prove that \(\mu\) is finite on every bounded interval \(\iff\) \(\mu\) is locally finite;
Prove that local finiteness implies \(\sigma\)-finiteness of \(\mu\);
Show that the converse of the previous part fails: give an example of a (nonnegative) \(\sigma\)-finite measure \(\mu\) that is not locally finite.




So, every Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure is finite on bounded intervals. Is the converse true? Yes! It is not hard to show that if \(\mu\) is a (nonnegative) measure, finite on bounded intervals, then setting
\[
  F(x) := \begin{cases}  \mu ((0, x]), &  0 < x \\ -\mu ((x, 0]), &  x \leq 0 \end{cases}
\]
we obtain a nondecreasing right-continuous finite function, with \(\mu = \mu_F\). Let us state this result.







Lemma 3 Let \(\mu\) be a (nonnegative) measure on \((\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\). The following conditions are equivalent:

\(\mu\) is a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure (for some nondecreasing right-continuous \(F: \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {R}\))
\(\mu\) is finite on bounded intervals.
\(\mu\) is locally finite.





Note that if \(\mu\) is a finite measure (for example, a probability measure), then instead of the \(F\) defined above one may take
\[
  F(x) = \mu ((-\infty , x])
\]
i.e. the distribution function.
crumbs: 13. Differentiating the Lebesgue integral. Absolutely continuous functions

title: Differentiation of the Lebesgue integral. Absolutely continuous functions
text:
3.2 An absolutely continuous Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure
Let us now consider not just a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure \(\mu = \mu_F\), but one that is absolutely continuous (with respect to Lebesgue measure): \(\mu \ll \lambda\). We know (the chapter on signed measures) that \(\mu_F\) is completely characterized by the function \(F\) — so the condition \(\mu_F \ll \lambda\) must somehow transfer to \(F\). Let us start with the cheapest observation: \(F\) will be continuous. In fact, a stronger statement holds: \(F\) will be locally uniformly continuous, i.e. uniformly continuous on every segment \([a,b]\).






ExampleExample 3





Show that if \(\mu_F \ll \lambda\), then \(F\) is locally uniformly continuous.






SolutionSolution





Indeed, on \([a,b]\) the measure \(\mu_F\) is finite, so by the lemma on the equivalent condition for absolute continuity of a measure, if \(\varepsilon > 0\) is an arbitrary fixed number, there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that for all \(a \leq x < y \leq b\) with \(\left|y - x\right| = \lambda ([x, y]) < \delta\) we have \[
  \left|F(y) - F(x)\right| = F(y) - F(x) = \mu _F([x,y]) < \varepsilon
\]






We have obtained a fairly strong restriction on \(F\) — local uniform continuity. That is good. However, is it enough for \(F\) to be locally uniformly continuous for \(\mu_F\) to have a density? Actually, no!






ExampleExample 4





Give an example of a nondecreasing, right-continuous, locally uniformly continuous function \(F: \mathbb {R}\to \mathbb {R}\) such that \(\mu_F\) is not absolutely continuous, i.e. does not have a density with respect to Lebesgue measure.






SolutionSolution





Let \(F\) be the Cantor staircase. Outside the segment \([0,1]\) it is constant. Hence it is uniformly continuous on any segment outside \([0,1]\).
What about on \([0,1]\) (or on any subsegment of \([0,1]\))? It is continuous there, hence it is uniformly continuous, since \([0,1]\) is compact.
In summary, the Cantor staircase \(F\) is locally uniformly continuous.
But is \(\mu_F\) absolutely continuous? No! Indeed, consider the Cantor set \(C\). \(\lambda (C) = 0\), \(\mu_F(C) = 1\). This violates absolute continuity.






We need a stronger form of continuity on a segment than uniform continuity.
crumbs: 13. Differentiating the Lebesgue integral. Absolutely continuous functions

title: Differentiation of the Lebesgue integral. Absolutely continuous functions
text:
3.3 Absolutely continuous functions
Note that in the uniform continuity condition on \([a,b]\) above, one could take not just \(2\) points \(x,y\), but arbitrarily many consecutive pairs of such points. Namely, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that for every \(N \in \mathbb {N}\) and for all
\[
  a \leq x_1 < y_1 \leq x_2 < y_2 \leq \ldots \leq x_{N} < y_{N} \leq b, \qquad \text{ such that } \qquad \sum _{k=1}^{N}(y_k - x_k) < \delta
\]
we have
\[
  \sum _{k=1}^N \left|F(y_k) - F(x_k)\right| < \varepsilon
\]
A function satisfying such conditions is called absolutely continuous on the segment \([a,b]\); locally absolutely continuous on \(\mathbb {R}\) if it is absolutely continuous on every segment. In other words, an absolutely continuous function does not oscillate on a set of measure zero.
Absolute continuity is stronger than uniform continuity on a segment \([a,b]\). And strictly stronger.






ProblemProblem 12





Show that the Cantor staircase is uniformly continuous but is not an absolutely continuous function on \([0,1]\).



We now have 2 notions of absolute continuity: for measures and for functions. The following theorem shows that for Lebesgue-Stieltjes measures these are exactly one and the same notion — and, moreover, connects it with the Radon-Nikodym derivative and with the ordinary, high-school derivative.
crumbs: 13. Differentiating the Lebesgue integral. Absolutely continuous functions

title: Differentiation of the Lebesgue integral. Absolutely continuous functions
section: 3.4 Synthesis: the Radon-Nikodym derivative is the ordinary derivative
text:
3.4 Synthesis: the Radon-Nikodym derivative is the ordinary derivative
We already know three things separately: the abstract Radon-Nikodym theorem (theorem Radon-Nikodym from the chapter on signed measures), the Lebesgue differentiation theorem (earlier in this chapter), and the notion of an absolutely continuous function (just introduced). Let us bring them together.







Theorem 4 (The “fundamental theorem” of Lebesgue integration on \(\mathbb {R}\)) Let \(\mu = \mu_F\) be a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure on \((\mathbb {R}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\). The following conditions are equivalent:

\(\mu \ll \lambda\);
\(F\) is locally absolutely continuous;
there exists a locally integrable \(f: \mathbb {R} \to [0,+\infty ]\) such that \(F(x) = F(c) + \int_{[c,x]} f \,  d\lambda\) for all \(c, x \in \mathbb {R}\) (in short: \(d\mu = f \,  d\lambda\)). Moreover, in this case \(f = F'\) \(\lambda\)-a.e. (and such an \(f\) is unique up to agreement a.e.), i.e. \(\mu (E) = \int_E F' \,  d\lambda\) for all Borel \(E\).











Mn-remarkRemark




3.5 the case of non-monotone \(F\)
If \(F\) is not necessarily monotone (for example, \(F = F_1 - F_2\) for some nondecreasing \(F_1, F_2\) — say, a function of bounded variation), no new theorem needs to be proved: the corresponding real Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure \(\nu := \mu_{F_1} - \mu_{F_2}\) is decomposed via Jordan decomposition, theorem Theorem 4 is applied to each of the (nonnegative) parts separately, and the results are added — this is exactly the same linearity we already used in the chapter on signed measures to pass from nonnegative measures to real ones, and at the very beginning of this chapter to pass from \(f \geq 0\) to an arbitrary integrable \(f = f^+ - f^-\).

title: Differentiation of the Lebesgue integral. Absolutely continuous functions
text:
3.6 Practice
So, where have we arrived? What is the practical meaning of this theory? We now have, for example, the ability to determine from the distribution function whether a random variable is absolutely continuous. Moreover, we can find the density: it turns out that it suffices simply to differentiate the distribution function.






ExampleExample 5





Let a random variable \(X\) have the following distribution function (here and below \(c: [0,1] \to [0,1]\) is the Cantor staircase, i.e. the Cantor function): \[
  F(x)= \begin{cases}  \frac{2}{10}e^{x+2}, &  -\infty < x< -2 \\ \frac{1}{10}c(x+2) + \frac{3}{10}, &  -2 \leq x < -1 \\ \frac{1}{10}x^3 + \frac{6}{10}, &  -1 \leq x < \sqrt[3]{2} \\ 0.85, &  \sqrt[3]{2} \leq x < 5 \\ 1 - \frac{1}{2x}, &  5 \leq x < +\infty \end{cases}
\]


                                                


Denote by \(\mu_F = \mathbf{P}_X\) the distribution of this random variable.

Decompose \(\mu_F\) into an absolutely continuous part \(\mu_a\) and a singular part \(\mu_s\) with respect to Lebesgue measure;
For the absolutely continuous part \(\mu_a\) find the density (Radon-Nikodym derivative) \(\frac{d\mu_a}{d\lambda }\);
Is the singular part \(\mu_s\) (relative to Lebesgue measure) absolutely continuous with respect to counting measure \(\#_{\mathbb {N}}\) on the natural numbers? What about with respect to \(\#_{\mathbb {Z}}\) on the integers? If so, find the Radon-Nikodym derivative.
Find the expectation \(\mathbb {E}\left[\sqrt{\left|X+2\right|}\right]\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(1)



We need to extract the locally absolutely continuous component from the function \(F\). We remove all singular fragments from \(F\). Note that the function \(F_a\), defined below, is continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb {R}\), hence locally absolutely continuous.
\[
  F_a(x)= \begin{cases}  \frac{2}{10}e^{x+2}, &  -\infty < x< -2 \\ 0.2, &  -2 \leq x < -1 \\ \frac{1}{10}x^3 + \frac{3}{10}, &  -1 \leq x < \sqrt[3]{2} \\ 0.5, &  \sqrt[3]{2} \leq x < 5 \\ 0.6 - \frac{1}{2x}, &  5 \leq x < +\infty \end{cases}
\]


                                                


Moreover \(F_{s} := F - F_{a}\) looks as follows:
\[
  F_{s}(x)= \begin{cases}  0, &  -\infty < x< -2 \\ \frac{1}{10}c(x+2) + \frac{1}{10}, &  -2 \leq x < -1 \\ 0.3, &  -1 \leq x < \sqrt[3]{2} \\ 0.35, &  \sqrt[3]{2} \leq x < 5 \\ 0.4, &  5 \leq x < +\infty \end{cases}
\]


                                                


Note that \(F_s\) generates a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure whose support is the set \(\left\{ -2, 1, \sqrt[3]{2}, 5\right\}  \cup (C-2)\), where \(C-2\) is the Cantor set shifted right by \(2\). This support has Lebesgue measure \(0\). Hence this measure is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure.
In summary, the absolutely continuous component is the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure generated by \(F_{a}\) (\(\mu_{a} := \mu_{F_{a}}\)), and the singular component is \(\mu_{s} := \mu_{F_{s}}\).








Enum-item(2)



\(F_{a}\) is absolutely continuous, so by theorem Theorem 4 it is differentiable a.e., and its derivative is exactly the density (with respect to Lebesgue measure). We have
\[
  \frac{d\mu _a}{d\lambda }(x) = F'_a(x)= \begin{cases}  \frac{2}{10}e^{x+2}, &  -\infty < x< -2 \\ 0, &  -2 < x < -1 \\ \frac{3}{10}x^2, &  -1 < x < \sqrt[3]{2} \\ 0, &  \sqrt[3]{2} < x < 5 \\ \frac{1}{2x^2}, &  5 < x < +\infty \\ \text{undefined}, &  x \in \left\{ -2, -1, \sqrt[3]{2}, 5\right\}  \end{cases}
\]


                                                


At the points \(\left\{ -2, -1, \sqrt[3]{2}, 5\right\}\) one may define \(f_a(x) = \frac{d\mu_a}{d\lambda }(x)\) however one likes. For example, by zeros.








Enum-item(3)



Consider the set \(A = \left(C-2\right) \;  \cap \;  (-2, -1)\), i.e. the Cantor set shifted \(2\) to the left, without the points \(-2, -1\). Note that \(\mu_{s}(A) = 0.1\), while \(\#_{\mathbb {N}}(A) = 0\) and \(\#_{\mathbb {Z}}(A) = 0\). Hence \(\mu_{s}\) is not absolutely continuous with respect to counting measure on \(\mathbb {Z}\) or on \(\mathbb {N}\).








Enum-item(4)



By definition
\[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\sqrt{\left|X+2\right|}\right] = \int _{\Omega } \sqrt{\left|X(\omega ) + 2\right|} \;  d\mathbb {P}(\omega )
\]
Let us use a change of variables in the Lebesgue integral: \(X(\omega ) = x\). Then \(\omega = X^{-1}(x)\), \(\mathbb {P}(\omega ) = \mathbb {P}(X^{-1}(x)) = \mathbf{P}_{X}(x)\). Hence,
\[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\sqrt{\left|X+2\right|}\right] = \int _{\mathbb {R}} \sqrt{\left|x+2\right|} \;  d\mathbf{P}_{X}(x)
\]
We decomposed \(\mathbf{P}_{X}\) as the sum \(\mu_{a} + \mu_{s}\). Let us find the integrals over each measure separately.

\(\mu_{a}\) has density \(f_a\) with respect to Lebesgue measure. Hence,
\[
\begin{align}  \int _{\mathbb {R}} \sqrt{\left|x + 2\right|} \;  d\mu _{a} & = \int _{\mathbb {R}} \sqrt{\left|x + 2\right|} \cdot f_a(x) \;  d\lambda =\\ & = \int _{-\infty }^{-2}\sqrt{\left|x+2\right|} \cdot \frac{2}{10}e^{x+2} \;  dx + \int _{-1}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}\sqrt{x+2} \cdot \frac{3}{10}x^2 \;  dx + \int _{5}^{+\infty } \sqrt{x+2} \cdot \frac{1}{2x^2} \;  dx = \\ & = \frac{2}{10}\Gamma (3/2) +\left[ \frac{3}{35}u^{7/2} -\frac{12}{25}u^{5/2} +\frac{4}{5}u^{3/2} \right]_{u=1}^{\, u=2+2^{1/3}} +\frac{\sqrt{7}}{10} -\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \ln \! \left(\frac{\sqrt{7}-\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{7}+\sqrt{2}}\right). \approx \\ &  \approx 1.107 \end{align}
\]
We omit the detailed computation of the Riemann integrals, since that is not the point of the example; what matters is understanding the general principle.
How do we find the integral with respect to \(\mu_{s}\)? Note that
\[
  \mu _{s} = 0.1 \cdot \delta _{-2} + 0.1\cdot \mu _{C-2} + 0.1 \cdot \delta _{-1} + 0.05 \cdot \delta _{\sqrt[3]{2}} + 0.05 \cdot \delta _{5}
\]
where \(\mu_{C-2}\) is the Cantor measure shifted \(2\) to the left. Then (recall that the integral with respect to a Dirac measure is simply the value of the function at the point)
\[
\begin{align}  \int _{\mathbb {R}} \sqrt{\left|x + 2\right|} \;  d\mu _{s} & = 0.1 \cdot \sqrt{\left|-2 + 2\right|} + 0.1 \cdot \sqrt{\left|-1 + 2\right|} + 0.05 \cdot \sqrt{\left|\sqrt[3]{2} + 2\right|} +\\ &  \qquad + 0.05 \cdot \sqrt{\left|5 + 2\right|} + 0.1 \cdot \underbrace{\int \sqrt{\left|x+2\right|} \;  d\mu _{C-2}}_{=\int _{[0,1]}\sqrt{x} \;  d\mu _{c} \approx 0.64} \approx \\ & \approx 0.322 + 0.064 = 0.386 \end{align}
\]
We omit the detailed computation of the integrals with respect to the Cantor measure, since that is not the point of the example; what matters is understanding the general principle.

In summary, \(\mathbb {E}\left[\sqrt{\left|X + 2\right|}\right] \approx 1.107 + 0.386 = 1.493\)














ProblemProblem 13





Consider the function \[
  F(x)= \begin{cases}  \frac{1}{2}x-1, &  x<0,\\ x^2, &  0 \le x < 1,\\ 3, &  1 \le x < 2,\\ 6 - \dfrac {4}{x}, &  x \ge 2. \end{cases}
\]


                                                


It is right-continuous. Hence one can construct from it a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure \(\mu_F\).

Decompose \(\mu_F\) into an absolutely continuous part \(\mu_a\) and a singular part \(\mu_s\) with respect to Lebesgue measure;
For the absolutely continuous part \(\mu_a\) find the density (Radon-Nikodym derivative) \(\frac{d\mu_a}{d\lambda }\);
Is the singular part \(\mu_s\) (relative to Lebesgue measure) absolutely continuous with respect to counting measure \(\#_{\mathbb {N}}\) on the natural numbers? What about with respect to \(\#_{\mathbb {Z}}\) on the integers? If so, find the Radon-Nikodym derivative \(\frac{d\mu_s}{d\# }\).
Find the integral

\[
  \int _{[-2, +\infty ]} \sqrt{\left|x\right|} \; \;  d\mu _F
\]

title: Differentiation of the Lebesgue integral. Absolutely continuous functions
text:
5.1 a dictionary: \(\mu \leftrightarrow F \leftrightarrow f\)
The diagram above actually encodes not only classes of measures \(\mu\), but also the fact that each of them is bijectively arranged also as a class of functions \(F\) and/or as a class of densities \(f\).

\(\mu \leftrightarrow F\). The correspondence from lemma Lemma 3 is a bijection between locally finite measures \(\mu\) and equivalence classes of nondecreasing right-continuous functions \(F: \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {R}\) under the relation \(F \sim G \iff F - G \equiv \mathrm{const}\) (indeed: \(\mu_F = \mu_G \iff F(b)-F(a) = G(b)-G(a) \;  \forall a<b \iff F-G \equiv \mathrm{const}\)). Finite measures correspond exactly to bounded such \(F\), again up to a constant. Outside the class of locally finite measures, such an (everywhere finite) function \(F\) simply does not exist — which is why the two outer rings of the diagram (arbitrary measures and merely \(\sigma\)-finite measures) carry no label with \(F\).
\(\mu \leftrightarrow f\). The correspondence \(\mu \leftrightarrow f\) is a bijection between measures \(\mu\) that are absolutely continuous (with respect to \(\lambda\)) and equivalence classes of measurable functions \(f: \mathbb {R} \to [0,+\infty ]\) under the relation \(f \sim g \iff f=g\) \(\lambda\)-a.e. Within the band of absolute continuity, \(\sigma\)-finiteness of \(\mu\) corresponds to finiteness of \(f\) \(\lambda\)-a.e., local finiteness to \(f \in L^1_{loc}(\mathbb {R})\), and finiteness to \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\) (everywhere, up to agreement \(\lambda\)-a.e.).
\(F \leftrightarrow f\). Where both correspondences are defined — i.e. for absolutely continuous locally finite measures — they are consistent by theorem Theorem 4: \(F' = f\) \(\lambda\)-a.e.

For example, the innermost lens of the diagram (finite \(\cap\) absolutely continuous measures) is simultaneously three descriptions of the same set of objects: finite absolutely continuous measures \(\mu\); bounded locally absolutely continuous functions \(F\) (up to an additive constant); functions \(f \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\), \(f \geq 0\) (up to agreement \(\lambda\)-a.e.).

title: Course program
text:
The course is designed for third-semester students at MIPT.

Discrete probability space. The classical model
Conditional probability. The law of total probability. Bayes’ formula. The multiplication rule for probabilities
Pairwise and mutual independence of events. The Bernoulli scheme
Discrete random variables. The distribution of a discrete random variable. The Bernoulli distribution. The binomial distribution. The geometric distribution. The Poisson theorem. Independent random variables
Expectation. Basic properties. Examples of computation for the distributions covered in the course
Variance. The computational formula. Basic properties. Examples of computation for the distributions covered in the course
Covariance. The computational formula. Basic properties. Additivity of variance for uncorrelated random variables. The relationship between independence and uncorrelatedness
Correlation. The Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz inequality. The covariance matrix, its symmetry and positive semidefiniteness. The relationship between positive definiteness of the covariance matrix and linear dependence of the components of a random vector
Markov’s and Chebyshev’s inequalities. The Law of Large Numbers in Chebyshev’s form. The Central Limit Theorem (in the form of Alexandrov’s theorem; without proof)
Semiring. Semialgebra. Ring. The relationship between semirings and rings. Algebra. Existence of the smallest ring/algebra generated by a system of sets. An equivalent definition of a semiring. The form of the minimal ring generated by a semiring. The “common refinement” proposition
The notions of \(\sigma\)- and \(\delta\)-rings and algebras. The relationship between them. The Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of the line and of a space
Measure on a system of sets. The notion of a \(\sigma\)-additive measure. Subadditivity and superadditivity of a measure on a semiring. Countable superadditivity of a measure on a semiring. The relationship between countable subadditivity and \(\sigma\)-additivity of a measure on a semiring
Extension of a measure from a semiring to the minimal ring. Inheritance of \(\sigma\)-additivity
Continuity of a measure from above and below. The relationship between continuity and \(\sigma\)-additivity of a measure on a semiring and on a ring
The Jordan and Lebesgue outer measures constructed from a \(\sigma\)-additive measure on a semialgebra. Their coincidence with the extended measure on the minimal ring. Countable subadditivity of the Lebesgue outer measure
Measurable sets. Lebesgue measure. An inequality characterizing measurability. The algebra of measurable sets. Additivity of Lebesgue measure. The \(\sigma\)-additivity property of Lebesgue measure on the \(\sigma\)-algebra of measurable sets
Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure and its \(\sigma\)-additivity
Construction of a \(\sigma\)-finite measure and its independence from the partition of unity. The relationship between continuity and \(\sigma\)-additivity of a \(\sigma\)-finite measure on a \(\sigma\)-algebra. Carathéodory’s extension theorem. The theorem on the structure of measurable sets. Borel measure
The classical Lebesgue measure, its \(\sigma\)-additivity. The classical Borel measure. Completeness of Lebesgue measure. Construction of a non-measurable subset within a set of positive classical Lebesgue measure
Measurable function. A criterion for measurability. Borel functions. Borel measurability of continuous functions. Measurability of the composition of measurable functions
Measurable functions with values on the extended line. The sum and product of measurable functions. Inheritance of measurability for the supremum, infimum, upper limit, and lower limit
Existence of simple functions converging pointwise to a measurable function. Existence of a Borel function equal almost everywhere to a measurable function
The Cantor set and its properties. The Cantor staircase and its properties. Incompleteness of the classical Borel measure. Construction of measurable and Borel functions whose composition is non-measurable
Convergence almost everywhere and in measure. Uniqueness of limits almost everywhere and in measure. A criterion for convergence almost everywhere on a space of finite measure. The relationship between convergence almost everywhere and in measure. Riesz’s counterexample. Riesz’s theorem
Almost uniform convergence and its relationship to convergence almost everywhere and in measure. Uniqueness of the almost uniform limit. Egorov’s theorem. Cauchy criteria for convergence almost everywhere, almost uniform convergence, and convergence in measure
Inheritance of convergence almost everywhere and in measure under addition. A criterion for convergence in measure on a space of finite measure. The theorem on inheritance of convergence almost everywhere and in measure under a continuous map. The image measure under a map (distribution)
The Lebesgue integral of a simple function. Basic properties.
A charge (finite signed measure), its continuity from above and below. Absolute continuity. The lemma on a set of measure zero. The indefinite Lebesgue integral. Its finiteness, absolute continuity, and \(\sigma\)-additivity
The limit of indefinite integrals of simple functions that are Cauchy in the mean, its finiteness and \(\sigma\)-additivity. Equi-absolute continuity of the indefinite integrals of simple functions that are Cauchy in the mean
The Lebesgue integral of a measurable function. Basic properties. The indefinite Lebesgue integral. Its finiteness, absolute continuity, and \(\sigma\)-additivity
Chebyshev’s inequality. The relationship between convergence in measure and convergence in the mean. The \(\sigma\)-finiteness property of the set on which an integrable function takes nonzero values. An integral property of measurable functions
(Without proof) The relationship between Riemann integrability in the proper sense and Lebesgue integrability. The relationship between Riemann integrability in the improper sense and Lebesgue integrability
The Cauchy criterion for convergence in the mean. A criterion for convergence in the mean. Lebesgue’s dominated convergence theorem. Its corollaries. Levi’s monotone convergence theorem, a corollary for series. Fatou’s lemma on the lower limit
The direct product of measures. The monotone class lemma. Propositions relating measure and integral, the measure of a subgraph. The integration-by-parts formula. Associativity of the product of \(\sigma\)-algebras and measures. Fubini’s theorem. Tonelli’s theorem
The Hahn decomposition. The Jordan decomposition. The Radon-Nikodym theorem. Absolute continuity of functions on the line. The Newton-Leibniz formula (without proof). The Lebesgue decomposition. The variation of a charge, total variation. Integration of functions with respect to a charge
Integration of complex-valued functions. The characteristic function of a charge. Its basic properties. The uniqueness theorem

title: Random Vectors
text: Real data is almost never one-dimensional: height and weight, stock price and oil price, response time and server load. A pair of random variables is not “two random variables” but a single object — a random vector: its distribution contains information not only about each coordinate but also about the dependence between them. Losing this information is costly: the 2008 financial crisis was, to a significant extent, a story about how risk models knew the marginal distributions of defaults individually but modeled their joint distribution incorrectly. In this topic we will learn to work with joint distributions: finding marginals, checking independence, and — the main computational technique — transforming densities under smooth changes of variables (the Jacobian).

title: Random Vectors
Convergence of Random Variables
text: The entire second half of the course consists of limit theorems, and before proving them we need to discuss the possible modes of convergence.

title: Convergence of Random Variables
section: 3.1 A metric for convergence in probability
text:
3.1 A metric for convergence in probability
For random variables \(\xi , \eta\) set \[
  \rho (\xi , \eta )= \mathbb {E}\left[\frac{\left|\xi - \eta \right|}{1 + \left|\xi - \eta \right|}\right].
\] Prove that \(\xi_{n} \xrightarrow {\mathbb {P}} \xi\) if and only if \(\rho \left(\xi_{n}, \xi \right) \to 0\).

title: The Law of Large Numbers
text: The law of large numbers is the promise on which all of empirical science rests: frequencies stabilize, averages converge. Insurance exists because the average loss over a large portfolio is almost deterministic; polls work because the sample fraction approximates the population fraction; the Monte Carlo method computes integrals because the average over simulations converges to the expectation. In this topic we will travel the path from a simple \(L^2\) argument (Chebyshev’s LLN) to Kolmogorov’s strong LLN — convergence almost surely under the minimal condition \(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi_1\right|\right] < \infty\) — and along the way collect tools valuable in their own right: Kolmogorov’s inequality, the theorem on convergence of series, and the Toeplitz and Kronecker lemmas.

title: The Law of Large Numbers
text:
1.1 Monte Carlo
Suppose we need to compute \(I = \int_{[0,1]^d} f(x)\, dx\). Take independent \(U_i \sim \operatorname {U}\left([0,1]^d\right)\) and average: \(\widehat{I}_n = \frac1n \sum f(U_i) \to I\). The error \(\sim \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}\) does not depend on the dimension \(d\) — this is the superpower of the method: deterministic grids in dimension \(d\) require \(\sim \varepsilon^{-d}\) nodes, while Monte Carlo requires \(\sim \varepsilon^{-2}\) simulations even in dimension \(1000\). This is exactly why it is used to compute multidimensional integrals in finance (pricing complex options), physics, and Bayesian statistics.

title: The Law of Large Numbers
text:
2.1 Nested disks
A point \(\xi_{1}\) is chosen uniformly in the unit disk; \(\xi_{n+1}\) is chosen uniformly in the disk of radius \(\left|\xi_{n}\right|\) centered at the origin. Prove that \[
  \frac{\ln \left|\xi _{n}\right|}{n} \xrightarrow {\text{a.s.}} c,
\] and find \(c\).

title: Characteristic Functions
text:
WarningDraft



This text is still being edited: it may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished spots. If you find something, please let the author know (contact details on the course page).


The characteristic function is the Fourier transform of a distribution, and its appearance in the course is dictated by sheer pragmatism: convolution turns into a product. The distribution of a sum of a hundred independent terms via convolution is a hundred-fold integral; via characteristic functions, it is the hundredth power of a single function. Add to this the uniqueness theorem (the characteristic function is a complete passport of the distribution) and the continuity theorem (pointwise convergence of characteristic functions is equivalent to weak convergence) — and you get the main computational tool of limit theorems: we will prove the CLT in topic 9 in five lines. This is the same trick an engineer uses to analyze a signal via its spectrum: an operation that is awkward in the time domain (filter convolution) becomes multiplication in the frequency domain.

1 Definition and properties







Definition 1 The characteristic function (CF) of a random variable \(\xi\) is \[
  \varphi _\xi (t) = \mathbb {E}\left[e^{it\xi }\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[\cos (t\xi )\right] + i\, \mathbb {E}\left[\sin (t\xi )\right], \qquad t \in \mathbb {R}.
\]




It is always defined (\(\left|e^{it\xi }\right| = 1\) — integrability comes for free, unlike for moment generating functions). Geometric interpretation: \(e^{it\xi }\) is a point on the unit circle, and \(\varphi_\xi (t)\) is the center of mass of the distribution wound onto the circle at speed \(t\); the more spread out the distribution, the closer the center of mass is to zero.







Proposition 1 (Properties of the CF)  

\(\varphi (0) = 1\), \(\left|\varphi (t)\right| \leq 1\), \(\varphi (-t) = \overline{\varphi (t)}\); \(\varphi\) is uniformly continuous on \(\mathbb {R}\).
\(\varphi_{a\xi + b}(t) = e^{itb}\varphi_\xi (at)\).
If \(\xi \;  \perp \! \! \! \perp \;  \eta\), then \(\varphi_{\xi + \eta }(t) = \varphi_\xi (t) \,  \varphi_\eta (t)\).
\(\varphi\) is real \(\iff\) the distribution of \(\xi\) is symmetric (\(\xi \overset {d}{=} -\xi\)).
If \(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi \right|^k\right] < \infty\), then \(\varphi \in C^k(\mathbb {R})\) and \(\varphi^{(k)}(0) = i^k \mathbb {E}\left[\xi^k\right]\); in particular,
\[
  \varphi (t) = 1 + it\, \mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right] - \frac{t^2}{2}\mathbb {E}\left[\xi ^2\right] + o(t^2), \qquad t \to 0.
\]





Item 3 is the heart of the topic (proof: \(\mathbb {E}\left[e^{it(\xi +\eta )}\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[e^{it\xi }\right]\mathbb {E}\left[e^{it\eta }\right]\) by independence — topic 1). Item 5 is “moments sit in the derivatives at zero”: smoothness of the CF at zero encodes lightness of the tails.







Theorem 1 (Uniqueness and inversion) The characteristic function uniquely determines the distribution. If in addition \(\varphi \in L^1(\mathbb {R})\), then the distribution has a bounded continuous density \[
  p(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi }\int _{\mathbb {R}} e^{-itx}\varphi (t)\, dt.
\]











Theorem 2 (Bochner-Khinchin; statement) A function \(\varphi\) with \(\varphi (0)=1\) is a characteristic function if and only if it is continuous and positive semi-definite: \(\sum_{j,k} \varphi (t_j - t_k) z_j \bar z_k \geq 0\) for any \(t_j \in \mathbb {R}\), \(z_j \in \mathbb {C}\).

title: Gaussian Vectors
text:
You already know the one-dimensional normal distribution well: it arises as the limit in the CLT, and describes measurement errors and the spread of traits in nature and society. But in practice one rarely encounters exactly one random variable — usually there are several, and they are dependent (a person’s height and weight, asset returns, the coordinates of a random point). The question arises: what should count as a “normal distribution” for a random vector?
Our task is to transfer the notion of a Gaussian distribution from the line to \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\), preserving all the important properties: stability under affine transformations, a simple description via parameters (a mean vector and a covariance matrix), and — especially valuable and far from obvious — the equivalence of uncorrelatedness and independence of the components. The multivariate Gaussian distribution is one of the central objects of probability and statistics: it arises in the multivariate CLT, underlies linear regression and the least-squares method, describes Gaussian processes (including Brownian motion, the stochastic processes course), and is actively used in machine learning (Gaussian processes, principal component analysis).
Plan for this topic: geometric language (affine subspaces) \(\to\) Gaussian distributions in dimensions \(0\), \(1\), \(n\) \(\to\) four equivalent definitions \(\to\) examples and counterexamples \(\to\) uncorrelatedness and independence \(\to\) conditional expectation in the Gaussian world \(\to\) the multivariate CLT.

title: Gaussian Vectors
text:
2.1 Dimension 0
Let us begin with the degenerate case. By definition \(\mathbb {R}^{0} := \left\{ 0\right\}\) — a set consisting of a single zero vector. There is exactly one probability measure on it: \(\mathbb {P}\left(\left\{ 0\right\} \right) = 1\).







Definition 2 The standard \(0\)-dimensional Gaussian distribution is the unique distribution on \(\mathbb {R}^{0}\): the measure assigning probability \(1\) to the point \(0\).




The definition looks like a joke, but it is a working part of the construction: it is exactly what will handle the degenerate cases in higher dimensions.

title: Gaussian Vectors
text:
2.2 Dimension 1
The standard normal distribution can be introduced in two equivalent ways — both familiar to you (topics 1 and 8):







Lemma 1 (The standard normal distribution) For a random variable \(Y\), the following are equivalent:

\(Y\) has density \(f(y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}e^{-y^2/2}\);
\(Y\) has characteristic function \(\varphi_Y(t)=e^{-t^2/2}\). We write \(Y \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\).





Now let us describe the entire family of one-dimensional Gaussian distributions — in a deliberately cumbersome form, which will then generalize verbatim to \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\).







Theorem 1 (Equivalent definitions of the one-dimensional Gaussian distribution) For a random variable \(X\), the following are equivalent:

\(X\) is an affine transformation of a standard normal variable: there exist \(\mu \in \mathbb {R}\), \(a \in \mathbb {R}\) such that
\[
  X = \mu + a Y, \qquad Y \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right);
\]
the characteristic function has the form \(\varphi_X(t) = e^{i\mu t - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 t^2}\) for some \(\mu \in \mathbb {R}\), \(\sigma^2 \geq 0\);
the support of the distribution of \(X\) is an affine subspace of \(\mathbb {R}\), and on it the distribution is “bell-shaped”: either \(X = \mu\) a.s. (the case \(\sigma = 0\): the support is a point, an affine subspace of dimension \(0\)), or \(X\) has density
\[
  f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }\, \sigma }\,  e^{-\frac{(x-\mu )^2}{2\sigma ^2}}, \qquad \sigma > 0
\]
(the support is the whole line, an affine subspace of dimension \(1\)). Here the parameters are consistent: \(\mu = \mathbb {E}\left[X\right]\), \(\sigma^2 = \operatorname {Var}\left[X\right] = a^2\). We write \(X \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\mu , \sigma^2\right)\).











NoteInteractive illustration placeholder



The interactive illustration has not been created yet. See the source: /home/nedosh/Documents/online_math_notes/math-notes_FPMI_2/courses/nedosh_courses/courses/04-probability/02_PT/contents/specials/100/03_gaussian_1d_cases_fig.tex.


Why such cumbersomeness, if the one-dimensional normal distribution lives perfectly well without it? Because it is exactly in this form — (1) an affine image of the standard distribution, (2) a special CF, (3) a support-subspace with a bell on it — that each item generalizes verbatim to the multivariate case.






Mn-remarkRemark




2.3 Rank
Notice how differently the cases \(\sigma = 0\) and \(\sigma > 0\) are structured. For \(\sigma = 0\) the standard \(\mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\) is not even needed: it suffices to take the \(0\)-dimensional standard distribution (definition Definition 2) and apply an affine map. Let us call these cases the rank of the one-dimensional Gaussian distribution: \(\sigma = 0\) — rank \(0\) (degenerate), \(\sigma > 0\) — rank \(1\) (full rank).









Mn-remarkRemark




2.4 Ambiguity of \(a\)
In representation (1), the coefficient \(a\) is not uniquely determined: both values \(\pm \sigma\) work, since \(-Y \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\). For instance, \(5 + 2Y\) and \(5 - 2Y\) have the same distribution \(\mathscr {N}\left(5, 4\right)\). The variance \(\sigma^2\), however, is uniquely determined.










Corollary 1 (Affine stability) If \(X \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\mu , \sigma^2\right)\) and \(a, b \in \mathbb {R}\), then \(aX + b \sim \mathscr {N}\left(a\mu + b, \, a^2\sigma^2\right)\).

For \(\sigma = 0\) the standard \(\mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\) is not even needed: it suffices to take the \(0\)-dimensional standard distribution (definition Definition 2) and apply an affine map. Let us call these cases the rank of the one-dimensional Gaussian distribution: \(\sigma = 0\) — rank \(0\) (degenerate), \(\sigma > 0\) — rank \(1\) (full rank).
