For instance, \(5 + 2Y\) and \(5 - 2Y\) have the same distribution \(\mathscr {N}\left(5, 4\right)\). The variance \(\sigma^2\), however, is uniquely determined.

title: Gaussian Vectors
section: 3.1 The standard vector and the general definition
text:
3.1 The standard vector and the general definition
Let us proceed by the same scheme: first the standard \(n\)-dimensional vector, then an arbitrary Gaussian vector as its affine image.







Lemma 2 (The standard Gaussian vector) For a random vector \(Y = (Y_1, \ldots , Y_n)\) in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\), the following are equivalent:

the components \(Y_1, \ldots , Y_n\) are independent and each \(\sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\);
\(Y\) has density \(f_n(y)=\frac{1}{(2\pi )^{n/2}}\, e^{-\left\| y\right\|^2/2}\), where \(\left\| y\right\|^2 = y_1^2 + \ldots + y_n^2\);
\(Y\) has characteristic function \(\varphi_{Y}(t)=e^{-\left\| t\right\|^2/2}\), \(t \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\). We write \(Y \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, I_n\right)\).











Mn-proofProof






\((1)\Rightarrow (2)\): the density of a vector with independent components is the product of the densities (topic 2): \(\prod_j \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}e^{-y_j^2/2} = f_n(y)\). \((2)\Rightarrow (3)\): from the multiplicative structure of \(f_n\), the characteristic function factors into a product of one-dimensional ones: \(\prod_j e^{-t_j^2/2} = e^{-\left\| t\right\|^2/2}\) (lemma Lemma 1). \((3)\Rightarrow (1)\): the joint CF factors into a product of the CFs of the coordinates — this is equivalent to independence of the coordinates (the factorization criterion, topics 2 and 8), and each coordinate is standard by lemma Lemma 1.




The density in item 2 depends only on \(\left\| y\right\|\): the standard vector is isotropic (invariant under rotations). The combination “independent coordinates + spherical symmetry” is a unique privilege of the Gaussian distribution (Maxwell’s theorem); it will come into play more than once below.






NoteInteractive illustration placeholder



The interactive illustration has not been created yet. See the source: /home/nedosh/Documents/online_math_notes/math-notes_FPMI_2/courses/nedosh_courses/courses/04-probability/02_PT/contents/specials/100/04_std_normal_2d_density_fig.tex.









Definition 3 A random vector \(X\) in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) is called Gaussian if there exist \(\mu \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\) and a matrix \(A\) such that \[
  X = \mu + AY, \qquad Y \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, I_m\right),
\] where \(A \in \mathbb {R}^{n \times m}\) (one may take \(m = n\); rectangular matrices are allowed — see the remark below).




No non-degeneracy of \(A\) is required — and this is essential: degenerate Gaussian vectors, whose entire mass lives on an affine subspace of smaller dimension, are ubiquitous in applications (regression residuals, frequencies with a fixed sum).

title: Gaussian Vectors
text:
3.2 Parameters: expectation, covariance matrix, CF
In the one-dimensional case the distribution was completely determined by the pair \((\mu , \sigma^2)\). Let us show that in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) too, a Gaussian vector is determined by two parameters — a mean vector and a covariance matrix, which replaces the variance.







Theorem 2 (Parameters of a Gaussian vector) Let \(X = \mu + AY\), \(Y \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, I_m\right)\). Then:

\(\mathbb {E}\left[X\right] = \mu\);
\(\operatorname {Var}\left[X\right] = AA^T =: \Sigma\) (the covariance matrix, \(\Sigma_{ij} = \operatorname {Cov}\left[ X_i, X_j \right]\));
the characteristic function
\[
  \varphi _{X}(t) = \exp \left(i\, \mu ^T t - \tfrac 12\,  t^T \Sigma \,  t\right), \qquad t \in \mathbb {R}^{n}.
\]











Mn-proofProof







Linearity: \(\mathbb {E}\left[X\right] = \mu + A\, \mathbb {E}\left[Y\right] = \mu\). (2) \(\operatorname {Var}\left[X\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[AY(AY)^T\right] = A\, \mathbb {E}\left[YY^T\right]A^T = AA^T\), since \(\mathbb {E}\left[YY^T\right] = I_m\) (ones on the diagonal — variances, zeros off it — independence). (3) \(\varphi_X(t) = \mathbb {E}\left[e^{it^T(\mu + AY)}\right] = e^{it^T\mu }\, \varphi_Y(A^Tt) = e^{it^T\mu }\, e^{-\frac12\left\| A^Tt\right\|^2}\), and \(\left\| A^Tt\right\|^2 = t^TAA^Tt = t^T\Sigma t\).





Thus the matrix \(A\) enters the distribution only through the product \(\Sigma = AA^T\) — \(A\) itself is nothing more than “scaffolding”.







Theorem 3 (Uniqueness of the parameters) The distribution of a Gaussian vector is uniquely determined by the pair \((\mu , \Sigma )\):

if \(A_1A_1^T = A_2A_2^T = \Sigma\), then the vectors \(\mu + A_1Y_1\) and \(\mu + A_2Y_2\) have the same distribution;
conversely, for any \(\mu \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\) and symmetric positive semi-definite \(\Sigma\), there exists a Gaussian vector with \(\mathbb {E}\left[X\right] = \mu\), \(\operatorname {Var}\left[X\right] = \Sigma\). We write \(X \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\mu , \Sigma \right)\).











Mn-proofProof







By theorem Theorem 2(3), both CFs equal \(e^{i\mu^Tt - \frac12 t^T\Sigma t}\); the uniqueness theorem for CFs (the multivariate version) identifies the distributions. (2) By the spectral theorem \(\Sigma = QDQ^T\) with orthogonal \(Q\) and diagonal \(D = \operatorname {diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots , \lambda_n)\), \(\lambda_i \geq 0\). Set \(A := QD^{1/2}\); then \(AA^T = QDQ^T = \Sigma\), and the vector \(\mu + AY\) is the one we sought.












Definition 4 The number \(k := \operatorname {rk}\Sigma \in \left\{ 0, 1, \ldots , n\right\}\) is called the rank of the Gaussian vector \(X \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\mu , \Sigma \right)\). When \(k = n\) the vector is called non-degenerate (full rank), when \(k < n\) — degenerate.











Lemma 3 For any \(A \in \mathbb {R}^{n \times m}\), \(\operatorname {rk}(AA^T) = \operatorname {rk} A\) — the rank of the vector can also be computed from the matrix \(A\) in the representation.










Mn-proofProof






It suffices to check \(\ker (AA^T) = \ker (A^T)\): the inclusion \(\supseteq\) is obvious, and if \(AA^Tx = 0\), then \(0 = x^TAA^Tx = \left\| A^Tx\right\|^2\), whence \(A^Tx = 0\). The nullities are equal — so are the ranks.

title: Gaussian Vectors
text:
3.3 Dimension reduction
If \(k < n\), then to construct \(X\) a \(k\)-dimensional standard vector actually suffices — as in the one-dimensional case, where for \(\sigma = 0\) the \(0\)-dimensional distribution sufficed.







Proposition 2 (Dimension reduction) Let \(X = \mu + AY\) be a Gaussian vector of rank \(k = \operatorname {rk}A\). Then there exist a matrix \(A' \in \mathbb {R}^{n \times k}\) of full column rank \(k\) and a vector \(Y' \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, I_k\right)\) such that \(X = \mu + A'Y'\).




The idea of the proof is the singular value decomposition: \(A = U_k \Sigma_k V_k^T\) (the zero singular values contribute nothing), \(A' := U_k\Sigma_k\), \(Y' := V_k^TY\); checking \(Y' \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, I_k\right)\) is a direct computation of the CF, using \(V_k^TV_k = I_k\).






ExampleExample 1 - Dimension reduction on a concrete example





Let \(n = 2\), \(\mu = 0\), \(A=\begin{psmallmatrix} 1& 1\\ 1& 1\end{psmallmatrix}\) — a matrix of rank \(1\). Find a representation of the vector \(X = AY\) via a single standard normal variable.






SolutionSolution





We have \(X = (Y_1+Y_2, \,  Y_1+Y_2)\). The variable \(Y' := \frac{Y_1+Y_2}{\sqrt2}\) is standard: the sum \(Y_1 + Y_2 \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 2\right)\) (convolution, topic 3), and dividing by \(\sqrt2\) normalizes the variance. Then \[
  X = \begin{psmallmatrix} \sqrt2\\ \sqrt2\end{psmallmatrix} Y' =: A'Y', \qquad A' \in \mathbb {R}^{2 \times 1}, \quad Y'\sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)
\] — the same distribution, but with one (rather than two) independent standard variable. The support of \(X\) is the diagonal \(\left\{ x_1 = x_2\right\}\), an affine subspace of dimension \(1 = \operatorname {rk}A\).












Mn-remarkRemark




The reduction shows that in definition Definition 3 one may freely allow rectangular \(A \in \mathbb {R}^{n \times m}\) for any \(m\): the class of Gaussian vectors does not change, and the notation becomes more economical. From now on we use both forms.










Lemma 4 (Affine image of a Gaussian vector) Let \(X\) be a Gaussian vector in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\), \(C \in \mathbb {R}^{m \times n}\), \(b \in \mathbb {R}^{m}\). Then \(Z = b + CX\) is a Gaussian vector in \(\mathbb {R}^{m}\), with \(Z \sim \mathscr {N}\left(b + C\mu , \; C\Sigma C^T\right)\).










Mn-proofProof






Substituting \(X = \mu + AY\): \(Z = (b + C\mu ) + (CA)Y\) — again an affine image of a standard vector (with rectangular matrix \(CA\), as in the remark above). The parameters follow from theorem Theorem 2.




The Gaussian world is closed under linear algebra: sums, differences, projections, and rotations of Gaussian vectors are Gaussian, and everything is computed by matrix multiplication.

title: Gaussian Vectors
section: 3.4 Marginal distributions and the criterion via linear combinations
text:
3.4 Marginal distributions and the criterion via linear combinations







Proposition 3 (Linear combinations of coordinates) Let \(X \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\mu , \Sigma \right)\) in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\), \(c \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\). Then \[
  c^T X = c_1X_1 + \ldots + c_nX_n \;  \sim \;  \mathscr {N}\left(c^T\mu , \; c^T\Sigma c\right).
\] In particular (\(c = e_i\)): each coordinate \(X_i \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\mu_i, \Sigma_{ii}\right)\).




This is a special case of lemma Lemma 4 with \(m = 1\). The converse is false: normality of each coordinate separately does not imply Gaussianity of the vector — counterexamples below (the “checkerboard” example and \((\xi , \eta \xi )\)). Normality of the marginals is necessary but not sufficient. But if we require normality of all linear combinations at once — that is already sufficient:







Theorem 4 (Criterion for Gaussianity via linear combinations) A vector \(X\) is Gaussian if and only if for every \(c \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\) the variable \(c^T X\) has a one-dimensional Gaussian distribution (possibly degenerate).










Mn-proofProof






(\(\Rightarrow\)) — proposition Proposition 3. (\(\Leftarrow\)) Each coordinate is Gaussian, so the second moments are finite and \(\mu := \mathbb {E}\left[X\right]\), \(\Sigma := \operatorname {Var}\left[X\right]\) are well defined. The variable \(c^TX\) is Gaussian with parameters \(c^T\mu\), \(c^T\Sigma c\), so its CF at the point \(s = 1\) equals \[
  \varphi _X(c) = \mathbb {E}\left[e^{i \,  c^TX}\right] = \varphi _{c^TX}(1) = e^{i c^T\mu - \frac12 c^T\Sigma c}.
\] The point \(c\) is arbitrary — so the CF of the vector \(X\) has exactly the Gaussian form from theorem Theorem 2(3), and by theorem Theorem 3(2) plus uniqueness of the CF, the vector \(X\) is distributed as \(\mathscr {N}\left(\mu , \Sigma \right)\).

title: Gaussian Vectors
text:
3.5 The full-rank density







Proposition 4 (Density) If \(\det \Sigma \neq 0\), then \(X \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\mu , \Sigma \right)\) has density \[
  f_X(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi )^{n/2}\sqrt{\det \Sigma }} \exp \left(-\tfrac 12 (x - \mu )^T \Sigma ^{-1} (x-\mu )\right), \qquad x \in \mathbb {R}^{n}.
\] The level curves are ellipsoids with axes along the eigenvectors of \(\Sigma\) and semi-axes \(\propto \sqrt{\lambda_i}\). When \(\det \Sigma = 0\), there is no density on \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\): the entire mass lies on the affine subspace \(\mu + \operatorname {Im}A\) of dimension \(\operatorname {rk}\Sigma\).




(Derivation — the change of variables from topic 2 applied to the representation \(X = \mu + AY\) with non-degenerate \(A\): the Jacobian \(\left|\det A^{-1}\right| = 1/\sqrt{\det \Sigma }\).)

title: Gaussian Vectors
text:
4.1 Scheme of the proof
\((1)\Leftrightarrow (2)\) — theorems Theorem 2(3) and Theorem 3; \((2)\Leftrightarrow (4)\) — theorem Theorem 4. The link with (3): in the direction \((1)\Rightarrow (3)\), dimension reduction (proposition Proposition 2) gives \(X = \mu + A'Y'\) with \(A'\) of full column rank \(k\); the support is the image of \(\mathbb {R}^{k}\) under a linear injection, i.e. the affine subspace \(H = \mu + \operatorname {Im}A'\), and in an orthonormal basis of \(\operatorname {Im}A'\) (the left singular vectors of \(A'\)), the coordinates of \(X\) are a non-degenerate linear image of \(Y'\), which has a Gaussian density (proposition Proposition 4 in dimension \(k\)). Conversely, \((3)\Rightarrow (1)\): the bell in coordinates on \(H\) is a linear image of a standard vector (spectral decomposition \(\Sigma ' = RDR^T\), the substitution \(W = D^{-1/2}R^Tz\)), and, unwinding the parametrization of \(H\), we obtain the representation \(X = \mu + (ERD^{1/2})W\), where \(E\) is the matrix of basis vectors.

title: Gaussian Vectors
section: 10.1 Gaussian marginals without joint Gaussianity, a threshold version
text:
10.1 Gaussian marginals without joint Gaussianity, a threshold version
Let \(X \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\), \(c > 0\), and \[
  Y = \begin{cases}  X, &  \left|X\right| \leq c, \\ -X, &  \left|X\right| > c. \end{cases}
\] Prove: (a) \(Y \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\); (b) the vector \((X, Y)\) is not Gaussian; (c) there exists \(c_0\) for which \(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated but dependent.

title: Conditional Distributions and Computing Conditional Expectation
text: The conditional expectation from topic 11 is the conditional mean; but often a full answer is needed: what is the conditional distribution of \(\xi\) given \(\eta\)? All two-stage models are built this way. A classic example (Klenke [@klenke2020probability]): a coin is “corrupted” at random, so that the probability of heads \(X\) is uniform on \([0,1]\), and then, given \(X = x\), it is tossed \(n\) times independently. Intuition immediately says: \(\mathbb {P}\left(Y_1 = \ldots = Y_n = 1 \mid X = x\right)\) “should be” \(x^n\) — but the event \(\left\{ X = x\right\}\) has probability zero, and the first-course definition cannot make sense of this expression. Topic 11 provided a workaround — \(\mathbb {P}\left(A \mid \eta \right) := \mathbb {E}\left[ \; \mathbb {1}_{A} \mid \eta \right]\) — but a “piecemeal” one, with its own null set for each event \(A\). In this topic we will build the full-fledged object — the regular conditional distribution: for each value of the condition, an actual probability measure. Along the way we will get the language of transition kernels (the stochastic processes course will use it to define Markov processes), the computational technique of conditional densities, the famous Borel-Kolmogorov paradox, and — as a bridge to statistics — sufficient statistics. We rely on Shiryaev [@shiryaev2016probability] (Ch. 2, §7) and Klenke [@klenke2020probability] (§8.3).

title: Conditional Distributions and Computing Conditional Expectation
text:
1.1 Checking measurability
Condition 2 need only be checked for \(B\) from some \(\pi\)-system generating \(\mathcal{E}_2\) (for instance, for rays \((-\infty , b]\) on the line): the collection of sets for which measurability holds forms a \(\lambda\)-system, and Dynkin’s lemma (topic 1!) finishes the job.

title: Conditional Distributions and Computing Conditional Expectation
text:
8.1 Rejection sampling
(Klenke, Exercise 8.3.6.) Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be distributions on a countable set \(E\), and \(f(e) := \frac{Q(\left\{ e\right\} )}{P(\left\{ e\right\} )} \leq c\) for all \(e\) with \(P(\left\{ e\right\} ) > 0\). A generator can produce independent \(X_1, X_2, \ldots \sim P\) and independent \(U_1, U_2, \ldots \sim \operatorname {U}[0,1]\). Set \[
  N = \min \left\{ n \colon U_n \leq f(X_n)/c\right\} , \qquad Y := X_N.
\] Prove that \(Y \sim Q\), and find \(\mathbb {E}\left[N\right]\).

title: Course Program
text: The course is built as a direct continuation of ETMT: overlaps with it are compressed to brief reminders, and the freed-up time is devoted to topics that are absent from self-contained probability theory courses or are given only in passing (uniform integrability, the Borel-Cantelli lemma and the zero-one law as a separate topic, the Lindeberg-Lyapunov conditions, conditional distributions with a Gaussian forecast). The throughline is computational technique for the continuous case: Jacobians, convolutions, and gamma- and beta-integrals.

title: Course Program
section: Part 1. Probability on the Foundation of Measure. Convergences
text:
Part 1. Probability on the Foundation of Measure. Convergences

The language of probability theory (1-2 seminars, “paying off debts” from ETMT). Kolmogorov’s axioms; independence and the criterion via \(\pi\)-systems; random variables and distributions; expectation as a Lebesgue integral, change of variables, generalized densities.
Random vectors. Joint distributions, multivariate distribution functions; the density transformation formula (Jacobian); marginals; independence criteria; the main continuous distributions in practice.
Convolution. Covariance and inequalities. The convolution formula as a technique; covariance and correlation in the general case, the covariance matrix; Jensen’s, Lyapunov’s, and Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz inequalities.
Convergence of random variables. The complete diagram of the four types of convergence with counterexamples; the criterion for almost sure convergence; inheritance of convergence, Slutsky’s theorem; uniform integrability and convergence of moments.
The Borel-Cantelli lemma and the zero-one law. Both parts of the lemma; problems on \(\limsup\) of events; tail \(\sigma\)-algebras, Kolmogorov’s zero-one law; optional — the three-series theorem.
Laws of large numbers. The Cantelli strong law of large numbers; Kolmogorov’s inequality, the Kolmogorov-Khinchin theorem; Toeplitz’s and Kronecker’s lemmas; Kolmogorov’s strong law of large numbers; applications: the Monte Carlo method, normal numbers.

Midterm exam 1.

section: Part 2. Limit Theorems and Conditional Constructions
text:
Part 2. Limit Theorems and Conditional Constructions

Weak convergence of probability measures. Convergence in the main sense; Alexandrov’s theorem; tightness of families of measures; Prokhorov’s theorem.
Characteristic functions. Properties, computational technique; moments and derivatives; the uniqueness theorem, the inversion formula; the Bochner-Khinchin theorem.
The central limit theorem. The continuity theorem; proof of the CLT; the Lindeberg and Lyapunov conditions; the Berry-Esseen inequality; the de Moivre-Laplace theorems, the Poisson approximation; optional — the law of the iterated logarithm (statement).
Gaussian vectors. Three equivalent definitions; independence \(\Leftrightarrow\) uncorrelatedness; density, linear transformations; the multivariate CLT.
Conditional expectation. The discrete case; definition via a \(\sigma\)-algebra; the complete set of properties (the foundation for martingales in the stochastic processes course).
Conditional distributions and computing conditional expectation. Conditional densities, \(\mathbb{E}[\xi \mid \eta = y]\); the best forecast in \(L^2\); the Gaussian conditional expectation as a linear forecast — a bridge to regression in statistics and to Gaussian processes.

Midterm exam 2.

title: Modes of Convergence of Random Vectors. The Delta Method

This set of notes is still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished spots. If you find something, please let the author know (contact information on the course page).


Let us continue studying the asymptotic properties of various estimators. Suppose we have a sample \(X_1, \ldots , X_n\) from the distribution \(\mathscr {N}\left(0, \sigma^2\right)\) with unknown parameter \(\sigma > 0\), which we want to estimate. Recall that
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {E}\left[X^p\right] = \begin{cases}  0, &  p \text{ -- odd} \\ \sigma ^p (p-1)!!, &  p \text{ -- even} \end{cases} \end{align}
\]
In particular, \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_1^2\right] = \sigma^2, \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^4\right] = 3\sigma^4\). Sample means approximately coincide with the corresponding expectations, \(\overline{X^2} \approx \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^2\right] = \sigma^2, \overline{X^4} \approx \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^4\right] = 3\sigma^4\). Consequently, one can try to estimate \(\sigma\) in several ways at once:
\[
  \widehat{\sigma }_1(X) = \sqrt{\overline{X^2}}, \quad \widehat{\sigma }_2(X) = \sqrt{\frac{\overline{X^4}}{3\overline{X^2}}}, \quad \widehat{\sigma }_3(X) = \sqrt[4]{\frac{\overline{X^4}}{3}}, \quad \ldots
\]
One can expect that these statistics will be approximately equal to the unknown parameter \(\sigma\). But will they, for example, be asymptotically normal? After all, we know that, by the CLT applied to the squares and fourth powers of the original sample, \(\overline{X^2}, \overline{X^4}\) are asymptotically normal estimators of \(\sigma^2, 3\sigma^4\).
To answer the questions above, we need a few new tools. First, we need a theorem on the so-called inheritance of asymptotic normality, i.e., some statement that would give asymptotic normality of the estimator \(f(\widehat{\theta })\) for some function \(f\), given that we know the asymptotic normality of \(\widehat{\theta }\). Such a statement would help in answering the question of the asymptotic normality of \(\widehat{\sigma }_1\), \(\widehat{\sigma }_3\).
Second, the samples \((X_1^2, X_2^2, \ldots , X_n^2)\) and \((X_1^4, X_2^4, \ldots , X_n^4)\) are dependent on each other. We cannot expect that applying the CLT separately to each of the samples will lead to an exact answer to the question about the limiting distribution of
\[
  \widehat{\sigma }_2 = \sqrt{\frac{\overline{X^4}}{3\overline{X^2}}}
\]
We need some new version of the CLT that would take these dependencies into account, that would answer the question about the limiting distribution of the two-dimensional random vector \((\overline{X^2}, \overline{X^4})^T\). We need a multivariate version of the CLT, which we would apply to the (infinite) sample from a 2-dimensional distribution
\[
  \begin{pmatrix} X_1^2 \\ X_1^4\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} X_2^2 \\ X_2^4\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} X_3^2 \\ X_3^4\end{pmatrix}, \ldots , \begin{pmatrix} X_n^2 \\ X_n^4\end{pmatrix}, \ldots .
\]
For this we need to give a definition of convergence for random vectors.

1 Convergence of Random Vectors
Modes of convergence in the multidimensional case are analogous to the one-dimensional case.







Definition 1 Let \(\left\{ \xi^{(n)}\right\}_{n \in \mathbb {N}}\) be a sequence of random vectors of dimension \(m\), defined on the same probability space \((\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mathbb {P})\), \(\xi^{(n)} = (\xi^{(n)}_1, \ldots , \xi^{(n)}_m)^T\).

The sequence \(\xi^{(n)}\) converges almost surely to a random vector \(\xi\) as \(n \rightarrow \infty\) (written \(\xi^{(n)} \stackrel{\text{ a.s. }}{\longrightarrow } \xi\)) if
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\omega : \lim _{n \to \infty } \xi ^{(n)}(\omega ) = \xi (\omega )\right) = 1
\]
The sequence \(\xi^{(n)}\) converges in probability to a random vector \(\xi\) as \(n \rightarrow \infty\) (written \(\xi^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} \xi\)) if for every \(\varepsilon >0\) we have
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\left\| \xi ^{(n)} - \xi \right\| _{2} \geq \varepsilon \right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} 0,
\]
where
\[
  \left\| \overrightarrow {x}\right\| _{p} := \sqrt[p]{\left|x_1\right|^p + \ldots + \left|x_m\right|^p}
\]
for \(\overrightarrow {x} = (x_1, \ldots , x_m) \in \mathbb {R}^{m}\).
Note that instead of the norm \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{2}\) one could use any other norm \(\left\| \cdot \right\|_{p}, \;  p \geq 1\) and even \(\left\| \overrightarrow {x}\right\|_{\infty } = \max \left\{ \left|x_i\right|, \;  i = 1, \ldots , m\right\}\), since in finite-dimensional spaces all norms are equivalent.
The sequence \(\xi^{(n)}\) converges in the Lebesgue space \(L^{p}\) to a random vector \(\xi\) as \(n \rightarrow \infty\) (written \(\xi^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{L^{p}} \xi\)) if
\[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\left\| \xi ^{(n)} - \xi \right\| _{p}^p\right] \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} 0,
\]
The sequence \(\xi^{(n)}\) converges in distribution to a random vector \(\xi\) as \(n \rightarrow \infty\) (written \(\xi^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \xi\)) if for every bounded continuous function \(f: \mathbb {R}^{m} \to \mathbb {R}\) we have
\[
  \mathbb {E}\left[f(\xi ^{(n)})\right] \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \mathbb {E}\left[f(\xi )\right]
\]
An equivalent definition: \(\xi^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \xi\) if the distribution functions of \(\xi^{(n)}\)
\[
  F_{\xi ^{(n)}}(\overrightarrow {x}) = \mathbb {P}\left(\xi ^{(n)}_1 \leq x_1, \xi ^{(n)}_2 \leq x_2, \ldots , \xi ^{(n)}_m \leq x_m\right)
\]
converge to the distribution function of \(\xi\) at every continuity point of the latter:
\[
  F_{\xi ^{(n)}}(\overrightarrow {x}) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} F_{\xi }(\overrightarrow {x}), \quad \forall \overrightarrow {x} \text{ such that } F_{\xi } \text{ is continuous at } \overrightarrow {x}.
\]












Theorem 1 (On relations among various modes of convergence) The following implications among modes of convergence hold


                                                


The implication \(L^q \Rightarrow L^p\) for \(q \geq p \geq 1\) is Lyapunov’s inequality: \(\left(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|\cdot \right|^p\right]\right)^{1/p} \leq \left(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|\cdot \right|^q\right]\right)^{1/q}\), applied to \(\left\| \xi^{(n)} - \xi \right\|_{p}\).











Theorem 2 (On relations between convergence of vectors and convergence of their components) Let random vectors \[
  \xi = \begin{pmatrix}  \xi _1 \\ \vdots \\ \xi _m \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \xi ^{(n)} = \begin{pmatrix}  \xi ^{(n)}_1 \\ \vdots \\ \xi ^{(n)}_m \end{pmatrix}
\] be given, where \(n \in \mathbb {N}\). Then for every \(i = 1,\ldots ,m\) we have \[
\begin{align}  \xi ^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\text{a.s.}} \xi & \iff \xi ^{(n)}_i \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\text{a.s.}} \xi _i, \\ \xi ^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} \xi & \iff \xi ^{(n)}_i \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} \xi _i, \\ \xi ^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{L^{p}} \xi & \iff \xi ^{(n)}_i \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{L^{p}} \xi _i, \\ \xi ^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \xi & \Longrightarrow \xi ^{(n)}_i \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \xi _i. \end{align}
\]




Note that for convergence in distribution the reverse-direction theorem does not hold. Convergence in distribution of random vectors implies componentwise convergence, but the converse is not always true, as the following example shows. Let \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) be independent identically distributed random variables. Let the sequences of random variables \(\left\{ \xi^{(n)}\right\}_{n \in \mathbb {N}}\) and \(\left\{ \eta^{(n)}\right\}_{n \in \mathbb {N}}\) be such that \(\xi^{(n)}=\xi\) and \(\eta^{(n)}=\eta\) for every \(n \in \mathbb {N}\). Then, obviously, \(\xi^{(n)} \stackrel{d}{\rightarrow } \xi\) and \(\eta^{(n)} \stackrel{d}{\rightarrow } \xi\), since \(\xi \stackrel{d}{=} \eta\) by assumption. But vector convergence does not hold: \(\left(\xi^{(n)}, \eta^{(n)}\right) \stackrel{d}{\not\to }(\xi , \xi )\), since \(\left(\xi^{(n)}, \eta^{(n)}\right) \stackrel{d}{\rightarrow }(\xi , \eta )\) and the distributions of the vectors \((\xi , \eta )\) and \((\xi , \xi )\) do not coincide, since all values of the second vector lie almost surely on the line \(y=x\), whereas for the first vector this is far from always the case.
However, if we have 2 componentwise-convergent-in-distribution sequences and the limit of one of them is a constant, then the reverse implication in theorem Theorem 2 does hold, as the following lemma states.







Lemma 1 Let \(\eta^{(1)}, \eta^{(2)}, \ldots\) be a sequence of random vectors of dimension \(k\), converging in distribution to \(\eta\): \[
  \eta ^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \eta
\] Let \(\zeta^{(1)}, \zeta^{(2)}, \ldots\) be a sequence of random vectors of dimension \(l\), converging in distribution to some constant vector \(c = (c_1, \ldots , c_{l})^T \in \mathbb {R}^{l}\): \[
  \zeta ^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} c.
\] Then the random vector \(\begin{pmatrix} \eta^{(n)} \\ \zeta^{(n)} \end{pmatrix}\) of dimension \(k + l\) converges in distribution to \(\begin{pmatrix} \eta \\ c \end{pmatrix}\): \[
  \begin{pmatrix}  \eta ^{(n)} \\ \zeta ^{(n)} \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \begin{pmatrix}  \eta \\ c \end{pmatrix}.
\]










Mn-proofProof






The distribution function of the limiting vector \((\eta , c)\) has the form
\[
  F_{(\eta ,c)}(x,y) = \mathbb {P}\left(\eta \leq x, \,  c \leq y\right) = F_\eta (x) \cdot \; \mathbb {1}_{y \geq c},
\]
since \(c\) is a nonrandom vector. By the definition of convergence in distribution via distribution functions, it suffices to check the convergence \(F_{(\eta^{(n)}, \zeta^{(n)})}(x,y) \to F_{(\eta ,c)}(x,y)\) at every continuity point of \(F_{(\eta ,c)}\) — that is, at points \((x,y)\) where \(x\) is a continuity point of \(F_\eta\) and \(y\) does not lie on any of the hyperplanes \(\left\{ y_i = c_i\right\}\), \(i = 1,\ldots ,l\). Fix such a point \((x,y)\).
Case \(y > c\) (strictly, componentwise). From the inclusions \(\left\{ \eta^{(n)} \leq x, \,  \zeta^{(n)} \leq y\right\}  \subset \left\{ \eta^{(n)} \leq x\right\}\) and \(\left\{ \eta^{(n)} \leq x\right\}  \setminus \left\{ \zeta^{(n)} \leq y\right\}  \subset \left\{ \zeta^{(n)} \not\leq y\right\}\) we obtain the bound
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\eta ^{(n)} \leq x\right) - \mathbb {P}\left(\zeta ^{(n)} \not\leq y\right) \;  \leq \;  F_{(\eta ^{(n)}, \zeta ^{(n)})}(x,y) \;  \leq \;  \mathbb {P}\left(\eta ^{(n)} \leq x\right).
\]
As \(n \to \infty\) both outer terms tend to \(F_\eta (x)\): the left one because \(x\) is a continuity point of \(F_\eta\), and \(\mathbb {P}\left(\zeta^{(n)} \not\leq y\right) \to \mathbb {P}\left(c \not\leq y\right) = 0\) (since \(y > c\)); the right one for the same reason. By the squeeze theorem, \(F_{(\eta^{(n)}, \zeta^{(n)})}(x,y) \to F_\eta (x) = F_{(\eta ,c)}(x,y)\).
Case \(y_i < c_i\) for some \(i\). From \(\left\{ \zeta^{(n)} \leq y\right\}  \subset \left\{ \zeta^{(n)}_i \leq y_i\right\}\) we obtain
\[
  0 \;  \leq \;  F_{(\eta ^{(n)}, \zeta ^{(n)})}(x,y) \;  \leq \;  \mathbb {P}\left(\zeta ^{(n)}_i \leq y_i\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \mathbb {P}\left(c_i \leq y_i\right) = 0,
\]
since \(y_i < c_i\). Hence, \(F_{(\eta^{(n)}, \zeta^{(n)})}(x,y) \to 0 = F_{(\eta ,c)}(x,y)\).
These two cases exhaust all continuity points of \(F_{(\eta ,c)}\) (at the remaining points either \(y > c\), or \(y_i < c_i\) for at least one \(i\)), which completes the proof.










ExampleExample 1





Prove that convergence in distribution of a sequence of \(m\)-dimensional random vectors \(\xi^{(n)}\) to a constant \(C \in \mathbb {R}^{m}\) implies convergence \(\xi^{(n)} \stackrel{\mathbb {P}}{\rightarrow } C\).






SolutionSolution





From theorem Theorem 2 it follows that for every \(i \in \{ 1, \ldots , m\}\) we have \(\xi^{(n)}_{i} \stackrel{d}{\rightarrow } C_i\), where \(\xi^{(n)}=\left(\xi^{(n)}_{1}, \ldots , \xi^{(n)}_{m}\right)^T, C=\left(C_{1}, \ldots , C_{m}\right)^T\). We know from the probability course that the latter convergence implies convergence in probability: \(\xi^{(n)}_{i} \stackrel{\mathbb {P}}{\rightarrow } C_i\) for every \(i \in \{ 1, \ldots , m\}\). But then from theorem Theorem 2 we have \(\xi^{(n)} \stackrel{\mathbb {P}}{\rightarrow } C\).








2 Inheritance of Convergence
The next important result we will need is the theorem on inheritance of convergence.







Theorem 3 (on inheritance of convergence / Mann-Wald / the continuous mapping theorem) Let \(\xi , \xi^{(1)}, \xi^{(2)}, \ldots\) be random vectors of dimension \(m\), and let \(h: \mathbb {R}^{m} \to \mathbb {R}^{s}\) be a function that is continuous almost everywhere with respect to the distribution of the random variable \(\xi\), i.e., there exists a set \(B \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{m}\right), \;  \mathbb {P}\left(\xi \in B\right) = 1\) such that \(h\) is continuous on \(B\). Then \[
\begin{align}  \xi ^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\text{a.s.}} \xi & \Longrightarrow h(\xi ^{(n)}) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\text{a.s.}} h(\xi ) \\ \xi ^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} \xi & \Longrightarrow h(\xi ^{(n)}) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} h(\xi ) \\ \xi ^{(n)} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \xi & \Longrightarrow h(\xi ^{(n)}) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} h(\xi ) \end{align}
\]











Corollary 1 Suppose we have a parametric model \(\mathcal{P} = \left\{ \mathbb {P}_\theta , \theta \in \Theta \right\}\) and a sample \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) from it. Let \(\widehat{\theta }\) be a consistent (strongly consistent) estimator of \(\theta\). Let \(h: \Theta \to h(\Theta )\) be some map that is continuous on \(\Theta\). Then \(h(\widehat{\theta })\) is a consistent (respectively, strongly consistent) estimator of \(h(\theta )\).




Convergence in the Lebesgue space \(L^p\) is inherited in a somewhat more subtle way, if only because \(h(\xi )\) does not always lie in \(L^p\), even if \(\xi\) is in \(L^p\) and \(h\) is everywhere continuous. However, if \(h: \mathbb {R}^{m} \to \mathbb {R}^{s}\) is a Lipschitz function:
\[
  \exists C > 0: \;  \left\| h(\overrightarrow {x}) - h(\overrightarrow {y})\right\| _{q} \leq C \cdot \left\| \overrightarrow {x} - \overrightarrow {y}\right\| _{p}
\]
\(\forall \overrightarrow {x}, \overrightarrow {y} \in \mathbb {R}^{m}\), then convergence of \(\xi^{(n)}\) to \(\xi\) in \(L^p\) implies convergence in \(L^q\) for \(h(\xi^{(n)})\):
\[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\left\| h(\xi ^{(n)}) - h(\xi )\right\| _{q}\right] \leq C \mathbb {E}\left[\left\| \xi ^{(n)} - \xi \right\| _{p}\right] \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} 0
\]


3 Convergence and Arithmetic Operations
By theorems Theorem 2 and Theorem 3, from the convergence of sequences of random variables \(\xi^{(n)} \stackrel{\mathbb {P}}{\rightarrow } \xi\), \(\eta^{(n)} \stackrel{\mathbb {P}}{\rightarrow } \eta\) we obtain the convergences
\[
  \xi ^{(n)}+\eta ^{(n)} \stackrel{\mathbb {P}}{\rightarrow } \xi +\eta , \quad \xi ^{(n)} \eta ^{(n)} \stackrel{\mathbb {P}}{\rightarrow } \xi \eta .
\]
For convergence in distribution, a similar conclusion cannot be drawn, since, as we already know, componentwise convergence in distribution does not imply convergence in distribution of vectors. For example, let \(\xi \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\) be an arbitrary standard normal random variable, \(\xi_n := \xi \;  \forall n \in \mathbb {N}\). Then we can write
\[
  \xi _n \xrightarrow [n\to \infty ]{d}\xi , \quad \xi _n \xrightarrow [n\to \infty ]{d} -\xi ,
\]
since \(\left(-\xi \right) \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\). But
\[
  \xi _n + \xi _n = 2\xi _n \stackrel{d}{\not\to } \xi - \xi = 0,
\]
since \(2\xi_n = 2\xi \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 4\right)\).
However, if one of the sequences converges in distribution to a constant, then the following statement holds.







Theorem 4 (Slutsky’s theorem) Let \(\xi_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \xi\) and \(\eta_n \xrightarrow {d} c \in \mathbb {R}\) be random variables. Then \[
\begin{align}  \xi _n + \eta _n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \xi + c \\ \xi _n \eta _n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \xi c \end{align}
\]










ProblemProblem 1





Prove Slutsky’s theorem.






HintHint





Use lemma Lemma 1 and theorem Theorem 3 on inheritance of convergence in distribution.








4 Inheritance of Asymptotic Normality, One-Dimensional Case
We are ready to move on directly to the question of inheritance of asymptotic normality. A consequence of theorems Theorem 3 and Theorem 4 is







Theorem 5 (The Delta Method) Let \(\xi^{(n)} \stackrel{d}{\rightarrow } \xi\) be random vectors of dimension \(m\), and let \(h(x): \mathbb {R}^{m} \to \mathbb {R}\) be a function differentiable at the point \(\theta \in \mathbb {R}^{m}\). Let \(b_{n} \rightarrow 0\), \(b_{n} \neq 0\). Then
\[
  \frac{h(\theta + \xi ^{(n)}b_n) - h(\theta )}{b_n} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \left\langle \xi , \nabla h|_{\theta } \right\rangle ,
\]
where \(\nabla h|_{\theta }\) is the gradient of the function \(h(x)\), taken at the point \(\theta\), and the right-hand side is a random variable (the dot product of the vector \(\xi\) with the vector \(\nabla h|_{\theta }\)).
In particular, if \(\xi^{(n)} \stackrel{d}{\rightarrow } \xi\) are random variables (\(m=1\)), and \(h(x): \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {R}\) is a function differentiable at the point \(\theta \in \mathbb {R}\), then
\[
  \frac{h(\theta + \xi ^{(n)}b_n) - h(\theta )}{b_n} \;  \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \;  h'(\theta ) \cdot \xi .
\]











Theorem 6 (on inheritance of asymptotic normality) Let \(\widehat{\theta } = \widehat{\theta }(X)\) be an asymptotically normal estimator of \(\theta\) with asymptotic variance \(\sigma^2(\theta )\), and let \(h(\theta )\) be a differentiable function on \(\Theta \subset \mathbb {R}\), whose derivative is finite and nonzero at every point \(\theta \in \Theta\). Then \(h(\widehat{\theta })\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(h(\theta )\) with asymptotic variance \(\sigma^{2}(\theta ) \cdot \left(h^{\prime }(\theta )\right)^{2}\).










Mn-remarkRemark




The condition \(h'(\theta ) \neq 0\) in the theorem is essential. If \(h'(\theta ) = 0\), while \(h''(\theta )\) is finite and nonzero, then the linear approximation degenerates, and \(h(\widehat{\theta })\) converges to \(h(\theta )\) faster than the standard rate \(\sqrt{n}\), with a limiting distribution that is no longer normal — the second-order delta method applies: \[
  n\left(h(\widehat{\theta }) - h(\theta )\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \frac12 h''(\theta )\sigma ^2(\theta ) \cdot \chi ^2_1.
\]



We are ready to move on to answering the question about the asymptotic normality of \(\widehat{\sigma }_1\).






ExampleExample 2





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be a sample from \(\mathscr {N}\left(0, \sigma^2\right), \sigma > 0\). Find for which parameter the estimator \(\widehat{\sigma }_1 = \sqrt{\overline{X^2}}\) is asymptotically normal, and find the asymptotic variance.






SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Let us apply the CLT to \(X_n^2, \;  n \in \mathbb {N}\). Recall that \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_1^2\right] = \sigma^2, \;  \operatorname {Var}\left[X_1^2\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^4\right] - \left(\mathbb {E}\left[X_1^2\right]\right)^2 = 3\sigma^4 - \sigma^4 = 2\sigma^4\). Let us apply the CLT:
\[
  \sqrt{n}\left(\overline{X^2} - \sigma ^2\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, 2\sigma ^4\right)
\]
Thus, \(\overline{X^2}\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(\sigma^2\) with asymptotic variance \(2\sigma^4\).








Enum-item2.



Let us use the theorem on inheritance of asymptotic normality. We have
\[
\begin{align}  h\left(\theta \right) & = \sqrt{\theta }, \quad h'(\theta ) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\theta }}, \quad h'(\sigma ^2) = \frac{1}{2\sigma } \end{align}
\]
\(h\) is differentiable on \((0, +\infty )\), and its derivative does not vanish. Consequently, \(\sqrt{\overline{X^2}}\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(\sigma\) with asymptotic variance \(2\sigma^4 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2\sigma }\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\):
\[
  \sqrt{n}\left(\sqrt{\overline{X^2}} - \sigma \right) \xrightarrow [n\to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, \frac{1}{2}\sigma ^2\right)
\]











AnswerAnswer





Parameter \(\sigma\). Asymptotic variance \(\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\).






Let us consider a few more examples.






ExampleExample 3





Let \(X_1, \ldots , X_n\) be a sample from a distribution with nonzero expectation \(a\) and variance \(\sigma^{2}\). Is the statistic \(1/\overline{X}\) an asymptotically normal estimator of some parameter? If so, what is the asymptotic variance?






SolutionSolution





By the central limit theorem, \(\overline{X}\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(a\) with asymptotic variance \(\sigma^2\):
\[
  \sqrt{n} \left(\overline{X} - a\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, \sigma ^2\right)
\]
Next, let us use the theorem on inheritance of asymptotic normality. We have \(h(y) = \frac{1}{y}\). This function is differentiable on \(\mathbb {R} \setminus \left\{ 0\right\}\). Here \(h'(y) = -\frac{1}{y^2}\). Consequently, \(\frac{1}{\overline{X}}\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(\frac{1}{a}\) with asymptotic variance \(\frac{\sigma^2}{a^4}\):
\[
  \sqrt{n}\left(\frac{1}{\overline{X}} - \frac{1}{a}\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, \frac{\sigma ^2}{a^4}\right)
\]












ExampleExample 4





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be a sample from \(U[1+\theta , \theta (1+\theta )]\), the uniform distribution on the interval \([1+\theta , \theta (1+\theta )], \theta >1\). Find an asymptotically normal estimator of the parameter \(\theta\) and its asymptotic variance.






SolutionSolution





Note that \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_1\right] = \frac{(1+\theta )^2}{2} =: m(\theta )\). By the central limit theorem, \(\overline{X}\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of the parameter \(m(\theta )\) with asymptotic variance \(\sigma^{2}(\theta )=\frac{\left(\theta^{2}-1\right)^{2}}{12}\). Note that \(m(\theta )\) takes values in the set \((2, \infty )\). Set \(h(x)=\sqrt{2 x}-1\) (a function differentiable on \((2, \infty )\)). Then \(h'(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2x}}\), whence \(\left(h'(x)\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2x}\), and, substituting \(x = m(\theta ) = \frac{(1+\theta )^2}{2}\):
\[
  \left(\left.h^{\prime }\right|_{m(\theta )}\right)^{2} = \frac{1}{2m(\theta )} = \frac{1}{(1+\theta )^2}.
\]
By the theorem on inheritance of asymptotic normality, \(h(\overline{X})\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(\theta\) with asymptotic variance
\[
  \sigma ^{2}(\theta )\left(\left.h^{\prime }\right|_{m(\theta )}\right)^{2}=\frac{\left(\theta ^{2}-1\right)^{2}}{12} \cdot \frac{1}{(1+\theta )^2} = \frac{(\theta -1)^2(\theta +1)^2}{12(1+\theta )^2} = \frac{(\theta -1)^{2}}{12}
\]









AnswerAnswer





Estimator \(\sqrt{2\overline{X}} - 1\), asymptotic variance \(\frac{(\theta - 1)^2}{12}.\)












ProblemProblem 2





Let \(X_1, \dots , X_n\) be a sample from \(\operatorname {Exp}\left(\alpha \right), \alpha > 0\). Find constants \(a(\alpha ), \sigma^2(\alpha )\) such that \[
\begin{align}  \sqrt{n} (\overline{X} \sin (\overline{X}) - a(\alpha )) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, \sigma ^2(\alpha )\right) \end{align}
\]









ProblemProblem 3





A sample \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) is given from the exponential law with parameter \(\lambda >0\). For which quantity \(h(\lambda )\) is the statistic \(\bar{X} \ln \bar{X}\) an asymptotically normal estimator? Compute the asymptotic variance of this estimator.









ProblemProblem 4





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be a sample from the exponential distribution with parameter \(\theta\). Show that for every \(k \in \mathbb {N}\) the statistic \(\sqrt[k]{k ! / \overline{X^{k}}}\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of the parameter \(\theta\). Find its asymptotic variance.



All the estimators constructed above were asymptotically normal at rate \(\sqrt{n}\). The following problem shows that this is far from always true: for the sample maximum \(X_{(n)}\), both the rate of convergence and the limiting distribution turn out to be quite different, so the delta method in its current form is not applicable here.






ProblemProblem 5





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be a sample from the distribution \(U[0, \theta ]\) (the uniform distribution on the interval \([0,\theta ]\)). Find a number \(\delta >0\) and a nondegenerate distribution law \(\mathbb {P}_{\theta }\) (i.e., not the distribution law of a constant) such that \(n^{\delta }\left(X_{(n)}-\theta \right) \stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow } \xi \sim \mathbb {P}_\theta\) as \(n \rightarrow \infty\).









ProblemProblem 6





Construct an asymptotically normal estimator of \(b\) from a sample \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) from the distribution \[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = 1\right) & = 1-a-a^{2}-6b, \\ \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = 2\right) & = 5 b, \\ \mathbb {P}\left(X_1 = 5\right) & = a+a^{2}+b, \end{align}
\] where \(a, b\) are unknown positive parameters.






HintHint





Choose a function \(g\) such that \(\mathbb {E}\left[g(X_1)\right] = b\) for all \(a, b\); for example, a quadratic polynomial with roots \(1\) and \(5\).












ProblemProblem 7





A sample \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) is given, \(X_{1}=\xi +\eta , \xi \sim U(0, \theta ), \eta \sim\) \(U(\theta , 2 \theta )\) — independent random variables, where \(\theta >0\) is an unknown parameter. Find an asymptotically normal estimator of \(\theta\) and its asymptotic variance.



Let us consider an example of applying the delta method that turns out to be useful in machine learning.






ExampleExample 5 - The curse of dimensionality





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be a sample from \(U[0,1]\), that is, \((X_1, \ldots , X_n)^T\) is a random point from the cube \([0,1]^n\) with the uniform distribution. Consider the statistic \[
  N = N_n := \sqrt{X_1^2 + \ldots + X_n^2}
\] — the \(2\)-norm of the vector, i.e., the Euclidean distance from zero to this random point. Find the distribution of \(N_n\) for large \(n\).






SolutionSolution





We have
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^2\right] & = \int _0^1 x^2\,  dx = \frac{1}{3}, \\ \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^4\right] & = \int _0^1 x^4\,  dx = \frac{1}{5}, \\ \operatorname {Var}\left[X_1^2\right] & = \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^4\right] - \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^2\right]^2 = \frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{9} = \frac{4}{45}. \end{align}
\]
By the central limit theorem, applied to the quantities \(X_1^2, \ldots , X_n^2\),
\[
  \sqrt{n}\left(\frac{N_n^2}{n} - \frac{1}{3}\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, \frac{4}{45}\right).
\]
Now let us apply the delta method to the function \(h(\theta ) = \sqrt{\theta }\) at the point \(\theta = \frac{1}{3}\), since \(h'(\theta ) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt\theta }\). Let us compute the asymptotic variance: \(h'\left(\frac13\right) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{1/3}} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), whence \(\left(h'\left(\frac13\right)\right)^2 = \frac34\), and
\[
  \frac{4}{45} \cdot \left(h'\left(\tfrac 13\right)\right)^2 = \frac{4}{45}\cdot \frac34 = \frac{1}{15}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
  \sqrt{n}\left(\frac{N_n}{\sqrt{n}} - \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, \frac{1}{15}\right).
\]
Note that on the left, after multiplying by \(\sqrt{n}\), we get the expression \(N_n - \sqrt{n/3}\). That is, approximately (for large \(n\))
\[
  \operatorname {Law}(N_n) \approx \mathscr {N}\left(\sqrt{n/3}, \frac{1}{15}\right),
\]
in other words, \(N_n\) is approximately normally distributed with expectation \(\sqrt{n/3}\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{1/15} \approx 0.26\).
This yields a curious geometric picture: a random point in the hypercube \([0,1]^n\), for large \(n\), lies practically on the surface of a sphere centered at zero with radius \(\sqrt{n/3}\). Meanwhile, the standard deviation of the distance is almost independent of \(n\) and is about \(0.26\). For large \(n\), this deviation turns out to be exceptionally small compared to the mean distance \(\sqrt{n/3}\), which grows without bound.







n = 10


Regenerate


distance between two random points






Conclusion for machine learning. In high-dimensional spaces, almost all points of a sample turn out to lie at comparable, practically identical distances from each other and from the origin. This phenomenon is one facet of the curse of dimensionality: methods based on the notion of distance (for example, the \(k\)-nearest-neighbors method or clustering by the Euclidean metric) lose their meaning, since distances between points cease to be informative — “close” and “far” points are practically indistinguishable from one another.












ProblemProblem 8





Let \((X_1, \ldots , X_n)^T\) and \((Y_1, \ldots , Y_n)^T\) be 2 independent random points from the hypercube \([0,1]^n\) with the uniform distribution. Consider the statistic \[
  D = D_n := \sqrt{(X_1 - Y_1)^2 + \ldots + (X_n- Y_n)^2}
\] — the Euclidean distance between them. Find the distribution of \(D_n\) for large \(n\).





5 Limit Theorems for Random Vectors
For random vectors, limit theorems analogous to the corresponding theorems for random variables continue to hold: the law of large numbers, the strong law of large numbers, the central limit theorem. Let us state them. Going forward, for a random vector \(\xi\) we will write \(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi \right]\), meaning the vector made up of the expectations of the components of the vector \(\xi\).







Theorem 7 (the multivariate analogue of the law of large numbers) Let \(\left\{ \xi^{(n)}\right\}_{n \in \mathbb {N}}-\) be independent random vectors, with the variance of each component of each random vector bounded by a constant \(C\). Then \[
  \frac{\xi ^{(1)}+\ldots +\xi ^{(n)}-\mathbb {E}\left[\xi ^{(1)}+\ldots +\xi ^{(n)}\right]}{n^{0.5+\delta }} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} 0,
\] where \(\delta\) is an arbitrary positive number.











Theorem 8 (the multivariate analogue of the strong law of large numbers) Let \(\left\{ \xi^{(n)}\right\}_{n \in \mathbb {N}}-\) be independent identically distributed random vectors, with the expectations of all components finite and equal to \(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi^{(1)}\right] = a\). Then \[
  \frac{\xi ^{(1)}+\ldots +\xi ^{(n)}}{n} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\text{a.s.}} a
\]











Theorem 9 (the multivariate analogue of the central limit theorem) Let \(\left\{ \xi^{(n)}\right\}_{n \in \mathbb {N}}-\) be independent identically distributed random vectors, \(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi^{(1)}\right] = a\), and let the covariance matrix of the random vector \(\xi^{(1)}\) be \(\operatorname {Var}\left[\xi^{(1)}\right] = \Sigma\). Then \[
  \sqrt{n}\left(\frac{\xi ^{(1)}+\ldots +\xi ^{(n)}}{n}-a\right) \stackrel{d}{\rightarrow } \eta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma ),
\] where \(\mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma )\) is the multivariate normal distribution (a Gaussian vector).






6 Inheritance of Asymptotic Normality, Multivariate Case
We are now almost ready to answer the question about the asymptotic normality of the estimator \(\widehat{\sigma }_2\) introduced at the beginning of the chapter. The last step is to state the multivariate version of the theorem on inheritance of asymptotic normality.







Theorem 10 (on inheritance of asymptotic normality, multivariate version) Let \(\widehat{\theta }(X)\) be an asymptotically normal estimator of a \(k\)-dimensional parameter \(\theta \in \Theta \subset \mathbb {R}^{k}\) with asymptotic covariance matrix \(\Sigma (\theta )\), and let \(h: \Theta \to \mathbb {R}\) be a differentiable function on \(\Theta \subset \mathbb {R}^{k}\) (the gradient \(\nabla h\) is finite and nonzero at every point \(\theta \in \Theta )\). Then \(h\left(\widehat{\theta }(X)\right)\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(h(\theta )\) with asymptotic variance \[
  \left(\nabla h|_{\theta }\right)^T \cdot \Sigma \cdot \nabla h|_{\theta }
\]




The proof is analogous to the one-dimensional case.






ExampleExample 6





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be a sample from \(\mathscr {N}\left(0, \sigma^2\right)\). Find for which parameter the estimator \(\widehat{\sigma }_2 = \sqrt{\frac{\overline{X^4}}{3\overline{X^2}}}\) is asymptotically normal, and find the asymptotic variance.






SolutionSolution











Enum-item1.



Let us apply the multivariate CLT to \(\xi^{(n)} := (X_n^2, X_n^4)^T, \;  n \in \mathbb {N}\). Let us find the expectation and covariance matrix of \(\xi^{(n)}\):
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^2\right] & = \sigma ^2, \quad \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^4\right] = 3\sigma ^4, \quad \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^6\right] = 15\sigma ^6, \quad \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^8\right] = 105\sigma ^8\\ \operatorname {Var}\left[X_1^2\right] & = \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^4\right] - \left(\mathbb {E}\left[X_1^2\right]\right)^2 = 2\sigma ^4, \quad \operatorname {Var}\left[X_1^4\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^8\right] - \left(\mathbb {E}\left[X_1^4\right]\right)^2 = 96\sigma ^8, \\ \operatorname {Cov}\left[ X_1^2, X_1^4 \right] & = \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^6\right] - \mathbb {E}\left[X_1^2\right]\mathbb {E}\left[X_1^4\right] = 12 \sigma ^6\\ \mathbb {E}\left[\begin{pmatrix}  X_1^2 \\ X_1^4 \end{pmatrix}\right] & = \begin{pmatrix}  \sigma ^2 \\ 3\sigma ^4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \operatorname {Var}\left[\begin{pmatrix}  X_1^2 \\ X_1^4 \end{pmatrix}\right] = \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}  2 \sigma ^{4} &  12 \sigma ^{6} \\ 12 \sigma ^{6} &  96 \sigma ^{8} \end{pmatrix} \end{align}
\]
Let us apply the CLT:
\[
  \sqrt{n}\left(\begin{pmatrix}  \overline{X^2} \\ \overline{X^4} \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}  \sigma ^2 \\ 3\sigma ^4 \end{pmatrix}\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, \Sigma \right)
\]
Thus, \(\begin{pmatrix}  \overline{X^2} \\ \overline{X^4} \end{pmatrix}\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(\theta := \begin{pmatrix}  \sigma^2 \\ 3\sigma^4 \end{pmatrix}\) with asymptotic covariance matrix \(\Sigma\).








Enum-item2.



Let us use the multivariate version of the theorem on inheritance of asymptotic normality. We have
\[
\begin{align}  h\left((x,y)^T\right) & = \sqrt{\frac{y}{3x}}, \quad \nabla h = \left(-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{y}{3x^3}}, \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{1}{3xy}}\right)^T, \quad \nabla h|_{\theta } = \left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma }, \frac{1}{6\sigma ^3}\right)^T \end{align}
\]
Let us separately compute \(\left(\nabla h|_{\theta }\right)^T \cdot \Sigma\):
\[
\begin{align}  \left(\nabla h|_{\theta }\right)^T \cdot \Sigma & = \begin{pmatrix}  -\dfrac {1}{2\sigma } &  \dfrac {1}{6\sigma ^3} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}  2\sigma ^4 &  12\sigma ^6 \\ 12 \sigma ^6 &  96\sigma ^8\end{pmatrix} \\ & = \begin{pmatrix}  -\dfrac {1}{2\sigma }\cdot 2\sigma ^4 + \dfrac {1}{6\sigma ^3}\cdot 12\sigma ^6 &  -\dfrac {1}{2\sigma }\cdot 12\sigma ^6 + \dfrac {1}{6\sigma ^3}\cdot 96\sigma ^8 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  \sigma ^3 &  10\sigma ^5 \end{pmatrix} \end{align}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{align}  \left(\nabla h|_{\theta } \right)^T \cdot \Sigma \cdot \nabla h|_{\theta } & = \begin{pmatrix}  \sigma ^3 &  10 \sigma ^5 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}  -1/2\sigma \\ 1/6\sigma ^3 \end{pmatrix} = -\frac{1}{2}\sigma ^2 + \frac{10}{6}\sigma ^2 = \left(\frac{10}{6} - \frac{1}{2}\right) \sigma ^2 = \frac{7}{6}\sigma ^2 \end{align}
\]
Consequently, \(\sqrt{\frac{\overline{X^4}}{3\overline{X^2}}}\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(h(\theta ) = \sigma\) with asymptotic variance \(\frac{7}{6}\sigma^2\):
\[
  \sqrt{n}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\overline{X^4}}{3\overline{X^2}}} - \sigma \right) \xrightarrow [n\to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, \frac{7}{6}\sigma ^2\right)
\]











AnswerAnswer





Parameter \(\sigma\). Asymptotic variance \(\frac{7}{6}\sigma^2\).












ProblemProblem 9





A collection of independent identically distributed random variables \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) with distribution \(\mathcal{N}\left(0, \sigma^{2}\right)\) is given. Consider the statistics \(Y=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|X_{i}\right|, Z=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}^{2}\) and \(T=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi }} \frac{Z}{Y}\). Prove that the statistic \(T\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(\sigma\), and find its asymptotic variance.






HintHint





If \(\xi \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, \sigma^2\right)\), then \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi \right|^p\right] = \sigma ^p (p-1)!!\begin{cases}  \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi }}, & p \text{ -- odd}\\ 1, & p \text{ -- even} \end{cases}
\]












ProblemProblem 10





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be independent random variables having the Laplace distribution with parameter \(\sigma > 0\), i.e., with density \[
  p(x)=\frac{1}{2 \sigma } e^{-\frac{|x|}{\sigma }} .
\] Consider \(Y=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|X_{i}\right|, Z=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}^{2}\). Prove that the statistic \(T := \frac{Z^2}{4Y^3}\) is an asymptotically normal estimator of \(\sigma\), and find its asymptotic variance.









ProblemProblem 11





A sample \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) is given from the distribution \(U[0, \theta ]\), where \(\theta\) is an unknown parameter. Find an asymptotically normal estimator of \(\theta\) as a function of \(\overline{X^2}/\overline{X^3}\). Find its asymptotic variance.

WarningDraft



This note is still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished passages. If you find something, please let the author know (contact information on the course page).
We have looked at convenient properties of estimators and learned how to find estimators. A natural question arises: which of two estimators possessing the same properties (e.g. consistency, unbiasedness, or asymptotic normality) is better? In this chapter we discuss the comparison of estimators.

title: Comparison of Estimators and Efficient Estimators
text:
2.1 The Score of the Sample
The likelihood function \(L(\theta ; \vec{x})\) is a density if, for fixed \(\theta\), it is varied over \(\vec{x}\). The area under the graph of the density equals \(1\):
\[
\begin{align}  1 = \int _{\mathbb {R}^{n}} L(\theta ; \vec{x}) \;  \;  d\vec{x} , \qquad \forall \theta \in \Theta \end{align}
\]
Let \(\Theta\) be an open set. Differentiate both sides with respect to \(\theta\), assuming that differentiation in \(\theta\) and integration in \(\vec{x}\) can be interchanged:
\[
\begin{align}  0 & = \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \int _{\mathbb {R}^{n}} L(\theta ; \vec{x}) \;  \;  d\vec{x} = \int _{\mathbb {R}^{n}} \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }L(\theta ; \vec{x}) \;  \;  d\vec{x} = \\ & = \int _{\mathbb {R}^{n}} \left[\underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }L(\theta ; \vec{x})\right) \cdot \frac{1}{L(\theta ; \vec{x})} }_{= \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \ln (L(\theta ; \vec{x}))=\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }\ell (\theta , \vec{x})}\right] \cdot L(\theta ; \vec{x}) \;  \;  d\vec{x} = \\ & = \int _{\mathbb {R}^{n}} \left(\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }\ell (\theta , \vec{x})\right) \cdot \underbrace{L(\theta ; \vec{x})}_{\text{density}} \;  \;  d\vec{x} = \mathbb {E}_{\theta }\left[\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \ell (\theta , \vec{X})\right], \qquad \forall \theta \in \Theta , \end{align}
\]
where \(\ell (\theta , \vec{x}) = \ln L(\theta , \vec{x})\) is the log-likelihood.







Definition 3 The random variable (depending on \(\theta\)) \[
  V = V(\vec{X}; \theta ) := \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \ell (\theta , \vec{X})
\] is called the score of the sample \(\vec{X}\).




As we have just established, the expectation of the score equals zero for every \(\theta \in \Theta\).

title: Comparison of Estimators and Efficient Estimators
section: 2.2 A Lower Bound for the Variance of an Unbiased Estimator: the Cramér-Rao Inequality
text:
2.2 A Lower Bound for the Variance of an Unbiased Estimator: the Cramér-Rao Inequality
Let \(\widehat{\tau } = \widehat{\tau }(\vec{X})\) be an unbiased estimator of some composite parameter \(\tau = \tau (\theta )\). Then, again assuming that differentiation in \(\theta\) and integration in \(\vec{x}\) can be interchanged, we obtain
\[
\begin{align}  \operatorname {Cov}_{\theta }\left[ \widehat{\tau }, V \right] & = \mathbb {E}_{\theta }\left[\widehat{\tau }V\right] - \mathbb {E}_{\theta }\left[\widehat{\tau }\right]\mathbb {E}_{\theta }\left[V\right] = \mathbb {E}_{\theta }\left[\widehat{\tau }V\right] = \\ & = \int _{\mathbb {R}^{n}} \widehat{\tau }(\vec{x}) V(\vec{x},\theta ) \cdot \underbrace{L(\theta ; \vec{x})}_{\text{density}}\;  d\vec{x} = \\ & = \int _{\mathbb {R}^{n}} \widehat{\tau }(\vec{x}) \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }L(\theta ; \vec{x})\;  d\vec{x} = \\ & = \int _{\mathbb {R}^{n}} \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \left[\widehat{\tau }(\vec{x}) L(\theta ; \vec{x})\right]\;  d\vec{x} = \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \int _{\mathbb {R}^{n}}\widehat{\tau }(\vec{x}) L(\theta ; \vec{x})\;  d\vec{x} = \\ & = \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \mathbb {E}_{\theta }\left[\widehat{\tau }\right] = \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }\tau (\theta ) = \tau '(\theta ) \end{align}
\]
On the other hand, applying the Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz inequality, we obtain \(\left(\operatorname {Cov}_{\theta }\left[ \widehat{\tau }, V \right]\right)^2 \leq \operatorname {Var}_{\theta }\left[\widehat{\tau }\right]\operatorname {Var}_{\theta }\left[V\right]\). Thus we have obtained







Theorem 1 (The Cramér-Rao Inequality: a Lower Bound for the Variance of an Unbiased Estimator) Let \(\widehat{\tau }\) be an unbiased estimator of \(\tau (\theta )\). Then for every \(\theta \in \Theta\) \[
  \operatorname {Var}_{\theta }\left[\widehat{\tau }\right] \geq \frac{(\tau '(\theta ))^2}{\operatorname {Var}_{\theta }\left[V\right]}
\]




The coefficient \(\operatorname {Var}_{\theta }\left[V\right] = \mathbb {E}_{\theta }\left[V^2\right]\) is called the Fisher information and is denoted \(I(\theta )\).
If equality is attained in the Cramér-Rao inequality, then \(\widehat{\tau }\) is called an efficient estimator of \(\tau (\theta )\). Recall that equality in the CBS inequality is attained if the 2 vectors are linearly dependent, i.e. one of the vectors is the other one multiplied by a constant.







Theorem 2 (Efficiency Criterion) Equality is attained in the Cramér-Rao inequality if and only if \(\widehat{\tau }-\tau (\theta ) = c(\theta ) V(X,\theta )\) for some \(c(\theta )\), i.e. when the estimator \(\widehat{\tau }\) is a linear function of the score1. Moreover, the latter equality holds if and only if \(c(\theta )=\frac{\tau^{\prime }(\theta )}{n i(\theta )}\).




Equality in the Cramér-Rao inequality can hold for only one unbiased estimator, and this estimator is the best in the mean-squared approach in the class of all unbiased estimators of \(\tau (\theta )\).
An efficient estimator will always be optimal, i.e. the best unbiased one. At the same time, an optimal estimator is not always efficient: the regularity conditions do not always hold, and in such cases one cannot speak of efficient estimators at all. However, an optimal estimator may still exist in such cases; see more on this below.

title: Comparison of Estimators and Efficient Estimators
text:
2.3 Regularity Conditions
The results obtained above hold only if the so-called regularity conditions are satisfied:

The Fisher information is always well defined: for every \(\vec{x}\) such that \(L(\theta ; \vec{x}) > 0\), the quantity
\[
  \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \ln \left(L(\theta ; \vec{x})\right)
\]
is defined and finite for all \(\theta \in \Theta\).
The operations of integration in \(x\) and differentiation in \(\theta\) can be interchanged when computing the expectation of \(\widehat{\tau }\), that is
\[
  \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \left[\int \widehat{\tau }(\vec{x}) L(\theta ; \vec{x}) \;  d\vec{x}\right] = \int \widehat{\tau }(\vec{x}) \left[\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }L(\theta ; \vec{x})\right] \;  d\vec{x}
\]
always holds whenever the right-hand side is finite.

More on regularity conditions can be found in (Боровков 2010). Let us just note that if the support of the unknown distribution depends on the parameter \(\theta\) (for example, \(U[0,\theta ]\)), then the regularity conditions do not hold.
The regularity conditions hold in either of the following cases:

all \(\mathbb {P}_{\theta }, \theta \in \Theta\) have a bounded support that does not depend on \(\theta\);
the family \(\left\{ \mathbb {P}_\theta , \theta \in \Theta \right\}\) is exponential (see the definition of an exponential family above), and \(\Theta\) is an open set: in this case the density \(p_\theta (x) = h(x)\exp \left(\sum_i a_i(\theta ) u_i(x) + v(\theta )\right)\) depends sufficiently smoothly on \(\theta\), the support is automatically independent of \(\theta\), and differentiation under the integral sign is justified.

title: Comparison of Estimators and Efficient Estimators
text:
2.4 Problems
Let \(i(\theta )\) be the amount of information contained in a single element of the sample \(X_{1}\).






ExampleExample 2





Show that \(I_{X}(\theta )=n i(\theta )\).






SolutionSolution





By the regularity condition, the integral of \(S(\vec{x}) p_{\theta }(\vec{x})\) can be differentiated under the integral sign. In particular,
\[
  \int _{\mathcal{X}} \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } p_{\theta }(\vec{x}) \mu (d \vec{x}) = \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \int _{\mathcal{X}} p_{\theta }(\vec{x}) \mu (d \vec{x})=0 .
\]
Here and below in similar cases we denote \(\mathbb {E}\left[X\right] =: \int_{x} \vec{x} p(\vec{x}) \mu (d \vec{x})\), meaning the Riemann integral in the case of an absolutely continuous distribution of the random variable \(\vec{X}\) with density \(p\), and a (possibly infinite) sum in the case of a discrete distribution of the random variable \(\vec{X}\) with \(p(\vec{x}) = \mathbb {P}\left(X = \vec{x}\right)\).
Thus,
\[
  \mathbb {E}_{\theta }\left[ \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \ln p_{\theta }\left(X_{1}\right)\right] = \int _{\mathcal{X}} \frac{\partial p_{\theta }(\vec{x})}{\partial \theta } \frac{p_{\theta }(\vec{x})}{p_{\theta }(\vec{x})} \mu (d \vec{x})=0 .
\]
Consequently,
\[
  I_{X}(\theta ) = \operatorname {Var}_{\theta }\left[\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \ln L(\theta ; \vec{X})\right] = \operatorname {Var}_{\theta }\left[\sum _{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \ln p_{\theta }\left(X_{i}\right)\right],
\]
and, since the summands are functions of independent \(X_i\), the variance of the sum decomposes into a sum of variances:
\[
  I_{X}(\theta ) = \sum _{i=1}^{n} \operatorname {Var}_{\theta }\left[\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \ln p_{\theta }\left(X_{i}\right)\right] = n i(\theta ) .
\]












ExampleExample 3





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be a sample from the Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(\theta\). Find an efficient estimator of \(\theta\) and the information \(i(\theta )\).






SolutionSolution





The regularity conditions hold for the parametric model considered in this problem. The likelihood function equals \[
  L(\theta ; \vec{X})=\theta ^{\sum X_{i}}(1-\theta )^{n-\sum X_{i}} .
\] Then \[
  V(X,\theta ) = \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta } \ln L(\theta ; \vec{X})=\frac{\sum X_{i}}{\theta }-\frac{n-\sum X_{i}}{1-\theta } = \frac{\sum X_{i}-n \theta }{\theta (1-\theta )}=\frac{n}{\theta (1-\theta )}(\bar{X}-\theta )
\] By the efficiency criterion, we obtain that \(\overline{X}\) is an efficient estimator of \(\theta\). Moreover, \[
  \frac{\theta (1-\theta )}{n}=\frac{1}{n i(\theta )}
\] Hence, \(i(\theta )=\frac{1}{\theta (1-\theta )}\).









AnswerAnswer





\(\overline{X}\), \(i(\theta ) = \frac{1}{\theta (1-\theta )}\).












ProblemProblem 3





Let \(X_1,\ldots , X_n\) be a sample from the binomial distribution with parameters \((m,p)\), with \(m\) known. Find the Fisher information \(i(p)\) in this model, and also an efficient estimator of the parameter \(p\).






HintHint





The probability mass function of \(\operatorname {Bin}\left(m, p\right)\) is conveniently written as: \(f(x) = C_{m}^x p^{x}(1-p)^{m-x}, \;  x \in \left\{ 0,1,\ldots ,m\right\}\)












ProblemProblem 4





Let \(X_1,\ldots , X_n\) be a sample from the exponential distribution with parameter \(\theta\). For which functions \(\tau (\theta )\) does an efficient estimator exist? Compute the Fisher information \(i(\theta )\) of one observation in this model.









ProblemProblem 5





Let \(X_1,\ldots , X_n\) be a sample from the normal distribution with parameters \((a, \sigma^2)\). Find an efficient estimator of

the parameter \(a\), if \(\sigma^2\) is known;
the parameter \(\sigma^2\), if \(a\) is known. Compute the Fisher information of one observation in both cases.

  p_{\theta }(x) = \frac{\exp (\theta -x)}{\left(1 + \exp (\theta - x)\right)^2}
\] Find the Fisher information \(i(\theta )\) of one observation in this model.
