In previous chapters we studied point estimators of parameters. Of course, in most cases the probability that the true value of the parameter coincides exactly with its estimator is zero. For this reason it is more convenient to consider, as an estimate, an entire interval of values of the unknown parameter. At the same time, the size of this interval should of course be as small as possible, while the probability of the true value of the parameter falling into it should, on the contrary, be as large as possible. In this chapter we discuss such intervals.

title: Confidence Intervals
section: 1.1 Constructing [Inexact] Confidence Intervals Using Chebyshev’s Inequality
text:
1.1 Constructing [Inexact] Confidence Intervals Using Chebyshev’s Inequality
To find a confidence interval one can, for example, use Markov’s inequality or Chebyshev’s inequality.






ExampleExample 1





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots X_{n}\) be a sample from the Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda >0\). Construct a confidence interval for \(\lambda\) of confidence level \(\gamma\).






SolutionSolution





By Chebyshev’s inequality,
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{\lambda }\left(\left|\sum X_{i}-\lambda n\right| \geq \varepsilon n\right) < \frac{\lambda }{\varepsilon ^{2} n}
\]
Hence,
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{\lambda }\left(\lambda -\varepsilon < \overline{X} < \lambda +\varepsilon \right) \geq 1 - \frac{\lambda }{\varepsilon ^2 n} = \gamma
\]
From the last equality we find \(\varepsilon =\sqrt{\lambda /((1-\gamma ) n)}\). Denote \(c := \frac{1}{(1-\gamma )n}\), then \(\varepsilon = \sqrt{c\lambda }\), and it remains to solve the inequalities \(\overline{X}<\lambda +\sqrt{c\lambda }\) and \(\lambda - \sqrt{c\lambda } < \overline{X}\) for \(\lambda\).
Let us start with the first inequality. Set \(u := \sqrt{\lambda } \geq 0\); then it can be rewritten as
\[
  u^2 + \sqrt{c}\, u - \overline{X} > 0.
\]
Complete the square:
\[
  \left(u + \frac{\sqrt{c}}{2}\right)^2 - \frac{c}{4} - \overline{X}> 0 \quad \iff \quad \left(u + \frac{\sqrt{c}}{2}\right)^2 > \overline{X} + \frac{c}{4}.
\]
Since \(u + \frac{\sqrt c}{2} > 0\), we may take the square root of both sides:
\[
  u > \sqrt{\overline{X}+\frac{c}{4}} - \frac{\sqrt{c}}{2}, \qquad \text{i.e.} \qquad \lambda = u^2 > \left(\sqrt{\overline{X}+\frac c4} - \frac{\sqrt c}{2}\right)^2.
\]
The second inequality (\(\lambda - \sqrt{c\lambda } < \overline{X}\)) is solved similarly with the same substitution \(u = \sqrt\lambda\) (only now the completed square is \(\left(u - \frac{\sqrt c}{2}\right)^2 < \overline{X} + \frac c4\)), giving \(\lambda < \left(\sqrt{\overline{X}+\frac c4} + \frac{\sqrt c}{2}\right)^2\). Finally, substituting \(c = \frac{1}{(1-\gamma )n}\) (so that \(\frac{\sqrt c}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4(1-\gamma )n}}\)), we obtain
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{\lambda }\left(\left(\sqrt{\overline{X}+\frac{1}{4(1-\gamma ) n}}-\sqrt{\frac{1}{4(1-\gamma ) n}}\right)^2< \lambda < \left(\sqrt{\overline{X}+\frac{1}{4(1-\gamma ) n}}+\sqrt{\frac{1}{4(1-\gamma ) n}}\right)^2\right) \geq \gamma
\]
A more precise (though not exact in the strict sense) interval can be obtained by using the fact that \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \operatorname {Pois}\left(n\lambda \right)\), and taking quantiles of this distribution instead of Chebyshev’s inequality — see the asymptotic version of this example at the end of the chapter.

title: Confidence Intervals
section: 1.2 Constructing Exact Confidence Intervals: the Central Statistic Method
text:
1.2 Constructing Exact Confidence Intervals: the Central Statistic Method
Chebyshev’s inequality, as a rule, gives a very crude bound on the probability of deviation from the mean. The diameter of such an interval usually turns out to be excessively large. Let us try to construct an exact interval.






ExampleExample 2





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be a sample from the distribution \(\mathscr {N}\left(\theta , \sigma^2\right)\) with known \(\sigma^2\). Construct an exact confidence interval for \(\theta\) of confidence level \(\gamma\).






SolutionSolution





Note that \(X_1 + \ldots + X_n \sim \mathscr {N}\left(n\theta , n\sigma^2\right)\) and \(\overline{X} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\theta , \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\). Hence,
\[
  \overline{X} - \theta \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, \frac{\sigma ^2}{n}\right), \qquad G(X, \theta ) := \frac{\overline{X} - \theta }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right).
\]
Notice that the distribution of the random variable \(G(X, \theta )\) does not depend on the unknown parameter \(\theta\). Such a random variable is called a central statistic. Let \(u_{\frac{1-\gamma }{2}}, u_{\frac{1 + \gamma }{2}}\) be the quantiles of levels \(\frac{1-\gamma }{2}, \frac{1+\gamma }{2}\) of the distribution \(\mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\). By the definition of quantiles,
\[
  \gamma = \frac{1 + \gamma }{2} - \frac{1 - \gamma }{2} = \mathbb {P}\left(u_{\frac{1-\gamma }{2}} < \frac{\overline{X} - \theta }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}} < u_{\frac{1+\gamma }{2}}\right).
\]
Let us solve the inequality under the probability for \(\theta\): multiplying by \(\sigma /\sqrt{n}\), we get
\[
  \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}u_{\frac{1-\gamma }{2}} < \overline{X} - \theta < \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}u_{\frac{1+\gamma }{2}},
\]
whence (subtracting \(\overline{X}\) and changing sign, i.e. reversing the inequality)
\[
  \overline{X} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}u_{\frac{1+\gamma }{2}}\sigma < \theta < \overline{X} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}u_{\frac{1-\gamma }{2}}\sigma .
\]
Hence,
\[
  \gamma = \mathbb {P}\left(\theta \in \left( \overline{X} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}u_{\frac{1+\gamma }{2}}\sigma , \; \overline{X} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}u_{\frac{1-\gamma }{2}}\sigma \right)\right).
\]









AnswerAnswer





\(\left( \overline{X} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}u_{\frac{1+\gamma }{2}}\sigma , \; \overline{X} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}u_{\frac{1-\gamma }{2}}\sigma \right)\)






Note the frequentist interpretation of the confidence level: it is the interval that is random, not the parameter. Upon repeated repetition of the experiment, the interval will cover the true \(\theta\) in approximately a fraction \(\gamma\) of cases:
“The dance of confidence intervals” (in Geoff Cumming’s terminology): a continuous simulation for the model \(\mathscr N(\theta,1)\) with known variance, \(\theta=0\) – the true (unknown to the statistician) value. Every few moments a new exact confidence interval of level \(\gamma\) is constructed by the central statistic method, \(\overline{X}\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt n}u_{\frac{1+\gamma}{2}}\); it appears at the bottom, the whole stack shifts up, and the oldest interval leaves the screen. It is the interval that is random, not the parameter \(\theta\): from experiment to experiment it shifts and either covers \(\theta\) (in black) or does not (in red). The circular gauge on the right shows the current empirical coverage fraction – it fluctuates, but on average stays near the nominal level \(\gamma\). Move the sliders \(\gamma\) and \(n\), and use pause/resume to examine the details.










γ = 95%
n = 20
speed = 500ms
Pause
















So, to find exact confidence intervals one needs to know the exact value of the probability, and hence one must use some function \(G(X, \theta )\) whose distribution does not depend on \(\theta\). Again, this function is called a central statistic, and the method of constructing an exact confidence interval based on such a random function is the central statistic method. Let us describe it in general form.
Let a random variable \(G(X, \theta )\) be such that its distribution is known and does not depend on \(\theta\). Suppose also that \(G(X, \theta )\) is strictly monotone (for example, increasing) and continuous in \(\theta\). Let \(0 \leq p_{1}<p_{2} \leq 1\) be such that \(p_{2}-p_{1}=\gamma\). For each \(i \in \{ 1,2\}\) consider the \(p_{i}\)-quantiles \(u_{p_{i}}\) of the distribution of \(G(X, \theta )\). Let \(T_{i}(X)\) be the solutions of the equations \(G\left(X, T_{i}(X)\right)=u_{p_{i}}, i \in \{ 1,2\}\). Then
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(T_{1}(X)<\theta <T_{2}(X)\right) = \mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(u_{p_{1}}<G(X, \theta ) < u_{p_{2}}\right) =p_{2}-p_{1}=\gamma ,
\]
i.e. \(\left(T_{1}(X), T_{2}(X)\right)\) is a confidence interval of confidence level \(\gamma\).
In general, for a given confidence level \(\gamma \in (0,1)\), when constructing a confidence interval one can take quantiles of levels \(p_1 = \frac{1}{2}-(1-\alpha ) \gamma\), \(p_2 = \frac{1}{2} + \alpha \gamma\), where \(\alpha \in \left(1 - \frac{1}{2\gamma }, \frac{1}{2\gamma }\right)\) is arbitrary (the latter condition is imposed so that \(0 < \frac{1}{2}-(1-\alpha ) \gamma , \frac{1}{2}+\alpha \gamma < 1\)). For example, for \(\gamma = 95\%\) one could take the quantiles \((u_{1\% }, u_{96\% }), (u_{4.5\% }, u_{99.5\% })\), etc. However, to minimize the length of the confidence interval, the levels \(p_{1}\) and \(p_{2}\) in the central statistic method are often chosen symmetric about \(0.5\), since the distribution of \(G(X, \theta )\) may have heavy tails. For \(\gamma = 95\%\) these would be \(u_{2.5\% }, u_{97.5\% }\).






ExampleExample 3





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be a sample from a distribution with density \[
  p_{\theta }(x)=e^{-(x-\theta )} \; \mathbb {1}_{x \geq \theta }
\] (an exponential distribution shifted by \(\theta\)). Construct a confidence interval of confidence level \(\gamma\) using the central statistic method.






SolutionSolution






Method 1. Note that \(X_{i}-\theta \sim \operatorname {Exp}(1) = \Gamma (1,1)\) (a distribution not depending on \(\theta\)). Further,
\[
  \sum _{i=1}^n \left(X_{i}-\theta \right) = n\overline{X} - n\theta \sim \Gamma (n, 1), \qquad \overline{X} - \theta \sim \Gamma (n, n)
\]
Take as the central statistic \(G(X, \theta )=\sum X_{i}-n \theta\). This statistic has distribution \(\Gamma (n, 1)\), since the sum of independent, identically distributed exponential random variables has a gamma distribution. Consider the \(\frac{1-\gamma }{2}-\) and \(\frac{1+\gamma }{2}\)-quantiles \(u_{\frac{1-\gamma }{2}}\) and \(u_{\frac{1+\gamma }{2}}\) of the distribution \(\Gamma (n, 1)\). By the definition of quantiles,
\[
  \gamma = \frac{1+\gamma }{2}-\frac{1-\gamma }{2}=\mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(u_{\frac{1-\gamma }{2}}<\sum X_{i}-n \theta <u_{\frac{1+\gamma }{2}}\right).
\]
Dividing the inequality under the probability by \(n\) (so that \(\sum X_i / n = \overline{X}\)) and solving it for \(\theta\) (subtracting \(\samplemean X\) and changing sign), we get
\[
  \gamma =\mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(\overline{X}-\frac{u_{\frac{1+\gamma }{2}}}{n}<\theta <\overline{X}-\frac{u_{\frac{1-\gamma }{2}}}{n}\right) .
\]
Method 2. By means of the statistic \(X_{(1)}\). Note that for \(x \geq \theta\):
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}\left(X_{1} > x\right) & = \int _x^{+\infty } e^{-(t-\theta )} dt = e^{-(x-\theta )} \\ \mathbb {P}\left(X_{(1)} > x\right) & = e^{-n(x-\theta )} \\ X_{(1)} - \theta & \sim \operatorname {Exp}(n) = \Gamma (1, n) \end{align}
\]
That is, \(X_{(1)} - \theta\) is a central statistic. Its quantile of level \(p\) equals \(u_p = -\frac{1}{n}\ln (1-p)\), whence
\[
  u_{\frac{1-\gamma }{2}} = -\frac{1}{n}\ln \frac{1+\gamma }{2}, \qquad u_{\frac{1+\gamma }{2}} = -\frac{1}{n}\ln \frac{1-\gamma }{2}.
\]
Hence,
\[
  \gamma = \mathbb {P}\left(u_{\frac{1-\gamma }{2}} < X_{(1)} - \theta < u_{\frac{1+\gamma }{2}}\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(-\frac{1}{n}\ln \frac{1+\gamma }{2} < X_{(1)} - \theta < -\frac{1}{n}\ln \frac{1-\gamma }{2}\right).
\]
Solving the inequality for \(\theta\) (subtracting \(X_{(1)}\) and changing sign), we get
\[
  \gamma = \mathbb {P}\left(X_{(1)} + \frac{1}{n}\ln \frac{1-\gamma }{2} < \theta < X_{(1)} + \frac{1}{n}\ln \frac{1+\gamma }{2}\right)
\]
(both endpoints lie to the left of \(X_{(1)}\), which is natural: \(\theta \leq X_{(1)}\) a.s.).
Method 3. Via Chebyshev’s inequality
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {E}\left[X_1\right] = 1 + \theta , \quad \operatorname {Var}\left[X_1\right] = 1 \\ \mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(\left|\overline{X} - (1 + \theta )\right| \geq \varepsilon \right) < \frac{1}{\varepsilon ^2 n} \\ \mathbb {P}_{\theta }\left(\overline{X} - 1 - \varepsilon \leq \theta \leq \overline{X} - 1 + \varepsilon \right) \geq 1 - \frac{1}{\varepsilon ^2 n} = \gamma , \quad \varepsilon = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n(1-\gamma )}}\\ \end{align}
\]













ProblemProblem 1





Let \(X_1, \dots , X_n\) be a sample from \(U[0, \theta ], \;  \theta > 0\). Construct a confidence interval for \(\theta\) of confidence level \(\gamma\), using the statistic

\(\overline{X}\);
\(X_{(1)}\);
\(X_{(n)}\).

*Note.** Each part is worth 0.5 points.









ProblemProblem 2





\(X_1, \ldots , X_n\) is a sample from a distribution with density \[
  p_{\theta }(x) = \frac{3}{8\theta ^3}x^2 \; \mathbb {1}_{x \in [0, 2\theta ]}
\] Using the statistic \(X_{(1)}\), construct an exact confidence interval of confidence level \(\gamma\) for the parameter \(\theta\).









ProblemProblem 3





Let \(X_1, \ldots , X_n\) be a sample from a distribution with density \[
  p_{\theta }(x) = \frac{1}{2}\exp \left(-\left|\left|x\right| - 6\theta \right|\right) \cdot \; \mathbb {1}_{\left|x\right| > 6\theta }
\] Construct a confidence interval for \(\theta > 0\) of confidence level \(\gamma = 1 - \alpha\).









ProblemProblem 4





\(X_1, \dots , X_n\) is a sample from the distribution of \(\xi + \eta\), where \(\xi , \eta\) are independent and have distribution \(\sim U[0, \theta ]\), \(\theta \in \Theta = (0,1)\). Construct a confidence interval for \(\theta\) of confidence level \(1 - \alpha\) using Chebyshev’s inequality.

text:

In this chapter \(\vec{X}\) denotes the observations.

title: Linear Regression
text:
1.1 Linear regression without an intercept






ExampleExample 1





There are 2 coins of different denominations, whose masses \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) are unknown. Using the same scale, the first coin was weighed separately, then the second, and then both coins together. Set up a statistical model for the experiment. Try to estimate \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\).






SolutionSolution





Denote the weighing results \(X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}\). If the scale gave error-free measurements, then we would have
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}  X_1 \\ X_2 \\ X_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  \theta _1 \\ \theta _2 \\ \theta _1 + \theta _2 \end{pmatrix} = \theta _1 \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \theta _2 \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}  
\]
or, in short,
\[
  \vec{X} = \theta _1 \cdot \vec{z}_{\cdot 1} + \theta _2 \cdot \vec{z}_{\cdot 2} = \mathbf{z} \cdot \vec{\theta }  
\]
where
\[
  \vec{X} = \begin{pmatrix}  X_1 \\ X_2 \\ X_3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{z} = (\vec{z}_{\cdot 1} \;  \vec{z}_{\cdot 2} ) = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 \\ 1 &  1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \vec{\theta } = \begin{pmatrix}  \theta _1 \\ \theta _2 \end{pmatrix}  
\]
In this case \(\vec{X}\) is non-random, linearly dependent on \(\vec{\theta }\). The 3rd measurement is superfluous; the first 2 would have sufficed to estimate \(\vec{\theta }\).
In practice, any scale admits some error, and it will differ slightly from one experiment to another. The errors in different experiments can be treated as random variables. Denote them \(\vec{\varepsilon } = (\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \varepsilon_3)^T\). Then the statistical model is:
\[
  \vec{X} = \mathbf{z} \cdot \vec{\theta } + \vec{\varepsilon },  
\]
where \(\mathbf{z}\vec{\theta }\) is an unknown non-random vector, and \(\vec{\varepsilon }\) is a random vector of errors. Thanks to \(\vec{\varepsilon }\), the observation vector \(\vec{X}\) becomes random.






In general, we are given a bag of coins of \(k\) different types, \(\theta_{1}\) is the mass of a type-1 coin, \(\ldots\), \(\theta_{k}\) is the mass of a type-\(k\) coin. The researcher estimates the masses of the coins. To do this, they weigh combinations of coins \(n\) times: at step \(i \in \left\{ 1,\ldots , n\right\}\) they weigh \(z_{i,1}\) coins of type 1, \(\ldots\), \(z_{i,k}\) coins of type \(k\). If the scale operates without error, then the measurement values will equal linear combinations of \(\theta_{1}, \ldots , \theta_{k}\). But since errors are nevertheless present, the observed quantity obtained at the \(i\)-th weighing \((i \in \{ 1, \ldots , n\} )\) equals
\[
  X_i = z_{i, 1} \theta _{1}+\ldots +z_{i, k} \theta _{k}+\varepsilon _{i},  
\]
where \(z_{i, j} \in \mathbb {R}\) are known coefficients of the linear combination, \(k\) is the number of coins participating in the \(i\)-th weighing, and \(\varepsilon_{i}\) is the measurement error at the \(i\)-th weighing. The full sample \(\vec{X}\):
\[
\begin{align}  \begin{pmatrix}  X_1 \\ X_2 \\ \vdots \\ X_n \end{pmatrix} & = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}  z_{1, 1} \theta _{1}+\ldots +z_{1, k} \theta _{k} \\ z_{2, 1} \theta _{1}+\ldots +z_{2, k} \theta _{k} \\ \vdots \\ z_{n, 1} \theta _{1}+\ldots +z_{n, k} \theta _{k} \end{pmatrix}}_{= \vec{z}_{\cdot 1} \theta _1 + \ldots + \vec{z}_{\cdot k} \theta _k} + \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}  \varepsilon _1 \\ \varepsilon _2 \\ \vdots \\ \varepsilon _n \end{pmatrix}}_{=\vec{\varepsilon }} \end{align}
\]
in short:
\[
  \vec{X} = \mathbf{z}\vec{\theta } + \vec{\varepsilon },  
\]
where
\[
\begin{align}  \vec{z}_{\cdot 1} & = \begin{pmatrix}  z_{1,1} \\ z_{2,1} \\ \vdots \\ z_{n,1} \end{pmatrix}, \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k} = \begin{pmatrix}  z_{1,k} \\ z_{2,k} \\ \vdots \\ z_{n,k} \end{pmatrix}, \\ \mathbf{z} = (\vec{z}_{\cdot 1} \;  \vec{z}_{\cdot 2} \;  \ldots \;  \vec{z}_{\cdot k} ) & = \begin{pmatrix}  z_{1,1} &  z_{1,2} &  \ldots &  z_{1,k} \\ z_{2,1} &  z_{2,2} &  \ldots &  z_{2,k} \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ z_{n,1} &  z_{n,2} &  \ldots &  z_{n,k} \end{pmatrix}, \\ \vec{\theta } & = \begin{pmatrix}  \theta _1 \\ \vdots \\ \theta _k \end{pmatrix}, \quad \vec{l} = \mathbf{z}\vec{\theta } \end{align}
\]
\(X_i\) is called the dependent variable, \(z_{i,1}, \ldots , z_{i,k}\) are called the independent variables or regressors, and \(\varepsilon_i\) is called the error or residual. Note that \(z_{i,1}, \ldots , z_{i,k}\) are known non-random values, even though they are called independent variables. The only random component in the model is the error \(\varepsilon_i\), and it is through this that \(X_i\) is random.
Suppose the column vectors \(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1} , \vec{z}_{\cdot 2} , \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k}\) are linearly dependent. Let \(\vec{z}_{\cdot i_1}, \vec{z}_{\cdot i_2}, \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot i_{k'}}\) be a maximal linearly independent subset of \(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1} , \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k}\). One can prove that the original model and the model \(\vec{X} = \vec{x}_{i_1}\theta_{\cdot i_1} + \ldots + \vec{z}_{\cdot i_{k'}}\theta_{i_{k'}} + \vec{\varepsilon }\) are equivalent, in the sense that whatever method we choose for estimating the unknown coefficients and the quality of the regression (more on this below), the quality of the model turns out the same in both cases. Going forward, for brevity we will assume that the original collection \(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1} , \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k}\) is already linearly independent by itself. Moreover, we will assume that the regressors are collectively nontrivial, namely that the space \(L := \operatorname {span}(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1} , \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k} )\) contains no vector consisting solely of constants. Regression with a constant regressor is discussed in the next section.
As a rule, \(k\) is much smaller than \(n\), and the matrix \(\mathbf{z}\) ends up extremely stretched vertically. The problem consists of estimating the true values \(\theta_{1}, \ldots , \theta_{k}\) from the observation \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\).
The observation \(\vec{X} = (X_1, \ldots , X_n)^T\) is a random vector from \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\), where \(\vec{l} = \vec{l}(\vec{\theta }) := \mathbf{z}\vec{\theta }\) is a fixed unknown vector, and \(\vec{\varepsilon }\) is a random vector.
About the vector \(\vec{l} = \mathbf{z}\vec{\theta }\) we know that \(\vec{l} = \mathbf{z}\vec{\theta } \in L\), where
\[
  L=\left\langle \vec{z}_{\cdot 1}, \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k}\right\rangle = \operatorname {span}\left(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1}, \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k}\right)  
\]
is a given linear subspace of \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) of dimension \(k<n\) (\(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1}, \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k}\) are basis column vectors of the space \(L\)). The parameters of the linear regression model described above are \(\vec{\theta }\) and \(\sigma^{2}\), whose estimation is discussed below.
Note that in this case, strictly speaking, according to our definition \(\vec{X}\) is not a sample of size \(n\), since the components of \(\vec{X}\) may have different distributions. However, \(\vec{X}\) can be viewed as a sample of size \(1\) from an \(n\)-dimensional distribution with parameters \(\vec{\theta }, \sigma^2\). Therefore, even in the absence of independence, one can, for example, speak of the existence of a likelihood function, apply factorization criteria to search for sufficient statistics, and so on. The likelihood function in this case is simply the density of the \(n\)-dimensional vector \(\vec{X}\).

title: Linear Regression
text:
1.2 Linear regression with an intercept
The model
\[
  X_i = \theta _0 + z_{i, 1} \theta _{1}+\ldots +z_{i, k} \theta _{k}+\varepsilon _{i}.  
\]
is called linear regression with an intercept. \(\theta_0\) is called the intercept of the regression. We have
\[
\begin{align}  \vec{X} = \begin{pmatrix}  X_1 \\ X_2 \\ \vdots \\ X_n \end{pmatrix} & = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  z_{1,1} &  \ldots &  z_{1,k} \\ 1 &  z_{2,1} &  \ldots &  z_{2,k} \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ 1 &  z_{n,1} &  \ldots &  z_{n,k} \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  \theta _0 \\ \theta _1 \\ \vdots \\ \theta _k \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}  \varepsilon _1 \\ \varepsilon _2 \\ \vdots \\ \varepsilon _n \end{pmatrix} = \\ & = \vec{z}_{\cdot 0}\theta _0 + \vec{z}_{\cdot 1} \theta _1 + \ldots + \vec{z}_{\cdot k} \theta _k + \vec{\varepsilon } = \\ & = \mathbf{z}\vec{\theta } + \vec{\varepsilon } \end{align}
\]
The vector of ones \(\vec{z}_{\cdot 0} = (1, \ldots , 1)^T\) is conveniently denoted \(\overrightarrow {1}\).

title: Linear Regression
text:
1.3 Conditions on the errors \(\vec{\varepsilon }\)
The following conditions are typically imposed on the error vector \(\vec{\varepsilon }\): it is square-integrable (expectations and variances exist), and moreover

\(\mathbb {E}\left[\vec{\varepsilon }\right] = \overrightarrow {0} \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\), i.e. all errors are centered;
\(\operatorname {Var}\left[\vec{\varepsilon }\right] = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_n\), where \(\operatorname {Var}\left[\vec{\varepsilon }\right]\) is the covariance matrix of the vector \(\vec{\varepsilon }\), and \(\mathbf{I}_{n}\) is the \(n \times n\) identity matrix. That is, all errors have the same variance \(\sigma^2\) and different errors are uncorrelated. This property is also called homoscedasticity, from Greek ὁμός (homos, “same”) + σκεδαστός (skedastos, “scattered”).

In practice these conditions on the errors are far from always satisfied, but often the original model can be reduced to one in which the conditions on the errors do hold. For example, under homoscedasticity the condition of centered errors can be relaxed: suppose \(\mathbb {E}\left[\vec{\varepsilon }\right] = \mu \overrightarrow {1}\), i.e. all errors have the same, but now unknown, nonzero expectation. Then from the model \(X_i = \theta_0 + z_{i, 1} \theta_{1}+\ldots +z_{i, k} \theta_{k}+\varepsilon_{i}\) we can pass to the model
\[
  X_i = \theta '_0 + z_{i, 1} \theta _{1}+\ldots +z_{i, k} \theta _{k}+\varepsilon '_{i}  
\]
where
\[
  \theta '_0 := \theta _0 + \mu , \quad \varepsilon _i' := \varepsilon _i - \mu .  
\]
In this model, the errors \(\varepsilon '\) have become centered. For more on reducing a model to standard form, see the problems below.

title: Linear Regression
section: 2.1 Explicit formula for the OLS estimate
text:
2.1 Explicit formula for the OLS estimate
Let’s find an explicit formula for \(\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\). Let’s solve a problem from linear algebra.






ExampleExample 3





Let \(\vec{y} \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\), and let \(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1} , \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k} \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\) be a collection of linearly independent vectors (\(k\leq n\)). Find \(\vec{t} \in \mathbb {R}^{k}\) — the coordinates of the projection of \(\vec{y}\) onto \(L = \operatorname {span}(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1} , \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k} )\) in the basis \(\mathbf{z} = (\vec{z}_{\cdot 1} , \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k} )\):
\[
  \operatorname {proj}_L(\vec{y}) = \mathbf{z} \cdot \vec{t} = t_1\vec{z}_{\cdot 1} + \ldots + t_k\vec{z}_{\cdot k}  
\]






SolutionSolution





We have
\[
\begin{align}  \left\| \vec{y} - \mathbf{z}\vec{t}\right\| ^2 & = \left\langle \vec{y} - \mathbf{z}\vec{t}, \vec{y} - \mathbf{z}\vec{t} \right\rangle = \\ & = \left\| \vec{y}\right\| ^2 - \underbrace{ \left\langle \vec{y}, \mathbf{z}\vec{t} \right\rangle }_{=\vec{y}^T \cdot \mathbf{z} \cdot \vec{t}} + \left\| \mathbf{z}\vec{t}\right\| ^2 = \\ & = \left\| \vec{y}\right\| ^2 - \left\langle \mathbf{z}^T\vec{y}, \vec{t} \right\rangle + \left\| \mathbf{z}\vec{t}\right\| ^2 = \\ & = \sum _{i=1}^{n}y_i^2 - 2\sum _{i=1}^{k}\left(\mathbf{z}^T \vec{y}\right)_i \cdot t_i + \sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathbf{z}\vec{t}\right)^2_i = \\ & = \sum _{i=1}^{n}y_i^2 - 2\sum _{i=1}^{k}\left(\mathbf{z}^T \vec{y}\right)_i \cdot t_i + \sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(\sum _{j=1}^{k}z_{i,j}t_j\right)^2 \end{align}
\]
Let’s differentiate the resulting expression with respect to \(t_{m}\) for each \(m \in \{ 1, \ldots , k\}\) and then simplify:
\[
\begin{align}  \frac{\partial }{\partial t_m} \left(\left\| \vec{y} - \mathbf{z}\vec{t}\right\| ^2\right) & = -2\left(\mathbf{z}^T\vec{y}\right)_m + \sum _{i=1}^{n}2\left(\sum _{j=1}^{k}z_{i,j}t_j\right) \cdot z_{i,m} = \\ & = -2\left(\mathbf{z}^T\vec{y}\right)_m + 2\sum _{i=1}^{n} z_{i,m} \cdot \left(\mathbf{z} \cdot \vec{t}\right)_i = \\ & = -2\left(\mathbf{z}^T\vec{y}\right)_m + 2\left(\mathbf{z}^T \cdot \left(\mathbf{z} \cdot \vec{t}\right)\right)_m \end{align}
\]
Setting these derivatives to zero to find the argument at which the minimum is attained:
\[
  \begin{cases}  \frac{\partial }{\partial t_1}\left(\left\| \vec{y} - \mathbf{z}\vec{t}\right\| ^2\right) = 0 \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\partial }{\partial t_k}\left(\left\| \vec{y} - \mathbf{z}\vec{t}\right\| ^2\right) = 0 \\ \end{cases} \iff \begin{cases}  -2\left(\mathbf{z}^T\vec{y}\right)_1 + 2\left(\mathbf{z}^T \cdot \left(\mathbf{z} \cdot \vec{t}\right)\right)_1 = 0 \\ \vdots \\ -2\left(\mathbf{z}^T\vec{y}\right)_k + 2\left(\mathbf{z}^T \cdot \left(\mathbf{z} \cdot \vec{t}\right)\right)_k = 0 \\ \end{cases}  
\]
In matrix-vector form:
\[
  -2\mathbf{z}^T\vec{y} + 2\mathbf{z}^T \cdot \mathbf{z} \cdot \vec{t} = 0  
\]
Consequently, \(\vec{t} = \left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{z}^T\vec{y}\). We obtain
\[
  \operatorname {proj}_L(\vec{y}) = \mathbf{z}\left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{z}^T \cdot \vec{y}  
\]
The matrix \(\mathbf{z}\left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{z}^T\) is called the projection matrix onto the subspace \(L\).
If the columns of \(\mathbf{z}\) are orthonormal, then \(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z} = \left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1} = \mathbf{I}_{k}\), and the projection matrix simplifies to \(\mathbf{z}\mathbf{z}^T\).
Check question. Where and how was the linear independence of the column vectors \(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1}, \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k}\) used in the solution?









AnswerAnswer





\(\vec{t} = \left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{z}^T\vec{y}\).






Altogether, the OLS estimation formula for linear regression is:
\[
  \widehat{\vec{\theta }} = \widehat{\vec{\theta }}(\vec{X}) = \left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{z}^T \cdot \vec{X}  
\]

section: 2.2 Geometry of OLS: regression without an intercept
text:
2.2 Geometry of OLS: regression without an intercept
Geometry of OLS regression without an intercept (Three.js version): \(\overrightarrow X\) is the vector of observations, \(\widehat{\overrightarrow X}=\overrightarrow X_L=\mathbf z\widehat{\overrightarrow\theta}\) is its orthogonal projection onto \(L=\operatorname{span}(\overrightarrow z_{\cdot 1},\ldots,\overrightarrow z_{\cdot k})\), and \(\widehat{\overrightarrow\varepsilon}\) is the error vector. The right angle at vertex \(B\) of triangle \(OBA\) illustrates that \(X-\widehat X\perp L\); the coefficient of determination is \(R^2=\cos^2\varphi=\operatorname{ESS}/\operatorname{TSS}\), where \(\varphi=\angle AOB\) — the larger it is, the closer \(\varphi\) is to zero, and the better the linear model. The labels are genuinely rendered LaTeX (KaTeX), anchored to their line/vector and rotated along it; they stay in place as you rotate the scene with the mouse. The mouse wheel zooms.











Isometric
Top
Side





Consider the graph @LinearRegr:GraphRegrWoParam. By the Pythagorean theorem we have
\[
  \left\| \vec{X}\right\| ^2 = \left\| \widehat{\vec{X}}\right\| ^2 + \left\| \widehat{\vec{\varepsilon }}\right\| ^2  
\]

The total sum of squares of the observations \(\left\| \vec{X}\right\|^2\) is called the total sum of squares, denoted \(\operatorname {TSS}\):
\[
  \operatorname {TSS} := \left\| \vec{X}\right\| ^2 = \sum _{i=1}^n X_i^2  
\]
The sum of squares of the estimated observations \(\left\| \widehat{\vec{X}}\right\|^2\) is called the explained sum of squares, denoted \(\operatorname {ESS}\):
\[
  \operatorname {ESS} := \left\| \widehat{\vec{X}}\right\| ^2 = \sum _{i=1}^n \widehat{X}_i^2  
\]
The sum of squares of the errors \(\left\| \widehat{\vec{\varepsilon }}\right\|^2\) is called the residual sum of squares, denoted \(\operatorname {RSS}\):
\[
  \operatorname {RSS} := \left\| \widehat{\vec{\varepsilon }}\right\| ^2 = \left\| \vec{X} - \widehat{\vec{X}}\right\| ^2 = \sum _{i=1}^n \left(X_i - \widehat{X}_i\right)^2  
\]

By the Pythagorean theorem, the total sum of squares splits into the explained sum of squares and the sum of squares of the error estimates:
\[
  \operatorname {TSS} = \operatorname {ESS} + \operatorname {RSS}  
\]

2.2.1 Coefficient of determination
The better the OLS-fitted regression describes the behavior of the dependent variable \(\vec{X}\), the smaller the length of the error vector \(\widehat{\vec{\varepsilon }} = \vec{X} - \vec{X}_{L}\) should be compared to the length of the observation vector \(\vec{X}\). The quantity
\[
  R^2 := 1 - \frac{\left\| \widehat{\vec{\varepsilon }}\right\| ^2}{\left\| \vec{X}\right\| ^2} = 1 - \frac{\sum _{i=1}^n \left(X_i - \widehat{X}_i\right)^2}{\sum _{i=1}^n X_i^2}  
\]
is called the coefficient of determination.
The coefficient of determination takes values between \(0\) and \(1\). The closer it is to \(1\), the better the regression.
Various formulas for the coefficient of determination:
\[
\begin{align}  R^2 & = 1 - \frac{\left\| \widehat{\vec{\varepsilon }}\right\| ^2}{\left\| \vec{X}\right\| ^2} = 1 - \frac{\operatorname {RSS}}{\operatorname {TSS}} = \\ & = 1 - \frac{\sum _{i=1}^n \left(X_i - \widehat{X}_i\right)^2}{\sum _{i=1}^n X_i^2} = \\ & = \frac{\operatorname {ESS}}{\operatorname {TSS}} = \frac{\left\| \widehat{\vec{X}}\right\| ^2}{\left\| \vec{X}\right\| ^2} = \frac{\sum _{i=1}^n \widehat{X}_i^2}{\sum _{i=1}^n X_i^2} \end{align}
\]
The coefficient of determination has several closely related interpretations. On one hand it is the fraction of the spread in the dependent variable \(\vec{X}\) that our model has managed to “explain”: \(\operatorname {ESS}/\operatorname {TSS}\).
On the other hand, one can say that our fitted model \(\widehat{\vec{X}}\) is being compared to the only model available for explaining \(\vec{X}\) in the absence of regressors — the model \(\vec{X} = \overrightarrow {0} + \vec{\varepsilon }\), i.e. \(\vec{X}\) is simply noise made of independent, identically distributed, centered errors. In this approach, the coefficient of determination is one minus the ratio of the spread in the first model to the spread in the second:
\[
  1 - \frac{\operatorname {RSS}}{\operatorname {TSS}}  
\]
The closer it is to one, the better our model performs compared to the most trivial model.
A simple model against which more complex models are compared is called a reference model or baseline model (English benchmark model). In this case the baseline model is independent, identically distributed noise. \(\operatorname {TSS}\) is the sum of squares of the errors when using such a model. \(\operatorname {ESS}\) is the sum of squares of the difference between the baseline model and our model.

title: Linear Regression
section: 2.3 Geometry of OLS: regression with an intercept
text:
2.3 Geometry of OLS: regression with an intercept
With an intercept \(\theta_0\) present, the baseline model for comparisons changes. Now, in the absence of regressors, the best model for explaining \(\vec{X}\) is the model of a constant \(\theta_0\) plus noise \(\vec{\varepsilon }\). The estimate of \(\theta_0\) minimizing the sum of squared errors in such a model is the sample mean \(\overline{X}\). The baseline model for modeling \(\vec{X}\):
\[
  \left(\overline{X}, \ldots , \overline{X}\right)^T = \overline{X} \cdot \overrightarrow {1},  
\]
where \(\overrightarrow {1} = (1, \ldots , 1)^T\) is the vector in \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) made up of ones.
\(\operatorname {TSS}\), \(\operatorname {ESS}\) are, respectively, the sum of squares of the errors when using the baseline model and the sum of squares of the difference between the baseline model and our model. Their computation now also changes. The computation of \(\operatorname {RSS}\) remains the same.

Total sum of squares:
\[
  \operatorname {TSS} = \left\| \vec{X} - \overline{X}\cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| ^2 = \sum _{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline{X})^2  
\]
Explained sum of squares:
\[
  \operatorname {ESS} = \left\| \widehat{\vec{X}} - \overline{X}\cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| ^2 = \sum _{i=1}^n (\widehat{X}_i- \overline{X})^2  
\]
Residual sum of squares:
\[
  \operatorname {RSS} = \left\| \vec{X} - \widehat{\vec{X}}\right\| ^2 = \sum _{i=1}^n \left(X_i - \widehat{X}_i\right)^2  
\]

Geometry of OLS regression with an intercept (Three.js version): \(D\) is the point of the baseline model \(\overline X\cdot\overrightarrow 1\), \(A\) is the vector of observations \(\overrightarrow X\), \(B\) is its projection \(\widehat{\overrightarrow X}=\overrightarrow X_L=\mathbf z\widehat{\overrightarrow\theta}\) onto \(L\). The right angle at vertex \(B\) of triangle \(DBA\) illustrates that \(X-\widehat X\perp L\); the coefficient of determination is \(R^2=\cos^2\varphi=\operatorname{ESS}/\operatorname{TSS}\), where \(\varphi=\angle ADB\) — the larger it is, the closer \(\varphi\) is to zero, and the better the linear model. The labels are genuinely rendered LaTeX (KaTeX), anchored to their line/vector and rotated along it; they stay in place as you rotate the scene with the mouse. The mouse wheel zooms.











Isometric

Side





Consider the graph @LinearRegr:GraphRegrWithParam. By the Pythagorean theorem for triangle \(ABD\) we again have (recall that \(\widehat{\vec{X}} = \vec{X}_{L}\) when the model is fitted by OLS):
\[
\begin{align}  \operatorname {TSS} & = \left\| \vec{X} - \overline{X}\cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| ^2 = \left|AD\right|^2 = \\ & = \left|BD\right|^2 + \left|AB\right|^2 = \left\| \widehat{\vec{X}} - \overline{X}\cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| ^2 + \left\| \vec{X} - \widehat{\vec{X}}\right\| ^2 = \\ & = \operatorname {ESS} + \operatorname {RSS} \end{align}
\]
Coefficient of determination:
\[
\begin{align}  R^2 & = 1 - \frac{\operatorname {RSS}}{\operatorname {TSS}} = 1 - \frac{\sum _{i=1}^n \left(X_i - \widehat{X}_i\right)^2}{\sum _{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline{X})^2} = \\ & = \frac{\operatorname {ESS}}{\operatorname {TSS}} = \frac{\sum _{i=1}^n \left(\overline{X} - \widehat{X}_i\right)^2}{\sum _{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline{X})^2} \end{align}
\]
For the same sample, the coefficient of determination for the model with an intercept can turn out to be either larger or smaller than the coefficient of determination of the model without one, despite the fact that the first model is obviously more flexible.


                                                
Linear regression with one regressor \(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1}\) and intercept \(\theta_0\), \(n=6\) (regression parameters denoted \(\theta_0, \theta_1\)). Orange points are the sample points \((z_{1,i}, X_i)\). Green points are the regression points \((z_{1,i}, \widehat{X}_i)\). The total area of the violet squares equals \(\operatorname{TSS}\), and of the red ones — \(\operatorname{RSS}\).

title: Linear Regression
text:
2.4 Properties of the OLS estimates
Recall, \(\widehat{\vec{\theta }} = \left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{z}^T\vec{X}\). Denote by \(\widetilde{k}\) the number of columns of the matrix \(\mathbf{z}\):
\[
  \widetilde{k} := \begin{cases}  k, &  \text{ if the regression has no intercept }\theta _0;\\ k+1 , &  \text{ if the regression has an intercept }\theta _0. \end{cases}  
\]

Expectation and covariance matrix of \(\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\):
\[
  \mathbb {E}_{\vec{\theta }, \sigma ^2}\left[\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\right] = \vec{\theta }, \qquad \operatorname {Var}_{\vec{\theta }, \sigma ^2}\left[\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\right] = \sigma ^2 \left(\mathbf{z}^T \mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}  
\]
Thus, the ordinary least squares estimator is unbiased.
Knowing the covariance matrix of the vector \(\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\), we can find the expectation of the (squared) distance from \(\vec{X}\) to the subspace \(L \subset \mathbb {R}^{n}\):
\[
  \mathbb {E}_{\vec{\theta }, \sigma ^2}\left[\left\| \vec{X} - \underbrace{\mathbf{z}\widehat{\vec{\theta }}}_{=\vec{X}_{L} = \widehat{\vec{X}}}\right\| ^2\right] = \mathbb {E}_{\vec{\theta }, \sigma ^2}\left[\left\|  \underbrace{\widehat{\vec{\varepsilon }}}_{=\vec{X}_{L^\perp }}\right\| ^2\right] = \mathbb {E}_{\vec{\theta }, \sigma ^2}\left[\operatorname {RSS}\right] = \left(n-\widetilde{k}\right)\sigma ^2  
\]
This last equality gives an unbiased estimator of the parameter \(\sigma^{2}\):
\[
  \widehat{\sigma ^{2}} := \frac{1}{n-\widetilde{k}}\left\| \vec{X}-\mathbf{z} \widehat{\vec{\theta }}\right\| ^{2} = \frac{\operatorname {RSS}}{n-\widetilde{k}}.  
\]






Sampling distribution of the OLS estimator

ExampleExample 4





There are 2 pieces of cheese with weights \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\). Using the same scale, the first, then the second, and then both pieces together were weighed. Find the least-squares estimates of \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\), and also an unbiased estimate of the variance of the measurement error. Find the coefficient of determination.






SolutionSolution





Suppose the weighings gave results \(X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}\). Set \(\vec{X}=\left(X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}\right)^{T}\). Then
\[
  \vec{X} =\mathbf{z}\vec{\theta } + \vec{\varepsilon }, \quad \text{where} \quad \mathbf{z} = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 \\ 1 &  1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \vec{\theta } = \begin{pmatrix}  \theta _1 \\ \theta _2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \vec{\varepsilon } = \begin{pmatrix}  \varepsilon _1 \\ \varepsilon _2 \\ \varepsilon _3 \end{pmatrix}  
\]
Let’s first compute \(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\), its inverse, and \(\mathbf{z}^T\vec{X}\):
\[
  \mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z} = \begin{pmatrix}  2 &  1 \\ 1 &  2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1} = \frac13\begin{pmatrix}  2 &  -1 \\ -1 &  2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{z}^T\vec{X} = \begin{pmatrix}  X_1+X_3 \\ X_2+X_3 \end{pmatrix}.  
\]
Then
\[
\begin{align}  \widehat{\vec{\theta }} & = \left(\begin{array}{c} \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_1 \\ \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_2 \end{array}\right)=\left(\mathbf{z}^{T} \mathbf{z}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{z}^{T} \vec{X}= \frac13\begin{pmatrix}  2 &  -1 \\ -1 &  2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}  X_1+X_3 \\ X_2+X_3 \end{pmatrix} = \left(\begin{array}{c} \frac{2}{3} X_{1}-\frac{1}{3} X_{2}+\frac{1}{3} X_{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} X_{1}+\frac{2}{3} X_{2}+\frac{1}{3} X_{3} \end{array}\right) \\ \widehat{\vec{X}} & = \mathbf{z} \widehat{\vec{\theta }} = \begin{pmatrix}  \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_1 \\ \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_2 \\ \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_1 + \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_2 \\ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  \frac{2}{3} X_{1}-\frac{1}{3} X_{2}+\frac{1}{3} X_{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} X_{1}+\frac{2}{3} X_{2}+\frac{1}{3} X_{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} X_{1}+\frac{1}{3} X_{2}+\frac{2}{3} X_{3} \\ \end{pmatrix} \\ \widehat{\sigma ^{2}} & = \frac{1}{3-2}\operatorname {RSS} = \| \vec{X}-\mathbf{z} \widehat{\vec{\theta }}\| ^{2}=\left(X_{1}-\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_1\right)^{2}+\left(X_{2}-\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_2\right)^{2}+\left(X_{3}-\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_1-\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_2\right)^{2} \end{align}
\]
Let’s substitute the explicit expressions for \(\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_1, \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_2\) (and for their sum — the third coordinate of \(\widehat{\vec{X}}\), found above) and simplify each residual individually:
\[
\begin{align}  X_1 - \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_1 & = X_1 - \left(\tfrac {2}{3} X_{1}-\tfrac {1}{3} X_{2}+\tfrac {1}{3} X_{3}\right) = \tfrac 13 \left(X_1+X_2-X_3\right), \\ X_2 - \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_2 & = X_2 - \left(-\tfrac {1}{3} X_{1}+\tfrac {2}{3} X_{2}+\tfrac {1}{3} X_{3}\right) = \tfrac 13 \left(X_1+X_2-X_3\right), \\ X_3 - \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_1 - \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_2 & = X_3 - \left(\tfrac {1}{3} X_{1}+\tfrac {1}{3} X_{2}+\tfrac {2}{3} X_{3}\right) = -\tfrac 13\left(X_1+X_2-X_3\right). \end{align}
\]
All three residuals are equal in absolute value to \(\frac{\left|X_1 + X_2 - X_3\right|}{3}\), so
\[
  \widehat{\sigma ^2} = 3 \cdot \left(\frac{X_1 + X_2 - X_3}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{\left(X_{1}+X_{2}-X_{3}\right)^2}{3}.  
\]
Further, we have a regression without an intercept, so by the Pythagorean theorem \(\operatorname {TSS} = \operatorname {ESS} + \operatorname {RSS}\), whence \(\operatorname {ESS} = \operatorname {TSS} - \operatorname {RSS}\); here \(\operatorname {RSS} = (3-2)\widehat{\sigma^2} = \widehat{\sigma^2}\) was already found above. We have
\[
\begin{align}  \operatorname {TSS} & = \sum _{i=1}^3 X_i^2 = X_1^2 + X_2^2 + X_3^2, \\ \operatorname {ESS} & = \operatorname {TSS} - \operatorname {RSS} = \left(X_1^2+X_2^2+X_3^2\right) - \frac{\left(X_1+X_2-X_3\right)^2}{3} = \\ & = \left(X_1^2+X_2^2+X_3^2\right) - \frac{X_1^2+X_2^2+X_3^2+2X_1X_2-2X_1X_3-2X_2X_3}{3} = \\ & = \frac{2}{3}X_1^2 + \frac{2}{3}X_2^2 + \frac{2}{3}X_3^2 - \frac{2}{3}X_1X_2 + \frac{2}{3}X_1X_3 + \frac{2}{3}X_2X_3, \\ R^2 & = \frac{\operatorname {ESS}}{\operatorname {TSS}} = \frac{2}{3}\frac{X_1^2 + X_2^2 + X_3^2 - X_1X_2 + X_1X_3 + X_2X_3}{X_1^2 + X_2^2 + X_3^2}. \end{align}
\]












ProblemProblem 1





In a quadrilateral \(A B C D\), independent measurements of the angles, all of equal precision,
\[
  A B D, D B C, A B C, B C D, C D B, B D A, C D A, D A B  
\] in degrees gave the results
\[
  50.78, 30.25,78.29,99.57,50.42,40.59,88.87,89.86  
\] respectively. Assuming that the measurement errors are independently distributed, have the same variance \(\sigma^2\) and zero expectation, find the OLS estimates of the angles \(\theta_{1}=A B D, \theta_{2}=D B C, \theta_{3}=C D B, \theta_{4}=B D A\) and of the unknown variance \(\sigma^{2}\). Find the coefficient of determination.









ProblemProblem 2





Let
\[
  X_{i}=\theta _0+i \theta _1+\varepsilon _{0}+\ldots +\varepsilon _{i},  
\] \(i=0,1, \ldots , n\), where \(\theta_0, \theta_1\) are unknown parameters, and the random variables \(\varepsilon_{0}, \ldots , \varepsilon_{n}\) are independently distributed, have the same variance \(\sigma^2\) and zero expectation. Reduce the problem to a linear model and find the least-squares estimates of \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta_1\), as well as an unbiased estimate of \(\sigma^{2}\). Find the coefficient of determination \(R^2\).









ProblemProblem 3






Prove that

\[
  \mathbb {E}_{\vec{\theta }, \sigma ^2}\left[\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\right] = \vec{\theta }, \qquad \operatorname {Var}_{\vec{\theta }, \sigma ^2}\left[\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\right] = \sigma ^2 \left(\mathbf{z}^T \mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}  
\]

Prove that

\[
  \mathbb {E}_{\vec{\theta }, \sigma ^2}\left[\underbrace{\left\| \vec{X} - \mathbf{z}\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\right\| ^2}_{=\operatorname {RSS}}\right] = (n-\widetilde{k})\sigma ^2 \qquad  
\]
and
\[
  \widehat{\sigma ^{2}} = \frac{1}{n-\widetilde{k}} \left\| \vec{X} - \mathbf{z}\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\right\| ^2  
\]
is an unbiased estimate of \(\sigma^2\).






HintHint





If \(\vec{\xi }\) is a random vector of dimension \(n\), then its covariance matrix can be computed as:
\[
  \operatorname {Var}\left[\vec{\xi }\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[\vec{\xi } \cdot \vec{\xi }^T\right] - \mathbb {E}\left[\vec{\xi }\right] \cdot \left(\mathbb {E}\left[\vec{\xi }\right]\right)^T.  
\] Moreover, if \(A \in \mathbb {R}^{m \times n}\) is a matrix of dimension \(m \times n\), then \(A\vec{\xi }\) is a new random vector of dimension \(m\), whose covariance matrix and the covariance matrix of the original vector are related as follows:
\[
  \operatorname {Var}\left[A \vec{\xi }\right] = A \cdot \operatorname {Var}\left[\vec{\xi }\right] \cdot A^T  
\]

title: Linear Regression
text:
3.1 Complete, sufficient statistic. Optimal estimators







Theorem 1 In the Gaussian linear model, the statistic \(\left(\vec{X}_{L}, \left\| \vec{X}_{L^\perp }\right\|^2\right)\) is complete and sufficient.











Corollary 1 In the Gaussian linear model, the statistic \(\left(\widehat{\vec{\theta }}, \widehat{\sigma^2}\right)\) is complete and sufficient.










ProblemProblem 4





Prove theorem Theorem 1. Prove corollary Corollary 1.



From the standard regression model it is known that the statistics
\[
\begin{align}  \widehat{\vec{\theta }} & = \operatorname *{arg\, min}_{\vec{t} \in \mathbb {R}^{k}} \left\| \vec{X} - \mathbf{z}\vec{t}\right\|  = \left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{z}^T \vec{X}, \\ \widehat{\sigma ^2} & = \frac{1}{n-\widetilde{k}} \left\| \vec{X} - \mathbf{z}\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\right\| ^2 = \frac{1}{n-\widetilde{k}} \left\| \vec{X} - \vec{X}_{L}\right\| ^2 = \\ & = \frac{1}{n-\widetilde{k}}\left\| \vec{X}_{L^\perp }\right\| ^2 = \frac{1}{n -\tilde{k}}\operatorname {RSS} \end{align}
\]
are unbiased estimators of \(\vec{\theta }, \sigma^2\). They are functions of the complete, sufficient statistic, and hence, by the Lehmann-Scheffé theorem, \(\widehat{\vec{\theta }}, \widehat{\sigma^2}\) are optimal estimators of \(\vec{\theta }, \sigma^2\) in the Gaussian regression model.






ProblemProblem 5





Two loads of masses \(a\) and \(b\) are weighed as follows: the first load is weighed \(n_{1}\) times (all measurement errors having distribution \(\left.\mathscr {N}\left(0, \sigma^{2}\right)\right)\), the second load is weighed \(n_{2}\) times on the same scale, then the first and second loads together are weighed \(n_{3}\) times on a different scale, all of whose measurement errors have distribution \(\mathscr {N}\left(0, 3 \sigma^{2}\right)\). Reduce the problem to a linear model and find the least-squares estimates of \(a\) and \(b\), as well as the optimal estimate of \(\sigma^{2}\).









ProblemProblem 6





Let the vector \(\vec{X}=\left(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\right)^T\) have distribution \(\mathscr {N}\left(a \cdot \vec{b}, \sigma^{2} \vec{\Sigma }\right)\), where \(\vec{b}\) is a known vector of dimension \(n\), \(\vec{\Sigma }\) is a known positive-definite matrix, and \(a\) and \(\sigma^{2}\) are unknown parameters. Reduce the problem to a Gaussian linear model and find the least-squares estimates of the parameters \(a\) and \(\sigma^{2}\).

title: Linear Regression
text:
3.2 Confidence intervals for the parameters
We have constructed point unbiased estimates of the parameters of the linear model, which in the Gaussian case turned out to be optimal. Let us now construct confidence intervals for these parameters.
Consider a motivating example.






ExampleExample 5





Let \(X_1, \ldots , X_n\) be a sample from \(\mathscr {N}\left(\mu , \sigma^2\right)\), where

\(\mu\) is unknown, \(\sigma^2\) is known;
\(\mu\) is known, \(\sigma^2\) is unknown;
\(\mu\) is unknown, \(\sigma^2\) is unknown. Construct confidence intervals of confidence level \(\alpha\) for the unknown parameters.







SolutionSolution





This model is the simplest example of Gaussian linear regression. Namely, let
\[
  \vec{X} = \mathbf{z}\vec{\theta } + \vec{\varepsilon }  
\]
where we set
\[
  \vec{X} := \begin{pmatrix}  X_1 \\ \vdots \\ X_n \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{z} := \begin{pmatrix}  1 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \vec{\theta } := (\mu ), \quad \vec{\varepsilon } := \begin{pmatrix}  X_1 - \mu \\ \vdots \\ X_n - \mu \end{pmatrix}  
\]
Why is this Gaussian regression? Most importantly, we need to check the conditions on the errors. From the assumption we know that the components of \(\vec{X}\) are independent and Gaussian. So \(\vec{X}\) is a Gaussian vector, and
\[
  \vec{X} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\mu \cdot \vec{1}, \sigma ^2 \cdot \mathbf{I}_{n}\right)  
\]
Hence
\[
  \vec{\varepsilon } \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\vec{0}, \sigma ^2 \cdot \mathbf{I}_{n}\right)  
\]
The conditions on the errors (independence, centeredness, identical Gaussian distribution) are satisfied.
Case c), where both \(\vec{\theta } = (\mu )\) and \(\sigma^2\) are unknown, corresponds fully to the regression model.
Let’s first note that \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \mathscr {N}\left(n\mu , n\sigma^2\right)\), so the sample mean has distribution
\[
  \overline{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n X_i \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\mu , \sigma ^2/n\right)  
\]
If we center and normalize (divide by the standard deviation), we get the standard normal distribution:
\[
  \frac{\overline{X} - \mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)  
\]
Recall that to construct a confidence interval, we need to find a pivotal statistic: its distribution must not depend on the unknown parameters.






Enum-item(1)



\(\mu\) is unknown, \(\sigma^2\) is known, so we can freely use \(\sigma\). Our pivotal statistic will be exactly
\[
  \frac{\overline{X} - \mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}}  
\]








Enum-item(2)



\(\mu\) is known, \(\sigma^2\) is unknown. We need to estimate the variance. A good estimate for the variance \(\sigma^2\) can be given by the sample variance computed using the true expectation:
\[
  \widehat{\sigma ^2} := \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n \left(X_i - \mathbb {E}\left[X_i\right]\right)^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n \left(X_i - \mu \right)^2  
\]
To construct a confidence interval, we need to find the distribution of \(\widehat{\sigma^2}\). Note that \(X_i - \mu \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, \sigma^2\right)\), so \(\frac{X_i - \mu }{\sigma } \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\). Consequently
\[
  n\frac{\widehat{\sigma ^2}}{\sigma ^2} = \sum _{i=1}^n \left(\frac{X_i - \mu }{\sigma }\right)^2  
\]
is a sum of squares of \(n\) independent standard normal random variables.







Definition 1 The distribution of a random variable equal to the sum of squares of \(n\) independent standard normal random variables is called the chi-squared distribution with \(n\) degrees of freedom. Notation: \(\chi^2_n\). One can prove that the chi-squared distribution is a special case of the gamma distribution: \(\chi^2_n = \Gamma \left(\frac{n}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)\).




The distribution of the statistic \(n\frac{\widehat{\sigma^2}}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^{2}_{n}\) does not depend on the parameter, so it is a pivotal statistic. Let \(Q_{\chi^2_n}(\alpha )\) be the quantile of level \(\alpha\). Then
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(0 \quad \leq \quad n\frac{\widehat{\sigma ^2}}{\sigma ^2} \quad \leq \quad Q_{\chi ^2_n}(\alpha )\right) = \alpha  
\]
Let’s solve the inequality inside the probability with respect to \(\sigma^2\). We get
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(n \widehat{\sigma ^2} \cdot \frac{1}{Q_{\chi ^2_n}(\alpha )} \quad \leq \quad \sigma ^2 \quad < \quad +\infty \right) = \alpha  
\]








Enum-item(3)



\(\mu\) is unknown, \(\sigma^2\) is unknown. If \(\sigma^2\) were known, constructing a confidence interval for \(\mu\) would present no difficulty (see the part above). In our case \(\sigma^2\) is unknown, so let’s try to estimate it. A good estimate for the variance \(\sigma^2\) is given by the sample variance \(S^2\):
\[
  \widehat{\sigma ^2} := S^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n \left(X_i - \overline{X}\right)^2  
\]
Now we need to find the distribution of \(\widehat{\sigma^2}\). Let \(L = \operatorname {span}(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1} ) = \operatorname {span}(\vec{1})\) be the one-dimensional linear subspace of \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) generated by the vector of ones. As we established above, the projection of \(\vec{X}\) onto \(L\) is the vector made up of sample means:
\[
  \vec{X}_{L} = \begin{pmatrix}  \overline{X} \\ \vdots \\ \overline{X} \end{pmatrix} = \overline{X} \cdot \vec{1}  
\]
Then
\[
  n\widehat{\sigma ^2} = \sum _{i=1}^n \left(X_i - \overline{X}\right)^2 = \left\| \vec{X} - \overline{X} \cdot \vec{1}\right\| ^2 = \left\| \vec{X}_{L^{\perp }}\right\| ^2  
\]
\(\widehat{\sigma^2}\) is a function of the vector \(\vec{X}_{L^{\perp }}\), while \(\overline{X}\) is a function of \(\vec{X}_{L}\).
Let \(\mathbf{z}_{L_2} \in \mathbb {R}^{n \times (n-1)}\) be the matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of the subspace \(L_2 := L^{\perp }\) (then \(\mathbf{z}_{L_2}\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T\) is the projection matrix onto \(L_2\), see the remark above about orthonormal columns). We have
\[
\begin{align}  n\widehat{\sigma ^2} & = \left\| \vec{X}_{L^{\perp }}\right\| ^2 = \left\langle \vec{X}_{L^{\perp }}, \vec{X}_{L^{\perp }} \right\rangle = \\ & = \left\langle \mathbf{z}_{L_2}\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T \vec{X}, \mathbf{z}_{L_2}\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T \vec{X} \right\rangle = \\ & = \left(\mathbf{z}_{L_2}\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T \vec{X}\right)^T \cdot \mathbf{z}_{L_2}\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T \vec{X} = \\ & = \vec{X}^T \mathbf{z}_{L_2} \underbrace{\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T \cdot \mathbf{z}_{L_2}}_{=\mathbf{I}_{n-1}}\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T \vec{X} = \\ & = \left\langle \mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T\vec{X}, \mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T\vec{X} \right\rangle = \\ & = \left\| \mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T\vec{X}\right\| ^2 \end{align}
\]
Note that in the last 2 lines the inner product is already taken in \(\mathbb {R}^{n-1}\).
We need to find the distribution of \(\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T\vec{X}\). This is a linear transformation of a Gaussian vector, so it is also a Gaussian vector, with expectation:
\[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T\vec{X}\right] = \mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T\mathbb {E}\left[\vec{X}\right] = \mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T \cdot \mu \cdot \underbrace{\vec{1}}_{\in \mathbb {R}^{n}} = \vec{0} \in \mathbb {R}^{n-1}  
\]
Why did we get \(\vec{0}\)? Because the columns of \(\mathbf{z}_{L_2}\) are orthogonal to \(L_1 = \operatorname {span}(\vec{1})\).
Covariance matrix:
\[
\begin{align}  \operatorname {Var}\left[\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T\vec{X}\right] & = \mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T \cdot \operatorname {Var}\left[\vec{X}\right] \cdot \mathbf{z}_{L_2} = \mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T \cdot \sigma ^2 \cdot \mathbf{I}_{n} \cdot \mathbf{z}_{L_2} = \sigma ^2 \cdot \mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T \cdot \mathbf{z}_{L_2} = \\ & = \sigma ^2 \cdot \mathbf{I}_{n-1} \end{align}
\]
In total,
\[
  \mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T\vec{X} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\vec{0}, \sigma ^2 \cdot \mathbf{I}_{n-1}\right)  
\]
Hence the components of \(\frac{1}{\sigma }\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T\vec{X}\) are independent standard normal random variables, \(n-1\) of them in total. So
\[
  n\cdot \frac{\widehat{\sigma ^2}}{\sigma ^2} = \left\| \frac{1}{\sigma }\mathbf{z}_{L_2}^T \vec{X}\right\| ^2 \sim \chi ^2_{n-1}  
\]
We have found the distribution of \(\widehat{\sigma^2}\)!
Next we need to find a pivotal statistic for the confidence interval for \(\mu\). In the part above we used \(\frac{\overline{X} - \mu }{\sqrt{\sigma^2/n}}\). In this case \(\sigma^2\) is unknown. Let’s replace \(\sigma^2\) with the estimate \(\widehat{\sigma^2}\):
\[
  \frac{\overline{X} - \mu }{\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma ^2}/n}}  
\]
We need to find the distribution of this expression. Let’s transform it:
\[
  \frac{\overline{X} - \mu }{\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma ^2}/n}} = \frac{(\overline{X} - \mu )/\sqrt{\sigma ^2 / n}}{\sqrt{\left(n \widehat{\sigma ^2}/\sigma ^2\right)/n}} = \frac{\xi }{\sqrt{\eta / n}}  
\]
where
\[
  \xi := \frac{\overline{X} - \mu }{\sqrt{\sigma ^2/n}}, \qquad \eta := n\frac{\widehat{\sigma ^2}}{\sigma ^2}  
\]







Definition 2 Let \(\xi , \eta\) be independent random variables, distributed according to the laws \(\mathcal{N}(0,1), \chi_{n}^{2}\) respectively. Then the random variable
\[
  \frac{\xi }{\sqrt{\eta / n}}  
\] has Student’s distribution with \(n\) degrees of freedom (denoted \(T_n\)).




In our case \(\xi \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\) and \(\eta \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\) are independent (\(\xi\) is a function of \(\vec{X}_L\), \(\eta\) is a function of \(\vec{X}_{L^\perp }\); independence is justified by Cochran’s theorem below), but in the denominator we have \(\sqrt{\eta /n}\), not \(\sqrt{\eta /(n-1)}\). Let’s correct the normalization:
\[
  \frac{\overline{X} - \mu }{\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma ^2}/(n-1)}} = \frac{\xi }{\sqrt{\eta /(n-1)}} \sim T_{n-1}  
\]
(equivalently, \(\frac{\overline{X} - \mu }{\sqrt{s^2/n}} \sim T_{n-1}\), where \(s^2 = \frac{n}{n-1}\widehat{\sigma^2}\) is the unbiased sample variance). This is a pivotal statistic, and the confidence interval for \(\mu\) at confidence level \(\alpha\) is obtained in the standard way:
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\mu \in \left(\overline{X} - \sqrt{\tfrac {s^2}{n}}\,  Q_{T_{n-1}}\left(\tfrac {1+\alpha }{2}\right), \; \;  \overline{X} - \sqrt{\tfrac {s^2}{n}}\,  Q_{T_{n-1}}\left(\tfrac {1-\alpha }{2}\right)\right)\right) = \alpha .  
\]
The interval for \(\sigma^2\) with unknown \(\mu\) is constructed as in part b), except now \(n\widehat{\sigma^2}/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\), i.e. with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom.














Densities of \(\chi^2_k\) and \(T_k\)
Left: densities of \(\chi^2_k\) for \(k=1,2,3,5,10\). Right: densities of \(T_k\) for \(k=1,3,10\) and the limiting \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) (dashed). The black/teal curve on each panel is the current \(k\) from the slider, recomputed continuously.

\(k=\)5.0
 Log scale for the tails (\(T_k\))






Deviation of the current \(T_k\) from \(\mathcal N(0,1)\): — (max. \(|T_k(x)-\mathcal N(0,1)(x)|\) over the grid \(x\in[-4.6,4.6]\))






In general, the following theorem holds.







Theorem 2 (Cochran’s theorem on the orthogonal decomposition of a Gaussian vector) Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots , X_n\) be independent standard normal random variables, i.e.
\[
  \vec{X} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\vec{0}, \mathbf{I}_n\right)  
\]
where \(\vec{X} = (X_1, \ldots , X_n)^T\). Let \(L_{1} \oplus \ldots \oplus L_{r}\) be an arbitrary decomposition of \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) into a direct sum of orthogonal subspaces. For each \(j \in \{ 1, \ldots , r\}\) set \(\vec{X}_{L_j} := \operatorname {proj}_{L_{j}} \vec{X}\). Then

\(\vec{X}_{L_1}, \ldots , \vec{X}_{L_r}\) are jointly independent random vectors;
\(\left\| \vec{X}_{L_j}\right\|^2 \sim \chi^2_{\dim (L_j)}\) for each \(j \in \{ 1, \ldots , r\}\).

Let
\[
  \vec{X} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\vec{a}, \sigma ^2 \mathbf{I}_n\right),  
\]
and let \(L_{1} \oplus \ldots \oplus L_{r}\) be a decomposition of \(\mathbb {R}^{n}\) into a direct sum of orthogonal subspaces. For each \(j \in \{ 1, \ldots , r\}\) set \(\vec{X}_{L_j} := \operatorname {proj}_{L_{j}} \vec{X}\). Then \(\vec{X}_{L_1}, \ldots , \vec{X}_{L_r}\) are jointly independent, and moreover
\[
  \frac{1}{\sigma ^2}\left\| \vec{X}_{L_j} - \mathbb {E}\left[\vec{X}_{L_j}\right]\right\| ^2 \sim \chi ^2_{\dim (L_j)}  
\]










ProblemProblem 7





Let \(\vec{X} = \left(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\right)^T\) be a sample from the normal distribution with parameters \(\left(a, \sigma^{2}\right)\). Prove that the statistics \(\bar{X}\) and
\[
  S^{2}=\frac{1}{n} \sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(X_{i}- \overline{X}\right)^{2}  
\] are independent, and compute the distribution of the statistic \(n S^{2}\).



In the general case \(\vec{X} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\mathbf{z}\vec{\theta }, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_n\right)\), we need to construct confidence intervals for the components of \(\vec{\theta }\) and for \(\sigma^2\). Let
\[
  L = \begin{cases}  \operatorname {span}\left(\vec{z}_{\cdot 1}, \vec{z}_{\cdot 2}, \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k}\right), &  \text{if the model has no intercept } \theta _0 \\ \operatorname {span}\left(\overrightarrow {1}, \vec{z}_{\cdot 1}, \vec{z}_{\cdot 2}, \ldots , \vec{z}_{\cdot k}\right), &  \text{if the model has an intercept } \theta _0 \end{cases}  
\]
Then the vectors \(\vec{X}_{L}, \vec{X}_{L^\perp }\) are independent Gaussian random vectors.

\(\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\) is linearly dependent on \(\vec{X}_{L}\),
\(\widehat{\sigma^2}\) is a function of \(\vec{X}_{L^\perp }\)

Hence \(\widehat{\vec{\theta }}, \widehat{\sigma^2}\) are independent. We have already computed above the expectation and covariance matrix of \(\widehat{\vec{\theta }} = \left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{z}^T \vec{X}\): \(\mathbb {E}\left[\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\right] = \vec{\theta }\), \(\operatorname {Var}\left[\widehat{\vec{\theta }}\right] = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{z}^T \mathbf{z})^{-1}\); in the Gaussian case this means
\[
  \widehat{\vec{\theta }} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\vec{\theta }, \sigma ^2 (\mathbf{z}^T \mathbf{z})^{-1}\right).  
\]
Further,
\[
\begin{align}  \vec{X}_{L^\perp } & = \vec{X} - \mathbf{z}\widehat{\vec{\theta }}, \qquad \mathbb {E}\left[\vec{X}_{L^\perp }\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[\vec{X} - \mathbf{z} \widehat{\vec{\theta }}\right] = \mathbf{z}\vec{\theta } - \mathbf{z}\vec{\theta } = \vec{0}, \\ \frac{1}{\sigma ^2} \left\| \vec{X}_{L^\perp } - \mathbb {E}\left[\vec{X}_{L^\perp }\right]\right\| ^2 & = \frac{1}{\sigma ^2 } \left\| \vec{X}_{L^\perp }\right\| ^2 = \frac{n-\widetilde{k}}{\sigma ^2}\widehat{\sigma ^2} \sim \chi ^2_{n-\widetilde{k}}. \end{align}
\]
Let \(\left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1} =: (a_{i,j})\). Then
\[
  \frac{\widehat{\vec{\theta }} - \vec{\theta }}{\sqrt{\sigma ^2}} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\overrightarrow {0}, (\mathbf{z}^T \mathbf{z})^{-1}\right), \qquad \frac{\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_i - \theta _i}{\sqrt{a_{i,i}\sigma ^2}} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right), \;  \forall i \in \left\{ 1,\ldots ,\widetilde{k}\right\}   
\]
In total, \(\frac{\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_i - \theta_i}{\sqrt{a_{i,i}\sigma^2}}, \frac{n-\widetilde{k}}{\sigma^2}\widehat{\sigma^2}\) are 2 independent random variables, where the first is distributed as \(\mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\) and the second as \(\chi^2_{n-\widetilde{k}}\). Then, by the definition of Student’s distribution, we have
\[
\begin{align}  \frac{\frac{\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_i - \theta _i}{\sqrt{a_{i,i}\sigma ^2}}}{\sqrt{\frac{n-\widetilde{k}}{\sigma ^2}\widehat{\sigma ^2}} / \sqrt{n-\widetilde{k}}} = \frac{\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_i - \theta _i}{\sqrt{a_{i,i}\widehat{\sigma ^2}}} & \sim T_{n-\widetilde{k}} \end{align}
\]






ExampleExample 6





In the Gaussian linear model, find confidence intervals for the parameters \(\theta_{i}, i \in \{ 1, \ldots , k\}\), and \(\sigma^{2}\) at confidence level \(\gamma\).






SolutionSolution






Denote by \(a_{i, i}, i \in \{ 1, \ldots , \widetilde{k}\}\), the diagonal element of the matrix \(\left(\mathbf{z}^{T} \mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\) in the \(i\)-th position. Then, by the theorem on the orthogonal decomposition, the random variable
\[
  \frac{\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_{i}-\theta _{i}}{\sqrt{a_{i, i} \widehat{\sigma ^{2}}}}  
\]
has distribution \(T_{n-\widetilde{k}}\). Let \(Q_{T_{n-\tilde{k}}}(\cdot )\) be the quantile function of the distribution \(T_{n-\tilde{k}}\). Then
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{\vec{\theta }, \sigma ^{2}}\left(Q_{T_{n-\tilde{k}}}\left(\frac{1-\gamma }{2}\right)<\frac{\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_{i}-\theta _{i}}{\sqrt{a_{i, i} \widehat{\sigma ^{2}}}} < Q_{T_{n-\tilde{k}}}\left(\frac{1+\gamma }{2}\right) \right) =\gamma ,  
\]
from which we get that the confidence interval at confidence level \(\gamma\) for \(\theta_{i}\) equals
\[
  \left(\widehat{\vec{\theta }}_{i}-\sqrt{a_{i, i} \widehat{\sigma ^{2}}}Q_{T_{n-\tilde{k}}}\left(\frac{1+\gamma }{2}\right), \widehat{\vec{\theta }}_{i}-\sqrt{a_{i, i} \widehat{\sigma ^{2}}} Q_{T_{n-\tilde{k}}}\left(\frac{1-\gamma }{2}\right)\right)  
\]
Further, let \(Q_{\chi_{n-\tilde{k}}^2}(\cdot )\) be the quantile function of the distribution \(\chi_{n-\tilde{k}}^2\). Then
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{\vec{\theta }, \sigma ^{2}}\left(\frac{(n-\widetilde{k}) \widehat{\sigma ^{2}}}{\sigma ^{2}}>Q_{\chi _{n-\tilde{k}}^2}(1 - \gamma )\right) = \gamma  
\]
The confidence interval at confidence level \(\gamma\) for \(\sigma^{2}\) equals
\[
  \left(0, \frac{(n-\widetilde{k}) \widehat{\sigma ^{2}}}{Q_{\chi _{n-\tilde{k}}^2}(1 - \gamma )}\right).  
\]













ProblemProblem 8





Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) be a sample from \(\mathscr {N}\left(a, \sigma^{2}\right)\) (both parameters unknown). Construct exact confidence intervals for each of the parameters \(a, \sigma^{2}\).









ProblemProblem 9





Let \(X_{i}, i \in \{ 1, \ldots , n\}\) be independent random variables, distributed according to the normal law with parameters \(\left(a+b i, \sigma^{2}\right), \;  a,b \in \mathbb {R}, \;  \sigma^2 \in \mathbb {R}_+\). Construct exact confidence intervals for the parameters \(a, b, \sigma^{2}\).

title: Hypothesis Testing in the Linear Gaussian Model
section: 3.1 The \(t\)-form of the \(F\)-test for one-dimensional hypotheses
text:
3.1 The \(t\)-form of the \(F\)-test for one-dimensional hypotheses
All the \(t\)-statistics listed above are “square roots” of \(F\)-statistics. The following theorem gives this precise meaning.







Theorem 2 Suppose that in the linear Gaussian model \(\overrightarrow {X} = \mathbf{z}\overrightarrow {\theta } + \overrightarrow {\varepsilon }\) we test a one-dimensional (\(m = 1\)) linear hypothesis: \(\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb {R}^{\tilde{k}}\) is a column, \(\tau_0 \in \mathbb {R}\), \[
  H_0: \mathbf{w}^T\overrightarrow {\theta } = \tau _0.
\] Denote \(\widehat{\tau } := \mathbf{w}^T\widehat{\overrightarrow {\theta }}\), \(b := \mathbf{w}^T\left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{w} > 0\), \(\widehat{\sigma^2} := \operatorname {RSS}/(n - \tilde{k})\). Then, under \(H_0\), the statistic \[
  T := \frac{\widehat{\tau } - \tau _0}{\sqrt{b \,  \widehat{\sigma ^2}}} \sim T_{n - \tilde{k}},
\] and the \(F\)-statistic for this hypothesis equals \(F = T^2\).










ExampleExample 7





Prove the theorem.






SolutionSolution





The estimator \(\widehat{\overrightarrow {\theta }} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\overrightarrow {\theta }, \sigma^2\left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\right)\), so its linear transformation \(\widehat{\tau } = \mathbf{w}^T\widehat{\overrightarrow {\theta }}\) is a one-dimensional Gaussian variable: \[
  \widehat{\tau } \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\mathbf{w}^T\overrightarrow {\theta }, \sigma ^2 \mathbf{w}^T\left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{w}\right) = \mathscr {N}\left(\mathbf{w}^T\overrightarrow {\theta }, \sigma ^2 b\right).
\] Under \(H_0\) we have \(\mathbf{w}^T\overrightarrow {\theta } = \tau_0\), whence \[
  \frac{\widehat{\tau } - \tau _0}{\sqrt{\sigma ^2 b}} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right).
\] By Cochran’s theorem the statistics \(\widehat{\overrightarrow {\theta }}\) (a function of \(\overrightarrow {X}_L\)) and \(\operatorname {RSS}\) (a function of \(\overrightarrow {X}_{L^\perp }\)) are independent, and \[
  \frac{n - \tilde{k}}{\sigma ^2}\widehat{\sigma ^2} = \frac{\operatorname {RSS}}{\sigma ^2} \sim \chi ^2_{n - \tilde{k}}.
\] By the definition of Student’s distribution (see the chapter on linear regression) \[
  T = \frac{\left(\widehat{\tau } - \tau _0\right)/\sqrt{\sigma ^2 b}}{\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname {RSS}}{\sigma ^2} \Big/ (n - \tilde{k})}} = \frac{\widehat{\tau } - \tau _0}{\sqrt{b\, \widehat{\sigma ^2}}} \sim T_{n - \tilde{k}}.
\] Finally, for \(m = 1\) the matrix \(\mathbf{b}\) is the number \(b\), and \[
  F = \frac{\left(\widehat{\tau } - \tau _0\right) b^{-1} \left(\widehat{\tau } - \tau _0\right)/1}{\operatorname {RSS}/(n - \tilde{k})} = \frac{\left(\widehat{\tau } - \tau _0\right)^2}{b \,  \widehat{\sigma ^2}} = T^2.
\]






Recall (see the chapter on linear regression) that as the number of degrees of freedom \(\nu\) grows, Student’s distribution \(T_\nu\) approaches \(N(0,1)\) — for large samples the difference between the \(t\)-test and the \(z\)-test disappears, and the “heaviness” of the tails of \(T_\nu\) matters primarily for small \(n\).
The density of Student’s distribution \(T_\nu\) compared with \(N(0,1)\): the more degrees of freedom \(\nu\), the thinner the tails and the closer the curve is to the normal one. Move the \(\nu\) slider to see how the curve “flows” into the standard normal; the switch below highlights the two-sided critical tail of level \(\alpha\) and shows how the critical value of \(t\) changes with \(\nu\).






ν = 5

A test of significance level \(\alpha\) based on \(T\) against the two-sided alternative \(H_1: \mathbf{w}^T\overrightarrow {\theta } \neq \tau_0\) coincides with the \(F\)-test:
\[
  S = \left\{ \left|T\right| > Q_{T_{n-\tilde{k}}}\left(1 - \tfrac {\alpha }{2}\right)\right\} , \qquad p\text{-value} = \mathbb {P}\left(\left|T_{n - \tilde{k}}\right| > \left|T(\overrightarrow {x})\right|\right).
\]
The advantage of the \(t\)-form is that, unlike \(F = T^2\), it “sees the sign” of the deviation, and thus allows testing one-sided alternatives as well, \(H_1: \mathbf{w}^T\overrightarrow {\theta } > \tau_0\) (the test \(\left\{ T > Q_{T_{n-\tilde{k}}}(1 - \alpha )\right\}\)) and \(H_1: \mathbf{w}^T\overrightarrow {\theta } < \tau_0\) (the test \(\left\{ T < Q_{T_{n-\tilde{k}}}(\alpha )\right\}\)). This is exactly why Excel’s output for the \(t\)-tests gives a pair of values: “\(t\) Critical one-tail” and “\(t\) Critical two-tail” (and the corresponding \(p\)-values).






ProblemProblem 9





(Duality of tests and confidence intervals.) Under the conditions of theorem Theorem 2, show that the two-sided \(t\)-test of significance level \(\alpha\) does not reject \(H_0: \mathbf{w}^T\overrightarrow {\theta } = \tau_0\) if and only if \(\tau_0\) is covered by the confidence interval of confidence level \(1 - \alpha\) for \(\mathbf{w}^T\overrightarrow {\theta }\): \[
  \left(\widehat{\tau } - Q_{T_{n-\tilde{k}}}\left(1 - \tfrac {\alpha }{2}\right)\sqrt{b\widehat{\sigma ^2}}, \; \;  \widehat{\tau } + Q_{T_{n-\tilde{k}}}\left(1 - \tfrac {\alpha }{2}\right)\sqrt{b\widehat{\sigma ^2}}\right).
\] Thus, one-dimensional hypotheses can be tested “by eye” — via the confidence interval.

title: Hypothesis Testing in the Linear Gaussian Model
text:
3.2 One-sample \(t\)-test
Given a sample \(X_1, \ldots , X_n\) from \(\mathscr {N}\left(\theta , \sigma^2\right)\) (both parameters unknown), we test \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\). We have already encountered this model in example Example 1 about the coffee machine:
\[
  \overrightarrow {X} = \overrightarrow {1}\cdot \theta + \overrightarrow {\varepsilon }, \qquad \tilde{k} = 1, \quad \mathbf{w} = 1, \quad b = \left(\overrightarrow {1}^T\overrightarrow {1}\right)^{-1} = \frac{1}{n}, \quad \widehat{\tau } = \widehat{\theta } = \overline{X}.
\]
Here \(\widehat{\sigma^2} = \operatorname {RSS}/(n-1) = s^2\) is the unbiased sample variance, and theorem Theorem 2 gives the statistic familiar from the chapter on confidence intervals
\[
  T = \frac{\overline{X} - \theta _0}{\sqrt{s^2/n}} \sim T_{n-1} \quad \text{under } H_0.
\]
In example Example 1 we already saw it in action (and the relation \(F = T^2\)).
In the “Analysis ToolPak” there is no separate button for the one-sample test: it is obtained from the paired test below if a column of constants \(\theta_0\) is supplied as the second “sample”.






ExampleExample 8





A power bank manufacturer advertises a capacity of \(10000\) mA\(\cdot\)h. A tech blogger measured the actual capacity of \(6\) units: \[
  9450, \quad 9800, \quad 10150, \quad 9300, \quad 9650, \quad 9550 \quad (\text{mA}\cdot \text{h}).
\] Assuming the capacity is Gaussian, test at significance levels \(5\%\) and \(1\%\) the hypothesis \(H_0: \theta = 10000\) against the one-sided alternative \(H_1: \theta < 10000\) (“the capacity is overstated”; a deviation in the other direction obviously does not concern the buyer).






SolutionSolution





We have \[
  \overline{X} = 9650, \qquad s^2 = \frac{1}{5}\sum _{i=1}^6\left(X_i - 9650\right)^2 = 89000, \qquad s \approx 298.3,
\] \[
  T = \frac{\overline{X} - 10000}{\sqrt{s^2/6}} = \frac{-350}{121.8} \approx -2.87.
\] The alternative is left-sided, so the critical region is the left tail \(\left\{ T < Q_{T_5}(\alpha )\right\}\). We have \(Q_{T_5}(0.05) \approx -2.02\), \(Q_{T_5}(0.01) \approx -3.36\) and \[
  -3.36 < -2.87 < -2.02,
\] so at significance level \(5\%\) the hypothesis is rejected (the capacity is significantly less than advertised), while at significance level \(1\%\) it cannot be rejected; the \(p\)-value equals \(\mathbb {P}\left(T_5 < -2.87\right) \approx 1.7\%\).









AnswerAnswer





\(T \approx -2.87 < Q_{T_5}(0.05) \approx -2.02\): at significance level \(5\%\) we reject (the capacity is overstated); at \(1\%\) we cannot reject (\(p \approx 1.7\%\)).












ProblemProblem 10





In example Example 1 we tested the coffee machine against a two-sided alternative and could not reject \(H_0\) at significance level \(1\%\). But the skeptic from the example is only concerned about underpouring. Using the same data, test the hypothesis \(H_0: \theta = 200\) against the one-sided alternative \(H_1: \theta < 200\) at significance level \(1\%\).

title: Hypothesis Testing in the Linear Gaussian Model
text:
3.3 Paired \(t\)-test
The tool “Paired two-sample \(t\)-test for means”. The data are \(n\) pairs \((X_i, Y_i)\): two measurements on the same object (before/after treatment, left/right eye, two instruments on the same part). Within a pair the measurements are dependent, so the two-independent-samples model does not apply. Instead, let us pass to the differences:
\[
  D_i := X_i - Y_i = \delta + \varepsilon _i, \qquad \varepsilon _i \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, \sigma _D^2\right) \text{ independent},
\]
and the hypothesis “there is no effect” becomes \(H_0: \delta = \delta_0\) (usually \(\delta_0 = 0\); Excel allows specifying a “hypothesized mean difference”). This is the one-sample \(t\)-test for \(\overrightarrow {D}\):
\[
  T = \frac{\overline{D} - \delta _0}{\sqrt{s_D^2/n}} \sim T_{n-1} \quad \text{under } H_0, \qquad s_D^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum _{i=1}^n \left(D_i - \overline{D}\right)^2.
\]
What is the gain of the paired scheme? If each object has its own individual level \(\mu_i\), i.e. \(X_i = \mu_i + \xi_i\), \(Y_i = \mu_i - \delta + \eta_i\), then in the differences \(D_i = \delta + (\xi_i - \eta_i)\) the individual levels cancel out: the between-object spread of \(\mu_i\) does not enter the variance of the statistic.






ExampleExample 9





Pulse (beats/min) was measured before and after a cup of espresso from the machine for \(8\) students:

Assuming the differences are Gaussian, test the hypothesis “coffee has no effect on pulse” at significance level \(5\%\).






SolutionSolution





Differences “after \(-\) before”:
\[
  \overrightarrow {D} = (7, 1, 6, -1, 5, 2, 8, 0)^T, \qquad \overline{D} = 3.5, \qquad s_D^2 = \frac{82}{7} \approx 11.71.
\]
We test \(H_0: \delta = 0\) against \(H_1: \delta \neq 0\):
\[
  T = \frac{3.5}{\sqrt{11.71/8}} \approx 2.89, \qquad \left|T\right| > Q_{T_7}(0.975) \approx 2.36,
\]
so at significance level \(5\%\) the hypothesis is rejected: coffee significantly speeds up the pulse (by \(3.5\) beats/min on average); the \(p\)-value \(\mathbb {P}\left(\left|T_7\right| > 2.89\right) \approx 2.3\%\). At significance level \(1\%\) we could not have rejected it (\(Q_{T_7}(0.995) \approx 3.50\)).
It is instructive to see what would happen if we applied a two-sample test (next section) to the same data, ignoring the pairing: \(\overline{X^{\text{after}}} - \overline{X^{\text{before}}} = 3.5\) — the same, but the between-individual spread of pulse (from \(61\) to \(95\) beats/min) enters the variance estimate: \(s_p \approx 9.6\), \(T \approx 0.73\), \(p \approx 48\%\) — no effect visible at all. The paired scheme removes this spread and makes the effect visible.









AnswerAnswer





Paired \(t\)-test: \(T \approx 2.89\), \(p \approx 2.3\%\) — the hypothesis is rejected (whereas a two-sample test would not have detected the effect: \(p \approx 48\%\)).
