title: Hypothesis Testing in the Linear Gaussian Model
text:
3.4 Two-sample \(t\)-test: equal variances
The tool “Two-sample \(t\)-test assuming equal variances”. The data are two independent samples with a common unknown variance:
\[
  X^{(1)}_1, \ldots , X^{(1)}_{n_1} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(a_1, \sigma ^2\right), \qquad X^{(2)}_1, \ldots , X^{(2)}_{n_2} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(a_2, \sigma ^2\right);
\]
we test \(H_0: a_1 - a_2 = \delta_0\) (usually \(\delta_0 = 0\): “the means are equal”).
This is exactly the model from example Example 3 about weighing coins: \(\tilde{k} = 2\), \(\mathbf{w} = (1, -1)^T\), and, as computed in example Example 5,
\[
  \widehat{\tau } = \overline{X^{(1)}} - \overline{X^{(2)}}, \qquad b = \frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}, \qquad \widehat{\sigma ^2} = \frac{\operatorname {RSS}}{n_1 + n_2 - 2} = \frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2} =: s_p^2,
\]
where \(s_i^2\) are the unbiased sample variances. The estimator \(s_p^2\) is called the pooled variance: both samples are combined into a common “pool” for estimating \(\sigma^2\). By theorem Theorem 2
\[
  T = \frac{\overline{X^{(1)}} - \overline{X^{(2)}} - \delta _0}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} \sim T_{n_1 + n_2 - 2} \quad \text{under } H_0,
\]
and the \(F\)-statistic from example Example 5 is its square (for \(\delta_0 = 0\)).






ExampleExample 10





An online store redesigned its checkout form and ran an A/B test: a random half of visitors were shown the old form, the rest the new one. Checkout time (seconds): \[
\begin{align}  \text{old } (n_1 = 10)& : \quad 104, \;  111, \;  72, \;  94, \;  104, \;  107, \;  101, \;  108, \;  98, \;  100 \\ \text{new } (n_2 = 12)& : \quad 87, \;  75, \;  77, \;  88, \;  80, \;  96, \;  97, \;  101, \;  85, \;  97, \;  77, \;  78 \end{align}
\] Assuming the samples are Gaussian with a common variance, test at significance level \(1\%\) the hypothesis that the mean checkout time has not changed.






SolutionSolution





Different visitors are in the groups (each saw exactly one form), the samples are independent — a paired scheme is impossible in principle here, this is a genuine two-sample problem. We have \[
  \overline{X^{(1)}} = 99.9, \qquad \overline{X^{(2)}} = 86.5, \qquad s_1^2 \approx 121.2, \qquad s_2^2 \approx 86.6.
\] The variances are close, so we apply the test with pooled variance: \[
  s_p^2 = \frac{9 s_1^2 + 11 s_2^2}{20} \approx 102.2, \qquad T = \frac{99.9 - 86.5}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{12}}} = \frac{13.4}{10.11 \cdot 0.428} \approx 3.10.
\] Since \(\left|T\right| = 3.10 > Q_{T_{20}}(0.995) \approx 2.85\), the hypothesis is rejected even at significance level \(1\%\): the new form speeds up checkout (by \(13\) seconds on average); the \(p\)-value \(\approx 0.6\%\).









AnswerAnswer





\(\left|T\right| \approx 3.10 > Q_{T_{20}}(0.995) \approx 2.85\): rejected even at significance level \(1\%\) (\(p \approx 0.6\%\)) — the new form is faster.







3.4.1 (*) Effect size: Cohen’s \(d\)
The \(p\)-value only answers the question “is there an effect” (more precisely, whether the data are compatible with “no effect”), but says nothing about how large the effect is. Because of this, a small, practically insignificant effect with a large sample yields just as small a \(p\)-value as a large effect with a small sample — statistical significance mixes up the effect size with the sample size. The standard way to separate one from the other is to convert the difference of means into dimensionless units by dividing it by the spread of the data.







Definition 2 Cohen’s \(d\) effect size for comparing two independent samples with a common variance is the standardized difference of the sample means: \[
  \widehat{d} := \frac{\overline{X^{(1)}} - \overline{X^{(2)}}}{s_p},
\] where \(s_p\) is the square root of the pooled variance defined above.




By construction, \(\widehat{d}\) is the difference of means measured in “number of standard deviations”: \(\widehat{d} = 1\) means that the means differ by one \(s_p\). Unlike the \(T\)-statistic, \(\widehat{d}\) does not depend explicitly on the sample sizes \(n_1, n_2\) — it is a feature of the data themselves (of the effect size), not of the precision of its measurement. This is exactly why, as the sample grows, the \(T\)-statistic and the associated \(p\)-value can grow arbitrarily, while \(\widehat{d}\) (for the same true effect) stays put.
J. Cohen proposed conventional benchmarks for interpreting \(\left|d\right|\) in the behavioral and social sciences: \(d \approx 0.2\) is a small effect, \(d \approx 0.5\) a medium one, \(d \approx 0.8\) and above a large one. These thresholds are conventional and depend on the subject area — in physics, for example, effects of \(d = 0.2\) are usually of no interest, while in psychology they are considered quite noticeable.






ExampleExample 11





Find Cohen’s \(d\) for the A/B test from example Example 10.






SolutionSolution





From the solution of example Example 10: \(\overline{X^{(1)}} = 99.9\), \(\overline{X^{(2)}} = 86.5\), \(s_p^2 \approx 102.2\), whence \(s_p \approx 10.11\). Then \[
  \widehat{d} = \frac{99.9 - 86.5}{10.11} = \frac{13.4}{10.11} \approx 1.33.
\] By Cohen’s benchmarks this is a large effect: the new checkout form is not only statistically significantly but also practically substantially faster than the old one — the difference in mean checkout time exceeds one standard deviation within each group.









AnswerAnswer





\(\widehat{d} \approx 1.33\).






Cohen’s effect size \(\hat d = \dfrac{\overline{X}^{(1)}-\overline{X}^{(2)}}{s_p}\) for the A/B test (old and new checkout form): two Gaussian distributions shifted by \(\hat d\) standard deviations. Move the \(d\) slider to see how the overlap of the distributions changes with the effect size, and how this same quantity relates to intuitive metrics: the overlap fraction (% overlap), the probability of superiority and the NNT. The default value \(d\approx1.33\) is exactly the one from the example in the text.

title: Hypothesis Testing in the Linear Gaussian Model
text:
3.5 Welch’s two-sample \(t\)-test: unequal variances
The tool “Two-sample \(t\)-test assuming unequal variances”. If \(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\), then homoscedasticity — the key condition of our linear model (\(\operatorname {Var}\left[\overrightarrow {\varepsilon }\right] = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}_n\)) — is violated, and the entire machinery of this chapter stops working. There is no exact analogue of theorem Theorem 2 here (this is the famous Behrens–Fisher problem), but there is a good approximation — the Welch test:
\[
  T_W = \frac{\overline{X^{(1)}} - \overline{X^{(2)}} - \delta _0}{\sqrt{\dfrac {s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac {s_2^2}{n_2}}} \approx T_{\nu }, \qquad \nu = \frac{\left(\dfrac {s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac {s_2^2}{n_2}\right)^2}{\dfrac {(s_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1 - 1} + \dfrac {(s_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2 - 1}}
\]
(the Welch–Satterthwaite approximation: a number of degrees of freedom \(\nu\) is chosen so that Student’s distribution best approximates the true distribution of the denominator). The number \(\nu\) is usually non-integer, \(\min (n_1, n_2) - 1 \leq \nu \leq n_1 + n_2 - 2\); Excel’s output rounds it to an integer.
Practical remarks. When \(s_1^2 \approx s_2^2\) and \(n_1 \approx n_2\), the statistics and conclusions of the two two-sample tests almost coincide. If, however, the variances differ noticeably (especially with different \(n_i\)), the test with pooled variance can badly misstate the significance level, while Welch’s test remains approximately honest. Hence the modern practical recommendation: if in doubt about equality of variances, use Welch’s test right away.






ExampleExample 12





A restaurant is comparing two delivery services. “Courier” delivers predictably, “economy” is cheaper, but hit or miss. Delivery time (minutes): \[
\begin{align}  \text{courier } (n_1 = 12)& : \quad 47, \;  53, \;  36, \;  53, \;  45, \;  41, \;  41, \;  40, \;  44, \;  49, \;  48, \;  48 \\ \text{economy } (n_2 = 6)& : \quad 26, \;  29, \;  85, \;  74, \;  96, \;  79 \end{align}
\] Test at significance level \(5\%\) the hypothesis of equal mean delivery times.






SolutionSolution





We have
\[
  \overline{X^{(1)}} \approx 45.4, \qquad \overline{X^{(2)}} \approx 64.8, \qquad s_1^2 \approx 27.5, \qquad s_2^2 \approx 891.0.
\]
The variances differ by more than a factor of \(30\) — the assumption of a common \(\sigma^2\) is obviously unreasonable here, so we apply Welch’s test. Denote \(u := s_1^2/n_1 = 27.5/12 \approx 2.29\) and \(v := s_2^2/n_2 = 891.0/6 = 148.5\):
\[
\begin{align}  T_W & = \frac{45.4 - 64.8}{\sqrt{u+v}} = \frac{-19.4}{\sqrt{150.79}} \approx \frac{-19.4}{12.28} \approx -1.58, \\ \nu & = \frac{(u+v)^2}{\dfrac {u^2}{11} + \dfrac {v^2}{5}} \approx \frac{150.79^2}{2.29^2/11 + 148.5^2/5} \approx 5.2. \end{align}
\]
Since \(\left|T_W\right| = 1.58 < Q_{T_{5.2}}(0.975) \approx 2.55\), the hypothesis cannot be rejected (\(p \approx 17\%\)): yes, “economy” took on average \(19\) minutes longer, but with such a spread and only \(6\) observations this could easily be chance.
It is instructive that the test with pooled variance on the same data would give \(T \approx -2.25\) and \(p \approx 3.9\%\) — “significant”! The pooled estimate \(s_p^2 \approx 297\) averages the huge variance of “economy” with the small variance of “courier” and overstates the precision of the comparison; a small sample with a large variance is the worst case for it. Welch’s test protects against this mistake.









AnswerAnswer





Welch’s test: \(T_W \approx -1.58\), \(\nu \approx 5.2\), \(p \approx 17\%\) — cannot be rejected (whereas the test with pooled variance would give a falsely “significant” \(p \approx 3.9\%\)).












ProblemProblem 12





Prove the bounds for Welch’s number of degrees of freedom: \[
  \min (n_1, n_2) - 1 \;  \leq \;  \nu \;  \leq \;  n_1 + n_2 - 2.
\]






HintHint





Denote \(u = s_1^2/n_1\), \(v = s_2^2/n_2\) and apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

title: Hypothesis Testing in the Linear Gaussian Model
text:
3.6 \(z\)-tests: known variances
The tool “Two-sample \(z\)-test for means”. If the variances \(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2\) are known (Excel asks you to enter them by hand), then there is no need to estimate \(\sigma^2\), no Studentization is required, and under \(H_0: a_1 - a_2 = \delta_0\) the statistic has an exact normal distribution:
\[
  Z = \frac{\overline{X^{(1)}} - \overline{X^{(2)}} - \delta _0}{\sqrt{\dfrac {\sigma _1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac {\sigma _2^2}{n_2}}} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right).
\]
Note: here \(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\) is allowed — the problem of the previous section arose only from estimating the variances. The one-sample variant is analogous: \(Z = \sqrt{n}\left(\overline{X} - \theta_0\right)/\sigma \sim \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\).
When can the variance be considered known? Either it is specified in the measuring instrument’s specification sheet (calibrated by the manufacturer on a huge amount of material), or the samples are large enough that \(s_i^2\) can be substituted for \(\sigma_i^2\): then the \(z\)-test is asymptotic (by the CLT it, incidentally, does not even require normality of the samples), and the \(t\)-tests for large \(n\) practically coincide with it (\(T_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\)).






ExampleExample 13





On a packaging line two dispensers pour sugar into “\(1\) kg” bags. The precision of a dispenser is known from its specification sheet: the bag mass is Gaussian with standard deviation \(\sigma = 5\) g. Over a shift, \(n_1 = n_2 = 40\) bags were sampled from each dispenser; the mean masses were \(\overline{X^{(1)}} = 1002.1\) g and \(\overline{X^{(2)}} = 999.3\) g (the operator did not keep the raw data). Test at significance level \(5\%\) whether the dispensers are set the same.






SolutionSolution





The variances are known — this is a \(z\)-test, and, conveniently, apart from the two means no other data is needed: \[
  Z = \frac{1002.1 - 999.3}{\sqrt{\frac{25}{40} + \frac{25}{40}}} = \frac{2.8}{1.118} \approx 2.50.
\] Since \(\left|Z\right| = 2.50 > Q_{\mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)}(0.975) \approx 1.96\), at significance level \(5\%\) the hypothesis is rejected: the dispensers are set to different average weights (\(p\)-value \(\approx 1.2\%\)). Note how small the “significant” difference is — \(2.8\) g with \(\sigma = 5\) g: samples of \(40\) bags make the test sensitive to small discrepancies. Significance is not the same thing as practical importance: whether a difference of \(2.8\) g matters is a question for the process engineer, not for statistics.









AnswerAnswer





\(\left|Z\right| \approx 2.50 > 1.96\): rejected, the dispensers are set differently (\(p \approx 1.2\%\)).

title: Hypothesis Testing in the Linear Gaussian Model
text:
3.7 \(F\)-test for equality of variances
The tool “Two-sample \(F\)-test for variances”. Here the hypothesis is no longer about the mean, but about the variances of two independent normal samples: \(H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2\). From the chapter on linear regression we know (essentially — from Cochran’s theorem for the constant-only model) that
\[
  \frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2}{\sigma _1^2} \sim \chi ^2_{n_1 - 1}, \qquad \frac{(n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{\sigma _2^2} \sim \chi ^2_{n_2 - 1},
\]
and these quantities are independent (the samples are independent). By definition Definition 1 of the Fisher distribution, under \(H_0\)
\[
  F = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2} = \frac{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2}{\sigma _1^2}\Big/(n_1 - 1)}{\frac{(n_2-1)s_2^2}{\sigma _2^2}\Big/(n_2 - 1)} \sim \operatorname {F}_{n_1 - 1, n_2 - 1}.
\]
The alternative is two-sided (\(\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2\)), so we reject if \(F \not\in \left(Q_{\operatorname {F}_{n_1-1,n_2-1}}\left(\frac{\alpha }{2}\right), Q_{\operatorname {F}_{n_1-1,n_2-1}}\left(1 - \frac{\alpha }{2}\right)\right)\). Excel gives a one-sided \(p\)-value \(\mathbb {P}\left(\operatorname {F} > F\right)\) — for a two-sided alternative it needs to be doubled (or, as is often done, the larger variance is put in the numerator in advance).
Two caveats. First, this test is often used to “check equality of variances” in order to choose between the two two-sample \(t\)-tests; such a two-stage procedure distorts the resulting significance level, and it is simpler to just use Welch’s test right away. Second, unlike the \(t\)-tests (fairly robust to non-normality of the samples thanks to the CLT), the \(F\)-test for variances is very sensitive to deviations from normality even for large \(n\).






ExampleExample 14





Next to the old coffee machine from example Example 1 a new one was installed. The same student measured \(8\) espresso servings from the new machine: \[
  199, \quad 202, \quad 197, \quad 200, \quad 201, \quad 198, \quad 200, \quad 203 \quad (\text{ml}).
\] Test at significance level \(5\%\) the hypothesis that the machines pour equally consistently (the variances are equal).






SolutionSolution





For the old machine \(s_1^2 = \frac{218}{7} \approx 31.1\) (we already computed the sum of squared deviations \(218\) in example Example 1). For the new one \(\overline{X^{(2)}} = 200\) and \[
  s_2^2 = \frac{1}{7}\left(1 + 4 + 9 + 0 + 1 + 4 + 0 + 9\right) = 4.
\] The statistic \[
  F = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2} = \frac{31.14}{4} \approx 7.79 \sim \operatorname {F}_{7,7} \quad \text{under } H_0.
\] Two-sided quantiles: \(Q_{\operatorname {F}_{7,7}}(0.025) \approx 0.20\) and \(Q_{\operatorname {F}_{7,7}}(0.975) \approx 5.00\); the statistic \(7.79 > 5.00\) falls into the critical region — the hypothesis is rejected: the spread of the old machine is significantly larger (\(p = 2\mathbb {P}\left(\operatorname {F}_{7,7} > 7.79\right) \approx 1.5\%\)). Note: underpouring (a shift in the mean) and instability (spread) are different defects, tested by different tests; as it turns out, the old machine is guilty of both.









AnswerAnswer





\(F \approx 7.79 > Q_{\operatorname {F}_{7,7}}(0.975) \approx 5.00\): rejected, the new machine is more consistent (\(p \approx 1.5\%\)).












ProblemProblem 13





For two independent normal samples, construct a confidence interval of confidence level \(1 - \alpha\) for the ratio of variances \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\). Compute it for the two coffee machines from example Example 14 (\(1 - \alpha = 0.95\)).






HintHint





Find a pivotal statistic: a quantity distributed as \(\operatorname {F}_{n_1-1,n_2-1}\) for any \(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2\).

title: Hypothesis Testing in the Linear Gaussian Model
text:
3.8 Analysis of variance (ANOVA)
“One-way analysis of variance” is exactly problem Problem 8: \(k\) independent groups of observations with a common variance, the homogeneity hypothesis \(H_0: \mu_1 = \ldots = \mu_k\) (\(m = k - 1\) linear constraints), the statistic
\[
  F = \frac{\operatorname {SS}_{\text{Treatments}}/(k-1)}{\operatorname {SS}_{\text{Error}}/(N-k)} \sim \operatorname {F}_{k-1, N-k} \quad \text{under } H_0
\]
(between-group spread against within-group spread). Excel outputs a table with \(\operatorname {SS}\), \(\operatorname {df}\), \(\operatorname {MS} = \operatorname {SS}/\operatorname {df}\), \(F\), the \(p\)-value, and the critical value.






ProblemProblem 14





Show that for \(k = 2\) one-way analysis of variance coincides with the two-sample \(t\)-test (with equal variances, \(\delta_0 = 0\)): the \(F\)-statistic of the analysis of variance equals \(T^2\).






HintHint





Substitute \(\overline{X} = \frac{n_1\overline{X^{(1)}} + n_2\overline{X^{(2)}}}{n_1 + n_2}\) into \(\operatorname {SS}_{\text{Treatments}}\).

A coffee shop chain is checking service standards at three branches. Time from order to pickup (minutes) for random customers:

Assuming the time is Gaussian with a common variance, test at significance level \(5\%\) the hypothesis of homogeneity across branches.






SolutionSolution





Here \(k = 3\), \(n_1 = n_2 = n_3 = 5\), \(N = 15\). Group means and overall mean:
\[
  \overline{X}_{\cdot 1} = 8, \qquad \overline{X}_{\cdot 2} = 11.4, \qquad \overline{X}_{\cdot 3} = 7.4, \qquad \overline{X} = \frac{134}{15} \approx 8.93.
\]
Sums of squares:
\[
\begin{align}  \operatorname {SS}_{\text{Treatments}} & = 5\left((8 - 8.93)^2 + (11.4 - 8.93)^2 + (7.4 - 8.93)^2\right) \approx 46.5, \\ \operatorname {SS}_{\text{Error}} & = 2 + 23.2 + 17.2 = 42.4 \end{align}
\]
(the three terms of \(\operatorname {SS}_{\text{Error}}\) are the within-group sums of squares for the branches). The statistic
\[
  F = \frac{46.5/2}{42.4/12} \approx 6.59 > Q_{\operatorname {F}_{2,12}}(0.95) \approx 3.89,
\]
we reject the homogeneity hypothesis (\(p\)-value \(\approx 1.2\%\)): the branches perform differently, and, judging by the means, Branch B is “lagging.”
Careful with the interpretation: analysis of variance only says that not all means are equal, but does not say which ones differ. Proper pairwise comparisons after the overall \(F\)-test are a separate topic (multiple comparisons, corrections such as Bonferroni), beyond the scope of this note.









AnswerAnswer





\(F \approx 6.59 > Q_{\operatorname {F}_{2,12}}(0.95) \approx 3.89\): rejected (\(p \approx 1.2\%\)) — judging by the means, Branch B stands out.

ProblemProblem 16





(Analysis of variance as regression.) Show that one-way analysis of variance is the \(F\)-test of overall significance of the regression (problem Problem 2) for a model with \(k - 1\) dummy regressors for group membership: \[
  X = \theta _0 + \theta _1 \; \mathbb {1}_{\text{group } 2} + \ldots + \theta _{k-1}\; \mathbb {1}_{\text{group } k} + \varepsilon .
\]
This problem is worth 2 points.



Two-way analysis of variance generalizes the picture: observations are classified by two factors at once (for example, crop yield: variety \(\times\) fertilizer). In the balanced model “with replication,” \(r\) observations are made in each cell \((i, j)\):
\[
  X_{ijl} = \mu + \alpha _i + \beta _j + \gamma _{ij} + \varepsilon _{ijl}, \qquad i = \overline{1,a}, \quad j = \overline{1,b}, \quad l = \overline{1,r},
\]
where \(\alpha_i\) is the effect of level \(i\) of the first factor, \(\beta_j\) of the second, \(\gamma_{ij}\) their interaction, and for identifiability the constraints \(\sum_i \alpha_i = \sum_j \beta_j = \sum_i \gamma_{ij} = \sum_j \gamma_{ij} = 0\) are imposed. This is again a linear Gaussian model, and the hypotheses “the first factor has no effect” (\(H_0^{A}\): all \(\alpha_i = 0\)), “the second has no effect” (\(H_0^{B}\)), “there is no interaction” (\(H_0^{AB}\)) are linear hypotheses of the form \(\mathbf{w}^T\overrightarrow {\theta } = \overrightarrow {0}\), to which the general theory applies. Let us write out the answer (the derivation is a direct, though cumbersome, application of the scheme of this chapter via the constrained least squares estimator; we leave it to the reader as an exercise of increased effort). In terms of the cell means \(\overline{X}_{ij\cdot }\), the factor-level means \(\overline{X}_{i\cdot \cdot }, \overline{X}_{\cdot j \cdot }\) and the overall mean \(\overline{X}\):
\[
\begin{align}  \operatorname {SS}_{A} & = br\sum _{i=1}^a \left(\overline{X}_{i\cdot \cdot } - \overline{X}\right)^2, &  \operatorname {SS}_{B} & = ar\sum _{j=1}^b \left(\overline{X}_{\cdot j\cdot } - \overline{X}\right)^2, \\ \operatorname {SS}_{AB} & = r\sum _{i=1}^a\sum _{j=1}^b \left(\overline{X}_{ij\cdot } - \overline{X}_{i\cdot \cdot } - \overline{X}_{\cdot j\cdot } + \overline{X}\right)^2, &  \operatorname {SS}_{E} & = \sum _{i,j,l} \left(X_{ijl} - \overline{X}_{ij\cdot }\right)^2, \end{align}
\]
and under the respective hypotheses
\[
  F_A = \frac{\operatorname {SS}_{A}/(a-1)}{\operatorname {SS}_{E}/(ab(r-1))} \sim \operatorname {F}_{a-1,\,  ab(r-1)}, \qquad F_B \sim \operatorname {F}_{b-1,\,  ab(r-1)}, \qquad F_{AB} \sim \operatorname {F}_{(a-1)(b-1),\,  ab(r-1)}
\]
(the statistics \(F_B, F_{AB}\) are built from \(\operatorname {SS}_{B}, \operatorname {SS}_{AB}\) analogously). The tool “without replication” is the case \(r = 1\): the interaction is then indistinguishable from noise (there is one observation per cell), so the model is taken to be additive (\(\gamma_{ij} = 0\)), and the role of \(\operatorname {SS}_{E}\) is played by the residual sum \(\operatorname {SS}_{\text{res}} = \sum_{i,j}\left(X_{ij} - \overline{X}_{i\cdot } - \overline{X}_{\cdot j} + \overline{X}\right)^2\) with \((a-1)(b-1)\) degrees of freedom.

title: Hypothesis Testing in the Linear Gaussian Model
text:
3.9 The “Regression” tool
The last and most substantive tool of the “Analysis ToolPak” fits a model with an intercept \(\overrightarrow {X} = \mathbf{z}\overrightarrow {\theta } + \overrightarrow {\varepsilon }\), \(\tilde{k} = k + 1\), and outputs three blocks, all assembled from the results of the chapters on linear regression and on hypothesis testing. Denote, as usual, \(\left(\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}\right)^{-1} = (a_{i,j})\), \(\widehat{\sigma^2} = \operatorname {RSS}/(n - \tilde{k})\).

Block “Regression Statistics”: the coefficient of determination “\(R\) Square” \(R^2 = \operatorname {ESS}/\operatorname {TSS}\); “Multiple \(R\)” \(= \sqrt{R^2}\) (as we will see in the chapter on correlation coefficients, this is the sample correlation between \(\overrightarrow {X}\) and \(\widehat{\overrightarrow {X}}\)); “Standard Error” \(= \sqrt{\widehat{\sigma^2}}\); “Adjusted \(R\) Square”
\[
  R^2_{adj} = 1 - (1 - R^2)\frac{n-1}{n - \tilde{k}}
\]
— a version of \(R^2\) penalized for the number of regressors: ordinary \(R^2\) never decreases when any regressor is added, even a useless one, whereas \(R^2_{adj}\) can decrease (unbiased estimators of the residual and response variances are used instead of biased ones).
Block “ANOVA”: rows “Regression” / “Residual” / “Total” with \(\operatorname {df} = k, \;  n - k - 1, \;  n-1\) and \(\operatorname {SS} = \operatorname {ESS}, \operatorname {RSS}, \operatorname {TSS}\); the statistic
\[
  F = \frac{\operatorname {ESS}/k}{\operatorname {RSS}/(n - k - 1)} \sim \operatorname {F}_{k, n-k-1} \quad \text{under } H_0: \theta _1 = \ldots = \theta _k = 0
\]
— the \(F\)-test of overall significance of the regression (“do the regressors explain anything at all”), familiar to us from problem Problem 2 (there also — its expression in terms of \(R^2\)); “Significance \(F\)” is its \(p\)-value.
Table of coefficients, one row per parameter \(\theta_j\) (including the intercept — “\(Y\) Intercept”): the estimator \(\widehat{\theta }_j\); its standard error \(\operatorname {se}_j := \sqrt{a_{j,j}\widehat{\sigma^2}}\); “\(t\) Stat”
\[
  t_j = \frac{\widehat{\theta }_j}{\operatorname {se}_j} \sim T_{n - \tilde{k}} \quad \text{under } H_0: \theta _j = 0
\]
— a test of significance of an individual coefficient: this is theorem Theorem 2 with \(\mathbf{w} = \overrightarrow {e}_j\), \(\tau_0 = 0\), \(b = a_{j,j}\); the (two-sided) “\(P\)-value” and the bounds of the confidence interval \(\widehat{\theta }_j \pm Q_{T_{n - \tilde{k}}}\left(1 - \frac{\alpha }{2}\right)\operatorname {se}_j\) at confidence level \(95\%\) (coincides with the interval from the chapter on linear regression).

Let us read it.

The model explains the data excellently: \(R^2 \approx 0.983\) (and \(R^2_{adj} \approx 0.979\) is not far behind), the typical spread of price around the line — “Standard Error” \(\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma^2}} \approx 21.4\) rubles.
“Significance \(F\)” \(\approx 10^{-5}\): the hypothesis “distance has no effect on price at all” (\(\theta_1 = 0\)) is soundly rejected — as expected. Note: for \(k = 1\) this \(F\)-test is equivalent to the \(t\)-test of the single coefficient, and indeed \(F = 286.25 = 16.92^2 = t_1^2\), and the \(p\)-values coincide.
Looking at the coefficient rows: both are significantly different from zero. The confidence interval for the pickup fee \((65.3, \;  151.2)\) covers the advertised \(100\) rubles, and the interval for the per-kilometer price \((27.2, \;  36.9)\) covers the advertised \(30\) rubles/km. That is, coefficient by coefficient there is no complaint about the fare.

Compare with example Example 2, where the joint hypothesis \((a, b) = (100, 30)\) gave \(p \approx 6.2\%\) — much closer to the boundary. There is no contradiction: the joint \(F\)-test looks at both parameters at once (its “confidence region” is an ellipse in the \((a,b)\) plane, accounting for the negative correlation between the estimators \(\widehat{a}\) and \(\widehat{b}\)), and the point \((100, 30)\) lies close to the boundary of this ellipse, even though it falls freely into the rectangle formed by the two separate intervals. We saw the reverse effect in problem Problem 7 about cubic regression: there each coefficient is insignificant by the \(t\)-test (multicollinearity inflates the standard errors), while the joint \(F\)-test does see the effect. Moral: coefficient-by-coefficient \(t\)-tests and the joint \(F\)-test answer different questions, and one must not substitute one for the other.

title: Correlation Coefficients
text:
WarningDraft



This lecture note is still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished passages. If you find something, please let the author know (contact information on the course page).
Let \(\overrightarrow {X} = \left(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\right)^T\) and \(\overrightarrow {Y}=\left(Y_{1}, \ldots , Y_{n}\right)^T\) be two paired samples from univariate distributions. That is, we have a sample from a 2-dimensional distribution \(\operatorname {Law}\left(X_1, Y_1\right)\):
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}  \overrightarrow {X} &  \overrightarrow {Y} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  X_1 &  Y_1 \\ X_2 &  Y_2 \\ \vdots &  \vdots \\ X_n &  Y_n \end{pmatrix}  
\]
We will be interested in whether \(\overrightarrow {X}\), \(\overrightarrow {Y}\) are samples from independent distributions: \(\operatorname {Law}\left(X_1, Y_1\right) = \operatorname {Law}\left(X_1\right)\cdot \operatorname {Law}\left(Y_1\right)\). In other words, we put forward the hypothesis
\[
  H_{0}: F_{X, Y}(s, t)=F_{X}(s) F_{Y}(t) \text{ for all } s, t,
\]
where \(F_{X}\) is the distribution function of \(X_{1}, F_{Y}\) is the distribution function of \(Y_{1}\), and \(F_{X, Y}\) is the distribution function of the vector \(\left(X_{1}, Y_{1}\right)\). The alternative to the hypothesis \(H_{0}\) is the hypothesis \(H_{1}\) that the samples \(\overrightarrow {X}\) and \(\overrightarrow {Y}\) are dependent, i.e.
\[
  H_{1}: F_{X, Y}(s, t) \neq F_{X}(s) F_{Y}(t) \text{ for some } s, t .
\]
Checking the independence property in general is problematic, since it must hold for all pairs \(s, t\); it is much easier to confirm that the samples are dependent via a correlation coefficient. Recall that if \(X_1\) and \(Y_1\) have finite second moments, then
\[
  \operatorname {Corr}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right] = \frac{\operatorname {Cov}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right]}{\sqrt{\operatorname {Var}\left[X_1\right]} \sqrt{\operatorname {Var}\left[Y_1\right]}}.
\]
By the Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz inequality, \(\left|\operatorname {Corr}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right]\right| \leq 1\), and if \(X_1\), \(Y_1\) are independent, then \(\operatorname {Corr}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right] = 0\).
For samples from unknown distributions, the true correlation coefficient \(\operatorname {Corr}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right]\) cannot be computed. Instead, sample correlation coefficients are used. The general decision rule in our problem is as follows: if the correlation coefficient lies sufficiently far from zero, we reject the hypothesis of independence.
Correlation analysis (namely, the analysis of dependencies between observations) plays an important role in regression problems, as well as in time series theory, in particular in the analysis of stationary sequences and autoregressive models.
In this chapter we consider the three most commonly used sample correlation coefficients: the Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlation coefficients.

title: Correlation Coefficients
text:
1.1 Definition and properties
Let \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) and \(Y_{1}, \ldots , Y_{n}\) be two samples with finite second moments: \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_1^2\right], \mathbb {E}\left[Y_1^2\right] < \infty\). To estimate the correlation, we need to estimate the variances \(\sigma_X^2\), \(\sigma_Y^2\) of each sample, as well as their covariance. We already constructed estimators for the variances back in the first chapter:
\[
  \widehat{\sigma _X^2} = s^2_X = \overline{\overrightarrow {X}^2} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n\left(X_i - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\right)^2, \qquad \widehat{\sigma _Y^2} = s^2_Y = \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n\left(Y_i - \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\right)^2  
\]
Let us estimate the covariance. Recall that
\[
  \operatorname {Cov}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right] = \mathbb {E}\left[\left(X_1 - \mathbb {E}\left[X_1\right]\right)\left(Y_1 - \mathbb {E}\left[Y_1\right]\right)\right].
\]
By analogy with the variance, the covariance can be estimated as follows:
\[
  \widehat{\operatorname {Cov}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right]} = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n\left(X_i - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\right)\left(Y_i - \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\right)
\]






ProblemProblem 1





Prove that \[
  \widehat{\operatorname {Cov}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right]} = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^nX_iY_i - \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n X_i\right) \cdot \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n Y_i\right) = \overline{\overrightarrow {X}\overrightarrow {Y}} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \;  \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}
\]










Definition 2 The Pearson correlation coefficient, or the ordinary (sample) correlation coefficient, is the following statistic: \[
  \widehat{\rho }(\overrightarrow {X}, \overrightarrow {Y}) := \frac{\widehat{\operatorname {Cov}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right]}}{\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma _X^2}}\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma _Y^2}}} = \frac{\sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(X_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\right)\left(Y_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\right)}{\sqrt{\sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(X_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\right)^{2} \sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\right)^{2}}}.
\] Two more equivalent expressions are useful. The geometric one — the cosine of the angle between the centered samples: \[
  \widehat{\rho }(\overrightarrow {X}, \overrightarrow {Y}) = \frac{ \left\langle \overrightarrow {X} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\cdot \overrightarrow {1}, \overrightarrow {Y} - \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\cdot \overrightarrow {1} \right\rangle }{\left\| \overrightarrow {X} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| \left\| \overrightarrow {Y} - \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| },
\] and the expression via sample means: \[
  \widehat{\rho }(\overrightarrow {X}, \overrightarrow {Y}) = \frac{\overline{\overrightarrow {X}\overrightarrow {Y}} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \;  \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}}{\sqrt{\overline{\overrightarrow {X}^2} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}^2}\sqrt{\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}^2}}.
\]






                                                
Scatter plots for 7 samples with different Pearson correlation coefficients \(r\): from an exact positive (\(r=1\)) to an exact negative (\(r=-1\)) linear relationship, passing through complete absence of a relationship (\(r=0\)).




                                                
Pearson coefficient for samples of linearly dependent quantities of the form \((X_1, Y_1)\): \(X_1 \overset{\text{a.s.}}{=} \theta_0 + \theta_1 Y_1\). The coefficient equals \(1\) if \(\theta_1 > 0\), equals \(-1\) if \(\theta_1 < 0\), and is undefined if \(\theta_1 = 0\) (in which case \(\operatorname{Var}[X_1]=0\)).


Before turning to the properties of \(\widehat{\rho }\), it is useful to train your eye: to be able to estimate the sign and the approximate magnitude of the correlation coefficient from the point cloud of a scatter plot alone.
A point cloud and the sample Pearson correlation coefficient \(\hat\rho\): the intuition behind the formula – how “stretched” the cloud is along a line, and in which direction. Move the target correlation slider \(\rho\) to see how the shape of the cloud changes; the button below regenerates the points with the same \(\rho\).






ρ (target) = 0.7
n = 80
New sample


sample coefficient: ρ̂ = 












Theorem 1 The sample Pearson correlation converges to the true correlation: \[
  \widehat{\rho } \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} \operatorname {Corr}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right]
\]










ExampleExample 1





Prove the property \(\widehat{\rho } \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} \operatorname {Corr}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right]\) of the Pearson correlation coefficient.






SolutionSolution





The proof consists of successively applying the strong law of large numbers (for independent identically distributed random variables with finite expectation) and the theorem on inheritance of convergence.
By the strong law of large numbers,
\[
  \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^n \left(X_i - \mathbb {E}\left[X_i\right]\right)\left(Y_i - \mathbb {E}\left[Y_i\right]\right) \xrightarrow [n\to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} \mathbb {E}\left[\left(X_1-\mathbb {E}\left[X_1\right]\right)\left(Y_1 - \mathbb {E}\left[Y_1\right]\right)\right]  
\]
and also \(\overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \stackrel{\mathrm{P}}{\rightarrow } \mathrm{E} X_{1}\) and \(\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} \stackrel{\mathrm{P}}{\rightarrow } \mathrm{E} Y_{1}\) (of course, even almost sure convergence holds). Consequently, convergence of the vectors \((\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}, \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}) \stackrel{\mathrm{P}}{\rightarrow } \left(\mathbb {E}\left[X_1\right], \mathbb {E}\left[Y_1\right]\right)\) also holds. Hence, by the theorem on inheritance of convergence,
\[
  \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\, \mathbb {E}\left[Y_1\right] - \mathbb {E}\left[X_1\right]\mathbb {E}\left[Y_1\right] + \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\, \mathbb {E}\left[X_1\right]-\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\cdot \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} \xrightarrow [n\to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} 0,
\]
and direct expansion of the brackets shows that this expression is exactly equal to the difference
\[
  \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(X_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\right)\left(Y_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\right) - \frac{1}{n}\sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(X_{i}-\mathrm{E} X_{i}\right)\left(Y_{i}-\mathrm{E} Y_{i}\right).
\]
Hence,
\[
  \frac{1}{n} \sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(X_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\right)\left(Y_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\right) \stackrel{\mathrm{P}}{\rightarrow } \mathrm{E}\left(X_{1}-\mathrm{E} X_{1}\right)\left(Y_{1}-\mathrm{E} Y_{1}\right)=\operatorname {cov}\left(X_{1}, Y_{1}\right) .
\]
As we proved in previous chapters, the sample variance \(s_{X}^{2}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(X_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\right)^{2}\) is a consistent estimator of \(\mathrm{D} X_{1}\), and an analogous statement holds for the sample \(Y_{1}, \ldots , Y_{n}\). Then, by the theorem on inheritance of convergence,
\[
  \widehat{\rho }=\frac{\sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(X_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\right)\left(Y_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\right)}{\sqrt{\sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(X_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\right)^{2} \sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_{i}-\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\right)^{2}}} \stackrel{\mathrm{P}}{\longrightarrow } \frac{\operatorname {cov}\left(X_{1}, Y_{1}\right)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{D} X_{1} \mathrm{D} Y_{1}}}
\]













Theorem 2 The Pearson coefficient is indeed a sample correlation coefficient in the sense of Definition Definition 1.










ProblemProblem 2





Prove the first property from Definition Definition 1 for the Pearson coefficient.










Theorem 3 (Relation to linear regression) If we have a linear regression model with an intercept
\[
  \overrightarrow {X} = \mathbf{Z}\overrightarrow {\theta } + \overrightarrow {\varepsilon }, \qquad \overrightarrow {Z}_{\cdot 0} = \overrightarrow {1}, \quad \dim (\mathbf{Z}) = n \times (k+1), \quad \dim (\overrightarrow {\theta }) = k + 1,
\]
then its coefficient of determination equals the square of the sample correlation between the dependent variable \(\overrightarrow {X}\) and the fitted model \(\widehat{\overrightarrow {X}}\):
\[
  R^2 = \widehat{\rho }^2\left(\overrightarrow {X}, \widehat{\overrightarrow {X}}\right)
\]
Moreover, if \(k=1\), i.e. we have a linear regression model with an intercept and a single regressor \(\overrightarrow {Y}:= \overrightarrow {Z}_{\cdot 1}\):
\[
  \overrightarrow {X} = \theta _0 \cdot \overrightarrow {1} + \theta _1 \overrightarrow {Y} + \overrightarrow {\varepsilon },
\]
then the coefficient of determination equals the square of the sample correlation between the dependent variable and the regressor:
\[
  R^2 = \widehat{\rho }^2\left(\overrightarrow {X}, \overrightarrow {Y}\right). \qquad \text{Moreover, } \widehat{\theta }_1 = \widehat{\rho }\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\sigma _X^2}}{\widehat{\sigma _Y^2}}}.
\]










ExampleExample 2





Prove the theorem.






SolutionSolution





Recall that if the regression has an intercept, then the coefficient of determination is defined as
\[
  R^2 = \frac{\operatorname {ESS}}{\operatorname {TSS}} = \frac{\left\| \widehat{\overrightarrow {X}} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| ^2}{\left\| \overrightarrow {X} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| ^2} = \cos ^2(\varphi )
\]
where \(\varphi\) is the angle between the vectors \(\overrightarrow {X} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \cdot \overrightarrow {1}\) and \(\widehat{\overrightarrow {X}} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \cdot \overrightarrow {1}\). It is easy to show that \(\overline{\widehat{\overrightarrow {X}}} = \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\). We have
\[
  \cos (\varphi ) = \frac{ \left\langle \overrightarrow {X} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \cdot \overrightarrow {1}, \widehat{\overrightarrow {X}} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \cdot \overrightarrow {1} \right\rangle }{\left\| \overrightarrow {X} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| \left\| \widehat{\overrightarrow {X}} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| },
\]
and, replacing \(\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\) in the second argument by the equal quantity \(\overline{\widehat{\overrightarrow {X}}}\), we recognize the definition of the Pearson correlation coefficient:
\[
  \cos (\varphi ) = \frac{ \left\langle \overrightarrow {X} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \cdot \overrightarrow {1}, \widehat{\overrightarrow {X}} - \overline{\widehat{\overrightarrow {X}}} \cdot \overrightarrow {1} \right\rangle }{\left\| \overrightarrow {X} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| \left\| \widehat{\overrightarrow {X}} - \overline{\widehat{\overrightarrow {X}}} \cdot \overrightarrow {1}\right\| } = \widehat{\rho }(\overrightarrow {X}, \widehat{\overrightarrow {X}}).
\]
Next, let \(k=1\). Let us prove that in this case the vectors \(\widehat{\overrightarrow {X}} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\cdot \overrightarrow {1}\) and \(\overrightarrow {Y} - \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}\cdot \overrightarrow {1}\) are collinear — this will give the required result, since both sides of the equality being proved do not depend on the sign of the cosine. We have \(\dim (L) = 2\), where \(L = \operatorname {span}(\overrightarrow {1}, \overrightarrow {Y})\), and both vectors under consideration lie in \(L\) and are perpendicular to \(\overrightarrow {1}\). Hence they are collinear (pointing the same way when \(\widehat{\theta }_1 > 0\) and opposite ways when \(\widehat{\theta }_1 < 0\)).
Next, \(\mathbf{Z} = \left(\overrightarrow {1} \;  \overrightarrow {Y}\right)\),
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbf{Z}^T & = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  1 &  \ldots &  1 \\ Y_1 &  Y_2 &  \ldots &  Y_n \end{pmatrix}, \quad \left(\mathbf{Z}^T \mathbf{Z}\right) = \begin{pmatrix}  n &  n\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} \\ n \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} &  n\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} \end{pmatrix}, \quad \left(\mathbf{Z}^T \mathbf{Z}\right)^{-1} = \frac{1}{n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}^2}\begin{pmatrix}  n\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} &  -n\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} \\ -n \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} &  n \end{pmatrix} \\ \widehat{\overrightarrow {\theta }} & = \left(\mathbf{Z}^T \mathbf{Z}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{Z}^T \overrightarrow {X} = \frac{1}{n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}^2}\begin{pmatrix}  n\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} &  -n\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} \\ -n \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} &  n \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}  n\overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \\ n\overline{\overrightarrow {X}\overrightarrow {Y}} \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}^2}\begin{pmatrix}  n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\; \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {X}\overrightarrow {Y}}\; \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} \\ -n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\; \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} + n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {X}\overrightarrow {Y}} \end{pmatrix} = \\ & = \frac{1}{\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}^2}\begin{pmatrix}  \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\; \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}\overrightarrow {Y}}\; \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} \\ \overline{\overrightarrow {X}\overrightarrow {Y}} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \cdot \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} \end{pmatrix} \\ \widehat{\theta }_1 & = \frac{\overline{\overrightarrow {X}\overrightarrow {Y}} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \cdot \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}} }{\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}^2} = \frac{\overline{\overrightarrow {X}\overrightarrow {Y}} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}} \cdot \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}}{\sqrt{\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}^2}\sqrt{\overline{\overrightarrow {X}^2} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}^2}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overline{\overrightarrow {X}^2} - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}^2}{\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - \overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}^2}} \end{align}
\]


                                                
Geometric interpretation of OLS with a single regressor: the vector \(X\) is projected onto the plane \(\operatorname{span}(\vec 1, Y)\); the projection \(\widehat X = X_L = \widehat\theta_0\vec 1 + \widehat\theta_1 Y\) is the point of this plane closest to \(X\), and the residual \(\widehat{\vect\varepsilon} = X - X_L\) is orthogonal to it. Numerical example: \(n=3\), \(Y=(1,2,4)\), \(X=(2.2,3.6,6.4)\). Interactive 3D model on geogebra.org: link.

title: Correlation Coefficients
text:
1.2 Gaussian samples
Let \((\overrightarrow {X}, \overrightarrow {Y})\) be a sample from a 2-dimensional normal distribution:
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}  X_1 &  Y_1 \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathscr {N}\left(\begin{pmatrix}  \mu _X\\ \mu _Y \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}  \sigma _X^2 &  \rho \cdot \sigma _X \sigma _Y \\ \rho \cdot \sigma _X \sigma _Y &  \sigma _Y^2 \\ \end{pmatrix}\right),
\]
where \(\rho := \operatorname {Corr}\left[ X_1, Y_1 \right]\). Since we are working with a sample from a 2-dimensional Gaussian distribution, independence of the components is equivalent to their being uncorrelated, i.e. \(H_0 \iff \rho = 0\).
In this case there exists an exact test for testing the hypothesis of independence, i.e. a test in which the distribution of the statistic is known.







Theorem 4 If the hypothesis \(H_0\) of independence of \(X_1, Y_1\) holds, then \[
  T=\frac{\hat{\rho } \sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1-\hat{\rho }^{2}}} \sim T_{n-2}
\]




The level-\(\alpha\) test for checking the hypothesis \(H_{0}\) for normal samples is as follows: if \(T \notin \left(Q_{t_{n-2}}(\frac{\alpha }{2}), Q_{t_{n-2}}(1 - \frac{\alpha }{2})\right)\), where \(Q_{t_{n-2}}(\cdot )\) is the quantile function of Student’s distribution with \(n-2\) degrees of freedom, then we reject the hypothesis \(H_{0}\) of independence.


                                                
Pearson correlation coefficient for 7 samples from 2-dimensional Gaussian distributions with different values of \(\rho\). The Pearson coefficient is especially effective at detecting dependence precisely for samples from a 2-dimensional normal distribution.








ExampleExample 3





Prove Theorem Theorem 4.






SolutionSolution





We have already encountered Student’s distribution in the chapter on Gaussian linear regression. Let us build from \((\overrightarrow {X}, \overrightarrow {Y})\) the linear regression model
\[
  X_i = \theta _0 + \theta _1 Y_i + \varepsilon _i, \quad i = \overline{1,n}
\]
Let us arrange for \(\varepsilon_i\) to be independent of \(Y_1\). Since we are dealing with components of a Gaussian vector, it suffices to arrange for them to be uncorrelated. We have
\[
  0 = \operatorname {Cov}\left[ Y_1, \varepsilon _1 \right] = \operatorname {Cov}\left[ Y_1, X_1 - \theta _0 - \theta _1 Y_1 \right] = \rho \cdot \sigma _X \sigma _Y - \theta _1 \sigma ^2_Y \;  \Rightarrow \;  \theta _1 = \rho \frac{\sigma _X}{\sigma _Y}
\]
Next, we require \(\mathbb {E}\left[\varepsilon_i\right] = 0\). We have
\[
  0 = \mathbb {E}\left[\varepsilon _i\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[X_i - \theta _0 - \theta _1 Y_i\right] = \mu _X - \theta _0 - \theta _1 \mu _Y \;  \Rightarrow \;  \theta _0 = \mu _X - \theta _1\mu _Y = \mu _X - \rho \frac{\sigma _X}{\sigma _Y}\mu _Y
\]
Let us find the variance \(\sigma^2\) of the resulting error. Substituting \(\theta_1 = \rho \sigma_X/\sigma_Y\):
\[
\begin{align}  \sigma ^2 & = \operatorname {Var}\left[\varepsilon _i\right] = \operatorname {Var}\left[X_1 - \theta _0 - \theta _1Y_1\right] = \sigma _X^2 - 2\theta _1 \rho \sigma _X \cdot \sigma _Y + \theta _1^2\sigma _Y^2 = \\ & = \sigma _X^2 - 2\rho \frac{\sigma _X}{\sigma _Y} \cdot \rho \sigma _X \sigma _Y + \rho ^2\frac{\sigma _X^2}{\sigma _Y^2}\sigma _Y^2 = \sigma _X^2 - 2 \rho ^2 \sigma ^2_X + \rho ^2 \sigma _X^2 = \sigma _X^2 \left(1 - \rho ^2\right) \end{align}
\]
For the given model, let us first find the auxiliary quantities entering the statistic \(T_{n-2}\). The element \(a_{1,1}\) of the matrix \(\left(\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{Z}\right)^{-1}\) corresponding to \(\theta_1\) (see the computation above):
\[
  a_{1,1} = \frac{n}{n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}^2} - n^2\overline{\overrightarrow {Y}}^2} = \frac{1}{n \widehat{\sigma _Y^2}}.
\]
Next, since the regression model contains \(k=1\) regressor and an intercept:
\[
\begin{align}  \operatorname {TSS} & = \sum _{i=1}^n\left(X_i - \overline{\overrightarrow {X}}\right)^2 = n\widehat{\sigma ^2_X}, \\ (n-2)\widehat{\sigma ^2} & = \operatorname {RSS} = \operatorname {TSS} - \operatorname {ESS} = \operatorname {TSS}\left(1 - R^2\right) = \operatorname {TSS}\left(1 - \widehat{\rho }^2\right). \end{align}
\]
Substituting what we found into the statistic:
\[
\begin{align}  T_{n - 2} & \sim \frac{\widehat{\theta }_1}{\sqrt{a_{1,1} \widehat{\sigma ^2}}} = \widehat{\rho } \sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\sigma _X^2}}{\widehat{\sigma _Y^2}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{a_{1,1} \widehat{\sigma ^2}}} = \widehat{\rho } \sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\sigma _X^2}}{\widehat{\sigma _Y^2}}}\frac{\sqrt{n\widehat{\sigma _Y^2}} \sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{\operatorname {TSS}(1 - \widehat{\rho }^2)}} = \\ & = \widehat{\rho } \sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\sigma _X^2}}{\widehat{\sigma _Y^2}}}\frac{\sqrt{n\widehat{\sigma _Y^2}} \sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{n\widehat{\sigma _X^2}(1 - \widehat{\rho }^2)}} = \frac{\widehat{\rho } \sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1 - \widehat{\rho }^2}} \end{align}
\]

title: Correlation Coefficients
text:
1.3 Drawbacks
Since, for normal samples, being uncorrelated is equivalent to independence, the Pearson correlation coefficient is best suited to working with normal samples. Unfortunately, as with many parametric methods, using this correlation coefficient can lead to inadequate values of the statistic (meaning that the resulting statistical decisions are incorrect), since the correlation coefficient is not robust to outliers (when the sample contains far-lying data points, for example due to measurement errors). A well-known example (the so-called “Anscombe’s quartet”) demonstrates how badly such methods of processing statistical data can “lie,” even when there is only a single outlier among 10 “ordinary” results.


                                                
Anscombe’s quartet (F. Anscombe, 1973): in all four datasets the Pearson correlation coefficient equals \(0.816\), and the regression line is the same — yet the scatter plots are completely different. Dataset I is the ordinary linear case, where the Pearson coefficient works adequately. Dataset II shows that the Pearson coefficient does a poor job of detecting nonlinear dependencies. Datasets III and IV show that it is overly sensitive to outliers.




                                                
The Pearson correlation coefficient estimates the degree of linear dependence between variables. It can be close to zero even when a dependence between \(X_1\) and \(Y_1\) exists — it is simply nonlinear (and, typically, symmetric).

title: Correlation Coefficients
text:
2.1 Ranks of a sample
Suppose we have a sample \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) from some continuous distribution, i.e. the sample elements do not coincide a.s. Let us order the sample elements in increasing order, i.e. construct the order statistics of the sample.







Definition 3 The numbers that the sample elements receive under such an ordering are called their ranks. Notation: \(\overrightarrow {R}^X\).










ExampleExample 4





Assign ranks to a realization of a sample of 10 elements in the experiment \(\omega_0\): \[
  \overrightarrow {X}(\omega _0) = \overrightarrow {x}_0 = \left(9.356, \frac{29}{5}, 2\pi , 3e, \frac{11}{2}, 5\sqrt{2}, 7\sin (1), 8.78, 4.51, \frac{e^\pi }{4}\right)^T
\]






SolutionSolution





We have \[
\begin{align}  \overrightarrow {X}(\omega _0) & = \left(9.356, \frac{29}{5}, 2\pi , 3e, \frac{11}{2}, 5\sqrt{2}, 7\sin (1), 8.78, 4.51, \frac{e^\pi }{4}\right) \approx \\ & \approx \left(9.356, 5.800 , 6.283 , 8.155, 5.500 , 7.071 , 5.890 , 8.780, 4.510, 5.785\right), \\ \overrightarrow {R}^X(\omega _0) & = \left(\; \;  10, \hspace*{6mm} 4, \hspace*{6mm} 6, \hspace*{6mm} 8, \hspace*{6mm} 2, \hspace*{6mm} 7, \hspace*{6mm} 5, \hspace*{6mm} 9, \hspace*{6mm} 1, \hspace*{6mm} 3 \quad \right) \end{align}
\]






The basic property of ranks:
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(R^X_1 = r_1, \ldots , R^X_n = r_n\right) = \frac{1}{n !},
\]
where \(\left(r_{1}, \ldots , r_{n}\right)\) is an arbitrary permutation of the numbers \((1, \ldots , n)\), since for any \(i<j\) we have \(\mathbb {P}\left(X_i > X_j\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(X_j > X_i\right)\), because the sample components are independent and identically distributed. The distribution of the ranks does not depend on the distribution of the sample.






ProblemProblem 3





Show that

\(\overline{R^X} = \frac{n+1}{2}, \quad \overline{(R^X)^2} = \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\);
\(\mathbb {E}\left[R^X_i\right] = \frac{n+1}{2}, \;  \forall i = \overline{1,n}\);
\(\mathbb {E}\left[(R^X_i)^2\right] = \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}, \;  \forall i = \overline{1,n}\);
\(\operatorname {Var}\left[R^X_i\right] = \frac{n^2 - 1}{12}, \;  \forall i = \overline{1,n}\);
\(\mathbb {E}\left[R^X_i \cdot R^X_j\right] = \frac{(n+1)(3n+2)}{12} , \;  \forall i \neq j\);
\(\operatorname {Cov}\left[ R^X_i, R^X_j \right] = -\frac{n+1}{12}, \;  \forall i \neq j\).

Notice that none of the characteristics of the ranks listed in this problem depend on the distribution \(\operatorname {Law}\left(X_1\right)\) from which the sample was drawn.

title: Correlation Coefficients
text:
2.2 Spearman Correlation Coefficient

2.2.1 Definition
As before, consider two samples \(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\) with distribution function \(F_{X}\) and \(Y_{1}, \ldots , Y_{n}\) with distribution function \(F_{Y}\).







Definition 4 The Spearman correlation coefficient \(\rho_S\) is the Pearson correlation coefficient between the ranks \(R^X, R^Y\): \[
  \rho _{S} := \frac{\sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(R^X_{i}-\overline{R^X}\right)\left(R^Y_{i}-\overline{R^Y}\right)}{\sqrt{\sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(R^X_{i}-\overline{R^X}\right)^{2} \sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(R^Y_{i}-\overline{R^Y}\right)^{2}}},
\tag{1}\] or, equivalently, via sample means of the ranks: \[
  \rho _{S} = \frac{\overline{R^X R^Y} - \overline{R^X} \cdot \overline{R^Y}}{\sqrt{\overline{(R^X)^2} - \overline{R^X}^2}\sqrt{\overline{(R^Y)^2} - \overline{R^Y}^2}}.
\]




Using the results of Problem Problem 3, we have
\[
\begin{align}  \overline{(R^X)^2} - \overline{R^X}^2 & = \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} - \frac{(n+1)^2}{4} = \frac{n^2-1}{12} \\ \rho _S & = \frac{12}{(n-1)(n+1)} \left(\overline{R^X R^Y} - \frac{(n+1)^2}{4}\right) = \\ & = \frac{12}{n(n-1)(n+1)} \left( \left\langle \overrightarrow {R}^X, \overrightarrow {R}^Y \right\rangle - \frac{n(n+1)^2}{4}\right) \end{align}
\]


                                                
The Pearson coefficient estimates the degree of linear dependence, while the Spearman coefficient estimates the degree of monotonicity of the dependence. Left: a strictly monotone but nonlinear relationship — the Spearman coefficient equals 1, while the Pearson coefficient is noticeably lower. Center: a weak, nearly absent relationship — both coefficients are close to each other and to zero. Right: an overall linear relationship spoiled by outliers — the Spearman coefficient is more robust to them than the Pearson coefficient.




2.2.2 Properties







Theorem 5 The following representation holds: \[
  \rho _S = 1 - \frac{6}{n^3 - n}\sum _{i=1}^n \left(R^X_i - R^Y_i\right)^2
\tag{2}\] In practice, the Spearman coefficient is computed from this formula. It is much simpler than formula Equation 1.










ExampleExample 5





Prove formula Equation 2.






SolutionSolution





Note that
\[
  \sum _{i=1}^{n}\left(R^X_{i}-R^Y_{i}\right)^{2} = \left\langle \overrightarrow {R}^X-\overrightarrow {R}^Y, \overrightarrow {R}^X-\overrightarrow {R}^Y \right\rangle = 2 \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} - 2 \left\langle \overrightarrow {R}^X, \overrightarrow {R}^Y \right\rangle ,
\]
whence
\[
  \left\langle \overrightarrow {R}^X, \overrightarrow {R}^Y \right\rangle = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} - \frac{1}{2}\sum _{i=1}^n\left(R^X_i - R^Y_i\right)^2.
\]
Substitute this expression into the formula for \(\rho_S\) above, and separately simplify the term that is free of the sum:
\[
  \frac{12}{n(n-1)(n+1)}\left(\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} - \frac{n(n+1)^2}{4}\right) = \frac{12}{n(n-1)(n+1)} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)(n-1)}{12} = 1.
\]
Hence,
\[
\begin{align}  \rho _{S} & = \frac{12}{n(n-1)(n+1)} \left( \left\langle \overrightarrow {R}^X, \overrightarrow {R}^Y \right\rangle - \frac{n(n+1)^2}{4}\right) = 1 - \frac{6}{n(n-1)(n+1)}\sum _{i=1}^n\left(R^X_i - R^Y_i\right)^2 \end{align}
\]













Theorem 6 The Spearman coefficient is indeed a sample correlation coefficient in the sense of Definition Definition 1. In particular, if the samples are drawn from independent distributions, then \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\rho _S\right] = 0, \qquad \operatorname {Var}\left[\rho _S\right] = \frac{1}{n-1}
\]










ProblemProblem 4





Prove that, if the hypothesis of independence of the samples holds, \(\mathbb {E}\left[\rho_S\right] = 0, \; \operatorname {Var}\left[\rho_{S}\right]=\frac{1}{n-1}\).






HintHint





Use the results of Problem Problem 3.








2.2.3 Testing the hypothesis of independence
To test the hypothesis \(H_0\) of independence of the distributions using the Spearman coefficient \(\rho_S\), we need to know the distribution of \(\rho_S\) under \(H_0\). Note that
\[
  -1 \leq \rho _S \leq 1 \iff 0 \leq \frac{6}{n^3 - n} \sum _{i=1}^n \left(R_i^X - R_i^Y\right)^2 \leq 2 \iff 0 \leq \sum _{i=1}^n \left(R_i^X - R_i^Y\right)^2 \leq \frac{n^3 - n}{3} =: \psi _n \in \mathbb {N}.
\]
Moreover, obviously \(\sum_{i=1}^n \left(R_i^X - R_i^Y\right)^2 \in \mathbb {Z}_+\). Hence, for any \(n\), the coefficient \(\rho_S\) is a discrete random variable taking values in the set
\[
  A_n = \left\{ 1 - 2\frac{k}{\psi _n}: \;  k \in \left\{ 0, 1, \ldots , \psi _n\right\} \right\}  = \left\{ -1, -1 + 2\frac{1}{\psi _n}, -1 + 2\frac{2}{\psi _n}, \ldots , -1 + 2\frac{\psi _n - 2}{\psi _n}, -1 + 2\frac{\psi _n - 1}{\psi _n}, 1 \right\}
\]
The distribution of \(\rho_S\) can be computed by finding the probability mass function on the set \(A_n\).
Since the distribution of \(\rho_S\) is discrete, computing the probability mass function of \(\rho_S\) is a combinatorial problem. It can be solved for any \(n\) simply by enumerating all possible values of the ranks \(\overrightarrow {R}^X, \overrightarrow {R}^Y\) by hand or by computer. However, as \(n\) grows, the number of cases to enumerate grows like \(n!\), i.e. very fast. In practice, statistical packages have exact values of the distribution of \(\rho_S\) only for \(n \leq N\), for some bound \(N\). For example, in the pspearman package of the R language the bound equals \(22\): \(N = 22\).
For \(n > N\), statistical packages use an approximation to the distribution of \(\rho_S\) when testing the hypothesis of independence. For example, from the CLT, for large \(n\) we have
\[
  \operatorname {Law}\left(\frac{\rho _S}{\sqrt{\operatorname {Var}\left[\rho _S\right]}}\right) = \operatorname {Law}\left(\sqrt{n-1}\rho _S\right) \approx \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right).
\]
Or, from the properties of the Pearson coefficient for normal samples, we have
\[
  \operatorname {Law}\left(\frac{\rho _S\sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1 - \rho _S^2}}\right) \approx T_{n-2}
\]
A corrected statistic can also be used, equal to the half-sum of the two previous ones:
\[
  \tilde{\rho }_S = \frac{\rho _S}{2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1 - \rho _S^2}} + \sqrt{n-1}\right).
\]
The distribution function and quantile function of \(\tilde{\rho }_S\) are approximately equal to the half-sum of the corresponding functions for \(\mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\) and for \(T_{n-2}\).
Other ways of computing an approximation to the distribution of \(\rho_S\) are also used. For example, the cor.test function of the R language uses algorithm AS 89 for \(n < 1290\). See (Best and Roberts 1975) for details.


Exact distribution of the Spearman coefficient under \(H_0\)
Blue bars — the exact probability mass function \(\probval{\rho_S = r}\) under the hypothesis of independence (computed by enumerating all \(n!\) permutations of the ranks; for \(n = 10\) — all \(3\,628\,800\) permutations, the values are precomputed and embedded in the page). The red dashed line — the density of the selected approximation, scaled by the lattice step \(12/(n^3-n)\). The bars of the critical region at level \(\alpha\) are shaded red.

Exact enumeration for \(n \le 10\); for larger \(n\), statistical packages use precomputed tables or approximations (see the text).


In summary, a level-\(\alpha\) test for checking the hypothesis \(H_0\) of independence can look as follows:

if \(n \leq 22\), reject the hypothesis \(H_0\) if \(\rho_S \not\in \left(Q_n(\frac{\alpha }{2}), Q_n(1 - \frac{\alpha }{2})\right)\), where \(Q_n(\cdot )\) is the exact quantile function of the distribution of \(\rho_S\);
if \(n > 22\), and we use, for example, the corrected statistic \(\tilde{\rho }_S\), reject the hypothesis \(H_0\) if
\[
  \tilde{\rho }_S \not\in \left(\frac{Q_{\mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)}(\alpha /2) + Q_{T_{n-2}}(\alpha /2)}{2}, \frac{Q_{\mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)}(1 - \alpha /2) + Q_{T_{n-2}}(1 - \alpha /2)}{2}\right)
\]







ExampleExample 6





Find the distribution of \(\rho_S\) for \(n=3\), given that \(H_0\) holds. Find the quantile function \(Q_3(\cdot )\) of this distribution.






SolutionSolution





Define the statistic \(T_{i}\) as follows: if \(R^X_{k}=\) \(i\), then \(T_{i}=R^Y_{k}\). That is, \(T_i = R^Y_{(R^X)^{-1}(i)}\):
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}  R^X_1 &  R^Y_1 \\ R^X_2 &  R^Y_2 \\ \vdots &  \vdots \\ R^X_n &  R^Y_n \\ \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  R^X_1 &  R^Y_1 \\ \vdots &  \vdots \\ 1 &  T_1 \\ \vdots &  \vdots \\ 2 &  T_2 \\ \vdots &  \vdots \\ R^X_n &  R^Y_n \\ \end{pmatrix}
\]
The Spearman coefficient between \(\overrightarrow {R}^X, \overrightarrow {R}^Y\) equals the Spearman coefficient between \(\overrightarrow {T}, (1, \ldots , n)^T\). The collection of values \(\left\{ T_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{n}\) is a permutation of the set \(\{ 1, \ldots , n\}\), and its distribution under the hypothesis \(H_0\) is, obviously, uniform. We have
\[
\begin{align}  \rho _S = 1 - \frac{6}{n^{3}-n}\sum _{i=1}^n \left(i - T_i\right)^2 = 1 -\frac{1}{4}\sum _{i=1}^3 \left(i - T_i\right)^2 \end{align}
\]

title: Correlation Coefficients
text:
2.3 Kendall Correlation Coefficient
Another example of a correlation coefficient robust to outliers, constructed using rank-based methods, is the Kendall correlation coefficient.

2.3.1 Definitions







Definition 5 A pair of 2-dimensional observations \(\left(X_{i}, Y_{i}\right), \left(X_{j}, Y_{j}\right)\) is called concordant if \[
  \left[ \begin{gathered}  X_i < X_j, \;  Y_i < Y_j \\ X_i > X_j, \;  Y_i > Y_j \\ \end{gathered} \right.
\] Equivalently: \[
  \operatorname {sign}\left(X_{i}-X_{j}\right) \operatorname {sign}\left(Y_{i}-Y_{j}\right)=1
\]






                                                
For the observation \((X_1, Y_1)\), the shaded zone contains observations concordant with it (the product of the signs of the deviations \(\operatorname{sign}(X_i-X_1)\operatorname{sign}(Y_i-Y_1)=1\)), while the unshaded zone contains discordant observations.


Let \(C\) be the number of concordant pairs of observations, and \(D\) the number of discordant pairs. The total number of pairs is
\[
  C + D = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}
\]
As before, we assume there are no identical elements within the samples. Note that the difference \(C - D\) can range from \(-\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\) to \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\), and if the hypothesis \(H_0\) of independence holds, then \(C - D \approx 0\).







Definition 6 The Kendall correlation coefficient is the statistic \[
  \tau =\frac{2}{n(n-1)} \left(C - D\right)= 1-\frac{4}{n(n-1)} D.
\]






2.3.2 Properties







Theorem 7 The following representation holds: \[
  \tau = 1-\frac{4}{n^{2}-n} \sum _{i<j} \; \mathbb {1}_{T_{i}>T_{j}},
\] where the statistics \(\left\{ T_i\right\}\) are taken from Example Example 6











Corollary 1 Like the Spearman coefficient, the Kendall coefficient is a rank coefficient, i.e. its value depends only on the ranks \(\overrightarrow {R}^X, \overrightarrow {R}^Y\) of the samples \(\overrightarrow {X}, \overrightarrow {Y}\).











Theorem 8 The Kendall coefficient is indeed a sample correlation coefficient in the sense of Definition Definition 1. In particular, if the samples are drawn from independent distributions, then \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\tau \right] = 0, \qquad \operatorname {Var}\left[\tau \right] = \frac{2(2n+5)}{9n(n-1)}
\]











Theorem 9 (Relation between the Spearman and Kendall coefficients) Under the hypothesis \(H_{0}\), the Spearman and Kendall correlation coefficients are strongly correlated: \(\operatorname {Corr}\left[ \rho_{S}, \tau \right] > 0.98\) for \(n>5\). However, the Spearman correlation coefficient is more sensitive to the number of discordant pairs.






2.3.3 Testing the hypothesis of independence
Like the Spearman coefficient, the Kendall coefficient is a discrete random variable. For small \(n \leq N\), the distribution function and quantile function of \(\tau\) can be computed fairly easily. For example, in the cor.test function of the R language, \(N = 50\). For \(n > N\), statistical packages use the normal approximation from the CLT: under \(H_0\), we have
\[
  \operatorname {Law}\left(\frac{\tau }{\sqrt{\operatorname {Var}\left[\tau \right]}}\right) = \operatorname {Law}\left(\sqrt{\frac{9n(n-1)}{2(2n+5)}} \tau \right) \approx \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)
\]
A level-\(\alpha\) test for checking the hypothesis \(H_0\) of independence can look as follows:

if \(n \leq 50\), reject the hypothesis \(H_0\) if \(\tau \not\in \left(Q_n(\frac{\alpha }{2}), Q_n(1 - \frac{\alpha }{2})\right)\), where \(Q_n(\cdot )\) is the exact quantile function of the distribution of \(\tau\);
if \(n > 50\), reject the hypothesis \(H_0\) if
\[
  \sqrt{\frac{9n(n-1)}{2(2n+5)}}\tau \not\in \left(Q_{\mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)}(\alpha /2), Q_{\mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)}(1 - \alpha /2)\right)
\]







ProblemProblem 7





Find the distribution of \(\tau\) for \(n=4\), given that \(H_0\) holds. Find the quantile function \(Q_4(\cdot )\) of this distribution.

Use Example Example 6 and Theorem Theorem 7.

text:
3.1 Generalized correlation coefficient
Suppose we are given samples \(\overrightarrow {X}=\left(X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\right)^T, \overrightarrow {Y}=\left(Y_{1}, \ldots , Y_{n}\right)^T\). Consider an arbitrary antisymmetric function \(f: \mathbb {R}^{2} \to \mathbb {R}\):
\[
  f(x_1, x_2) = -f(x_2, x_1).
\]
For any \(1 \leq i < j \leq n\) and for \(\overrightarrow {x} \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\), set \(c_{i j}(\overrightarrow {x}) := f\left(x_{i}, x_{j}\right)\).







Definition 7 Consider some \(n\)-dimensional characteristic \(\tilde{\overrightarrow {X}} = \tilde{\overrightarrow {X}}(\overrightarrow {X})\) of the sample \(\overrightarrow {X}\). For example, \(\tilde{\overrightarrow {X}}\) may be the sample \(\overrightarrow {X}\) itself or the vector of ranks \(\overrightarrow {R}^X\). Similarly for \(\overrightarrow {Y}\). The generalized correlation coefficient is the following statistic: \[
  \widehat{r}_f(\overrightarrow {X}, \overrightarrow {Y}) = \frac{\sum _{i<j} c_{i j}(\tilde{\overrightarrow {X}}) c_{i j}(\tilde{\overrightarrow {Y}})}{\sqrt{\sum _{i<j} c^2_{i j}(\tilde{\overrightarrow {X}}) \sum _{i<j} c^2_{i j}(\tilde{\overrightarrow {Y}})}}.
\]

title: Correlation Coefficients
text:
3.2 Fechner Sign Correlation Coefficient







Definition 8 The Fechner sign correlation coefficient is defined by the formula \[
  I = \frac{C-H}{C + H},
\] where \(C\) is the number of pairs for which the signs of the deviations of the values from their means agree, and \(H\) is the number of pairs for which the signs of the deviations of the values from their means disagree.

title: The simple random walk
text:
WarningDraft



This lecture note is still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished passages. If you find something, please let the author know (contact information on the course page).
Suppose that the step of a random walk takes only 2 values: \(1\) and \(-1\) with probabilities \(p\) and \(1-p\):
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(\xi _1 = 1\right) = p, \qquad \mathbb {P}\left(\xi _1 = -1\right) = 1-p =: q
\]
A random walk with such steps
\[
  S_0 = 0, \qquad S_n := \sum _{i=1}^n \xi _i, \;  n \geq 1
\]
is called simple. If \(p = \frac{1}{2}\), it is called symmetric.
In this chapter we will study only the simple random walk. We will often drop the word “simple.”
In general, the initial position \(S_0\) is also a random variable, independent of \(\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\), with an arbitrary distribution on \(\mathbb {Z}\). In this case \(S_n = S_0 + \sum_{i=1}^n \xi_i\) (\(n \in \mathbb {N}\)) is a random walk. Going forward, it will be convenient for us to assume that \(S_{0}\) has some distribution on \(\mathbb {Z}\) such that \(\mathbb {P}\left(S_0 = k\right) > 0\) for all \(k \in \mathbb {Z}\), so that we can study conditional probabilities
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left( \cdots \;  \mid S_{0} = k\right)
\]
If we want to go back to a walk starting a.s. at \(0\), it suffices to take the conditional probability \(\mathbb {P}\left( \cdots \;  \mid \;  S_0 = 0\right)\).
We will periodically use the following notation:
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}_{a}\left(A \right) := \mathbb {P}\left( A \mid S_{0} = a\right), \qquad \mathbb {E}_{a}\left[Y\right] := \mathbb {E}\left[Y \mid S_{0} = a\right] \end{align}
\]
where \(A\) is some event and \(Y\) is some random variable.
A trajectory of the simple random walk corresponding to some elementary outcome ω₀.

title: The simple random walk
section: 1.1 Reference: how to solve some recurrence relations
text:
1.1 Reference: how to solve some recurrence relations
Let us recall how to solve second-order linear recurrence relations:
\[
  y_{t} = \alpha _1 y_{t-1} + \alpha _2 y_{t-2} + F(t), \qquad t \in \mathbb {Z}
\]
If \(F(t) \equiv 0\), the recurrence relation is called homogeneous. Otherwise it is inhomogeneous.
Consider first the homogeneous case \(y_{t} = \alpha_1 y_{t-1} + \alpha_2 y_{t-2}\). We first need to write down the characteristic polynomial:
\[
  p(\lambda ) = \lambda ^2 - \alpha _1\lambda - \alpha _2
\]
Let its roots be \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2\).

If \(\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2\), the solution has the form \(y_t = c_1\lambda_1^t + c_2 \lambda_2^t\);
If \(\lambda_1 = \lambda_2\), the solution has the form \(y_t = (c_1 + c_2 t) \lambda_1^t\).

The numbers \(c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb {R}\) are determined by the initial (boundary) conditions.
The solution of the inhomogeneous relation is given as \(y_t = y_t^h + y_t^n\), where \(y_t^h\) is the solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation (without \(F(t)\)), and \(y_t^n\) is any particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation. We can find a particular solution explicitly only in certain cases. For example, if \(F(t) = P(t) \cdot \gamma^t\), where \(P(t)\) is a polynomial of degree (at most) \(2\), \(\gamma \in \mathbb {R}\), and \(\gamma\) is a root of multiplicity \(m = 0,1,2,\ldots\) of the characteristic polynomial of the homogeneous relation, then the inhomogeneous solution has the form
\[
  y_t^{n} = Q(t) \cdot t^m \cdot \gamma ^t
\]
where \(Q(t)\) is a polynomial of degree at most that of \(P(t)\).
