section: 2.1 The ballot theorem: the probability that the winning candidate led throughout the vote count
text:
2.1 The ballot theorem: the probability that the winning candidate led throughout the vote count
The famous “ballot theorem” is a consequence of these elementary results; it was first proved by W. A. Whitworth in 1878, but is named after J. Bertrand, who rediscovered it in 1887.







Theorem 2 (Bertrand’s ballot theorem) Two candidates, Alice and Bob, took part in an election. Suppose we know that Alice received \(a\) votes in this election and Bob received \(b\) votes, where \(a>b\), i.e., Alice won. Suppose the votes were counted in random order. Then Alice was ahead throughout the entire count with probability \(\frac{a-b}{a+b}\).










ProblemProblem 6






Prove that the fraction of paths from \((0,0)\) to \((n, b)\) (\(b > 0\)) that do not cross the zero level, out of the total number of paths from \((0,0)\) to \((n, b)\), equals \(\frac{b}{n}\).
Prove Bertrand’s ballot theorem.

title: The simple random walk
section: 2.2 The maximum of the random walk: its distribution and the time it is attained
text:
2.2 The maximum of the random walk: its distribution and the time it is attained
Another interesting characteristic is the maximum value attained by the random walk. Denote
\[
  M_{n} = \max \left\{ S_{i}: 0 \leq i \leq n\right\}
\]







Theorem 3 (on the joint distribution of the random walk and its maximum) For \(r \geq 1\) we have \[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(M_{n} \geq r, S_{n} = b\right) & = \\ & \quad \begin{cases} \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{n} = b\right) &  \text{ if } b \geq r, \\ \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{r-b} \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{n} = 2 r-b\right) &  \text{ if } b < r .\end{cases} \end{align}
\]










ExampleExample 5





Prove the theorem on the joint distribution of the random walk and its maximum.






SolutionSolution







                                                
Reflection principle for finding the joint distribution of Sₙ and Mₙ: after the first time the level r is reached, the tail of the trajectory is reflected about r.


We may assume that \(r \geq 1\) and \(b < r\). Let \(N_{n}^{r}(0, b)\) be the number of trajectories from \((0,0)\) to \((n, b)\) that include some point at height \(r\), i.e., some point (\(i, r\)) with \(0 < i < n\); for such a path \(\pi\) let \(\left(i_{\pi }, r\right)\) be the earliest such point. We may reflect the portion of the path with \(i_{\pi } \leq x \leq n\) across the line \(y = r\) to obtain a trajectory \(\pi^{\prime }\) connecting \((0,0)\) to \((n, 2 r-b)\). Any such trajectory \(\pi^{\prime }\) arises in this way from a unique trajectory \(\pi\), and therefore \(N_{n}^{r}(0, b) = N_{n}(0,2 r-b)\). It follows that
\[
  \begin{aligned}  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(M_{n} \geq r, S_{n} = b\right) &  = N_{n}^{r}(0, b) p^{\frac{1}{2}(n+b)} q^{\frac{1}{2}(n-b)} \\ &  = (q / p)^{r-b} N_{n}(0,2 r-b) p^{\frac{1}{2}(n+2 r-b)} q^{\frac{1}{2}(n-2 r+b)} \\ &  = (q / p)^{r-b} \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{n} = 2 r-b\right) \end{aligned}
\]






What is the probability that the walk reaches a new maximum at a specific moment in time? More precisely, what is the probability that a walk starting from 0 reaches the point \(b > 0\) for the first time at the \(n\)-th step? Denote, as before, the moment of the first crossing of the level \(y=b\) by the random walk \(S_n\) (the hitting time of \(b\)) as \(\tau_b\):
\[
  \tau _b := \min \left\{ n \geq 0 \;  : \;  S_n = b\right\}
\]






ExampleExample 6





Let \(S_0 = 0\). Find the distribution of the random variable \(\tau_b\) for arbitrary \(b \geq 1\).






SolutionSolution





Let us find the probability mass function. For \(n \leq 0\) we have \(\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\tau_b = n\right) = 0\). For \(n \geq 1\) we have \[
  \begin{aligned}  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\tau _b = n\right) &  = \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(M_{n-1} = S_{n-1} = b-1, \;  \frac{}{} S_{n} = b\right) = \\ & = \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(M_{n-1} = S_{n-1} = b-1, \;  \frac{}{} \xi _{n} = 1\right) = \\ &  = \underbrace{\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\xi _n = 1\right)}_{=p} \cdot \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(M_{n-1} = S_{n-1} = b-1\right) \\ &  = p \cdot \bigg[\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(M_{n-1} \geq b-1, \;  \frac{}{} S_{n-1} = b-1\right) \\ & \quad -\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(M_{n-1} \geq b, \;  \frac{}{} S_{n-1} = b-1\right)\bigg] \\ &  = p\cdot \bigg[\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{n-1} = b-1\right) - \frac{q}{p} \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(S_{n-1} = b+1\right)\bigg] = \\ &  = \frac{b}{n} \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{n} = b\right) \end{aligned}
\]






We have proved the following theorem.







Theorem 4 (on the distribution of the hitting time) The probability \(\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\tau_b = n\right)\) that the random walk \(S\) first reaches the point \(b\) at step \(n\), starting from \(0\), is: \[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\tau _b = n\right) = \frac{|b|}{n} \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{n} = b\right)\quad \text{ for } \quad n \geq 1
\]




The probability mass function of the hitting time \(\tau_b\) (the first time the level \(b\) is reached): \(\probval[0]{\tau_b = n} = \frac{b}{n}\probval[0]{S_n = b}\); the mass is concentrated on \(n\) of the same parity as \(b\). Move the sliders \(b\) and \(p\): for \(p = \frac{1}{2}\) the tail is heavy, of order \(n^{-3/2}\) (this is precisely why \(\tau_b\) is finite a.s., yet \(\mean[0]{\tau_b} = +\infty\)), while for \(p > \frac{1}{2}\) the tail decays geometrically. The dashed line shows the asymptotic \(\frac{b}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\, n^{-3/2}\), valid for \(p=\frac12\) (for \(p \ne \frac12\) it no longer describes the true tail — this is visible from the divergence of the curves). At the bottom is the running sum of probabilities: it tends to \(1\) if \(p \ge \frac12\), and to \((p/q)^b\) if \(p < \frac12\).







b = 3



p = 0.50








Above, using conditional probabilities, we already found with what probability \(\tau_b\) is finite and in which case its expectation is finite. Now we have obtained a much more general result: we found the probability mass function for \(\tau_b\), which uniquely determines the distribution. One can check the results obtained in the previous section using the new formulas:
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\tau _{b} < \infty \right) = \sum _{n=1}^{\infty } \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\tau _{b} = n\right), \qquad \mathbb {E}_{0}\left[\tau _b\right] = \begin{cases}  +\infty , &  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\tau _{b} = +\infty \right) > 0 \\ \sum _{n=1}^{+\infty } n\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\tau _{b} = n\right), &  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\tau _{b} = +\infty \right) = 0 \end{cases}
\]
If anyone is interested, feel free to check this yourself.
Altogether, we have fully characterized the distribution of the time \(\tau_b\).






ProblemProblem 7





Let \(p = \frac{1}{2}\), i.e., the random walk is symmetric. Show that in this case the mass function of the maximum can be computed as follows: \[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(M_n = r\right) = \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{n} = r\right) + \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{n} = r+1\right)
\]

title: The simple random walk
section: 2.3 The probability of never returning to the origin
text:
2.3 The probability of never returning to the origin
We have already introduced the hitting time of some level:
\[
  \tau _{i} = \min \left\{ n \geq 0 \;  : \;  S_{n} = i\right\}
\]
Let us introduce the hitting time after step \(1\):
\[
  T_{i} := \min \left\{ n \geq 1 \;  : \;  S_{n} = i\right\}
\]
(these are all standard notations). These random variables are very similar: if the walk does not start from state \(i\), they coincide:
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{j}\left(T_{i} = \tau _{i}\right) = 1, \qquad i \neq j
\]
Above we have already fully studied \(\tau_{i}\), so we also fully understand the distribution of \(T_{i}\) in this case.
However, if the chain starts from state \(i\), then \(\tau_{i}\) is not particularly meaningful, being identically zero. But \(T_i\) will denote the return time to \(i\), which is something meaningful. Let us find the distribution of \(T_i\) in this case. Without loss of generality, let \(S_0 = i = 0\), i.e., the chain starts from zero. We will look for the survival function of \(T_{0}\):
\[
  \underbrace{\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(T_{0} > n\right)}_{\text{survival function}} \quad = \quad 1 - \underbrace{\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(T_{0} \leq n\right)}_{\text{cumulative distribution function}} , \qquad n \geq 1
\]
This is the probability that the random walk does not return to its starting point in the first \(n\) steps. Like the cumulative distribution function, the survival function fully determines the distribution itself.






ExampleExample 7





Find \[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(T_{0} > n, S_{n} = b\right)
\]






SolutionSolution





Suppose that \(S_{0} = 0\) and \(S_{n} = b > 0\). The event under consideration occurs if and only if the random walk’s trajectory does not visit the \(x\)-axis during the time interval \([1, n]\). The number of such trajectories equals \((b / n) N_{n}(0, b)\), and each such trajectory has \(\frac{1}{2}(n+b)\) steps to the right and \(\frac{1}{2}(n-b)\) steps to the left. Therefore \[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(T_{0} > n, S_{n} = b\right) = \frac{b}{n} N_{n}(0, b) p^{\frac{1}{2}(n+b)} q^{\frac{1}{2}(n-b)} = \frac{b}{n} \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{n} = b\right)
\] A similar computation holds for \(b < 0\).









AnswerAnswer





\(\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(T_{0} > n, S_{n} = b\right) = \frac{\left|b\right|}{n}\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{n} = b\right)\)












ProblemProblem 8






Find the survival function for \(T_0\). Namely, prove that
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(T_{0} > n\right) = \frac{1}{n} \mathbb {E}_{0}\left[\left|S_{n}\right|\right]
\]
Find the probability that the random walk never returns to its starting point. Namely, show that
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(T_{0} = +\infty \right) = \left|2p - 1\right|
\]




Thus, for \(p \neq \frac{1}{2}\), a random walk, having left zero, will never return to it with some nonzero probability: \(\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(T_{0} = +\infty \right) > 0\). Of course, in this case \(\mathbb {E}_{0}\left[T_{0}\right] = +\infty\). If, on the other hand, \(p = \frac{1}{2}\), then \(T_{0}\) is a.s. finite: \(\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(T_{0} < +\infty \right) = 1\). But what about its expectation?






ProblemProblem 9





Let \(p=\frac{1}{2}\), i.e., we consider the symmetric simple random walk.

Find the probability mass function for \(T_0\) given \(S_0 = 0\). Namely, show that the distribution of \(T_0\) is concentrated on even points, with

\[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(T_0 = 2m\right) = \frac{1}{2m - 1}\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{2m} = 0\right) = \frac{1}{2m-1} C_{2m}^{m} \frac{1}{2^{2m}}, \quad m \in \mathbb {N}
\]

Show that \(\mathbb {E}_{0}\left[T_0^{\alpha }\right] < \infty\) if and only if \(\alpha < \frac{1}{2}\). In particular, show that \(\mathbb {E}_{0}\left[T_0\right] = +\infty\).







HintHint











Enum-item(1)



Use problem Problem 5








Enum-item(2)



use the corollary of Stirling’s formula: \(C_{2m}^m \sim \frac{2^{2m}}{\sqrt{\pi m}}\) as \(m \to +\infty\).

title: The simple random walk
text:
3.1 The last zero crossing
Fix \(n \in \mathbb {N}\). Denote by \(\operatorname {LZ}_{n} = \operatorname {LastZero}_{n}\) the time of the last visit to \(0\) of the random walk before time \(n\). Note that \(\operatorname {LZ}_{2m} = \operatorname {LZ}_{2m + 1}\), since zero cannot be hit on an odd step. Therefore, going forward, we will study the distribution of \(\operatorname {LZ}_{n}\) for \(n = 2m\), i.e., for even \(n\).






ExampleExample 8





Find the distribution of \(\operatorname {LZ}_{2m}\), \(m \in \mathbb {N}\). Namely, show that it is concentrated on the even numbers from \(0\) to \(2m\), and \[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {LZ}_{2m} = 2k\right) = \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{2 k} = 0\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{2 m-2 k} = 0\right)
\] for \(k = 0,1,\ldots ,m\).






SolutionSolution





\(\operatorname {LZ}_{2m}\) is a discrete random variable that can only take even nonnegative values \(0,2,4,\ldots ,2m\), since zero can only be hit on an even step. Let \(0 \leq k \leq m\). We have
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}\left(\operatorname {LZ}_{2m} = 2k\right) &  = \mathbb {P}\left(S_{2k} = 0, \quad S_{2k + 1}, \ldots , S_{2m} \neq 0\right) = \\ & = \mathbb {P}\left(S_{2 k} = 0\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(S_{2 k+1} S_{2 k+2} \cdots S_{2 m} \neq 0 \mid S_{2 k} = 0\right) \\ &  = \mathbb {P}\left(S_{2 k} = 0\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(S_{1} S_{2} \cdots S_{2 m-2 k} \neq 0\right) = \\ & = \mathbb {P}\left(S_{2 k} = 0\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(T_{0} > 2m-2k\right) = \\ & = \mathbb {P}\left(S_{2 k} = 0\right) \cdot \frac{1}{2m-2k} \mathbb {E}\left[\left|S_{2m-2k}\right|\right] \end{align}
\]
So far we have not used the fact that the random walk is symmetric.
To get the answer, we need to recall (see Example Problem 5) that for the symmetric random walk
\[
  \frac{1}{2m-2k} \mathbb {E}\left[\left|S_{2m-2k}\right|\right] = \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{2m-2k} = 0\right)
\]






The exact distribution of the last zero \(\operatorname{LZ}_{2m}\) of the symmetric random walk: \(\probval[0]{\operatorname{LZ}_{2m} = 2k} = u_{2k}\, u_{2m - 2k}\), where \(u_{2j} = \probval[0]{S_{2j} = 0} = C_{2j}^{j}/2^{2j}\) (blue stems), plotted against the asymptotic U-shaped curve \(\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{k(m-k)}}\) (red), which yields the arcsine density in the limit. Move the slider \(m\) to see how, as \(m\) grows, the stems “condense” onto this curve: the last zero most often ends up very close to the beginning or the end of the observation interval. Below is one simulated random-walk trajectory of length \(2m\) with its last zero marked; the button regenerates the trajectory.







m = 10





New trajectory






Consider the normalized random variable \(\frac{1}{n}\operatorname {LZ}_{n}\). This is a random variable with values in \([0,1]\), showing how long ago the last \(0\) was relative to the entire elapsed time.






ExampleExample 9





Find the limiting distribution of \(\frac{1}{n}\operatorname {LZ}_{n}\).






SolutionSolution





Let us look for the limiting distribution of \(\frac{1}{2m}\operatorname {LZ}_{2m}\).
By Stirling’s formula:
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{2k} = 0\right) & = C_{2k}^{k}\frac{1}{2^{2k}} \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi k}} \end{align}
\]
as \(k \to +\infty\). Then
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {LZ}_{2m} = 2k\right) \sim \frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{k(m-k)}}
\]
This holds for values of \(k\) that are close to neither \(0\) nor \(n\). Then
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}\left(\frac{\operatorname {LZ}_{2n}}{2n} \leq x\right) & \sim \sum _{k \leq x n} \frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{k(n-k)}} \\ & \sim \int _{u = 0}^{x n} \frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{u(n-u)}} d u \\ & = \frac{2}{\pi } \arcsin (\sqrt{x}) \end{align}
\]









AnswerAnswer





The arcsine distribution.






The distribution on \([0,1]\) with cumulative distribution function \(\frac{2}{\pi }\arcsin (\sqrt{x})\) is called the arcsine distribution and is denoted \(\operatorname {Arcsine}\). Its density:
\[
  f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{x(1-x)}} \cdot \; \mathbb {1}_{[0,1]}(x)
\]
That is, this is a special case of the Beta distribution: \(\operatorname {Arcsine} = \operatorname {Beta}(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2})\).
We have proved







Lemma 2 (Arcsine law for the time of the last zero) Let \(S_{n}\) be the symmetric simple random walk starting from zero. Then \[
  \frac{1}{n}\operatorname {LZ}_{n} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \operatorname {Arcsine}
\]






                                                
Arcsine distribution: the distribution function F(x) = (2/π)·arcsin(√x) and the density f(x) = 1/(π·√(x(1-x))), x ∈ [0,1] (the density plot is capped at y ≤ 3 — the density is unbounded at the endpoints of the interval).


The arcsine law is quite remarkable. One might think that in a long series of \(2 m\) tosses of a fair coin, periods in which the number of heads and tails is equal should occur fairly often. However, it turns out that with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\) no such moment occurs during the last \(m\) tosses, and, moreover, with probability roughly \(\frac{1}{5}\), no such moment occurs after the first \(\frac{1}{5} m\) tosses.
One might think that in a long series of \(2m\) tosses of a fair coin, the last moment at which the number of heads and tails was equal tends to lie closer to the end. Reality strongly contradicts this intuition: the distribution of this time is symmetric around the midpoint (\(m\)).

title: The simple random walk
section: 3.2 How much time the walk spends in the positive half-line
text:
3.2 How much time the walk spends in the positive half-line
How much time does the symmetric random walk spend on the positive half-line? We say that the random walk spent the time interval \((k,k+1)\) in the positive half-line if \(S_k > 0\) or \(S_{k+1} > 0\) (adjacent values differ by exactly \(1\), so in this case the segment of the trajectory between them lies above the axis — except possibly at one of the endpoints). Let \(\operatorname {SI}_{n} = \operatorname {SojournIntervals}_{n}\) be the number of such (unit-length) intervals from time \(0\) to \(n\):
\[
\begin{align}  \operatorname {SI}_{n} & := \; \mathbb {1}_{\left\{ S_{0} >0 \text{ or } S_{1} > 0\right\} } + \; \mathbb {1}_{\left\{ S_{1} >0 \text{ or } S_{2} > 0\right\} } \\ & \quad + \ldots + \; \mathbb {1}_{\left\{ S_{n-1} >0 \text{ or } S_{n} > 0\right\} } \end{align}
\]
Note the “or” in this convention: an interval adjacent to a zero of the trajectory is assigned to whichever side the trajectory occupies during the interval itself. Under an “and” convention, the statement of the next problem would be false (check this for \(n = 2\)!).






ProblemProblem 10





Prove that \(\operatorname {SI}_{2m}\) has the same distribution as \(\operatorname {LZ}_{2m}\): \[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {SI}_{2m} = 2k\right) = \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{2 k} = 0\right)\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{2 m-2 k} = 0\right)
\]



We have already found the limiting distribution for \(\frac{1}{n}\operatorname {LZ}_{n}\). It will be the same for \(\frac{1}{n}\operatorname {SI}_{n}\). We obtain







Lemma 3 (Arcsine law for sojourn intervals in the positive half-line) Let \(S_{n}\) be the symmetric simple random walk starting from zero. Then \[
  \frac{1}{n}\operatorname {SI}_{n} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \operatorname {Arcsine}
\]




Again, one might intuitively expect the answer to be around \(n\) with high probability, but in fact things are quite different. With high probability, the fraction of time spent to the right (or left) of the origin is close to 0 or to 1, but not close to \(\frac{1}{2}\). In other words, in a long sequence of fair coin tosses there is a high probability that one of the two faces (heads or tails) will lead the other by a disproportionately large amount of time.

title: The simple random walk
section: 3.3 The time at which the maximum is attained
text:
3.3 The time at which the maximum is attained
Let \(\operatorname {AM}_{n} = \operatorname {ArgMax}_n := \min \left(\operatorname *{arg\, max}_{k \in \left\{ 0,\ldots ,n\right\} }S_{k}\right)\) be the time at which the random walk first attains its maximum on the time interval \(\left\{ 0, \ldots , n\right\}\). It turns out that for \(0 < 2k\) and \(2k + 1 < 2m\) we have
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {AM}_{2m} = 2k\right) = \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {AM}_{2m} = 2k + 1\right) = \frac{1}{2}\,  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{2k} = 0 \right) \cdot \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_{2m-2k} = 0\right) \end{align}
\]
(cf. (Feller 1968, Ch. III, 7)).






ExampleExample 10





Prove the formula for the distribution of the first maximum time \(\operatorname {AM}_{2m}\). Also work out the boundary cases: what are \(\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {AM}_{2m} = 0\right)\) and \(\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {AM}_{2m} = 2m\right)\)?






HintHint





Cut the trajectory at the point of the first maximum; on the left piece, reverse time. The facts from step 1 of the solution of the \(\operatorname {SI}_{2m}\) problem will be useful.









SolutionSolution





Let \(0 \leq l \leq 2m\). The event \(\left\{ \operatorname {AM}_{2m} = l\right\}\) is the intersection of two events depending on disjoint sets of steps (and hence independent):

\(A_l\): the maximum on \(\left\{ 0, \ldots , l\right\}\) is first attained exactly at \(l\), i.e., \(S_i < S_l\) for all \(0 \leq i < l\) (depends only on \(\xi_1, \ldots , \xi_l\));
\(B_l\): after time \(l\) the trajectory does not rise any higher, i.e., \(S_{l+j} - S_l \leq 0\) for all \(1 \leq j \leq 2m-l\) (depends only on \(\xi_{l+1}, \ldots , \xi_{2m}\)).

Probability of \(B_l\). The process \((S_{l+j} - S_l)_{j \geq 0}\) is again a symmetric walk from zero, so, using the symmetry \(S \mapsto -S\),
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(B_l\right) = \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_1 \geq 0, \ldots , S_{2m-l} \geq 0\right)
\]
In step 1 of the solution of the \(\operatorname {SI}_{2m}\) problem we showed that for even lengths \(\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_1 \geq 0, \ldots , S_{2j} \geq 0\right) = u_{2j}\); an odd length \(2j-1\) gives the same probability, since \(S_{2j-1} \geq 0\) automatically implies \(S_{2j} \geq 0\) by parity. Hence for both \(l = 2k\) and \(l = 2k+1\)
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(B_l\right) = u_{2m - 2k}
\]
Probability of \(A_l\). Reverse time over the first \(l\) steps: set \(\xi '_{j} := \xi_{l-j+1}\), which are again independent symmetric steps, and for the corresponding walk \(S'_j := \xi '_1 + \ldots + \xi '_j = S_l - S_{l-j}\), the condition \(\left\{ S_i < S_l \; \;  \forall \,  i < l\right\}\) becomes \(\left\{ S'_j > 0 \; \;  \forall \,  1 \leq j \leq l\right\}\). Again by step 1: \(\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(S_1 > 0, \ldots , S_{2k} > 0\right) = \frac{1}{2}u_{2k}\), and an odd length \(2k+1\) gives the same probability: \(S_{2k} > 0\) is an even number, i.e., \(S_{2k} \geq 2\), whence \(S_{2k+1} \geq 1 > 0\) automatically. Hence for \(l \in \left\{ 2k, 2k + 1\right\}\), \(l \geq 1\),
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(A_l\right) = \frac{1}{2} u_{2k}
\]
Putting it together. Multiplying, for \(l = 2k \geq 2\) and for \(l = 2k + 1 \leq 2m - 1\) we obtain
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {AM}_{2m} = l\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(A_l\right) \cdot \mathbb {P}\left(B_l\right) = \frac{1}{2}\,  u_{2k}\,  u_{2m-2k}
\]
Boundary cases: for \(l = 0\) the event \(A_0\) is trivial (\(\mathbb {P}\left(A_0\right) = 1\)), so \(\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {AM}_{2m} = 0\right) = u_{2m}\) — the factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) disappears; for \(l = 2m\) it is \(B_{2m}\) that is trivial, and \(\mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {AM}_{2m} = 2m\right) = \frac{1}{2}u_{2m}\) (this is a special case of the general formula at \(k = m\)).






Let us add the probabilities in pairs \(\left\{ 2k, 2k+1\right\}\): for \(1 \leq k \leq m-1\)
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {AM}_{2m} \in \left\{ 2k, 2k+1\right\} \right) = u_{2k} \,  u_{2m-2k} = \mathbb {P}_{0}\left(\operatorname {LZ}_{2m} = 2k\right)
\]
That is, up to boundary terms (which are of order \(u_{2m} \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi m}} \to 0\) and do not affect the limit), the time of the first maximum has the same distribution as the time of the last zero! The limiting argument is therefore verbatim the same as before, and we obtain the third arcsine law.







Lemma 4 (Arcsine law for the time at which the maximum is attained) Let \(S_{n}\) be the symmetric simple random walk starting from zero. Then \[
  \frac{1}{n}\operatorname {AM}_{n} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \operatorname {Arcsine}
\]




What other arcsine laws are there? The family of such results is noticeably wider than the three facts we proved.

By the symmetry \(S \mapsto -S\), the same laws hold for the fraction of time in the negative half-line and for the time at which the minimum is attained; the first time of the maximum may be replaced by the last — the limit does not change.
All three laws (P. Lévy, 1939) also hold for Brownian motion on the interval \([0,1]\): the time of the last zero, the fraction of time above zero, and the location of the maximum of the trajectory are all arcsine-distributed. We will encounter this last fact again in the chapter on stopping times.
Universality (the Sparre Andersen theorem): the limiting arcsine law for the fraction of time in the positive half-line holds for any random walk with a symmetric, atomless step distribution — the result is essentially combinatorial and does not depend on the specific distribution.
Generalized arcsine laws (Spitzer, Lamperti): if \(\mathbb {P}\left(S_n > 0\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \rho \in (0, 1)\), then the fraction of time in the positive half-line converges in distribution to \(\operatorname {Beta}(\rho , 1 - \rho )\); for \(\rho = \frac{1}{2}\) this is exactly the arcsine distribution.

title: The simple random walk
text:
Footnotes


On the left of the equality are conditional probabilities with respect to random variables (not events). If you have not encountered this construction before in probability courses, interpret this equality as meaning that \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(S_{m+n} = j \;  \left| \;  \begin{array}{rl} S_{0} & = k_0 \\ S_{1} & = k_1 \\ \cdots &  \cdots \\ S_{m-1} & = k_{m-1} \\ S_{m} & = k_{m} \end{array}\right.\right) \;  = \;  \mathbb {P}\left(S_{m+n} = j \mid S_{m} = k_{m}\right)
\] holds for all possible \(k_0, k_1, \ldots , k_m \in \mathbb {Z}\) for which the conditional probability makes sense, i.e., for which the events being conditioned on have positive probability.
We will discuss the rigorous general definition of conditional probability with respect to a random variable later on.↩︎

As already mentioned, a random process \(X=\left(X(t,\omega ), t \in T\right)\) can be viewed from three different perspectives.
Going forward, \(X\) without a subscript will denote the map \(\Omega \to \mathsf{}^T\).

title: Distributions on the space of trajectories
section: 2.1 Constructing a distribution on the space of functions from finite-dimensional distributions
text:
2.1 Constructing a distribution on the space of functions from finite-dimensional distributions
We have established that the distribution \(\mathbf{P}\) (i.e., a probability measure on \((\mathsf{S}^T, \mathscr {B}^T)\)) is uniquely determined by the finite-dimensional distributions
\[
  \mathbf{P}_{t_1,\ldots ,t_n} := \mathbf{P} \circ \pi _{t_1,\ldots ,t_n}, \qquad t_1,\ldots ,t_n \in T
\]
A natural question arises: under what conditions can the distribution \(\mathbf{P}\) on the whole (typically infinite-dimensional) \((\mathsf{S}^T, \mathscr {B}^T)\) be recovered from given finite-dimensional distributions \(\mathbf{P}_{t_1,\ldots ,t_n}\)?
If \(\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{P}_X\), i.e., \(\mathbf{P}\) is the distribution of some random function \(X\), then note that
\[
  \mathbf{P}_{t_1, \ldots , t_n}\left(B_1 \times \dots \times B_n\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(\bigcap _{k=1}^n X_{t_k}^{-1}(B_k)\right),
\]
where \(B_1, \ldots , B_n \in \mathscr {B}\). From this relation follow the symmetry and consistency conditions for finite-dimensional distributions: \(\forall n \geq 2, \;  \forall t_1, \ldots , t_n\) a collection of distinct points from \(T\), \(\forall B_1, \ldots , B_n \in \mathscr {B}\)

\(\mathbf{P}_{t_1, \ldots , t_n}\left(B_1 \times \dots \times B_n\right) = \mathbf{P}_{t_{i_1}, \ldots , t_{i_n}}\left(B_{i_1} \times \dots \times B_{i_n}\right)\) for any permutation \((i_1, \ldots , i_n)\) of the numbers \((1, \ldots , n)\);
\(\mathbf{P}_{t_1, \ldots , t_n}\left(B_1 \times \dots \times B_{n-1} \times \mathsf{S}\right) = \mathbf{P}_{t_1, \ldots , t_{n-1}}\left(B_1 \times \dots \times B_{n-1}\right)\).

It turns out that, under certain topological restrictions on \((\mathsf{S}, \mathscr {B})\), conditions ,  are sufficient for \(\mathbf{P}\) to exist.







Theorem 1 (Kolmogorov) Let a collection of distributions be given \[
  \left\{ \mathbf{P}_{t_1,\ldots ,t_n}\text{ -- a distribution on } (\mathsf{S}^n,\mathscr {B}^n) \;  : \;  n \in \mathbb {N}, t_1, \ldots , t_n \in T, \;  t_i \neq t_j\right\}
\] satisfying the symmetry and consistency conditions , . Then there exists a distribution \(\mathbf{P}\) on \((\mathsf{}^T, \mathscr {B}^T)\) whose finite-dimensional distributions are exactly the distributions given above.




We have obtained a probability measure \(\mathbf{P}\) on \((\mathsf{}^T, \mathscr {B}^T)\). But how do we now obtain a random element (random function) \(X\) with this distribution? Recall the canonical model:
\[
  (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) := \left(\mathsf{}^T, \mathscr {B}^T\right), \qquad X := \operatorname {Id}
\]
That is, we define \(X\) as the identity map on the space of trajectories. In this case
\[
  (X_t)_{t \in T} = (\pi _t)_{t \in T},
\]
since \(X_t = \pi_t \circ X = \pi_t \circ \operatorname {Id}\). In other words, the (one-dimensional) projections of the space of trajectories themselves play the role of the random process. This construction is called the canonical model.

title: Distributions on the space of trajectories
section: 2.2 Consistency conditions via characteristic functions for random functions with values in
text:
2.2 Consistency conditions via characteristic functions for random functions with values in 
Recall that there is a one-to-one correspondence between probability measures on \((\mathbb {R}^{n}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{n}\right))\) and their characteristic functions. Let us reformulate conditions ,  in terms of characteristic functions.







Theorem 2 Let a collection of distributions \(\mathbb {P}_{t_1, \dots , t_n}\) on \((\mathbb {R}^{n}, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}^{n}\right))\) be given, \(n \in \mathbb {N}, \;  t_1, \ldots , t_n \in T, t_i \neq t_j\) for \(i \neq j\). Denote by \(\varphi_{t_1,\dots ,t_n}\) the characteristic function of \(\mathbb {P}_{t_1, \dots , t_n}\). Then the symmetry and consistency conditions ,  are equivalent to the following conditions:

\(\varphi_{t_{i_1}, \ldots , t_{i_n}}(\lambda_{i_1}, \ldots , \lambda_{i_n}) = \varphi_{t_1, \ldots , t_n}(\lambda_1, \ldots , \lambda_n)\) for any permutation \((i_1, \ldots , i_n)\) of the numbers \((1, \ldots , n)\);
\(\varphi_{t_1, \ldots , t_{n-1}, t_n}(\lambda_1, \ldots , \lambda_{n-1}, 0) = \varphi_{t_1, \ldots , t_{n-1}}(\lambda_1, \ldots , \lambda_{n-1})\).

title: Distributions on the space of trajectories
section: 2.3 A special case of constructing a distribution: independent increments
text:
2.3 A special case of constructing a distribution: independent increments
Let us recall the definition.







Definition 2 A process \(\left(X_{t}, t \geqslant 0\right)\) is called a process with independent increments if \(\forall n \in \mathbb {N} \;  \forall 0 \leqslant t_{1}<\ldots <t_{n}\) the random variables \(X_{t_{n}}-X_{t_{n-1}}, \ldots , X_{t_{2}}-X_{t_{1}}, X_{t_{1}}\) are jointly independent.




Note that in discrete time, a process with independent increments is nothing but a random walk. Thus, it is natural to view processes with independent increments as the continuous-time generalization of random walks.







Theorem 3 (Kolmogorov’s existence theorem for processes with independent increments) Let the initial (one-dimensional) distribution of the process \(\mathbb {Q}_0\) and a collection of (one-dimensional) probability distributions of the increments of the process \(\left\{ \mathbb {Q}_{s,t}: \;  0 \leq s < t < +\infty \right\}\) with characteristic functions \(\left\{ \varphi_{s,t}\right\}\) be given. A process \((X_t, t \geq 0)\) with independent increments satisfying \(X_0 \sim \mathbb {Q}_0, \;  X_{t}-X_{s} \sim \mathbb {Q}_{s, t}, 0 \leq s < t\), exists if and only if \[
  \varphi _{s,t} = \varphi _{s,u} \cdot \varphi _{u,t}, \quad \forall 0\leq s < u < t.
\]










ExampleExample 1





Prove Theorem Theorem 3.






SolutionSolution





In one direction: obvious.
In the other direction: without loss of generality, let \(\mathbb {Q}_0 = \delta_0\). Let \(\varphi_{s,t} = \varphi_{s,u} \cdot \varphi_{u,t}\). Let us prove that the process exists. Let \(\varphi_{t_1, \ldots , t_n} = \varphi_{X_{t_1}, \ldots , X_{t_n}}\), \(t_1 < \dots < t_n\), be the characteristic function of its finite-dimensional distribution. Let us check that the consistency condition holds. Let \(\lambda = (\lambda_1, \dots , \lambda_n)^T \in \mathbb {R}^{n}\). We have
\[
\begin{align}  \varphi _{t_1, \ldots , t_n}(\lambda ) & = \mathbb {E}\left[e^{i \left\langle (X_{t_1}, \ldots , X_{t_n})^T, \lambda \right\rangle }\right] = \\ & = \mathbb {E}\left[e^{i \left\langle A^{-1}A(X_{t_1}, \ldots , X_{t_n})^T, \lambda \right\rangle }\right] = \\ & = \mathbb {E}\left[e^{i \left\langle A(X_{t_1}, \ldots , X_{t_n})^T, (A^{-1})^T\lambda \right\rangle }\right] = \\ & = \varphi _{A(X_{t_1}, \ldots , X_{t_n})^T}((A^{-1})^T\lambda ), \end{align}
\]
where
\[
\begin{align}  A & = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  0 &  0 &  0 &  \dots &  0 &  0 \\ -1 &  1 &  0 &  0 &  0 &  \dots &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  -1 &  1 &  0 &  0 &  \dots &  0 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  -1 &  1 &  0 &  \dots &  0 &  0 \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \ddots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ 0 &  0 &  0 &  0 &  0 &  \dots &  -1 &  1 \\ \end{pmatrix}, \\ A^{-1} & = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 &  0 &  0 &  0 &  \dots &  0 &  0 \\ 1 &  1 &  0 &  0 &  0 &  \dots &  0 &  0 \\ 1 &  1 &  1 &  0 &  0 &  \dots &  0 &  0 \\ 1 &  1 &  1 &  1 &  0 &  \dots &  0 &  0 \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \ddots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ 1 &  1 &  1 &  1 &  1 &  \dots &  1 &  1 \\ \end{pmatrix}, \\ (A^{-1})^T & = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  1 &  1 &  1 &  1 &  \dots &  1 &  1 \\ 0 &  1 &  1 &  1 &  1 &  \dots &  1 &  1 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 &  1 &  1 &  \dots &  1 &  1 \\ 0 &  0 &  0 &  1 &  1 &  \dots &  1 &  1 \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \ddots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ 0 &  0 &  0 &  0 &  0 &  \dots &  0 &  1 \\ \end{pmatrix} \end{align}
\]
Therefore, denoting \(\lambda ' := (A^{-1})^T\lambda\), i.e., \(\lambda '_k = \lambda_k + \ldots + \lambda_n\), and using independence of the increments, we have
\[
\begin{align}  \varphi _{t_1, \ldots , t_n}(\lambda ) & = \varphi _{X_{t_1}, X_{t_2}-X_{t_1}, \ldots , X_{t_n} - X_{t_{n-1}}}(\lambda ^\prime ) = \\ & = \varphi _{0, t_1}\left(\sum _{i=1}^n\lambda _i\right) \cdot \prod _{k=2}^{n} \varphi _{t_{k-1}, t_k}\left(\sum _{i=k}^n\lambda _i\right) \end{align}
\]
This calculation was carried out for a hypothetical process \(X\) (which does not yet exist); let us now take its right-hand side as the definition of the characteristic functions \(\varphi_{t_1, \ldots , t_n}\) for ordered collections \(t_1 < \ldots < t_n\) (extend to unordered collections by symmetry, so that condition  holds automatically), and check the consistency condition from Theorem Theorem 2, doing so directly in the strengthened form: with any coordinate \(\lambda_k\) set to zero, not just the last. For \(\lambda_k = 0\) we have \(\lambda '_k = \lambda '_{k+1}\), and two adjacent factors merge into one exactly by the condition of the theorem:
\[
  \varphi _{t_{k-1}, t_k}(\lambda '_{k+1}) \cdot \varphi _{t_k, t_{k+1}}(\lambda '_{k+1}) = \varphi _{t_{k-1}, t_{k+1}}(\lambda '_{k+1}),
\]
and we obtain exactly the characteristic function of the collection without the point \(t_k\) (at \(k = n\) the last factor simply becomes \(\varphi_{t_{n-1}, t_n}(0) = 1\)). It is precisely here that the condition \(\varphi_{s,t} = \varphi_{s,u} \cdot \varphi_{u,t}\) is used. The consistency conditions have been checked, and by Kolmogorov’s existence theorem (Theorem Theorem 1) the desired process exists.













Definition 3 Let \(\Lambda\) be some measure (i.e., a nonnegative countably additive set function) on \((\mathbb {R}_+, \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}_+\right))\) with density \(\lambda (t)\) with respect to Lebesgue measure \(\mu\): \[
  \Lambda (B) = \int _{B} \lambda (t) \;  \mu (dt), \qquad B \in \mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}_+\right)
\] A random process \(\left(N_{t}, t \geqslant 0\right)\) is called an (inhomogeneous) Poisson process with intensity function \(\lambda (t)\) if the following three conditions hold:

\(N_{0}=0\) a.s.;
\(N_{t}\) has independent increments;
\(N_{t}-N_{s}\) has a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\Lambda (s,t]\) for all \(0 \leq s \leq t < \infty\).





Note that these conditions are imposed only on the distribution of the process on the space of trajectories. In this sense, this definition is really a definition of the distribution of the Poisson random function on the space of trajectories. However, in most sources the notions of a random process and its distribution are used interchangeably.
If \(\lambda (t) \equiv \operatorname {const}\), then the Poisson process with such intensity is called homogeneous. We have already encountered precisely the homogeneous Poisson process earlier. Note, moreover, that we constructed the homogeneous Poisson process explicitly, as a renewal process. And it immediately had nice trajectories: they were all right-continuous with finite left limits.






ProblemProblem 2





Prove that the inhomogeneous Poisson process exists.
This problem only requires proving the existence of a distribution on \((\mathbb {R}^T, \mathscr {B}^T)\) with the stated properties. For practical purposes we would like more: that, as in the homogeneous case, the inhomogeneous process has trajectories that are right-continuous with finite left limits. This is exactly how a store’s customer counter behaves in practice. For more on obtaining nice trajectories, see below.






HintHint





Characteristic function of the Poisson distribution: \(\varphi_{\operatorname {Pois}\left(\alpha \right)}(t) = \mathrm{exp}\left(\alpha (e^{it} - 1)\right)\)






The top panel shows the intensity ((t) = 0 + A(1.5t-1)); the bottom panel shows a trajectory of (N_t) simulated by thinning, with red marks at the jump times: a homogeneous Poisson process of rate ({}=0+A) is generated, and each point is independently retained with probability ((t)/{}). Move the sliders (_0) and (A) to see how the density of jumps tracks the intensity, and click “New realization” to regenerate the trajectory for the same ((t)).

title: Distributions on the space of trajectories
text:
5.1 Continuous trajectories
For simplicity let \(T = [0,1]\) (one could take \(\mathbb {R}_+\) or \(\mathbb {R}\); the computations in this section would not change).
Suppose that all (or almost all) trajectories of the process \(X(\omega ) = X(t,\omega )\) are continuous, i.e., \(\mathbb {P}\left(\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega ) \in C[0,1]\right) = 1\). Denote the cylindrical \(\sigma\)-algebra on the space \(C[0,1]\) by \(C[0,1] \cap \mathscr {B}^{[0,1]}\) and define it as the intersection of elements of the cylindrical sigma-algebra \(\mathscr {B}^{[0,1]}\) on \(\mathbb {R}^{[0,1]}\) with \(C[0,1]\):
\[
  C[0,1] \cap \mathscr {B}^{[0,1]} := \left\{ C[0,1] \cap B: \;  B \in \mathscr {B}^{[0,1]}\right\}
\]
It is not hard to prove that this is indeed a sigma-algebra, and moreover it is generated by the intersections of cylinders with \(C[0,1]\):
\[
\begin{align}   C[0,1] \cap \mathscr {B}^{[0,1]} & = \\ & \quad \sigma \left(\left\{ C[0,1] \cap \pi ^{-1}_{t_1,\ldots ,t_n}(B) \;  : \;  n \in \mathbb {N}, \;  0 \leq t_1 < \ldots < t_n \leq 1, \;  B \in \mathscr {B}^n\right\} \right) \end{align}
\tag{1}\]
Recall that \(C([0,1])\) carries yet another sigma-algebra — the Borel sigma-algebra \(\mathscr {B}\left(C[0,1]\right)\), generated by the open balls in the supremum metric
\[
  \rho (f', f'') = \sup \limits _{t \in [0,1]} \left|f'(t) - f''(t)\right|.
\]
It turns out that the following lemma holds.







Lemma 2 On \(C[0,1]\), the Borel sigma-algebra \(\mathscr {B}\left(C[0,1]\right)\) and the cylindrical sigma-algebra coincide: \[
  \mathscr {B}\left(C[0,1]\right) = C[0,1] \cap \mathscr {B}^{[0,1]}
\]










ProblemProblem 6





Prove Lemma Lemma 2.



We obtain the following result.







Theorem 4 Let \(X = (X_t, t \in [0,1])\) be a real-valued random process such that almost all its trajectories are continuous, i.e., \(\mathbb {P}\left(X \in C[0,1]\right) = 1\). Then the process \(X\) is \(\mathcal{F}|\mathscr {B}\left(C[0,1]\right)\)-measurable as a map \[
  X: (\Omega , \mathcal{F}) \to (C[0,1], \mathscr {B}\left(C[0,1]\right)).
\]










ProblemProblem 7





Let \(X = (X_t, t \in [0,1])\) be a real-valued random process with a.s. continuous trajectories. Prove that in this case \[
  \left\{ \sup _{t \in [0,1]} X(t) \leq \alpha \right\}  = \left\{ X \in M_\alpha \right\}  = X^{-1}(M_\alpha ) \in \mathcal{F}, \;  \forall \alpha \in \mathbb {R}.
\]
This problem shows that if we have an a.s. continuous process \(X\), we may freely find the probability that its trajectories do not exceed an arbitrary level \(\alpha\).



Recall that Kolmogorov’s existence theorem allowed us to construct a process with prescribed consistent finite-dimensional distributions, with values in an arbitrary Borel space, for example, in the space \((\mathbb {R},\mathscr {B}\left(\mathbb {R}\right))\). However, this theorem said nothing about the trajectories of this process. Obtaining continuous trajectories for a process is aided by the following theorem, also proved by Kolmogorov.







Theorem 5 (Kolmogorov’s continuous modification theorem) Let \(X = (X_t, t \in T)\), where \(T = [0,1]\) or \(\mathbb {R}_+\) or \(\mathbb {R}\), be a real-valued random process such that there exist \(\alpha , \varepsilon > 0\), \(C = C(\alpha , \varepsilon ) > 0\) such that \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\left|X_t - X_s\right|^\alpha \right] \leq C \left|t-s\right|^{1 + \varepsilon }, \quad \forall t,s \in T.
\tag{2}\] Then the process \(X\) has a continuous version (modification).




Recall that \(Y = (Y_t)\) is a modification of the process \(X = (X_t)\) if they coincide a.s. at each point \(t \in T\): \(\mathbb {P}\left(X_t = Y_t\right) = 1\), \(\forall t \in T\). This theorem says that if the distribution of the process \(X = (X_t)\) satisfies condition Equation 2 (i.e., the expectations of the increments of the process are, in some sense, bounded by the increments of the argument), then this process can always be “slightly” redefined at each point \(t\) (i.e., redefined on a set of measure zero) so that the new version of the process has a.s. continuous trajectories.






ProblemProblem 8






Prove that a stationary Poisson process \(\left(X_{t}, t \geq 0\right)\) of intensity \(\lambda >0\) has no continuous modification, i.e., no modification all of whose trajectories are continuous.
Using the previous part, show that if we set \(\varepsilon = 0\) in condition (Equation 2), the theorem need not hold in general.

title: Distributions on the space of trajectories
text:
5.2 Càdlàg trajectories
Càdlàg is an abbreviation of the French continue à droite, limite à gauche, right-continuous with finite left limits. Processes with such trajectories are very common in the theory of random processes and in stochastic calculus. The theory of random processes was actively developed in France in the second half of the 20th century, which is why this French abbreviation is conventionally used to refer to such trajectories concisely. All possible càdlàg trajectories on \(T\) are called the Skorokhod space on \(T\) and are denoted
\[
  D(T)
\]
The space \(D(T)\), like \(C(T)\), has a wealth of nice properties. To avoid overloading the exposition, we will not present them here. For more detail, see (Биллингсли 1977). Here we will give a certain analogue of Kolmogorov’s continuous modification theorem.







Theorem 6 (On the nondecreasing càdlàg modification) Let \(X=\left(X_{t}, t \geq 0\right)\) be a random process that is

stochastically nondecreasing, i.e., \(\mathbb {P}\left(X_{s} \leq X_{t}\right) = 1\) for all \(0 \leq s \leq t<\infty\);
right-continuous in probability: at every point \(s\) of the ray \([0, \infty )\) we have

\[
  X_t \xrightarrow [t \to s+0]{\mathbb {P}} X_s, \quad \forall s \geq 0.
\] Then \(X\) has a modification with a.s. nondecreasing càdlàg trajectories.










ProblemProblem 9





Show that for the inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity function \(\lambda (t)\), one can obtain a version with nondecreasing càdlàg trajectories.










Lemma 3 Let \(f(x)\) be a function on \([0,1]\) that is nondecreasing along rational points. Then the function \(\tilde{f}(x)\), defined as \[
  \tilde{f}(x)=\lim _{r \rightarrow x+0, r \in \mathbb {Q}} f(r), \quad x \in [0,1), \qquad \tilde{f}(1) := f(1),
\] is right-continuous and nondecreasing.










ProblemProblem 10






Prove Lemma Lemma 3;
Using Lemma Lemma 3, prove Theorem Theorem 6.

title: Discrete-Time Markov Chains (DTMC)
text:
WarningDraft



This lecture note is still being edited: the text may contain typos, inaccuracies, and locally unpolished spots. If you find something, please let the author know (contact details on the course page).
The simple random walk and the Galton-Watson branching process had the following property: conditionally on the value at step \(n\), their future values did not depend on the previous values. This property turned out to be very useful in their analysis, and we now turn to the general theory of processes with this property.

title: Discrete-Time Markov Chains (DTMC)
text:
3.1 Communicating states
In the theory of Markov chains, states \(i,j \in \mathcal{X}\) are called communicating if they are strongly connected in the transition graph: it is possible with positive probability (in some finite number of steps) to go from \(i\) to \(j\) and from \(j\) to \(i\). The strongly connected components are called communicating classes.
A state is called transient if it is possible to leave this state and, with some positive probability, never return to it. Otherwise, i.e. when starting from the state one returns to it eventually with probability \(1\), the state is called recurrent.







Lemma 3  

Within the same class all states are either simultaneously recurrent or simultaneously transient. In other words, each communicating class is either entirely recurrent or entirely transient.
Determining the type of a class (recurrent/transient) is simple: if the class is closed, i.e. there are no transitions out of it, then it is recurrent. Otherwise it is transient. 1











ExampleExample 6





The (one-step) transition probabilities of some Markov chain are given as a graph.


                                                
Transition probability graph of a Markov chain (the vertices are deliberately left unlabeled — the task is to determine the communicating classes and their type on your own).



Determine the communicating classes of states.
For each class, determine whether it is recurrent or not.
Number the classes so that the transient ones come first, followed by the recurrent ones. Moreover, number the transient ones so that transitions are only possible from a smaller to a larger number.
Number the vertices. Write down the transition matrix of this chain.







SolutionSolution







                                                
The same graph with numbered states and highlighted communicating classes: I, II are transient, III, IV, V are recurrent.


The transient classes (I, II) are shaded in yellow-orange tones, and the recurrent classes (III, IV, V) in blue tones; the border color of each vertex reflects this same division.


                                                
The full transition matrix P in the canonical numbering of the states from the example above. Color highlights only the diagonal blocks corresponding to communicating classes: yellow and orange are the transient classes {1,2,3} and {4,5}; blue, teal, and purple are the recurrent (closed) classes {6,7,8}, {9}, and {10,11,12,13}. Hover over a cell to see the transition probability.


Why the \(2 \times 2\) blocks in the lower-right submatrix (shown in teal, corresponding to class V) are highlighted will become clear a bit later.






The numbering of states obtained in the example above is called canonical. This is a numbering under which the transition matrix has the block form \[
\mathbf{P} =
\left(
\begin{array}{c|c}
\mathbf{T}_{11} & \mathbf{T}_{12} \\ \hline
\mathbf{0} & \mathbf{T}_{22}
\end{array}
\right)
\]
Block form of the transition matrix under the canonical numbering of states: \(\mathbf{T}_{11}\) is the transitions within and between transient classes, \(\mathbf{T}_{12}\) is the transitions from transient classes into recurrent ones, \(\mathbf{T}_{22}\) is the transitions within recurrent classes, and \(\mathbf{0}\) is the block accounting for the (impossible) transitions from recurrent classes into transient ones. The block sizes depend on the specific chain, so the matrix is shown schematically.

\(\mathbf{T}_{11}\) is responsible for transitions within transient classes and between transient classes. Let \(r\) be the number of transient classes. Then \(\mathbf{T}_{11}\) is a square matrix with block structure
\[
  \mathbf{T}_{11} = \begin{pmatrix}  \mathbf{P}_{11} &  \mathbf{P}_{12} &  \cdots &  \mathbf{P}_{1r} \\ \mathbf{0} &  \mathbf{P}_{22} &  \cdots &  \mathbf{P}_{2r} \\ \vdots &  \ddots &  \ddots &  \vdots \\ \mathbf{0} &  \cdots &  \mathbf{0} &  \mathbf{P}_{rr} \\ \end{pmatrix}
\]
The matrix is upper triangular (viewed block-wise). Under the canonical numbering, transitions are only possible from a transient class of smaller number to one of larger number.
\(\mathbf{T}_{12}\) is responsible for transitions from transient classes to recurrent ones. Let \(m\) be the total number of classes. Then \(\mathbf{T}_{12}\) has the form
\[
  \mathbf{T}_{12} = \begin{pmatrix}  \mathbf{P}_{1,r+1} &  \cdots &  \mathbf{P}_{1m} \\ \vdots &  \cdots &  \vdots \\ \mathbf{P}_{r,r+1} &  \cdots &  \mathbf{P}_{rm} \\ \end{pmatrix}
\]
\(\mathbf{T}_{22}\) is responsible for transitions within recurrent classes (transitions between recurrent classes are impossible by definition). It has block form
\[
  \mathbf{T}_{22} = \begin{pmatrix}  \mathbf{P}_{r+1,r+1} &  \mathbf{0} &  \mathbf{0} &  \cdots &  \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{0} &  \mathbf{P}_{r+1,r+1} &  \mathbf{0} &  \cdots &  \mathbf{0} \\ \vdots &  \cdots &  \cdots &  \cdots &  \vdots \\ \mathbf{0} &  \mathbf{0} &  \cdots &  \mathbf{P}_{m-1,m-1} &  \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{0} &  \mathbf{0} &  \cdots &  \mathbf{0} &  \mathbf{P}_{mm} \\ \end{pmatrix}
\]

Any DTMC with a finite number of states can be brought to this form.

title: Discrete-Time Markov Chains (DTMC)
text:
3.2 Limiting behavior
We are interested in the behavior of the chain as \(n\) grows. As we have already established, the distribution at step \(n\) is given by \(\Pi^{(n)} = \Pi^{(0)} \cdot \mathbf{P}^n\). Let us examine the behavior of the matrices \(\mathbf{P}^n\) as \(n\) grows, as well as the sequence of arithmetic means
\[
  \frac{1}{n}\left(\mathbf{P}^0 + \mathbf{P}^1 + \ldots + \mathbf{P}^{n-1}\right)
\]
(\(\mathbf{P}^0 = E\)).
We say the sequence of matrices \(\mathbf{P}^0, \mathbf{P}^1, \mathbf{P}^2, \ldots\) converges if each of its entries converges. We say the same sequence is Cesàro summable (Cesàro convergent) if the sequence of arithmetic means \(\frac{1}{n}\left(\mathbf{P}^0 + \mathbf{P}^1 + \ldots + \mathbf{P}^{n-1}\right)\) has an entrywise limit.
Recall that if a numerical sequence converges (in the ordinary sense), it also converges in the Cesàro sense, with the same limit. However, Cesàro convergence is a more general notion. For example, the sequence \(1,0,1,0,1,0, \ldots\) does not converge, yet the sequence of arithmetic means
\[
  \frac{1}{1}, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{2}{3}, \frac{2}{4}, \frac{3}{5}, \frac{3}{6}, \ldots , \frac{n}{2n}, \frac{n+1}{2n+1}, \ldots
\]
converges to \(\frac{1}{2}\). That is, the sequence is Cesàro summable. It is therefore convenient to first study the Cesàro limit, and then the ordinary limit.
Let us look at heat maps of the sequences \(\mathbf{P}^n\) and \(\frac{1}{n}(\mathbf{P}^0 + \ldots + \mathbf{P}^{n-1})\) for the example above.


                                                
Animation of the evolution of Pⁿ for n = 0,1,2,…,40 (the same matrix as in the example above). Use the slider or the Play button to track how the matrix entries change as n grows.




                                                
The limit lim Pⁿ (to 2 decimal places, where it exists). The diagonal blocks of the transient classes {1,2,3}, {4,5} tend to zero (the chain leaves the transient states almost surely). The block of the recurrent class {6,7,8} and the absorbing state {9} converge to their stationary values. But for the periodic (period 2) class {10,11,12,13}, as well as for all transitions from transient states into this class, the limit of Pⁿ does not exist – the matrix merely oscillates between two limit points as n grows (see also the animation above and the Cesàro limit below, which always exists).




                                                
Animation of the evolution of the Cesàro averages Cₙ = (1/n)(P⁰+P¹+…+Pⁿ⁻¹) for the same transition matrix P. Unlike Pⁿ (see the animation above), this sequence converges entrywise as n → ∞ for all blocks of the matrix, including the periodic recurrent class {10,11,12,13}.




                                                
The Cesàro limit lim(1/n)·(P⁰+P¹+…+Pⁿ⁻¹) for the transition matrix P from the example above. Unlike the ordinary limit of Pⁿ, the Cesàro limit exists for all blocks – including the periodic recurrent class {10,11,12,13}. The values are computed exactly: for each recurrent class, the row of the limit coincides with its stationary distribution, and for transient states it is the absorption probability into the class multiplied by the stationary distribution within it.


As can be seen from the heat-map animations, some of the entries of the sequence \((\mathbf{P}^n, \;  n \in \mathbb {Z}_+)\) converge, while others do not. At the same time \((\mathbf{P}^n, \;  n \in \mathbb {Z}_+)\) is Cesàro summable. In fact, \(\mathbf{P}^n\) will always be Cesàro summable. See below.
What is the probabilistic meaning of the Cesàro limit? Let us examine \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbf{P}^{k}\). Its \(i,j\) entry equals
\[
\begin{align}  \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbf{P}^{k}\right)_{ij} & = \frac{1}{n}\bigg(\mathbb {P}_{i}\left(X_{0} = j\right) + \mathbb {P}_{i}\left(X_{1} = j\right) + \ldots + \mathbb {P}_{i}\left(X_{n-1} = j\right)\bigg) = \\ & = \frac{1}{n} \bigg( \mathbb {E}_{i}\left[\; \mathbb {1}_{X_{0} = j}\right] + \mathbb {E}_{i}\left[\; \mathbb {1}_{X_{1} = j}\right] + \ldots + \mathbb {E}_{i}\left[\; \mathbb {1}_{X_{n-1} = j}\right] \bigg) = \\ & = \mathbb {E}_{i}\left[\frac{\; \mathbb {1}_{X_0 = j} + \; \mathbb {1}_{X_1 = j} + \ldots + \; \mathbb {1}_{X_{n-1} = j}}{n}\right] = \\ & = \mathbb {E}_{i}\left[\frac{1}{n} \sum _{k=0}^{n-1} \; \mathbb {1}_{X_k = j}\right] \end{align}
\]
Let us introduce the notation:
\[
  V^{(n)}_{j} := \left|\left\{ 0 \leq k \leq n \;  : \;  X_{k} = j\right\} \right| = \sum _{k=0}^{n} \; \mathbb {1}_{X_k = j}
\]
The sum of indicators \(V^{(n-1)}_j = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \; \mathbb {1}_{X_k = j}\) is the number of visits (hence the letter \(V\)) to state \(j\) at times \(0, 1, \ldots , n-1\). Dividing by \(n\), i.e. by the total time, gives the visit frequency of state \(j\). Hence the \(i,j\) entry of the matrix \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbf{P}^{k}\) is the expected visit frequency of state \(j\) over \(n\) steps, given that the chain started at state \(i\).
Note that (for fixed \(j\)) the process \(V^{(n)}_{j}, n \geq 0\) is almost a renewal process. Namely, let \(\tau^{(k)}_j\) be the time of the \(k\)-th visit to state \(j\). These can be defined inductively:
\[
\begin{align}  \tau _{j}^{(1)} & := \min \left\{ n \geq 0 \;  : \;  X_n = j\right\}  \\ \tau _{j}^{(k)} & := \min \left\{ n > \tau _{j}^{(k-1)} \;  : \;  X_n = j\right\} , \;  k \geq 2 \end{align}
\]






Mn-extraAdditional material






Relation to the old notation from the random walk: \(\tau_j = \tau^{(1)}_j\) is the time of the first visit to \(j\), \[
  T_j = \min \left\{ n \geq 1 \;  : \;  X_n = j\right\}  = \begin{cases}  \tau ^{(1)}_j, &  X_0 \neq j \\ \tau ^{(2)}_j, &  X_0 = j \end{cases}
\] is the time of the first visit to \(j\) after step \(1\). Along the way, note that by definition state \(j\) is called recurrent if \[
  \mathbb {P}_{j}\left(\tau ^{(2)}_j < \infty \right) = 1 \quad \text{or, equivalently, } \quad \mathbb {P}_{j}\left(T_j < \infty \right) = 1
\]




In this case \(V^{(n)}_j\) is a visit counter built from
\[
\begin{align}  \xi ^{(1)}_j & := \tau _{j}^{(1)}, \\ & \quad \xi ^{(2)}_j := \tau _{j}^{(2)} - \tau _{j}^{(1)}, \\ & \quad \xi ^{(3)}_j := \tau _{j}^{(3)} - \tau _{j}^{(2)}, \ldots \end{align}
\]
We have already studied such processes in detail, renewal processes in particular. Let’s try to apply what we know!
Recall that in the definition of a renewal process we required \(\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots\) to be nonnegative i.i.d. random variables with a nondegenerate distribution. We need to understand how \(\xi^{(1)}_j, \xi^{(2)}_j, \xi^{(3)}_j, \ldots\) are distributed. Are they i.i.d.?
What follows is a slightly informal argument, since writing it out formally would be long and tedious, and after all these are seminar notes rather than lecture notes. The Markov property: the process, upon entering state \(j\), forgets its previous behavior. Hence, for any initial distribution \(\Pi\) (i.e. under any \(\mathbb {P}_{\Pi }\)) these random variables are independent. Moreover, again due to the Markov property, \(\xi^{(2)}_j, \xi^{(3)}_j, \ldots\) will be identically distributed (and this distribution also does not depend on \(\Pi\), since it is characterized only by the fact that the process has entered state \(j\) at some fixed step, and hence it no longer matters how it got there). The distribution of \(\xi^{(1)}_j = \tau^{(1)}_j\), however, may differ from the rest. For example, if the process a.s. starts at \(j\), i.e. \(\Pi_i = \delta_i^j\), then \(\xi^{(1)}_j \equiv 0\),
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{j}\left(\tau ^{(1)}_j = 0\right) = 1,
\]
while \(\xi^{(2)}_j, \xi^{(3)}_j, \ldots\) will still have some nontrivial distribution.
So, \(\xi^{(1)}_j, \xi^{(2)}_j, \xi^{(3)}_j, \ldots\) are independent random variables, all identically distributed except for the first time. Recall that \(\tau^{(m)}_j = \xi^{(1)}_j + \ldots + \xi^{(m)}_j\). The process
\[
  V^{(n-1)}_j = \max \left\{ m \geq 1 \;  : \;  \tau ^{(m)}_j \leq n-1\right\}  = \sum _{k=0}^{n-1} \; \mathbb {1}_{X_k = j} , \qquad n \geq 1
\]
(the maximum over the empty set is taken to be \(0\)) is called a delayed renewal process.
What are the limiting properties of a delayed renewal process? It turns out that the elementary renewal theorem remains valid in many cases.







Theorem 3 (Elementary renewal theorem for a delayed process) Let \(\xi_1, \xi_2, \xi_3, \ldots\) be independent random variables with values in \([0, +\infty ]\), where \(\xi_2, \xi_3, \ldots\) are identically distributed and \(\mathbb {E}\left[\xi_2\right] > 0\). Then, if \(\mathbb {P}\left(\xi_1 < \infty \right) = 1\), the delayed renewal process built from them, \(N_t = \max \left\{ n \;  : \;  \xi_1 + \ldots + \xi_n \leq t\right\}\), satisfies the elementary renewal theorem for the ordinary renewal process built from \(\xi_2, \xi_3, \ldots\): \[
  \frac{\mathbb {E}\left[N_t\right]}{t} \xrightarrow [t \to +\infty ]{} \frac{1}{\mathbb {E}\left[\xi _2\right]}
\]




See the proof in (Grimmett and Stirzaker 2020, Theorem 10.4.15).
Let us first consider some special cases.

title: Discrete-Time Markov Chains (DTMC)
text:
3.3 Irreducible chains
A Markov chain is called irreducible if all its states form a single communicating class (which in this case must be closed). Studying a chain with more than one communicating class essentially reduces to studying its “restrictions” to the various classes.
One can show that if a chain is irreducible and has a finite number of states, then
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{i}\left(\tau _j < \infty \right) = \mathbb {P}_{j}\left(T_j < \infty \right) = 1, \qquad \forall i,j \in \mathcal{X}
\]
That is, from any state, any other state is reached in an a.s. finite time, and all states are recurrent. Such a chain is not transient2.
Returning to the delayed renewal process, in this case we have
\[
  \mathbb {P}_{i}\left(\xi ^{(1)}_j < \infty \right) = 1
\]
(recall that \(\xi^{(1)}_j = \tau^{(1)}_j = \tau_j\)). That is, starting at state \(i\), the process reaches state \(j\) a.s. in finite time. The counter overcomes the first barrier \(\xi^{(1)}_j\) a.s. in finite time. In this case, \(\xi^{(2)}_j, \xi^{(3)}_j, \ldots\) then come into play, which are i.i.d., so the limiting properties of the process are the same as for the ordinary renewal process built from \(\xi^{(2)}_j, \xi^{(3)}_j, \ldots\). In particular, the elementary renewal theorem holds:
\[
\begin{align}  \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbf{P}^{k}\right)_{ij} & = \frac{1}{n} \cdot \mathbb {E}_{i}\left[ V^{(n-1)}_j\right] \quad \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \\ & \quad \frac{1}{\mathbb {E}_{i}\left[\xi ^{(2)}_j\right]} \end{align}
\]
Note that \(\xi^{(2)}_j = \tau^{(2)}_j - \tau^{(1)}_j\) is the time between the first and second visit to \(j\). Since the process has already visited \(j\), by the Markov property its distribution, in particular the distribution of \(\xi^{(2)}_j\), does not depend on the initial distribution. In other words,
\[
  \mathbb {E}_{i'}\left[\xi ^{(2)}_j\right] = \mathbb {E}_{i''}\left[\xi ^{(2)}_j\right] = \mathbb {E}_{j}\left[\xi ^{(2)}_j\right]
\]
for all \(i', i'' \in \mathcal{X}\). And if the chain started at \(j\), then \(\tau^{(1)}_j \equiv 0\) and
\[
  \xi ^{(2)}_j = \tau ^{(2)}_j - \tau ^{(1)}_j = \tau ^{(2)}_j = T_j
\]
is the return time to state \(j\). This brings us to the theorem.







Theorem 4 Let \((X_n)\) be an irreducible DTMC with a finite number of states and transition matrix \(\mathbf{P}\). Then the matrices \(\mathbf{P}^0, \mathbf{P}^{1}, \ldots\) have a Cesàro limit: \[
  \frac{1}{n}\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbf{P}^{k}\qquad \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \qquad \begin{pmatrix}  \left(\mathbb {E}_{1}\left[T_1\right]\right)^{-1} &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{2}\left[T_2\right]\right)^{-1} &  \cdots &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\left[T_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\right]\right)^{-1} \\ \left(\mathbb {E}_{1}\left[T_1\right]\right)^{-1} &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{2}\left[T_2\right]\right)^{-1} &  \cdots &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\left[T_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\right]\right)^{-1} \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ \left(\mathbb {E}_{1}\left[T_1\right]\right)^{-1} &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{2}\left[T_2\right]\right)^{-1} &  \cdots &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\left[T_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\right]\right)^{-1} \end{pmatrix}
\] That is, the limit does not depend on the row index \(i\), but only on the column index \(j\), and equals the reciprocal of the mean return time to state \(j\).

title: Discrete-Time Markov Chains (DTMC)
text:
3.4 Stationary distribution
For a homogeneous DTMC, an (initial) distribution \(\Pi\) is called stationary if it does not change with time, i.e.
\[
  \Pi = \Pi \cdot \mathbf{P}
\]
In essence this is a left eigenvector (i.e. a row vector) for the matrix \(\mathbf{P}\). Or, \(\Pi^T\) is a right eigenvector (column vector) for the matrix \(\mathbf{P}^T\). Note that the sum of all columns of the matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) itself equals the column of ones. That is, \((1,1,\ldots ,1)^T\) is a right eigenvector for the matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) with eigenvalue \(1\). The eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{P}\) and \(\mathbf{P}^T\) coincide, so for this eigenvalue there is also a left eigenvector. Moreover it can always be normalized, i.e. turned into a distribution. This brings us to the theorem.







Theorem 5 A DTMC with a finite number of states always has a stationary distribution.




How is the stationary distribution related to the Cesàro limit? Note that
\[
\begin{align}  \Pi \cdot \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbf{P}^{k}\right) & = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\Pi \cdot \mathbf{P}^{k} \\ & = \frac{1}{n}\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\Pi = \Pi \end{align}
\]
Suppose we have an irreducible chain, as in the previous section. Let us pass to the limit as \(n \to \infty\). We get
\[
  \Pi \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  \left(\mathbb {E}_{1}\left[T_1\right]\right)^{-1} &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{2}\left[T_2\right]\right)^{-1} &  \cdots &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\left[T_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\right]\right)^{-1} \\ \left(\mathbb {E}_{1}\left[T_1\right]\right)^{-1} &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{2}\left[T_2\right]\right)^{-1} &  \cdots &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\left[T_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\right]\right)^{-1} \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots \\ \left(\mathbb {E}_{1}\left[T_1\right]\right)^{-1} &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{2}\left[T_2\right]\right)^{-1} &  \cdots &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\left[T_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\right]\right)^{-1} \end{pmatrix} = \Pi
\]
Let us expand the left-hand side:
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}  \sum _{i=1}^{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|} \Pi _i \cdot \left(\mathbb {E}_{1}\left[T_1\right]\right)^{-1}, &  \sum _{i=1}^{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|} \Pi _i \cdot \left(\mathbb {E}_{2}\left[T_2\right]\right)^{-1}, &  \cdots , &  \sum _{i=1}^{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|} \Pi _i \cdot \left(\mathbb {E}_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\left[T_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\right]\right)^{-1} \end{pmatrix}
\]
But \(\sum_{i=1}^{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|} \Pi_i = 1\). In the end we obtain
\[
  \begin{pmatrix}  \left(\mathbb {E}_{1}\left[T_1\right]\right)^{-1} &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{2}\left[T_2\right]\right)^{-1} &  \cdots &  \left(\mathbb {E}_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\left[T_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\right]\right)^{-1} \end{pmatrix} = \Pi
\]
In other words, the Cesàro limit consists row by row precisely of stationary distributions! From this, incidentally, one can conclude that for an irreducible chain the stationary distribution can only be unique, since the limit is unique. In other words, the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue \(1\) for the matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) equals \(1\). Let us state the theorem.







Theorem 6 Let \((X_n)\) be an irreducible DTMC with a finite number of states and transition matrix \(\mathbf{P}\). Then its stationary distribution is unique and equals any row of the Cesàro limit of the matrices \(\mathbf{P}^0, \mathbf{P}^{1}, \ldots\).

title: Discrete-Time Markov Chains (DTMC)
section: 3.5 Period of a state, ergodic chain
text:
3.5 Period of a state, ergodic chain
We have worked out in detail the Cesàro limit of the transition matrices \(\mathbf{P}^0, \mathbf{P}^1, \ldots\) for an irreducible DTMC with finitely many states. But what about the ordinary limit? It turns out this does not always exist.






ExampleExample 7





Consider class \(V\) from the example above as a separate chain:


                                                
Transition graph of an auxiliary 4-state chain with period 4: the class {1,3} and the class {2,4} alternate at every step, so the sequence P⁰, P¹, … has no ordinary (entrywise) limit, although the Cesàro limit exists.


Show that the sequence \(\mathbf{P}^0, \mathbf{P}^{1}, \mathbf{P}^{2}, \ldots\) has no limit.






SolutionSolution





We have \[
  \mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  0 &  1 &  0 \\ 0 &  0 &  0.6 &  0.3 \\ 0 &  1 &  0 &  0 \\ 0.3 &  0.7 &  0 &  0 \end{pmatrix}
\] This matrix is block-structured: \[
  \mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix}  \mathbf{0} &  \mathbf{A} \\ \mathbf{B} &  \mathbf{0} \end{pmatrix}
\] That is, \[
  \mathbf{P}^2 = \begin{pmatrix}  \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} &  \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{0} &  \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A} \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{P}^{3} = \begin{pmatrix}  \mathbf{0} &  \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A} \\ \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} &  \mathbf{0} \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{P}^4 = \begin{pmatrix}  (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^2 &  \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{0} &  (\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A})^2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \ldots
\] There is no limit, since the zeros keep hopping around.






What is the issue with the chain above? It has periodic behavior: starting from any state, one can return to it only after an even number of steps. An even simpler example of such a chain is:


                                                
The simplest periodic chain with 2 states: deterministic transitions 1→2→1→…, with period 2.


Its transition matrix:
\[
  \mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  1 \\ 1 &  0 \end{pmatrix}
\]
In this case
\[
  \mathbf{P}^{2k} = \begin{pmatrix}  1 &  0 \\ 0 &  1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{P}^{2k + 1} = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  1 \\ 1 &  0 \end{pmatrix}
\]
It has no entrywise limit. However, it does have a Cesàro limit:
\[
  \frac{1}{n}\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbf{P}^k \quad \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \quad \begin{pmatrix}  1/2 &  1/2 \\ 1/2 &  1/2 \end{pmatrix}
\]
The period of state \(j\) (notation: \(d(j)\)) is the gcd of all step counts at which one can, with positive probability, return to \(j\) after leaving \(j\). In other words,
\[
  d(j) := \operatorname {gcd} \left\{ k \geq 1 \;  : \;  \mathbb {P}_{j}\left(T_j = k\right) > 0\right\}
\]
A state is called aperiodic if \(d(j) = 1\).







Lemma 4 The period, like recurrence, is a characteristic of the entire communicating class. That is, if \(i,j\) are communicating states, then \(d(i) = d(j)\).




In particular, all states of an irreducible chain have the same period. That is, one can speak of the period of the entire (irreducible) chain. For the chains above the period equals \(2\).
For an irreducible chain, periodicity arises, as we saw, when there is some nontrivial period (i.e. greater than \(1\)). It turns out that if an irreducible chain is aperiodic, then \(\mathbf{P}^{n}\) converges. An irreducible, aperiodic chain is called an ergodic chain.
Let us state the theorem.







Theorem 7 (The ergodic theorem) Let \((X_n)\) be an ergodic DTMC with a finite number of states. Then

its stationary distribution \(\Pi\) exists, is unique, and equals the reciprocals of the return times to the states:
\[
  \Pi = \left(\frac{1}{\mathbb {E}_{1}\left[T_1\right]}, \quad \frac{1}{\mathbb {E}_{2}\left[T_2\right]}, \quad \cdots , \quad \frac{1}{\mathbb {E}_{|\mathcal{X}|}\left[T_{\left|\mathcal{X}\right|}\right]}\right)
\]
The matrices \(\mathbf{P}^{n}\) converge, both in the ordinary sense and in the Cesàro sense, to the matrix whose rows all equal \(\Pi\):
\[
  \lim _{n \to \infty }\mathbf{P}^n \quad = \quad \lim _{n \to \infty }\frac{1}{n}\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbf{P}^k \quad = \quad \begin{pmatrix}  \Pi \\ \Pi \\ \vdots \\ \Pi \end{pmatrix}
\]





The distribution \(\Pi\) from the ergodic theorem is itself called ergodic. Note that if \(\Pi^{(0)}\) is some other initial distribution, then
\[
  \Pi ^{(0)} \cdot \mathbf{P}^{n} \quad \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \Pi ^{(0)} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  \Pi \\ \Pi \\ \vdots \\ \Pi \end{pmatrix} = \Pi
\]







Corollary 1 (Sometimes this is also called the ergodic theorem) The limiting distribution of an ergodic chain always exists (i.e. \(X_n\) always converges in distribution), and it equals the ergodic distribution. In particular, the limiting distribution does not depend on the initial distribution of the chain \(\Pi^{(0)}\), but only on the transition matrix \(\mathbf{P}\), and equals its normalized left eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue \(1\).




An ergodic chain, as time goes on, effectively forgets where it started, stabilizing at the stationary distribution.






ExampleExample 8





Consider the DTMC \((X_n)\) from problem Problem 1.

Find all stationary distributions of the chain.
Is this chain irreducible? Is it ergodic? If so, find the ergodic distribution.
Find the limit of the sequence \(\mathbf{P}^0, \mathbf{P}^{1}, \mathbf{P}^{2}, \ldots\) in the ordinary sense and in the Cesàro sense (if they exist, of course).
Find the limit in distribution of \(X_n\), depending on the initial distribution \(\Pi^{0}\).
Find the mean return time \(\mathbb {E}_{i}\left[T_i\right]\) for each of the states \(i \in \mathcal{X}\).







SolutionSolution











Enum-item(i)



Let us find all left eigenvectors for the matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) (for eigenvalue \(1\)):
\[
  \Pi \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  3/7 &  3/7 &  1/7 \\ 1/11 &  2/11 &  8/11\\ 1/11 &  4/11 &  6/11 \end{pmatrix} = \Pi
\]
We solve the homogeneous linear system
\[
  \Pi \cdot \begin{pmatrix}  -4/7 &  3/7 &  1/7 \\ 1/11 &  -9/11 &  8/11\\ 1/11 &  4/11 &  -5/11 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &  0 &  0 \end{pmatrix}
\]
… The solution:
\[
  \Pi = \alpha \begin{pmatrix}  91 &  209 &  363 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \alpha \in \mathbb {R}
\]
We normalize to obtain a distribution:
\[
  \Pi = \begin{pmatrix}  \frac{91}{663} &  \frac{209}{663} &  \frac{363}{663} \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix}  13.73\%  &  31.52\%  &  54.75\%  \end{pmatrix}
\]








Enum-item(ii)



All states communicate, so the chain is irreducible. Moreover, for instance, from state \(1\) one can return to itself in \(1\) step. Hence the gcd of the step counts at which one can return to \(1\) equals \(1\). So \(1\) is an aperiodic state. All states of the chain form a single communicating class, so the chain is aperiodic. It follows that it is ergodic (being irreducible and aperiodic). The ergodic distribution coincides with the stationary one, found in the previous part.








Enum-item(iii)



By the ergodic theorem,
\[
  \lim _{n \to \infty } \mathbf{P}^{n} = \lim _{n \to \infty } \frac{1}{n}\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbf{P}^k = \begin{pmatrix}  \Pi \\ \Pi \\ \Pi \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}  \frac{91}{663} &  \frac{209}{663} &  \frac{363}{663} \\ \frac{91}{663} &  \frac{209}{663} &  \frac{363}{663}\\ \frac{91}{663} &  \frac{209}{663} &  \frac{363}{663} \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix}  13.73\%  &  31.52\%  &  54.75\%  \\ 13.73\%  &  31.52\%  &  54.75\%  \\ 13.73\%  &  31.52\%  &  54.75\%  \end{pmatrix}
\]








Enum-item(iv)



By the ergodic theorem,
\[
  X_n \xrightarrow [n \to +\infty ]{d} \Pi
\]
The limiting distribution does not depend on the initial distribution.








Enum-item(v)



By the ergodic theorem,
\[
  \begin{cases}  \mathbb {E}_{1}\left[T_1\right] = \frac{663}{91} \approx 7.3 \\ \mathbb {E}_{2}\left[T_2\right] = \frac{663}{209} \approx 3.2 \\ \mathbb {E}_{3}\left[T_3\right] = \frac{663}{363} \approx 1.8 \\ \end{cases}
\]

Is this chain irreducible? Is it ergodic? If so, find the ergodic distribution.
Find the limit of the sequence \(\mathbf{P}^0, \mathbf{P}^{1}, \mathbf{P}^{2}, \ldots\) in the ordinary sense and in the Cesàro sense (if they exist, of course).
Find the limit in distribution of \(X_n\), depending on the initial distribution \(\Pi^{0}\).

The transition matrix of \(Y_n\): \[
  \mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix}  3/7 &  4/7\\ 1/11 &  10/11 \end{pmatrix}
\]












ProblemProblem 4





Consider the DTMC \((X_n)\) from example Example 1. Recall its transition matrix: \[
  \mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix}  0.5 &  0.5 &  0 &  0 \\ 0.3 &  0.3 &  0.3 &  0.1 \\ 0 &  0 &  1 &  0 \\ 0.4 &  0.4 &  0 &  0.2 \end{pmatrix}
\]

HintHint





You may renumber the states for clarity.






For an irreducible chain (with a finite number of states) there is a useful criterion for ergodicity (i.e. aperiodicity).







Lemma 5 (Frobenius’s aperiodicity criterion) Let \((X_n)_{n \geq 0}\) be an irreducible DTMC with a finite number of states. It is ergodic if and only if there exists \(m \in \mathbb {Z}\) such that in this many steps one can go from any state to any other with positive probability: \[
  \mathbb {P}\left(X_{m} = j \mid X_{0} = i\right) > 0, \qquad \forall i,j \in \mathcal{X}
\] In matrix terms: \[
  \mathbf{P}^{m} > \mathbf{0} \quad \text{(entrywise comparison)}
\]




See the proof in (Meyer 2001, 678).

Let us now consider chains consisting of several communicating classes.

To find the limits of \(\mathbf{P}^{0}, \mathbf{P}^{1}, \ldots\), you may use the results obtained above.









ProblemProblem 8





Prove that for any DTMC (even an infinite one, looking ahead) the sequence \(\mathbf{P}^{0}, \mathbf{P}^1, \ldots\) converges in the Cesàro sense. What is the probabilistic meaning of the limit \[
  \lim _{n \to \infty } \left(\frac{1}{n} \sum _{k=0}^{n-1} \mathbf{P}^k\right)_{ij}
\] for arbitrary states \(i,j \in \mathcal{X}\)? Namely, write down a formula for this limit in terms of probabilities and expectations. In particular, what is the probabilistic meaning of the numbers in the upper-right corner of the Cesàro limit for the large Markov chain (with 13 states) from the example above?
What do you think is the equivalent condition on the chain for the sequence \(\mathbf{P}^{0}, \mathbf{P}^1, \ldots\) to have an ordinary limit? Under what condition does the chain converge in probability?






HintHint





Apply the elementary renewal theorem for delayed renewal processes (theorem Theorem 3).

title: Discrete-Time Markov Chains (DTMC)
text:
4.1 Irreducible chains
For a DTMC with transition matrix \(\mathbf{P}\), a stationary measure \(\Psi\) is a measure on \(\mathcal{X}\) (i.e. a row of nonnegative numbers indexed by \(\mathcal{X}\)) such that
\[
  \Psi \cdot \mathbf{P} = \Psi
\]







Theorem 8  

An irreducible DTMC has a stationary distribution \(\Pi\) \(\iff\) it is positive recurrent. In this case the stationary distribution is unique and equals the reciprocal return times:
\[
  \Pi _{i} = \frac{1}{\mathbb {E}_{i}\left[T_i\right]}, \qquad \forall i \in \mathcal{X}
\]
If an irreducible chain is recurrent (either null recurrent or positive recurrent), then there exists a measure \(\Psi\) on \(\mathcal{X}\), unique up to multiplication by a constant, consisting entirely of positive values (\(\Psi_i > 0\) for all \(i \in \mathcal{X}\)). Moreover the chain is

positive recurrent if \(\sum_{i \in \mathcal{X}}\Psi_{i} < +\infty\);
null recurrent if \(\sum_{i \in \mathcal{X}}\Psi_{i} = +\infty\);

For an irreducible, aperiodic DTMC,
\[
  \left(\mathbf{P}^{n}\right)_{ij} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \frac{1}{\mathbb {E}_{j}\left[T_j\right]}, \qquad \forall i,j \in \mathcal{X}
\]
That is, whatever the initial distribution \(\Pi^{(0)}\),
\[
  \left(\Pi ^{(0)} \cdot \mathbf{P}^{n}\right)_j = \mathbb {P}_{\Pi ^{(0)}}\left(X_{n} = j\right) \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{} \frac{1}{\mathbb {E}_{j}\left[T_j\right]}
\]





See the proof in (Grimmett and Stirzaker 2020, sec. 6.4).






ProblemProblem 9





Let \(\frac{1}{2} < p \leq 1\), \(q = 1 - p\). Consider the chain


                                                
An infinite chain ‘condensing’ toward zero: from state 0 there is a transition to ±1 with probability q and a self-transition with probability 1−2q; from any other state there is a transition toward zero with probability p and away from zero with probability q (here 1/2 < p ⩽ 1, q = 1−p).



Find \(\mathbb {E}_{i}\left[T_i\right]\) for each of the states \(i \in \mathcal{X}\) and all stationary distributions of the chain.
Is this chain irreducible? Ergodic? Positive recurrent?
Find the (entrywise) limit of the sequence \(\mathbf{P}^0, \mathbf{P}^{1}, \mathbf{P}^{2}, \ldots\) in the ordinary sense and in the Cesàro sense (if they exist, of course).
Find the limit in distribution of \(X_n\), depending on the initial distribution \(\Pi^{0}\).







HintHint





From the theory of the random walk we know that in this case \(\mathbb {E}_{-1}\left[T_0\right] = \frac{1}{p-q}\).
