4.3 Donsker’s construction (multivariate CLT)
Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) be i.i.d. random variables with finite variance. Without loss of generality, we may assume \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_i\right] = 0\) and \(\operatorname {Var}\left[X_i\right] = 1\). Indeed, if this is not the case, we can always pass to the centered, normalized random variables
\[
  \tilde{X}_i := \frac{X_i - \mathbb {E}\left[X_i\right]}{\sqrt{\operatorname {Var}\left[X_i\right]}}
\]
.
As you know from the probability theory course, the CLT holds for such a sequence:







Theorem 16 (The central limit theorem) Under the conditions above, \(\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{n}} \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{d} \mathscr {N}\left(0, 1\right)\).










ProblemProblem 13





Let \(m \in \mathbb {N}\) be some fixed number. Under the conditions above, find the limit in distribution of the random vector \[
  \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \;  \cdot \;  \begin{pmatrix}  0 \\ S_{\lfloor n/m \rfloor } \\ S_{\lfloor 2n/m \rfloor } \\ \cdots \\ S_{\lfloor (m-1)n/m \rfloor } \\ S_{n} \end{pmatrix}
\]










Theorem 17 (Donsker’s theorem, the infinite-dimensional CLT) Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) be i.i.d. random variables with \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_i\right] = 0\), \(\operatorname {Var}\left[X_{i}\right] = 1\). For a fixed natural number \(n \in \mathbb {N}\), consider the random function \[
  Y^{(n)} = Y^{(n)}_t = Y^{(n)}_t(\omega ), \qquad t \in [0,1], \; \omega \in \Omega ,
\] which at the points \(\frac{k}{n}\), \(k \in \left\{ 0,1,\ldots , n\right\}\), equals \[
  Y^{(n)}_{k/n} := \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}S_{k},
\] and between these points is equal to the linear interpolation of these values. In other words, \[
\begin{align}  Y_{t}^{(n)} & := \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}S_{\lfloor nt \rfloor } + \left(nt - \lfloor nt \rfloor \right) \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}S_{\lfloor nt \rfloor + 1}, \qquad t \in [0,1] \end{align}
\] where \(S_{n} := X_1 + \ldots + X_{n}\). Then \(Y^{(n)}\) is a random element of the space \(C[0,1]\) for each \(n\), and \(Y^{(n)}\) converges weakly to some probability measure on \(C[0,1]\) as \(n \to \infty\). This measure is precisely the Wiener measure on \(C[0,1]\), i.e., the distribution of the Wiener process.




For a proof, see (Биллингсли 1977, Theorem 8.2).
A visualization for \(X_i \sim \frac{1}{2}\delta_{-1} + \frac{1}{2}\delta_1\), i.e., for \(S_n\) — the simplest symmetric random walk: the scaled trajectory \(Y_t^{(n)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt n} S_{\lfloor nt \rfloor} + (nt - \lfloor nt \rfloor)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt n} X_{\lfloor nt \rfloor + 1}\), extended to \(t \in [0,4]\) (the theorem uses \(t\in[0,1]\); here the range is extended so that more of the walk’s “history” is visible). Move the slider \(n\) to see how, as the number of steps increases, the scaled walk increasingly accurately approximates a trajectory of the Wiener process (Donsker’s invariance principle); use the “Show more trajectories” slider to add independent realizations, and click the button to regenerate the steps \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) (new trajectories).

title: The Wiener Process, Gaussian Processes
section: 5.1 Proof of theorem Theorem 15 (a.s. convergence of the series \(\sum_n \xi_n \tilde{e}_n\) in \(C[0,1]\))
text:
5.1 Proof of theorem Theorem 15 (a.s. convergence of the series \(\sum_n \xi_n \tilde{e}_n\) in \(C[0,1]\))
We follow the proof in (Kwapien and Woyczynski 1992, Theorem 2.5.1, pp. 49–51). It relies on two tools: the Itô–Nisio theorem on the convergence of series of independent random elements of a Banach space (we shall state it and use it as a black box) and fractional integration operators, whose properties we shall work out from scratch. The proof is essentially self-contained: the Wiener process is nowhere assumed to have been constructed in advance — on the contrary, the series itself constructs it.
First, the idea. Let \(D^1\) denote the operator of taking an antiderivative: \(\left(D^1 f\right)(t) = \int_0^t f(s) \,  ds\); then \(\tilde{e}_n = D^1 e_n\), and our series is \(\sum_n \xi_n \,  D^1 e_n\). Proving convergence directly in \(C[0,1]\) is hard: one would have to control the suprema of a Gaussian process. On the other hand, in the space \(L^4[0,1]\) the norm is computed as an integral, and for Gaussian terms everything reduces to moments; and it is the Itô–Nisio theorem that will carry us from mean convergence to almost sure convergence. The plan is this: we decompose \(D^1\) as a composition of two “fractional antiderivatives”
\[
  D^1 = D^{3/8} \circ D^{5/8}
\]
An intermediate object — the series \(\sum_n \xi_n \,  D^{5/8}e_n\) — converges almost surely in \(L^4[0,1]\), and the operator \(D^{3/8}\) will turn out to be continuous from \(L^4[0,1]\) to \(C[0,1]\) and will carry that convergence over to the one we need.

5.1.1 Part 1: the Itô–Nisio theorem







Theorem 18 (Itô–Nisio; {}) Let \(V\) be a separable Banach space, and let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) be independent \(V\)-valued random elements having symmetric distributions: \(-X_n \overset {d}{=} X_n\) for all \(n\). Let \(S_N := \sum_{n=1}^{N} X_n\). Then the following conditions are equivalent:

\(S_N\) converges a.s. (in the norm of \(V\));
\(S_N\) converges in probability;
\(S_N\) converges in distribution (i.e., the distributions \(\operatorname {Law}(S_N)\) converge weakly);
there exist a \(V\)-valued random element \(S\) and a set \(\mathcal{D} \subseteq V'\) of continuous linear functionals separating the points of \(V\) (for any \(v \neq u\) there is \(\varphi \in \mathcal{D}\) with \(\varphi (v) \neq \varphi (u)\)) such that \(\varphi (S_N) = \sum_{n \leq N} \varphi (X_n) \to \varphi (S)\) in probability for every \(\varphi \in \mathcal{D}\).





The substantive meaning: for series of independent symmetric terms, all types of convergence — from the weakest, coordinate-wise in distribution, to the strongest, almost sure in norm — coincide. This is an infinite-dimensional generalization of the classical Lévy theorem (“for series of independent quantities, convergence in distribution implies almost sure convergence”). The proof is beautiful but would require a separate seminar — see (Kwapien and Woyczynski 1992, 2.1). We shall need the implication (ii) \(\;  \Rightarrow \;\) (i).


5.1.2 Part 2: fractional integration
For \(0 < \alpha \leq 1\) set
\[
  k_\alpha (s) := \frac{s^{\alpha - 1}}{\Gamma (\alpha )}, \quad s \in (0, 1], \qquad \qquad \left(D^\alpha f\right)(t) := \int _0^t k_\alpha (t - s) f(s) \,  ds
\]
The operator \(D^\alpha\) is called the fractional integration operator (of order \(\alpha\)). For \(\alpha = 1\) the kernel is \(k_1 \equiv 1\), and \(D^1\) is the ordinary antiderivative; for \(\alpha < 1\) the kernel has an integrable singularity at zero. We shall need three properties.







Lemma 6 (Semigroup property) Let \(\alpha , \beta \in (0,1]\), \(\alpha + \beta \leq 1\), \(f \in L^2[0,1]\). Then \(D^{\beta }\left(D^{\alpha } f\right) = D^{\alpha + \beta } f\).










Mn-proofProof






For fixed \(r\) we change the order of integration (Fubini; justification below): \[
\begin{align}  \left(D^{\beta }\left(D^{\alpha }f\right)\right)(r) & = \int _0^r k_\beta (r - t) \int _0^t k_\alpha (t-s) f(s) \,  ds \,  dt = \\ & = \int _0^r \left(\int _s^r k_\beta (r-t) \,  k_\alpha (t - s) \,  dt\right) f(s) \,  ds \end{align}
\] The inner integral is computed by the substitution \(t = s + (r-s)u\), \(u \in [0,1]\): \[
\begin{align}  \int _s^r (r-t)^{\beta - 1}(t - s)^{\alpha - 1} \,  dt & = (r-s)^{\alpha + \beta - 1}\int _0^1 (1-u)^{\beta - 1} u^{\alpha - 1} \,  du = \\ & = (r-s)^{\alpha + \beta - 1} \cdot B(\alpha , \beta ) \end{align}
\] and, since \(B(\alpha ,\beta ) = \frac{\Gamma (\alpha )\Gamma (\beta )}{\Gamma (\alpha + \beta )}\) (a well-known property of the beta function), \[
  \int _s^r k_\beta (r - t) k_\alpha (t-s) \,  dt = \frac{(r-s)^{\alpha +\beta -1}}{\Gamma (\alpha + \beta )} = k_{\alpha + \beta }(r - s)
\] which is exactly \(D^{\alpha +\beta }f\). Justification of Fubini: the same computation for \(\left|f\right|\) (Tonelli’s theorem, everything nonnegative) gives \(\left(D^{\alpha + \beta }\left|f\right|\right)(r) < \infty\) for almost every \(r\), i.e., absolute integrability.











Lemma 7 Let \(\alpha > \frac{1}{2}\). Then for \(f \in L^2[0,1]\) \[
  \sup _{t \in [0,1]} \,  \left|\left(D^{\alpha }f\right)(t)\right| \leq c_\alpha \left\| f\right\| _{L^2}, \qquad c_\alpha := \frac{1}{\Gamma (\alpha )\sqrt{2\alpha - 1}}
\] In particular, \(D^{\alpha } f \in L^4[0,1]\) and \(\left\| D^\alpha f\right\|_{L^4} \leq c_\alpha \left\| f\right\|_{L^2}\).










Mn-proofProof






The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in \(L^2(0,t)\): \[
  \left|\left(D^\alpha f\right)(t)\right| \leq \left\| k_\alpha (t - \cdot )\right\| _{L^2(0,t)} \cdot \left\| f\right\| _{L^2} = \frac{1}{\Gamma (\alpha )}\left(\int _0^t u^{2\alpha - 2} \,  du\right)^{1/2} \left\| f\right\| _{L^2} = \frac{t^{\alpha - \frac{1}{2}}}{\Gamma (\alpha )\sqrt{2\alpha - 1}}\left\| f\right\| _{L^2}
\] and \(t \leq 1\). The exponent \(2\alpha - 2 > -1\) precisely because \(\alpha > \frac{1}{2}\).











Lemma 8 Let \(\beta > \frac{1}{4}\). Then \(D^{\beta }\) is a continuous linear operator from \(L^4[0,1]\) to \(C[0,1]\): for \(f \in L^4[0,1]\) the function \(D^\beta f\) is continuous on \([0,1]\) and \[
  \left\| D^{\beta } f\right\| _{\infty } \leq c'_\beta \left\| f\right\| _{L^4}, \qquad c'_\beta := \left\| k_\beta \right\| _{L^{4/3}[0,1]} < \infty
\]










Mn-proofProof






Hölder’s inequality with exponents \(4\) and \(\frac{4}{3}\):
\[
  \left|\left(D^\beta f\right)(t)\right| \leq \left\| k_\beta (t - \cdot )\right\| _{L^{4/3}(0,t)} \cdot \left\| f\right\| _{L^4} \leq \left\| k_\beta \right\| _{L^{4/3}[0,1]} \cdot \left\| f\right\| _{L^4}
\]
where \(\left\| k_\beta \right\|_{L^{4/3}}^{4/3} = \Gamma (\beta )^{-4/3}\int_0^1 u^{(\beta - 1)\cdot \frac{4}{3}} \,  du < \infty\), since \((\beta - 1)\cdot \frac{4}{3} > -1 \iff \beta > \frac{1}{4}\).
Continuity of \(D^\beta f\) in \(t\) (this point is omitted in the book): let us write \(k_\beta (t-s)\; \mathbb {1}_{0 < s < t} = g(s - t)\), where \(g(u) := k_\beta (-u)\; \mathbb {1}_{(-1,0)}(u) \in L^{4/3}(\mathbb {R})\). Then
\[
  \left|\left(D^\beta f\right)(t') - \left(D^\beta f\right)(t)\right| \leq \left\| g(\cdot - t') - g(\cdot - t)\right\| _{L^{4/3}(\mathbb {R})} \cdot \left\| f\right\| _{L^4} \xrightarrow [t' \to t]{} 0
\]
by continuity of translation in \(L^{q}(\mathbb {R})\) — a standard fact of functional analysis (continuous functions are dense in \(L^q\), and for them the statement is obvious).






5.1.3 Part 3: convergence of the “intermediate object” in \(L^4[0,1]\)
Take \(\alpha = \frac{5}{8} > \frac{1}{2}\) and \(\beta = \frac{3}{8} > \frac{1}{4}\), so that \(\alpha + \beta = 1\). Set
\[
  \varphi _n := D^{5/8} e_n \in L^4[0,1], \qquad S_N := \sum _{n=1}^{N} \xi _n \varphi _n
\]
— independent symmetric random elements of \(L^4[0,1]\) and their partial sums. Let us estimate, for \(M < N\) (Tonelli’s theorem — the integrand is nonnegative):
\[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\left\| S_N - S_M\right\| ^4_{L^4}\right] = \int _0^1 \mathbb {E}\left[\left(\sum _{n=M+1}^{N} \xi _n \varphi _n(t)\right)^4\right] dt = 3\int _0^1 \left(\sum _{n = M+1}^{N} \varphi _n(t)^2\right)^2 dt
\]
— for each \(t\), the quantity \(\sum_{n=M+1}^N \xi_n\varphi_n(t)\) is Gaussian \(\mathscr {N}\left(0, \; \sum_{M < n \leq N}\varphi_n(t)^2\right)\), and the fourth moment of \(\mathscr {N}\left(0, \sigma^2\right)\) equals \(3\sigma^4\).
Now for the key estimate. Note that \(\varphi_n(t) = \left\langle k_{5/8}(t - \cdot )\; \mathbb {1}_{(0,t)}, e_n \right\rangle_{L^2[0,1]}\) are the Fourier coefficients of the function \(h_t := k_{5/8}(t - \cdot )\; \mathbb {1}_{(0,t)} \in L^2[0,1]\). By Bessel’s inequality and lemma Lemma 7
\[
  \sum _{n=1}^{\infty } \varphi _n(t)^2 \leq \left\| h_t\right\| ^2_{L^2} \leq c_{5/8}^2 \qquad \forall t \in [0,1]
\]
Hence the tails \(R_M(t) := \sum_{n > M}\varphi_n(t)^2\) decrease monotonically to zero at each \(t\) (tails of a convergent numerical series) and are uniformly bounded by the constant \(c_{5/8}^2\). By the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem
\[
  \sup _{N > M} \,  \mathbb {E}\left[\left\| S_N - S_M\right\| ^4_{L^4}\right] \leq 3\int _0^1 R_M(t)^2 \,  dt \;  \xrightarrow [M \to \infty ]{} \;  0
\]
i.e., \((S_N)\) is Cauchy in fourth mean, and hence (by Markov’s inequality) also in probability; the space \(L^4[0,1]\) is complete with respect to convergence in probability in the following sense: a sequence that is Cauchy in probability converges in probability to some limit (a standard fact: pass to an almost surely convergent subsequence). So \(S_N \to S\) in probability in \(L^4[0,1]\). The space \(L^4[0,1]\) is separable and Banach, and the terms \(\xi_n\varphi_n\) are independent and symmetric — by the Itô–Nisio theorem (implication (ii) \(\;  \Rightarrow \;\) (i))
\[
  S_N \;  \xrightarrow [N \to \infty ]{\text{a.s.}} \;  S \qquad \text{in } L^4[0,1]
\]


5.1.4 Part 4: assembly
It remains to apply the operator \(D^{3/8}\). By the semigroup property (lemma Lemma 6) and linearity
\[
  D^{3/8} S_N = \sum _{n=1}^{N} \xi _n \,  D^{3/8}\left(D^{5/8} e_n\right) = \sum _{n=1}^{N} \xi _n \,  D^{1} e_n = \sum _{n=1}^{N} \xi _n \tilde{e}_n = W^{(N)}
\]
— this is exactly the original partial sums! The operator \(D^{3/8}: L^4[0,1] \to C[0,1]\) is linear and continuous (lemma Lemma 8), so on the same event of full probability where \(S_N \to S\) in \(L^4\),
\[
  W^{(N)} = D^{3/8}S_N \;  \xrightarrow [N \to \infty ]{} \;  D^{3/8}S \qquad \text{in } C[0,1]
\]
The theorem is proved; the limit \(W := D^{3/8}S\) is an almost surely continuous function.
Remarks.

Where do the exponents \(\frac{5}{8}\) and \(\frac{3}{8}\) come from? We need \(\alpha > \frac{1}{2}\) (lemma Lemma 7), \(\beta > \frac{1}{p}\) (lemma Lemma 8 for \(L^p\)), and \(\alpha + \beta = 1\). For \(p = 2\) we would get \(1 = \alpha + \beta > \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1\) — a contradiction: \(D^1\) can only be split into two suitable factors via \(L^p\) with \(p > 2\). We took \(p = 4\) (the first even exponent) so that the moment \(\mathbb {E}\left[\eta^4\right] = 3\sigma^4\) could be computed in one line; in (Kwapien and Woyczynski 1992) the same computation is carried out for arbitrary \(2 < p < \infty\) via \(c(p) := \mathbb {E}\left[\left|\xi_1\right|^p\right]\).
Completeness of the ONB was not used in Parts 3–4: Bessel’s inequality, which holds for any orthonormal system, sufficed. Therefore the proof carries over verbatim to “thinned” series \(\sum_{n \in A}\xi_n \tilde{e}_n\) (see the problem in section Section 4) and does not depend on the order in which the basis is enumerated. Completeness is needed only at the next step — when we identify the limit with the Wiener process via Parseval’s equality (the problem after theorem Theorem 15).
Bonus (Remark 2.5.1 in (Kwapien and Woyczynski 1992)): for \(\beta > \frac{1}{p} + \gamma\) the operator \(D^\beta\) is continuous from \(L^p[0,1]\) to the space of \(\gamma\)-Hölder functions. Choosing \(p\) large and \(\beta\) slightly less than \(\frac{1}{2}\), we get for free: the paths of the limiting process are \(\gamma\)-Hölder for any \(\gamma < \frac{1}{2}\) — in full agreement with the section on local properties of the paths of WP.
For the Haar system there is also a completely direct proof, without fractional integration or the Itô–Nisio theorem (essentially, Lévy’s original 1940 argument): group the series by generations. The tent functions \(\tilde{\psi }_{m,k}\), \(0 \leq k < 2^m\), have disjoint supports, so
\[
  \sup _t \,  \left|\; \sum _{k} \xi _{m,k} \tilde{\psi }_{m,k}(t)\right| = 2^{-\frac{m+2}{2}} \max _{k} \left|\xi _{m,k}\right|,
\]
and from the Gaussian tail bound \(\mathbb {P}\left(\left|\xi \right| > x\right) \leq e^{-x^2/2}\) (for \(x \geq 1\)) and the Borel–Cantelli lemma: \(\sum_m \mathbb {P}\left(\max_k \left|\xi_{m,k}\right| > 2\sqrt{m}\right) \leq \sum_m 2^m e^{-2m} < \infty\), i.e., almost surely for all large \(m\) the generation contributes no more than \(2^{-\frac{m+2}{2}} \cdot 2\sqrt{m}\) — a convergent numerical series. By the Weierstrass criterion the series (by generations) converges uniformly almost surely. The drawback of this route: it is tied to a specific basis; for an arbitrary ONB this does not work.

Footnotes


Do not confuse the Schauder functions with the Faber–Schauder system or with the Schauder basis. The Faber–Schauder system is obtained from the Schauder system by normalizing in the supremum norm and adding the function identically equal to \(1\). What a Schauder basis is (sometimes it is simply called a basis for an infinite-dimensional Banach space) you should cover in functional analysis. Interestingly, the Faber–Schauder system is a Schauder basis in the Banach space \(C[0,1]\).↩︎

title: Martingales
text:
3.1 Markov \(\overset {?}{\;  \Rightarrow \; }\) martingale
A martingale is necessarily an integrable process, while a Markov process may be non-integrable. From this we immediately get an example of a Markov process that is not a martingale: a random walk with a step distributed according to the Cauchy law.
In the case of integrability, the following theorem holds:







Theorem 2 A real-valued Markov process \((X_t, \mathcal{F}_t, t \in T), \;  T \subset \mathbb {R}\) is a martingale (with respect to the same filtration \((\mathcal{F}_t)\)) if and only if \((X_t)\) is an integrable process and \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[X_t \mid X_s \right] = X_s
\tag{1}\] holds for \(s \leq t, \;  s,t \in T\).




For the process \((X_t)\) to satisfy condition Equation 1, it is necessary that its mean function be constant. From this we get a second example of a Markov process that is not a martingale: the Poisson process.
Furthermore, even if a Markov process is integrable and has a constant mean function, this still does not guarantee that it is a martingale, as the following problem shows.






ExampleExample 5





Let \(X_0 \sim \frac{1}{2}(\delta_1 + \delta_{-1})\), i.e. \(\mathbb {P}\left(X_0 = -1\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(X_0 = 1\right) = \frac{1}{2}\). Let \[
  X_n = \begin{cases} X_{n-1} + 1, &  X_{n-1} > 0 \\ X_{n-1} - 1, &  X_{n-1} < 0\end{cases}, \qquad n \in \mathbb {N}
\] Sketch the sample paths of \((X_n)\). Prove that \((X_n, n \in \mathbb {Z}_+)\) is an integrable Markov process with a constant mean function that is not a martingale.






SolutionSolution





Integrability and the Markov property are obvious, and \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_n\right] = 0\) by symmetry: \(X_n \sim \frac{1}{2}\left(\delta_{n+1} + \delta_{-(n+1)}\right)\). At the same time \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right] = X_{n-1} + \operatorname {sign}(X_{n-1}) \neq X_{n-1} \quad \text{a.s.},
\] so \((X_n)\) is not a martingale: it “stays put” only on average unconditionally, but not conditionally.






The only possible trajectories (up to sign) of the process from the example: \(X_0 = \pm 1\) with equal probability, and then \(X_n = X_{n-1} + \operatorname{sign}(X_{n-1})\) — the process moves deterministically away from zero. The button below flips the coin again (a new \(X_0\)), and the slider \(n\) highlights a point on the current trajectory and shows next to it the conditional forecast \(\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\): it coincides exactly with the next point of the trajectory — “standing still” is impossible for any \(n\), even though unconditionally \(\mathbb{E}[X_n]\equiv 0\).

ProblemProblem 3





If a real-valued random process \(\xi_t\) is Markov, then so is the process \(f(\xi_t)\), where \(f\) is an injective map. In particular, if \(W_t\) is a Wiener process, then \(W_t^3\) is Markov. But show that \(W_t^3\) is not a martingale.

title: Martingales
text:
3.2 Martingale \(\overset {?}{\;  \Rightarrow \; }\) Markov
Producing an example of a martingale that is not a Markov process is a bit trickier:






ExampleExample 6





Let \(\left(X_{n}, n \geqslant 0\right)\) be independent random variables uniformly distributed on the set \(\{ -1,0,1\}\). Consider the process \[
  Y_{n}= X_{0} X_{1}+X_{1} X_{2}+\ldots +X_{n-1} X_{n}
\] Prove that \(Y_{n}\) is a martingale with respect to the filtration \[
  \mathbb {F}=\left(\sigma \left(X_{0}, X_{1}, \ldots , X_{n}\right), n \in \mathbb {Z}_{+}\right),
\] but is not a Markov process with respect to it.






SolutionSolution





\[
  Y_n = \left(BX \bullet S\right)_n
\]
where \(S_n = X_1 + X_2 + \ldots + X_n\), \((Bf)(n) = f(n-1)\), where \(f: \mathbb {Z}_+ \to \mathbb {R}\) is an arbitrary function. \(B\) is the time shift, the backward shift.
\[
  B: \mathbb {R}^{\mathbb {Z}_+} \to \mathbb {R}^{\mathbb {N}}
\]
Martingale:
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {E}\left[Y_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n\right] & = Y_{n} + \mathbb {E}\left[X_n X_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n\right] = Y_{n} + X_n \mathbb {E}\left[X_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n\right] = \\ & = Y_n \end{align}
\]
Not Markov: if \((Y_n)\) were Markov with respect to \(\mathbb {F}\), then the conditional probability \(\mathbb {P}\left(Y_2 = 1 \mid \mathcal{F}_1\right)\) would a.s. be a function of \(Y_1\). But on the event \(\left\{ X_1 = 0\right\}\) we have \(Y_1 = 0\) and \(Y_2 = X_1\left(X_0 + X_2\right) = 0\), whence
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(Y_2 = 1 \mid X_1 = 0\right) = 0,
\]
while on the event \(\left\{ X_0 = 0, \;  X_1 = 1\right\}\) we also have \(Y_1 = 0\), but \(Y_2 = X_2\), and
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(Y_2 = 1 \mid X_0 = 0, X_1 = 1\right) = \mathbb {P}\left(X_2 = 1\right) = \frac{1}{3} \neq 0
\]
Both events lie in \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and have positive probability, i.e. the conditional distribution of \(Y_2\) given \(\mathcal{F}_1\) is not determined by the value of \(Y_1\).

4.1 Doob decomposition







Definition 3 The process \(\left(X_{n}, n \in \mathbb {N}\right)\) is predictable with respect to the filtration \(\left(\mathcal{F}_{n}, n \in \mathbb {Z}_{+}\right)\) if \(X_{n}\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\) for all \(n \in \mathbb {N}\).











Theorem 3 (Doob decomposition) Let \(\left(X_{n}, n \in \mathbb {Z}_{+}\right)\) be an \(L^{1}\)-process, adapted to the filtration \(\mathbb {F}=\left(\mathcal{F}_{n}, n \in \mathbb {Z}_{+}\right)\). Then there exists a unique (up to stochastic equivalence in the narrow sense) decomposition of the form \[
  X_{n}=M_{n}+A_{n}, \quad n \in \mathbb {Z}_+
\] where \(M_{n}\) is a martingale with respect to \(\mathbb {F}\), \(A_{n}\) is a predictable process with respect to \(\mathbb {F}\), and \(A_{0}=0\) a.s.




Note, in connection with the theorem, that the process \(\left(X_{n}, n \in \mathbb {Z}_{+}\right)\) is a submartingale with respect to \(\mathbb {F}\) if and only if, in its Doob decomposition, the sequence \(A_{n}\) is a.s. non-decreasing.






ProblemProblem 4





Prove the Doob decomposition theorem for representing an \(L^1\)-process as a sum of a martingale and a predictable process.






HintHint





For the existence proof, set \[
\begin{align}  M_n & = X_0 + \sum _{k=1}^n \left(X_k - \mathbb {E}\left[X_k \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}\right]\right) \\ A_n & = X_n - M_n = \sum _{k=1}^n \left( \mathbb {E}\left[X_k \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}\right] - X_{k-1}\right) \end{align}
\]












ProblemProblem 5





Let \(\left(X_{n}, n \in \mathbb {Z}_{+}\right)\) be a Galton-Watson branching process with offspring distribution \(\operatorname {Pois}(3)\). Find the Doob decomposition for this process.



The Doob decomposition “up close”: for the simple symmetric random walk \(S_n\), the submartingale \(X_n = S_n^2\) splits into the sum of a martingale \(M_n = S_n^2 - n\) and a predictable nondecreasing compensator \(A_n = n\) — all of the submartingale’s “systematic growth” is concentrated in the compensator. The slider \(\theta\) animates the subtraction of the compensator: at \(\theta = 0\), \(X_n\) is shown; at \(\theta = 1\), \(M_n = X_n - A_n\); intermediate values show \(X_n - \theta A_n\). The checkbox shows/hides \(A_n\) itself, and the button regenerates the random walk.

4.2 Convergence of martingales
The statements and problems below are formulated for discrete time, but they are in fact also true for continuous time.







Theorem 4 (Boundedness in \(L^1\) suffices for a.s. convergence of a martingale) Let \(\left(X_{n}, n \in \mathbb {Z}_+\right)\) be a submartingale such that \(\forall n \in \mathbb {Z}_+: \;  \mathbb {E}\left[X_n^+\right] \leq M\) for some \(M > 0\) (i.e. the family \((X_n^+)_{n \in \mathbb {Z}_+}\) is bounded in the norm of the space \(L^1\))1. In particular, this holds if \(X_n\) is simply bounded in \(L^1\). Then there exists a random variable in \(L^1\), conventionally denoted \(X_\infty\), such that
\[
  X_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\text{a.s.}} X_\infty
\]
If, in addition, \((X_n, n \in \mathbb {Z}_+)\) is uniformly integrable, then \(X_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{L^1} X_\infty\).




Recall that a family of random variables \((X_\alpha , \alpha \in A)\) is called uniformly integrable if there exists a function \(G: \mathbb {R}_+ \to \mathbb {R}_+\), growing faster than linearly (i.e. \(\frac{G(x)}{x} \xrightarrow [x \to +\infty ]{} + \infty\)), such that the expectations \(\mathbb {E}\left[G(\left|X_{\alpha }\right|)\right]\) are uniformly (in \(\alpha\)) bounded2. For example, boundedness (in norm) in the space \(L^1\) is not sufficient for uniform integrability, but boundedness in the space \(L^p\) for an arbitrary \(p > 1\) is already sufficient.
Let us recall a few properties of uniform integrability (UI):

\(X_t \xrightarrow [t\to \infty ]{L^1} X\) if and only if \(X_t \xrightarrow [t\to \infty ]{\mathbb {P}} X\) and the family \((X_t, t \in \mathbb {R}_+)\) is uniformly integrable.
Conditional expectations of an integrable random variable are UI. Namely, let \(X \in L^1 = L^1(\Omega , \mathcal{F}, \mathbb {P})\) and let \(\mathcal{G}_\alpha \subset \mathcal{F}, \;  \alpha \in A\) be some family of sigma-subalgebras. Then the family \(\left(\mathbb {E}\left[X \mid \mathcal{G}_\alpha \right], \;  \alpha \in A\right)\) is UI.








Theorem 5 (\(L^p\)-convergence of martingales) Let \(p>1\) and let \(X_n\) be a martingale bounded in the space \(L^p\). Then there exists an \(\mathcal{F}_\infty\)-measurable random variable \(X_\infty \in L^p\), such that \(X_n \xrightarrow [n \to \infty ]{\text{a.s.}, L^p} X_\infty\).










ProblemProblem 6






Let the process \((X_t, \mathcal{F}_t, t \in \mathbb {R}_+)\) be a Lévy martingale for \(Z \in L^1\), i.e. \(X_t = \mathbb {E}\left[Z \mid \mathcal{F}_t\right]\) a.s. \(\forall t \in \mathbb {R}_+\). Prove that then \((X_t)\) converges a.s. and in \(L^1\) to some random variable \(X_\infty\), with \(X_\infty = \mathbb {E}\left[Z \mid \mathcal{F}_\infty \right]\) a.s., where \(\mathcal{F}_\infty = \sigma \left(\bigcup_{t \in \mathbb {R}_+} \mathcal{F}_t\right)\).
Prove that a uniformly integrable martingale \((X_t, \mathcal{F}_t, t \in \mathbb {R}_+)\), converging a.s. and in \(L^1\) to \(X_\infty\), is a Lévy martingale with respect to \(X_\infty\).




The statements above show that UI martingales and Lévy martingales are one and the same thing. Moreover, such processes are uniquely (up to a modification, i.e. up to a.s. agreement at each point \(t \in T\)) characterized by their filtration and the limit \(X_\infty\).






ProblemProblem 7





Let \(Z_1, Z_2, \ldots\) be independent random variables such that \[
  Z_n =\begin{cases}  a_n, &  \text{with probability } \frac{1}{2n^2} \\ 0, &  1 - \frac{1}{n^2} \\ -a_n, &  \frac{1}{2n^2} \end{cases},
\] where the sequence \(a_n\) is defined recurrently: \(a_1 = 2, \;  a_n = 4\sum_{j=1}^{n-1} a_j\). Show that \(Y_n := \sum_{j=1}^n Z_j\) is a martingale. Show that \((Y_n, n \in \mathbb {N})\) has an a.s. limit, while there is no \(M > 0\) such that \(\mathbb {E}\left[\left|Y_n\right|\right] \leq M, \;  \forall n \in \mathbb {N}\).
The problem shows that, in general, a martingale can converge a.s. even without the conditions of Theorem Theorem 4 holding.









ProblemProblem 8





Give an example of a nonnegative martingale \(X_n\) such that \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_n\right] = 1\), while \(X_n \xrightarrow [n\to \infty ]{\text{a.s.}} 0\).



A nonnegative martingale \(X_n = \xi_1 \cdots \xi_n\), where the \(\xi_i\) are independent and take the values \(\frac12\) and \(\frac32\) with equal probability (so that \(\mathbb{E}\left[\xi_i\right] = 1\)): \(12\) simulated trajectories. Almost all of them die out (\(X_n \to 0\) a.s., since \(\mathbb{E}\left[\ln \xi_i\right] < 0\)), even though \(\mathbb{E}\left[X_n\right] = 1\) for all \(n\) — there is no convergence in \(L^1\), and the family is not uniformly integrable. The button regenerates the bundle and simultaneously recomputes the sample mean of \(X_{80}\) over a much larger (unseen) batch of trajectories: the counter accumulates over all clicks and stays close to \(1\) thanks to rare but enormous outliers among the dying-out paths.

4.3 Optional stopping of a martingale







Theorem 6 (Optional stopping theorem: a stopped martingale is still a martingale) Let \(\left(X_{n}, \mathcal{F}_n, n \in \mathbb {Z}_+\right)\) be a submartingale (martingale). Let \(\tau\) be an arbitrary stopping time with respect to the filtration \(\mathbb {F} = (\mathcal{F}_n, n \in \mathbb {Z}_+)\). In particular, \(\tau\) may equal \(\infty\) with nonzero probability. Then the stopped process \[
  X^\tau _n := X_{\min (\tau , n)} = \begin{cases}  X_n, &  n < \tau \\ X_\tau , &  n \geq \tau \end{cases}
\] is also a submartingale (respectively, a martingale) with respect to \(\mathbb {F} = (\mathcal{F}_n, n \in \mathbb {Z}_+)\).




The stopped process \(S^\tau_n = S_{\min(\tau, n)}\) for seven simulated trajectories of the simple symmetric random walk started at \(s_0 = 3\), where \(\tau\) is the exit time from the strip \([a, b]\): once the boundary is reached, the trajectory “freezes” (a dot). By the optional stopping theorem, \(S^\tau\) is still a martingale: \(\mathbb{E}\left[S^\tau_n\right] = s_0\) for all \(n\). Move the sliders for the strip boundaries and click “Regenerate”: the sample mean of the stopped value accumulates over all runs and stays close to \(s_0 = 3\) regardless of the strip’s width.

title: Martingales
text:
4.4 Optional sampling of a martingale







Theorem 7 (The optional sampling theorem, sometimes also called the optional stopping theorem) Let \((X_n, n \in \mathbb {Z}_+)\) be a martingale, let \(\sigma \leq \tau\) be two stopping times with values in \(\mathbb {Z}_+ \cup \left\{ +\infty \right\}\), and let the stopped process \((X_n^\tau )\) be uniformly integrable (on the event \(\left\{ \tau = +\infty \right\}\) we set \(X_\tau := \lim_{n\to \infty } X^\tau_n\); the limit exists a.s. by uniform integrability). Then \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[X_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_\sigma \right] \stackrel{\text{a.s.}}{=} X_\sigma
\] and, in particular, \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[X_\tau \right] = \mathbb {E}\left[X_\sigma \right] = \mathbb {E}\left[X_0\right]
\] Uniform integrability of \((X_n^\tau )\), in turn, holds under any of the following conditions:

\(\tau \in L^\infty\), i.e. \(\tau\) is a.s. bounded: \(\exists M > 0: \;  \mathbb {P}\left(\tau < M\right) = 1\). Here we have strong restrictions on the stopping time and no restrictions on the martingale.
\(\tau \in L^1\) and there exists a constant \(c > 0\) such that

\[
  \; \mathbb {1}_{(n, +\infty )}(\tau ) \cdot \mathbb {E}\left[\left|X_{n+1} - X_n\right| \mid \mathcal{F}_n\right] < c, \qquad \forall n \in \mathbb {Z}_+
\]
(the conditional increments of the martingale are bounded up to time \(\tau\)). In particular, this holds if \(\left|X_n - X_{n-1}\right| \leq c\) a.s. for all \(n\).
Here we have moderate restrictions on the stopping time and moderate restrictions on the martingale.

\(\tau\) is arbitrary, but the process \((X_n)\) is itself UI. Here we have no restrictions on the stopping time and strong restrictions on the martingale.





The optional stopping theorem means that the mean value of a martingale at random time instants remains the same as at deterministic ones.







Corollary 1 Let \(S_n\) be a martingale, with \(S_n - S_{n-1}\) uniformly bounded by some constant. Let \((C_n)\) be a predictable process, also uniformly bounded by a constant, and let \(\mathbb {E}\left[T\right]<\infty\) for some stopping time \(T\). Then \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[\left(C \bullet S\right)_{T}\right] = 0
\]










ExampleExample 7





Give an example of a martingale \((X_{n}, n \in \mathbb {Z}_+)\) and stopping times \(\tau , \sigma\) with respect to its natural filtration such that \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_{\tau }\right] \neq \mathbb {E}\left[X_{\sigma }\right]\).






HintHint





Take a random walk.









SolutionSolution





Consider the simplest symmetric random walk on the line \(\left(S_{n}, n \in \mathbb {Z}_{+}\right)\) and set \(\tau =\min \left\{ n: S_{n}=\right.\) \(1\} , \sigma =\min \left\{ n: S_{n}=2\right\}\). Recall that \(\tau , \sigma < \infty\) a.s., i.e. these are not merely stopping times in the general sense but stopping times that are a.s. finite. Furthermore, \(S_{n}\) is a martingale. But \[
  \mathbb {E}\left[S_\tau \right] = 1 < 2 = \mathbb {E}\left[S_\sigma \right]
\]






We have already solved the following problem by combinatorial methods, but it is instructive to solve it by martingale methods as well.






ExampleExample 8 - The gambler’s ruin problem





Let \(a<{s_0}<b\) be integers, and let \(S_{n} = {s_0} + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \xi_i, \;  n \geqslant 0\), be the simplest random walk with probability \(p\) of a step to the right, started at the point \(s_0\). Denote by \(\tau = \min \left\{ n: S_{n} \in \left\{ a, b\right\} \right\}\) the time at which the process \(S_{n}\) exits the strip. Compute the distribution of \(S_\tau\) and \(\mathbb {E}\left[\tau \right]\) in the case \(p = \frac{1}{2}\) (i.e. the symmetric case).






HintHint





\(p = \frac{1}{2}\). To compute \(\operatorname {Law}\left(S_\tau \right)\) one must consider the martingale \(S_n\). To compute \(\mathbb {E}\left[\tau \right]\), prove that \(M_n := S_n^2 - n\) is also a martingale. Next, for an arbitrary \(k \in \mathbb {N}\) take the stopping time \(\tau_k := \tau \wedge k \in L^\infty\) and apply the optional sampling theorem to it and to \(M_n\). Then let \(k \to +\infty\).









SolutionSolution





We have \(a < {s_0} < b\) integers, \(S_n = {s_0} + \sum_{i=1}^n \xi_i\) a random walk:
\[
\begin{align}  \mathbb {P}\left(\xi _i = 1\right) = p, \quad \mathbb {P}\left(\xi _i = -1\right) = 1-p =: q \end{align}
\]
Here \(\tau := \min \{ n: S_n \in \{ a,b\} \}\).

Distribution of \(S_\tau\). \(S_n\) is a martingale. Note that \(\left|S_n^\tau \right| \leq \max (\left|a\right|,\left|b\right|)\), so we can use the optional stopping theorem: \(\mathbb {E}\left[S_\tau \right] = \mathbb {E}\left[S_0\right] = {s_0}\). At the same time
\[
  \mathbb {E}\left[S_\tau \right] = a \mathbb {P}\left(S_\tau = a\right) + b \mathbb {P}\left(S_\tau = b\right) = a \mathbb {P}\left(S_\tau = a\right) + b (1 - \mathbb {P}\left(S_\tau = a\right) )
\]
We obtain the equation:
\[
  {s_0} = a \mathbb {P}\left(S_\tau = a\right) + b (1 - \mathbb {P}\left(S_\tau = a\right) )
\]
Distribution of \(S_\tau\):
\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(S_\tau = a\right) = \frac{{s_0}-b}{a-b} \quad \mathbb {P}\left(S_\tau = b\right) = \frac{a - {s_0}}{a-b}
\]
Expectation \(\mathbb {E}\left[\tau \right]\). \(S_n\) is an \(L^2\)-process with independent increments and a constant mean function. Moreover \(\operatorname {Var}\left[S_n\right] = n \operatorname {Var}\left[\xi_1\right] = n\). Then \(M_n := S_n^2 - n\) is a martingale. Hence \(s_0^2 = \mathbb {E}\left[M_0\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[M_{\tau \wedge k}\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[S^2_{\tau \wedge k}\right] - \mathbb {E}\left[\tau \wedge k\right]\).
Let us prove that \(\mathbb {E}\left[\tau \wedge k\right] \xrightarrow [k \to \infty ]{} \mathbb {E}\left[\tau \right]\). Note that \(\tau \wedge k \xrightarrow [k \to \infty ]{\text{a.s.}}\tau\), and for every \(\omega\) the sequence \(\tau (\omega ) \wedge k\) is non-decreasing in \(k\). Hence, \(\mathbb {E}\left[\tau \wedge k\right] \xrightarrow [k \to \infty ]{} \mathbb {E}\left[\tau \right]\).
Let us prove that \(\mathbb {E}\left[S^2_{\tau \wedge k}\right] \xrightarrow [k \to \infty ]{} \mathbb {E}\left[S^2_{\tau }\right]\). Note that \(S^2_{\tau \wedge k} \xrightarrow [k \to \infty ]{\text{a.s.}} S^2_{\tau }\), and \(\left|S^2_{\tau \wedge k}\right| \leq \max (a^2, b^2)\), so we have \(L^1\)-convergence.
As a result we obtain
\[
\begin{align}  s_0^2 & = a^2\frac{{s_0}-b}{a-b} + b^2 \frac{a - {s_0}}{a-b} - \mathbb {E}\left[\tau \right] \\ s_0^2 & = {s_0}(a+b) - ab - \mathbb {E}\left[\tau \right] \\ \mathbb {E}\left[\tau \right] & = -s_0^2 + {s_0}(a+b) - ab \end{align}
\]










AnswerAnswer





\[
  \mathbb {P}\left(S_\tau = a\right) = \frac{{s_0}-b}{a-b}, \;  \mathbb {P}\left(S_\tau = b\right) = \frac{a - {s_0}}{a-b}, \qquad \mathbb {E}\left[\tau \right] = -s_0^2 + {s_0}(a + b) - ab
\]












ProblemProblem 9





Solve the gambler’s ruin problem (see the previous example) by the martingale method for the case \(p \neq \frac{1}{2}\)






HintHint





To compute \(\operatorname {Law}\left(S_\tau \right)\) consider \(Y_n := \frac{1}{\theta^{S_n}}\), where \(\theta = \frac{p}{1-p}\). Prove that \(Y_n\) is a martingale.
To compute \(\mathbb {E}\left[\tau \right]\) consider the process \(Z_n = S_n - (2p-1)n\), prove that \(Z_n\) is a martingale.






The gambler’s ruin problem: the probability of reaching \(b\) before being ruined at \(a = 0\), as a function of the starting capital \(s_0\): \(\mathbb{P}\left(S_\tau = b\right) = \dfrac{\varrho^{a} - \varrho^{s_0}}{\varrho^{a} - \varrho^{b}}\), where \(\varrho = q/p\) (for \(p = \frac12\) this expression is the limit \(\varrho \to 1\), which degenerates into the linear function \(s_0/b\)). Move the slider \(p\) to see how the curve deforms from a straight line into an exponential “cliff” — even a slight bias in the step probability makes winning with a small capital nearly impossible — and the slider \(b\) to change the width of the strip.







p = 0.50



b = 20













ExampleExample 9 - A monkey types ABRACADABRA





Suppose that at times \(1,2,3, \ldots\) a monkey types a capital letter at random, and the sequence of typed letters forms an independent and identically distributed sequence of random variables, each of which is chosen uniformly from 33 possible capital letters (of the Russian alphabet).

Let \(T = T_{\text{Ж}}\) be the first time at which the monkey has typed the letter Ж. Prove that \(T\) is a.s. finite and find \(\mathbb {E}\left[T\right]\);
Let \(T = T_{\text{АБРАКАДАБРА}}\) be the first time at which the monkey has typed the sequence of letters АБРАКАДАБРА (ABRACADABRA). Prove that \(T\) is a.s. finite and find \(\mathbb {E}\left[T\right]\).







SolutionSolution





Let \(A_1, A_{2}, \ldots\) be the letters typed by the monkey.






Enum-item(1)



Let \(\xi_i = \; \mathbb {1}_{\text{Ж}}(A_i)\). Then \(\xi_1, \xi_2 ,\ldots\) are i.i.d.r.v.’s, distributed as \(\operatorname {Ber}(1/33)\).
\[
  T_{\text{Ж}} = \min \left(i \in \mathbb {N} \;  : \;  \xi _i = 1\right) \sim \operatorname {Geom}(1/33)
\]
by the definition of the geometric distribution. Then \(\mathbb {E}\left[T_{\text{Ж}}\right] = 33\).








Enum-item(2)



It is easy to prove that \(T < \infty\) a.s., and even that \(\mathbb {E}\left[T\right] < \infty\). Indeed, let
\[
  \xi _{i} = \; \mathbb {1}_{\text{АБРАКАДАБРА}}(A_{11i + 1}\ldots A_{11i + 11}), \qquad i \geq 0
\]
Let
\[
  T' = \min \left(i \in \mathbb {Z}_+ \;  : \;  \xi _i = 1\right)
\]
\(T\) is the time of the first occurrence of ABRACADABRA, while \(T'\) is the index of the first block of \(11\) consecutive letters (blocks do not overlap) in which ABRACADABRA is written in full; such a block ends at step \(11(T'+1)\). The first occurrence overall could happen earlier, so \(T \leq 11(T' + 1)\). Moreover \(T' + 1 \sim \operatorname {Geom}\left((1/33)^{11}\right)\), i.e. \(T' \in L^1\). Hence \(T \in L^1\), it has finite expectation. But how do we find the exact value of this expectation?
Let us set up a casino next to the monkey! In our casino there is only one game: one can bet on the next letter the monkey will type. Moreover, let the casino be fair: the payout odds for a win are \(33\). In that case the expected result of the game is exactly \(0\).
Suppose that immediately before each time instant \(n=1,2, \ldots\) a new player arrives. They bet \(1\) ruble that the \(n\)-th letter will be А. If they lose, they leave. If they win, they receive \(33\) rubles, all of which they bet on the \((n+1)\)-th letter being Б. If they lose, they leave. If they win, they bet their entire fortune of \(33^{2}\) on the \((n+2)\)-th letter being Р, and so on through the sequence ABRACADABRA.
Let \(X_n\) be the combined capital of all players at time \(n\) (we take \(X_0 = 0\)). Suppose we prove that \(X_n\) is a martingale, and that there exists a constant \(C > 0\) such that \(\left|X_n - X_{n-1}\right| < C\) a.s. for all \(n\). Then, by the optional sampling theorem, we get \(0 = \mathbb {E}\left[X_0\right] = \mathbb {E}\left[X_{T}\right]\). How do we find \(X_T\)? At every time instant a new player arrives, and they spend exactly \(1\) ruble on the game, regardless of whether they are still playing (i.e. have won every round they have played) or have already dropped out. Hence, the total expenditure of the players by time \(T\) is exactly \(T\). But how are the earnings determined? Only those still in the game at time \(T\) have earnings (everyone else has lost their ruble). There are 3 such people:

the player who arrived at step \(T - 1\), and correspondingly named А. Their earnings equal \(33\);
the player who arrived at step \(T - 4\), and correspondingly guessed АБРА (ABRA). Their earnings equal \(33^4\);
the player who arrived at step \(T - 11\), and correspondingly guessed the entire word АБРАКАДАБРА (ABRACADABRA). Their earnings equal \(33^{11}\);

The other players have already lost. For example, the player who entered at round \(T - 6\). They correctly guessed the first А. But then they called the letter Б, while the monkey typed Д.
As a result we have \(X_T = 33^{11} + 33^4 + 33 - T\), \(\mathbb {E}\left[X_T\right] = 0\) and
\[
  \mathbb {E}\left[T\right] = 33^{11} + 33^4 + 33
\]
What follows is a justification of the points left unproven.

Let \(C_{n}^{j}\) be the bet of player \(j\) at time \(n\).
\[
  C_{n}^{j}= \begin{cases}  0 &  \text{ if } n<j \\ 1 &  \text{ if } n=j \\ 33^{k} &  \text{ if } A_{j}, \ldots , A_{j+k-1} \text{ were correct and } n=j+k \\ 0 &  \text{ otherwise } \end{cases}
\]
It is easy to see that each \(C_{n}^{j}\) is a predictable process, since it is determined using only information up to and including the \((n-1)^{\text{th }}\) bet. Now let us define the martingale \(M_{n}^{j}\) as the winnings after \(n\) bets for player \(j^{t h}\). Note that this definition of \(M_{n}^{j}\) already incorporates \(C_{n}^{j}\), since we defined \(M_{n}^{j}\) as the total winnings, not the winnings per unit stake. It will be easier to solve the problem by defining \(M_{n}^{j}\) this way. Also note that each player leaves the game if they lose even one of their bets. Thus, if the \((n+1)^{t h}\) bet is to be made, then \(M_{n}^{j}= 33^{n}\) and \(M_{n+1}^{j}=33^{n+1}\) with probability \(1 / 33\) and \(0\) with probability \(32 / 33\). This happens because the monkey types each letter at random and independently of the previous letters, with each letter having an equal probability of being typed at any given moment. To show that \(M_{n}^{j}\) is a martingale, we must show that

Is \(M_{n}^{j}\) adapted? \(M_{n}^{j}\) is determined by the event \(A_{n}\) and by whether the letter typed at time \(n\) is correct.
Is \(E\left(\left|M_{n}^{j}\right|\right)<\infty , \forall n\)? \(M_{n}^{j}\) is always nonnegative and the maximum value of \(M_{n}^{j}\) is \(33^{n}\), i.e. attained when the player has won all \(n\) previous times. Since \(33^{n}<\infty\) and \(E\left[\left|M_{n}^{j}\right|\right]=E\left[M_{n}^{j}\right]<33^{n}\), (2) holds.
Is \(E\left[M_{n}^{j} \mid \mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]=M_{n-1}^{j}, n \geq 1\)? There are two cases. If the player has lost at some point before time \(n\), then, given this information, \(E\left[M_{n}^{j} \mid \mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]=0=M_{n-1}^{j}\). If the player has won the first \((n-1)\) times, then

\[
  E\left[M_{n}^{j} \mid \mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]=33^{n} \cdot \frac{1}{33}+0 \cdot \frac{32}{33}=33^{n-1}=M_{n-1}^{j}
\]
Is there a constant \(C>0\) such that \(\left|X_{n} - X_{n-1}\right| \leq C\) a.s. for all \(n\)? Yes: at every moment there are at most \(11\) players in the game (those who arrived over the last \(11\) steps), and a player who has made \(k\) winning bets by this moment holds capital \(33^{k}\), \(k \leq 10\). In one step such a player either loses all their capital (\(-33^k\)) or increases it by \(32 \cdot 33^{k}\); also \(1\) ruble is spent by the newly arrived player. In total
\[
  \left|X_{n} - X_{n-1}\right| \leq 1 + \sum _{k=0}^{10} 32 \cdot 33^{k} = 1 + \left(33^{11} - 1\right) = 33^{11} =: C
\]












AnswerAnswer











Enum-item1.



\(\mathbb {E}\left[T\right] = 33\).








Enum-item2.



\(\mathbb {E}\left[T\right] = 33^{11}+33^{4}+33\).

Foundations of Probability and Measure Theory

Classic Informatics Mathematics NES CSE-sp



⏸
n = 1








The “typewriter sequence”: a bump of width \(2^{-k}\) and height \(2^k\) sweeps across \([0,1]\). The sequence converges to zero in measure but diverges at every point, so it does not converge almost everywhere. Nor does it converge in \(L^1\), since \(\|f_n\|_1 = 1\) while \(\|0\|_1 = 0\). The subsequence highlighted in red, however, does converge almost everywhere.


Syllabus

Part I. Foundations of Probability

1. Probability space. Classical models. Independence
2. Probability distributions. Random variables. Expectation
3. Covariance, convergence of random variables, limit theorems

Part II. Measure Theory

4. Systems of sets. Borel sigma-algebra
5. Set functions on semirings and sigma-algebras. Measure
6. Outer measure, Carathéodory’s extension theorem
7. Lebesgue measure, Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure
8. Measurable functions and their convergence
9. Lebesgue integral: integral with respect to a measure
10. Product measures
11. Lebesgue spaces \(L^p(\mu)\)
12. Signed measures, densities
13. Differentiating the Lebesgue integral. Absolutely continuous functions




Probability Theory

Classic NCS/CSE Informatics CSE-sp Mathematics NES AMI base






⏸
N ≈ 10¹



The law of the iterated logarithm, the central limit theorem, and the law of large numbers on a single chart: 100 simulated trajectories of \[
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2n \ln \ln n}}S_n.
\] Almost surely the limit superior of each is \(1\) and the limit inferior is \(-1\). The histogram on the left shows that, for each fixed \(n\), the distribution itself is well approximated by a normal distribution and shrinks toward zero.


Syllabus

Part 1

1. The language of probability theory
2. Random vectors
3. Convolution, covariance
4. Convergence of random variables
5. The Borel-Cantelli lemma, 0-1 laws
6. The law of large numbers

Part 2

7. Weak convergence
8. Characteristic functions
9. The central limit theorem
10. Gaussian vectors
11. Conditional expectation
12. Conditional distributions
